name: Fate/Samurai Remnant
detailed_description: Content featured in the Digital Deluxe Edition - The main game - Digital Artbook - Soundtrack - Season Pass - Season Pass Bonus: Hallowed Relic Sword Mountings (Equipment) Note: The Season Pass and the Digital Artbook & Soundtrack are also available for purchase separately. Included in the Season Pass: - Additional Episode 1, planned to be released before the end of April 2024 - Additional Episode 2, planned to be released before the end of July 2024 - Additional Episode 3, planned to be released before the end of September 2024 - Season Pass Bonus: Hallowed Relic Sword Mountings (Equipment) , released on the same day as the game Note: All items (except Season Pass Bonus) included in the Season Pass can be purchased separately at a later date. In order to play the content featured in the Season Pass, you need to reach a certain point in the game. Fate/Samurai Remnant DEMO In this demo, you can play the early stages of the game. The Apprentice difficulty level is recommended for players who seek a casual combat experience and would like to focus on enjoying the story. Please visit the official website for more information about the gameplay. Note: Save data from the Fate/Samurai Remnant DEMO can be carried over to the full version if there is no existing save data for the full version. About the Game The battle over the Waxing Moon which could grant any and all wishes — the Waxing Moon Ritual. The seven individuals seeking their wish, or Masters, are the bearers of the Ritual. The seven Heroic Spirits, or Servants, are summoned to this world by their Masters. The curtain rises on the battle between the seven Masters with their seven Servants. Traverse the city of Edo and become victorious in the Waxing Moon Ritual. Fight, explore, converse... Many elements are deeply intertwined in this action RPG! - Master and Servant work together during battles Control the Master and Servant during battles and use their bond with each other to survive. Use a variety of attacks to gain an advantage while assessing the enemy and situation of the battle. - Explore Edo Yoshiwara, Kanda, Akasaka... Various famous places in Edo will act as the stage of the Ritual. As you explore the city, you may fight with other Masters, or you may also learn things that will help you grow as a Master. You can interact with the people who live in Edo, replenish your energy at a food stall, or play with dogs and cats. - Various encounters In the town of Edo, you may encounter Rogue Servants. If you deepen your interactions with them and form a bond, they will become reliable allies who will help Iori with their great strength. - Rogue Servants Once you form a bond with Rogue Servants through the Waxing Moon Ritual, you will have the chance to fight alongside them or even control them directly in combat. Overwhelm any enemies that stand in your way with their unrivaled power. “I suppose...you're the one who summoned me?” Supervision: Kinoko Nasu / TYPE-MOON Character Design: Rei Wataru Story Supervisors: Hikaru Sakurai, Yuichiro Higashide Development: KOEI TECMO GAMES In Cooperation with ANIPLEX Opening Animation Production: CloverWorks Genre: Action RPG ※Screens are taken from an in-development build.

_childDocuments_.review: Whilst I can't review Fate/Samurai as a part of the Fate series as I've had very little interaction with it - I've only played a small chunk of the VN, a couple of hours into FGO and outside of those, just looking at the myriad of art across Twitter. What I can do is review the game as a standalone project.Fate/Samurai is a scaled back take on the Musou (Dynasty Warriors) genre, with a very different albeit similar style of play. The game doesn't feature the usual level-based structure, nor does it feature an open world like the recent Dynasty Warrior, instead you'll have a rather similar take to Yakuza's map. It ain't AS deep or intricate as you'd find in Yakuza, but there's a lot of similarities between the two, overall presentation is similar (the way NPCs walk the streets, fade in/out constantly, the way their speech is presented to the player, etc.) Challenges/overall map design feels like something straight out of Yakuza. Sidequests themselves have similar writing to those you'd find in that series. Again though, it ISN'T as deep or interactive as Yakuza, it's more superficial comparisons, don't go buying the game expecting musou-yakuza.Combat wise, Fate/Samurai's combat lends itself to being very different from the usual style. You won't be playing some superhuman warrior who can take on hundreds of guys with the press of the button, instead fights will consist of 8-15 enemies, or even less if they're demons/possessed units or even mini-bosses. Iori (The protagonist.) feels very detached from any other Musou, whilst he's strong enough to hold his own, combat is played rather evasively/defensively in comparison to the other games in the Musou series. The second you begin fighting demons/boss fights you'll feel that human nature of Iori slip straight into the combat with him dealing little damage until you're able to deplete the enemies stance. However... Switching out to Iori's servant, Saber. You'll instantly feel right at home with the usual Musou style, Saber will tear through any and all enemies like butter, she's able to dish-out incredible damage withing a short amount of time and is a stark difference from her human Master. Switching between the two throughout combat is incredibly satisfying and feels great *every* time.Writing wise. I feel this is where the game truly shines, the characters are incredibly well written even minor characters. The dynamic between Iori and Saber his Servant is incredible, you can feel each character grow as the story progresses and their bond strengthens, unlocking new abilities for both characters (including movesets as Iori who's able to access five sword-stances.) The sidequests with Gilgamesh had me in stiches every time, the awkwardness of Iori dealing with Tamano, etc. It's all incredibly well done. I absolutely adored the characters in the game, and I was sad when the credits finally rolled on my playthrough, I want more adventures with the characters, and I'm interested to see where the DLC next year takes the game. Overall, I'm really pleased with the game. I hope the game was successful enough to have Koei/TypeMoon colaborate again, whether for a direct sequel or just an outright entirely new game set within the universe Nasu created.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr Worth the wait if you're a musou fan and you don't hate TYPE MOON or a TYPE MOON fan and you don't hate musou games.---------------Based on my initial impressions of the game, I'd say it's more or less following a more open version of the Persona 5 Strikers formula. It's really technically smooth too for me; haven't run into any crashes or anything like that. Some occasional stutter while loading shaders but that goes away the more you play. I have heard about the cutscene skipping bug some people are experiencing; I really hope that Omega Force fixes it, since this game is pretty darn good at first shot.You got an open world with different zones to walk around and do missions in, you got some navigation that can be done with the help of your servant, dual techs, follow-up strikes, you can temporarily swap to your servant and fight as them for a while, you equip gear, learn spells that use consumables... it's pretty expansive, and has a lot of strong RPG elements that give each character a strong progression curve. The musou combat is on point, though I wish the battles were larger. I hope they get larger later in the game.I've seen some people liken the game to the RGG Studios games as well; walking around town, doing small missions and favors and errands for people, and yeah I would say that's present but not really that oppressive. The point of the game is to ease you into the battles and get you used to these micro-encounters with 25-50 enemies at once, much like Persona 5 Strikers did.I think the main problem with this game though, for most people, is probably going to be that it's pretty niche for what it is; you have to really be a neutral-to-positive fan of both musou games and TYPE MOON, particularly Fate, to really like this. If you are, then this will probably be one of your favorite games to come out this year; and you also probably don't need to be convinced by me to buy it.But, for the rest of the internet, I think it's probably worth waiting for a sale. This definitely isn't a game that you can use to get into Fate; the story is a mimicry of the core beats of the original Fate/stay Night story, but it won't tell you about anything you'll see in the other big name Fate franchises, instead being more of an isolated story that uses similar themes and ideas. It might be a game you can use to get into the musou genre, but because of its open world and RPG elements, it's very different from the more mission and campaign-based structure of the mainline Dynasty Warriors games, or even the earlier spinoff licensed titles like One Piece: Pirate Warriors, Berserk & The Band Of The Hawk or Hyrule Warriors.The bottom line is, for fans this is exactly what they want, but for anyone who isn't already in on this type of game or franchise, there's nothing here that will blow your mind or turn you into a fan of either that couldn't be found in one of the games I mentioned earlier in this review. Because of that, while I can easily recommend this to a certain type of person, if you're not really familiar with TYPE MOON or with the musou genre, I would wait for this one to go on sale before you experiment with it.For the rest of you, you've probably already made up your mind about this game; go download it and play it! It's great.

_childDocuments_.review: The -franchise has been around for 20 years now, and as such, it’s hardly surprising that a new entry is usually first met with the question “can I play it even without previously engaging with the franchise?”. Usually, the answer to this is either “no” (e.g. ) or some form of “yes, but” – for example, you may engage with  first but it’s better if you read  before. The latter applies to  as well – it’s a standalone story that works perfectly fine even if this would be your first interaction with  but expect a few fan-favorite characters to return as well. is an action-RPG co-developed by Koei Tecmo’s Kou Shibusawa () and Omega Force (), which – unsurprisingly considering their previous releases – takes place in Keian era Japan, specifically the year 1651. As a  story, the basic set-up is the same as most other entries in the franchise: The protagonist (“Miyamoto Iori”) is taking part in a magic ritual (“Waxing Moon”) by chance and becomes a “Master”, which means that a “Servant” (a Heroic Spirit, usually historical or based on legends) is summoned in order to help him win the battle against other masters, which in turn promises the fulfillment of a wish through powerful magic. Again, this should be a familiar set-up for -veterans but  still explains the system in finer detail for those new to the franchise, making for a good point of entry in that regard.A slight departure from the usual  formula would be protagonist Miyamoto Iori, a well-trained swordsman, able to hold himself in battle instead of letting his Servant (“Saber”) do all the work. Additionally, apart from the usual Master & Servant pairings, there are also several “Rogue Servants” present during the Waxing Moon ritual, who were summoned without a Master at all. But before we get to the story, let’s talk about the gameplay first.Perhaps surprising for an Omega Force game,  is much less of a musou game than one might expect. Instead, it’s an action-RPG with a focus on battles against more powerful individuals (other Servants or certain monsters) who are only accompanied by a handful of basically harmless “cannon fodder” enemies with little health at max. Most of the fighting is done as Miyamoto Iori, with Saber (or other helpers) being controlled by the AI. One button unleashes normal attacks, one heavy attacks, both of which can effortlessly be chained into combos. There’s also an “affinity gauge”, which - once sufficiently filled – allows you to order Saber to unleash specific powerful abilities. Finally, there’s also a “substitution gauge”, which – once filled – allows for temporal (~ 20 secs unless upgraded) control of Saber, meaning you can perform her powerful combos yourself.The combat system is easy to get into – you simply spam combos using normal & heavy attacks, unleash techniques once possible and occasionally play as Saber for a short burst phase. It’s a shame that you can only play as Servants for a longer time during very select opportunities, but it does center Iori as the protagonist of the game. Additionally, only Iori can switch between various sword stances during combat, which offer different benefits (e.g. combat against many enemies or against a single powerful one) and reward switching with temporal buffs. As for the RPG-component – besides a very light equipment system, it’s mostly present through a levelling & skill system for each character, which allows you to either increase character stats (attack, defense, etc.) or unlock new battle abilities.In general, the combat system proves to be fun to play, providing additional depth by allowing you extra attacks if you evade enemy attacks at the right time for example. However, as fun as the combat system is, it also suffers from one big flaw: Over the course of the game, you’ll simply spend way too much time fighting similar battles instead of doing something else.  has little gameplay variety – you’ll spend most of the game running from point A to point B, listening to dialogue and then fighting the same battles against the few enemy types – the designs of which are mostly taken from the mobile game . Battles against other Servants are supposed to be exciting boss encounters, shaking things up, but as you fight almost every servant multiple times throughout the game, they’re quickly “just another battle”Making things even worse is the “Shell” system. Powerful enemies (usually at least one per battle) are protected by a shield (“Shell”) which makes them almost invincible to your attacks as long as it’s up. The shield is only breakable through (multiple) powerful attacks, mainly coming from your Servant during your first playthrough & thus take some time to recharge. As shields are usually re-applied (!) multiple times (!!) during many encounters, they quickly turn battles into a tedious affair of using your shield breaking attacks & then mostly waiting for them to recharge. You gain more ways to break shields throughout the game but that won't improve the mechanic itself: Shields don’t make battles more difficult (the game is easy to beat  & higher difficulties are only available after your first playthrough), just tediously long & annoying. Fewer battles, less shields and more actual gameplay variety would’ve given the game some much needed breathing room.It doesn’t help that  really wants you to do more than your first playthrough (~20h long on normal difficulty) either, as it features three (!) different ending chapters (guide ), one of which is only accessible through New Game+. The game tries to sell you a second playthrough by promising additional dialogues und side quests, but frankly, these additions turned out to be so small/uninteresting that they’re hardly worth doing an entire “new” playthrough for. The three endings are also quite short considering their build-up, ending quite abruptly when an epilogue would’ve been needed to give everyone a proper send-off.Even apart from the final acts, the story of  unfortunately doesn’t live up to its strong first impression, turning out just okay in the end. The general premise is interesting, many of the characters are fun and the first half of the game is decent – but just as the gameplay gets tedious, the story does get worse too. The main problem here is that some Servant/Master pairings are incredibly underdeveloped compared to others, which is caused by simply too many characters being crammed into the game - mainly the huge number of additional Rogue Servants. Many of them are only there for fanservice reasons, which would be completely fine if they didn’t take away much needed time to flesh out the characters that are actually important to the story. I also feel like the master-pupil relationship between Iori and his come-to-life-again mentor was surprisingly underutilized, even though it would’ve made for an potentially interesting tale.Overall,  is a still mostly enjoyable action-RPG with an okay story, it simply doesn’t know its limits when it comes to the amount of (shield) battles or characters present in the story. It’s a game that doesn’t respect the players time but can still be entertaining as long as you know what you’re getting into.

_childDocuments_.review: Fate/Samurai Remnant is a VN/Musou/ARPG game.I would say it's 60%-70% VN, while 30%-40% Musou/ARPG. I've been enjoying the game so far and would definitely recommend it. I think the price of $60 is fine for some more hardcore fans, but if you are a casual player, I would wait for a sale since that might happen sometime in the future. Here's a TLDR for those that want a summary of this review. Amazing cutscenes, amazing sounds (VA and music), amazing dialogues and interactions, amazing graphics, great characters, good story, combat is okay, enemies are okay, equips are okay, skill tree is okay, leylines are okay, commissions are okay, digressions are okay, exploration is not so great, and errands not so great. Flaws include lacking playable servants (possible DLCs), errands too simple, digression types should vary, easy town loot, and no secret areas. Another flaw is Iori's less expressive personality. Also, currently has a bug with cutscenes for some, most likely will be patched (temp fix on the bottom). Otherwise, great game and 8/10. Possibly wait for a future sale if casual player. Quicktime events (Riposte,Saber's Techs,Clashes,Phantasms) - J = left click & I = right click & L = middle scroll clickGraphicsI think the game has great graphics. a minority might dislike the graphics, but it's an anime artstyle as expected. Character art is also great. Like this one time where the town atmosphere was nailed down. Slightly foggy, night/sunset time, low lighting, cherry petals falling, trees, flowers, banners swaying, shadows are aligned, and even little details like petals on roofs, fishes splashing, and butterflies hovering. Though, flooring textiles could be better. Cutscenes are incredibly amazing, especially Saber's first time using their noble phantasm. The cutscenes' fight scenes are incredible and did a great job.SoundThey nailed the sound and music. With same town atmosphere, I could hear the incredible background music, hearing the wind, fish splashing, own walking sounds, Saber walking, Saber's misc idle sounds (procedural gen of NPCs, so no walking sound). Main and side character VAs also did a great job. Perfectly nailed each scenario, including the cutscenes. Even the VAs for the random NPCs are incredibly good too.CharactersIori, the MC. Some people might not like him since he's the less-expressive type of personality. In other words, resting b**ch face. Also, his tone of voice doesn't change much. However, almost all the other main and side characters are expressive, like Kaya (little sister personality) and Musashi (outgoing personality) are very expressive when you first meet them. Aria is my favorite lately, giving me yandere loli vibes from her. Can't say much about character development yet. Wish you could play other servants more (2%), while 90% Iori and 8% Saber. (-2nd half of game, you play other servants more often-)Dialogue and InteractionsIt's amazing... It's more focused on the VN part, so this is incredibly important too. Like Kaya, the expressions and action animations of characters during the VN mode are very great. For example, when you first meet Kaya, the sister of Iori, she goes from a greeting > pouting > geez moment > worried > "I told you so" > embarrassed. Just saying, this is only ONE scene and that tells you a lot already. Dialogue itself is solid, a minority may not like it since it sounds like they're talking in phrases. Also, doggo and neko interactions are cute, though a bit redundant after a while.StoryI think it's good so far. Can't explain much since spoilers, but there's some kind of progression so far. Pacing feels good. However, slightly lacking in context, though maybe will be revealed later. But just story context. There's info boxes in the menu in case you missed anything or need an explanation on the info needed.CombatCombat in this game isn't too difficult. Know that the game is VN heavy rather than combat. Technically, you could spam both click buttons while evading, but I don't think you could do that for elites or servant battles. Both battle types have a shell (shield) you have to break to deal some massive damage. So, you end up using several skills. Just note, pay attention to health management. Could go from 1000 hp to 100 hp real quick, especially in servant battles. At least food is instant with one click. Small note, Rogue Archer is somewhat difficult.EnemiesEnemies are fine. There are some variations in enemies, but majority are probably reused assets. I think the Servant (boss) battles are definitely different, and elite enemies also vary a little too, but still uses reused assets.LeylinesSome players dislike this, but it's not bad. It's like a mini-game of chess, but to a lesser degree. I think what they don't like are the enemy battles in between. Enemy battles are similar to random town battles. Developers could of made a new battle format while playing the leyline mini-game, but that's just my opinion.Skill TreeI think the skill tree is okay, but they could of made adjustments. You usually find frags and jewels from errands, town loot, and commissions. You gain some skill points while leveling up. Saber gets some points from random map events too. Some skills are locked behind requirements or even progression, and majority of them aren't too difficult. Skills aren't much of a game changer. There are some skills that would probably matter, like the revive skill and skill upgrades for your stance, ex. additional attacks or ability to block.EquipmentFor equipment, just loot whatever you get and equip the best one. Once you find a decent equip that has higher stats and 2-3 good effects, you usually upgrade that with the hammers. Just note that upgrades are from a future workshop upgrade unlock. You most likely will unlock it before Chapter 2 starts.CommissionsCommissions are like achievement quests, very similar to errands except they vary more. Majority are kill X amount with this type of attack. Some are different where you do X amount of counter attacks or win X amount of battles with no damage or win X amount of battles within 20 seconds or kill X amount of this type of elite enemies or regular enemies.DigressionsOne of the flaws. Digressions are side quests. Like, where I played as Archer. Only went through the mini story dialogue and fought. They should have more quest types like stealth or tracking. Might be difficult to implement anyways, especially tracking quests since enemy mobs are limited and town maps are small. Stealth might work since enemies could get a visible radar and require you to sneak past. Despite this, you use Archer's attacks and skills instead, so different combat style is more fun.ExplorationExploration might be a miss for me. I keep finding items way easily on town map and could be more hidden. Two loots are required for an errand and could find skill frags in town loot, so you're required to look for loot in town. There are "hidden" paths in the town sometimes, but not hidden at all. Kinda like alternative paths. So there's no secret areas, especially since the map reveals everything. Couple areas that you can't reach that time, but it seems like you could revisit them in the future. Some errands are a type of exploration in this game.ErrandsAnother flaw for my opinion. Errands are too simple. Basically, errands are like town quests that give small bonuses if completed. The errands pretty much sum up as kill X amount of this type of enemies, click X amount of times for this pet or object, or collect 2 special town loot. The last 2 objective types ties in to the exploration too. The developers could made more variations for the errands.BugsSeems like there's a cutscene bug so far, probably will be patched in a future update. The temporary solution for now is either turn off your Anti-Aliasing settings for NVIDIA users or download VP9 video extensions.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been a big fan of Fate since 2006, so I was excited to play this game. However, I was disappointed with it and cannot recommend it. While the story and characters are great, and there are some amazing cameos and new versions of existing servants (Tamamo Aria <3), the game part itself is just bland. The fighting system is tedious, even with all the available stands. The enemies are repetitive, with just some reskinned mobs and boss battles that are more of a check to see if you have enough real-life time to beat a huge HP sponge with the same 3-5 attack patterns. Additionally, you need to buy all the food in all of the maps to heal continuously because the hitboxes are ridiculously big and the "evade system" is more of a luck system". I was expecting more from the 2vs2 fights, where two masters and their servants fight together with different tactics and strategies.Especially the last chapter is a Sisyphean labor. "Hey, do you remember all of the micro-bossed that you had to fight repeatedly for the past 40-ish hours? well now you need to fight them again all and together, it will be so fun!" And the final boss is so unimaginable that it hurts. OG God of War on PS2 almost 20 years ago had way more interesting boss stages with proper multiphase fights.I will force myself to do the 3 DLC but I'm not expecting much.Do yourself a favor and just watch a recap video on YouTube to understand the main story and some lore. Avoid this grind fest and save your time and money.

_childDocuments_.review: I've wanted to write this review for a while now, but I wanted to wait until I got the platinum trophy (103 hours in) before doing so; now that I have it, here it is.I'm not going to lie, I went into this with lower expectations; I was basically expecting this to be at about the quality level of Extella or Extella Link. Imagine my surprise when it still captures the musou spirit, but actually adds particularly compelling gameplay! Just for context, my first clear was on hard mode, every clear afterward was on Sword Demon difficulty. Below are my ratings for the various aspects of the game.Gameplay: 8.5/10As mentioned earlier, this game falls under the musou category, but it distinguishes itself heavily from its cousins in the Extella family. Extella's gameplay almost entirely revolved around zone capture, and ultimately, every ability the characters had ultimately boiled down to just damaging everything in the vicinity, barring very few exceptions. In FSR, some things make a return such as Noble Phantasms (obviously), but the main difference comes in the form of stances. Each stance offers various benefits while also holding some level of demerit; water stance is extremely fast, mobile, and has a wide range, but the attacks aren't very powerful. Earth stance is comparatively slow and focuses extensively on single targeting, but it comes with a nifty shield that makes it particularly valuable for boss battles. Suffice to say, you will find yourself changing stances constantly to reap the unique benefits each provide. Besides these, the game also provides you with spells, which basically do what you'd expect between damage, buffs, and healing, and combat mechanics including link strikes and ripostes. All of these come into play; there's a ton of spells that are very useful throughout the game, link strikes are amazing for disrupting enemy charge attacks, and RIPOSTES. Oh man, on Sword Demon, you'd better learn the timing on them, but when you do, the game really starts to feel good to play. I personally believe ripostes are one of the most vital parts of the game, and they lead to some of the most exciting gameplay moments during boss fights. It is because ripostes work through dashing that I believe the gameplay captures the ideal of fighting servants better than in any other Fate game to date. I remember fighting Rogue Lancer for the first time, who likewise dashes around the stage looking for you to leave an opening; it really felt to me like what I imagine a duel between two servants would, almost like a dance around the arena where you and your opponent circle each other, trying to get pokes in while also dodging those of the foe. The only real complaint I would have to give here is the NONcombat gameplay. Most of it is honestly fine, it might include going to find some items and bring them somewhere, or talk to a particular person, nothing really crazy, but sometimes you get the Rumor missions. These suck lol. They require you to talk to specific NPCs, but the map doesn't show you which ones to talk to even though it does normally show you which NPCs have dialogue options (since many of them are just there to fill the world and cannot actually be interacted with). It's a slight pain that might leave you wondering where to go for 15-20 minutes, but this is a pretty minor complaint when the combat is as good as it is. There is no question; while the bar is admittedly pretty low, FSR has by FAR the best gameplay of any Fate game.Graphics: 8/10I personally found the graphics in the game to be pretty good. I don't think they match up to the highest tier graphics of games out there necessarily, but the world itself is pretty beautiful. I actually really enjoyed exploring all of the cities/temples because of just how pretty some of them are (looking at you, Shinagawa! GLORIOUS cherry blossom display). They remain pretty good through combat as well; enemy attacks are easily discernable and the hitboxes are exactly where you'd think they are (for the most part). Story: 9/10If you're playing FSR, there's like a 99% chance you're doing it specifically because you're a Fate fan. As a Fate fan, one should probably expect a LOT of reading, since that is a hallmark of the franchise, and FSR is no different in that regard. I would say that at least on the first clear, the game is 70% reading, 30% gameplay. I like reading, so this is not a problem for me, but I do understand that some people may feel differently. Regardless of that, the actual content of the story is excellent. FSR even steps above its visual novel and mobile game counterparts in one key regard; the game is almost fully voiced. Additionally, the game features an extremely colorful cast including some new servants that I urgently want in FGO, as well as some familiar faces and even fan favorites. I legitimately would like all of the new servants to migrate over, they were done extraordinarily well, and I found myself extremely interested in all of the newcomers. There are also some genuinely emotional moments in the game, such as the tragedy that happens near the end of Chapter III. Most importantly, Iori is a compelling main character. The Ray of Light ending is pretty on-point for what you'd expect on a first clear, but the Entreat the Darkness and Flames of Resentment endings both add a new dimension to Iori (a rather unexpected one, at that). It definitely tries to recreate the type of rivalry Shirou had with Kotomine in the original VN but with Iori and Chiemon, and admittedly I don't think it's quite at that same level of intrigue, but it's still quite good. Regardless, I think the story should overall be an easy sell for existing Fate fans, and whoever is playing FSR that isn't somehow in the rabbit hole already might like it too.Music: 9/10I'm pleased to say, FSR channels its best from FGO with an excellent soundtrack. The OST features a lot of new songs unique to the game, many of which are simply city BGMs, but they do a great job of capturing the tranquility in places like Torikoe Shrine, while also capturing the tension in story moments where all sorts of bad things are happening. Most importantly to me, however, the game also features remixed versions of tracks from other Fate properties, like Blood Wind from FGO and Cosmic Air from CCC, and they are absolutely amazing. My only point deduction here is that sometimes the city BGMs can be a little repetitive, since they do reuse themes between certain locations. Besides that, the OST is brilliant, I'm extremely happy I bought the collectors' edition for the soundtrack.Performance: 9/10I didn't really have many issues with things like slow down, bugs, or glitches, but I did find a couple. First, the game DOES chug under some circumstances; I found that the game slows down to a crawl sometimes, specifically in cities where there are a LOT of NPCs, such as the main street in Asakusa. The only major bug I found was in Edo Castle during the Flames of Resentment ending; there is an area where you can jump up to find a rare item (I think it was a Pale Moon but don't quote me on that). It wasn't a problem for me the first time around, however when I went into that ending for the second time to unlock Rogue Saber, immediately after pressing the button to jump up a level, Iori fell through the floor all the way down to the moat. I tried to wiggle out of it but unfortunately there was no way out without loading my save. Luckily, the autosave feature brought me to the room right before that, so it was really only about 5 minutes of trouble. Overall: 8.7/10The game is great, I think new and old fans alike will find plenty to enjoy. I hope if you read my inane ramblings and weren't immediately repulsed, you give the game a try.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been on the fence with the Fate franchise for a long time. This game really proved to me that it's a universe that is capable of good stories and characters and can do those things while for the most part being very original. The game has a visual style that is absolutely stellar, and while it has fanservice it does enough with characters that such things can be entirely overlooked. Samurai Remnant is very much a visual novel that still services fun gameplay extremely reminiscent of the Yakuza and Dynasty Warriors games. At first I was just going to beat the game once and get the ending I got and move on, but I find myself replaying the game just to find out small details I missed and the alternate paths that are possible. It takes me back to the PS2 era in terms of game replayability, and that is not a bad thing. Certainly worth full price, even if you're not a huge fan of Fate. The amount of effort put into the game shows, and while it is not a perfect game by any means it somehow leaves me truly excited to see what they have in store moving forward.

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVE FATE.Straight to the point, game is good, if you like Fate, buy, the game has a lot of very nice little references here and there which make it very enjoyable if you know the franchise already.-Story is good, if you like Fate Zero, you'll like this, similar enough to be cool without being really a "copy", engaging with lots of exposition so you have to be patient, but if you like Fate, you're used to this. They explain everything very clearly which is helpful if you don't know much about Fate universe, so I can see it as a relatively decent entry point for new people.-Gameplay is cool, played max difficulty in all 5 playthroughs and only really struggled a bit in ng+1 with the new max difficulty added. The game is as difficult as you want it to be no matter what difficulty selection you have, since you can just spam items if you can't be arsed to fight normally, or if you're a real man and use no items ever (like me 😎) it can actually be difficult when it comes to boss fights that have oneshot or difficult to avoid attacks. Perfect dodging is extremely rewarding and very satisfying, I feel like the majority of negative reviews complaining about enemies being tanky just don't know how to perfect dodge, as it's easily the best way to deal massive damage.At the start you don't play as servants much which is a big downside for a lot of people, gets better (a LOT better) as you go into further ng+ cycles with upgrades that let you play as them more often, but of course that's a big time commitment.Iori feels good to play, has very good varied moveset with every stance other than water feeling fantastic and useful to use in each fight, especially in bossfights, and you become an actual monster, way stronger than servants, by the endgame.-OST is a banger, that's it really, very good.-My main gripes with the game are for one how hollow the world feels, every town is just going from A to B a lot of times, random encounters placed in big areas, not very interesting, also no chapter selection is a VERY bad feeling when you end up wanting to fully 100% the game and doing 5 playthroughs, the lack of freedom and everything being tied to chapters feels pretty meh, not a big fan of that, not the end of the world though.-Side quests (digressions) are very fun to do, give you a lot of insight on the characters and feel very enjoyable to sort of "bond" with them, alas, it did take me 5 playthroughs to get every single one, but I'm pretty sure it can be done in just 3(maybe 4?) if saves are used properly. (This is a bad thing)Conclusion: I like it a lot, can't wait for the dlcs, absolutely recommended if you have the time/dedication to fully immerse yourself in it, it's not a game for impatient people, and that's okay.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not the Holy Grail War that you know. Enter the era of the Tokugawa Shogunate, the Edo period of (mostly) isolation. Gods and Spirits, the old ways, still predominately influence the day to day lives of this new time of peace. A young man, born in the shadows of a bloody era and now in a world frozen in strange new ideals and government - was surely born years too late. He wishes to achieve greatness in the sword, but there is no longer any honor in the taking of lives.  However, an unexpected ritual has taken grasp of the nation's capitol and not all the mysterious heroes that have manifested to partake in it are local. Fate/Samurai Remnant is a musou game. When you allow yourself to think about what this word means, you realize it was practically a perfect fit for the Fate series. Not only that, but the musou genre is a celebration of heroic figures throughout history, fictional and real and all the in-between - identical to what Fate plays most into.The gameplay... is actually very good and decently varied for a musou game. All of this is augmented and amplified by the masterful animation, art direction and character design of the Servants and cast. The game itself is very repetitive and relies heavily on copy-pasting and retreading through the story, which is a haymark for both Fate and musou games.I don't have much to say, because if you hate musou games, you'll definitely enjoy this more than most. If you love musou games, this game is easily one of the best in the genre. In terms of gameplay, Fate/Samurai Remnant is competent but held back by some small things. As a product overall, in terms of story, presentation, characters, it is very worth the investment of money and time. Truly, for musou game, it must be promoted above its peers and as a Fate game, it should be lauded for being so ambitious and succeeding within the frame work of this specific gameplay genre.Ultimately, I love most if not all type-moon projects. Without Fate, I would not have gotten into the arguably better stuff like KnK, Tsukihime, Melty Blood, etc. That being said, type-moon's Fate is a series that actually holds up better than most shonen and seinen out there. Normies will call it perpetually 7/10 and that is true. But Fate is 90% 7/10 but has moments of HYPE that is 11/10. I think this is true for other type-moon IPs, which are admittingly more driven by original ideas that outshine the reliance on historical figures in the Fate series. This no doubts elevates them above their contemporaries. (especially Nasu's pre-Fate stuff, both the original and revisisted/remakes) But Fate being consistently 7/10 actually makes thse 10/10 moments the 11/10 I mentioned earlier. Much like a Fate series of episodes or light novel, the intro is incredible and the rest of the first third is a slog. Then there is a center piece that is arguably better than the main finale and then there is a haunting conclusion. I believe this game mostly follows the same formula.While this story in particular, borders more on the original Fate/Stay Night in many ways, its narrative is more on par with the arguably more entertaining entries, but story-wise, the more underwhelming. Fate Apocrypha is the closest equivalency, but with a far more likable central protagonist and endings with a lot more value. But like FA, this game's story simply feels like it didn't have enough time to cook. But what we do get, as far as something raw goes, is still sushi or sashimi. Therefor good, but not as filling as you'd hope. The characters and character writing is fantastic, there are some great story beats, but it is hard to appeciate everything for what it is (including the lame and bad moments) until you've experienced the full game, endings and all, alternate routes included. The bad ending is arguably the best, in terms of it actually having a far more meaningful impact and the fact that the game nudges you toward it with a single ominous sentence in the other endings.I think for Fate fans, it will provide great entertainment but not take you on a ride like the rest of the IP has successfully. But for newcomers or casual fans, it is actually a fantastic introduction and unlike other Fate games, you don't need to know too much about the conventional Holy Grail War mechanics as these rules are broken often regardless.It is amusing that, despite a very basic albeit interesting premise of a battle royale in a magical ritual with numbered servents, the Fate stories never fully adhere to the structure promised. The twists and turns are often what actually elevates Fate over its imitators and most shonen and seinen. Each series tends to leave me with a haunting feeling. There is a conclusion, all character arcs close, but there is still so much story left afterwards for our minds to fill in the blanks. Usually, the romances in Fate can distract or enshrine this feeling to great effect.Interestingly, this game has no actual romance (and to the decry of perverts everywhere, no 'mana-transfer' scenes) and it tells about mostly platonic relationships in contrast to the more toxic ones in rivals. It is a breath of fresh air, but some romance would have helped humanize some character and add more personality-building. Some argue that they were disappointed you don't play servants enough and that the main protagonist is "just some guy", which is a hilarious notion considering he stands toe to toe with servants in the late game (practically making them easily one of the strongest non-servant, human protagonists in all of Type-Moon) with relatively minimal mage skills and reliant mostly on the peak of their martial prowess. Not to mention, the protagonist was a real person in history and at a young age, became arguably one of the most accomplished swordsman in his rare, peaceful time. As for the servants, I feel like you end up playing them a LOT more than people think. Not only are there battle recollections, that allow you to replay mini boss, boss and horde fights with any servant you have unlocked - but by the end of the game, I was actually annoyed you couldn't skip some Noble Phantasm cutscenes because I had seen them a total of a hundred times, lol.The DLC is expensive individually, but I got this game with the season pass via pre order and simply only now got to play it in full. I believe the DLC is actually... very good for this game and its genre. The first one is easily 5-7 hours if you play through every possibility and is a nearly straight forward tournament mode. The second one is underwhelming if you don't recognize the historical figures involved (Unless you are Japanese or very knowledgeable about older Japanese myth, some names will surely blindside you in the same way some Biblical ones will for those not raised in or around it in familiarity.) but is still fairly decent in length. It is more or of the same, which is exactly as you expect it to be. But the third DLC is actually a very nice way to bring the cast together in an oddly wholesome, temporary alliance. Ironically, moments like this really help the unique characters of this setting shine so much and you really do wish for more Fate content where servants are co-existing more often. The story is nothing too epic compared to the main plot and its conclusions, but it was always meant to be something "in-between". In presentation and content alone, you get a fair amount out of it. The expansions also add entirely new playable servants, sometimes several, which certainly adds to the overall replayability of the game. Fate/Samurai Remnant is a bold step forward for Musou and Fate, but it may not impress long time megafans as much as one would hope. But we are so utterly starved for good Fate content that isn't a gacha, that its hard to say anything truly bad about an otherwise top tier game of this sort.

_childDocuments_.review: A nice game that, despite its noteworthy flaws, is still better than the sum of its parts. It's certainly the best thing Fate has had recently.The Gameplay is a few steps above what you'd find in a Musou game. Very simple "combos", wide windows of time for dodges+ripostes, instant healing, and a lot of harmless enemies. That being said there's still some pretty fun fights, in 1v1 or 2v2 fights using spells and abilities becomes becomes a bit more tactical and therefore rewarding when done correctly. The Stances are also interesting, they're a cool way of executing character progression and they compliment each other well as far as combat goes. The plot and characters are pretty good too for the most part, this is a great execution of a Grail War, with the alliances and backstabbing one would come to expect from them. The characters all bounce of each other pretty well, there's plenty of good dynamics and interactions in this game, and the potential of the Master-Servant concept is used pretty well. However I will note that the ending section of the game is clearly rushed. With some character stories not receiving as much attention as they should, or even a proper conclusion, which obviously doesn't sit well even if they did have some nice scenes. This doesn't really ruin the game but the wasted potential is there.

_childDocuments_.review: First, a video overview Taking on the spin-off of the Fate franchise without prior knowledge is difficult, considering how it spans across so many games and media projects. Fate/Samurai Remnant serves as a great introduction to the franchise, being a terrific action RPG in its own right that combines many different systems without feeling overwhelming, while still keeping its core combat system satisfying, especially for anime fans (and if you've noticed, it probably is).The story of Fate/Samurai Remnant is set in 1600s Japan during the Keian Rebellion. A young samurai named Miyamoto Iori is drawn into a conflict called the Ritual of the Growing Moon, where seven men battle each other for the prize of wish fulfillment. Each of these seven "Masters" is given a Servant, a mystical being who fights alongside them, all based on historical or mythological figures such as Joan of Arc. Iori is given Saber, a Servant who suffers from amnesia and wields water, and they both must endure the machinations of the Ritual of the Growing Moon as more enemies invade their home.Key DetailsRelease date:September 29, 2023.Platform:Nintendo Switch, PC, PS4 and PS5.Price: $59.99 USD.Developer: Omega ForcePublisher: Koei TecmoThe combat system is the highlight of Fate/Samurai RemnantAlthough Fate/Samurai Remnant is an action RPG, its combat system has a lot in common with Musou games, as you'll often face large groups of humanoid or monstrous enemies, with reinforcements arriving in waves as the battle progresses. Some elite units and bosses take significantly more damage, and larger enemies have a "projectile scale" that must be depleted before you can deal proper damage to them.Fortunately, Iori has plenty of weapons at his disposal. You have two swords that you can upgrade as the game progresses, as well as different fighting styles that you can switch between during combat. Iori has access to magic spells, though these are powered by gems you earn in battle, which deplete when used.The main gimmick of Fate/Samurai Remnant is the Servants, as you'll have Saber by your side for most of the game, as well as other Ravaging Servants that you unlock as the story progresses. You can have two Servants with you at a time, and they perform several functions related to their Kinship streak, which grows in battle. This allows them to perform powerful super moves and gives you temporary control over them in battle.All of this may seem like too much, but the various systems work well together to keep the combat feeling fresh throughout the game. The brightly colored anime special moves are spaced far enough apart so as not to overwhelm the gameplay, as you'll want to keep them from interrupting your opponent's attacks. Juggling all of the systems in combat is all about maximizing all of your abilities while trying to survive an enemy attack. It's a fine balance, but Fate/Samurai Remnant pulls it off and the combat never gets boring.There are some issues with the combat system, one of which is food. You can heal at any time by eating food, which is done immediately through the pause menu. This causes the same problem as Final Fantasy XVI: you can stock up on items before battle and outrun your enemies while healing. Fate/Samurai Remnant would be improved if there were limits to the amount of food you could carry, or if healing was tied to an animation that enemies could interrupt, as the current system makes combat much easier.The dodge mechanics are also a bit of a mess. You can perform a dash by pressing R2, and if you dodge a punch at the last second, Iori can retaliate with a punch that does a ton of damage. The problem is that the jerk feels a bit late and you can't cancel actions, which forces you to play more conservatively than you'd like, especially in a flashy anime-style fighting game.Balance between exploration and combatOutside of battles, you'll be exploring various cities and locations, as well as completing quests, improving your workshop, buying new items, and interacting with NPCs. The design of the outside world isn't all that interesting, though it's limited by the setting, and many of the decrepit cities seem interchangeable.Fate/Samurai Remnant utilizes a skill point system for Iori and Servants, allowing you to unlock abilities spread across several different trees. Your home/workshop can also be improved by spending money and finding rare items. Together, these aspects ensure that you're always gradually improving as the game progresses and you have a reason to keep fighting and completing quests.There is also a world combat system, where cities are connected by power lines and you move Iori and his Servants around the board. You have a home base and link different city nodes together, fighting enemies for control of different regions and strategically cutting their ties, allowing you to destroy all of their units in certain areas. This mode is a lot of fun and offers a different way to divide up combat scenes. VerdictFate/Samurai Remnant is a great introduction to the franchise. A few issues aside, the combat system is fantastic and manages the difficult task of staying interesting for long periods of time, something that games like this can struggle with. The story is also great and serves as a major motivator for you to pull out your sword as you advance towards the next mob of enemies.

_childDocuments_.review: I have to say I'm not a big fan of anime nowadays, not even a great KOEI TECMO fan, though I did play some Dynasty Warriors. _childDocuments_.review: I've been pretty addicted to this one all week. I'm not sure how far I am into the story but tackling all side missions and objectives that pop up has kept the grind going steady. For people who play a lot of musous I'd say the combat feels along the lines of Age of Calamity, where enemies have overshields that need to be broken down through perfect dodges/parries and spells which is nice because it keeps the combat from feeling mindless but still fun. That's all I'm going to say about the straight combat because there's lots info out there.I would like to use this post put focus on the Laylines/grid battle system (just because I hadn't really seen it covered much in reviews that I was digging through here or youtube) and its a shame because I think it's a highlight of the game.It's a network of nodes that the player is supposed to travel along to concur and buff your party with limited moves/actions and different ways to engage the enemy. Whether it be cutting off their route for an effort free win, knocking their piece off the board or meeting that piece head-on to jump out of the board and into an arena to hack n slash them musou style. It gets tricky because they can cut off your route as well, turning back your progress and causing you to use up your limited moves. There are resources that you can use to extend your actions, leap to different spots on the board or prevent the enemy from moving but they are kept to a limit and the enemy will occasionally use them against you as well. This all adds a layer of thinking to the quests they're part of and feels pretty satisfying when you wrap up the encounter and get bombarded with XP and loot drops.I hope more people give this one a shot because even if they're not a big fan of Dynasty/Samurai warriors. Koei approached this one with the same level of creativity that they brought to the Zelda and Persona crossovers making it fun for fans of the respected IPs even if they don't usually dabble in musou games.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:- This game takes Fate back to its roots. You have a roster of very cool and mysterious servants who all of their true names hidden. The masters are interesting and the dynamic between master-servant pairs is actually relevant again.- Character designs have returned to that grounded Fate/Stay Night and Fate/Zero style. This game is a breath of fresh air from the overly "Tropey and Anime" designs that FGO and Fate/Apocrypha started to introduce.- The cutscenes are fantastic. I feel like I'm watching Unlimited Blade Works again for the first time when a fight scene is being shown.- Character progression is easy to understand and meaningful. The moves you learn are flashy and fun to use. Changing stances actually changes the way you play- Enemy designs are either completely new or taken from FGO and given a nice makeover. If you remember the little Onis from Shimousa or the Kintoki rider event, those make an appearance and they actually look creepy.- There's a saint quartz joke.- Grail Front inspired combat makes it in the game with a fresh coat of paint and is very fun.- You get paid to pet dogs and cats.- Noble Phantasms look pretty badass.- Voice acting is pretty great.    - GilgameshCons:- This style of JRPG isn't for everyone. It plays similar to Extella or Hyrule Heroes in the sense that its designed kind of like a hoard hack and slash. It's redeemed by the fact that major targets/bosses have cool moves and are fun to fight against. I was hesitant my money was well spent at first but the gameplay improved.- Your servant is another saberface, which is a minor critique at best. Her character design is changed enough that she definitely looks unique.- If you aren't on controller you're gonna need to do some serious work on key-bind remapping to make the game feel good. Once you find your sweet spot though it plays pretty good.- That's it. Those are all my problems with the game.

Engaging story world divided by town segments and their local problems, character bonds as expected from Fate series with nice cutscenes. New servants and old ones (Gilgamesh, Lancer, Jalter) these are always good to see. Gameplay considering that you have only two type of attacks that you can mix into combos is good because of the characters swapping in combat. Special moves + tech tree for powering servants.World when moving around feels nice a lot of random materials to find, shrines to visit for skill points, things to buy including accessories for your weapons improving stats. Eating food, petting cats and dogs, this one never gets old. Side quests there is a lot to do and it feels like home. Ah and also an FGO mechanic covering Grail Wars where you basicly play chess on tactical map against other servants and their masters. Mini games in which you can create wooden figures or repair your katana. There is more but summing it up, it just feels relaxing to have various leisure activities implemented this way.Samurai Remnant has a lot to offer in a small package. Even if it doesn't stay spectacular at all times it still keeps me happy once I am in a mood to play. It's fun to move around blooming city of the japan Edo period and interacting with locals. _childDocuments_.review: I had only loosely followed the news surrounding this game, so I had come in expecting a primarily Musou game, akin to Dynasty Warriors or Fate/Extella. I was pleasantly surprised to discover that while Fate/Samurai Remnant does have the Musou battle basics and DNA within it, it is much more than that.As a Fate related product, there is a lot of Visual Novel style storytelling. I enjoy this personally, but I know this won't be up a lot of people's alley - especially if they were coming in primarily to hack-and-slash ala Musou gameplay. Other than the VN storytelling and Musou-style combat though, there are plenty of RPG style systems that - while a bit awkward at first to get used to - start to flow together very well.As for these RPG systems themselves, let me start with the one I consider the most important: The Magecraft Workshop. This is where you'll spend a lot of your money and materials that you'll gather from fighting, discovering random items in the towns and villages you travel to, and selling. The Workshop will help you unlock both helpful buffs - such as decreasing the cost of items and food bought at shops - and important sub-systems within the Workshop such as allowing you to both Upgrade your Mounting equipment to either increase the performance of the gear you have equipped, or Dismantle unneeded equipment to gain raw materials that can be used elsewhere.Mountings are essentially your gear in this game, and you'll gain them in various ways - though the most often will be by fighting. There appears to be a quality system to Mounting gear, of which I have currently only discovered Tiers I and II, which I'll call Bronze and Silver here, though I am sure higher tier/quality equipment will appear in time. Higher tier Mountings will more likely have a greater number of modifiers that will increase Iori's stats, such as increasing his damage in a specific combat stance, heal him after an enemy is defeated, increase the rate at which the Affinity gauge recovers, and several others that I won't list here for levity.These are just a few of the parts of the game that I have enjoyed thus far, and I hope that anyone that reads this review will find the information helpful in order for them to decide to purchase it themselves, or to help get themselves started along their journey in Fate/Samurai Remnant. :)

_childDocuments_.review: no you don't need prior knowledge to play this. there are cameo characters here from other fate works, but it's basically just for fun and not structurally important. miniature rant here, but i hate how much people overexaggerate needing prior knowledge to play or read type moon stuff, they are all standalone, with very few exceptions, just read/watch/play what you think looks interesting. spoilers followflawed in a lot of ways, but when it matter it really hits. there is so much care put into the overall production. all the character portraits, the animations, the 3d environments and all the million other fine details, you can just tell the developers were type moon fans themselves and wanted to bring this setting to life out of that love, it is absolutely stellar on that front. writing wise it is good in broad strokes. i do have complaints about the cast being too large and a lot of characters not getting more development, a bunch of the rogue servants in particular were basically just fan service and wasted in the story. The main cast is pretty great, though (and this is probably another minus) you won't get to see a lot of that until the second playthrough. iori and saber are the centerpiece obviously and by far the best part of the game, but i ended up liking all of the master/servant pairs by the end except like tsuchimikado and caster, who really suffered from the writing in general. tsuchimikado was always just a stereotypical cackling villain (or comic relief in dlc1) in his scenes, he practically gets more development in the digression about his brother than he gets in the entire rest of the game (also in the short story). i got a laugh from caster telling iori their true name and them immediately saying "i bet you don't even know who that is". also didn't pick up on this until i saw a post afterwards, but chiemon never actually killing anyone innocent (except arguably whoever was in edo castle in his ending) is such a subtle and good detail. by the end of entreat the darkness, which was i think the perfect end to the game, i just felt so bad for kaya, lol. i do wonder how much she understood iori, it's never spelled out but it felt like she knew more than she let on, but maybe that's just me coping.it really feels like they should have forced the snake ending for the first play, it just makes significantly more sense. I also suspect there were supposed to be more differences across playthroughs but they had to pare back whatever their plans were due to scale. snake -> rat -> entreat the darkness just so perfectly follows the lineage of the original fsn's storylines that i have a hard time believing it wasn't intended.gameplay wise i'm fine with it. not a musou player but this was more small scale fights than large fights, people compared it to p5strikers or yakuza which i've never played. lot of small irritating things, like dialogue happening during combat, or the way ranged servants worked. counterattack moves seem like by far the strongest thing in the game against strong enemies, outside of affinity np charges and nps/valor strikes, so i ended up abusing earth h1 a lot once i unlocked that. against trash mobs, water stance is great, but so is fire h4 (the multi stabbing move). h3 and h2 spam are also bonkers. void is just silly lol. honestly the most fun i had in actually playing the game was in the leyline battles, give me more of that.dlc1- should be saved for after first playthrough- decent, a little tiresome by the end. it's extremely funny how like 80% of gil and ibuki's lines are repeated across routes. the ending cgs are extremely cute, especially yui/rider's.dlc2- should be saved for after second playthrough.- short standalone story, young munenori is just a really fun character, writing and gameplay wise. loved the teamup at the end.dlc3- not played yet, will update later.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time Fate fan, I really really wanted to like this game. But alas, this game is a flawed piece of entertainment with a good story buried under a pile of bloated gameplay and filler fetch quests. When you boot up the game, the banger of an opening plays and you are like ohhhhhh this is going to be a good time. But a couple hours into the game, you realise that the gameplay loop is basically go here, interact with this object, go to somewhere else, fight a horde of monsters, dialogue telling you to go somewhere else, oh hey saber just ran off gotta chase her/him? down, rinse and repeat before you can get to the next major story cutscene. I mean I guess information gathering is an important part of a HGW, but it does not excuse the sheer excessive amount of running around the map when some of the conclusion can be easily reached without going through all that. And don't get me started on the god-awful grail front sections. The cutscenes themselves looks cheap, some of the free-to-play games out there have better looking cutscenes than this 80 dollar game. The battle system is alright, a mixture of souls-like gameplay and hack-and-slash. Now for my biggest gripe, the characters. The story is set in Edo period Japan, so obviously a ton of Japanese servants will be summoned, but the majority of the western audiences lacks the knowledge on that front and the game refuses to tell you who they are straight when you are almost at the end of the game. You can try looking it up but by doing that, you might encounter spoilers. I might just be nitpicking here, but I really expected more out of a game set in the intricate and expansive Fate universe, makes you wonder what they did with all that dough made from FGO. This game fails both as a competent game and as an extension to the Fate universe. If you are interested in Fate, there are much better introductions to the franchise. Hopefully F/EX record will be better. Now if you'll excuse me, those FGO dailies won't do themselves, adieu.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an okay JRPG, nothing too special, but for a Fate fan, this game is truly wonderful. The gameplay itself is just okay, and perhaps this is a pc only issue but the handling of combat is quite clunky and takes some getting used to. One of the highlights are of course the servants, which there are 11 playable, with few of them locked behind NG+. The servants really give you the sense of powerful mythical characters that are way beyond the capability of a human and also manages to balance them so that they do not trivialise the encounters in this game. The main character Iori is also nice to play with and has 'four' forms which suits different playstyle so there's something for everyone and encounter. Overall I can't really give a remark for the story as many of my thoughts have to do with spoiler territory, but I think its not bad and can make for a fun experience. Overall a 7/10 for average gamers, and a 8/10 for Fate fans. Highly recommend to purchase when its on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: It's been such a drag so far.In my 8h the first thought that comes to my mind is sleepy music while running from point A to B in an endless maze like town that looks the same in every corner. The environment and VFX look decent at best. At least the characters do have some style and they look cool, except for the goofy big hands.I'm playing the game on the hardest difficulty. Attack animations of some enemy types are barely visible. Many attacks have some visible long windup, but as soon as the enemy swings his weapon I can't dodge with my average 200 ms reaction time. The dodge timing is either below that or you need to learn how long the windup is for every attack and dodge according to that.Furthermore, bigger enemies are not really difficult or fun to play against. They usually just harden themselves, so your light attacks become useless. But then it just turns into a waiting game, 5 seconds looking at the enemy, then dodging an attack, then going for 2 attacks. Rinse and repeat for 30 seconds (for regular big enemies) or up to 2 minutes (when facing servants). I'm using heavy attacks already to break their shield which the game told me to do, but maybe I'm missing something. Comments are open.In general the combat feels like a watered down version of Fate Extella Link. You fight less but tougher enemies. Therefore, your abilities are adjusted accordingly. Smaller dodge range, smaller attack range, smaller attack speed.I'm not into RPG level systems or grinding, but if I had to judge, the skill trees and upgrade systems look fine. Some changes are meaningful, but you also have your +2% some random stat in between.I think the story could be interesting with some potential plot twist or surprises, but it's all washed down in an ocean full of "your partner is hungry" jokes, "your sister thinks your partner is your waifu and everything is embarassing and awkward", "your partner is from an ancient time and is missing human/social trait xyz". For me, the dialogue in general is way too much. So much talking happens and in the end you just have to run from point A to B to pick something up.Otherwise the game occasionally throws time wasters at you. Silly stealth mechanics, where you have to press a button and automatically crawl. Or you move along a wall. You have to pet cats/dogs to get HP back, but this action takes like 10 seconds and button mashing (in addition to combat button mashing to make sure you really get that repetitive strain injury). Redundant cutscenes where your partner walks through walls or doors to open them. Another scene where you press a button and then your characters jump on wood planks to cross a river, not even a mini game, just some random things that have no value. There is also a chess like 300 IQ board system, where you are supposed to move strategically and fight enemies at certain points. But there is so many extra rules where you or the enemy can move across the entire board, I don't know why this even exist.I was hoping things would get better after I took my first big break after 2.3h (where I went above the refund playtime), but it's just dragging and dragging. I was hoping to unlock stronger characters that do more on the field, but it seems the starting character is the peak already and it stays with summoning and playing the fun characters for only 15 seconds.I'm sad I got lured in by the 85% score and paid the premium price of 70, just to waste 8h of my life for this.

_childDocuments_.review: Aside from certain gripes I feel towards how the endings were done, the new Game+ being essentially forced, and granted even an issue where I had to install "VP9 Video Extensions" to simply see cutscenes, the story and gameplay are something special. It's very reminiscent of Fate/Stay Night while adding a lot of personality of its own, primarily that Iori is a compelling protagonist and most of the other Masters as well, even down to the more brief characters, all felt as thoughtful as the Masters in Fate/Zero, which easily could've gotten messy with the concept of Rogue Servants and other characters to develop. My only critique of the story perhaps comes from how I don't think Iori would've acted so suddenly evil to have achieved what he wanted - I've seen some discourse on that part - but the option is there as far as endings go, so the story is at least a little richer for that as it elevates the heroic path more. The gameplay itself also has many special moments, unlocking new stances often accompanies a development in the story. There are many memorable fights, especially if you're bold enough to fight against Rogue Berserker while inexperienced... Despite its flaws, perhaps because everything else is so good, especially as it fuses parts I love from across the franchise, I'd still give this game a 9/10. It's a great starting point in the franchise as well. Just be careful there are some flaws to be found here and they may feel worse as the game is otherwise near perfect. I'm hoping these may get fixed in time.

_childDocuments_.review: Musashi herself is already one of my favorite characters from Fate/Grand Order, and I'm happy to say that this game amplifies her even further. I'm already personally bias enough to have bought the game on multiple platforms several times.Fate/Samurai Remnants is a Action RPG and is very different from the typical hack-n-slash nature of Koei Techmo's other titles. It's a healthy mix between exploration and battles. The exploration aspect has the player visiting different locations set within the Edo period within Japan. While battles are a simplified real time action RPG. Both do not overstay it's welcome, and the main focus of the game is the bond between Iori and Saber.Miyamoto Iori is the adopted son of Musashi, and Saber is Iori's servant who are both part of the Holy Grail War. The game is fluid for the most part, and doesn't experience any major frame rate or resolution drops throughout the adventure. Fate/Samurai Remnants does NOT have online play, however the game does feature multiple endings, encouraging replay-ability with New Game+, including additional content to allow the player to use the other servant and master pairs albeit for a short amount of time. As stated above, the story is about Iori and Saber, and the game does feature many side quests that will nail you an easy 50 hours of play time.I highly recommend the game to any avid Fate series fan, and especially Fate/Grand Order players as the story takes place between the events of Shimosa and the Lost Belts. If you're new to Fate, the game will explain the basic fundamental concepts to you such as Holy Grail Wars, Servants/Masters, Command Seals etc. However, at it's core, the game (and series as a whole) is a visual novel. If you're not a fan of reading or visual novel games, this many not be the best game for you.Either way, I love this game and it's my game of the year for 2023. Thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: Writing this review right after completing the game and stepping into NG+, so don't give me that ♥♥♥♥ about "damn didn't clear the game and already hating on it".I didn't even know they could make musou game that would genuinely be bad, as the genre itself is not really know for being complex when it comes to mechanics, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, this game is BAD. How could they ♥♥♥♥ up such a premise when there are two EXTELLA games that exist? All you had to do is to give us a musou game with servants. In the meantime you see comments like "MOMMY MUSASHI" and "JALTER MY BELOVED", but you are playing Musashi for a total of 15 minutes, and then JAlter you play for like 15 seconds, only for A SINGLE SECTION they let you control Jeanne. This is ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up. Actually, no, this is beyond ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up. I don't even care if that spoils the game to someone because I bought this game for the premise of playing as JAlter because I thought they'll give you like a Free Mode type thing where you can replay encounters with anyone you want, BUT NO, THERE IS NO SUCH THING. Don't be lured in by all the positive feedback. Maybe they'll give you more servant gameplay through season pass, but have you seen the price for that ♥♥♥♥?! Doubt it'll be worth it. And if that means that you're playing more Iori, then double no from me. Game does look amazing, and I love the artstyle of it, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ am I just empty after clearing it.Also, three billion tutorials.Your main gameplay loop is playing the weakest musou character they could come up with, Iori. Why is he the weakest? Well cause everyone gets hyper armor whenever you are fighting as him. The only way to actually deal damage to anyone larger than you is to break their armor by countering or just waiting till their move is done and then time your strikes while their defence is "lowered". You wanna have fun and play a cool character, which is basically like any servant in the game? We got you. Here's a bar that lasts ~20 seconds that you have to grind for 30 years as Iori, and then maybe by divine intervention you can play a servant until you've just barely familiarized yourself with their movesets. People who played through the game will tell me "BUT THERE ARE TIMES WHEN YOU PLAY SERVANTS ONLY" and yeah, sure, that would be an argument if you could play them for more than 15 minutes of in-game time. But alas, this is not what Fate game is about I guess. Totally not. Don't be fooled, you're not playing servants in this game for the most part. Even NG+ is just that, it's same game but with your progress already being there. I'm disappointed beyond belief. I pre-ordered it because I dreamed of a musou game with servants, given Extella was the only thing closest to that, so I had hopes when I saw Koei making a Fate game. Beaten it because that's the only way I can justify spending money on this piece of ♥♥♥♥. And even then it just left me with a bigger feeling of disappointment. Cause the whole time I played, I was hoping that the game will allow me to just pick servants I wanna play as and ditch the stupid and weak Iori. I just wanted a musou game with servants that's not riddled with stupid tile-conquering gameplay shtick and I couldn't even get that, unbelievable. Do not buy this. Just don't. Maybe on sale 10 years later along with whatever content comes out for it later, but not full price. This is a huge flop and I hope that whoever is writing those positive reviews will wake up and see the game for what it is.UPD: They added choice for characters exclusively for battle recollections. While you could say that this is negating some of my complaint and now I can in fact play any servant featured as playable, BUT it's only for the glorified boss rush mode in a musou game WHERE MAIN CONTENT IS PVE, JUST LET ME MOW DOWN HORDES, I DON'T CARE TO REPLAY ONLY BOSS BATTLES. _childDocuments_.review: Went into this game expecting nothing from it considering past Fate games were good fanservice but rather mediocre games, but Samurai Remnant took me completley by surprise by actually being a very good game. The gameplay feels pretty nice for an action game, much better than most small or middle sized action JRPGs, though it obviously can't quite compete with something like a Platinum Games game. Compared to musou games though, where this game still has noticeable roots in, the gameplay is almost mindblowingly good.Story and writing is quite decent so far though I don't feel like I'm far enough to actually rate that.Characters alas their personalities, backgrounds, dialogs, etc. are very good and where this game shines most, this is absolutely on the level you expect from anything Fate related. Graphics are as you can see in the trailers not exactly good, but with the art style they choose for the game they actually just work and look pleasant enough. This is further assisted by the fact that, unusually for Koei Tecmo, this game is actually a technically decent port. The Antialiasing works flawless and produces a sharp and calm picture, the framerate is stable and high, no hiccups or whatsoever, fast loading times, there's nothing really to criticize. All in all this makes this the by far best Fate Game to date and thus an absolute must have for any Fate fan. And even if you're not a fan of Fate but just like Action games and/or JRPGs this is still a solid recommendation, even for the high price they ask for it.
