_childDocuments_.review: As a Fate fan, I'm naturally somewhat biased, but I had a great time with the story. Alliances are forged, allies are betrayed and cities are leveled. It really feels like you're watching a (good) Fate anime adapation.Unfortunately it takes a while to get going - there are quite a few uninteresting tasks like chasing random enemy goons around or asking shopkeepers about their whereabouts in the beginning hours. But once it gets going, it goes full throttle.The side stories (digressions) were a nice addition to the main story as they gave more insight on the individual Master / Servant pairs, although some made you face the same bosses a little too often in my opinion.This game uses musou-type combat, which means that most of the time, you will string together fast normal attacks that all lead into different heavy attack finishers, depending on the length of your combo. While this core aspect of the combat never changes, you get multiple sword stances with different attacks and effects, spells and the ability to order your servants to use special skills during battle to spice things up.Sadly, the first few hours paint a rather boring picture. Most encounters revolve around depleting an enemy's shell (shield) gauge and once it's broken, you're meant to unleash hell on them since they take increased damage for a while. Problem is, during the first few hours you don't have many tools to unleash so the enemies feel like damage sponges. As you level up and gain more options, this feeling then quickly fades. You can also play as the servants themselves, although only for rather short periods.All in all, the combat stays rather simple and needs little strategy, but I loved annihilating foes with the magical equivalent of a nuclear blast.I would recommend this game to not only Fate and / or Musou fans, but to all fans of action JRPGs. Story and combat take a while to truly get going, but once they do, you don't want to put your controller down. As it also has multiple routes and NG+ (which also unlocks more digressions not available on your first playthrough), replayability is great.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Fate, you'll very likely enjoy this game. The bond between Iori and Saber is generally great stuff. Their relationship and it's development throughout the game is one of the highlights of the game's story. It's good the main characters are as good as they are, because the actual plot of the story is quite messy and borderline confusing at times. Especially near the end of the game where everything starts feeling rushed and nonsensical. Thankfully, the other supporting characters/servants you encounters are full of personality and play well off each other. If you're going into this game expecting an epic story like Fate Zero, then you'll be a bit disappointed. You need to play this game for the amusing character interactions and fun spectacle.The combat is very satisfying for the first half of the game. It's fun switching between different stances, dodging/parrying attacks, and pulling off team attacks with your Saber. All of this accompanied by some quite good music which helps make the combat encounters grand and emotional. Unfortunately, the combat does get quite repetitive in the later half of the game. The game starts to throw endless waves of spongy enemies at you, and all of this becomes quite fatiguing. I only unlocked one of the endings, but I'm not sure if I'm willing to do another playthrough to see the game's true ending at this point. The fights in this game are simply tiring. I did play through the game on the highest difficulty, it's possible the encounters are more enjoyable on the easier difficulties if you're simply here for the story.Definitely worth a play, but have the expectations that you'll likely burn out on the game before you reach the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Embark on a journey into a world of masters, servants, magic, and war with Fate Samurai/Remnant as it summons you to fight your way in a hidden war set during the Edo Period in Japan. If you're a big fan of the Fate series as I am, then this game is perfect for you! On a side note, I'm in the middle of Chapter 2 of the game and have completed a number of quests after 8 hours. So, join me as I discuss my thoughts and experiences in this game, as this is my fate.SOUNDS AND GRAPHICSAs we immerse ourselves in the world of Fate/Samurai Remnant, the game delivers a captivating audio and visual experience for our inner weeb and future Fate fans. The game welcomes you with striking visuals and immersive background music that sets the tone of the game right from the start. The sound effects, including those for attacks, clashing weapons, magics, and enemies, contribute to the immersive experience of the gameplay. The Japanese voice acting is top-notch, as they chose the perfect lineup of popular voice actors for which the emotions conveyed are spot on! Unfortunately, the English dub, which some players are looking forward to, is not yet available. The game also has a dynamic soundtrack that fits the atmosphere; from ambient background music of various towns to intense background music as the tension also heightens during combat scenarios. Notably, the satisfaction derived from the combat dialogues also takes the game experience to the next level. On the other hand, the game's graphics are simply incredible. It truly feels like you're in an anime, particularly a Fate anime. It enhances our visual experience with its bright anime art style, bringing the Edo era to life. It is highly detailed, particularly the character models and environments. All of the color palettes selected complement each other very well. Additionally, the characters' eyes are so gorgeous that they melt my heart, especially Saber's. That being said, it is truly an absolute feast for the senses—both auditory and visual.STORYAside from the captivating audio and visual experience, the story of the game also has an engaging narrative. Imagine this: In the 4th year of the Keian Era during the Edo Period in Japan, people were enjoying peace and tranquility. However, as the "Waxing Moon Ritual" comes, a hidden battle between seven pairs of masters capable of summoning heroic spirits known as servants is set for a battle royale to claim the Waxing Moon's wish-granting power. Each of these seven pairs of servants has a distinct class, such as Saber, Archer, Lancer, Caster, Berserker, Assassin, and Rider. Unexpectedly, you are one of the selected masters who is about to face the violence of this war. Furthermore, I enjoy how there are multiple endings that you must achieve in order to uncover different perspectives or, most likely, what-ifs in the plot. As I'm still in my first playthrough, I'm not sure how different the endings are or how much they'll impact them. Nonetheless, I hope it is worth the wait.CHARACTERS But what would Fate be without its memorable masters and servants? In Fate/Samurai Remnant, you can play as Miyamoto Iori, a master, or Saber, a servant. Starting with Miyamoto Iori, he is the student and adopted son of Miyamoto Musashi. He is a ronin from Asakusa, Edo, who studied Niten Ichiryu swordsmanship. Then, he was suddenly chosen as a Master of Saber during the Waxing Moon Ritual. Also, he wields two katanas and uses various sword stances, each of which has a specific purpose in combat. The next one is Saber (my all-time favorite class and character); she is a heroic spirit that was surprisingly summoned by Miyamoto Iori during an intense battle with a master and servant. She refuses to reveal her true name to Miyamoto Iori because she feels insulted; he cannot determine who she is just by looking, and it is for strategic reasons. She possesses superhuman combat skills and carries a jagged, curving-edged sword with water abilities. She also resembles Artoria Pendragon, the best-known saber-class heroic spirit in the Fate series in terms of facial features and hair.The other masters and servants in the game are just as amazing and intriguing as the ones I've already mentioned. If you're a fan of the Fate series, you'll very much enjoy both the new and returning characters. I'll let you discover the remaining ones because I don't want to spoil the enjoyment of discovering who the other masters and servants are.PERSONAL OPINION AND RATINGIn addition to my previous review of the game, here are some pros and cons based on my observations and opinions.Pros:Cool combos:There are different moves, combos, abilities, and sword stances offered in the game, which you can learn as you progress. Combining these can create effective attacks and nail a sick combo for both the master and servant. Original game:Fate/Samurai Remnant has no anime equivalent or major connection for it yet. It's simply a new entry in the Fate series; the fact that it's being released as a game first is cool.It lets you strategize:The game allows you to carefully plan your battle strategy. To increase your chances of success, you must select various sword stances, combos, and abilities. Also, you need to efficiently switch between master and servant. Another game feature that needs strategy is the Leylines, in which you must capture all points or spirit fonts, as shown previously in the screenshots.Cons:Hardest difficulty ain’t that hard:The hardest difficulty seems to be lacking. It hasn't changed much over my playtime; it simply increases the enemies' attack power and health. But they still lack attack actions and movesets. They sometimes stay still during the fight.Japanese text translates on its own:Sometimes, when I launch the game, it occasionally translates itself to Japanese even when I set the language to English. I was challenged to read the Japanese texts, but I wasn't ready. Well, I’d like to take that as a sign for my future profession and language skills. Kidding aside, I hope this is fixed as soon as possible.No English dub:As I mentioned previously, the English dub is currently unavailable. This could be due to budget limits or other issues. Some players might find it difficult to play the game if they do not want to read the subtitles.A lot to take in for some players:Some players, particularly those unfamiliar with the Fate series, may find the game perplexing. This may have an impact on their comprehension of the story or how things unfold in Fate, particularly for the series' returning characters. Although the story was properly stated, they will most likely have a lot to process.Despite all its pros and cons, Fate/Samurai Remnant is an extremely enjoyable game that introduces a different approach and experience to the Japanese action role-playing game genre and the Fate games, particularly the Musou-style gameplay like Dynasty Warriors. It's a game that people, especially Fate fans will enjoy because of its intriguing auditory and visual experience, memorable characters, and engaging story. However, it would have been amazing if you could choose who to summon as your servant, giving the game a unique and immersive feel. Finally, the game provides an unforgettable experience for role-playing game lovers, casual gamers, and newcomers alike, making it well worth a try. Given everything considered, and with the game's fate sealed, I give it a whopping, one of the most sought-after but well-deserved 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I decided to give Fate Samurai Remnant a shot. My familiarity with the Fate series was mostly limited to the anime adaptations, yet I hadn't deeply explored the franchise beyond that. Surprisingly, this game has the potential to transform me into a dedicated fan of the Fate universe. The developers have impressively balanced fan service with accessibility for newcomers. I particularly enjoyed the combat system, which offers a variety of stances and the ability to switch between servants, adding depth and excitement to battles. The narrative captivated me for the most part, especially with its intricate portrayal of masters outmaneuvering each other, leading to unexpected plot developments.The character dynamics were a highlight for me, particularly this version of Saber, which stands out as my favorite portrayal yet. It's a refreshing departure from the usual Artorias that fans have come to expect. Iori, too, caught me by surprise with his calm and rational demeanor, often delivering lines with a deadpan delivery that sharply contrasts with Saber's more brash and outspoken personality. This interplay between the characters led to some genuinely humorous momentsHowever, I believe the game's weakness lies in its execution of boss fights. While a few boss encounters were engaging, many felt painfully average The primary issue seems to be the inadequate signaling of bosses' moves, which hampers the player's ability to anticipate and react effectively. Additionally, the shell gauge mechanic didn't hit the mark for me, lacking a sense of satisfaction in its implementation.All in all, still loved my time with it so much , I'm doing a NG+ do get the other endings and most likely get the DLCS

Characters are very flat, outside of Tamano who is well played and Saber who is your main side kick. Ironically, Iori (you) has pretty much zero character, his sister gives him the tiny bit he has. The villian has an unexplained hatred for the main character, zero explanation there outside of 'meh, meh meh, I hate Iori and have an Alter Servant. Speaking of servants, building bonds only really works for Boss and Tamano, maybe even Rogue Saber, that's it. The game is a very short one gameplay wise, meaning my first playthrough took me 40 hours, a solid 25 0f those are spent in cutscenes at least. Equipment is shallow, slight stat altercations, nothing more, looks are fine though. Skills are well done, I must say, while magic is very meh. To really get every cutscene / moment in the game you will have to beat the game about three times for all endings and digressions. YES SOME SIDEQUESTS ARE LOCKED BEHIND MAIN QUEST CHOICES WHICH IS ABSOLUTELY STUPIDThe game has one good quality of life feature, that being in ng+.The game will give you a red line warning if you try to skip a line you haven't heard before, which semi decent if you do really care about the ng+ expansion lore. _childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game, but with a few considerations before hand, let me explain.TLDR: ---------Not the deepest combat system you've seen (but still nice) and some technical limitations with the engine, but the enjoyable combat, environments and different characters makes it worthwhile. More enjoyment is to be felt if you like anime and in particular if you're familiar with the "Fate" series.Very decent and easy to enjoy title in the series.More depth:-----------------First of all, you probably need to enjoy anime. Second, I truly feel you need to have watched something (anime, manga, videogame) concerning the "Fate" series beforehand. I'm only an explorer of it on and off, I can feel it goes way deep, you don't need to know all that was made before, but if you come into this without any clue this will probably feel confusing. Just watch one anime in the series and - especially Fate/Stay Night - and you'll be fine.Very basically and without spoilers, it goes something like this: periodically on Earth the "holy grail" appears - where different "Masters" (magically attuned real-world people) are paired with Servants (embodiments of historic heroic figures) to have a mega duel to the death where last Master standing is granted one wish that will actually come true do to the mystical powers of the "Holy Grail". Different Masters come from different backgrounds and have their own personal interests and you'll find all this along the journey.This time, it happens in Tokyo closely after the Sengoku Jidai era as the "Waxing Moon Ritual" and your main character is one the Masters that gets all this thrown on his lap involuntarily.The gameplay is not the most deep you'll find out there, but if you're OK with that you'll get an enjoyable action packed experience that is not simply a "button masher", it has some depth, but it's not the most complex either. You have some different stances and can make combos of N light attacks finished by a heavy attack. There's no parry, there is a dodge - which if you time perfectly you can do a riposte leaving enemies staggered. Then, you have some magical attacks. The different stances focus on different types of combos so you'll be switching it up on the fly.Also, you can take control of your Servant and allied Servants making use of their character for a limited time - which is very powerful and fun as they have their unique combos. As you control the main character you can also do a "pair move" with your servant that is very impactful. Both of these are on a sort of "cooldown" gauges that fill up as you do your attacks with the main character.It's more "reigned in" compared to the typical "Samurai Warriors" style of combat, but still not as "personal" or "engaged" as something like a From Software game or "For Honor".If these caveats are OK with you I feel you will get a good experience with this. Currently I'm about 24h in (which is quite a lot for a gamer who has a full time job) and I feel things are going at a nice pace: I wish it could be faster but also I'm enjoying the combat.Other than that, the story leans a lot on some anime tropes, but all the characters (including Masters and Servants) have their own personality traits, motivations and backstories, and things move along at a good pace: not too fast, not too slow - with varied and unique combat encounters along the way.Visually it's barely above a PS3 gen game, but different times of day and more modern coloring and lightning makes it fun to go along the different Japanese environments. The graphics engine unfortunately does not support VRR (freesync, g-sync) or upscaling (DLSS, FSR) and it doesn't seem to handle refresh rates other than 60Hz or 120Hz well. If you try to set a framerate cap different than that you will get poor frame pacing, which is immediately apparent by just turning the camera with a controller. To get around this, in my case I set my monitor refresh rate to 120Hz and a framerate cap of 120 FPS (since my GPU can 99% handle that FPS) and only by doing this I could get the fluidity you'd expect of a locked frame rate with smooth frame pacing at that refresh rate. If you're going for 120 FPS there's a multitude of graphics settings you can lower in order to achieve that. Of course going for locked 60 FPS is probably much easier for many GPUs (i have an RTX 3080 Ti, playing at 1440p)

The OST is good as well.I think doing a second run is pretty essential for this game though, I'd say my second run was better than my first. Story-wise, it unlocks pretty much all disgressions  and as for the gameplay it allows you to experiment a lot more with the combat. _childDocuments_.review: For anyone who is a Fate fan, you'll enjoy this game in some way or another. But if you're coming from the Extra/Extella games, you might be a little disappointed to hear that you don't play as the Servants too often/for very long. It's a bit of a shame as characters like Lancer  or Musashi are crowd favourites, though in NG+ Lancer does get a bit more spotlight, and a new playable side story, but imo Iori is fun enough when you get a hang of switching forms, the overwhelming combo lists and the like. The game is sort of a mix of Dark Souls and the Warriors games gameplay wise. Not that it's terribly difficult (does present some challenge at least), but you are fighting waves of enemies Warriors style, with a dodge, timing, and enemy attack pattern mechanic similar to that of the Souls games. It can be a little tedious at times, as Mini boss enemies, and bosses, are a bit spongy. But once you've got the Wind form (which is optional), getting rid of Shell Gauges (Basically an enemy's shield before you can do any real damage) becomes less of a chore. Either way, I found it enjoyable to learn each enemy type and try to perfectly dodge every attack, which grants a bonus if you pull it off. The story is written as you'd expect from the Fate IP. So pretty good. Graphically it's a treat, animations are just wonderful, art is brilliant, and the visual effects are just on point. Overall it's a good game, I'm the type of person who doesn't finish games all that often, but Samurai Remnant did hook me in for the long ride. The main story is about 30 ish hours long, with 3 endings, and one joke ending. And after your first play through, expect to spend maybe another 10 or so hours getting the other two endings. Luckily, when you start NG+ the game will grey out text you've already read, and will warn you before you skip a cutscene if there is new story, text, or otherwise so you won't miss anything, if you care. A shame that Boss/Ruler  isn't playable. But there is a boss fight with him if you do a few things. I won't spoil how, but it was amusing, as is always with this character. 8/10 game, I can't wait to see what the DLCs bring.

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the Fate series, I consider this game the most polished Fate related game despite it not being my personal favorite. On its own, I'd say it's a very enjoyable albeit not excellent entry in the vast story-rich action/RPG sub-genre worth checking out if you're into that sort of experience.The most accomplished aspects of the game lie in my opinion within its cast, setting and underlying ideological clashes, which are a staple of Fate stories. The characters involved knit a mesh of beliefs and personalities that make for very compelling exchanges and interactions. My highlight is the game's protagonist Miyamoto Iori, I think the people charged with developing his character deserve special credit for the patience shown in fleshing him out as for most of the time he is portrayed as a pretty generic videogame playable character with a pretty bland personality and a relatable but risk-free moral compass that a player can just step into with neither much struggle nor care. However the story, through its clearly intended multiple playthroughs calmly deconstructs his real motives and reason for his seemingly unassuming behavior and twist it into what I found to be a pretty fascinating outlook on life that perfectly fits with the real doctrine he followed in the real world, culminating in a refined mixture between authentic records and creative freedom signature of Type Moon's most celebrated works. Iori's servant is an excellent compliment to his evolution as well as being a wonderful character on their own with an endearing blend of a carefree mischievous demeanor concealing a tragic life.The setting is utilized to the fullest and it intelligently integrates both new and familiar servants in a non disruptive manner, the most relevant servants all hail from Japanese myth and are novel inclusions to the series while recurring servants are relegated to the secondary rogue category. Allowing both gameplay and setting to benefit from the mixture of novelty and familiarity.The game's presentation is memorable but flawed, the art style is simply superb with lead artist Rei Wataru successfully creating a new identity for this title not just as a game but as a universe within the whole of the Fate series. If Fate/stay Night is synonymous with Takashi Takeuchi and Fate/Extra with Wada Arco, Samurai Remnant is the Rei Wataru Fate.This brilliant identity is however held back by the frankly mediocre technical aspects of the game's software, specially when it comes to environment graphics. The spectacle that are the character sprites and models is damaged by the muddy terrains and landscapes. A shame since even those are clearly made with care to replicate ancient Japanese scenery which they can if you overlook their dated graphical quality.As far as the gameplay goes it's entertaining without impressing, a trend very much pertaining to all Fate games with varying degrees. This game has however the most engaging gameplay I've yet experienced from any Fate title as it constantly adds new systems and mechanics that while not particularly sophisticated on their own they add on to each other to make for a whole better than the sum of its parts complimented by very visually impressive special attacks. My only gripe with these is that late game additions to the gameplay make some of the early game systems obsolete which I see as a sign of more amateur game design.All things considered, I think this was a very memorable story told through a competent game and I thoroughly enjoyed it despite its flaws. I'd say this is a must for any fan of the Fate series as this provides with a story the quality of which holds up to the Type Moon's standard with its own unique identity carved in the familiar and beloved setting of the Holy Grail War and I'd still recommend it to those who aren't fans of Fate but looking for a compelling story-rich game to sink their time into.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played Fate/Samurai Remnant through to completion and I can give this game my full recommendation. I initially got the game as I am a Fate fan and was intrigued at an RPG in the setting as that is a type of game I love playing. Fate/Samurai Remnant is an extremely well put together game. The gameplay, visuals, story, and soundtrack all come together wonderfully. Each is strong in its own right, but taken together you have an exceptional game. I will be upfront on one extremely important issue. This is not a create your own character and play in an open world type RPG. This is very much a story focused RPG. Iori, the main character, is not some blank slate that acts as your avatar. He is a character just as much as everyone else. You control him in all ways that matter for gameplay. However, you cannot get Iori to take an option to 'roleplay' that is against his established character. If you are a fan of the Fate series you will want to pick this up as soon as you can. If you are a RPG fan who loves story focused games than you should pick this game up as soon as possible. A general RPG fan should at the very least put this game on their wish list to grab on the next sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Fate/Samurai Remnant is a decent game. A 7/10 kind of decent game. Why do I think that? I'll try to explain.Firstly, the soundtrack is mediocre, but music is always subjective. All I'm saying is that it ain't no YS or Dark Souls soundtrack.Secondly, the gameplay is a mixed bag of tedium and kind of entertaining boss fights, but I did play it on the hardest difficulty that was available to me as a fresh start. All combat for anything short of a boss is just your typical dynasty warriors thing, but with different sword stances for your protagonist, that pretty much just amount to being the same thing. Water is borderline useless for anything short of just moving fast af boy, and earth is just what you swap to to not take damage. Wind is just a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ stance that I don't even know why exists. The heavy attacks are abysmally slow for every stance short of fire and void, but are especially slow for wind, so your best bet will just be to spam normal attacks. Well, the only good earth attack is just spamming the heavy attack once and moving. Seriously, what the hell is the point of the wind stance? Why does the game tell you that it's good for monsters when it does literal ♥♥♥♥ for damage?     The bosses and "miniboss" enemies have shells, which basically just means more health, but done in an obnoxious way. What are the shells? They're just a barrier that makes you do borderline 0 damage to said enemy until you break it, but now you can't do any damage at all unless said enemy finishes their attack and is glowing blue. This seems fine in theory, but when the game is mostly just throwing mobs at you, and most of the enemy movesets are too easy to avoid, or ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ attacks that give you barely any time to hit them after they finish (♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Arjuna), then the fights start to just become kind of tedious. Maybe I shouldn't have done every side thing and clapped many monster cheeks on my first (and probably last run anytime soon), because that ♥♥♥♥ had me bored real quick. At about the midpoint of the game, combat for bosses just devolves into spamming affinity moves, normal attacks, and devouring food that restores affinity and hp.Too long don't read, the only good and decent fights are the actual bosses. The mob enemies barely exist, and the "miniboss" enemies are just a complete slog to kill, because I feel like they're wasting my time with how long it takes to kill them.Thirdly, the skill tree for the protagonist and his servant,  are almost entirely just stats, the occasional skill (which almost always ends up being the same damage but different looking animation), or some gimmick like reviving upon death when in earth stance. Basically, it's your typical nothing burger skill tree that doesn't really add anything except the illusion of "evolving" your combat play style.My fourth and lost point for my opinion on this game is the story. Now once again, the story, just like music, is very subjective. For me, the story ends up being decent. It's not bad by any means, but it's not particularly interesting either. It's your typical Fate story, but with different characters in a different setting, so if that sounds good to you, then go for it. I was fine with it, since I kind of enjoy this style of story.My main issue with the story is that it's just the same old, same old, but with a different set of paint, but this set of paint is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ than most of the previous ones. The only interesting or entertaining characters in the entire story are Iori (protagonist), your servant (Saber), Gilgamesh, and Miyamoto. Gilgamesh is just there for the sake of being amusing. Most of the characters in the story just aren't super fleshed out, especially not Chiemon, and they mostly exist as either obstacles, or being mostly irrelevant. The worst offenders of being mostly irrelevant are J'alter (but not really J'alter), Crimson Codex, Kaya and the pseudo-servant inside of her, Tsuchimikado, and the caster dude.I have one more final point, which is that every ending except for the "true"/"bad" ending actually just sucks ass. That true/bad ending or whatever requires NG+, but I looked up every ending after having beaten it because I didn't wanna go through the inane combat again. The ending I got didn't even have Saber's in it, and Iori was in it for a second just standing around not saying anything. After Yui Shousetsu says something about bright lights or whatever, it cuts to Zheng and the ginger chick talking about not giving up on achieving their objectives, and how they'll probably fight each other in the future. That ending was a whole lot of nothing, and not the vague artsy nothing, but nothing burger nothing. The "true/bad" ending is actually a pretty good ending.Too long didn't read summary of my ♥♥♥♥♥ review is that the game's barely good, but it ain't bad or anything. It has mostly inane dynasty warriors style combat, and a story that's kind of good, but has already been done before in a better way. I don't regret playing this game, so it's a positive from me, but I don't really see the appeal in playing through this again on NG+.

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10, weak recommend as this game has some real flaws that fanservice cant solvefor fate fans this game is sprinkled with homages, references, and returning charactersfor fate newbies, this is a somehwat accessible entry to the fate universe, but ultimately i would recommend either reading the visual novel or watching an anime than playing thiswhile the story has a handful of shining moments, it is otherwise shallow and underdeveloped. foreshadowing that never pay-offs, characters that have no motivations, no development, no arc. in other fate grail war stories, there's a lot of intrigue and surprises that upset your understanding of the conflict and characters. here? only in trace amounts. theres a lot of potential here in the setting that just isnt being realized.mechanically this is a musou game. you press light attack a few times and heavy attack to complete a combo. thankfully unlock and upgrade a robust set of combat stances that keep it fresh and interesting. there is a bit of a learning curve for knowing when to burn your 6 different combat resource meters to make combat not a slog, and failing to do so forces you to slog through otherwise difficult fights. unlike other musou games you dont have to worry about conquering and reconquering territory, all fights are restricted to a set arena and after you defeat the enemies in that area you can move on.on letdown is there is no real post-game mode where you can just do combat challenges with all the different characters in the game. if you want to continue beating up enemies after cleaing the game you have to start a new game+, and you are still restricted to the enemies and playable characters the story has at the time.mild spoilers: there is a fairly interesting structure to the game that the human player character starts out quite weak when fighting monsters and enemy servants when compared to his servant, and early on you must rely quite a bit on your servant to help turn the tide of battle. as you upgrade your stats, gear and skills the gap between the player and servant diminishes, eventually the human master surpasses his servant in some ways. this is strength is acknowledged and addressed by the plot of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr: A really solid Musou where they over-delivered with loads of game mechanics, a rich story and memorable characters.Gameplay-wise, there's lots of skills and abilities to unlock for the main duo through the whole game to keep it fresh. The ability to play all of the Heroic Spirits at one point or another is great fun too since they all have custom move-sets, skills and Noble Phantasms. The game also has good difficulty balancing too, enemies are tough when they need to be and they're varied.Story-wise, I think that the game is approachable to people not familiar with the Fate Franchise, but for those that are it's really something. I'm talking up there with the animes in my opinion. There's a lot of reading sure but it is fully voice acted (in Japanese) and they really blew budget on art and animations here and there, so it still manages to be very engaging. For the characters there are some returning cast-members for people that have played FGO or seen UBW, and I really enjoyed the new characters despite my lack of knowledge in Japanese/Chinese history and mythology. The main character is about the only muted character (he's a classic Fate self-insert), but he's carried by the interactions with Saber so it's alright. There is also multiple endings and NG+ which I'm trying now.I think it's been worth it at full price =)

_childDocuments_.review: Fate Samurai Remnant is a game that combines Musou, RPG, and VN story telling. They blend nicely in this game. The story is engaging and feels like it is its own unique story, while drawing inspiration from the existing Fate (specifically FSN, UBW, and HF) stories. This probably isn't a good entry point into the Fate/ universe; This seems like a game specifically targeted at fans of Musou and Fate/.I haven't encountered any major bugs yet; though one minor annoyance is that using the desktop shortcut to launch the game, launches it in Japanese; regardless of your launch settings. I also believe the game needs an accessibility setting that allows for "hold" instead of "tap" for button mashing sequences.The art design is what you would expect from an anime style game; I think it looks great! If you're a fan of Fate/ and Musou, you probably don't need me to convince you to pick this game up. _childDocuments_.review: A great new entry into the Fate series. It clearly pulls a lot from Grand Order's successes and while I would like it to have been more separate, the benefits outweigh the faults.The game itself is an RPG, there's some classic Koei Tecmo waves of enemies (this is my first KT game - going off what I've seen) layered with harder foes and bosses. Plenty of side questing to explore Japan in this era, learning about the different areas was really fun.You also get to pet maybe 1000 dogs and cats so it cant be a bad game.The full story seems to require a second play through, there were only 2 main choices, not sure how many endings in total there are. I was pretty satisfied from getting an ending first, and I didn't really do a lot of the challenge quests facing boss' again.Ok on subsequent playthroughs with game data carrying over, its full muso brainless action for a lot of it, but it was fun to memorize some of the bosses. If I had to go through it another time immediately I could see it being tiring. Hence why I put off completing everything in the game. Namely some of the minor sidequests and stuff that was a bit of a pain if you don't keep track of what you're doing specifically. _childDocuments_.review: This is a great game for Fate fans. The story focuses on Miyamoto Iori, who is the adopted son of Miyamoto Musashi. Iori finds himself embroiled in the Waxing Moon ritual--a Holy Grail War. The story is a fairly simple grail war compared to a lot of other Fate series. The masters and servants fight it out, make alliances, and try their hand at winning the wishing granting Waxing Moon. Iori is a much more interesting character than he initially seems, and I find the other characters to be interesting and compelling as well.Gameplay isn't quite musou, but I call it a "musou-lite" because while combat is encounter based rather than big battlefields where you're trying to capture strongholds, the combat is the same style. I like musou games, but tend to get fatigued of them. The combat in Samurai Remnant is broken up into digestible chunks though. You'll be playing as Iori for around 90% of the game, but you can build up a gauge to switch out with Saber or one of the rogue servants you can recruit. The game does a great job of making Iori feel like a competent fighter but making the servants feel on another level. Iori's different stances also do a good job diversifying the combat as they give him several completely different move pools. Lastly, going for 100% completion can be fairly tedious. There are 3 different endings, and if you want the game to register 100% completion you have to do one particular ending twice. With strategic saving you can get every ending with only 2 playthroughs, so maybe look up the endings if you want 100%. And for the "All-Knowing" achievement, which requires you to complete the logbook, you need to find a few very missable entries, which required me to do a whole other playthrough to find. I still had fun with the game though, and was very happy to see my waifu in a non-gacha game.

_childDocuments_.review: A fair warning to those expecting your typical Musou-style game like Fate/Extella, this plays much closer to a typical action RPG than a Musou style game, though battle animations are very much reminiscent of one. Lots of story, dialogue, and exploration, much less hack and slashing through hordes of enemies.For those looking to play this game, about 75% of your time on your first playthrough will be spent reading dialogue, as this is a very heavily story driven game, much like most of the Fate franchise. If you don't mind a lot of reading, the game is captivating from start to finish, though the ending(s) end somewhat abruptly. The gameplay itself is very snappy and responsive, though expect to control the same 2 characters for the majority of the game, only occasionally swapping to some of the others in the cast. You will not get to play as Musashi or Jeanne Alter often, if that's what you're here for.It is highly recommended to play with a controller, as at the time of writing, KB+M controls are very jank and your gameplay experience will be greatly diminished with them.Overall, I'd rate the game a solid 8 or 9/10. It's not for everyone, but absolutely amazing for its intended audience with some minor nitpicky issues here and there.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently the best game in the Fate series. Not a high bar to beat, but it does beat it well, and I recommend it for that if you are a fan of the Fate series or games with an anime aesthetic.The combat is a little clunky thanks to the lack of animation canceling into dodges, so you have to time against your own attack animations but, aside from that aspect, it is quite fluid, well-paced and at least offers invincibility-frames. The game itself isn't hard at all and, if you know what you're doing, becomes an avenue for power fantasy (at least in the normal difficulty, I haven't tried the highest yet).The story's engaging, and serviceable. For the most part, characters aside from the main two (who are lovable as heck) are not deeply fleshed out, but you get enough of a feel for them that you look forward to interacting more with your favorite characters whenever they come up into the story. The MC, in my opinion, is a Gary Sue who other non-villainous characters tend to immediately warm up to after a first encounter. In my view, that aspect does not fit the battle-royal nature of the competition underlying the story, but it is only a small gripe, however. Aside from those two faults, I'm enjoying the story and the cutscenes.Graphically, it's passable, looking as if it was developed primarily for the Switch. At the very least, any subpar PC should have no problems running this game at the highest settings.I have encountered 0 bugs or technical issues that negatively effect the game or serve to stall your progress or enjoyment of it. Though sporadic, graphical glitches do occur but offer nothing in the way of actually impeding your gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally done!!!!!! whew so first i will go ahead and say for my Musou fans this game has elements of Musou all in it but it is not the main focus of the game its much more smaller scale then what Musuo fans are used to. _childDocuments_.review: Surprisingly good, I'd recommend picking it up on sale. Combat is fun, there are 5 unique fighting styles Iori has access to as well as a variety of spells and servant skills. Certain boss fights can get tedious however due to ridiculous health bars combined with minuscule damage windows, but this is alleviated somewhat as you gain access to more sword styles, servants, and servant abilities. The gap closes a little bit when you unlock the final sword style, but combat is absolutely at its best when you're playing as any of the servants.

_childDocuments_.review: Only a few hours in, you can see this game as a culmination of Fate's history.  The starting story beats are very reminiscent of the OG visual novel while adding in new elements that serve both narrative and in-game purposes. Don't let the musou-like gameplay fool you, combat encounters can be challenging, especially servant fights when controlling Iori. Fans of the series will catch some references and important characters from other Fate franchises, especially FGO; as most of the "monsters" are FGO mobs and two of the titular character Musashi and Jeanne Alter both started as FGO originals. The composer borrowed from his other titles to remix various OST's giving them a new life to fit the Edo period vibes. From Gil's theme having a more lighthearted and comedic tone, to Musashi's and Tamamo's being remixed to fit the Edo period and the amazing remix of Blood Wind when Jalter shows up Keita Haga once again proves to be an amazing composer. Overall this is a quintessential Fate story that can serve as both a starting point and an extension for both new and old fans.

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent Fate spinoff for both fans and newcomers alike.The combat is super solid and a much better showing than Omega Force's other non-"actual Musou game" efforts like Persona 5 Strikers.The story is excellent, on par at least with most of the better Fate stories/scenarios/FGO chapters, but not quite on the level of the absolute best ones. This is partly because it's an action game though, and the game avoids any of the heavy narration or flowery prose that Sakurai's actually really good at in favor of not having the player spend too long a time between gameplay bits.Overall the presentation is really good too. The major fight cutscenes really hyped me up, and the characters are extremely expressive in their sprites (I especially love Saber and Musashi's expressions).The music is great too but it's Type Moon + Omega Force so that's basically a given.Overall a definite 9/10 and one of the best games I've played this year in a ridiculously strong year for video games.

If you like action RPGs with a heavy focus on story also a must buy.Edit.Having beat the game I want to add one thing real quick.This game has a "forced" 2nd play-through to get the full story.  But it really didn't and shouldn't have done that.  the cut-scenes/dialogue that is in the 2nd play-through as well as the digressions should've been in the first play-through.Honestly I was hoping for a big change in story but the 2nd play-through is basically the exact same story with missing dialogue/context added.

_childDocuments_.review: So I will begin this by saying that I am a big Fate fan. There are various styles of game play that is used so there isn't anything that becomes too boring. There is a great story and the graphics, art, and music are gorgeous.  This is also a good story for anyone who doesn't know the Fate universe well since they do explain everything pretty well. Now my only issue is that since I got the deluxe edition, I was hoping to have an art book and soundtrack as separate, downloadable items from the game that I could save on my computer. That is sadly not the case. I do love the music and I am not flipping through the art book just yet to avoid spoilers. This does present a problem for me since I paid extra for it and I was hoping to be able to have the soundtrack on my library to play as background music for other things. It is a great experience for those that have or have not experienced Fate. Just forewarn that the soundtrack and art book are within the game, so please keep that in mind when you contemplate your purchase. If this changes, then I will update this review.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll sum up my five problems with the game first before speaking of the positives. There is one fight in this game that just sucks. I won't go into detail but it pits you against two damned strong enemies that can one-tap you and your controls are not normal. Further you have to play through a bit to get back to this fight even if you retry it making the whole encounter annoying. _childDocuments_.review: EDIT: A year after release. Granblue Fantasy Relink was amazing, the Elden Ring Shadow of the Erdtree DLC was great. Stellar Blade on PS5 had some good gameplay. This is still one of the best ARPGs we've had in the last year. Bar has been getting set pretty low by other games. FF16, for example, is still the worst game I've ever played in my life. And I played Too Human. I've watched a ton of Fate anime, I've played some of the previous games like Fate/Extella and Fate/Extra, I enjoy myself some long winded story and action RPG gameplay. At the time of writing this, I'm only in Chapter 2, not sure how many chapters there are yet.This is the second best ARPG I've played this year in terms of combat, but it has the best story of any ARPG I've played this year so far. Voicing, world building, theme, character building, it all hits the marks that typically all Kinoko Nasu properties have. I love the aesthetic of having animated portraits for dialogue, and the game has voicing for basically everything. Upon thinking about it, I can't recall anything that doesn't have some voicing, but I think I'm just used to filling in the hypothetical blanks with voicing when it comes to Anime. What ARPG was better than this, this year? Stranger of Paradise, but for wholly different reasons. Strangers took a Final Fantasy paint job to a Soulslike game, and it was a match made in heaven. This game takes the similar Fate/Extella formula for the Warriors-style games and gives it a fresh coat of paint. No playing King of the Hill on large sprawling maps with thousands of enemies in giant armies. Just the main character fighting alongside his Servant, Saber, against 5-30 enemies at a time on a Chess/Checkers node control battlefield and engaging in battles from there.The game isn't all about combat though. Anyone that has played Persona will feel where this game lands. Combat is part of the equation, but so is roaming towns and talking to people, doing side missions for allied Servants that give backstory or just doing a mission that doesn't take itself too seriously. These side missions don't overstay their welcome either, something that some other AAA ARPGs this year could have seriously learned. If you like Fate, or Persona, or Warrior's style games, will you like this game? There's a good chance you'll enjoy it as much as I am. If you don't know what the hell Fate is, but enjoy some simple Warriors combat, will you still enjoy it? Probably! Fate is wonderful in that you don't need to know anything about any of the other dozens of properties to jump into it. This game is no exception. It goes for a bit of a slow burn and explains everything to you, but it never gives you more than you can handle, and doesn't leave you wanting for hours on end with no reward.If you don't like Fate or Warriors stuff? Well, seems kind of obvious at that point. It's more of the same. You may not like this. But it sure as hell won't be worse than FF16 was. This game is a major improvement over FF16 in literally every single way, and probably had 1/10th of the budget. And the regular version of the game is even cheaper too!Edit: I completed the game after doing a ton of the side content, and have found that New Game+ offers another game difficulty and even new activities for challenging content (Beyond the difficulty increase) like harder boss enemy kills. Looking forward to doing another full completion now. There is a skill curve to the combat by end of game, between Servant swaps and your own combos and the story between Iori and Musashi goes out on a good note. The only thing I'm wondering about is the access to one of the Rogue Servants, and a bunch of people seem to have issues recruiting them, since they have barely any overlap to your story progression. Hopefully this becomes more clear or easier.Edit2: I've done a nearly 100% full completion of the game for achievements. Cannot get the last 2 because I didn't get credit for the joke ending in the game. I've repeated all of that servant's digressions and the ending several times and still cannot get it. Stuck at 99% Logbook completion and 43/45 achievements. One for Logbook completion, one for full achievement completion.

_childDocuments_.review: The story takes place in 17th-century Japan during the Keian Uprising. You take the role of of Iori Miyamoto, disciple of the legendary Miyamoto Musashi. Iori earns his living by doing odd jobs, following his code of honour to keep the peace. After a strange mark appears on the back of one of his hands, the young man finds himself unwillingly drawn into the Waxing Moon Ritual. In a desperate situation, Iori manages to summon a Servant and confirm his participation in the Ritual as Master. Saber is summoned...For a newcomer to the Fate franchise, the beginning is usually difficult. Even though Fate has anime adaptations and one of the longest-running mobile games, it's still difficult to introduce a newcomer to the Fate Series without giving them a link to a 5k page wiki... Nevertheless, it was difficult before Fate/Samurai Remnant. The game gently introduces you to the Fate universe, explaining absolutely everything you need to know to fight effectively in a Holy Grail War. I was surprised at how simply and effectively the game explained what are relatively difficult concepts!Although Fate/Samurai Remnant is essentially an action-RPG, it offers a long, detailed and complete story, a quality that lives up to the standards of the Fate franchise. Veteran fans of the franchise will find all the ingredients of a good Type-Moon title here. The story explains every element and rule of a Holy Grail War in detail, ensuring that those unfamiliar with the franchise will be able to follow the story smoothly and easily. Once you've completed the game, you can start a new game to access an extended storyline, a modified ending and brand new scenes that give you even more information about the lore. A classic Type-Moon.Of course, I can't talk about Fate/Samurai Remnant without mentioning Saber. Ah, Saber... I've lost count of the number of times my quest told me to go right when Saber was on my left, gazing at a food stall... Probably one of the most endearing characters in the entire Fate series! The bond that develops between Iori and Saber is one of the highlights of the game. Little by little, Iori gets to know and understand Saber. In exchange, Saber will get used to Iori's calm and peaceful character, while trying to understand how Miyamoto Musashi's student sees the world... The other characters won't leave you unmoved either. You'll quickly feel a sense of friendship for the Rogue Servants, while surprising yourself with compassion for the other Master-Servant duo, who all have their own stories to tell. You'll also be given a few lessons in history and mythology to help you understand the "power" of the True Names of the Servants!In terms of Gameplay, it would be a bit reductive to say that this is a simple Musou. While Saber can wipe out weak enemies with a single blow, the bosses are... Much more difficult. If you want to understand why I thought first of a "inspired" Souls-like game, just play Iori and turn the difficulty up to the max... The boss stages will be a real challenge! The different styles of Iori's swords prevent repetition in battle and force you to rethink your strategy, as Iori adapts his style to his opponents in order to win. I particularly liked the stark difference in power between Iori and Saber. You feel all the weakness of a simple, brave human and the monstrous power of a true Heroic Spirit! This difference is also felt when Iori confronts a Servant. Without Saber's help, it's hard to imagine Musashi's adopted son winning... Each Servant has their own unique fighting style, so you'll enjoy trying them all!In conclusion, Fate/Samurai Remnant is an excellent introduction to the Fate Series. Beginners will discover all the basics of the universe while enjoying a story full of twists and turns and terribly engaging characters. As for confirmed fans, I'm not taking the slightest risk in saying that you'll find what you're looking for as a Fate series fan in this title! This new Type-Moon x Koei Tecmo game is an unforgettable Fate experience!

_childDocuments_.review: I am a huge Fate/ franchise fan. I was probably going to like this game regardless, so feel free to let that color everything else I have to say.I was immediately apprehensive when it was announced and in the trailer there was the Omega Force logo. Omega Force are excellent developers, but they live in their niche and thrive there. As great as Omega Force are at diversifying the gameplay in their licensed Warriors titles, it's already been done in the franchise with both Extella and Extella Link being musou games. Thankfully, they managed to find an excellent balance with what they know and new mechanics. Combos initially flow like those in a musou game, linear chains of light attacks followed with a heavy, but they inject a need to react and play off the opponents that is so often missing from their more typical fare.They also manage to make the player character feel strong and useful, while demonstrating the huge gulf that exists between Masters and Servants as far as their strength. You don't feel underpowered or useless, but you absolutely do need your Servant to survive. Enemies aren't like those in other Omega Force titles, they can take a beating and if you fail to stay on your toes, they will punish you and easily deplete your HP bar.Strictly viewing this as a Fate/ game, this is the best adaptation of a Holy Grail War in any non-Visual Novel game so far. It perfectly captures the delicate act of having to balance the facade of daily life while also uncovering the other Masters, preparing for nightfall when the veil of secrecy is easier to maintain and all out Servant vs Servant combat can really take place. As far as the story they do retread some well-worn story beats, borrowing from tropes established in more than a few Fate/ stories. It does make for an excellent introduction to the franchise for first timers though, and a entrenched fan will probably find it nostalgic. Omega Force and Koei Tecmo as a whole have really out done themselves with this release

_childDocuments_.review: Part Musou/Part ARPG... all FATE![-First impressions-] (No SpoiIers)If you're a fate veteran or new to the series, there's plenty to like here,It's a stand alone story, and explains the basics well, so no prior knowledge is needed.It has all the crazy over the top action you'd expect from the fate series, But with tons of options in combat, and without the repetitive zone capping of Fate/Extella!I have a quick comparison of Samurai vs Extella here: The mob count is SIGNIFICANTLY smaller than most other musou games, so it feels much less mindless,and there are plenty of options to mix up combat, so you won't be stuck spamming light and heavy attacks everywhere.The story is pretty interesting so far, and I'm enjoying the characters,There are plenty of RPG elements, you can upgrade your skills, weapons etc,And while it doesn't quite offer the expansive variety of some top teir ARPGs,Not the nonsensical drop in/out grindy excitement of a musou game...It manages to find a great balance between Flash and function, choices and carnage, power and plot. to offer a really fun and unique experience!It's not just fan service, and makes great strides over other musou/ARPG hybrids,But it's still a musou at heart, so some ARPG fans may still prefer a little more content in terms of side activities, and combat variety.In short, if you can't stand musou combat, (for more than just the lack of options/decision making), this won't change your mind.But if you're looking for a stylish hack and slash game that still contains substance, Or are a huge fan of the fate series, I'd say give this a shot!Code Provided by publisher, but I can say whatever I want :P (they just asked that I avoid spoiIers.)[Reuploaded, long story...]

name: Killer Frequency
detailed_description: The year is 1987, and as the clock strikes midnight in small-town Gallows Creek, USA, former big city radio DJ Forrest Nash is live on air in what will turn out to be the graveyard shift of a lifetime... In this horror comedy, you must solve puzzles to save callers from being hunted down by a mysterious killer. Where every call is life and death, can you save the inhabitants of Gallows Creek? Unique 1st person narrative: Step into the shoes of a late-night radio talk-show host – new in town and fallen from grace. The Police Chief is dead… so the townsfolk turn to you for help, as apparently you, Forest Nash are the only person in town who can run a phone line. Real-time decisions and puzzle solving: Use branching dialogues to interact with a variety of eccentric small-town personalities including potential victims and suspects. Explore your surroundings, gather clues, make decisions, solve satisfying riddles, and try to help each of your callers survive the night. Retro Slasher setting: Jump back in time to 1987 with this slasher inspired puzzler – explore an authentically detailed radio station and interact with dozens of physics-based objects straight from a bygone era, including a working cassette and record player. With a fully voiced cast and a killer original soundtrack of 80's inspired tunes from rock classics to synthwave!

_childDocuments_.review: My favorite game I've played this year. The game looks great and plays great. The puzzles and dialogue trees are perfect for casual and fun game-play, especially since you can save and pick up where you left off at any time (while still having incredibly high stakes involved to make you feel the consequences if you screw up).  The game also has a great atmosphere, while staying away from the excessive gore or jumpscares that keep me from playing most horror games.However, the best part about this game is definitely the soundtrack. It has amazing original songs that you get to play throughout the night (as you are a radio host) and there is great variety in the music. I find myself listening to the soundtrack a lot even outside the game.The game is a bit on the short side (3.5 to 4 hours, depending on how fast you solve the puzzles) but I didn't mind, since your first play-through will probably leave you wanting to run through it again to save everyone. If you can grab it on sale it is definitely worth it. Simply amazing game.

_childDocuments_.review: Good overall, but has some sour spots. I'll be upfront in saying I'd call it a 7/10 or so. The dialogue is good when it's on, and painful when it's not. Ponty's Pizza being a reference to Pontypool, which this game takes tons of inspiration from, alongside Scream 2, is fun, but I don't want to listen to the guy go on and on and on when I already get the deal and want to hang up on him. Humor is subjective, but it would've been funny as hell to just cut him off instead of listening to Forrest and Peggy buy into his stupid antics for the 4th time. Line delivery is mostly fine, but again, when it's off it's seriously off. The only time Forrest shows all that much emotion is yelling at Ponty to stop trying to get free advertising. It's plodding and while it's well-acted, it sounds like a well-acted diction class more than anything.The gameplay just isn't there, and it's not very fun. I busied myself during some breaks by cleaning up the office, and that was more fun than many of the puzzles. It's also annoyingly easy to find the stuff you need way before you need it, thus allowing you to skip the process of finding it at the intended time...and thus missing a lot of the clues left for you. SPOILERS past this point: The most egregious of these is when Roller Ricky's life is on the line, the only victim I lost. In retrospect, the clues were all there to realize something wasn't right, but I'd found the code book half an hour beforehand and thought I had it all figured out. It's one part clever puzzle trickery, one part leave your clues aside until their proper time to allow people to put the pieces together when the information is fresh.Other miscellaneous issues: I know it might be a bit much to expect, but there's absolutely no replay value, and this game costs $25. In essence, it's asking $5/hr and for what's on offer, with absolutely no reason to go through it again short of seeing different endings to calls or the game, or slightly different dialogue you could just as easily look up on YouTube, it's probably not worth it. Going through the puzzles in the game, I was excited to see the different variations. Would the "next target" puzzle be Kim or Ant or Rebecca this time? Would I need to send a different fast food place to the frat to save Virginia? Would the killer search different places in Russell's office? Etc. To see there was nothing at all was seriously disappointing. The game also never places you in actual danger, aside from the very end, and that's purely tied to saving [x] callers and looking at the extremely obvious birthday card. Once I cottoned on to the fake tension, it sucked the air out of the room and made me never fear turning another corner again, even despite the tense, scary music trying to make me think otherwise. Hell, if it had lowered my guard just to genuinely surprise me and force me into a situation where I was being hunted, I would've loved that. As well, there were wasted opportunities with what few mechanics there were, especially timed choices (there are maybe a few that really matter, most just let the story continue) and situations where it's better to say nothing (I counted one that actually saved someone's life, and even it was misleading, as you hear rustling and a door closing, but if you wait until the very end, and still pick an option, he dies despite sounding like he's hidden). So ultimately, the game hinges entirely on its story, dialogue and whether you care about these characters, and little else.Luckily, where the game shines is its aesthetic, atmosphere and the strength of its characters. Some of them are seriously annoying, and I wasn't sad to see Jimmy die, but for the most part, I bought in and was invested in helping them survive the night, so it succeeded in that regard. These are dumb. small-town folks, and grating personality traits aside I really wanted to help them. It just might have been more compelling if Forrest wasn't constantly doing his radio man patter. The game takes you through a classic 80s neon-bathed murder mystery slasher flick. It's a shame so much of it really is just spent watching with no personal dread.On the whole, I recommend it on sale, unless you love this kind of experience that much.

_childDocuments_.review: Killer Frequency has a fantastic premise, but fails to execute in some keys areas that really drag the overall experience down. Because of that, I can't recommend it.I'm not going to go over every aspect of this game because there are plenty of reviews that already cover that information. I mostly want to focus on the voice acting and writing, which I think are the weakest part of this entire experience, and because they are such a big part of that experience, it really spoils the whole thing.You play as Forrest and you'll spend a lot of time listening to him attempt to talk to people, but it feels as if he has never spoken to another human being before. His tone is all over the place. Sometimes he'll go from being somber in one sentence, to then awkwardly yelling (in a cheering way) in the next sentence. It feels so jarring and out of place. Even when it's a serious conversation, it often feels almost too serious. This is a hard issue to explain, but as an example, think about how you would deliver the line "I'm so sorry." to a close friend who just lost their job, versus that same friend who just lost their spouse. You obviously understand the difference, but Forrest does not. His delivery is so sporadic and rarely in line with what is happening in the current conversation. And it's not just Forrest's voice acting that's off; everyone's lines sound off to some extent. It feels like all the voice actors were on different pages, with a totally different understanding of what the goal of the writing was trying to achieve in a certain scene. The trick of good voice recording and sound design is to make the player believe that the people talking to each other are actually in the same room, even though their lines were all recorded separately (in most cases). However, it's very, very obvious that everyone's lines were recorded separately, and with what seems like very little direction. I'm not sure if this is a failure of the voice actors, or just poor writing/direction, but it kills the vibe of a game and makes conversations something that I wish I could just read through or even skip at times. As for the writing, it doesn't help the situation. It's pretty weak overall. I'm not expecting this to be Disco Elysium, but the written dialogue isn't great to begin with. Even if you removed the voice acting, you'd probably fall asleep trying to make it through these drawn out, tensionless conversations. By the time I reached the ending, I didn't care much to find out the story of the killer behind it all, and even when I did, it was as boring as every other conversation.There are other aspects of the game which are fine -- the music, exploring the radio station, light puzzles -- but those aspects aren't big enough or good enough to warrant your money or time. This is a game you buy specifically for a good story and dialogue, but it fails on both accounts. So, save your money and hope someone else takes a stab at this premise and does a better job.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ (5/5)Killer Frequency is a masterclass in blending suspense, humor, and atmospheric storytelling. The game takes players into a uniquely thrilling experience, immersing them as a radio DJ in the heart of a small town facing a series of chilling events. From the start, *Killer Frequency* hooks you with its clever, interactive gameplay mechanics, effectively integrating puzzle-solving elements with an engaging narrative that keeps you on edge.The voice acting is stellar, bringing depth and authenticity to each character, while the sound design enhances the tension, turning the crackle of the radio and distant sounds into pulse-raising cues. The setting feels meticulously crafted; it’s not just a backdrop but a character in itself, with each interaction adding layers to the story.What truly sets *Killer Frequency* apart is its ability to keep players invested in every decision. The interactive radio segments are brilliantly implemented, giving you the feel of a live broadcast where every choice matters. This game doesn't just provide scares—it gives players a sense of agency and responsibility, raising the stakes with every call that comes in.  Overall, Killer Frequency is a polished, unique experience that elevates the horror genre. It’s a must-play for fans of suspenseful storytelling and interactive adventures, promising hours of tense, satisfying gameplay.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an excellent narrative and really fun mechanics. Your choices make a difference on the outcomes of the game, but you don't have any real danger to yourself in the radio station booth. Killer Frequency combines witty humor with an excellent 80s-style soundtrack into a cheesy retro slasher story reminiscient of the original Scream, Halloween, and other movies from that time.Killer Frequency is relatively short, with my first playthrough only taking around five hours, but I considered the money well-spent. I've since played through it a couple more times to get the rest of the achievements and personally have zero regrets on the $25 spent. If price point is an issue, I would wait until it goes on sale, because it DOES go on sale for $10 relatively often. It IS incredibly well made, I didn't experience any bugs, so at least it's very polished. Overall I give this game an 8.5/10, with the only real downsides being the price point and the brevity.

_childDocuments_.review: What happens if you stick an egomaniac behind a microphone and give him a killer running around town to square off with? That is the fundamental question asked in Killer Frequency.Kidding, but the main character is an overwhelming douche, which is fitting, honestly. in KF you play as Forrest Nash, former nationally syndicated radio host and now host of 189.16 The Scream, a late night call in show with 30-ish affectionate listeners. Right off the bat the game throws you in the deep end in a good way, setting up the premise believably *enough* that you are now going to be a 911 operator for the town until backup can arrive. You get to run around the radio station looking for anything to help the ensuing callers escape the Whistling Man's knife, and honestly, there's actually quite a few fun puzzles to solve. It does boil down to active listening more often than not and then responding on a timer, but I have problems paying attention to... everything? So at one point if I stopped listening for a little bit, I usually missed important information and ending up getting someone shanked. I uh... I got a lot of people shanked.The story is interesting enough for the time you'll spend experiencing it, but one of the huge highlights in KF is the voice acting. I am so glad that good voice acting is becoming more commonplace because ho-ly sh*t it makes a difference. The dialogue is decent but the delivery brings it home.Now, there are some issues, namely that you are very much on rails for most of the game. Thats not a huge problem if you know what to expect, but it is something worth mentioning because in the marketing it shows you running all over the radio station all the time. Typically the game locks you into the booth until you have to go and find something to help the current caller, so do with that what you will. That being said, the game really does allow for you to mess around with most of the things in the environment. You can toss paper balls into the basket across the room while people are getting stabbed, play stupid soundboard noises while they're trying to hide, and while the game doesn't really penalize you for doing this which would have been nice, I still appreciate that they allow you to do it at all.There's more to be said but I made a Youtube video covering any other points I had if you're interested: And I review lots of games both indie like this and not on my curator page, so drop a follow there if you wanna have my reviews pop up for ya if I've done one for a game already. Thanks for reading.

The 'puzzles' are a tad easy and the dialogue, while overall enjoyable and well voiced, does get a bit tedious at times, especially since it is completely impossible to skip or accelerate it. So, this is not a game for the ADHD types; or just do what I did and have a second screen to browse while you listen to the delivery.(Update): It's been over a month since I finished this little gem, and I still occasionally think about it. It does such a nice job of conveying the "1980s small-town radio host, holed up while scary stuff stalks the town" vibe. A very cozy game indeed. If anyone ever makes a similar themed game, with the same style of music and art-style and vibe, but just makes the puzzles 10x more difficult and involved and perhaps adds some more horror elements - well, then that would be a true 10/10 game my dear friends. /Pray There's just something about the template they have here that makes it very cutesy and cozy to melt your reality into. If you like this sort of 'style' check this game out and let your imagination fill in the gaps.

_childDocuments_.review: Killer Frequency is a surprisingly very good game for its genre.The most important parts, the story and gameplay are good. _childDocuments_.review: If you are expecting a "realistic" story, do not indulge.Set in 1987, you play as Forrest, a radio show host recently demoted to a local radio in a small town, and in your first night you basically become the 911 operator after the sheriff is murdered. There’s a serial killer on the loose.So, whenever any of the locals call 911, they are routed to you, and it becomes your job to guide them to safety by telling them what to do.The premise sounds like it could be fun, but it gets old pretty fast… both in terms of gameplay and credibility.As for gameplay, it’s a dialog simulator slash fetch game. Find this “thing” that has the exact information that you need, give the right answers. In terms of the story, there’s a lot of plot holes and “this makes no sense” moments.The game just takes too many licenses that break immersion or credibility. Whether because potential victims can call you from a corn maze or from 4 different offices while the killer is in the same building or because you can take 30 minutes to solve something that seems to be urgent.And the thing is, everyone with a radio can tune in and hear whatever you discuss on the phone line while the killer is on the loose… so, guiding a person through a building while the murderer is in the same place becomes pretty lame, because whatever you are telling them to do, the murderer could just be listening.Anyway, to get the “good ending” and "win", you have to piece together this intricate vengeance story behind the murderer's motive, but I didn't really bother with it. The game expects you to become interested enough to do it, and I think that's expecting too much.At times it tries to be funny, and at times it tries to be more serious, but it ends up failing at both, or at least that is my opinion. I’d say it's a rather forgettable experience.If you are after a narrative experience that involves radio talk, go play Firewatch. It is going to be more fun.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like text-based, narrative-driven games, definitely give Killer Frequency a try!
