_childDocuments_.review: I am giving this game a positive review really for anyone who is just getting into the series rather than for those people who have been playing the series for years and as an overall game - yes - it is good. But as an improvement worth £30 on FM22.........err.........no.There's a fair bit of moaning as I do agree with a lot of the content in the negative reviews that there has been very little added. If you had a product selling 1000000 copies at £30 pounds a pop (30mil from sales) then your fan-base is quite rightly expecting clear progress from year to year - if you can't manage that - release it every two to three years and just patch over the 48/36 months and don't get them to spend!As a bit of background. I have watched (live) over 1200 games of football ranging from mainly Prem level and Champ level with a lot of games also being viewed at Conference levels and also Regionals. I have also accumulated over ~2500hrs of gameplay over FM20-22. I will first start off by saying that I consider (unike many others - and I'm not saying I'm right and they're wrong by the way) the match engine to be mere window dressing to the game in all honesty, and something where SI will probably hit a ceiling real soon unless they want to diminish other functionalities in the game. So I will start there!Match Engine: Yes. There have been improvements to this and you can never really judge it in the first months anyway as we all know there are issues and that it will be patched to death to solve these. In all honesty, the match engine is okay and is a lot more realistic in terms of movement, passing and especially the goalkeeping than it ever has been. I personally still have roll your eyes moments at some of the defending which is the real oddity, as across most divisions in England, the standards in defending really only differ in ball-playing ability. The positioning and physicality of defenders across the leagues is actually fairly close and in fact you could argue the "physicals" of non-league defenders are better. The real differentiation in the match engine should have come in some "poorer" forward players not being able to hit a barn door with a huge stick, and 90% of free-kicks either hit the wall or sailing wide and high rather than pin-point hitting the top corner. But, it is what it is and at the end of the day is a performance based on the stats the game has. But.........better than previous iterations in terms of realism.Tactics: To be honest, I think this is a good part of the game although you could always argue that it could be more detailed in terms of fine detail. E.g. would it be possible to say where you wanted individual players on the pitch to be when the ball was in a certain position - but I think this is maybe going a bit too far in all honesty. I think there is more than enough variation here what with the player roles and how competent they are in these so for me - I think this is any area that each year will only undergo minor refinement.Interactions and management: Sigh..........right.........here comes my real moan. Okay........so I make life difficult for myself. I couldn't care less about all these wonder-kids and elite level players. I manage with settings as Sunday league footballer with no coaching badges with all attributes not visible, have DoF buying players. (I'm forcing myself to be as real life as possible and also forcing myself to use the data hub as much as possible....which I do think is good)1) Pre-match conferences - Scrap them or make the comments have greater impact; so players like me don't just click the second one on the left. What is my manager personality? I am brusque like Mourinho or Van Gaal? Am I a nice guy who despite having a poor win % - I can do no wrong like Martinez and good old Gareth? No jeopardy or real outcome in these interviews - same with the press so why bother?2) Player interactions. I get SI for wanting to stop players who are struggling from praising their players all the time to get the morale up, but come on guys - can we be realistic here? I speak to football players (Isthmian level) who play and they all agree that even if you do have a manager who "praises"all the time, they take it with a pinch of salt but it won't actually harm morale!! In this game I praised a CD for 7.6 and a 7.7 performance two games in a row and after the second bit of praise he threw his toys out of the pram with a massive decrease on morale. However, the juxtaposition on this is that they never react badly to you praising their conduct when you never get any feedback on the game about said conduct (this could be expanded far more and would give players a much better idea on certain attributes too - such as not turning up to a community event, being praised by a local charity for donations, previous tweets coming up, etc, etc, etc). I have no clue about their conduct really but I know I can give them all a boost............urghhh. Either improve or get rid. Team meetings...........I almost got sacked cos my team wanted to know why I wouldn't let a player leave yet its the DoF in my save that deals with all that. Absolutely no option for me to respond in that way or go.....yeah I know guys........it was bad idea but not my fault........nope they all blamed me whilst my DoF was down his local club having a cigar and brandy.........sigh3) Shouts...........utterly pointless. Just get rid4) Board and Club vision stuff: Right. I do like the fan confidence idea and think this is a good thing that although embryonic in its development could have a future. But.......here comes my moan again. In order to make the game "tougher" they have taken a broad brush stroke approach to how EVERY board will look at performance. I agree. If you've been given a three year contract at a PL club and you look like you might get relegated then we all know its "bye bye". However......having had some interactions with non-league directors, some clubs at Conf regional level and national level are quite happy with keeping the manager as long as they stay in the div. What they certainly don't do is sack managers after 8 games, a month, half a season - even with a 40% win ratio. E.g. Got sacked at Concord after a few games even though they have a track record of liking managers there for the long term and give them time (Cowley brothers were here about 7 years!). I think this is lazy in an effort to add jeopardy to the game......but it is taking away the realism.Transfers: Like the Transfer Centre but have very little to do with these as I operate under a DoF model where they do all the recruiting/selling. One thing I think that could be improved is Agent approaches so that a player with say 10 months on their contract is willing for their player to sign a pre-contract with you behind their clubs back.......etc. I do think agent interactions being brought into the game in FM22 was a good thing and adds another layer of depth but this could be developed a lot more.Other areas:1) Loan manager feedback could be improved and to be fair there has been a bit more info regarding this. Interactions here with opposition managers is generally poor. They moan......you say you don't have a choice.......they go okay then.......they come back in two weeks..........rinse and repeat.2) Technical director should report back 6 monthly on staff performance, and suggested actions. Rather than just a.......Bob should go on a management course or........Dave is struggling on his course........add some info like........therefore we are not looking to extend his contract. You know........add little nuances3) Half time team talks - whats the point with the range of options you have? Window dressing4) New cup draws - ooo..look at all the pretty colours.....jeez...Overall: A good game but not enough development in the key, underlying areas that run the game. And I  didn't even get onto attributes..(ran out of space)

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Woodwoork Manager 2023.It's so easy to write Football Manger reviews. Copy/paste one from the previous version, and you're done. There are no major changes for years, and it's unlikely they'll ever be.No multi-monitor support (no one wants to see a match on a separate screen, as SI believes). No female football, only prostate cancer ads. No possibility to create sandboxed leagues not dependent on the default game DB. I won the Champions League countless times, played everywhere on Earth, and I'm sick of it to death. I want to play some ancient Greece or Mars league, for example. Without agents and transfers. Why not?But all we get is more and more micro-management. In the 2000s, a season per weekend in a relaxed mode was a norm. Or even in one day if you're dedicated enough. Now it's not. Be prepared for 4-7 full-time (not paid!) days to babysit your players, handle all that inbox spam, and please agents. And if you decide to handle the media yourself...Is there anyone who uses those "pat on the head" buttons for interactions? I never did. What's the point? Is it trendy? Emotional? Friendly? Using communication skills? For me, it's just a time waste and not a real improvement.Since the beginning, Football Manager had three main plagues: woodwork, pep-talk goals, and goal droughts.I'm happy to see that pep goals (those scored between 46 and 50 min after the opponent manager yelled at the team) are somewhat better now and closer to realism. In the earlier versions, sometimes it was better NOT to score in the first half to improve your chances of winning. I hope they'll not "fix it back" in the next release.Goal droughts, though, are worse. I never had all four strikers at the same time on the goal drought before. And 10 droughts per season is too much unrealistic if you ask me.Woodwork. At some point, it was that bad, so SI even removed this stat from the game. Later they returned it, but it's hidden by default. The average increased from 1.8 in the previous version to 2.7(!) in the current. Also, I saw 5 woodworks in one game for the first time (for my team only). If you strive for realism, it should never happen. Or call the game "No Match Without Woodwork", someone will buy it for sure.The match engine is pretty good (as of 23.4-23.5), except for those problems (features?) listed above. My tactic perfected many years ago still works with minor adjustments. That means nothing serious was broken.Finances are a bit crazy. A decent striker demands 400-500k per week. The asking price for a good player is in the range of 200-300M. Come on. There is some inflation in the football world, but not that much.I didn't encounter any serious bug (probably, 'cause I started to play with 23.4 this year), but one minor issue is pretty annoying. Every time you open tactics during the match, the sort order of players is randomly messed up. Fix it, SI. It's infuriating.Well, I could've written most of this for any previous version. And, probably, it'll be valid for a few future versions, at least. In the end, you pay every year for the updated database and some (unneeded) micromanagement features.And yes, after all those whinings, I still recommend Football Manager. There are no alternatives, it's fun (sometimes), it's annoying (sometimes), and it's the best value for the money compared to those 14 hours of gameplay games.And, finally, a piece of useful advice you'll never find at any FM site: NEVER EVER make any promise. Your targets will find a way to blame you (maybe it's a bug or just human nature).Have fun!

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DRIf you play FM a lot - its worth getting (FM continues to be one of the best value games out there), but if you only get <100 hours a year out of the game, don't bother. It is a very small change to FM 22, and half of the new features are poorly implemented/don't add anything. If they work at all.If you haven't bought an FM since 2019, then this will be a nice upgrade.---OK, So it's FM, you will get your money's worth. But FM23 is not a good vintage. I have given it a thumbs up - because of the value it offers, but it is a very reluctant thumbs up.I got over 1000 hours out of FM 22, and felt that was a poor year. Initial reaction (30 hours of beta) is this year is worse still (by worse i mean fewer changes and less improvements on the previous years).Some of the new features are nice , i like the fan info/expectations, i quite like the end of season manager timeline (which i wasn't expecting to), but neither of these are game changing. However, that's about where the good ends for the new features.The scouting changes are clunky, and make it feel more awkward to set up (and also don't work some of the time, but i will put this down to actual bugs in the beta, rather than design, and hope i am right). Also the old system still is there for some competitions for some reason, just to add to the confusion.The squad planner is a good idea, but poorly implemented (and the layout for it is god awful - hopefully skins will help here). I keep just going back to the squad depth view as used in previous version, only it now takes me 3 more clicks to get there from my squad page.Player traits are nearly impossible to see anymore, because SI choose to put them in the world's smallest box on the player screen for some reason - again skins may come to the rescue here.In game changes/ match engine, improvements are noticeable, but small (you will loose the ball in midfield more often, and the AI won't wait until the 72nd minute to change their tactic against you any more), but overall feels very similar to FM22. I heard a lot about the game being harder - its not. As always with FM (and i don't say this as a bad thing) difficulty is down to the team you choose/ restrictions you give yourself.For a game i know i will still play ~1000 hours of, i am disappointed. I knew the changes were small from the feature videos/release notes etc, however even those "new" features they have introduced in FM 23 are either poorly done and/or not very impactful on the game itself.I understand why FM 21/22 were weak years, but i had hoped they would get their act together for FM23. However i was wrong,As always, FM is fantastic value - it offers hundred of hours of replayability and is one of my favourite games, but this year really is just a glorified database update.

_childDocuments_.review: Football Manager, the game that makes you question your life choices and wonder if you should've pursued a career in sports management instead of whatever it is you're currently doing. It's like having a part-time job, but instead of a paycheck, you get the satisfaction of guiding your virtual team to glory. And by glory, I mean avoiding relegation.The game starts innocently enough, with you choosing your favorite team, or perhaps a struggling lower league side that you hope to take to the Premier League. You'll find yourself drawn into the world of tactics, transfers, and temperamental players faster than you can say "sacked in the morning."Your first task is to figure out the tactics, and this is where you realize that the beautiful game is also the most complicated. It's like trying to solve a Rubik's Cube while blindfolded and wearing oven mitts. You'll mess around with formations, roles, and instructions, hoping to stumble upon that magical combination that turns your bunch of misfits into a winning machine.And then there are the transfers. You'll spend more time negotiating contracts and scouting potential players than you'll care to admit. You'll have a notebook filled with wonderkids from obscure countries and a growing disdain for agents who think they can demand a private jet for their client.The match days are where the real stress sets in. You'll watch the games unfold with bated breath, hoping that your tactical genius pays off. When things go well, you'll feel like a footballing genius. But when your star striker misses an open goal for the tenth time, you'll question why you ever decided to manage a football club in the first place.The press conferences and player interactions are where you'll hone your skills in diplomacy. One wrong word, and you could have a mutiny on your hands. Praise your players too much, and their heads will swell faster than a hot air balloon. Criticize them, and you'll have a full-blown crisis on your hands. It's like juggling fragile egos while walking on a tightrope.But despite all the stress and frustration, there's something undeniably addictive about Football Manager. The thrill of finding that hidden gem of a player, the satisfaction of getting a lower league team promoted, and the heartache of a last-minute defeat in the cup final – it's all part of the rollercoaster that is football management.In conclusion, Football Manager is not just a game; it's a way of life. It's a test of your tactical prowess, your negotiating skills, and your ability to handle pressure. It's the only game where you can be simultaneously adored and vilified by virtual fans, where you can achieve greatness or experience heartbreak, all from the comfort of your computer. So, if you've ever dreamed of being the next Sir Alex Ferguson or Arsène Wenger, here's your chance. Just don't forget to save before that crucial Champions League final.

_childDocuments_.review: Football Manager 2023 (FM 2023) continues to be what it has been for the past 2-3 years - a game that holds true to its roots. While the absence of major changes might leave some longing for innovation, I can't help but appreciate its consistency. This game has managed to maintain its essence, and that's precisely why it remains my absolute favorite.Sure, one could argue that a lack of significant alterations might lead to stagnation, but there's a certain comfort in knowing that FM 2023 offers the familiar experience that many of us have grown to love. The tried-and-true mechanics, the intricate tactics, and the nail-biting matches all come together to provide the engaging football management simulation that fans have come to expect.It's like returning to a well-worn, beloved stadium where every corner and every roar from the crowd feels like home. FM 2023's steadfast dedication to its core gameplay ensures that players can dive right into the action without a steep learning curve. It's this accessibility that makes it a great entry point for newcomers while still catering to the tactical minds who revel in its intricacies.While a breath of fresh air in terms of new features would undoubtedly be invigorating, there's something oddly comforting about knowing that FM 2023 is a dependable constant in an ever-changing gaming landscape. It's not just a game; it's a tradition, a ritual that fans like me eagerly partake in year after year.In the end, Football Manager 2023 might not be a revolution, but it certainly is an affirmation of its own legacy. Its commitment to authenticity, strategy, and the love of the beautiful game makes it a standout in a sea of flashy releases. So, as I guide my virtual team through wins and losses, I can't help but feel grateful for FM 2023's unwavering dedication to being exactly what it is - a game that captures the essence of football management in its purest form.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Football Manager, you'll like this. The almost meme worthy comment of a glorified spreadsheet is somewhat true, as the game is a lot of number and statistics. But that is part of the core of the game and has been for 30 years or so.It's the best football manager game out there, and it's not even close.The match engine is better than previous versions.Updated squads and players.People, clubs, and leagues are close to real life and it's very impressive how detailed it is.Various tactical setups works and the old 4-2-3-1 gegenpress is no longer the only viable setup.Various general improvements and QoL stuff.The graphical engine is still lacking behind. Although news of big changes are coming in a future version, it's not that great here. Of course, not everyone cares about the graphical side of things, and 2D is still an option.AI squad building is still not good enough. It's been improved from earlier versions, but the AI squads are still unbalanced and the longer into a save it goes, the more obvious it is.Some of the new features are underwhealming.The game lacks a bit of polish in general. As the devs have said themselves, they missed a few deadlines with this game, so there are issues with a few things.As I've played thousands of hours of the series and most versions since the early 90s, I do consider myself quite well versed in the franchise, and it's still the game I spend most time on. And I really enjoy the game every year, there are still issues with it. With news of FM24 being a "love letter to the fans" and FM25 bringin the Unity engine for matches, I have hopes for the future of the series. And while FM23 has it's issues, I still think it's the best version of Football Manager yet.

_childDocuments_.review: For those who buy every edition and put in hundreds if not thousands of hours you are going to find this one of the weakest FMs in recent memory. Especially if you are more of a sim or comp highlights only sort of manager who tries to go 10+ years into a save. This is because the only area of the game that has actually seen any significant improvement is the match engine. Games are much more chaotic in midfield; possession turns over more frequently, players take heavier and worse touches, defenders are better at compressing space and nullifying attacks. As such, more defensive tactics are actually viable this year. Although, the 4-2-3-1 gegenpress is still fairly meta. Overall, the match engine provides a more fluid, realistic and dynamic replication of football than previous FMs. But, if you are the type of player to plug and play (or sim) your gegenpress tactic, all these improvements to the match engine are not very noticeable. Away from the match engine improvements, the licencing for UEFA club competitions is nice, but nothing that a real name fix+logo pack couldn't already add to prior games. The improvements to scouting and recruitment are nice and make it easier and less tedious to set up your scouts to find that next batch of wonderkids... and now I'm seriously struggling to think of any noticeable improvements. - Player interactions are still tedious button mashing (once you know what response works 95% of the time you just button mash through the screens).- Press conferences are still best left to you assman and serve no apparent purpose.- The new squad planner screen does nothing to impact gameplay: the list is purely for you to 'organise' your team by ranking players... This does nothing for me as I assess my starting XI + bench in the old squad view using ability/potential, match ratings/form, fitness/injuries and morale/happiness, which influences my thinking week to week.- International football is still dull and unchanged... with a winter WC round the corner this is a massive PR missed opportunity for SI.- Set pieces are still annoying to set up and still require constant tweaking to stop them breaking mid match (why can we still not set them up based on players rather than position?)- ps2 era graphics and horrific newgen faces remain... it is actually embarrassing how bad the game can look at times. Whilst FM22 was a big improvement to 21, 23 feels more like a minor update. Definitely not worth the money if you have last years version.

_childDocuments_.review: For those who are familiar with Football Manager and simply wish to know if the upgrade is worth it, I personally would say "yes". The majority of the improvements have come in the match engine. The CPU-controlled managers are more responsive, faster to react to problems and when the reaction comes, it's often effective. What I have noticed is that players are in two camps regarding the higher difficulty. I am a member of Camp A, where if you previously knew of a tactical setup that the CPU simply did not know how to counter, then the people in this camp should definitely find the game far more difficult to achieve the same insane records they could strike up in older games. Camp B are the guys who did not know of these exploits, perhaps running a standard 442/424, not really messing around with individual instructions, and just playing the game on the strength of the players in their team. These people may find not much has changed in the difficulty department, since for them, those exploits were never something they used or knew about, so they wouldn't be seeing large drops in points season by season in the new version.Some people in Camp A actually WANT the game to be much easier, less stressful, they want to just have a Football Management power fantasy. There is nothing wrong with that at all, but you might want to not bother buying this game if this sounds like you. Everyone else, if you never knew of the sorts of exploits that would allow you to put together runs of 200 games without defeat, or if you like the idea of the game being a little more challenging and better reflecting reality, then this would be a worthy little time-sink.                                                                                                                                        For those who don't know what this game is, it is one of the longest-running, most-successful game franchises of any genre in the history of gaming. Football Manager is not a direct competitor to FIFA or Pro Evolution Soccer, rather it runs parallel in the same sort of way iRacing runs parallel to something like Forza Horizon. FM is very 'spreadsheety', you are encouraged to spend hours pouring over the finest-details of the statistics available to you in the name of extracting a extra 0.1% of performance out of your team. You can take over any club (or national team) in one of dozens of leagues from around the world, including the usual places such as the English Premier League and it's associate pyramid right down to the 6th tier, Spain, Italy, Germany and France, but also many smaller European league pyramids, and the league systems of countries elsewhere in the world ranging from MLS in the US, the major South and Central American leagues, Asia, Australia, South Africa and more. You can increase this to hundreds of national pyramids with mods. Take your tiny club from San Marino to glory in the Champion's League. Go be the manager of some malnourished North Korean village club. Other mods can introduce special situations: put the two Glasgow giants of Scottish football in the English pyramid and see how they both do. You could even download databases of players from bygone eras of the sport, playing for the clubs as they did back in the 70s, 80's, 90's or 2000's, with real-life youngsters coming through just like, how and where they did IRL.FM covers, in great detail, every painstaking element of Football Management, allowing you to prove that you do indeed know better than your favourite club's real life manager, putting all those theories you discussed with your pals down the pub to the test, and constantly evolving, forcing you to evolve your ideas along with it. You are going to have to test your mettle against intelligent AI opponents, their managers employing endless arrays of methods to get one over on you, and the further up the pyramids you climb, the more fiendish your opponents become. And it's not just on the field you have to win, the game often kicks off before the actual day of the game, in the media, with you and the other team's manager playing mind-games. Will you be a wily, old fox like Alex Ferguson or an emotional, somewhat naive but very inspiring Kevin Keegan type? You will watch the games and look for patterns in the play, listen to advice from your assistant, read the commentary for clues as to what kinds of changes you might make tactically in order to better your odds of winning. You will train the lads, selecting all kinds of different training modules to buff their skills over time, changing your bunch of amateurish hoofball-merchants into a proper team of silky tiki-taka specialists even Pep Guardiola would be jealous of...or turn them into the next Wimbledon Crazy Gang, or Mourinho Park-The-Bus merchants. You will spend months putting together shortlists of potential new signings, pouring over each candidate, sleuthing into every single aspect of their abilities, personalities, relationships, their tendencies, ambitions and professionalism (or lack of) in order to come up with the best possible signings come the transfer window. You will be keep tabs on who the referee is for you upcoming game so that you are not blindsided by his tendencies, such as handing out yellow and red cards like sweeties. You will keep an eye on the weather, and learn that depending on what time of year it is will have a big effect on certain players, as well as what sort of playing style you might employ, for example, in a Scottish winter with the field all cut to shreds, that nice passing game that worked so well for you when the season started in late July/early August suddenly isn't working so well, you will find you need to adapt tactically to such changing conditions. You'll request the board give you funds to extend scouting ranges, increase the stadium capacity (according to what kinds of crowds you can realistically expect to attract based on city size, club size and reputation, even things such as how working class the people in the town tend to be and what kind of spare income they might have for watching football), or move stadium entirely. You may ask your board to open up a partnership with another club in order to have a place to easily send promising youngsters on loan or to open a channel into a country your club never had a presence in before either to increase your merchandising revenue, or simply gain a better scouting knowledge of that country by sharing scouting knowledge with the club you're partnering with. FM is about as deep a simulation of it's subject matter as there is in the gaming world. There are people been playing this series since the early 90s, still learning new things to this day. If you are looking for a quick kickabout, FM is not for you; This game is as deep as it gets and demands you throw yourself willingly into it's finer points. If you think you can make it through the very difficult learning-curve at the beginning of your Football Manager journey, what you will find is the ultimate football simulation. While it lacks the flashy graphics seen in the likes of FIFA, it makes up for this in it's depth as well as it's ability to keep you playing "just one more match before bed".Start playing this game and you, too, may lose your wife, children, family, dog, house, car, job, self-respect and life-savings. But hey, as long as the boys can manage to make the playoffs this year it'll all be worth it. I just need someone who can ping the ball into the box for the big man to get his head on and we'll dominate this league...Oh, sorry. I'm just saying that's all. I'm not talking about myself or anything.

_childDocuments_.review: FM23 continues the long string of minimally-updated annual releases from SI, with the now-typical mostly-cosmetic, mostly-inconveniencing changes that you've come to know and love. BUT... it really is an improvement on its predecessors.The match engine really does have a special something about it this year, the UCL/UEL/UECL branding really does add something to the atmosphere of the simulation, and the shortened VAR review times really are an upgrade to the playing experience.But more than all that, if past trends continue, I have a strong feeling that FM23 will be remembered as the last good FM game. With women's football on the horizon, the already thin veneer of investment from SI will almost certainly crumble into an attitude of "we barely tried and you deserve it" as they shore up their defenses and center women's football as the scapegoat that it is destined to become. I imagine that, starting with FM24, the game will see a long, slow descent with worse and worse annual releases until it either fades into an eFootball-esque pathetic half-existence or a FIFA-esque tweaker-style addiction to Ultimate Team cash.All that to say, in light of what we've had and in the trepidation of what's to come, FM23 is our final push, our golden hour, our great paean to Ozymandias - not yet crumbled in the sand, but juuuuust starting to crack.

_childDocuments_.review: Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)Football Manager 2023 brings the familiar thrill of managing your own football team to the table, but while it delivers on core gameplay, it falls short in some areas where improvement was hoped for. As an avid fan of the series, I found myself once again engrossed in the world of tactics, transfers, and triumphs, but I couldn't shake the feeling that more could have been done to truly elevate the experience.**Pros: Gameplay Excellence**The gameplay, as always, remains the highlight of Football Manager 2023. The depth and complexity of managing every aspect of a football team are unparalleled, and this installment doesn't disappoint in that regard. The intricate tactics system, detailed player management, and in-depth match simulations all combine to create an incredibly immersive and authentic football management experience. Whether you're leading a lower-league underdog to glory or managing a football giant to European dominance, the joy of crafting your own narrative remains unparalleled.**Cons: Familiar Stagnation and Subpar Graphics**While the core gameplay remains strong, it's disheartening to see that Football Manager 2023 doesn't bring substantial improvements compared to its predecessors. Many of the mechanics and features seem almost identical to those of previous titles, and this lack of innovation can leave long-time fans yearning for more. Moreover, the game's graphics continue to be a sore point. In an era where gaming technology is pushing boundaries, the dated visuals of Football Manager 2023 are a stark reminder of the game's stagnant visual evolution.**Final Thoughts**Football Manager 2023 is a testament to the addictive nature of football management simulations. The gameplay's depth and authenticity are more than enough to keep both newcomers and veterans engaged for hours on end. However, the game's lack of innovation and failure to address longstanding visual shortcomings are difficult to overlook. While the core experience remains compelling, it's disappointing that Sports Interactive hasn't pushed the envelope further with this latest iteration.For fans of the series who are content with the tried-and-true formula, Football Manager 2023 is a solid addition to their collection. However, those hoping for substantial advancements in gameplay and visual fidelity might find themselves longing for more. Goals are conceded not due to tactical inferiority or player fatigue, but due to 'once-in-a-lifetime' mistakes that happen every single match. For example, the last goal that we conceded came from my defender holding onto the ball for too long and being tackled. The resulting goal was ruled offside, then my goalkeeper passed the free kick straight to the same striker, who scored again. Goals like this happen so frequently, and there is no tactical answer because it comes from a mis-pass.If you go onto the Sports Interactive forums, the bug threads are full of hundreds of people posting thousands of complaints, most of them ignored. I myself posted several legitimate AI or graphical glitches before the winter update a month ago; all of the posts have been ignored, and the bugs were not patched in the latest update.I genuinely think this will be my last year playing the FM franchise. SI is too small a developer to keep up with the need to constantly improve the game, especially since every year they attempt to improve the Match Engine, they take one step forwards and two steps back.....all this without even mentioning the graphics, which have barely improved in almost a decade.

The game play (match engine) is extremely buggy and results in the player being utterly confused by what they should be doing. Football Manager's tactical inputs haven't been very intuitive for a while now, but this version leaves you creating tactics that could easily contradict one thing with another, and the player none the wiser as to why. To have to repeatedly send players to the tactics section of the SI Forum should possibly give the developer pause for thought as to why players struggle, and whether there is a better way to organise this. Far from being a reflection of real football management, SI have become locked into a presentational style which it does not provide adequate coaching for. 23 does not feel like it has moved anything on from 22. Press conferences, scouting etc have not changed at all and remain the same tedious process. It feels like the series has gone a little stale and the introduction of licenses for European competitions doesn't disguise this.I am disappointed that Football Manager 2023 has been released in it's current form. It's been mentioned elsewhere that there will be a big update to come out and fix some of the glaring issues around the defending within the match engine. It cannot be good practice to release a product for it only to be fixed months later.

But I feel like the game becomes a bit monotonous. But what can you expect? The game is straight forward and there are limits of how un-monotonous it can be.Everything you do regarding in-game choices is highly meaningful. This is because everything you do will influence the team. When playing you get rewards for progresses which is satisfying enough. The presentation and immersion of the game is very decent. The base “story”, if we can call it that is moderately interesting. I feel moderately immersed into the game, and that’s even more than I thought based on it being a “manager game”. The visual art style of the game is slightly appealing. I don’t feel the style of the game meets the standards of 2023. The style of a match feels a bit “cheap made”. A very small piece of the game makes this a big part of the game. And I feel every match looks a bit sad and not that immersed. In my opinion every match could be a lot better. I just feel like watching a normal football match as a viewer. But only with less quality, immersion, style and without commentary. It looks like a FIFA game from 2001. Sounds and music is slightly engaging. Sounds are repetitive and overlapping.  The HUD is user-friendly but sometimes during matches it can be a bit hard to use without pausing the match.Game mechanics are well designed, and the content is anywhere from moderate to extensive. General I would say that the AI’s are good. Where also the games settings are flexible. During my playtime I’ve experienced minor to nontechnical issues or glitches. Of my overall experience with the game, I feel very neutral. There are no micro-transactions or in-game purchases. _childDocuments_.review: So here is the thing... This is the only extremely repetitive game that I love. It is the exact same every time and it can be difficult to create and live out what it would be like to manage one of the worlds most premier clubs or even one of the worlds least prestigious. Every Football Manager has a wish list of improvements they would like to see, not necessarily a negative thing; however mine would start with the revamping of youth development. I would love to see a more in depth and expansive addition of U-17, U-16, U-15, and U-14. This does not necessarily mean that there needs the ability to treat them as the first team (that level of depth) and or immediately promote them to first team (even though it might be beneficial to have the next Jude Bellingham start at 14 if you play in the Non-League Football). A good starting point might be the annual or even bi-annually report on players with notes from coaches about potential and recommendations on what positions to train them in over the coming years. Take Reece James and Trent Alexander-Arnold for example. They came up as forwards and midfielders and found their way to RB later on in the academy. These decisions you could also automate to the Director of Youth Development and the 1st team manager could take over manually. From a back end perspective idk if that would increase the total amount of automated teams needing to simulate results or not, but I if it was an algorithm based on possible growth trajectories, possibilities of training far better in a certain position, academy facilities, and junior development budget that was ran let's say twice a year before the Development Center is updated with the corresponding email based , then that may be a good short term solution until the players reach U-16 and can be promoted into the first team. If it is just an algorithm and you do not need to make all of the youth teams playable, then you could go all the way down to U-10 maybe? Earlier then that and it gets too messy. One other thing to look at is you could prompt the director of youth development to give him a budget for youth trials for academy players by region vs. just the ability to ask your board to increase the overall fund. Obviously, the nation that a club is in will have the highest of that nationality, but you could have academy scouts or designate scouting assignments for academy players in the scouting department for overseas candidates. Those players will have an increased likelihood of dual nationalities to maintain domestic league requirements. At this point I am just ranting, but I have over 1,250+ hours on FM21, and I strongly believe that FM23 is a major upgrade. I personally buy in 2 year cycles because I get too invested into my team and will try to take my first elite academy players until they retire before I move on the the next club. Look forward to playing this game more, and I do hope to see what improvements will be made in the future!! - GG

_childDocuments_.review: I have 10k hours in all FM games combined. And it's a tough marriage. And here's why:The game leans on data, insights and all things which make you feel you're in control, really in control of your own 'success'. And I truly thing this system is 'rigged'. Meaning; the game is correcting itself when things are going too linear or easy. Unexplainable thing keep happening in a successive order. Not just in FM23, but in all of them. It's a pattern which is getting very annoying and it gives you a bad taste in your mouth.   Usually, when you know a little bit how to get the right players in the right situation, you will get a winning formation and staff and you can watch your team grow and do well. This does not mean you're winning all the time in the same way, but there is a line in the way your team plays. Then suddenly your team is all over the place. Suddenly you will get a 'bad streak'. And not that having a bad streak is not common but the way how it presents itself leaves questions. Your team will suddenly start to miss the greatest of chances, where the other team will tap in any opportunity. Your team will make a lot of forced mistakes. Some players weird moves on the pitch, like they would not now who to follow. Your keeper starts to make the weirdest mistakes too. And it happens in EVERY GAME, in every version. Because of 10k hours I can identify them very easily too. It's funny. So, I am forced to put a thumbs down here, even though the game has brought me many happy moments too.

_childDocuments_.review: Although there are no HUGE innovations in both game mechanics and visual style, the core gameplay experience is so good that I gladly come back for another year, even though I was still playing FM22 until like a few days before release of 23. It's just fun and if you install mods and packs the experience gets even better, so thanks to the devs for allowing this. The only 3 slightly negative things: - the interviews with media become boring and repetitive after a while and you kind of don't want to click through them (or do as I do, which is clicking on random stuff without reading the answers). I also don't feel like they made any updates to the answer texts or the questions. - there is no auto-simulation button by default. There are games where I just don't want to bother sitting through them, like playing against the last team on the table late in the season, and it would be great to have this button so that I can progress through the game faster if needed. This can be added through Mods but I am a bit puzzled why the devs don't put it in by default (or allow the option to enable it in the settings). - the player and character models aren't the prettiest but I don't mind it much. But that really is it. 9/10 would choose a 2nd division tier team to the Champions League Finals again.

name: Agatha Christie - Murder on the Orient Express
detailed_description: Reviews Check out Blazing Griffin's upcoming game About the Game Discover a modernized and revisited version of the Agatha Christie's classic. Set in 2023, Murder on the Orient Express brings the classic tale to life in a way that will surprise even the most dedicated fans. With brand-new elements added to the original story, experience the mystery and suspense like never before and rediscover one of the most famous case of Hercule Poirot. A crime is committed on board the Orient Express. Hercule Poirot, during this trip, is surrounded by a group of singular characters, all suspects, each with their own secrets and motivations, and will then try to elucidate the murder that has just taken place. Solving the mystery won’t be easy. Through numerous twists and turns, you will have to use your little grey cells and your detective skills to unravel the truth and bring it to light. Whether you’re a fan of the iconic book or movies, a lover of murder mysteries, or just looking for a thrilling adventure, this new proposal has something for everyone. So step aboard the Orient Express, and let the journey begin! FEATURES Experience a thrilling investigation Prepare for major twists and turns that will keep you hooked until the very end, as 'Murder on the Orient Express' is renowned for having one of the best plot twists in literary history. Not one, but two detectives Rediscover Murder on the Orient Express, adapted to the modern era of 2023 with a faithful but augmented adaptation that introduces a new character named Joanna Locke. Embody the private detective allows you to lead a second investigation during playable flashbacks in the United States. Mind Map & Timeline Resolving Enter Hercule Poirot's head to discover mind maps and make deductions there, adding an extra layer of depth to the gameplay. Take on the roles of Poirot and Joanna to solve puzzles and make deductions to uncover the truth behind the murder, playable in third person as you inspect sets and talk to all the protagonists and confront them.

short_description: Step on board the legendary Orient Express and immerse yourself in the most famous detective suit in a race against the clock to unmask the murderer.

_childDocuments_.review: Good detective game, bad Poirot game.Putting aside the new looks of Poirot (which I cannot accept as an extreme traditionalist in this matter), the game does a bad job of portraying the famous detective. His voice, his manners, his appearance, his convictions - all gone. To me it's a completely different person having the same name.With this out of the way I can focus on the game itself and in general it's surprisingly good. I really enjoyed my playthrough and I'm hoping to see a sequel.The game is full of contradictions. It was a very interesting move to try to reimagine the well known history in modern times, but at the same time a lot of actions and events felt stuck in the past (who writes notes and letters nowadays?). And I couldn't help but cringe when Poirot was talking about vapes.The game is low budget, so don't expect AAA audio-visuals. Graphics looked a bit outdated but stylised and once I got used to it I started to enjoy it. The character design was top notch, especially Princess Dragomiroff. Unfortunately some locations (Venice, Bank) felt straight up from 1990s adventure games with static, empty world. Invisible walls (e.g. Armstrong's driveway) didn't help.Music is really good and perfectly fits the atmosphere of Orient Express. Sadly most voices are subpar. Either they don't fit the characters (e.g. Poirot) or the accents are imitated to a comical level (e.g Hotaru) and which you can hear are almost always fake. In a game where dialogues play such a big role it's a serious detriment. The only exception is Joanna Locke, who does a great job playing an American detective.The main part of the game which is investigating is done brilliantly. You need to actually read what you find, pay attention to small details, often take screenshots or take notes in addition to what the game saves for you. This in combination with fact gatherings from conversations made me easily overlook shortcomings mentioned above. The mind map, while it could be a bit clearer and easier to navigate, is much better than in the other recent Poirot games. The amount and variety of puzzles and minigames make it a worthwhile addition to the game (unlike in the "young Poirot" series). It helps to keep track of the progress and helps with the next steps in a logical manner just like a real detective.Mechanically some design decisions are weird to say the least. The fog/smoke transition between screens which adds nothing but a delay and quickly becomes really annoying. Poirot not able to run is certainly the "Poirot doesn't run" trope from the books, however with the chosen Poirot design it makes no sense at all. Having to walk the train back and forth from one end to another chapter after chapter quickly loses it charm. All characters seem to be talking very, very slow and dialogues can't be skipped.The changes and additions to the story known from the book were done well. Being able to set out of the train and see the places, events, meet the characters which lead to the main story was a well needed change of pace. Joanna Locke is an interesting character and I hope she will be back for another story. In all honesty I wouldn't mind her as a lead in a new game while the "modern Poirot" is phased out.All in all a game worth playing if you like detective games and don't mind some budgetary and/or gameplay shortcomings.
_childDocuments_.name: Agatha Christie - Murder on the Orient Express

_childDocuments_.review: If you love Agatha Christie's famous novel Murder on the Orient Express, you'll enjoy this game despite knowing the whole story. You'll play the legendary detective Hercule Poirot, who is taking a prestigious train to his new destination. Still, an unexpected murder occurs on the first night on this train after it is such by an avalanche. Help Poirot by using his little grey cells in this modernized game with new twists and characters. Instead of 1934 setting, you'll play a fully voiced story in 2023, with all the modern tools to help our detective to find the murderer by taking a photo and analyzing it with his phone or searching through emails. On the side, we are introduced to a new character, Johanna, who adds an extra layer of depth to the story.The puzzles are good, but some of them are difficult; you can also enter into Poirot's head to discover mind maps and make deductions, which helps to tie all the evidence and character relations together. You can also check the character's profile through the menu any time; he will keep taking notes of each character he encounters; make sure to check those occasionally. I liked the character's designs, especially Poirot; although he doesn't look like the original except for the mustache, his personality is pleasant and sassy. The artwork is outstanding; I even bought the artbook, which was worth the price and even more. The new character Johanna fits very well in the game, I could see her having an exclusive game for herself. The soundtracks are excellent as well.Pros:+Interesting story with new twists.+Different ending than the original novel.+Fully and amazing Voice-overs.+Beautliful soundtracks.+Interesting new and likable characters.+Characters profiles.+Good game length.+Mind-map+Collectables (Golden mustache)+Manual save.+Steam achievements.Cons:- Sometimes, while playing on the keyboard the keybindings disappear, and you have to restart the game.There are different numbers of collectibles in each chapter, but if you miss any of them, you could always go to the extra menu and choose the chapter to collect those golden mustaches. I highly recommend this game to anyone who enjoys Agatha Christie's stories or detective games. Pick it up even if you know the story because it has multiple twists and different ending from the original novel.

_childDocuments_.review: From a technical point of view this game is good. I didn't hit any bugs or anything. The writing however is terrible. The additional story is a bunch of nonsense right out of an American cop show, bringing with it every cliche and a character seemingly based entirely on Jesse Fayden from Control. As the story progresses this just gets worse. English voice acting is fine at best and painful at worst. The Swedish character's accent wavers in and out of Welsh, and the poor Japanese chef stretches all his words to about twice their normal length. In-game text that should be in Cyrillic for plot reasons is in English, with no explanation. Every step of the way is blocked by an unrelated puzzle. Several times you can't interview someone until you help them with a problem represented by a derivative, irrelevant puzzle, like arranging gears correctly to fix a heretofore unseen juicer or arranging oddly-shaped packages in a fridge. Here's a list of some particularly non-Poirot plot devices if you're interested, spoiler's ahead: If you like Poirot or Agatha Christie I'd give this a miss unless you also like melodramatic action and don't mind bad writing.
_childDocuments_.name: Agatha Christie - Murder on the Orient Express

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a massive letdown.The familiar Orient Express story is about 60-70% of the game. In it the game is on rails. You can't really make decisions on how to investigate, and you are held by the hand to make every connection and deduction. What gameplay there is lies in things like opening puzzle boxes, fitting a bunch of weird boxes into a container, etc. For the deductions you can make as many mistakes as you want with no penalty, so picking the right answer doesn't feel like much of an accomplishment. The story "twist" is the same as the book's, so no surprise there even if, like me, you last read it maybe 30 years ago.Then the game tacks on a few extra chapters that feel completely disjointed. All of a sudden Poirot becomes a mix of Arsene Lupin and James Bond. There's a chase and a bank robbery. The mystery makes little sense, the new characters are not interesting, and the puzzles are tedious. This extra story really makes you appreciate Agatha Christie's craft by being a very pale imitation.Overall a game that had brilliant source material and wasted it with poor execution and not trusting the player enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Agatha Christie - Murder on the Orient Express

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't finished this Agatha Christie game yet but so far I am VERY impressed with the quality of this game. If there's one thing that I've been confused about with Agatha Christie games over the years, it's that each new iteration of Poirot seems to be made with a different studio, a different engine, different user interface, etc. It's difficult to get excited for these games sometimes because even though Poirot is the same, the gameplay varies so much between Orient Express, The First Cases, and ABC Murders. At least with Nancy Drew by HeR Interactive, you know the games are part of a series. The disparity between Hercule Poirot games just feels a bit off and it's hard to communicate to audiences which game they should play first, if they are connected, if they are part of a series, etc. So the marketing is not great and it's even more confusing that there's no specific dev team that works on these games. It's just all around confusing. That being said, Murder on the Orient Express is a very solid mystery game. For starters, the game works wonderfully on my Steam Deck. Even though the game doesn't say steam deck approved, the game runs PERFECTLY on the Steam Deck. So thank you for the Steam Deck consideration. As for the actual mystery, this game is a modern take on Agatha Christie's original "Murder On the Orient Express". I literally laughed out loud when Poirot took out a literal iPhone to take photos. It blew my mind seeing Poirot in the modern age using modern tech. I loved it. The game somehow feels like a special world where modern meets classic, especially with how the train itself is more on the traditional historical side of things. The game aesthetically is beautiful, from the luscious train landscapes to the interior of a bustling hotel, to a regal mansion and even a spooky cabin in the woods, the game is beautiful. Granted, it's not AAA cinematic quality that's like breathtaking, but we as adventure gamers don't need that either. Not every game needs to be a cinematic masterpiece and with Agatha Christie, the game does a fine job at bridging the balance between aesthetically beautiful and stylistic. The gameplay doesn't stray too far from Hercule Poirot: The First Cases. Back is the mind map, but this time around the mind map feels like an integral part of the game. In the First Cases, the mind map got in the way and it just wasn't fun at all using it. I actually was annoyed by the mind map in the First Cases because it forced you to draw conclusions with bubbles all over the place. It was a mess to be honest. I couldn't even finish The First Cases, because the mind map drove me mad. This time around, the mind map in Murder on the Orient Express has been simplified A LOT. I always say, when it comes to Game Development, KEEP IT SIMPLE (KISS). The mind map serves as a todo list which is super helpful. The mindmap also serves as a mini-game hub for when Poirot needs to recount evidence or events. I also love that the mindmap has it's own soundtrack. The song that plays in the mindmap is very soothing and relaxing. One other thing that I love about the mindmap is the way the game sometimes lets you draw your own conclusions based on survey questions. They don't impact gameplay but it lets you feel more like Poirot. So thank you for the simplification of the mindmap. I could easily play 30 Hercule Poirot games with this mindmap feature. The investigation gameplay is a lot of fun. I love how the camera shifted from a ceiling view to a Life is Strange shoulder view. The switch in camera prospective is very welcome. I love it. I think future Poirot games should maintain this camera prospective. It feels more intimate and up close in the action. The hotspot integration with a gamepad is very smooth and fluid. Moving the camera around allows you to choose which hotspot Poirot should focus on. The game blends 3D environments with 3D objects as well. Poirot will often times zoom into 3D areas to find more evidence. All of it is done very smoothly. The game also gives us insight into Poirot's headspace with voice recorded dialogue. It all reminds me so much of Life is Strange. I'm glad that the developers went that direction too. Making the inspiration Life is Strange was the PERFECT way to go. The puzzles in this game were a very nice and welcoming addition. I am a big Nancy Drew game fan, so seeing puzzles being implemented is great. The puzzles range from Mindmap puzzles (coming up with a sequence of events, mixing and matching, memory based challenges) to environment puzzles (jigsaw puzzles, weight puzzles, sequence puzzles). The puzzles break up the investigation gameplay quite nicely and I loved every minute of them. Seeing Poirot's smug smile at the end of each puzzle also made it a blast. I felt like I was there with him. It's a fun dose of artificial affirmations that just feels so good. This characters in this game are great. The voice acting is believable and fun. My favorite character is Beuc, Poirot's assistant. This game takes creative liberties in being a little comedic. In one scene, Poirot has to be quiet to listen to the sounds a puzzle makes, and halfway through the puzzle, Beuc starts having a full blown conversation with Poirot, disrupting the puzzle. The only way to solve the puzzle is to literally tell Beuc to be quiet. It's the smallest things like that that make this game charming and fun, and give it that comedic flair that I don't really see in adventure games that often. The rest of the suspects are all very fun to talk to, some having more of a memorable impact on me than others. Joanna is a new protagonist to the game. I was quite surprised by her inclusion. Her character works the same as Poirot, but having us step into her shoes made the game very fun as well. I'm equally invested in her character. She reminds me a lot of the Phoenix Wright/Maya Fey dynamic. This game also sort of borrows from that concept and even though we are playing as Joanna, we can't fully trust her either. It's a really cool plot point and I can't wait to see how it all plays out. The soundtrack in this game is incredible. I love jazz, and hearing jazz on the train just feels amazing. It's cozy. It's relaxing. It's ironic considering the murder but just sounds wonderful. The mindmap music is AMAZING. I want this soundtrack badly. I want the mindmap music to be my new focus playlist at work. It's sooo good. Thank you so much to the musicians in charge because the OST of this game is wonderful. Also special thanks to the Poirot voice actor. Thank you for your wonderful work in helping us get in Poirot's head. It must have been a lot of work not only voicing the main lines but also the internal dialogue lines (like Life is Strange) and it works very well here. I can't wait to finish this game. I hope that Microids considers making more Agatha Christie games with this game engine. Please consider using the same developers for next time because this game feels like the first and best iteration of the Poirot games compared to all the others. The other games sort of feel like prototypes where this game feels like a real, honest fully finished Poirot game that has the best of the best in it. I highly recommend this game. Even if you've seen the film, read the book, or maybe even played past games like this mystery. It's really good.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game.   I am a BIG Agatha Christie fan and love the novel, but after playing I am left with the question  "who is this game for?"On the plus side the game runs smoothly,  the character animations are good,  and I had no trouble running or playing the game.   I see a lot of positive reviews and I am glad people are enjoying it.  I just wanted to share my thoughts from someone who really loves the book.There are a LOT of story elements I questions, and  a lot of over simplified puzzles -  for example you speak with a character, they tell you all about themselves, then you get a pop quiz about something they just said and Poirot says "Voila ! I am correct"   even though he hadn't deduced anything.  There are flashbacks and another detective that also limit what Poirot is actually doing.  Is he actually solving anything or just being dragged through the story?At first I was going along with the modern setting - but the more I traversed through the game  (and walked constantly back and fourth up and down the corridors)   I realized that the story really works best in the past, and Poirot does, too.    I LOVE Poirot as a detective and throwing in another detective, Joanna Locke, really threw everything off for me.   Poirot's deductions were too simple, and after a while it started to drag on.  I just wanted to get to the end.And get to the end I did, and without spoilers, the end really isn't the end.    And I DO understand developers wanting to change elements of a book so that readers of the book will be surprised (as a lot of us know the plot)   but this became something very un-Christie like. And I think that was my primary trouble with the game.  If you love the character and the novel, you may find,  like me,  something vastly different from what you love about Christie's work -  and you will find yourself continuing to play thinking it will merge with the novel at some point, only to discover it veers further and further away.In the end, I would have preferred this just be a Joanna Lock adventure with no mention of Agatha Christie, and just be her own mystery,  and I may have enjoyed it more.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR - If you like murder mysteries with lite puzzle elements (ala - Sherlock Holmes games), you will likely really enjoy this game. It has some flaws, but the clear dedication and love that the development team put into this far outshines the small blemishes. The story starts a bit slow, but builds into a very intriguing tale of a murdered man, a kidnapped child, and the previously branched (and now intertwining) story lines of an American detective in Boston (presented in flashbacks) and present time Europe, as Poirot. The way the story weaves between the two character's POV really pulls you in, and is well done. I also really liked the choice of artistic design. The characters are pretty awesome looking, in their comic-like appearance and the locations are very well presented. The Orient Express itself looks fantastic! The voice acting throughout is good to very good.The movement, interactions, some puzzles, some voice acting, can be a bit spotty, at times, but again, I think the rest of this game is done well enough to still play this, and really enjoy it. I didn't expect a AAA polished game, when this is clearly a smaller dev team, and that's pretty standard for this genre.If you played the previous Agatha Christie game (like I unfortunately did), disregard everything about that, when considering this. That was (thank Jeebus) a different developer, and everything about this title is completely different.If I could give a rating on Steam, rather than a thumbs up, I would give it a solid 8/10. If you like murder mystery/visual novel/puzzle-lite games, there's a very good chance you will not regret buying this.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm giving this game a positive review because I have no reasons to give it a bad review, BUT... There are some reasons I wouldn't recommend it, at least not for the full price.The story is obviously awesome, and the fact that they "modernized" it without making it ridiculous is a great thing.The game is actually an "interactive story" though, don't expect to find challenging misteries to solve, because the way is straight and you're driven through all the events, there's no way to make mistakes, to skip things, to misjudge people or anything else.There are a few puzzles to solve during the gameplay, but nothing actually challenging, they're all very basic puzzles (for instance the famous "Hanoi Tower" puzzle)The game is actually pretty short, Steam says it took me 16.5 hours to complete it, but consider that I left it on pause a few times, I'd say it took me about 12 hours in the end. Considering that the gameplay is already not engaging at all, and that it is composed mostly in cutscenes, and that there are no side quests or similar to do, it has a pretty low duration for a 40€ game.Another thing that slowed down the gameplay was the doors on the train. In the long term it became pretty annoying to open those doors and going from a train car to another, expecially when if have to go back and forth from the first to the last train car, even for just a small talk.The voice acting is TOTALLY A NO. It was ok for the english/american characters, but for non-english characters it was at times embarassing, at times even insulting and annoying.I'm Italian and I can assure you nobody talks like the characters in this game. One of the main characters is Italian and speaks english with a very bad italian accent. In Venice some italians speak english, others speak a very bad italian with english accent. Why doing something like that? The game was dubbed in english by english speakers, let all the characters speak english. It really felt like a mockery in some points.Also the sweden character speaks in a very weird accent. I'm not swedish, but I spoke in english with a few swedish people and none of them sounded like that.In conclusion, it's worth playing this game if you like the genre of interactive stories, for sure it's not worth the full price, so care about buying it only if you find it in discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not terribly far into the game at the time of this review but even now, it feels incredibly tedious. _childDocuments_.review: Though I'm not yet done with the game, I think I know enough to write a review. It's an okay-ish, low budget puzzle game with mediocre graphics and voice acting, and puzzles so mundane that you could solve them in your sleep. I'm not even sure that's an exaggeration.The plot is for the most part jsut the original Christie story, with a few tweaks (like having a second playable character experiencing the Armstrong case first hand instead of it just being "Poirot remembering the events" like in the book). A lot of the dialogue is ripped straight out of the book. That's not necessarily a bad thing, as that's the story I expect. One of the major changes is the addendum after the the conclusion of the original main storyline. Suddenly there's a twist, and the story continues. However, this extra plotline feels so forced and out of place, that I'm unsure why the developers even bothered.Another big change from the original book, at least in theory, is the developers' decision to set the game in modern times. But the game never utilizes any of the possibilities a modern setting could provide. You live in a world with smart phones with the internet at your fingertips, but they brush this off by having characters state that there's no reception in the area where the train stopped. It's fair, but it begs the question; why not just set the game in the original time period? Maybe the devs just couldn't be bothered researching architecture and clothing styles specific to the early 1900s.The plot being a carbon copy of the original book's story (until the shoehorned additional part at the end), that wouldn't be so bad if the game had some redeeming gameplay mechanics. But it doesn't. It feels stale and... on rails (and not in a good way). You just walk around and click things. You can never fail a challenge, it'll just tell you that you're wrong and then you press the correct option and move on. Poirot constantly pats himself on the shoulder every time he completes all these banal tasks; like being able to deduce that someone who is using their right hand to write a note in front of Poirot, is right handed. Woooow, what a genius! This is the level of challenge you can expect to face while playing.The game isn't terrible, it's just not very good. The main problem is the asking price. It's insanity to charge this much for something that feels so cheap, unoriginal and uninventive. At $20, it could be passable. But it's sold at twice that. Looking back, I would have had a better experience if I had listened to one of the old audiobooks or radio plays. I would've gotten better narration too.Buy it at a discount if you buy it at all. But don't expect to be thrilled.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game and maybe it has potential, but it is (so far) overly simplified and drawn out. Most of the "mind map" is really just the quests you have to do and most of the quests you have to do are so boring.   This would have been much better if they made it a more dense story with more intense puzzles, in my opinion.  Minimize the walking back and forth, minimize the repetitive puzzles (like asking at LEAST 6 people person to write their address, then asking me what hand they are using when I can see them on the screen) and eliminate the irrelevant puzzles (like stacking random boxes) altogether.If you want a great mystery game I recommend Blacksad by the same devs

_childDocuments_.review: As my partner and I continued through the game, we started referring to it as "baby's first mystery game." I'm still playing through it (chapter 10/12 complete), but I just want it to end at this point. It doesn't evoke any of the wonder and discovery and excitement of Christie's works; it just feels tedious. I often find myself wishing I could refer to the clues and notes I've collected during decision points, but there's no way to get to them during these. Also, when I did refer to them in-game, I was forever popping in and out of clunky menus. At other points, and this might just be me, I feel you need to straight up guess the correct answers without any (or flimsy) reasoning. Of course, there's no penalty, and you can just click every answer until it says, "Good job!"Disclaimer: I've not read this book, but I've read a few others and seen The Mousetrap on stage.

_childDocuments_.review: Poirot games tend not be all that good. This newest Microids offering, however, was a home run for me. On one occasion, I managed to ruin my sleep schedule because I couldn't stop playing until 4AM, In a nutshell: Looks great, plays great, interesting take on the classic story with some added extra twists. Very enjoyable background music, too.The only negatives I have are mostly due to it not being a big budget fare, in that there's a quite a lot of "euro jank" present, even though I don't personally usually mind lower production values.The most glaring weak area is the voice acting. Accents are all over place, with some being cartoonishly exaggerated to the point of being halfway offensive (think those old Dolmio ads), while others sound like native English speakers who suddenly forgot how to pronounce basic words.The rest of the very few negatives are mostly about abrupt breaks from otherwise great game design. Interviewing suspects, completing mindmap items etc are all fine and par for the course. But, for example, there is a a larger area, where you're forced to hunt for small points of interest with no hotspot icons, armed only with fairly uninteresting clues related to the 3D area itself.That said, I really recommend this take on the Orient Express, since the modernized version with its extra storyline and good atmosphere is very captivating and chances are you really, REALLY do want to catch the culprit and find out what's going on.

Even though the narrative is pretty liniar, the plot is well delivered and additions keep it entertaining. Especially the new perspective of Joanna Locke, who I wouldn't mind to see in her own game one day. The puzzles are fair and don't feel out of place. The stylized graphics for the characters are fine, if that matters to you. Choices didn't have to seem any impact on the narrative. All in all the game seems to be well polished and I can't say that I encountered any bugs.I should also mention that I played in German where not every nationality of the characters, was that eaasily to determin.
