_childDocuments_.review: Coming a little out of nowhere, I was very pleasantly surprised with Trinity Fusion. Looking for a roguelite to play between big releases or on the side ? Look no further, this game could be what exactly what you need.Set in a futuristic and dying world where robots, animals and plants (and a mix of those) will be your enemies, Trinity Fusion follows a classic roguelite formula. You pick one of three characters, each with her own weapons and abilities, and grow stronger by defeating monsters, finding upgrades and obtaining new weapons.Your playground will be 10 worlds, ranging from desolate landscapes to robotic infrastructures and you will face half as many bosses, learning the mechanics along the way.But let's not beat around that desolate bush any longer, the appeal and why I would recommend this game is the gameplay. The general movement and animations are satisfying. Attacking enemies with the different weapons is satisfying. Dodging attacks while triggering your perks and abilities is satisfying. Word of the day : Satisfying ! When you're having fun simply moving and platforming around, you know something was done right. This makes experimenting with weapons and skills all the more pleasant and you're bound to find something you enjoy.The game is probably on the easier side, but will offer a good challenge at first and the permanent perks you can unlock are well balanced. There's even a hardcore mode that only allows you to get hit a limited number of times in a row, a Boss rush, and an Endless mode. You can expect to beat the final boss for the first time in 5 or 6 hours, and 10 to 12 hours to see everything. It's short, but the first of several dlcs is already out, and it's free !As for the story, it seems interesting and the introduction is quite engaging. Unfortunately, it gets pretty obscure and is only told through dialogues with (voiced) characters or logs hidden in the world. Oh well. You'll be too busy having fun to really care.I had a blast with Trinity Fusion. There aren't that many worlds or bosses and the story is a little hard to grasp, but the gameplay is amazing. Fluid and rewarding, it's fun no matter how you play. This could be your gaming obsession for the next few days, like it has been mine. I could see it being one day worth much more than the  I'll give it today. Short, but I loved it !

_childDocuments_.review: First, the hopeful bits.When I first tried opening the game, it froze and crashed repeatedly on the loading and menu screens, even closing Steam on some attempts.  It took closing Discord to get the game running, which probably means it has steep ram requirements.  I wasn't impressed looking at the graphical settings, where everything was set to maximum by default, including unlimited FPS.  I call this hopeful, because it's easy to hope that a game will have optimization fixes in the future.  I remember Risk of Rain 2's early access days, and I'm sure this game can get the same treatment.Now, the less hopeful bits.The in-game models look really derpy compared to the art on the cover and on the store page.  The voice acting, while not objectively lacking in quality, doesn't seem to add much to the game, and could probably use some supplementary animations and audio effects.  It seems like a good deal of effort went into the game's artistic areas, and the audio-visual experience still came out mediocre.  We can hope for improvements to the game's appearance, but it would likely require work no shorter than an overhaul of the models and the voice acting.The thing I'm most concerned about is the gameplay.  I should say that I've only played 1 run so far, and it's probable that the experience will vary between runs.  That said, I found myself descending down a chasm very early on, which kept going down until I eventually reached a dead end about 15 rooms in, and I had to learn I had a double jump without a tutorial to make it back up.  The enemies are painfully simple, with seemingly no variance to their behavior other than a very telegraphed attack and a long wind down, and an idle where they either block all damage or just sit there completely vulnerable.  I opened a sort of "risky chest", which states that it gives you a relatively high rarity alternative weapon and a temporary debuff, but what I got was essentially a freeze ray, which only stopped a single target in place, no damage bonus, no shatter chance, not even less energy cost than my default secondary that electrocuted enemies for damage over time.  The debuff was an extra 30% damage taken until I killed 10 enemies without taking damage.  I hope there's more creativity to the debuffs than that, but I don't know if I can expect that from this game at this point.It's important to remember that there's a reason early access is distinguished from full release, and this game can certainly change for the better in the future.  I'm not leaving a negative review because I think the game is bad and will stay bad, but moreso that I don't think it's ready for the world to see yet.  I'll play this game some more, and I'll revisit this review in the coming days.

_childDocuments_.review: Trinity fusion is an impressive feat and an immensely satisfying game to play through. With only 4 devs on the game, to say this game exceeds what should be possible is an understatement. As many people have said, the gameplay loop is similar to Dead cells, although, I vastly perfer the combat, asthetics and overall gameply of Trinity Fusion over it. The music composed by Synthwave Goose (sorry can't remember the other composers) is excellent and really naisl the overall atmosphere. The powerups, platforming, and exploration are extrememly fun and immerse you into a cybernetic dystopian future oozing with style. Visually, the game is reminiscent of Metroid Dread, which admittedly, is what drew me to the game to begin with.Combat is of the typical Metroidvania variety, except that some of the wepons have "combos" that you need to imput for them to perform certain functions. Seeing how there's a large swathe of different weapons to upgrade and swap through, this leads to some decisive moments. Do I want to upgrade to a weapon that does more base damage, but attacks slower due to the button inputs for comboing my current weapon equipped? I would love to see even more of these combos developed further in the future to make each weapon more unique and some of the slower weapons more viable. SOTN is still the only Metroidvania game to offer "fighting game" combos to execute certain actions to this day, and it was released almost 25 years ago. I really hope the devs expand this feature in depth to its fullest potential!The story is ok, but its kind of all over the place near the end since you can sequence skip some segments, so story beats seem to happen out of order sometimes, and can leave the player a bit confused. Some of the voice datalogs are more sparse than others, so it would be nice to see these fleshed out more as well. By the way the story ended, it does seem like the devs are going to add on more, plus there a handful of dialogue boxes near the end that arent voiced at all.This game still seems very much like a work in progress, and not quite complete imo, though for what it offers, it's extremely satisfying. Easy 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Trinity Fusion:~~~~~~~~~~~ Prime is the centre of the multiverse.  It controls the three worlds within it: The Hyperworld (a scientific and artistic world), the Overworld (an orderly, manufacturing world), and the Underworld (which has an abundance of resources and lives). Unfortunately, Prime has lost control, and the multiverse is collapsing.  The result is that the Ewer have now proclaimed themselves the superior beings for the Hyperworld, robots are now running the Overworld, and the energy that made the Underworld fertile has created massive monsters. The only way to salvage what was the multiverse is to fuse what is left of each world and hope for the best, in Trinity Fusion.Trinity Fusion is an action roguelike 2D platformer game developed and self-published by Angry Mob Games on the 14th of April, 2023, on the Steam platform. This game is currently on early access and might have significant changes upon its full release (version 1.0).There are three characters, one for each world.  All three characters are the same and they each have similar weapons, a combination of melee, range and energy. The only variation is that each character is more skilled with a different weapon.  In your first playthrough, you’ll only be able to play Altara, the character of the Underworld. You will be able to choose between all three characters when you reach two specific areas in one of your playthroughs.Currently on early access, each world has two stages to complete and a boss fight. Each stage is average in length, well-designed, and full of action from the beginning until you reach the door at the end of the stage. Within each stage you’ll be able to pick up coins. You’ll need these coins for two purposes, to purchase new weapons and gizmos, and to open special workstations.  There are two types of workstations, one is free and the other needs coins. There are usually one or two paid and several free workstations per stage. When you open them, you can choose one of the two items from inside, which could be coins, weapons, perks or an artifact. There are also several teleport stations spread around the stage, which you can use to teleport your character around the map to see if you’ve missed any secret rooms or forgotten to explore parts of the map. You probably won’t use them in the beginning, but they come in pretty handy when you know the stage. Another item you’ll come across once per stage is the Cursed Rock, where you can get either a free perk or a weapon.  It will, however, give your character a negative effect for a certain time, such as 30% less health until you either reach the end of the stage, or kill a certain number of enemies. There are three specific chambers in each stage, one where you can purchase goodies (this chamber is usually close to the exit gate), one where you can combine your current character with one of the other world characters (giving you access to both characters’ energy weapons), and the last chamber where you’ll fight several enemies at close quarters and be rewarded at the end of the fight with a weapon, coins or a perk. You’ll find a red gate somewhere within the stage; you can’t access it right now, but it will be available in future updates.One of the main aspects of platformer games is the combat system which I was really impressed with. As you have to evade enemies swiftly and then attack, I am always worried about the input from when you press the button and when the action is executed, as it can make the game unplayable. I am happy to report that the input is sharp and precise. Trinity Fusion has over 60 different types of enemy, and three bosses fights. It might take you a few attempts to pinpoint each of the bosses’ moves and attacks before you can successfully kill them. I would appreciate the developer adding a few extra difficulty levels to spice up the game. Yes, there is permanent death, and you might die every now and then within the stage, depending on the perks that you collect, but as soon as you fuse two characters and build up your persona skills at the citadel, the difficulty decreases rapidly.Graphically, the game looks great, and the story is pretty good too. As an early access, you expect to encounter issues, which I did in the form of enemies getting stuck in walls, but is wasn’t too frequent, which is great. But I had a crash to the desktop once while playing in one of the Hyperworld stages. Thankfully, the game saved my progress, and I could restart from the beginning of the stage without losing my coins and weapons.Positives:~~~~~~~ +	Nice graphics+	Interesting story+	Fun and pleasant to play+	Good combat mechanism+	Over 60 different types of enemies within three different worlds, and three bosses fight+	A large number of weaponsNegatives:~~~~~~~~ -	Needs additional levels of difficulty-	A few glitches here and there-	One crash to desktop-	No achievements or trading cards as yetTrinity Fusion is a solid early access that will appeal to fans of roguelike platformer games.7/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: Trinity Fusion is a bit janky here and there, but overall it's a good action platformer roguelite with a notably different feel from the norm.  A big aspect of that different feel comes from making enemies solider and more imposing.  You get far fewer hit-stuns from your attacks, and you can dash by enemies but not simply walk through them.  There's a distinct feel to the combat here that takes some getting used to, so be patient with it.For fighting play, you have a main weapon and two slots for side weapons (generally charged by main weapon hits), jump, dodge, and a couple slots for consumables/cooldown abilities.  There are also some traversal abilities you get depending on character, which can make the gameplay a little confusing since sometimes you can double jump and sometimes you cannot.  A post-release update added parry, which you need to unlock and slot through the metaprogression.  It's not a flashy parry, but it works, and if you are a parry type player you will find it easy and effective with a generous window, so for me, a substantial gameplay upgrade.Metaprogression--aside from the parry--is pretty boring and rudimentary stuff with two currencies split between upgrades and space to slot upgrades, so you are doubly constrained and have to manage which currencies you choose in runs.  There are also a few ability unlocks requiring passing the various main stage bosses, and the bosses are tough, so that takes some time to open play up.

_childDocuments_.review: This is more lite-rogue than metroidvania but nonetheless, it is a fun hack & slash mixed with some shooting here and there despite the Dark Souls-like penalties. The soundtrack has a nice atmospheric vibe to each level as it slightly intensifies whenever in a battle. The scenes in each level has a nice cyberpunk vibe to it as well with some abstract design areas like "The In-Between" levels. It definitely would make for a nice wallpaper on a desktop like "The Forge" level for example. When you first play the game (or demo) it may seem a bit difficult and yes- you WILL die several times... which is a GOOD thing! While you lose your weapons and power level (even if you successfully clear the stage and end boss), you do collect two primary currencies to buy perks, which will help you get better as you progress and lesser chances of dying per run.Don't be ashamed to start off on Survivor mode to get a good feel of the controls. Dodging attacks is very simple as long as you know to time it right and know your enemies' patterns. As you level up in your runs IMO, I think the fights get easier once you hit at least level 10+ and you find any gate that takes you to "The In-Between" levels. In-Between levels are what I consider as bonus stages, but varying on the "skull" difficulty indicator, you're going to have to put your best effort into earning a higher weapon, currency, perk, etc, etc. Eventually, you'll start kicking up the difficulty a notch either for a challenge, the Steam achievement, or both. Therefore, have patience each time you lose. You'll begin to like each run more and more as you get better amid earning perks.

_childDocuments_.review: Trinity Fusion is about a 9 / 10 for me. Maybe 8 / 10.I'll try not to spoil too much of the story, but here's what you might want to know.There are four parallel universes. You play as a woman named Mara who lives in Prime. There are cross-universe shenanigans happening that threatening the balance between then which could collapse or destroy all of them. They have diverged too much even though, once you visit them, you'll wonder how they were ever considered "in harmony". Each universe is aware of this impending collapse and is trying to save itself in one way or another.You are the only person who still has a counterself in each universe and Prime has a fancy machine that lets you take over those people temporarily ("hitch-hiking").The gameplay loop is you jump into another one of them in their universe and fight to the boss of that particular biome to defeat them. When you die, you are sent back to Prime and your counterself "resets" so that they don't permanently die.The levels are randomly generated like a rogue-like. Any weapons or upgrades you have when you fail a biome are lost.You earn orbs that can be used to unlock permanent upgrades back in Prime. You have a limit of how many you can equip so you can tailor your playstyle a bit as you unlock them.It's kind of a metroidvania but not really. There are sometimes places that you need a specific traversal ability for, but since the levels reset when you die, its not really the same. More like Dead Cells in that respect. If you have the ability you can get to a bonus area, but if you don't , you can still finish the level.Normally, enemies do not repop after you kill them, so if you clear a level and want to spend time exploring, you won't have to worry about them coming back. Time is not on your side in Hardcore mode, so this doesn't count when you play that difficulty level.Each counterself has a different personality, different abilities, different weapons, and different traversal abilities. As the game progresses, the line blurs but I won't spoil anything else.There is also a place called The In Between that you can sometimes find entrances for. It has different rules and plays more like Hades than Dead Cells. You fight an arena then choose a path based on the reward you will receive and then keep doing that until you reach the end.If you are new to this type of game or just want to play around, you can use Survivor difficulty which makes everything easier. If you are still having problems making it to the end, you can turn on Hypermode which permanently boosts your damage resistance every time you die. I think it maxes at 65%. I played a lot of hours in Survivor with Hypermode just to get a full understanding of how everything works.I've been playing on Veteran difficulty for a while and it is comparable to how I was doing on Survivor when I had no idea what I was doing.Hardcore difficulty is a completely different thing with its own complications. I don't make it very far in Hardcore difficulty but I plan to keep playing until I can.The primary reason I don't give this a definitely 9 out of 10 or even a 10 out of 10 is a minor quibble. I play on my SteamDeck and it runs great on it; they even have a specific SteamDeck mode that really does optimize it. Before that, it would lag if you turned on shadows. But, late in each run, you have too many actions and not enough buttons. They only let you map to Y, RB, LB, RT, D-pad left, and D-pad right. You may have two or three more things. A weapon, a secondary weapon, a tertiary weapon, a consumable, and one or more special abilities. There are additional buttons they could have mapped. R3 and L3 where you push down the analog stick. There are 4 back buttons. They could have had a quick switch option to switch between presets. It's just a weird limitation that I'm sure came up in testing, but they decided it wasn't a big deal? You can pause at any time and remap the controls so that's good enough?Regardless, I enjoy playing this game.I beat it many times in Survivor. I've beaten in once in Veteran so far. But I'm still playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: "Trinity Fusion" emerges as a standout title in the realm of Metroidvania games, skillfully blending elements from well-known titles like "Dead Cells," "Cult of the Lamb," and "Hades," while adding its unique flair.In comparison to "Dead Cells," "Trinity Fusion" offers a more narrative-driven experience. While "Dead Cells" is renowned for its fluid combat and roguelike elements, "Trinity Fusion" elevates this with its engaging storyline set in a captivating sci-fi multiverse. This narrative depth adds an extra layer of immersion and purpose to the gameplay.When it comes to "Cult of the Lamb," "Trinity Fusion" shares the aspect of exploring diverse, beautifully designed worlds. However, "Trinity Fusion" leans more towards action-packed platforming and combat, whereas "Cult of the Lamb" combines action with strategic base-building and resource management.Comparing it with "Hades," another highly acclaimed title in the genre, "Trinity Fusion" holds its own with its intricate character development and world-building. While "Hades" is celebrated for its unique storytelling and character interactions, "Trinity Fusion" matches this with its own compelling narrative and a multiverse that is rich in detail and lore.Overall, "Trinity Fusion" stands out in the Metroidvania genre by combining the best elements of its peers—fluid combat from "Dead Cells," diverse world exploration akin to "Cult of the Lamb," and the narrative depth and character development reminiscent of "Hades." This synthesis, along with its own unique features, makes "Trinity Fusion" a highly recommended title for fans of the genre and newcomers alike. The game offers a thrilling experience that is both familiar and refreshingly new, setting a high standard for future entries in the Metroidvania and rogue-lite genres.

_childDocuments_.review: Below is my original review. I am editing it and changing it to "Not Recommend". Edits: The procedural generation of each level makes the game super random and inconsistent. Also, getting shot through walls and floors from off screen is where I draw the line. Skip this ♥♥♥♥ until they fix that, at least. Very much on the fence about this one. There are some balance issues and some problems that seem related to procedural generation. The upgrades are so specific it's kind of insulting. "Deal additional 20% damage to non-elite and non-boss enemies for 2 seconds after a successful evade if there are 3 or more enemies nearby and you are at or below 50% health."Ok, that's an exaggeration, but it's honestly not that far off. For a 2D game, there are times when you get swarmed, blocked and stun locked and there appears to be no counterplay. You can only dash and parry so much. Eventually you'll get hit, and then you will get hit again, and again and again, and you'll get stunned by electricity on the ground and frozen by the little flying guys and the water will prevent you from dashing and some enemy from off screen and 3 floors up is able to hit you through all the floors for some stupid reason. Meanwhile, I launch homing missiles at the only enemy visible on the screen and they just fly straight up and do jack s***, leaving me stuck for half a second in this useless animation, which is just enough time for the enemy to close the gap and hit me for poison damage that gradually drains over a quarter of my health, and there's nothing I can do about it. On the flip side, it does feel really good getting some of the abilities and chaining together synergistic upgrades. The combat feels pretty solid and the reward structure on each level feels pretty good. The combat is tight and snappy, even if the hit boxes and collision detection can somtimes leave a lot to be desired. Overall, I think Trinity Fusion is a good example of an average to slightly above average experience. Like a true 6 or 6.5 out of 10. If you like the genre and/or you find this game on sale, like I did, I would say pick it up and give it a try. Just don't expect a super polished, perfect game that's going to break any of the established moulds.

_childDocuments_.review: Very badly designed enemies or upgrades/weapons, it feels like these two facets of the game were designed by independantly of each other. In that context having several weapons that are borderline unusable and clearly unusable against certain enemies/bosses makes this game simply unfun. Imagine getting to a boss with a weapon that is so close ranged that you can rarely strike the boss without automatically walking into its attack (even when the boss is aiming in the other direction) during your attack animation. There are also bosses that are mainly in the air, when there are several weapons and secondary weapons that either only ground-based or very very bad with aerial attacks.If this would not be enough there are many situations in this game where all you can do is parry, and the parry is in my opinion pretty annoying. The parry timing window is fine, the problem is the enemies animations which are very fast, they often go from being on the other side of the screen to being through you very fast which makes timing your parry hard.Overall the enemies are easy but the bosses a nightmare, which makes for a jarring experience. Often just running through boring enemies, boring hallways to "train" on the hard bosses and get face stomped. Especially if you get weapons which are sometimes useless against said boss, same is true for upgrades. Bosses are the hardest in the game but MOST upgrades are useless on the bosses

_childDocuments_.review: This game reminds me of Dead Cells, but with smoother movement like in Metroid Dread. The combat is really fluid and responsive, and you need to be careful with your attacks, dash through incoming attacks, and combo your enemies to death. Some tougher ones can even be stunned with an extra stun bar.It gets more risky in some rooms where you get swarmed by several at once, and need to properly strategize some crowd control.Once you beat the first boss and meet the second character, Kera, the game and challenges really open up. Kera has lots of melee combos available. And the third one’s gameplay feels more bullet-hell, with long range aiming.You still have to get in close, as all the better/special weapons use an energy bar, which only gets filled when you use your main weapon.Run lengths are not too long, from 7-15 minutes per stage, but it’s well worth exploring the whole map, to increase the power level and get better weapons.The mods are pretty basic right now, but maybe they'll add more special ones or some clearer synergies.Overall, game is most definitely worth recommending. _childDocuments_.review: This game is only about 3 months old and any little bit of exposure helps; I'll probably write a few of these as I go through the game, maybe get a little bit better at it; speaking of, this game is my introduction to the Roguelike space, so take my assertions about its difficulty with a grain of salt. I'm about as baby as it comes with this.The visuals of this game are phenomenal. All the different places are vibrant in their own way, between the putrid underworld, the ordered overworld, and the expansive hyperworld. Each of the worlds have their unique color schemes, and each of their areas have very distinct styles without ever losing the overall feeling of its world. The character and mob animations are gorgeous and fluid. The music is very fitting for the genre, but just enough variety between the different worlds - well, between the underworld and the hyperworld, at least, I've only done one run with Kera and I couldn't quite get a handle on her extra jump, so I didn't get very far."Roguelike" was the description of the game, but this is the first one I've played, so you'll have to bare with me if what I end up describing is just the basic roguelike experience.The gameplay loop was quite satisfying to go through. I'm not used to the "having to go through all the levels again when you die," but doing it that way meant I was able to learn the level's layout, all the enemies, all the best ways to avoid them and traverse the level quickly. There were also movement ability unlocks from mid-level arenas, meaning I had more to explore, more secrets to uncover in the level when I died and started again. The fusing mechanic was also cool... the one time I used it; I tend to save my cash for weapon upgrades and health restores, but it was neat to mess around with.The boss fights are absolutely infuriating. They're incredibly difficult to try and navigate; if you're good at the game, you've got up-to-gear weapons, good skills and a health restore on stand-by, but most of the time you'll have, at best, two of the above listed. And then it's a pattern recognition deal, and if you don't learn it on the first go, you have to trudge all the way back through all the previous areas - which is a lot of time to forget the pattern recognition you worked to learn. And with health restoration being one of the areas this game isn't big on, taking a few hits to learn the patterns - the go-to strategy for most of the others I've played - would most likely cost you the run. It's a pain in the ass sometimes; like I said at the top, it's entirely possible the answer to making the boss fights easier is just for me to "get good" but I feel like there's a bit of refinement that could be done. A checkpoint on the bosses maybe, or extra lives somewhere for boss fights only.The variety of weapons and specialties, as well as abilities, is astounding. And the system they have, randomized ability pools, and the randomly dropped weapons by enemies or in the mini shops, means you can never get to comfortable. Sure, you might find your favorites - Deceleration Field being a personal go-to - but the chances you're going to get it are low in the best of cases. So you work with what you got as you go. Really cool system I haven't seen with many other games.The lore of the game is fascinating. Both the world lore and the inter-character relationships is awesome. The dialogue of the game is some of the best I've seen, and finding bits and pieces of lore around the world as you go if always super satisfying. I admittedly haven't found to much of it, but it seems like a very in-depth world they've got going on, and I can't wait to explore more of it.As of this review, I'd give it 8/10. Very good stuff so far, even if some of the difficulty spikes can verge on unfair. Look forward to seeing what else the devs have up their sleeve!

_childDocuments_.review: Despite being in Early Access, I can already tell you I love this game...The most important thing that Angry Mob got right in a game of this genre is the combat and the controls.  There's a good variety of enemies and tactics that makes the core game actually, you know, FUN.  I find myself always coming back for just one more run, which says a lot about Trinity Fusion's replayability.That's not to say that this game is perfect; far from it actually.  However, knowing that this is still a work in progress is exciting as the dev brings balancing and updates.  So far I've only had one crash and had to restart a run, so not much in the way of game-breaking bugs.  They are still working on removing some of the more useless perks and consumables which is great, because I often find myself skipping some of these items or leaving them in my inventory (looking at you Rally Banner).Going back to the combat, it's critical that Trinity Fusion offers enough variety to keep you interested, and in my opinion they've nailed it.  Lots of different enemy types specific to their biomes requiring different approaches to victory.  My only gripe is that flying enemies tend to keep their distance, and it can be tough to get at them considering you can't swing vertically.  That being said, having a weapon with longer range can help.On to the controls, I've played a lot of titles in the action platformer genre that failed to be engaging because movement or attacking were just outright frustrating.  Thankfully TF is fast, fluid, and gives you the sensation that you're totally in control.  One negative that comes to mind is that the ledge grip is a bit sticky, but this only becomes a problem when you're trying to get the drop on an enemy from above.  The other negative, and this one is big, is that there is no invulnerability after you are attacked (unless you have that perk) and this can be irritating especially during boss fights.  Your life can be drained extremely quickly if you get stuck in a laser or other trap, and unless you time the dash right you can't move.  Naturally you should be avoiding these situations altogether if you git gud, but just a warning that you can be killed often by this, so stay agile.Finally, the visuals.  Trinity Fusion looks great.  Mostly.  The Citadel is particularly stunning, but some of the levels can be a bit bland.  For the most part I love the gritty post-apocalyptic vibe and it works.  The enemy models are well done and feel appropriate for each biome.  I have no qualms here.  And the biggest plus of all is that it runs FLAWLESSLY on Steam Deck out of the box.  If you're worried about battery life you can tone down the graphics settings as it will eat your charge quickly, but it runs like butter regardless.All in all this is a fantastic Action Roguelite that will be in my play rotation for a long time.  Highly optimistic to see where the devs go from here; they've already got the solid core that I feel many games lack, Early Access or not.  Angry Mob, excellent work!

_childDocuments_.review: Trinity Fusion is a remarkable Rogue-Lite action platformer that sets itself apart from other games in terms of its stunning design and immersive story. The game's dark and sci-fi worlds are beautifully crafted, and the attention to detail is truly impressive. From the atmospheric lighting to the intricate level design, Trinity Fusion creates a world that feels both haunting and awe-inspiring.But it's not just the design that sets Trinity Fusion apart - the game's story is equally engrossing. As you explore the doomed multiverse, you'll uncover a rich and complex narrative that will keep you invested in the game's world and characters. The story is expertly woven into the game play, creating a truly immersive experience that will leave you wanting more.Of course, no action platformer would be complete without solid gameplay, and Trinity Fusion delivers in spades. The combat is fast-paced and precise, and the platforming elements are challenging without ever feeling frustrating. With a variety of weapons and abilities to master, there's always something new to discover in Trinity Fusion.Overall, Trinity Fusion is a fantastic game that any fan of action platforms will love. Its stunning design and immersive story, combined with its challenging game play, make it a must-play for anyone looking for a truly engaging gaming experience. So if you're looking for a game that will transport you to another world and keep you on the edge of your seat, Trinity Fusion is definitely worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: Early Access ReviewInteresting setting, very good art direction/asset quality/animations for an indie.  Currently it's a bit basic in its initial early access state, but it's clear that the game has potential to turn into a very solid metroidvania/roguelite.There are 3 "worlds" with the main character having a different version of herself for each one (though functionally this doesn't amount to much yet).  As you beat the boss of each world you unlock a new traversal ability for that specific character.  You gain 2 different meta-resources (orange and blue) to help you strengthen your upgrades, though currently they are pretty lackluster, just minor stat increases.  Orange unlocks new upgrades to be purchased or increases your upgrade slots, blue is what you use to purchase the upgrades.  The second tier of upgrades includes a revive, very useful, work towards that ASAP.The "fusion" mechanic isn't really fleshed out at the moment.  In later updates it looks like the 3 different worlds will be fused together in a way that promotes more thoughtful planning and preparation from the player.  Currently, you can find a terminal in a run to "fuse" with one of the other 2 versions of yourself from the other worlds, increasing your health, granting you one of their spells/abilities, traversal ability and giving you a new unique look for the remainder of the run.  It's a nice touch, I just wish it was more accessible and more than just a flat combination of the 2 characters.  So far nothing is in the game that requires you to have 2 different traversal abilities, but it's clear to see how it will be utilized in the future (hopefully).All in all it's a fun enough game while it lasts.  The current state of the game is somewhat short, I got to the end of the current content in around 4-6 hours (a good understanding of how to dodge enemies will almost trivialize the game and shorten your playtime) but I enjoyed what I played.  Looking forward to the games progress.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has got to have the most awful controls of any 2D game I've played in recent memory. Playing the game feels like wading through sludge - every action feels slow and unresponsive, with the dash being in contention for quite possibly the all-time worst of the genre. Double jumping is also incredibly inconsistent due to what seems to be poor platform detection - the game is very finicky about whether it thinks your character is standing on a platform or not. This problem also affects ledge grabbing and dropping through platforms, as visual indicators of when those things should be possible do not match when you can actually do them. The result is that the entire game world feels soft and undefined, as you're liable to 'slip' around platforms in ways that feel unnatural. This is exacerbated by how enemies also function as semi-permeable walls, slowing you down when you try to pass through them. It's an odd choice that makes moving through the game world feel even less intuitive.There are other things I can nitpick, like how NPCs' hideous, creepy-doll faces don't move whatsoever despite having voice-acted dialogue, but those aren't worth getting into when the core feel of gameplay is as bad as it is. Perhaps you think me histrionic, but these issues are bad enough to make me stop playing and contemplate a refund after about 20 minutes. Buyer beware.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a roguelite game with dystopian scifi theme. You start from the base, then move to the first stage. During your run, you discover portals that take you to the next stage. You may ignore the portal and try to find another, if you don't want that stage. This makes the transition feel a bit more natural than some other roguelites, where you simply choose a stage at the end. You get temporary powerups that are lost after the run, and also credits to upgrade your character permanently. If you die, you return to base, losing the temporary upgrades. Pretty standard stuff for a roguelite. Regions have distinct appearance. Overall the graphics look very good and detailed. Voice acting is also a plus, and it's decently done. There are 3 different characters with slightly different playstyles (focus on melee vs. ranged).It starts easy, enemies do hardly any damage. You can also dodge attacks pretty effectively. Dealing with multiple enemies at the same time might get you killed, though. The game seems to focus on smooth movement and anticipation, rather than quick reflexes. This makes the controls seem a bit laggy at times, because the reactions are somewhat tied to character animations. Also, every weapon has a speed value. It can feel a bit awkward at first, but I got used to it. There are other games like that, such as Lost Ruins.Good:+ Looks great+ Voice acting+ Good difficulty progression+ Stable, no major bugs or crashesBad:- Laggy controls not for everybody

_childDocuments_.review: I feel bad leaving a negative review on a competent game that I'm sure many would enjoy, but I have to be honest. The game is pretty well made, nice graphics and sound, gameplay is okay. The problem is the roguelike elements. First, the levels are procedurally generated, which means they are generally very uninteresting. Even the best procedural routines can't match a good designer, and it shows badly here. Secondly, the game is designed for you to die and start over, with some meta-progression to ease the next "run". All standard tropes, and it can work in some games, but here it just emphasises how dull the levels are. Starting over again and again, fighting the same enemies in samey environments - but without being able to develop muscle memory from well-designed levels like in classic games. No thanks, it's not for me.

Better hope you stood there the 1 time in 20 that it fell or hope that you didn't use a ranged weapon or hope that you didn't defeat that enemy in the air.  Maybe you should try the heal a point or two on crit with a 20 second cooldown.  At least you might see that one work once.  The abilities between runs are equally useless. If they do add another dozen worlds with a dozen new enemies on each, I'd never see them because the level design is so unbalanced and uninteresting.

enemy design is really cool, the main characters feel unique in their looks and personality, despite them being pretty much the same person and the bosses I think are the main highlight, they look _childDocuments_.review: I have 74 hours in this game, and beat it on hardest difficulty on all the characters... So I come from this perspective as a hardcore fan of the game.  PROS:I can describe this game as "Sci-Fi Dead Cells." If you're familiar with Dead Cells, this has a similar loop, mechanics, and progression system. However, this game jettisons some unnecessary things from Dead Cells, but improves in other key areas as well. The combat is actually better here, with a faster and more responsive dash mechanic. In-run progression is also better, and you can quickly become stronger as enemies become stronger. So the in-run satisfaction is higher. Also, there is more variety of enemies. In Dead Cells the same enemies can be found throughout the game, i.e., level 1 enemies on the first map will appear on later maps. But in this game, each map has its own set of unique enemies. Also, the enemies are more nuanced, and there are many tactical/strategic approaches to gameplay. CONS: -The beginning of the game is deceptively simple. So new players might be turned off from playing more. It takes a good 5-10 hours to begin to see its variety and complexity.-Most importantly though, the biggest con to this game is its too short. Compared to Dead Cells---which has 5 difficulty levels and hundreds of hours of replay value---this game only has Normal and Hardcore difficulty. So once you beat it on Hardcore, there is no incentive to play more. After about 40 hours in the game, I had already beat everything multiple times on Hardcore and there was nothing left to do. I wish there were higher difficulties, or more replay incentives like Leaderboard, etc. SUMMARY:In short, this game is criminally under-rated. It is by far the best side-scroller I've played in years. Buy it. You will not regret it. Don't let the simplicity in the beginning fool you. It gets complex quickly, with rewarding progression and an enjoyable loop. It was fun to strategize and figure out what works best. I enjoyed this more than I enjoyed the Ori games. I also loved the clean sci-fi [Mass Effect] theme (we need more games like this today!). Everything about this game was smooth and polished, and incredibly well thought out; the music, weapons, abilities, progression, all work together well. Love the epic soundtrack too!  👍

_childDocuments_.review: In a world where we have Dead Cells, there is no point in playing this. In every aspect, this game is subpar. I cannot list a single thing worth mentioning (well maybe music). It's just a sloppy, B grade copy. Someone please explain to me, what is the point of having 3 characters? To have 3 classes of weapons? So why don't you start with one weapon, and slowly upgrade to 3? Why are all the characters the same (the only difference I noticed is one not having double jump). I cannot understand the idea behind this, and it doesn't add absolutly nothing to gameplay. I would refund it, but games in this genre require a bit more than 2 hours to fully understand and get a hang of the game. I should have known better. Still, me and my friend kept playing, hoping for something to change, expand, whatever. It never happened.And oh, internet version worked fine. So did the Steam version. But then we got a few patches... Now the game randomly crashes, infinite loading times, glitching enemies... Thank you, no.EDIT: To make some actual points in the review:- compared to other games in the genre, this one is very short and doesn't offer anything substantial in other aspects. When talking about similar games in the 20€ range, there are plenty more that offer way more enjoyment, deeper mechanics, lore, and overall tighter gameplay. I gave it a go, but quickly went back to other games that do things better. Or, just more enjoyable. In either case, do some research in 20€ bracket, there are lots of games in this genre.- visual style is pretty nice IMO, looks quite different to other similar games, but moving and traversing in this pretty world is not so fun. Controls are not bad, but not great either. I don't mind missing a jump here and there if I know I messed up, but when I get hit, can't dodge or move away from attacks due to inprecise and sloppy controls? That is a no go. There are secrets in the levels, but again, compared to other games, they are just slightly hidden, can't really call them "secrets" or "secret rooms". Big minus for me.- sound design/music is on par, nothing special, but it gets the job done. I quite like some songs, but that is subjective. If you like 80s vibe and synths, you might enjoy it as well.- difficulty is hit and miss; most enemies are "easy" once you learn  their attacks, it can get tricky when you have to fight a mob of them tho. Couple that with dodgy controls, and you have a problem. Otherwise it's not either hard or easy, middle of  the road (provided you take it slow and easy and don't eat cheap hits). - lenght is also a big problem. This types of games are made to be played hours upon hours. Die, learn something, repeat. Use the knowledge, die, upgrade, repeat. But when you can actually see the majority of what game has to offer in ~30min... It's not even funny.I did enjoy the game to some degree, I'd say about 10 hours were quite ok, when you still learn, experiment, explore... But when that stopped, I lost interest very quickly and got frustrated often due to little things... Which as always, quickly stack up.I do not recommend the game in it's current state, and even if developers expand, fix and tweak some things, I believe other products in the genre would still offer more content, more gameplay, more lore, and are tweaked and polished to a higher standard. If you see it on sale (like 50% off or so), then go for it.

_childDocuments_.review: "Meh" or "ugh" would be the appropriate improvisatorial adjective here.This game is pretty contrasting in the things it does well and poorly in my opinion. The good are all the bits where it attempts to be simple, whereas the mediocre are everything else. The enemies are the highlight in this game; they're simple and follow a distinct pattern that requires the player to deal with them in a unique way. Because they're simple yet quite expressive fighting multiple at once feels quite good and dynamic. They hazards are generally well communicated too, like incoming strikes having a clear recognizable particle cue. Unfortunately the game suffers a bad case of the "just run by them", which is addressed in the small arena sections. The latter are consequently also the most challenging part of a run.Then comes the core gameplay loop, which starts strong but starts to deteriorate in its confusion really rapidly. You have your standard melee strike and a ranged option which empties a resource generated by the first. Simple formula. Worked in the past, works here. You also have a dash with some i-frames and a perfect "evade" when close to the enemies' active frames. Again proven formula, works well. On top of that the player has two forms of consumables and an ability on a cooldown. Here things start to show the first signs of deterioration in the design. The game offers ZERO urgency outside the arenas, which means cooldowns are *rewarding* defensive and slow playing. You have the original "ranged option only available when first getting into melee combat" copied, which is designed exactly to battle this issue, and then you make the mistake anyway with abilities on cooldowns? Remarkable.The consumables don't really compliment the game and feel more like a "free out of jail"-card. I'm unsure what exactly was intended with them but they're fairly bland.The melee combat feels BAD. Like actually outright bad. Animations are way slower than they should be, making the game feel unresponsive and clunky. But worse yet: weapons have massive deadzones. The most obvious examples are the weapons that have *no upward strike*. I complained about this in the demo and instead of fixing it they added it as "roguelite element" (further reinforcing what absolute cancer this genre is to indie developers). The consequences are that some enemies fall perpetually in the players deadzone, forcing them to awkward hop around and try to hit them with a directional attack that isn't suited for the job. Flying enemies and those sticking to the geometry are a nightmare to fight because of this.Then there are the roguelite elements. This is the part where we go beyond bad in my opinion. The roguelite elements manifest themselves twofold: linear progression by collecting resources and crates containing upgrades and weapons. The first are part of the hub area, the latter lootboxes you can find in the map. Both of them are extremely invasive to the pace of the game. Just cleared a room with a lot of flair and speed? Hold up, gotta investigate this loot-box and pick my random boon for a minute. Momentum gone. And it happens constantly. Hub areas pretty much always suck so I don't really need to explain myself there. They're just an inferior menu to waste more time than necessary.Because the game needed linear progression for whatever reason the maps sport a wealth of resources used for meta-progression. Resources in the form of coins and upgrade orbs. Some lootboxes contain an option: a meta-progression blue orb or something you would actually want to make the game fun? Brilliant. Punish the player for having stupid meta progression.But the game goes even further by making the boons, random small perks you can obtain, extremely poorly designed. Almost a third of the boons I've seen REWARD bad playing. "You get hit you get X", "if an enemy hits you you get Y". WHY? Why REWARD the player for not playing the game properly? Even by roguelite standards this is dumb, and that's a big insult in my eyes.The whole game is just another shining example of roguelites being perceived as this free "look mom i designed a game xd"-crutch that indie developers fall for by the dozen. Almost everything bad about it originates from the fact that it didn't just double down on the fundamentals. It had to be another crappy roguelite, because indies must make roguelite games.Real disappointment.

_childDocuments_.review: Melancholy and squandered potential. (my life, not the game)As I stand at the precipice, screaming into the wilderness at the unassailable Mountain of Regret I've built, for standing between me and my sight of happiness and casting its shadow on all I see, I am smothered in an avalanche of excuses. Melancholy and squandered potential is all I have to hold me. To tell me who I am, to tell me where I have been.As we age and gain perspective on time and our significance in the course of the universe, what gives us mooring and holds us fast to life and our memories is the continuance of the things we've built and accomplished. Our families and children, the friends and connections we've made as well as the literal edifices we've built and the mark we've left in our wake. As ephemeral is it all may be... Like the forlorn cliche of Dust in the Wind, the dust holds a truth of what it once was and what it could have been... Melancholy and squandered potential. Doesn't even amount to dust. I've come to find that as I've passed a certain threshold in the course of my life, a sense of detachment has begun to grow in regards to my place and purpose in life. More and more I feel as though I'm sailing into a great wide open, not of unknown potential, but a void of untethered meaninglessness, a bleak uncertain future...but certainly bleak.I've built nothing. I've accomplished nothing. I have nothing to stand on to connect me to my past and the dreams I once cherished....It all feels more and more like a dream and like this was who I always was. I watch, blinking apathetically as it all falls away from me in slow motion... But hey, I can still make run-on sentences and play video games so far as now and this one ain't too shabby. _childDocuments_.review: Full disclosure, I'm friends with one of the voice actors who worked on this project.I didn't like this game. But I dislike all rogue-likes or rogue-lites or whatever the hell they're calling them now. I firmly believe rogue-like developers do so because building a game with a standard difficulty curve is too hard. So they make players play the same levels over and over again (instead of having an actual wealth of content), and implement a difficulty curve that's a smooth, straight line until it shoots upward at a near 90-degree angle like you're slamming into a brick wall.And your reward for the 30-60 minutes of your life? You might see a number tick up by one. But no ACTUAL progress, just the SENSATION of it. And then you get to slam into a brick wall again. This is not fun. This is frustrating. I don't understand how ANYONE enjoys this kind of game. But sadly, enough people (masochistic people, I have to assume) enjoy this kind of thing enough so that game devs with budgets large enough to hire people as talented as the voice actors in this game get their game made, and now I have to try and play it out of misguided loyalty.To be fair, Angry Mob Games tries to alleviate some frustration by implementing "Hyper Mode" which gradually ups your damage resistance every time you die - but again, it's watching a number tick up, and you won't really notice the difference. I didn't. This is a halfway measure. If Angry Mob Games was really serious, they would let us set that number to whatever we want.This game is not for me. It might be for you. If it is, I will never understand you.
