_childDocuments_.review: Personally a huge fan of arcade wrestlers. I feel like the game is a solid replication of the original "No Mercy" and "WCW/NWO Revenge" era of wrestling games on the N64. The graphics are definitely cartoonish and that's okay (for me). This is mostly a brawler style wrestling game that is self-aware. As an AEW fan I'm pretty happy with it, however If you are more used to the WWE 2k series, you may/may not enjoy this as it is NOT a realistic wrestling sim (and that's the point).
_childDocuments_.name: AEW: Fight Forever

_childDocuments_.review: I've not played a Wrestling Game since WWE 2k14 and for good reason. I wasn't satisfied with how malformed and annoying the mechanics became. Though this game hardly has the suites and creation options of WWE games, it has far better gameplay, which is what I've wanted instead of making a slew of created wrestlers, while never touching a single match. I had to stop playing the WWE games because I didn't enjoy the kick out system for pins. It made matches last forever and online matches never ended because of it. I'd be far better than people at the game but I couldn't win the match because they just kicked out. The last match I played, went for an hour and I quit the match myself. They can just win, if they prefer to suffer for that long. I've only dabbled in a bit of this game. Did a lot of training to get down counters and attack patterns. I like the dodging mechanic as well as how you're able to transition a grapple to the corner or ropes. The lack of Free Run is so good. I could not stand that in WWE games people would abuse it and run a marathon around the ring in online modes. I quit right away when that happened. I don't care that much about winning, I just don't want to suffer. Matches are very quick, as they should be. Instead of needlessly lasting an hour or even 30 minutes while both wrestlers lumber about the ring in quicksand. The quicker pace is definitely the way to go and I can feel needing to get better at this game instead of needing to learn 1 or 2 mechanics to exploit.
_childDocuments_.name: AEW: Fight Forever

_childDocuments_.review: Ultimately, the game is -really fun- and that's the most important thing I got out of it. The gameplay feels good, the move animations are crisp, and it plays nicely. Every wrestler feels very different and playing someone like Yuka Sakuzaki is a joy. I also appreciate the herculean challenge of creating a scratch game engine and animating every single move by hand - and how that will affect development time, particularly in adding new wrestlers to the game. This plays fine on PC, and I'm happy to have purchased it. My complaint is the game is not done and has a dearth of content you'd think would be standard in a modern wrestling game. That affects replayability and ultimately how many hours I'm going to put into this. A more robust create a wrestler, backstage areas, and multi-person gimmick matches are omissions that you can just -feel- looking at this game.
_childDocuments_.name: AEW: Fight Forever

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. Not only does it bring you back to the golden era of wrestling games, it has some cool unique twists to it. Yeah the game isn't exactly cheap, and no it doesnt have the content that other recent wrestling games have, But as a first AEW game I think it does really well. The most important part of a game, is being fun which we know the rival wrestling game is not, its also not nearly as broken either as said rival game.

_childDocuments_.review: AEW: Fight Forever is not a perfect game, nor is it going to be what everyone wants in a wrestling game. Like a lot of people in the reviews here, I stopped playing wrestling games heavy when the WWE 2K series was introduced. I've picked up a couple of yearly iterations of the game, not once feeling excited to play it. They're not bad, just not my thing. I missed the dumb fun in older games like SvR, No Mercy, Here Comes the Pain. If you were a fan of those older titles I HIGHLY recommend giving this game a go. Worst case, you really won't enjoy it, play less than 2 hours and ask Steam for a refund.The gameplay is solid, it's a lot of fun. I mean A LOT of fun. I have the game on PC and PS5 and have played a total of about 15-20 hours so far across both platforms. This game is incredibly simple to pick up and get the hang of, HOWEVER, every time I play I am finding new things that we can do as players that the game didn't announce to us but were left for us to find out. It provides some real life "HOLY SH%T" moments.The story mode experience, "Road to the Elite" is a fun experience. Each situation, decision, and outcome is said to alter the path of the story, thus providing you with a different experience each time you play. It's quick enough, to not feel like you're sinking too much time trying to figure out how to unlock some missing characters, but long enough that it doesn't feel pointless.The creative suite is by far the weakest part of this game. As a player you're provided with very minimal options up front. They have a good variety of moves, music, and entrances, however, the actual CAW customization features are disappointing. Luckily, THQ has seemed to rescind their original stance on modding, allowing for ProWrestlingMods to create their own offline launcher, release modding tutorials, and even will be adding official channels to the discord for them. The devs have already shown us that they are willing to listen to the players, we can only hope that they keep this up. Who's to say they won't do an overhaul on the creative suite in the future?With all of this said, Fight Forever is fantastic. I have heard that this game was released with the planned to be built onto and added to in the future, rather than going the yearly release route. I am excited to see what the devs end up doing with this game, but if it was left the way it is, I wouldn't feel that my money or time was wasted.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say the game isn't fun. Gameplay wise, Fight Forever will remind you of older arcade style wrestling games. Huge fan of the gameplay, it's fast paced and a great alternative to WWE 2K's more simulation based gameplay. However, the game is most definitely not worth its $60 price tag. The lack of content makes it hard to recommend the game to anyone for more than $20 or maybe $30 if you're a really big fan of AEW and 2000s wrestling games. With time and updates I'm sure the game will be able to solve these issues, but it's not a day 1 purchase. Super solid foundation and set up for a potentially amazing pro wrestling game, just give it time and see how Yukes, THQ, and AEW handle the game post launch.

_childDocuments_.review: Ive never felt so conflicted on a review. I enjoy what the game offers and I can tell what they wanted to go for but it feels like they either didnt have a big budget or just had to meet a deadline. The game is fun and easy to pick up but the roster is very dated, which always seems to happen in wrestling games. Alot of current stars are not an option which isn't a big deal as they could be added. This game could be good with some content and a few patches. I personally haven't encountered any bugs but at the time of this review, Im aware they exist.I dont want to refund because I know this can turn into the game we all want in future titles but $60 is a hard sell for what is offered currently. At best $40 is what should be the current price. While it is simple fun, It can feel rather (mid). I do think this will become a solid series with future titles but this one isnt quite hitting the itch....yet but definitely in the right direction. Overall I recommend but at a discount. Dont expect this to replace a 2k style game as far as content goes

_childDocuments_.review: I'm recommending this because at it's core it's fun and is a good game.HOWEVERThis game is trying to be WWF No Mercy a little too much where the game feels like it has the same limitations that No Mercy had. The difference is that you could forgive those limitations for No Mercy because No Mercy came out in 1998.Entrances are in short clips like No Mercy. This is terrible design choice in my opinion. It destroys the atmosphere of a good entrance which in turn kills some of the buildup to the match. In No Mercy, one could forgive this because full entrances weren't really a thing in wrestling games at the time. Now they are. That same vibe is consistent throughout this game. These design choices would be fine... in a bubble. This game suffers from the fact that it didn't take basically anything from what WWE 2K was doing. It feels like 1998 in both the good and the bad. The arcade feel is fine. It needs something to distinguish it from it's competition, but you should still pay attention to what your competition is doing right. Things like community creations, large varieties in match types, extensive rosters, in-depth wrestling with highly varied movesets. This game lacks those and if you have played the WWE 2K games. Those missing features stick out badly.I am in full support of AEW making more arcadey games than WWE. I really like the variety of weapons in the game and the fact you can play an exploding barbed wire deathmatch. I really like some of the mechanics like riding the skateboard or throwing the propane tank to explode your opponent. I also like that you can control the pyro and camera cuts during entrances. But they should still have full entrances and some preset pyro, they should still have a community creations, they should still have an extensive roster (hell because its arcadey they have even less of an excuse there because they don't need to have as much attention to detail or mocap wrestlers like WWE).Overall, the game is fun and does have some great features. It just feels like it's lacking a lot when compared to its competition. They will be adding more wrestlers in DLCs and hopefully other new stuff but yeah definitely fell short of some of the hype.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a high quality wrestling game, very reminiscent of the games of the N64 and PS2 era. It has a few bugs as of the time of me writing this, but they do not make the game unplayable. I clipped into the crowd on occasion when brawling on the outside and and a few goofy hit detection moments, but it's a far sight better than 2K20.It is VERY easy to pick up and play. My wife is a somewhat casual and cozy gamer who is fairly new to the genre and, once she realized that in training mode she could just beat up on Christian until she learned the game controls she was quite pleased and learned quickly.The minigames are fun diversions and good ways to play the game in party mode when you get tired of exploding barbed wire death matches, and the story mode is very similar to a classic Street Fighter or Mortal Kombat experience with a little bit of management thrown in to allow you to choose different ways to organically advance the story down different pathways. From what I've seen after two play throughs, losing doesn't mean the story is over, you just go on to a different branching path of the storyline.AEW: Fight Forever isn't the absurdly polished next gen photorealistic wrestling game WWE puts out, but does that really matter if they weren't aiming for that as the goal? They prioritized accessibility and arcade feel over realism, and it turns out creating something that's supposed to be fun rather than realistic makes for a pretty fun video game. The addition of the in-game currency is a bit odd as you'll likely buy out the store after 20 hours of play by my estimation, but it leaves me hopeful for additional free content down the road.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a cellphone model game, There is nothing here. The game play is fun, but how many times over the course of this game can you play online matches or exhibition mode? All of the content is locked behind multiple season passes. Thus to get a whole roster you need to buy 3-4 season passes at over $20 a pop just to play as wrestlers, without dated attires and entrances in even more exhibition matches. The career mode is a joke, a trash pile, a waste of time. I see what they were trying to go for with the multiple branching paths thing. When you can't be bothered to add voice acting and instead use text and a JPEG background for everything, it doesn't exactly make me want to play the career more than once. 5 / 10... It functions, but its not the 90s anymore. I'm not going to get pizza and play random matches with the boys over and over all damn day.  At least release the DLC with character + addition stories for each character. The lack of tangible content is laughable. A bunch of mini games that the average person has zero interest in. It functions though and could be fun for a day if you can get it on a Deep DEEP discount.

_childDocuments_.review:
Developed by YUKE's Co, Ltd., creators of numerous, multi-million unit selling wrestling games, AEW: Fight Forever combines that nostalgic arcade-wrestler feel with innovative All Elite Wrestling finishers and tandem offensive moves. All Elite Wrestling is currently taking TNT and TBS networks by storm every week with their Rampage and Dynamite shows, featuring some of the biggest legends to enter the ring plus a stable of brand new, high-flying, AEW talent. AEW: Fight Forever brings the best of the best from that talent roster together in one game! Online co-op wrestling is going completely next level in Fight Forever with Tag Team matches that feature sequences of team maneuvers performed with simple commands. A deep career mode, wrestler customization, signature AEW arenas, and more match types than you can count, including some good ol' fashioned, unsanctioned fun, all await!

* Single, tag-team, 3-way, 4-way, ladder, Casino Battle Royale, Falls Count Anywhere, Unsanctioned Lights Out, Exploding Barbed Wire Death and online co-op multi-player matches!
* Online co-op multi-player!

* Deep career mode
* Wide range of customization modes: wrestler attire and appearance, move sets, entrances, teams, and arenas.
* More than 40 weapons!
* Mini-Games!
* Daily and weekly challenges!

name: SUPER BOMBERMAN R 2
detailed_description: The latest title of the party battle games series SUPER BOMBERMAN R! With new adventures and game modes, it has the largest content volume in the series' history! The game features not only offline battles that can be played with family and friends, but also online battles that connect players from all over the world, as well as a single player mode. In addition to the well-known 'Standard', 'Grand Prix' and 'Battle 64' a new battle mode called 'Castle' in which players are divided into Attack side and Castle side to battle for the treasure! A 'Stage Editor' function has also been added, allowing players to create their own stages for 'Castle' and share them online with players around the globe. Let's have fun together in 'SUPER BOMBERMAN R 2'! • Battle Mode Enjoy 4 battle modes, including the new 'Castle'! “Castle”: Asymmetrical battle between the Castle side, which protects the treasure chest, and the Attack side, which aims to win the treasure chest! “Standard”: The classic battle mode loved by fans! “Grand Prix”: Battle of two teams! Work with your allies to defeat the opposing team! “Battle 64”: Battle for survival with up to 64 players! Aim for Bomber One! • Grade Match Battles between users with similar abilities! Fight online with players from all over the world! • Room Match Set freely battle modes and rules! Get your friends together online and have a good time! • Offline Battle With one console you can enjoy Bomberman! Connect additional controllers and play with family and friends! *Controllers for the number of persons are required. • Stage Editor Customized stages with blocks and gimmicks can be shared online! Create, play, share, and explore various stages with the Stage Editor! • Story Mode Enjoy the Story Mode that has been enhanced! Visit new planets with Bombermans new friends “Ellons” and face the threat of the universe!

_childDocuments_.review: They took down the F2P Bomberman R Online and repackaged its content with barely anything new for $50. Took away the freedom of choice in the online multiplayer from the original R in favor of a rotation based ranked mode. No way to find and join private lobbies from within the game instead requiring a code. Also since there's no F2P option and Konami barely marketed the damn thing good luck ever finding a full lobby. The story mode might be worth something but I kind of don't wanna risk accidentally going over 2 hours. If you want to play an online Bomberman game you can do so SO much better. Play the original R over Parsec, play Live/Ultra on PS3 and 360, or better than all of those just play Power Bomberman.
_childDocuments_.name: SUPER BOMBERMAN R 2

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time fan who has played Bomberman for over 25 years... wtf is this game? I almost want to say this game was falsely advertised. So many features made to sound better than they are. This game is just SBRO with extra features at a 50$ price tag. "All new story mode"... with 3 boring levels and lazy still frame cutscenes featuring bad voice overs. "Create your own maps"... only for castle mode AND using pre set templates only. "Couch multiplayer"... only with a few bland stages, no team battle options, none of the variety that made past games have replay value. "Online multiplayer"... with rotating game modes where you cant choose classic or b64 as you please. And this is 50$? I truly thought after the failure of SBRO Konami would actually make it up to us fans with a true labor of love kind of game. To see an already unpopular IP get treated this way is awful. If this game was free to play i would not give it such a harsh review.
_childDocuments_.name: SUPER BOMBERMAN R 2

_childDocuments_.review: As a longtime fan of the franchise, I'm not sure if this the worst game in it's catalog, but it's certainly the one I dislike the most.I don't know where to begin with this game, game development is tough and I hate using this term because I understand things regarding it aren't so simple, especially with publishers and deadlines, but SBR2 feels worthy of the claim regardless, this is one of the laziest releases in a long time, and I'm positive the series niche status is the only reason why this hasn't become more widespread. 85% or so of this game was simply lifted from SBR Online and pressed onto a disc(physical ver), and to begin with much of that game was lifted from SBR1.I'm fully convinced this game was an attempt to salvage the remains of SBRO after it's failure, and isn't actually an original title of it's own, this is hardly worth calling a sequel and if it really is, it's astonishing how it could release 6 years later in this state, there are: . No new or returning power-ups . Next to no new customization features. Missing features that SBR1 had . No new battle stages and Less Battle Stages unfortunately(only the same 8 from SBRO, as opposed to the 22 or so from SBR1) . Less characters,(24 additional ones from SBR1 are not present) . No team standard battles, . One stage for Battle 64(missing Orion Town). No CPU difficulty option(a standard for Bomberman games) and this game is home to the worst AI in the franchise.. Less Grand Prix modes("Checkpoints" and "Civilians" are both absent.) and stages . Dead Online That's just the start sadly, What's "new" here?Well Castle Mode, but let's talk about Story Mode, Since they're related, Story serves as a tutorial for Castle and is almost entirely built on assets from said mode, just with a few cinematics and text boxes slapped in, the game is exploration focused where you control White, and only White(baffling considering you could play as the entire roster in story mode in SBR1) and essentially collect a set number of creatures trapped in blocks or containers called "Ellons" to open up areas gating your progression with a required number of them saved to proceed. This is certainly different from other Bomberman games but I still would call it uninspired, open ended Adventure based Bomberman games were done before this over 2 decades prior in games like Bomberman Quest (GBC), Bomberman Tournament(GBA), and Bomberman Jetters Densetsu no Bomberman(GBA) all of those games had visually distinct worlds to roam full of fun puzzles and layouts that invited curiosity, and RPG elements that weren't temporary and gave the player the proper feeling of growth that you typically want from this kind of format, along with skills or abilities unseen that aren't simply the standard ones expected from Bomberman. In SBR2 no matter where you venture, you're always looking at the same ugly and dull environments devoid of any character, there are no NPCs to talk to, villages or towns to check out, Item stores, and no caverns to discover, lakes to cross etc. everything is essentially one elongated castle map, you gain exp by blasting blocks or enemies and collecting it, and each time you reach a threshold you level up and get stat increases, extra lives, and/or skills such as bomb punch and bomb kick, but none of these are ever necessary to proceed, which is a shame there's no neat puzzles or obstacles that take advantage of your abilities like there were in those older games I mentioned, its just one monotonous slog to get stronger and there's really not too many ways to speed it up, killing multiple enemies at once does not give any multiplier bonus like I feel it should have given how scoring worked in older Bomberman games, that could've at least rewarded players for skilled or risky play.Like the last game, I don't know why they keep doing this but your stats from one world do not carry over to the next, meaning you have to do all of this tedium again in each world, leaving the game with no proper difficulty curve and no genuine sense of momentum, seriously even if you were trying to speedrun this it would feel like playing 3 repetitive sessions rather than one cohesive run, oh yeah there's only 3 worlds btw a paltry number compared to just about any attempt at a single player mode in any of these games before this, to be fair they do pad out each world and on average they'll probably take 90 minutes to 2 hours each to complete, but quite frankly it's dreadful the game only has a pathetic total of 4 enemy types, shared across all 3 worlds and they all feel very uninvolved and basic, you can run past all of them and I don't know if that's a good thing or a bad thing quite frankly considering this game isn't very enjoyable. no unique gimmicks or terrains or anything to shake up the gameplay loop, at best each world just utilizes different arrangements of the same castle gimmicks.Occasionally as you progress your home base will be attacked and you're forced to drop whatever you're doing and play a 3 minute defense session of Castle Mode, all of which can be cheesed in hilarious ways thanks to the games abysmal AI, there's a community post showcasing this if you'd like to see for yourself but essentially when these happen, just put your controller down and go make a sandwich, you'll be fine.I'm unsure when I'll hit the character limit so let me rush a bit, The boss fights are maybe the highlight of this mode but I'm not even sure because they're terrible, they reuse attack patterns from earlier Super Bomberman games, and unfortunately due to the rest of the game I don't think that's as an homage so much as it is the developers not bothering to think of new ones, and unfortunately these retreads are worse than their original forms because the boss design is much like SBR1 where you'll need to take out a bunch of weak points before you can actually access the bosses weak point, you do this 3 times or so and the fights end, there's a lot of aimless standing around and waiting while these bosses are out of frame or completely invincible until they're done attacking and then you get to make a move, slow and boring. Co-op is gone, I want to say due to the nature of the story mode this time it's understandable, but it really isn't, if players got too far apart the screen could've just split, like the Lego games. if anything this story mode could've been 4 players, it would drastically make this otherwise tedious experience more enjoyable if everyone could focus on their own tasks, unlocking parts of the map together. Story writing is bad, same problems as SBR1, but magnified, characters are still one note and annoying(Pink the sole exception in SBR1), but now they get more screen time and don't develop at all(and now there's pee humor) i still don't like the presentation, the artstyle is way too cutesy compared to Shoji Mizuno's work which had a balance of cute, cool and weird, and now everyone just looks like Bomberman instead of a range of designs for the cast, the cinematics are not really animation so much as tweening and playing around with vectors in Toon Boom, a lot of recycled art is used to the point where I don't know why they didn't just make text based scenes with dynamic portraits, could've saved space and allowed for 60fps.Castle Mode feels like a draft of an idea coded in before it could be properly realized, seriously if attackers get a key and open a chest they simply stop playing until matches end, its weird when it happens early, also they finally add a stage builder for a modern Bomberman and its locked to this mode only for some reason.No positives that weren't in older games.There's so so much more I want to say but Steam reviews can only go so far sadly. I love Bomberman(single and multi!) and I know it can be much more than this today, but it needs developers who care for it and unfortunately that doesn't seem to be the current folks chosen to lead.
_childDocuments_.name: SUPER BOMBERMAN R 2

_childDocuments_.review: Good grief Konami, if you're going to be this lazy with bomberman can you at least just port one of the good games for twenty bucks or something? I can't blame people in the slightest for not wanting to pick this up, for some reason they thought the rotating mode selection from splatoon would be a good idea when they don't even have a playerbase to fill the modes with. _childDocuments_.review: While I do not absolutely hate what I've played so far, I don't think I can in good heart recommend this game.So basically this game compiles the three game modes seen in Super Bomberman R and the now defunct R Online, plus a new mode, Castle mode, exclusive to this game, and they're pretty lackluster compared to what other Bomberman games from the Hudson Soft era had to offer.Standard battle of course is simple by nature, as it always has been in prior titles, but here the stage and gimmicks diversity is bare bones, and there have not been any new power ups added since the last game. Louies do return from R Online, but they're just the green ones that go fast, what happened to the ones that could do other things like kick bombs or soft blocks, jump over obstacles, make a line of bombs (since the power up that does that is also missing), or even one that just dances?Grand Prix is fine I suppose, although I do find it weird that because of this mode, the option to set teams in standard battle is absent, like what if I just want to play a game with normal rules but divided in teams and with more than six players?Battle 64 is a neat concept but that mode is just riddled with pretty mindless bots that are not a threat in the slightest, there's also no stage or gimmick variety at all which makes this mode repetitive very quickly.Castle mode is just a mess of a game mode, the main new selling point of this game and what half of the story mode is based on, like I kinda see where they were going for with this idea, but it's an unbalanced mess and not all that fun.On top of this, the only way to play with strangers seems to be through ranked matches, which are always rotating, so the game mode that you want to play may not always be available, I suppose this is made so that the likelihood of finding a match with real players is higher than if everyone could just pick whichever mode they want, but to not have a casual online mode where to host your own game with your own rules seems like a miss opportunity to me, you do have the freedom to do so in offline battles, but the AI is so terrible that they destroy themselves with their own bombs at the start of the game, why aren't there any AI difficulty settings? Offline is probably not what you're here for anyways unless you have a group of friends who to play with on the couch.This game takes pride in having a diverse amount of battle modes, but I believe older games had better modes, like reversi battle where you have change the floor panels to your color and win by covering the most area, hyper battle where you battle to collect three orbs that you bring to a gate and nuke everyone, countdown battle where a ticking clock appears on you when a bomb explodes you, so you have to tag it to another player before it ticks down to 0 or you lose, or dodge battle where you can't place down bombs but instead have to dodge those that fall from the sky.My final verdict, every Bomberman game put out by Konami just feels like wasted potential, Bomberman can be so much more than what has been being offered in the R series.

_childDocuments_.review: While I love the Bomberman series, it makes me sad to say this feels like another lazy entry that has such potential to be a good game. Starting off with the price... yikes. The price for this game as of reviewing is $49.99 when not on sale. I believe I bought it for $30 when on sale recently because I love the franchise regardless and want to support the devs whenever a Bomberman game comes out. However, I just can't recommend this game to somebody who isn't a Bomberman fanatic for either of those prices. Even then, it's hard to recommend this over an older entry in the series. This is so unfortunate, because I along with many people miss the days of playing Bomberman with friends either locally or via a cheaper release such as Bomberman Live on the Xbox360. Some older Bomberman games at least gave us slightly more captivating missions or worlds to explore. Single Player: There's not much at all. I tried to 100% this game for achievements, but the single player experience is just so bland and boring I stopped. You work through 3 worlds that contain different rooms containing puzzles, which allow you to collect these little creatures called "Elons" that help Bomberman and friends save the day or whatever. It uses traditional Bomberman movement, but just rehashes the same enemies and barriers to make you solve puzzles that aren't too challenging. Whether they're just vague or overly obvious, I like the concept but the execution is just simply poor. I couldn't bother wasting my time to get through the entire campaign. Even if I was a kid again, I'd find this to be so boring compared to other games I could be playing. There's no character interaction in-game besides the cutscenes you get. Even then, the voice acting is a little tough, but hey, it's a Bomberman game, I can forgive that. I just wish we could have more single player experiences like old Bomberman games. Characters to meet, levels that are at least cool to look at, and fun puzzles to play around with. If we could have another game with a formula like Bomberman Jetters or 64, I guarantee fans would be happy if it just had some love and work put into it. Konami, please give the devs enough time to show this game more love. I will say that I enjoy the idea of Bomberman leveling up and gaining stronger abilities, it just doesn't support the rest of the lackluster ideas here.Multiplayer: Fun ideas and modes, but just doesn't have the playerbase to keep it fresh. This comes back to price. The game is too expensive to catch and keep attention from an audience that isn't seeking out these games in hopes of them being fun. The online is so dead, you have to either connect with players online via third party sites, or just play with bots for a couple days until you're bored out of your mind due to a lack of variation in skill or variety in play styles. It's now 2024. We had Super Bomberman R Online for free and it was great and accessible. We have most of the same content, but just in a $49.99 game with a half-baked singleplayer attached. There is a new game mode called "Castle" where one person defends multiple treasure chests against a horde of Bomberman characters. It's fun for a few games, but just doesn't hit the spot. The content and character customization doesn't require and microtransactions which is awesome, but it just falls on deaf ears with such a lackluster platform. It truly feels like another game that was pumped out to get a few dollars. I don't know if devs aren't given time or if there's just a lack of resources for these games, but man it hurts.I wish I could say I'd rather have a free-to-play Bomberman game, but it would consist of microtransactions and battle passes. Maybe that trade off is all we can hope for these days if we just keep getting games like this. Who knows, but it really feels like this franchise is sadly beyond saving at this point. Paying this much for something that feels like a cash grab Unity game half the time is absurd. I really wish I could recommend this game. I love the core gameplay of Bomberman. I love the crossover characters you can play as. I love the art style of the cutscenes. It's just that this game and the original Super Bomberman R were both massive letdowns at this point in terms of holding any value beyond playing multiplayer against bots for a few days. I hope we get at least one more good Bomberman game for a fair price that can get people playing it again.

Way to ♥♥♥♥♥♥' high, for me $50 as a bomberman fan wasn't too bad but if you're just casually interested in bomberman please just do yourself a favor and emulate the classics on the snes/pce/etc. I disagree with the sentiment that this game has a lot of "content", a long story mode due to grinding doesn't really sound fun to most people, and again price does not equal the amount of content in a game, games should not bloat themselves and should focus on the core of what makes them fun. _childDocuments_.review: Looking past the online timed rotations and lack of public lobbies, the story isn't that great either. I did a 100% completion and man it was a let down compared to the first Bomberman R in terms of gameplay. TL:DR, story is a grindfest and repetitive with forgettable boss fights.The story itself is basically on par with the first game, but the gameplay gets way too repetitive and grindy. Instead of collecting power-ups on a board, you collect experience and level up which gives you your typical upgrades (fire up, bombs, power glove, etc). You're thrown into huge board segmented in a metroidvania-esqe map where you'll need to rescue 100 Ellon for one world. You need about 80 in each world in order to progress the story and most of them just require you to run past a few enemies and collect them. You'll also be interrupted by an enemy ambush whenever you enter certain areas and dragged back to the base to protect it. It was fun for the first few times but needing to do it roughly 5 time in each world with little to no variance to the enemies made it feel like a slog so I ended up making a base that cheesed the AI so I could just sit back and watch until the timer rung so I could get back to the map. Also good luck getting back to where you were before the ambush because the game places you all the way back at the start. Not getting any of the warp points would mean you'll have to walk all the way back. All the enemies and blocks you destroyed respawn whenever you return to base or protect it from an ambush so you'll need to run past them or grind for exp on the trip back. You'll occasionally have to attack enemy bases too which are a cakewalk for the most part. I don't like the fact that if one of your teammates successfully grab the key and make it to the end, it counts as a loss. In regular castle mode rules this would result in a victory but I guess they wanted the player to achieve it?Boss fights were underwhelming and forgettable. Instead of a 1v1 into a giant boss fight for phase 2 like in the first game, it's only the giant boss fight and they only have 2-3 moves that are easily avoidable. You place bombs to damage them as usual, but now they added another mechanic where Ellons spawn in the arena. You'll have to gather them up and throw them into a cannon to deliver actual damage. You're basically staggering the boss with bombs then attacking with the Ellons which roam around the arena haphazardly. After the first world, you've pretty much experienced everything the story has to offer in terms of gameplay. Aside for an extra stage hazard thrown into the mix, you won't find anything that impressive.Along with the stuff I mentioned above there's no 2P co-op and you are only able to play as White. Major downgrade compared to the first game.So yeah. If you got a group a friends to play with and have some quick fun then sure this game should be fine. It's the usual Bomberman 4P mayhem. Stay away if you're looking for matchmaking online and the story.EDIT:Spent a lot of time doing online matches. Multiplayer is definitely still fun when standard mode is in rotation. Any other mode besides for Standard and Battle 64 is dead unfortunately. 99% of my matches in modes like Castle, Grand Prix, and sometimes even Battle 64 are full of only bots. Earlier today I spent a full rotation matchmaking for Battle 64 matches, and of them all, I only had 1 real player show up in a single match while the other 62 were bots. Every other match I had that rotation were only against bots.There are no skill based matchmaking from what I can tell. Casuals getting matched with Grandmasters which is expected considering the small player base this has currently. As of writing this review, KONAMI seems to have shifted to only having one mode in rotation which is sort of better than having it be a toss-up between two modes. Still would vastly prefer a lobby system though. A weird thing I noticed is that for Standard, 2 maps only ever appear in rotation. Old-school and Full Power. Old-school is exactly what it's called. Normal, no-frills, Bomberman. The Full Power map seems like this game's "1V1" mode when it's in rotation. Only 2 players in a match, first to 5, with max fire and bombs. Wish the other maps showed up in rotation too.TL:DR2: Opinion still unchanged. Don't buy. Online is mostly dead. Even if you do find players it's a 80/20 if they're a grand master or a similar skill to you if you're coming to this as a casual.

_childDocuments_.review: Super Bomberman R 2 offers much the same setup as the installments from the series' heyday in the early 1990s had - you have a Story Mode and a Battle Mode, which offers a selection of competitive games with settings that can be tailored to your liking. The idea is that you organically learn how to play across the course of the single-player game (and the game does a good job of teaching this), and then take those skills to the battlefield after that. Indeed, Battle Mode takes up more space on the main menu than any of the other options, so the game is clear from the outset about what the focus is. The menus are more similar to those of Super Bomberman R Online than the first Super Bomberman R, and might seem a little overwhelming at first if you skipped R Online; However, everything is clear and intuitive, so it won't take too long to pick it all up.Criticisms about the first Super Bomberman R have been taken on board here, and the story-mode seems to be A LOT bigger. R 2 plays out like a combination of exploring numbered areas in a manner somewhat similar to classic Monster Hunter, light RPG elements, and tower-defense, all whilst gathering up Ellons - cute collectable creatures who aid progress and open up fast-travel points and hidden puzzles. Unfortunately, the story can only be played through solo this time around, unlike the previous game which also offered couch co-op. These changes do mean that the story-mode gets off to a slower start than in the previous game, but it soon opens up once you get the hang of what the new game brings to the table.Battle Mode is as great as it's ever been. Unfortunately, the computer-players in solo battle-mode games no longer have a difficulty-setting, though, and they're as dumb as a stump - hopefully a future update will reinstate the ability to alter their level of challenge!A new battle-game called Castle debuts here, which combines Bomberman with tower-defense gameplay, and it works great. This is also integrated into the main story to represent the Bomberman Brothers' base-camp, which occasionally needs to be protected whilst exploring planets, as well as to represent the protagonists' attacks on enemy bases, which places the Bombermen on the attacking side instead.Much like the rest of the series (except for the notorious Bomberman Act: Zero - the less said about that the better...), Super Bomberman R 2 has a tone and feel much like a playable 1980s/1990s Saturday-morning cartoon, and the elements that make it this way are all on-point. The graphics are suitably cute-and-cuddly, and are full of neat little details (for example, narcissistic Black Bomberman is shinier than his other robotic siblings - a tiny detail carried forward from the previous two games). The cutscenes are fairly frugal animated-comic-book type affairs, but they're still plenty of fun to watch as they're full of personality. The voice casting for Bomberman and his family is absolutely perfect - each has their own quirks and they all bounce off of one another in fun ways; There's more emphasis on that this time around, which is very welcome because it's all so wholesome!The loading-times can sometimes be a little long, but I'm sure that this will be addressed in future updates, as this was also the case for the previous two modern Bomberman titles early on.The Bomberman series has its roots in a 1983 Hudson Soft title for a number of Japanese home microcomputers plus the British ZX Spectrum, and as such (barring a few fully-3D console installments in the late 1990s and early 2000s) has always been keyboard-friendly, and that continues to be the case here. Between this and the easy-to-understand controls, whether you prefer a gamepad or a keyboard you'll always be on even footing with opponents in this game. Gamepad configuration is handed off to Steam Input when playing on a Steam Deck, and will automatically pop up the relevant menus when you try to change it; This does seem to have the side-effect of the game not showing the correct controller glyphs, though.Cosmetic options were introduced to the Bomberman series back in the days of the Nintendo 64, but they've now been greatly expanded upon, with the official literature claiming that this installment has the largest amount of content in the series' history. There's a wide selection of clothing and antenna-toppers to dress your robot protagonists with, entrance/victory animations and banners for displaying your username for multiplayer games, and so on and so forth. You use an in-game currency called "Gems" (earned through playing offline and online multiplayer matches) to unlock these items, but don't worry, this isn't related to microtransactions - it's just a reference to a similar progression scheme in a Japan-only Nintendo Wii installment in the series.Going beyond cosmetics, the selection of unlockables also includes character cameos from various other franchises owned by Konami (including some of the Hudson Soft series that were taken in alongside Bomberman when Konami absorbed the company in 2012), all redesigned as Bomberman-style robots. Want to play as Castlevania's Alucard? No problem, he's here. Fan of Gradius? Vic Viper Bomber's your man. Metal Gear? There are multiple variations of Snake - all voiced by beloved voice-actor David Hayter, no less. Most of the cameo characters feel like they fit the tone and setting of the Bomberman series. However, that said, the Silent Hill Bomber characters feel quite out-of-place, both in terms of fitting the setting, and, though cutesyfied like the rest, also in terms of the game's age-rating (since Silent Hill isn't comic-bookish like, say, Metal Gear or Castlevania); Adult players who grew up with earlier Bomberman installments won't be bothered by this, but kids will be playing too, so it's at least worth mentioning.Whether Super Bomberman R 2 is worth the money mainly comes down to how much you'll get out of the multiplayer modes and the large amount of unlockable cosmetics, but that said, the launch price of £44.99 seems a bit too high. Even as a huge fan of the series who'll definitely spend a lot of time with the game over the coming years, I took advantage of a 20% pre-order discount when it was available, which I feel would have made for a much more reasonable base price. Hopefully the starting-price won't impact uptake of the online modes too much, and perhaps this is part of why cross-play with other platforms is included; This is off by default at the time of writing this review, but can be activated from the Settings > Basic Settings menu (EDIT: I got this wrong, oops! Oddly, the menu says "Enable cross-platform play" when it's already on!).I play on Linux, and the game ran perfectly via Proton on release-day, with no tweaks needed on my part. With the addition of a few extra controllers, it's also an excellent fit for the Steam Deck and its Docking Station due to the local multiplayer offerings. There are no anti-cheat and/or anti-tamper rootkits to punish legitimate customers here, and although this is most likely simply because Konami and their shareholders don't see Bomberman as being as big as their other franchises, this respect for users and their computers is nonetheless appreciated and I hope that it stays this way for future installments - I'm very happy to be able to play day-and-date with everyone else in the way that I prefer.For fans who've been waiting for years for some substantial new Bomberman content to get their teeth into, this game's for us. For those who like maze-chase games but somehow have never tried Bomberman at any point in the last 40 years, this is more experimental than how the series usually plays but it might still be your sort of thing. For the devs, thankyou - I haven't played anything so engrossing in a very long time. And, for Bomberman himself, happy anniversary, and congratulations on getting a game worthy of marking that milestone.Bombs away!

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly don't know where to begin with this one. Oh, wait, I know! "Super Bomberman R2 has more content than ever!" - This is a flat out lie. That would be Bomberman Generation () for Nintendo GameCube which had 5 battle modes (), and a Story Mode with 5 worlds that were 3 stages each plus a final level and boss.Nearly every Bomberman game before this one has had more content than this game in their single player mode alone unless you go by sheer gameplay hours, then this game is the longest only due to the sheer amount of padding and backtracking it has with lackluster uninspired level design, one dimensional characters and writing, only 5 unique enemies throughout the whole game that just get reskinned in each world, and only 4 bosses - not counting repeats in the Boss Rush area. The story mode, if you can even call it that, is written very poorly and serves mostly to train the player in Castle Mode - which the CPU is so bad at that you can win with little to no effort if you make use of just conveyor belts and blocks. Meanwhile the puzzles in the game range from effortless to completely opaque and unintuitive. Last but not least, the number of multiplayer stages are painfully low as well.Konami slapped the absolute bare minimum they could on top of the previously free Super Bomberman R Online in order to sell us this corpse of what Bomberman USE to be while having the audacity and gall to ask for the price of what feature length games go for. This should've honestly be priced to $20 at most and I'm being generous. To add insult to injury, the high price means an even smaller player base for online... and let me put it this way: When Super Bomberman R Online was free, we never once had a full Battle 64 lobby and I played it enough to get Grandmaster in every season before it was discontinued. Now they slap a $50 price tag on it, how much smaller do you think the lobby is gonna be now? Spoiler, I'm lucky to play against more 4 to 5 humans during any given match; the rest of the empty seats are filled with bots.I love Castle Mode, this is the only redeeming thing this title has to offer, however even that is ruined because Bean Bomber can cheese every castle effortlessly thanks to his ability to jump over any obstacle, of any size, with minimal cooldown.I WANT to see Bomberman succeed, as a lifelong fan I've been playing Bomberman since Super Bomberman 2 for the SNES, but Bomberman succeeding as a franchise can only happen if Konami would actually not be cheap for once and stop trying to gut him like a hollowed out ellonite husk.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a streamer, have been for years, and have done first-impressions reviews of review keys I've received. I rarely add a written Steam review to this, preferring my videos to stand on their own as a review, but Super Bomberman R2... My word. This triggered me enough that I need to summarize my experience as a review here. If you want to see the full gameplay experience I had, the video's over here: The Story Mode somehow manages to turn Bomberman power-up acquisition into a boring grind-fest, with you collecting medals to (slowly) fill an experience bar which then drip-feeds you power ups when you level up. Essentially, you break like 20-40 blocks, hoping for coins to spawn, and then eventually get 2-3 power-ups for that, and rinse and repeat. It also adds a weird base-defense mode to the story which feels simultaneously over-complicated and confusing (including having a very-intricate edit mode to customize your defense area), yet entirely too basic and scuffed at the same. There's a million things going on and to consider, but you basically just have to defend one particular objective, meaning you can ignore most of the details and just focus on surviving out the timer. And of course, the Bomberman Brothers from R1 are still here and still as sociopathically-noncaring as they were there, making them frankly-lousy characters and ruining the story imo. They're the same one-note characters with only White Bomber actually seeming to care about saving the day. Cutscenes are done in the same style as R1, with lazy cutouts and basic animation, and similar passable-but-basic dubbing (probably the same voice actors from R1).The battle mode technically gives you tons of customization and game modes and options, but there is a very LARGE catch to this. R2 is actually just the F2P Bomberman R Online reskinned and renamed, with the Story Mode tacked on and the whole thing sold for a frankly-unreasonable $50 USD. This fact, as well as this price tag, has kept people away from the game...which also means that the multiplayer modes are DEAD. On Steam, I believe the player count -capped- at 300 a little after release; when I played it mid-day the other day, it had merely 18 players online. I couldn't even find an online match and was forced to play with bots...which btw, had seemingly-real-player-like names, but basic un-customized Bomberman characters and clear bot behavior as well. While I understand padding some multiplayer games with bots for low-activity periods, I only think that's okay if it's made clear when you're facing bots. In R2, it's pretty obvious Konami were trying but failing to pass bots off as real players, which I consider to be a very tricky business practice I don't approve of.So yeah... R2 is an absolute disaster. R1 isn't very good either, but it's still at least a more streamlined and playable and ORIGINAL experience compared to the many tricky business practices behind R2.

_childDocuments_.review: Non-whiney launch day review (for online players):Pros:- I've played for less than half an hour and managed to get into several matches filled to the brim with non bot players.- Same fast paced action you're used to and want from multiplayer bomberman.- In the previous online, I was faced with the terrible lag that comes with Australian internet vs East Asian internet. This appears to have been worked on, as I feel like that has (almost) disappeared.- Castle mode has been surprisingly fun (although I still prefer battle 64).Cons:- Same game as the last. Same engine, same graphics, same music, same assets. (+Less lag for Australians IMO).- The major issue is a lack of choice for battle mode. I prefer to player the 64 player matches, as do most people in my opinion. Reading the reviews, most people seem to believe that you should be able to pick which mode you want, but the problem with that is, you'll end up with a more spread out player base and therefore more bots. Some people like the rotating modes that is currently in the game but the problem with that is a lot of people feel that if they can't play battle 64 right here right now, they'll refund the game/ not buy it at all.It's a shame because I feel there is a very simple solution to this: 4 game modes, each has a 25% chance of being picked. every player has a choice of their preferred mode, which slightly increases the chance of their mode being picked. (mode is chosen after players have been grouped). This will cause the majority that want their mode to have theirs more often while still having a chance to play the other modes, so that no one completely misses out, and you have the occasional refreshing break from the same mode.I recommend getting this game

name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration
detailed_description: Expand the Celebration with two DLC Packs! Atari and developer Digital Eclipse are excited to share a significant addition to Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration with two all new DLC content packs:  The Wider World of Atari and The First Console War. Each pack offers 19 additional games as well as a new interactive timeline, featuring more exclusive interviews, historical artifacts, and context for the games themselves. See more details about each DLC and their release dates below: DLC 1: The Wider World of Atari Release Date: 09/26/2024 The story’s not over yet! THE WIDER WORLD OF ATARI introduces a new timeline with more games, historical artifacts and video interviews that explore the creation of Atari games. Features: 19 new games including Berzerk, Atari Football (the first Trak-ball game), and underappreciated gems of the 2600 library New timeline with eight new video segments, including: Al Alcorn’s story on the creation of Breakout, the search for rare prototype games, and a spotlight on artist Evelyn Seto, who helped create the famous Atari Fuji logo DLC 2: The First Console War Release Date: 11/08/2024 It’s about to go down! Well before the current day console wars dominated social media and message boards, Atari's VCS and Intellivision collided in the first major video game rivalry in 1979. Features: 19 new games including several rare M Network prototypes available here for the first time New timeline video interviews with M Network programmer Jane Terjung, Activision’s David Crane & Garry Kitchen, homebrew programmer Dennis Debro, and historians Leonard Herman & Mike Mika Players can also acquire both DLC packs through the following methods: Atari 50: Expanded Edition DLC Bundle  includes immediate access to DLC 1 and will grant access to DLC 2 upon its release. Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration Digital Expanded Edition includes the full Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration game plus the Expanded Edition DLC Bundle. About the Game Join the celebration! Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration takes you on an interactive journey through 50 years of video games. At the heart of Atari 50 are the Interactive Timelines, which combine historical trivia, digital artifacts, over 60 minutes of new interviews, documentary footage, and playable games into one cohesive experience. When you encounter a game in the Timelines, you can immediately play it without losing your place. The massive selection of over 100 games spans seven different platforms: Arcade, 2600, 5200, 7800, Atari 8-bit computers, and, for the first time ever on modern consoles, Atari Lynx and Jaguar! Play the classics like Tempest 2000, Asteroids, and Yars' Revenge, or dive into some deeper cuts. Behind every game are the stories of Atari, what was happening at the company, and what went into the creation of the games and the hardware on which they ran, all told by the people who were there. Also includes six new games: Swordquest: AirWorld – Yes, you read that right: After nearly 40 years of waiting, the team at Digital Eclipse has created a new entry in the legendary Swordquest series, inspired by the design concepts of original Swordquest creator Tod Frye. Who will be the first to solve its mysteries – and finally complete the quest? Haunted Houses – The original “survival horror” game for the Atari 2600 gets a modern 3D voxel-based sequel, featuring more houses, more spooky situations, and more urns. VCTR-SCTR – This mashup celebration of the vector era of gaming combines the gameplay from Asteroids, Tempest, and other vector-based arcade classics into a single, continuous challenge. Neo Breakout – An amazing and addictive two-player competition that combines the best features of Breakout and Pong, with a modern graphic style Quadratank – The first new entry in the classic Tank series since 1978 combines features from the original games with four-player fun in team or free-for-all modes. Yars’ Revenge Reimagined – The Atari 2600 masterpiece gets a whole new look. Swap between original and modern graphics at any time!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a lightbulb moment when you realise - "Context". Context is what’s been missing from Retro Collections before now, and that goes for both the official and the less-than-legitimate packages.Let’s be honest, after 50 years of video game evolution most Atari titles have been dated to unplayability. I imagine glancing eyes will roll when they see the price, "£30! For a bunch of ROM's! In this economy!" but the games themselves aren't the sales pitch here, the sales pitch is In Atari 50 you’ll find the games presented on a chronological timeline alongside supplementary documentation. This documentation takes the form of advertising flyers, behind-the-scenes design plans and, most interesting of all, video interviews with the developers. Enough time has passed that these developers are talking truthfully and frankly about their experiences which makes for a refreshing change in today’s world of sanitised PR output. Seeing this evolution is rewarding because the absolute bare essentials of gaming are drip-fed and you get that  when something we take for granted was once absolutely groundbreaking, like music or colour sprites.If development war stories and archival archaeology aren't really your thing then Atari 50 does become more difficult to recommend. Aside from the inclusion of Lynx and Jaguar games this arguably isn't the most "complete" Atari set out there. Additionally, with no Activision representation, the scope of this collection is firmly about the history of "Atari as a company" not a comprehensive "experience of owning Atari hardware". An important distinction!Regardless, if these retro collections wish to remain relevant the blueprint on how to do so has been laid and the bar for quality has been raised. To any folks fascinated about the history of game development do not hesitate to pickup Atari 50 - Video games are an interactive medium, their museums should be interactive too.With my best wishes to Pong, I hope you’re having a wonderful 50th birthday.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: The various people who've owned the Atari license have released and rereleased a ton of collections over the years - a collection with Centipede, Combat, and all the other 2600/early arcade staples is pretty old hat and you'd be hard pressed to find someone with any interest in those games that hasn't played the heck out of them.Atari 50 isn't that, it's like buying a well-produced Criterion edition of their history. Instead of a bunch of roms with a front end, it's a extras packed museum exhibit with well edited and entertaining clips from people who were there (or prominent big fans). It's all set in a timeline that provides full context to the long story of a company that was at the top of the world and slowly fell apart. Without having played everything at this time, the emulation seems excellent across the various supported platforms (including Lynx and Jaguar) and I really like the various visual CRT-effect styles they do, which usually fall apart for me in collections like this, but really worked this time.And yeah, in addition to all the games everyone who is looking at this store page has played a million times, it digs deeper and gets the aforementioned Lynx and Jaguar representation, which includes the great and highly entertaining Tempest 2000. There's a ton of oddball games too like say, Ninja Golf a game that sounds like it was developed for Newgrounds, but was instead made for the 7800.Playing something like this that is so well and smartly put together makes me wish that this is the beginning of a series for long-running companies. A real treat for big nerds.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: I've bought this mostly for the Atari Jaguar (and Lynx) content. So will mostly cover those, rather than much else. So there are a variety of Arcade games, plus games from the Atari 2600, 5200, 7800, 800, Lynx and Atari Jaguar. The Atari ST/STE systems are almost completely ignored, as though they don't exist at all, in terms of there being any games available, but the Atari ST is mentioned extremely briefly in the history section. You can play and learn about the games and the history of the systems, or you can bypass the history lessons and select the games you want to play directly. There are two options when starting: OpenGL, or DirectX, I went for OpenGL (with Nvidia 2060) and it worked perfectly, whilst DirectX was glitchy in the menus. So skipping all the other systems, here are the Atari Jaguar games available, with brief ratings from when I originally played them on the console:- Atari Karts – this is almost impossible to get for a real Atari Jaguar, so it’s good to see here, but it doesn’t compete with Mario Kart (on the SNES) in terms of fun- Club Drive - this was terrible on the console- Cybermorph - this was okay- Dino Dudes - OK- Fight for Life - this was the "cool" looking game (at the time), but not much fun- Missile Command 3D - quite good- Ruiner Pinball - another pinball game, the likes of which you've seen on the Amiga 500 / Atari ST/E- Tempest 2000 - the best version of Tempest ever, this whole package is worth buying for this alone - Trevor McFur in the Crescent Galaxy - a forgettable sideways scrolling shooter that I completely forgot about, even after playing it, end level baddies are quite big thoughThere are obvious omissions from this list, including Alien vs Predator (not included), which was very slow on the Atari Jaguar, but very scary and fun to play. The other game that I think is worth playing on the Jaguar is Super Burnout, which was very impressive and very fast for the time (60fps), but again, not included with this compilation. Rather frustratingly each Atari Jaguar game you play has the controls assigned to different keys, perhaps there’s some reason behind this, but it does make switching between games frustrating. Atari Lynx games include: - Basketbrawl- Malibu Bikini Volleyball- Scrapyard dog- Super asteroids / Missile Command- Turbo SubThe best Atari Lynx games are missing, such as California Games, Paperboy, Robotron 2084, and of course as mentioned, all the great Atari ST/STE games are nowhere to be found (Lemmings, IK+, Stunt Car Racer anyone!?). There are also arcade versions of Missile Command, and Tempest, so there is some duplication. There are also 6 new games, but who wants to play new games, when they want to relive their childhood?The history included is really interesting, with lots of information including old adverts, old video interviews and features, as well as new stories, interviews and information. There is a lot to watch, and play here!

_childDocuments_.review: £30 for a bunch of old Atari games would frankly be a rip-off, but that's not what this is. This is essentially a virtual museum of the history of Atari. The presentation is great, it takes you year by year through the history of Atari, with original interviews, old footage, advertisements and all the other promotional stuff, and then of course there are the games. You don't just jump blindly into a game, it gives you a story of why that game mattered, so even if you don't like it, you can still appreciate it. As the title states this is a celebration of Atari not just a collection of games.

_childDocuments_.review: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration is what I'd consider to be the gold standard of game collections and retrospectives. Are all the games good? Frankly, no.. some really haven't aged well and are pretty terrible. That said, they are included and explained contextually within the history of Atari. But don't worry, there are great games in this collection, including many genuine classics and some that hold up surprisingly well! Also included are several new Atari games, mostly re-imagined versions of Arcade/2600 classics. Despite a few obvious gaps, such as the absence of any Atari ST games or certain externally licenced properties, it gives a fair sample of the different eras of Atari. The video interviews alone are incredibly interesting, especially within the section covering the startup and early years of the company. Contemporary TV and magazine advertisements, promotional material, box art, posters, concept art, design drawings, photos and internal company memos are also included. If you have any interest in the history and development of video/computer games, then you owe it to yourself to experience this collection.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: So, is this game a masterpiece? No, but it contains a bunch of (very old) masterpieces. It is like a book, a book about one of the most iconic computer game companies of all time. Atari was the first company that became synonymous with computer games in the early days before Nintendo pushed it off the throne (only to be knocked off by Sony in later years, but that's a different story). This game is an interactive book, detailing the cornerstones of the brand name "Atari". From its foundation in the early 70s, releasing the first ever arcade machines (Pong anyone?), to its later years with far more advanced arcade machines and various consoles and home computers. The brand name has gone through difficult times, first after the gaming industry crash around 1985, which lead to the splitting of Atari in a company making arcade machines and a company making consoles and computers. Later the arcade industry became smaller every year, with consoles being able to offer the same quality of gameplay for use at home. Atari also lost in the home computer war and their machines were, like nearly everyone else in the market, destroyed by the so-called IBM compatibles running MS-DOS and then Windows. After Atari also failed with their last console, the Falcon, the brand name was resold a few times and finally acquired by Infogrames to rebrand their company into Atari. During the last few years this new "Atari" has brought back some of their age-old classics in "Recharged" editions, which are actually quite nice little action games, especially for players who experienced the originals a long time ago. Atari also developed a game called Atarimania, which is a funny nostalgic trip using a large bunch of their old IPs and adding them in dozens of minigames into the new game - nothing stellar but a refreshing action adventure with challenging action sequences and bringing a smile on the face of seasoned players when the meet the heroes (or villains) from the old games. The Atari museum brings back such smiles, too, because it contains about 90 (!) full games from the old Atari catalogue. These are quite well emulated versions from the arcade machines, home computers and consoles. You can play now games made for the Atari VCS, the Atari 5200 and 7800, for the Atari 800, Lynx and for the Jaguar... only their most iconic computer, the Atari ST is completely missing. Of course only a small selection of all the old games once available for the systems are included, but it gives you a nice overview of how games looked and played like in the 80s. Young players might be shocked because of the low visual quality and high difficulty, but this is how games were when I was a kid. As an additional bonus, there are also six brand new re-imaginations of old games included. They are not emulated versions of the originals and look and play a bit more like current games, but keep in mind they are still based on the gameplay of old classics. Actually they are similar to the reimagined games released under the "Recharged" series. An interactive history book of the iconic "Atari" brand from 1972 to today, with about 90 emulated classics for various systems to let you actually play those games you read about. Kind of a museum with playable exhibits.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: The hype is well deserved, this is a fantastic compilation of old games - best ever maybe - but what you get out of it will depend on what you expect going in. If you, like me, were hoping for a fully playable encyclopedia of Atari history, you should know that's not what this is. It is not a textbook or a documentary. The games themselves are front and center, with just enough bite-sized snippets of info to put them into the most basic historical context. There's very little in the way of supplementary materials: some cover art, a very few internal documents, and a handful of non-revelatory video interviews with the people where were there. But the juiciest and most fascinating stories - the legal battles with Magnavox, the conflict between Bushnell and Dabney, Cyan Engineering and the development of the VCS, Bushnell's eventual ouster, etc - are glossed over or absent entirely. What's here is accurate, but it's so condensed it feels like you're skimming over the syllabus for a 101 level course. It is very much videogame history for people who have no interest in videogame history.Having THAT said, as a compilation of some of the most important and influential games ever made (alongside quite a few less essential ones), it may well be the best there's ever been. Emulation is flawless, weaved into slick new menus that make doing laborious things such as choosing game modes easy breezy. QoL features make some of the denser games such as Star Raiders more approachable and playable than they have been in decades. There's a few all-new "reimagined" reboots that are (mostly) neat but not deep or engaging enough to be standalone games. The two biggest treats are the graphically remastered Yars Revenge built on top of Howard Scott Warshaw's original VCS code (you can toggle between classic and modern graphics on the fly), and the never-before-released Swordquest: Air World, newly programmed from the ground up based on Tod Frye's original notes.  is what going above and beyond looks like.As a compilation, the care that went into this is astounding. It really is the new gold standard for retro game packages. I just wish there were more history in my history sandwich.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Just like in the 90's, when I purchased the Jaguar brand new, I purchased this compilation for one game.  Tempest 2000. The $45 CAD I paid for this compilation is a no brainer just for this one game. Got my ass handed to me on level 25.  Got angry.  Knew I was hooked immediately.  The grid hasn't seen the last of me.

_childDocuments_.review: Lets preface this by saying that I wasn't born during any of Atari's console (I'm 25) so I have no nostalgia for any of the games in particular. I have some experiences on a real 2600 (we found my dad console), but thats about it ( had a fun time, need to buy a new TV cable for it tho haha).So I'm not really in the target audience of this product, but I still bought it day one. Why? Well, the number of games is a really good argument. 104 or 3 (don't remember) is a huge number of new experiences. And while some games are very simplistic and a bit so-so, you get a ton of great fun and I think its really fun to revisit the past, and I personally love retro-gaming (more of a SNES guy tho lol). Also, finally good Jaguar emulation. Its one of those system I would like to own one day because its a really unique one.But I think the bigger selling point for my purchase was for the historical value. I love video game history, from start to today. Its a really fun subject to explore and I would hope some younger gamers gets interested in it. You get a treasure trove of fun facts, ads and interviews with the people that made Atari, well Atari (shoutout to the drugs interview, my favorite one, its really hilarious). The way it is set up is ingenious, its really like a museum display, you get to explore on your own rythm and stuff. I have 16-ish hours of game time and I just got through everything. There is alot packed here.So if you're not sure if you should pick it up or not, get it for the history. The games are great to have, but the museum feature and the love put through to it by the devs we're super apparent and fun. Also the 6 new games are fun too. Must buy for any fan of video game history.
