_childDocuments_.review: I'm lucky enough to have been a youngster who experienced the dawn of video games ( I remember queues of people waiting to play Space Invaders, Pacman and Galaxian, and was fortunate to have parents who thought the Grandstand video console would rock my world - how  right they were!).  Now as a middle aged man I feel lucky again to have Digital Eclipse and Atari take me back to my childhood.  Rose tinted glasses?  A big ol' pint glass of nostalgia?  Sure, why not. Because progress, boys and girls, ain't all that.. gaming today has lost the magic of anticipation, the unknown, the sheer delight of coming back from a store with a physical copy of a game you saved your pocket money for months for.. My first exposure to Atari was my friend's 2600 VCS  - we played Decathlon/Space Invaders/Donkey Kong for A WHOLE WEEKEND, and I'm talking 7am to 9pm for 2 days solid!  I can't tell you how happy I am that projects like Atari 50 exist, because the current climate of video game rights and live service delivery mean that the sacred art of video gaming will be lost to the dusty ether of cloud storage history.. I know, I know, I'm typing this on Steam which could be regarded as one of the biggest obstacles to gaming preservation, but I'm only a member here because of a little game called Half Life 2 which arrived at a difficult time in my life and renewed my faith in digital storytelling and the power of video games.. If there's one thing I would suggest that might remind GenZ that video games didn't start with Zelda or Call of Duty, it would be to insist that all current and new coders (regardless of whether they work at Microsoft or Nintendo or Electronic Arts or Rockstar or Ubisoft or Epic or an independent studio etc.) are required to code a game as a homebrew 2600 project.. that could be the great levellerPeace Out Friends
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I think this is a great retro gaming collection, with a few things that could be improved.  I've played this for over 7 hours at the time I'm reviewing it.   The emulation is very well done and there's a lot of games here.   All of the games I've played have worked flawlessly, especially the Jaguar games which are notoriously difficult to emulate well.  The other big attraction is the interactive history mode. It's a treasure trove of concept/production art, internal memos, photos, and interviews that are all well done.  It does a great job of capturing the history of Atari from it's founding through the Jaguar era.  There's a lot of funny moments in the interviews and it's a wonderful peek behind the scenes.  Taken as whole, it's worth the $40 asking price.  So, what could they improve?  First, there's a number of odd omissions in the games, and I'm talking about Atari owned games that they have the rights to.  It's understandable that 3rd party games (Activision, Imagic, M-Network, Parker Bros., etc.) aren't included due to licensing costs/issues.  But there are some Atari developed games that have been in previous collections that are oddly missing.  Take for example, Star Raiders.  The original version was for Atari 400/800, and the Atari 2600 port is by far the most well known.  Yet neither of those are here.  We get the Atari 5200 version, which while similar to the 400/800 version is probably the one the fewest people have played given how poorly the 5200 sold.  So, why that version and not the original or the one most people had.  Or better, yet, why not all three?  [edit] Since originally writing the review I've had a chance to try the 5200 version of Star Raiders included here.  It's not really advertised as a feature, but the 5200 version of Star Raiders is enhanced in this collection with an external HUD in the bezel that shows system status and the controls are mapped nicely to the controller.  It's a nice way to play Star Raiders, but it would still be nice to have the original Atari 400/800 and 2600 versions as they represent what the game was historically.The Atari 5200 and Atari 8-bit computer library are anemic with only 4 games each.  Where's the Atari 5200 versions of Asteroids, Centipede, CounterMeasure, all of the Atari 5200 RealSports, etc.  Same with the Atari 8-bit computer games, just a lot of odd omissions.  The part I'm really not a fan of, many of these games were in the Atari Vault, which they removed from sale 1 day before this collection went live.  There are currently no options for the arcade game difficulty.  They're configured one way and that's how you're going to play them, even if the game has settings for different amount of starting lives, different difficulty settings, different point targets for bonus lives.  They really need to open these up.  Especially because they provide the sales flyers for a lot of these games that tout these features.Another area for improvement is achievements.  There's only a handful and they're tied to the Reimagined games and a few Jaguar games.  Atari Vault had an achievement for most (all?) games for every console.   This seems like a simple thing to add and they really should add these for all the games.One last thing that was a bit disappointing were the display options.  The CRT filter isn't great.  There's much better examples in open source offerings like Stella that do an excellent job of emulating a CRT display, including adding interference. It could really do with some more options there.  I think what they have is works, but it could be so much more authentic.Overall, despite those issues, there's a lot of value here.  I'd like to see these things addressed, but I think the collection is definitely worthwhile in its current state.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Atari and Digital Eclipse have raised the bar for not only game preservation, but documentaries as well.The idea of a docu-game is really interesting to me, and this (along with Digital Eclipses other recent docu-games) is an incredible step to realizing the concept of a non-fiction, informational video game.In terms of gameplay, you have roughly 100 Atari games from the 70's to the 00's, along with 6 new games by Digital Eclipse made as spiritual successors or modernizations of a handful of choice games. Overall, if one was to entirely ignore the documentary aspect of this, you'd still have a good gameplay experience.In terms of "story", Atari 50's historical timeline is fantastic. Going through the cardinal history of Atari, and their rise and fall along with the game industry. Interviews, letters, promotional material, and the pertinent games being placed to be played at their places along the timeline. For example, in 1972, you've go interviews about Pong, development and promo materials, and along with all that, a prompt to play the game for yourself as you learn about it, who made it, and its place in history.It also really holds its own as a local multiplayer game, with so many great 2-4 player games in the package. From co op to competitive. I love this, and I really, really want to see more like it. If you have *any* interest in classic games, and/or the history behind them, this is absolutely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: A lot of love went into the making of this, I was around 9-10 years old went my Dad got us a Atari 2600 then a few years later a 5200 that's when I was introduced to Star Raiders "great game" and the awful 5200 non centering joystick, it wasn't a problem until I was playing Miner 2049er which was impossible to pass level 4 but now thanks to this and my "submarine grade" logitech gamepad I have finally made it to level 5... only took 45 years.  Big thanks to all the programmers back in the day at Atari and the Dev's that put this together!   10/10

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a STAR RAIDERS fan, look elsewhere, it's broken.First off, I  think they did a fantastic job on the Star Raiders port,the controls are spot on, it works seamlessly with a controller,all the keyboard controls were mapped brilliantly, great job.But....Although the NOVICE and PILOT missions work well, those who adorn the game willselect WARRIOR or COMMANDER and sadly, these higher levels are broken.Once you get down to the remaining 8 enemies or so on the map, the difficulty ramps up to insanity.Come out of a warp, get plummeted by 3+ meteors in a row.Photons gone.Rinse and repeat until you just give up, it's relentless, and I've yet to be able to finish a game on COMMANDERlevel because of this.I've tried all the different speed modes, original, opengl and direct3d, nothing helps, it's broken.Another minor gripe is that the "Destroyed Engines" mode is just the "Damaged Engines" and barely impactsyour speed.I really hope that this is patched, I'll gladly revise the review once it is.Everything else is great, the arcade ports are fine, the controls are practically 1:1 in the trackball games,they all feel just like the arcade (unlike Atari Vault, cough cough).The Jaguar games are a blast, T2K still rules. I would have loved to see AvP, perhaps a future DLC.But the main reason I spent $40 was for Star Raiders, one of my all time favorite games, and in it's currentstate, I feel like I've wasted my money, sadly I spent so much time troubleshooting it, my refund window is gone.I'd say wait for this on a heavy sale and if you're a die hard Star Raiders fan, don't do it until it's patched!And still no word from the developers on any patches.........you guys out there?!?

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really well-done anthology and I'm impressed with the amount of care and effort that went into producing it. You start off with a history of Atari, broken down into 4 or 5 channels (arcade, console, pc, etc). Each channel has a timeline with information on the company and its decisions - this includes videos from prominent personnel, media like game boxes (rendered in 3d) and advertisements, and notes and pictures from the time. At the points where games are presented, you can jump in and play them from there. The reproduction of these images/videos is really good and it's a wonderful trip back for anyone that recalls it fondly.Skipping the historic timeline, you can jump right into the games, which are all accessed through the interface. You can sort by type (arcade, console etc), or name or chronologically. In my opinion the arcade games are the star of the show. The games are rendered faithfully, and you can not only play them, but often see things like the original cabinets or advertising materials. Within the game, you often have specific options like displaying the cabinet/screen overlay art (includes authentic looking scratched glass in some cases!), remapping controls, screen width (original, etc). Games allow for controller or keyboard use. Multiplayer is a little weird, but does work. To get true multiplayer to work (meaning each player is using their own controls, and not just swapping one set on alternate turns), you need to have 2 controllers plugged in.  The game does allow remote multiplayer through steam's "Let's play", but the host machine will need to have more than one controller installed or the players will share the same controller (which might be fun for some games). Natively though, the game doesn't support remote multiplayer, which is perhaps the largest negative for me.The arcade selections are perhaps the best of the bunch - a lot of good old atari games here, from legends like Asteroids, Pong and Lunar lander to some of its later classics like Tempest, Missile Command, Major Havoc and Centipede. The 2600 titles are probably the worst - there's some nostalgic factor, here, and the games are presented well (with 3d box models and manuals), but some of these games were horrible when they were released and the years have not been kind. I'd have wished for more 400/800 games, some ST games, and less repetition (did we really need to see missile command on every platform?), but all in all, the selection presented is pretty good. Still, it's a really good anthology and packaged exceptionally well. While I haven't played all of the games yet at time of this writing, I've had no issues loading/playing any of the games. I'll update this review if I encounter anything.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: As a collection alone, it's hard to recommend at the price point. Some of the Reimagined games softlock (notably on Neo Breakout - crushers can get trapped balls lodged in bricks which still need to be broken to progress but lose collision), but they're still a respectable addition.Fortunately, this is more than just a collection. As many others have pointed out, it's a well-presented historical exhibit that may as well be from a museum.  At that, it's an exhibit I hope is imitated by other storied companies. It feels almost natural, like this is supposed to be how these things are handled.$40 for a pass that doesn't expire to a nicely arranged exhibit with an interactive section that lets you come and go as you please. While I might not have grown up with these games and some might not have aged well, I still feel that this is worth the price of admission.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: For someone who was around ten years old, when the neighbor kids got a 2600 (the Sears version) for Christmas...this has a lot of nostalgia, and interesting content for the now-mature mind...who didn't know how terrible most of these games were at the time. We had no frame of reference! Interviews with old dudes (older than me!) talking about their craft in the early days, are quite fascinating.If you were into these games (and arcades) in your younger years, and later shared a similar passion for the world of personal computers...there is a TV series you must watch, called "Halt and Catch Fire." It's a show about people working for a company that made IBM-compatible personal computers in the 80s. If you're a computer nerd, you'll love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: An absolutely stand-out project. This is part documentary, part fan-tribute, part game collection. The level of effort put into it should be a benchmark for any similar projects in the future; the amount of high-quality scans of original materials, the level of effort put into including 3D recreations of many relevant props, the quality of the interviews, and overall presentation are all great. The fact they went so far as to create original re-imaginings and sequels to several games in the collection is really cool too.I'd be lying if I said I'd rate most of the games highly, the 2600 collection in particular was fairly dire, but there's also still some fun to be had with the likes of Basketbrawl, Fatal Run, Tempest, and the  versions of Asteroids, Breakout, and Missile Command included. Genuinely a really wonderful way to celebrate the history of Atari while also acknowledging the mistakes that lead to its eventual decline as a major player in the games industry. Would love to see this project taken as a template and used for other companies in the future, particularly Midway.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: After the most recent DLC update, I think I can finally recommend Atari 50. For Context, my original review criticized Atari 50 for most of the new games not being that great (with the exception being Vctr-Sctr), the existence of multiple emulation issues / design choices that hurt the overall package, and the fact that Atari Vault was delisted when this game came out, despite the fact that it contained different games. That all remains true, and I really hope that Digital Eclipse addresses the emulation issues / design choices that I noticed (The wobble effect on the Vector Arcade games where the lines aren't consistently drawn in the same place, making the games look like they're playing on displays that need service, and the pitch issues on certain Raster Arcade games where certain sound effects aren't at the correct pitch; an easy example of this is Centipede, where the sound of firing is an octave higher than it should be, for reference compare it to the Centipede firing sound effect that is used in the menu theme, which is pitched correctly).With that all being said, while the emulation issues remain true, I've come to appreciate more of the content on offer. Jaguar games are great to play here, and every game here has a reason to be here: there are lots you have heard of, and some you probably never knew existed. In addition, the interviews and artifacts from Atari's History serve to retell the history of both Atari and the video game industry in a way that's never been done before.Next, the paid DLC came out, and $8 for Berzerk & Frenzy is an absolute steal. I'm usually not keen on video game company / property acquisitions, but Atari's rereleases of Berzerk and its ports in different formats has shown that they are good stewards of the IP. In addition, they reworked the controls of Arcade Berzerk so in addition to playing it normally, you can also play it like a Twin-stick shooter, which is an awesome new take on the classic, albeit it takes away from some of Berzerk's challenge.Overall, the game is good, and I'd recommend picking it up, even if it's just for Berzerk. However, I'd still like Digital Eclipse to fix the emulation issues / design quirks on some of the games already in this collection. Also please put all of the games in Atari Vault in this collection so the issue of exclusive content can be put to rest.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: "Atari 50: The anniversary Celebration" is more than a mere game. It is a very well done, thought out, interactive museum. To say it was a history buff's dream come true would be a severe understatement...especially when it gives you the opportunity play most of the games of note in the company's history.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very cool collection of games, and while I think there could have been MORE documentaries and interviews, there is still a lot here, a lot more than with most classic game collections on the market right now, so I think it's a big step in the right direction. It reminds me of some of those Atari/Activision/Taito/Namco PS1 collections back in the day.I think game preservation is very important, and this game does a great job at that, and deserves support. I will say however, that my second point of disappointment (the first being that I wish there was MORE video interviews/documentaries, as what's here is very well done), is that it's kind of a bummer that there aren't any Activision games here (maybe one or two? I don't think so though). Now, I get it, Blizzard Activision are going to be a bunch of C-units on a good day, and would probably try to strong-arm the devs out of some cash to hand over the rights to publish some of them, but surely there has to be *SOME* semi-reasonable deal that could have been reached, yeah? Just  a damn shame to not have a near perfect collection of games here.Speaking of which (and I know this would be a stretch), it would have been cool to have gotten some of the notoriously bad licensed games, like Spider-Man, Ghostbusters, and ESPECIALLY the legendary ET game. Now, I know that Hollywood would be their typical soul-less subversive, money-grubbing selves and try to charge out the ass to hand over the licenses for these games, but I have the strong inkling that the devs here didn't even bother to try. Just a shame. I'm not saying it would be easy, but I think it would have been possible.Anyway, the presentation here is awesome and deserving of praise, but short of the complaints and disappointments I listed above, I do think this game is a solid purchase.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: This is quite possibly one of the greatest game compilation releases I've ever seen. As someone who has been using emulators for over twenty years now I often think "what does this offer me compared to what fans provide for free" when it comes to these type of releases. The big thing about this that separates it from the others along with fan projects is that it's less of a game compilation(though it is one and a great one) and more of an interactive museum about an era of gaming history frequently ignored in favor of the NES onward. There are so many fascinating interviews, historical documents, and overall insight into the history of Atari and video games as a whole from the 70s and early to mid 80s that makes this a must buy if you're either an Atari fan or someone interested in the history of video games.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: The 8-bit era of Atari was before my time. I started the next generation with the Sega Genesis and Super Nintendo as a young toddler. I still respect and have enjoyed iterations and ports of Atari 8-bit games over the years. What hasn’t been done well is anything outside of bundles of seemingly random collections. They’re nearly countless at this point and have spanned to nearly every console imaginable. Atari anniversary collections, various Atari-themed packs, and various retro packages with fancy UIs or presentations. However, no single retro package has been as cohesive or beautifully created as Atari 50. Even Sega’s recent Genesis Collection with its retro 90’s bedroom and bookshelf display can’t beat this.The entire game is presented like an interactive history lesson. You go through four timelines. Atari’s origin story and their arcade routes. You get to see photos, printouts, commercials, and interviews with various Atari developers and industry veterans such as Tim Schafer (Psychonauts) and Cliff Bleszinski (Gears of War). These are presented in chronological order. A game is presented when its release comes up in the timeline. Some games have cover art, photos, and even comics underneath them to view. As you advance in the timeline you get a feeling like you’re playing an interactive museum tour. There are no fancy 3D menus or anything, but the clean and simple UI works well. There are a few surprises peppered in like unreleased prototypes and Digital Eclipse’s own recreations of iconic games like Yar’s Revenge and Haunted House.As you advance to the home console and PC timeline things get more interesting. You will eventually get to Atari 5200 and 7800 games which are a bit more advanced. You will also get to play a few PC games for the Atari home computers. Then you will finish up in the 90s with the Atari Lynx and Jaguar. Sadly, there aren’t many games in this timeline, and the biggest issue with this entire game is the lack of third-party titles. You only get to play Atari-published and own games. That’s very limiting, and while I understand this is Atari’s own history there are many games that helped make their systems great outside of internal developers. The few Jaguar games range from Cybermorph to Tempest 2000 and Missle Command 3D. They aren’t great, but interesting to dive into. That’s another thing about this whole collection. Very few games are fun to play longer than five minutes. Some are pretty clunky and bad. This isn’t a “greatest of” collection which I really appreciate. You will most likely go back to the more fun games like Missle Command, Centipede, Millepede, Tempest, or their latest versions in this game. You get special bezels, backgrounds, overlays, and control options for every game as well. You can also select various modes and some games support save states which is cool. You also get a digital view of every manual for the game including the arcade operator’s manuals. They didn’t leave anything out.By the time I spent around 5 hours in the game, I got to the end of the timelines. You can go back and play any game in the library view and pick your favorites. These games run really well and look great, but many gamers who didn’t grow up in the 80s will probably find this nothing more than a history lesson. Even more, will find pretty much every game boring or uninteresting. However, that’s not a knock to the games, but just a warning to younger audiences. Anyone younger than 30-35 will most likely not find this game interesting or fun. If you have a curiosity about Atari’s history or games then this is the best place to get that. If you have an itch for trying out 8-bit games or want to go back without emulating anything then this will give you nearly 100 games. I also appreciate how few ports and copies of the same game are in here. Each game was hand-picked and placed with relevancy.Overall, Atari 50 is one of the best retro packages you can ever play. Telling an entire developer’s history with games placed in their correct time slots and even including unreleased games and reimaginings of some is just fantastic. The videos are entertaining and interesting and you will learn a lot. There are so many details added from commercials, print ads, posters, manuals, customizable controls, save states, and more. It’s a complete and cohesive package for Atari lovers out there. Just be warned that there are no third-party games and less of the 90s stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: "This game should belong in a museum" - Indiana JonesNot only do you get a documentary on the genesis of gaming, there are over a hundred games that comes with it. The documentary's honesty deserves 300 thumbs up. All the glory days are covered, and it doesn't tip toe around the bad decisions either, namely, the broken 5200 controller, the video game crash of 83, the E.T landfill and the Jaguar.If I have one recommendation : We know E.T was bad, but please include it in the collection, it's a cult classic by this point.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: This feels more like a history lesson of video game, but in a fun way. Not even boring at all.Lots of historical facts with interview videos, photos of variant products, cool retro ads, instruction manuals with original package designs of each games and detailed descriptions with accurate timelines.We can gain knowledge while also playing the very first (....okay, let's be real. The first video game system is actually Magnavox Odyssey, but Atari is more popular at that time. So, yeah...)  and the most best video games from the earliest days of Atari to the modern era ones.Thank you, Atari. For being a pioneer in the history of gaming. :3Nowadays photorealistic games or insanely lifelike VRs can never be existing without: Pong time!b(^_^)d
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Might be the most comprehensive and fascinating collection I've ever played. Other game collections often just have the games and some concept art unlockables or something of that nature. They went above and beyond for this one, producing several new reimaginings of older games, creating a version of a game that never got released based on original design documents, and putting in all new documentary-style footage and interviews from across Atari's history. If you have even the slightest fondness for Atari, or just love gaming history, this is an amazing showcase of it in interactive form.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: This is by far the greatest "classic game compilation" that has ever been made. Instead of just a collection of ROMS, Atari 50 greets you with a digital museum and tour of the history of the company that helped create the industry, with games lovingly emulated for you to simply hop into or enjoy as a part of their ride. Even if you're not a fan of 2600ish era retro gaming, if you at all care about the founding years of video gaming as a whole, I cannot recommend this highly enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: While the idea of the ""game"" itself really peaked my interest, It is not executed properly. There are several games here that do not work at all. Quadratank doesn't let you play the game. All you can do is put AI enemies and watch them fight. In the Fire Truck game after a collision you can just pass right by the buildings without collision. Even the Remade version of Breakout doesn't hide your mouse. I want to cut the developers some slack for building this without a game engine I assume. It's Atari that I'm disappointed in for it's lack of quality control over something that could've been flawless.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: If you try to report a bug mad community managers will erase you and call you a liar and will make insane claims which are disproven by their own advertising. They they will block you and re-edit all their own inflammatory posts, entirely changing the replies. But steam always marks edited posts. Digital Eclipse is a scam.This release from Digital Eclipse is a new form of media. It was conceived as a merge between a reference book on the publisher, and an actual anthology of games. But since not everything present in the encyclopedia is playable, the concept doesn't actually work. It's not an all-encompassing absolute definitive final word on the topic.But this can and should be treated as a separate collection of games. There's a button in the menu to jump directly to the one-dimensional list of games. And there are a lot of games, so this GUI sucks. You have to go through each of the games one by one. At the fastest you can skip one letter at a time by pressing Shift+=. So there's still 26 letter in the latin alphabet plus some numbers.This software offers easy to use emulation, which is especially important for the arcade games.The rendering options are very limited. And as an attempt at an interactive reference book, this is not a series of emulated or re-enacted games, but a separate app baked into a 16:9 render. So if you have a vertical 4:3 screen, CRT or not, you can't play these properly, without severe windowboxing. The arcade games have dip switches options. There are no rebinds, even when the default controls make barely any sense. In most of the games the input lag is insane. At a light tap it can even refuse to register. You can press a button then release it, and the game will react after you've already released the button. In the 18 years i barely ever talked about input lag, and this is the most insane i've ever seen. There are save states even in the score-attack games, but not in the modern games in this collection. Sometimes it crashes. 3/10 3/10 3/10 3/10 3/10 2/10 0/10 IT DOES NOT WORK 2/10
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: On a first glance, this may seem like a compilation of Atari's greatest and best, presented in a way that almost feels like an interactive documentary, with developer interviews, quotes, pictures of memorabilia and pretty much everything you may want to know about Atari on its heyday. However, appearances may be deceiving. This is, in reality, Ninja Golf with extras. The only game that matters here is Ninja Golf, nothing else on this collection matters. Not even Tempest 2000 can change my mind. Hell, not even the Berzerk DLC can change my mind. This is a Ninja Golf rerelease.TL;DR: Play Ninja Golf.Jokes aside this is an incredible showcase of videogame history, compiling everything in this company's messy history. From successes to failures, everything is here. The fact that it includes Atari Jaguar and Lynx videogames speaks of its quality and commitment to accuracy. This is not a mere game collection, this is a videogame documentary where you can actually play the games they're talking about. Absolutely brilliant and highly recommended for retro enthusiasts and even those who are just curious about videogame history. A must have in every dedicated gamer's collection.But of course, the true important thing here is that it includes Ninja Golf. Everything else is a plus of course, but Ninja Golf is the catch here. So go ahead, get this and score some hole in ones and kick sharks in the face. They just don't make them like they used to, do they?
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: THIS is exactly how a retrospective collection should be done. Sublime timeline-based navigational system, with everything from interviews, design documents, official advertisements, hell even some scans of inter-company correspondence (written and typed!). I already knew a lot about the history of Atari from books, yet I'm still learning a lot of new things about their rich history. To top it all off, as you come to the games in the timeline you can immediately play them, and they even include zoomable instruction booklets (even arcade titles)! P.S. You don't have to go through the timeline at all if you don't want, one button brings up the games only menu. But don't do that, you'll have more fun "discovering" the games while learning, I promise.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Let me get one thing out of the way that I want to make perfectly clear. I'm really not a big fan of old school Atari games. I'm talking mainly on the ones developed or published by Atari for the 2600. Not knocking some of the quality 3rd party stuff found on Atari 2600. A lot of that was good. Especially from the likes of Activision. But Atari themselves released a lot of pretty basic stuff. That's not to say it was all bad. They had some fun titles scattered. But it was mostly pretty bland. This is one of the reasons I could not without any good conscience recommend the previous Atari Vault collection that was delisted and replaced with this title. And because of this I had my doubts on Atari 50 being any good.I'm glad I was wrong. Atari 50 is fantastic. They trimmed a lot of the fat from the 2600 line. Not to say they got rid of all the duds. Some of those are still here. As it stands they dropped the 2600 collection down to about 50 titles (after the free update added a few more titles), and expanded their arcade collection by a good amount adding in some really fun titles. They also added in games from the 5200 and 7800, as well as the Lynx and Jaguar, and some of the Atari home computers as well. In total over 100 classic titles. Much like before they are not all winners, but there is a lot more to be exicted about with this one, such as Tempest 2000, Cloak & Dagger, Ninja Golf, Miner 2049er and more. What's more is that for this collection Digital Eclipse actually did some remakes of a few of the titles such as Haunted House, Yar's Revenge and more. They even did a new Sword Quest title! The real winner here though is not the games. Instead it is the overly impressive interactive documentary style wrapper that holds everything together. Digital Eclipse really nailed this. You can either just browse the game list at will, or what I'd really recommend doing is going through the documentary which is loaded with documentation, scans, blurbs, video interviews, old footage, and a lot more spanning nearly the entire history of Atari's console and computer legacy. At different points in the documentary you will also come across games that are in the collection ready to play. It's a really novel way to do a retro compilation and it just works perfectly and adds value to this collection. I'd love to see other companies take note when handling their own compilations and maybe give us a similar type of presentation on the legacy of their own games.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Makes me feel closer to my dad and to my father-in-law, whose main memory of and exposure to videogames remains mostly this particular pantheon and period of gaming.This particular release is nostalgic not only in-and-of-itself but also because I had a similar Atari collection cartridge back on my GameBoy Advance SP as a kid. And I have fond memories of similar collections like various Namco Museums and Midway Arcade Treasures and Intellivision Lives! and whatnot on assorted platforms.Overall, I love the presentation here. I’ve barely scratched the surface, there’s so much content, and more added semi-regularly even still, it seems. Works well enough on Steam Deck—not so much the museum and documentary and photo history aspects though, sadly.I got it as part of a Humble Bundle, luckily. I don’t think I would’ve been too eager to spend more than $20 on this by itself, so I spent that for this and several other games. I did still want it at $28 on sale at points, but I’m glad I waited. If you’re reading this far into my review, I think you already know that you’ll be glad to play this collection whether you wait for a deeper discount or not.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: My first console was an Atari 400 so, I may be a bit partial and nostalgic.However. its not like I haven't played these games in forty years.This is a truly amazing release that I hope other developers follow.It's a documentary, a museum, and a games collection. They meld into brilliance. This is well worth the price of admission. You get documentary segments interwoven with artifacts, internal documents AND THE GAMES.Did you just watch a segment, read the internal documents from development? Yeah? Why not give the game a quick go!?!Tons of games spanning the beginning arcade to the Jaguar, with all the tasty history thrown in.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: I fully expected to be bored of it in about an hour or so, but this whole presentation is actually a great way to present older material like this. This has got to be one of the best uses of an interactive timeline I've ever seen. I loved all the movies and promotional material. Of course, the games are there too, but they are just another part of the entry. I don't know about you, but I'm probably not going to dump 40+ hours into playing Canyon Bomber, but it's great to hear the stories and see the beautiful box art and then dive in for a brief nostalgic trip back in time.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: The sheer love and care put into this package is to be commended. This sets a new standard for how these collections should be produced. Digital Eclipse went so far as to resurrect prototypes, build an unmade game in a series, re-imagine classic games, and on top of it all create their own Jaguar emulator because a decent one doesn't really exist.There are a thousand different ways to play these games but this is a brilliant way to give these games (and the people who made them) context for why they matter which in my opinion is much more valuable than just playing the games themselves.I hope this does really well for Digital Eclipse because I would love to see this same presentation done to every company or game property they can get their hands on. Bravo! You made me care about Atari in 2022 and that's more than Atari themselves can say.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who grew up playing Atari games on the original hardware from the 80's and 90's this is a very, very nicely packaged collection with gorgeous photography and overall presentation. It feels like you stepped into a museum of Atari. It is by no means a "complete Atari" collection but it does provide nostalgia seekers young and old with something special to enjoy for hours on end.  I hope more games from the 8-bit computers and 16/32 bit ST era get added (Atari didn't release much in the way of games for the ST per se, but some classics did make it to the early days of the ST).
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Rather than a slap-dash compilation of emulated games thrown together, this is a comprehensive time capsule of Atari's history, from arcade games to consoles faithfully restored for the modern age, complete with a timeline of highs and lows from the company itself along with interviews and behind the scenes of some of the most prolific games. Absolutely worth your time for over 90 games across several console eras, as well as some new additions by Digital Eclipse themselves.Pleasure.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Its not perfect yet. Needs updates and tweaks.The menu is brutal, the color palettes, the presentation, the perfect artwork in 4k of the game deserves game of the year. The sound and quality of the videos its really professional, it beats videos ive had seen on youtube or netflix.Its a tear dropping of nostalgia in a magical way, not a fan of new atari games, always been a 2600 fan and have a great rooster of games. Some are missing like Galaxian, Pitfall, joust or defender.Im not sure but i counted more than 100 games. Its a steal for this price of 15 dollars.The badFor example the Voileyball game makes weird sounds randomly. The sticks are kot perfectly tune up. This is a shame.Emulators like Stella or Retroarch does a better job, sometimes you die for a bad input. And these emulators does a great job in emulating the original joysticks and improving them, here is a big miss, some tunning in future updates will make the game a perfect 100 score.Games like Warlords or pong are super hard to control with an xbox series x controller.Also the remade game Block lags in versus mode player vs player. Hope they fix it.If you are a Gen X gamer this needs to be in your library.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: I grew up with a lot of "retro collection" titles back in the 2000's and 2010's. I had Namco and Atari plug and plays, and I played the heck out of things like Namco Museum. All I can say is, 12 year old me would have loved Atari 50 to death. The way this is presented feels like what I can only describe as 'an interactive documentary,' which is something I have NEVER experienced playing a game. Atari did an incredible job preserving their history, which is something that will likely never be said for companies like Nintendo. As someone with ADHD, the excitement that the games (especially the older ones) give are usually short-lived, and I quickly move on to the next, but this is made up for by the extensive history it explains. Most game collections usually have the history lessons in the extras menu, but here it's front and center, easily accessible to anyone interested in learning about game history. Color me impressed, Atari.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: If I didn't have memories of going to my cousin's house on holidays and playing for hours, it might be a harder recommend.  I was showing my kids the games and they basically didn't understand why I liked it so much.   I personally think this is wonderful and I am having a good time remembering times from my childhood.  Thank you very much for this!
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: I was very young during the Nintendo Entertainment System years so I missed the excitement of this Atari era. As I got older I started appreciating the retro games more and more. This collection is the best tribute I have seen to an era of gaming that I missed and really gives me a much deeper appreciation of the time. I have played several retro game collections. This goes above and beyond.I used to find the pre-NES games to be far too low tech but hearing the excitement about building these games within the tech limitations of the time from the people that were there and also seeing the very cool retro marketing has opened my eyes to something beautiful in gaming history. So even if these games are not as complex as the stuff that came after, that's part of the beauty of them. Highly recommended for original Atari fans or people that are curious about the era that find themselves with a deeper appreciation of retro games.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic both as a collection of games (and modern re-imaginings of games) that would not be accessable elsewhere in so authentic a form, and as a museum of Atari (and therefore videagame) history, with an amazing selection of key people to interview. You would be doing yourself a disfavor not to buy this title.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Digital Eclipse did a great job on the emulation for the Atari Jaguar, offering up the best, most playable emulated version of Tempest 2000 in this collection that I've played compared to the real cart (which is still superior, but the version herein is very, very good). For this game alone, I was interested in playing this collection, but then pepper in a bunch of Atari gems like Asteroids, Asteroids Deluxe, Centipede, Milipede, Missile Command, the original Tempest and some rarities like Akka Arrh, and that's just two categories. They have a bunch of Atari 2600 and a small few (a complaint, really) of the Atari 5200. There are more Atari 7800 titles and a few Atari Lynx, another one wished they had more, but there's plenty to play here including a few new games with the standout for me there being Vctr-Sctr.Add to this the timeline history and several very well done videos from former Atari employees talking up the good ole days, and this one scores historical points galore. Would love to see more collections like this from other publishers (cough, cough, Nintendo). For those that love a trip down memory lane with their collection of games, many with tons of replay value.It's not all great here, like they are missing some publishers that were noteworthy with Atari (ahem, Activision) but it *is* an Atari collection.  There is enough to keep any retrogaming fan busy for quite some time.  I see a number of my friends have this on their wishlist but haven't pulled the trigger and bought as of this writing. Get this in the next big sale (Winter, Summer, whatever). I paid full price for it and feel like it's worth every penny.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: I wish I could go back to the Arcades of old and the consoles of my past.....whoa....wait...what, you say I can, in Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration I get to relive the fabulous history of the icon of the industries Golden era.  Visit great memories tucked away in the corners of the game designers themselves, play the games, play some more, learn some more, this game offers an great amount of both.  A keeper for any Arcader, and a welcomed piece of history for almost anyone else, I highly recommend Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: yNot going to lie, a bunch of the games in this collection are just terrible.  That being said I was surprised at how much fun I had with the games.  I don't think this is meant to be approached quite how it is presented (consuming the games in their chronological order as you experience the amazing historical aspects Digital Eclipse has woven for us), rather absorb and enjoy the history, look at the boxes and art, then play the games you would have played had you been there eyeballing them back in the day.Loved this package.  The presentation is an obvious evolution of the SNK Collection.  Problem is, I'm going to expect this all the time!
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Atari 50 is tremendous, and sets a new standard for how a video game collection/retrospective should be handled.  Atari 50 is an interactive timeline containing both documentary style entries and emulated games.  There is so much great historical content including old interviews, tv news clips, newspaper articles, photographs, design documents, etc, to go along with recent interviews with both the people who were there, and people in the game industry now, who were influenced by Atari along the way.  Then, right after learning all about a game, and its development, and how influential it was, you can jump right in and play an excellently emulated version of it!  The visual design of the interface is fantastic, as is the sound, there is really almost nothing to complain about.  The period of time covered is expansive, documenting the entire history of the company, as is the swath of playable games.  You get everything from Pong to Jaguar games, and everything in between.  Top it off with some very well done modern takes on some Atari classics, and you have what basically amounts to a perfect package.  I enjoyed this so much, and I am so impressed.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: I'm just 50% in of the first chapter, but after playing the Lunar Lander/Asteroids/Tempest hybrid I felt compelled to write a small review. Really amazing collection of old games with excellent remakes, stunning presentation and all the videos and history snippets are interesting for any videogame fan. Although I'm younger and didn't grow up with an Atari, I've always been interested in the company, legacy, and games. This collection is packed with info that I didn't know. Amazing job to the Digital Eclipse team and Atari, can't wait to play more.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Atari was my first gaming love, but prior to now, I would play an Atari compilation and dip into the games for a few seconds, minutes at most. This one has me actually playing the games for fun again. The secret formula to retro compilations has been unlocked. It's not the games themselves, it's not galleries of historical material, it's CONTEXT. Putting everything together in a package and explaining WHY this stuff is important and interesting is so obvious, yet nobody thought of it until now. Genius.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: I loved all the interviews with the different people involved in the development of the Atari line of video games systems and computers. Playing the games help reminded me why I love the Atari 2600 so much growing up. It was the only game system that my Dad would take time out of his schedule and play Combat with me. Thanks Atari
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely LOVE this compilation!When I first heard about it at California Extreme 2022, I knew that I had to pick it up. Not only was it worth buying, but it exceed my expectations. Completely blew away the Atari Anniversary Edition compilation from 2001.If you are a retro games fan—especially one who loves all of the lore and technicalities of said games and gaming hardware—you should absolutely purchase the Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration.It's a blast!
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: It feels like we've been here before. I lived through the original history and had most of systems, and played all the games in the arcade. Then game the endless stream of archive collections, Flashback units, and of course emulation. In no way did I think I could take yet another one of these... but I gave it a try, and this really is the best one they've ever put out.The history stuff is fun, but I'm here for the games. Yes, it's mostly the same games, with a few new ones (VCTR-SCTR is the standout)... but it's the way they are presented. Everything just feels right. The menus, the way the games look, the way they play... it's a lot of little adjustments and improvements that just make the games feel great.This just makes the games not present feel all the more missed... Red Baron, Battlezone, Gauntlet... a ton of 2600 games... wish they could game gotten Activision and Imagic games.... and there are a lot of Lynx games that are much better than what they've included... California Games chief among them. Yes, I can play all those in numerous other ways, but I'd to see them in this excellent format.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: A great collection for any Atari fan! It would be nice to have more Lynx/Jaguar added in the future though.The best love letter to Atari, and its role as one of the founders of the video game industry, imaginable. A fantastic collection that not only includes most if not all of the arcade and 2600 games you'd expect to be there, but also a number of 7800, Lynx, and Jaguar games that, quite frankly, I'm just glad to see available legally, in some cases for the first time since the late 80s. Combine that with a rose-tinted but self-aware collection of video interviews and facts about Atari's rise, fall, and corporate issues, and you have a collection that loves its subject matter enough to not only celebrate its beauty, but to acknowledge and face some of its flaws head-on.If you're gonna get it it's worth getting the Expanded Edition: even though the second DLC isn't out yet, the games included in the first one are great additions to the overall package.If I have one serious criticism of the collection, it would be that I want to see more Lynx and Jaguar titles available. While I understand that that's a hard ask, given the complexity of licensing it would take to get hold of some of the most important titles on the systems (I don't even know who you'd contact for Epyx's California Games nowadays, and there's just no way the Jaguar Alien Versus Predator game is ever gonna see the light of day again unfortunately,) seeing some more love given to these two late-life and underappreciated systems would be more than welcome.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: THIS IS VERY UNUSUAL COLLECTION.SOME OF THE GAMES ARE *VERY* OLD AND SIMPLISTIC.THEY ARE BEST SEEN AS FIRSTS - THERE WOULD BE NO MODERN GAMES WITHOUT THESE TRAILBLAZERS.6/10 FOR OVERALL GAME CONTENTBUT9/10 AS A SET OF ATARI HISTORY YOU WILL STRUGGLE TO FIND ELSEWHERE.After that preamble, I have been getting into retro gaming – SNK, capcom etc – and if there was one thing missing from them was a collation of the how and why all these greats come to prominence.  You have to remember that pre-pong, there were games like chess, draughts or the various card games.  Then billiards and so on – which kind of evolved into pin ball and other electric arcade attractions.  From Pong onwards, Atari led the pack on development and innovation.  I was taken by the documentary aspect of this which is very professionally done for those that they spoke to from the period and industry.  I also found myself wincing at the old family console phenomenon of the promo graphics and concept art was more compelling that the actual blocky graphics which booped and pinged around the screen.  You can also see the progression and development of what is missing from a lot of modern games – playability and novelty.  Cloak and Dagger is a manic Bezerk variant with some very funny cut scenes (depending on how bad you mess up the level).I, Robot is so unique (if cursed by fiddley controls) it is essential for any gamer if you ask me. As are Tempest, Akka Arrh and Quantum.  Most of these games are best dropped in and out of, but games like Food Fight, Black Widow, Missile Command Yars Revenge and Asteroids are so addictive – and some have remakes included - that I can see myself blazing away quite happily on a very regular basis.  Some of these games have bought together before – and of course some ‘retro’ games have plundered/homaged these proto video games to build on the lack of modern technology when they first appeared – but I have never seen such a professional package of history and emulation put together. I hope my marks out of ten are clear – the whole package is a 9 – but if you look solely at a fair amount of the games in comparison to modern games, I think most people will feel a bit under served for the price.  It is best seen as an interactive, detailed documentary of one of the most important gaming companies in the industry.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: When I was 5, I asked my dad for a Nintendo so I could play Mario like my friends. He told me that if I wanted a Nintendo, I'd better get a job so that I could afford to buy one. However, he did give me an Atari 2600 that he found in a dumpster. While other kids had their Nintendos with Mario and Contra, I had my Atari with Pong and Tank.Anyways, this game is an interactive museum exhibit that delivers the Atari nostalgia.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a well put-together collection of games with timelines full of old adverts, anecdotes, and interviews that makes me appreciate the games even more than before!  Since I bought this, it's the only thing I've been playing. _childDocuments_.review: It's quite entertaining seeing all the reviews for this game just glowing about Tempest 2000 being available for the first time since 1994, because I could definitely end the review there and just say nothing else. However, there is quite a bit more to say about this release other than that, after perusing and (more or less) taste-testing the library.Granted, at least half of the time I've put in so far is just playing Tempest 2000. I did spend $39.99 USD just to play that. But, there is also so much more than just T2K. There's lots of neat interviews, lots of promotional artwork and even cartridge box recreations (all in a very nice high resolution, save for maybe the video being compressed some). It's the effort that went into this whole thing being as nice as they could make it- well, kind of.The new games are quite neat. I'm much more a fan of Yars' Revenge than the others, and VCTR-SCTR is very neat, but quite unforgiving (I've spawned into enemy shots and gotten a game over) also has a bonus hidden "GIT GUD" message if you die with an extremely low score... Now that's just mean. Just don't play with two ships unless you're a masochist. The Haunted House remake is neat, and the Swordquest Airworld game feels really, really accurate to how the actual game would have been, had we lived in a world where that made it to market. Quadratank feels janky, though. You have to play it quite a bit to get a hand of it, and it doesn't even have the more conventional tank controls as a selectable control setup. Neo Breakout is neat. That's all there is to say about it.I have two nitpicks. One may not even be the compilation's fault, but the game doesn't like me being in a Discord voice call when I'm playing it. It takes a while to load and it also sometimes has weird lag spikes that lock up the program for a while. However, that can be eschewed as that may just be a fault of the Discord app being... infamous for being an out of date version of Electron and sometimes just being somewhat weird. However, my bigger issue is the audio emulation on the arcade games. I played a few in particular; namely Major Havoc and it sounded a bit choppy and not as I remembered it sounding, either on the Atari app for iOS that I'd played a while back, or even the DE-developed Atari Anthology on the PlayStation 2 that also used emulation. A slight bit of irony in the fact that that compilation is nearly two decades old and has more accurate audio emulation by the same people isn't lost on me... The emulation of all the other systems is good. Nearly everything other than the Jaguar has been fine tuned (and if you screw up 2600 emulation you may not be the right developer for this job) by free projects done by fans, so I can't exactly say that I'm blown away by anything other than Jaguar emulation, as it works well enough and I have no complaints to level here. The game selection is neat, and not too shabby, even if most people buying this collection aren't gonna end up playing most of the games.Now, it's time for what everyone bought this collection for. The singular Jaguar game.Jaguar emulation has been a bit of an enigma for a long time. Being that it was built with arcade hardware in mind much like the Sega Saturn (though probably not as well documented since Sega had the Saturn planned for a very long time) in that it has a bunch of co-processors running in parallel, most people that know how to do that sort of coding don't really have interest in the Jaguar, it's just too niche. I've tried VirtualJaguar, Project Tempest and the much more unknown Russian-developed Phoenix Emulator that tends to be good for most. I've personally only had a great experience with Project Tempest as VJ is undercooked and hasn't been touched in many years, and Phoenix just felt... off. Here, the emulation is as on point as it needs to be. I'm not looking for a low level emulator that gets Jaguar right down to a T, I just want an emulator that plays the game well enough. And it does. Having the legal license to play Tempest 2000 without, you know, paying some schmuck on eBay a down payment on a car to have a legitimate cartridge is nice. That's not including getting the equipment to dump it and... all that. It's not fun.I have the Saturn version, but High Voltage Software really seems to have had trouble with getting the Particle Laser right as well as the hitbox on the Fusers (the rainbow colored star enemies), making for a (while smoother than Jaguar) somewhat frustrating experience. This feels as good as an emulated version should, and should you want to play this, I just recommend waiting for the game to go on sale. I'm an Atari diehard and have been for a very long time, so I was willing to dump the cash for it.The rest of the games on the Jaguar are neat, though of course they're not the real reason people bought this collection. I recommend giving them a try, though they're not gonna be any sort of masterpiece and most of them haven't had staying power for most for one reason or another.It comes highly recommended, but if $40 US (or however much it is in your currency) is too much, wait for it on sale. If you want to just play Tempest 2000, think about how much you wanna spend to play it now. This beats spending however much on a legitimate Jaguar and copy of Tempest 2000, that's for sure.EDIT: One thing I forgot to note is that I've not found a way to change the arcade game settings yet. It may be something I have to unlock, but at this time I am not sure about that part. For someone like me who likes changing the settings to make the game easier to get into it or harder once I've gotten used to it, I do find that a bit unfortunate.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only an hour in at the time of this review, but I have to say, I really like what I'm seeing so far.  It's really a love letter to Atari/Video Game history.  The documentary aspect is really well done, with some tidbits that I didn't know about (despite being very into retro gaming since before these games were considered retro).The timeline layout is nice and intuitive.  Food Fight was a favorite of mine on the Atari 7800.  The 7800 version is not here, but the arcade and Atari XE version ARE.If you're on the fence, $40 may be high for you.  But if you grew up with these games, this package is nicely put together and the re-imagined offerings are a nice addition to the slate of games.For all the Atari compilations that exist, Atari 2600 is what's typically out there.  This version gets you 2600, 5200, 7800, Lynx, Jaguar, arcade, and the before mentioned re-imagined ones.  Again, only one hour in, but I'm really really liking this so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: My impressions video: This package is not only Digital Eclipse's most ambitious project to date, I would dare to call it important to the cause of games preservation.From the games perspective alone, Atari 50 has a lot going for it:As usual, Digital Eclipse's emulators are as spot on as you can get and will provide a fantastic experience. The number of options you have to tweak is limited compared to something like an M2 collection, but they cover all the bases the vast majority of people want.Where Atari 50 goes from good to important is with the historical timeline function. Never before has a retro collection provided as much interesting education as this one has. From high resolution scans, to video interviews with Atari legends, to the ability to jump into each game's full manual from the menu, this is a retro nerd's dream, but also very interesting and engaging for anyone who just wants to learn about where video games came from. It's all presented on an easy to navigate timeline, that lets you jump right into any of the relevant games being talked about.It does take some baffling historical liberties at times, such as completely omitting how Epyx actually developed the Lynx, later selling it to Atari due to their financial issues and I think it merely glosses over Atari's long history in computers, which does a disservice to a major era of the company. More coverage of the computers and especially, more than just a sprinkling of 400/800 games would have been nice. For the hardcore nerd in me too, I'd love to see uncut versions of the interviews and would even pay extra for those. You also won't find any third-party games from the likes of Activision in this collection, it's all Atari stuff. It also doesn't talk about the shall we say, complicated history of Atari after the original company folded, but that probably wouldn't have been very interesting for most people anyway.Overall though, this is an incredible package that does a great job at conveying the core historical beats of one of the most iconic companies in the games industry. I really hope this package succeeds enough to draw interest from other companies who want similar things done for them. Games are important and preservation is important. To see it done in such a datailed and passionate way is fantastic.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended for any gaming history buffs out there. This package is so far above and beyond, it basically redefines what a historical gaming collection can be. The vast majority of the games can be accessed from a list, just like you'd expect from any collection, but the primary mode actually has the game walk you through different aspects of Atari's history along a timeline of events. The timeline includes the games themselves but also documentary features, archival footage, marketing material, and fully realized 3D models. The level of detail is incredible.This would all be more than enough on its own but the game also includes 6 brand new games which are mostly modernized, remix-style games imagining what a 2022 version of a classic title may look like. They even created Airworld, the unfinished finale of the Swordquest series, based on original design documents. Many of the original games that are included are also exceedingly rare or may never have been released in an accessible fashion on PCs or consoles before, such as many of the Atari Lynx and Jaguar titles.Digital Eclipse is well known for their historical compilations but they have outdone themselves with Atari 50. This completely redefines what a game compilation can be and hopefully will set a new standard going forward. For anyone even remotely interested in gaming history, Atari 50 is the best we have ever gotten, bar none.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Great collection and piece of Atari history. For those so inclined to learn more about the company, and its lifecycle, for the askingprice you get a fair amount of stuff. Game selection is solid, the interviews and documents add more "humanity" into a company, aswell as teaching us the follies of shortsightedness. The presentation is very well done, kind of cute, actually.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Essentially you buy this documentary if you are interested in the video game history. This documentary contains alot of interviews from the people who have worked with the Atari consoles from 2600 to Jaguar. As a bonus this documentary contains games from different platforms starting from the 2600 to Jaguar (this includes 5200, 7800, 800 and Lynx) including 6 original games that serves as reimagines of popular Atari titles.For what the bundle contains, I would say that for its price, its a steal however I can also understand why some may disagree since not everyone is interested in playing 2600-7800 era games and if you are one of them, then you may want to hold it off once it goes for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: If you grew up playing ATARI at home and in the arcades this title is a must have. The historical information contained in this is absolutely amazing. So cool to follow the timelines and hear the stories directly from the mouths of the actual folks involved in the creation of these games. This release provides a complete history of ATARI from Pong to the Jaguar console.  The selection of titles you can play exceeds that of ATARI VAULT and there are a few really special gems in there. Especially excited that it includes the final installment of Swordquest, AirWorld.  Sixteen year old me has been waiting 38 years to play this game! Whether you are interested in ATARI specifically or gaming industry history in general you won't want to miss out on this.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: great collection filled with a lot's of bonus.they're mostly first party Atari games from the arcade and 2600 up to the jaguar and also including remixed and reimagined games , so far it's the most solid atari collection I've seen even if it's missing some big first party Atari games like Red Baron and Battlezone.the collection offer a timeline mode where you can go throught all of the games in their release orders while having access to various paper documents , Interviews , ads materials , gamebox and game manuals. you can expect over 5 hours and nearly 10 hours even if you barely try each games while having a look at the whole bonus materials.it's not just a collection of random games , it's a virtual museum that give you the context of how the games evolved over the yearsand seriously the jaguar games are better then what I anticipated , especially the atari Kart games and Cybermoprh. Yeah , the ''where did you learn to fly game ?'' is actually playable and I've beaten a few levels before getting the game over screen on my first try.

_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: This is a must-purchase for Atari fans! The emulation is near perfect to perfect on all of the games that I played; however, I didn't grow up with these games, and most of the time, I used an emulator to play these games, so you may want to take my emulation comment with a grain of salt. My one minor complaint is the lack of online multiplayer for games like PONG & Combat, but other than that, there's a lot of attention to detail with the games, as well as enhancements that make it feel like you're playing the games on a real machine. One example is lit-up vectors in Asteroids. Now, the biggest question is, how is the Atari Jaguar emulation? Well, I have fantastic news, it's incredible! Both Cybermorph & Tempest 2k run very well. The price tag is a bit high at $40, but I think it's worth it if you love Atari.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly one of if not THE best retro game compilations released, I can only hope this has raised the bar for this genre going forward. In short:Pros: -Amazing game lineup, extremely solid emulation-Very interesting Documentary timeline, with interviews and tons of original assets-The new games are the addicting cherry on top-extreme attention to detail in nearly every aspect of the game, clearly Digital Eclipse put a ton of love into this-YoompCons: -Lack of certain modernizations (No built in online multiplayer or leaderboards, and a very tiny set of achievements), many of which would go a really long way to encourage me to play and master these older arcade style games-Some missing games, mostly due to copyright (The lynx library really suffers here I think)Any other complaints aren't really the games fault so much as circumstance with copyright and timing, in regards to games I'd like to see included, historical content I'd like to see added, and people I'd like to see interviewed. So I really hope this collection can get some expansions in the future!
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: Ah, my childhood comes back to me. Not only do we have the arcade games that took untold number of quarters from me, but the 2600, 5200, 7800, and other Atari systems that I never was able to experience! With the recent additions of certain third-party games, this has just made me all the happier. The only thing now is for Atari (or the company that owns them) to get the rights to the Activision, Imagic, and other third-party games to truly bring me back to the simpler days of my youth. For now, I'm very happy, and I fully encourage the younger generation to look into this, not only for the entertainment, but for the history that led to the games you know and love now in the 21st centuery.

_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: I considered myself a major Atari-head until I bought this game. I've learned quite a few new things about Atari from playing it, and I'm not even halfway through yet.I hesitate to even call it a game in the traditional sense. It's equal parts book, documentary and video game; and the format works incredibly well.The interface of using a timeline to select which part of the game to delve into is innovative and very satisfying. You can progress linearly, playing titles in the order that the company released them, or jump straight to your favourites.I really dig the revitalised Breakout, an arcade classic I spent many an hour on in my pre-teenage years. This update beats the Recharged title for replayability by a large margin.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

_childDocuments_.review: If you're not a huge Atari fan or don't care much for video game history, this collection could be a bit of a hard sell as the games aren't for everyone. But this collection has so much going on that it absolutely justifies its current price tag, with exclusive dev interviews that can be funny or insightful to tune into, flyers and memorabilia, information about the company's highs and lows over the years, and tons of games to explore. It's not just some Rom collection, the interactive museum feeling is great.The only disappointment is that there's a lot of Jaguar and Lynx games that didn't make the cut. If there's anyway they could work with third party publishers to get the rights to release more games as DLC, that would make an already great collection into an even more fantastic one. But even with that nitpick, this is still a release that is absolutely worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Atari 50: The Anniversary Celebration

Usually these remakes the controls are awful and unplayable. In this case you can use keyboard or x box 360 controller. Both at best suck. at worst unplayable. Atari Football (Which i actually own the machine), Is completely unplayable on this as its a 2 player game and theres no way for both players to choose plays and lock them in. IMPOSSIBLE TO RUN A PLAY. CANNOT BE PLAYED. REALLY? Try playing Breakout or Avalance with keyboard or a xbox controller. IMPOSSIBLE. Missle Comnmand or Centepede with a x box controller? lol good luck.  They mention Atari pinball but no playable games. Shame. They could have made those playable as you know there are many pinball emulators out there. Next up is the library overall is pretty small. for this price they could have added a ton more games.Notable omissions are Berzerk, (NOW INCLUDED IN THE DLC) Space Invaders,  ET (The game that killed the industry, but the guy who made the game is featured in several video presentations in here but only touches that he made the game, nothing more). MY ADVICE: Simply download Stella for the Atari 2600 and Mame for the coin op stuff. I ave a tankstick with a trackball platform set up its so much easier. I bought a real arcade spinner and a usb attachment as well. This is far better then these unplayable controls.On a more positive note they did do the boxes and inserts really well.
