_childDocuments_.review: I muddled for a long time on what to say about this game. People complain a lot about how the game runs. Aside from an unacceptable frame rate of 0.02fps on the title screen, I had no technical problems with the game. Mechanically, it was excellent. The game's systems reminded me a lot of what I liked about Mass Effect. Combat felt good, stealth felt pretty good, the ability to talk your way out of sticky situations felt good. Movement was not perfect, but reasonably responsive. There was a (minor, optional) platforming bit I failed on several times, before I realized I was trying to do it while over-encumbered. My bad there. What didn't feel good was the writing. I felt like it couldn't tell what it wanted to be, and it suffered from tonal whiplash at many points. The characters are living through hell, but you constantly run into slapstick, zany situations. The 'retro-future corporate apocalypse' could work, but there's so much 'wink wink, nudge nudge' that my ribs ache. The companion characters are one-dimensional and dry. I had one character's personal quest begin and end in the space of a single conversation, and then suddenly he trusts me like we're best friends and I get an achievement. The others have no narrative complexity either, but their quests took longer due to having to travel halfway across the star system for each progressive step. Toward the end of act 2 I got punished for not immediately betraying someone I had just agreed to help, so that was fun. I get that a lot of the theme of this game is a criticism of corporate culture, but there were certain points when I felt like the narrative slipped from being a self-aware criticism of commercialism to unironic communist propaganda. I finished this game, with as many sidequests as I could find.  I did not play the DLC content, because by the time I finished the main story, I just wanted the game to be over. I had several regrets about choices I had made earlier in the game, and I was unwilling to replay 6+ hours of content in order to correct them. I'm certainly not willing to start the game over so I can make different choices. I wish there was a middle option for this game, because I can understand why people might like it, but overall it's like I ate something bland that gave me mild indigestion. I didn't hate it, but, all in all, I don't think it was worth my time.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun retro style shooter game, unique in its game-play and authentic in its storytelling.I am currently still completing TOW as I write this review, but so far my journey with this game has been one of intrigue and enjoyment, so much so that every time I return to the game I am reminded of my love for action role-laying games and how this style genre is one of my top 5 favourites.I originally played this game on the PlayStation 4, but never got into it due to my lack of time playing at that particular time in my life. However, repurchasing it for PC has NOT been a mistake. The game-play itself is smooth and loading is fast. The conversations within the game are not long winded and are full of seriousness but also wit, as you yourself can choose how sarcastic you want to be in situations. This often plays out in interesting ways.The first-person shooting is categorically similar to other shooter games, but comes with a unique arsenal of basic and sci-fi style weaponry and armour. As well as this, the enemies are fantastically designed and consistently remind you that you are a mere human amongst creatures, ghouls and other humans with agendas.Overall, if you are into sci-fi fantasy style games and enjoy that classic first-person shooting experience within a unique open-world (mostly) full of surprises, then this is the kind of game for you. Your choices along the way will determine what kind of game you have, so make the game yours and enjoy what results you get from it.

_childDocuments_.review: The outer worlds caught my eye back when it came out. As a big fan of the Fallout franchise, a game made by the original creators of Fallout & the creators of Fallout New Vegas this seemed to be the perfect game for me. I kind of forgot about it after I didn’t buy it at launch, and just recently acquired it.I expected it to be just like the old Fallout games. Turns out it’s not. But it does have some mechanics & systems that are almost exactly the same and clearly expired by Fallout. Some systems like VATS, terminals with information and logs, the skill upgrades are all very similar. NPC’s also have the same stale Bethesda look on their faces, and dialog options with skill checks also remind me of Fallout. The biggest difference between the two for me is the world and its setup. Instead of one big open world, you travel the galaxy and enter smaller semi-open worlds, comparable to the Borderlands games for example. Locations are well crafted, look beautiful and are fun to explore, but don’t have nearly the amount of content Fallout has for example. Yes you can roam around and find the occasional side quest, but it doesn’t have the lore and small hidden spots to discover that Fallout games have.So enough comparisons with Fallout. Let’s look at the Outer Worlds as its own game.I’ve had a lot of fun with the game. The main story can be hard to follow at first, but picks up towards the end. It’s nothing to write home about, but good enough to keep it interesting. It’s short however, I would guess around 12 hours if you skip the side quests. I played the Spacers Choice edition, which also included 2 new story lines. Both are really fun and if you ask me, even better than the main game. There’s some side quests as well, and if you love those, I think you can count on some 40-50 hours of gameplay(with the DLC’s). Don’t expect too much of those either though, they’re mostly fetch quests.The game itself looks great, and has some fun environments to explore. They are however, quite empty besides the main locations, and you should not expect to bump into too many special spots or sudden side quests, most of these are acquired in the main cities. Speaking of which, the cities are really nice! They’re fun, well crafted and big/interesting cities to explore.Dialog is fun and the decisions you make actually make a difference towards the end result of the game. I did find the skill checks on dialog a bit too easy though. Soon enough you can persuade anyone to do what you want.Overall, The Outer Worlds is a lot of fun. It’s on the shorter side for these types of games, but you ask me that’s not that big of an issue. It’s comparable to Fallout on a lot of aspects, but also adds its own flavor to the mix. I do feel however, that on some mechanics they tried to match the Fallout counterparts too much. Obsidian clearly has the talent to create amazing games, and there is no need to try and copy existing systems. In the end, I would really recommend this game for people who like the RPG genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I prefix this that I played this well after launch of the Spacer's Choice edition and encountered none of the technical issues mentioned by other users.Overall, I would recommend The Outer Worlds (either version), its skill systems offer a level of variety and depth to build a character to achieve your style of play, whether that be the charismatic rogue captain with a quick tongue or quicker sidearm. The sneaky stealth characters rooting through computers or demonstrating a brazen disregard for private property. And of course, the "keep on smashing till the problems solved". It feels, and I appreciate this cliche given its lead creators, reminiscent of Fallout pre-4. The setting blends sci-fi with styles of the early 1900s which presents an interesting world to explore, I often found myself staring at the advertisement artworks and the unique gun designs. The story sees you set off to save Halcyon colony from the board and itself and sees numerous moral dilemma that usually leaves you picking the least bad shade of grey. My only complaints of the game are that it felt that just as it was getting going, it came to an end. Whilst I enjoyed myself in the nearly 20 hours, before doing DLC, what could be considered Acts 1 and 2 had some meat to the bones to play around in. But as it approached the third and final act it all came about rather abruptly and rushed to the finish line. I suppose in a way it is good that I was left wanting more, but it feels a missed opportunity in this regard.I did appreciate the addition of the "Slideshow" endings, detailing how my actions had lasting consequences. An off-shoot minor complaint is the companions, for the most part I considered them all interesting banter machines but their personal quests, with perhaps the exception of Max and Parvati, felt noticeably short and to the point. I was more than eager to keep going and learn what made them tick, but they seemed dis-interested in that once I ticked their box off.I look forward to seeing how they build from this with their upcoming sequel. Other notable neat bits- Music was cool- Planet designs were vibrant, wish there were more maps to explore.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start off by saying I didn't play this game on release, but after a few patches once performance seems to have been worked out.For me, the game runs great. On max graphics with a 3060 12GB, and i5-9600k @ 1440p I'm getting a fairly consistent 144 FPS indoors, and averaging 80-110 FPS outdoors. Occasionally it'll drop down to about 60 FPS, but never lower. _childDocuments_.review: This is a very strange game. Thing is - it feels like the game itself doesn't know what it want to be. It supposed to be an Action RPG, right? FPS with RPG elements? Many people compare it to Fallout, but...- This is not a good RPG game. Why? Well, I wanted to go full sneaky stealthy crit dealer when I created my character. Invested into Stealth & Perception, big guns (as I consider a Sniper rifle to fall into that category) and well... After just couple of quests I interrogate, plasma kill stuff, engineer my choices out and basically covering all of the skill tree choices without even thinking of developing some skills over other ones. So your build choices are not really taken into account. You pissed off a faction in game and have a quest to talk to their leader? Gun your way in, find the guy, press Ctrl to sneak for couple of seconds, talk and walk out like as if the massacre never happened. - This is also not a good shooter. You got lots of guns and blades and whatever. All of them feel like made of cardboard. Impact is not satisfying. Recoil, critical hits, focus fire? Hitting enemy into the "soft spot" - that should be a thing, right? But it's not. There's a bunch of skills that are aimed to boost your headshotting potential, but it doesn't work well. Plus all the guns are supposed to be modified/upgraded by the player. Guess what? You find +- fine barrels in your first hour of the game and then just keep upgrading them spreading death. No need to change. - This could be a good Action Adventure game, but there's just too much talking and running back & forth. I mean, seriously. Most of the quests are: fly there, find that guy, talk to him, then go back to your base and talk to other guy, then back to the guy #1, who will tell you where to look for an item to bring to guy #2, and guess what? After doing this - go back to guy #1, get his approval and yet again - back to base to speak to some people. This is a futuristic game, ok? You got AI  leaded ship & stuff. Was a walkie-talkie too much rocket science or something? Now on the bright side: aesthetics & general design is pretty nice. Loved the retro futuristic vibe. In general this game feels like Borderlands meets Bioshock. But unfortunately - it doesn't inherit fun or complexity from those two titles. Pseudo open-world brings more harm than joy. At times you just can't understand why you can't climb this particular hill, as you've just did a dozen times before. In general - this is not a bad game. It has it's ups and downs, yet after 8 hours I'm extremely bored with shooting same guys with the same weapons and looting the same yellow boxes over and over and over again.

_childDocuments_.review: The problem with performance when it comes to this game has to do with framerate pacing, so it doesn't matter if you're getting 60 or over 60 fps because the game feels stuttery; however, there's a fix.Either use the in-game vsync and framerate limiter in conjunction, limiting your fps to your monitor's refresh rate, or simply use an external fps limiter (such as RTSS) in conjunction with vsync. Vsync can either be forced through control panel or through the game, same with fps limiter, but it's necessary to use both to fix the frame pacing issues plaguing this game.So for example, you have a 60hz screen, then you limit the fps to 60fps, and simultaneously use vsync; this worked for me and the game is running really well for now.PCGamer wrote an article about this with Durante as their source; it's an 8 year old article, but it's still relevant and useful: As for the game?This is a streamlined Fallout game, if you don't mind a much more forgiving and commercial game that takes those Fallout games as an inspiration, you're going to love this, if you're expecting something as profound and/or crazy as "Fallout: New Vegas" then you'll probably be left disappointed.I personally love the game, I think it's fun, I like the characters and the story, I enjoy the decisions you have to make, I like all the quality of life improvements and the combat, I like the world and the enemies, I just really think is a fun game. This version also includes all the DLC which is a plus if you already like the base game like me.If I can complaint about something is the lack of replayability in the form of a NG+ mode or an alternate mission replay that allowed me to experiment with my power ups and abilities, I get why it isn't here, but I don't like it.I also don't like how the game looks too much, it isn't horrible, but after a while the color balance ends up feeling a bit to overwhelming, like everything is overtly saturated and I end up not liking the look too much. The game does look a tad bit better than the original, but in my opinion it isn't that much of a difference to justify the asking price if you already own the original version.The only way that I could recommend this, over that one, is if you can find it for a much cheaper price, like I did, I got this game through Humble, I hadn't played through the DLC, I had just played a bit of the Game Pass version when it came out, so I'm happy with my purchase.The performance is good with the fix I mentioned, otherwise the game is a stutter fest, remember, vsync, fps limit to your refresh rate, IN CONJUNCTION.Try it and see if it works, it resolved the performance issues for me completely, now the game runs even better than the original one at that, strangely enough...

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is a great game.  It has passing similarities to Obsidian's other games but that is misleading, this is a multifaceted game of interconnected decisions that does a very good job of allowing you a great deal of freedom.You will make a lot of choices in this game.  Even the most straightforward choice is never good vs evil, rather shades of grey.  Once you leave the first planet you can deviate from the 'led by nose' plot, throw someone under the bus and then wend your merry way righting wrongs (or wronging rights) and the game copes with it.  You can shoot important characters and the game copes - at the beginning of one of the DLCs you can shoot the main protagonist and the game copes.  Not always in dramatic ways but it is very adaptable and makes for considerable replay ability.I liked the companion characters, they are fun to spend time with and I felt a connection.  I wanted to be on that spacecraft with them, they weren't out there but they are multifaceted.  They react to your behaviour, have great dialogue and regularly surprise.  Most of the companion quests are pretty good too - Parvati's and Nyoka's in particular.  Unlike BG3, there is no romancing the companions and I think I prefer that.The combat becomes pretty easy after a while, the DLCs are more challenging but don't play this game for the gunplay.   Play it for a vibrant set of characters undertaking a bunch of interesting missions against the backdrop of social and cultural decay.  In space. With a sarcastic flight computer.To quote Nyoka "I. Am. A star"

_childDocuments_.review: Spacer's Choice. True to its motto, The Outer Worlds did not really excel at anything. Straight out of the box, you can't escape the feeling of being visually overwhelmed by the tremendously absurd contrast and gamma on the first planet. Soon after, you also realize that the game world is truly vast, but disappointingly repetitive and empty.Eventually, you get used to it— especially once you realize it goes well with the over-the-top and, most of the time, absurd storyline. Alas, although I usually enjoy a sprinkle of borderline stupidity in my games, this time I cannot really say I enjoyed the dialogue options. Just as a person repeating the same jokes in your face every 5 bloody minutes would be very punchable in real life, the same can be said for The Outer Worlds. We get it, crony capitalism bad and absurd... but it's kind of cheap when you dedicate 65 hours just to that? Sadly, it's an utterly forgettable game.However, I ought to admit I enjoyed the DLCs as they brought me more joy with more focused (although predictable) storylines and game time value.I ran the game with no glitches or any technical issues.

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: I solved the crashing issue. Having rebar on in the bios and a 120Hz monitor (whether I had Freesync off and just set the monitor's refresh rate to 120hz in the regular Windows display settings didn't matter - it has to be set to 60Hz) yielded the crashes. Now, with rebar off and my monitor set to 60Hz the game runs smooth.The game kept crashing during the character creation screen. So, I cleared the DX12 cache and ran the game as administrator. _childDocuments_.review: My previous review has  gone by the wayside and this is the newer one.I've played through the game,and despite the glitches first encountered,a patch has since been released and with a bit of tweaking said glitches have almost all disappeared.They will never be able to get rid of the periodic hesitation when walking,but I will take that over the others they rid the game of.In this form it is a far more enjoyable game ,as the colours have  been given a new life and it is visually very nice to look at.I have also been able to complete all achievements(hurray for me!).But I might offer a word of advice in that department.A) When  going for Hard to Supernova levels,contrary to many vids on Youtube,do NOT worry about your fellow  fact it's better if you let them die.On these levels(especially Supernova) they are a drain on resources which many times you just do not have.Remember YOU have to buy their armour,etc and that could be better used for you.I played Supernova virtually by myself and did it successfully I might add and could easily see how much of a burden having Parvatti or Nyoka along would have been.B) I went from playing Normal straight to Supernova.First timer players I wouldn't recommend to do this.But long time players should do alright.Because if you do this and succeed you get credit for Supernova level AND Hard level! A 2 for 1-er.C) Another thing about vids on You Tube is they say that on Supernova that in order to save you must travel back to the ship all the time.NOT true.Sometimes this is the case,but remember this:Any building in which you "transition" into,the game itself automatically saves it,so if you get out,you don't start back at the ship but at the door at which you entered.D)I'm a conservative player and like to err on the side of caution.If your ship is the only save point in the game,I would recommend-1)avoiding as much as possible ANY fighting and running past /around your foes,and 2)as you progress in your fighting within buildings stop,go back to your ship and save then walk back.It only takes a short time before your back but if you get out it saves you from starting over from scratch,which to me is more of a pain than anything.E)On Supernova find your own rhythm /cadence and stick with what works for you.Because that's all the game is,finding what works and what doesn't.F) There is no need to do all quests,side or other wise,to get completion credit at the end.If you want to,hey all the power to you.Since Supernova is the hardest,why make the game any longer and involved than it already is and do only the main quests throughout.The more quests you do means the more involved you become,the more resources you use and the more chance you have of getting killed.On that level you don't need any more stress than you already have,right?and finally G)Another canard from You Tube videos is that of your initial character build.They want this attribute higher and these one's lower,right? I tried different character builds and in the end all my attributes went below average! So I played "dumb" throughout the game,but I ultimately succeeded just fine,once again contrary to their "expert" opinions".You do what you want and don't listen to anyone.We all play differently and that's fine.And while i sound anti-Youtube vids,I'm not.I am picky of what I see and hear for sure, but generally I can find ones that are good if stuck trying to get an achievement of one type or another.They are overall pretty reliable in that department.Any ways I hope some of these tips help some folks out there.Good luck out in The Outer Worlds.It's a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first time I can remember having trouble deciding whether or not I "recommend" a game. The binary rating system doesn't give itself to nuance, so I'll endeavor to explain my decision here.The Outer Worlds is a good game. The Spacer's Choice edition includes the DLCs, so if youre going to buy the game I'd recommend opting for this edition, however I have heard a lot of people saying that this edition has serious performance issues. I have a very powerful PC which easily ran this game at 120+ FPS, so I cannot comment on that aspect of the game. The Outer Worlds is a good game. It is fun to play, has memorable characters and builds an interesting world that can keep you occupied for a good amount of time. There are many different ways to play the game, both in terms of playstyle and narrative choices, giving the game reasonably good replayability. The DLCs add significant content to the game, and in my opinion were probably the most fun and interesting parts of the game. The Outer Worlds is a good game. However, even after all I've said I cannot in good conscience recommend it to others. I just finished getting every achievement. I've played this game for 133 hours, and most of that time was pretty enjoyable... but this isn't the game you should be spending your money on. I'm sure many people will come here because this game was developed by Obsidian Entertainment, famed developer of one of the most well-liked RPGs in recent memory, Fallout: New Vegas. However, Obsidian does not deserve as much credit as they get for the success of Fallout: New Vegas. FNV was built upon the shoulders of giants, so to speak. Fallout 3 laid the groundwork; FNV had the engine and core mechanics already set up for them. The same cannot be said about The Outer Worlds.The Outer Worlds is a good game, but it could have been so much better. Its shortcomings do not make it a bad game, but they can make it frustrating to enjoy. It has a wide variety of systems and mechanics, of which many are poorly explained or poorly implemented, so much of the game's content goes unappreciated or underutilized. The Outer Worlds has many of the mechanics one expects from a Fallout game: a time-dilation ability, looting of enemies and items, unique items, lockpicking, hacking, stealth, attributes/perks/skills, the list goes on. However it fails to strike the right balance to be fun. Looting in general feels tedious; there are items and containers everywhere, and most of it is worthless or nearly so. You'll find extremely difficult to open containers that will contain pocket change and a half eaten piece of candy. Junk items pile up in your inventory while playing, weighing you down until you can drag yourself to somewhere they can be sold for minimal profit. Unique weapons are almost universally inferior to the standard fare because they cannot be customized to your playstyle  and because the system for upgrading equipment makes it nearly impossible to hold onto the equipment you like, as it is prohibitively expensive to keep it at your level, requiring you to constantly swap out for new, higher level gear you find lying around. The attributes you select at character creation cannot be changed, so you must make crucial decisions about your character before you have learned anything about the game. My list of complaints continues, but this review is already long enough that most readers have skipped it over, so I'll stop here.The Outer Worlds is a good game, but you will find it is at its best after you have already learned how to play, which means your first (and possibly only) playthrough will be the most frustrating, and that's not how games should be. It feels as though the developers designed their game forgetting that players would not know the intricacies of its systems the way they do. I've heard that a sequel is in the works, and my hope is that the well-documented failures of this game will be heeded so that the next is all that much better because of it. tl;dr The Outer Worlds is a good game, but not as good as it should have been. Spend your money elsewhere or maybe wait for the sequel when they (hopefully) will have learned from their mistakes. If you do buy this, try to get it on sale, and do a little research before building your character so you can avoid irreversible mistakes.

_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Worlds is an action RPG made by Obsidian Entertainment and then later "improved" by Private Division in Spacer's Choice Edition. I would love to blame all the problems on Private Division, but be honest for one second. In terms of story and gameplay The Outer Worlds is one of the worst games in Obsidian's portfolio. Spacer's Choice Edition did screw with the performance and created new issues, but the base game was already average at best. If I could, I would give it a mixed review, just for the expansions. There's some good stuff here, but it's hidden behind a bland main story, bugs, and joyless gameplay.The main story of The Outer Worlds is just plain and boring. Some weirdo scientist saves us from the hibernation chamber and then asks us to help him wake up the others. This is not easy and we need to do some other stuff beforehand. And that stuff is just... weak. There's no oomph, no emotions, and zero surprises. At least the choices matter - usually in small ways, but still. There's some good and bad stuff here. The fetch quests aren't great, but you can find some gems with fun sub-stories. The faction quests are way better in terms of design and they entwine with the main story very nicely. I liked that we could quickly resolve some quests just by using our attributes during the conversation.The real "meat" of The Outer Worlds. The world created by Obsidian is a fascinating mix of sci-fi, post-apo, and cyberpunk. There are heartless corporations, cruel gangs, cults, weirdos - everyone that you would expect in a world like this.It's hard to exactly describe all the details and nuances - there are too many of them. Obsidian was able to create something fairly interesting and unique.Parvati was easily the best companion. Well written, well voice-acted, has some character development, and her companion quests are fun. It helps that we have lots of time to bond with her. Everyone else? Depends on what you like. Vicar Max has an interesting backstory, but his quest line is just meh. Nyoka and Ellie - they aren't bad, but they lack IT. SAM is fun for his one-liners. Felix is... not good.  There's no romance, only some flirting. Instead, you can help one of your companions to date another person. Interesting replacement, but I would prefer to have both things in the game. First story expansion. You can complete it in less than 10 hours (main story and all side quests). Unfortunately, the new planet feels like a rehash of what we already saw. There are some exceptions, but most of the new places felt dull. Too much walking and shooting the same enemies over and over. At least the story is intriguing. The new characters aren't bad either. I would even dare to say - both are more interesting than stuff from "vanilla" game.The second story expansion and probably the biggest reason why someone would want to play The Outer Worlds. You can finish it in around 5 hours. Add ~4 hours if you want to complete all side quests. The new planet is medium-sized. It looks way prettier than most of the locations from the rest of the game. There are also lots of easter eggs and environmental storytelling.I especially liked the story of this expansion. It starts as a mystery, but very quickly everything gets weirder and sometimes unsettling. The plot twist near the end is also great. Unlike in the first expansion, the Murder on Eridanos adds a new gameplay element to the game - a tool that helps you find the clues.The gameplay is very shallow. It feels like Obsidian wanted to create Skyrim/Fallout in their own universe, but they didn't have enough money to make it good. The foundations are solid and the ideas aren't bad, but the execution leaves much to be desired.We start with the character creation - it feels like in a classic RPG. A decent amount of options to choose from. Different faces, hairs, details, etc. You can also pick your attributes, skills, perks, and background story.Unfortunately, it doesn't take much to see the worst sides of this game. Small locations, repetitiveness, the world around us is pretty much dead, lack of balance, boring crafting, and much more. The melee combat is awful. The gunplay is not bad, but the lack of weapons variety is noticeable. There's a big problem with the enemies' variety. You'll fight humans, robots, and five or six types of animals. This is not enough to NOT make you bored after 15-20 hours of playing. It doesn't help that their AI is super dumb. They won't give you any challenge, no matter the difficulty level.The reputation system could be better. Besides discounts in shops and some different speech lines, it doesn't affect the gameplay at all. I appreciate the freedom to pick your playing style. The good guy, the bad guy, something in between - you can play however you want.The game is just... ugly. There are worse-looking titles on the market, but I would expect something better from a game released in 2020. Besides some specific designs, most of the stuff looks dated. The models are too simple, the textures are often low quality, and the animations are extremely wooden. What's the point of the face close-ups, when the faces are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awful?There's nothing negative that I can tell about the audio. Everything is at least fine.The soundtrack fits the game well, but it's not particularly memorable. The sounds (guns, effects, etc.) and voice acting are solid. I wouldn't expect anything less from some well-known names that did the voice acting.It didn't bother me, but it may be a problem for some - the main character is not voiced.The performance is bad. My FPS were never stable, even inside the buildings. They usually fluctuated between 100 and 144, but some bigger drops (below 70 FPS) also occurred.There are also tons of other problems. Crashes (two), a broken quest (Electric Fling from DLC), and an insane amount of small bugs (from flying corpses to getting stuck inside the objects).

Third time is the charm, I bought the Spacer's Choice edition on sale on Steam and I'm glad I did....this game deserves your attention. Don't go into it thinking it is New Vegas in space....it knows what it wants to be and beneath the surface it is a well-built new RPG from a talented development studio with a great track record. The world is interesting, and the lore is enough to keep you invested in the outcome, which has enough choice that you can easily do multiple playthroughs with completely different results. _childDocuments_.review: After just beating the game a few minutes prior I can say, confidently, that this is one of the best games I've played in recent years, even with an objective look at the issues it has.I can't say much about performance issues, I didn't have so much as one stutter throughout my playthrough, but I would suppose that comes down to your computer specs.Don't come at this expecting a huge focus on space travel and combat, as there's basically none of that, and space travel is just an extension of fast traveling.Gameplay is, admittedly, tedious at times; the combat can be boring and one-sided, and the excessive focus on looting can get old quickly, but if you've played Fallout 4 or 76, then you already know about those issues well.Otherwise, this is an amazing game. The choices you get really do let you feel like you have some effect on the colony in the end, and the number of skills and frequency at which they come up in-world and in dialogue lets you actually feel like you get something out of building your character. The companions are all well-written and have stories that are interesting enough, though they do become a tad bland outside of companion-companion banter and their additions to dialogue. Don't let the yappers and people who jumped on the bandwagon to hate this game influence you, give it a try, especially if you love the overall feel of Obsidian games and have been looking for something akin to New Vegas.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not going to get into the base story/gameplay. What I AM going to comment on is something not found in any documentation about this version as compared to the original version; I have both of them and beaten both of them.The key here is about tinkering. This is when you use a workbench to modify/upgrade armor and weapons. Since SCE raises the level cap to 99 from 36, it also raises the level cap on gear from 41 to 104. That said, there is one key note in all of this. You can tinker weapons to level 104 (or 5 levels above you current player level, which ever is the lower) with corresponding increases in base damage. Armor, however, cannot be improved after level 50. You CAN tinker a piece of armor to level 104, but, you gain no improvement to the base defense rating past level 50. This is not common knowledge.

_childDocuments_.review: Terrible, but in a way that arises from many small flaws adding together rather than a single crippling one, and so is hard to express in a review. The plot isn't funny, and it isn't clever, which means that the characters don't have much to say or do about it. The characters aren't fun to talk to, which means that the gameplay has to pick up the slack. The gameplay is that supremely dull type of FPS RPG where you have to grind to get a gun that deals +1.6% more DPS so you only have to shoot an alien in the face 17 times instead of 18 times, which means that it can't carry the game. So the only reason to play is if you're really, really into spacesuits. My vote is to skip this one.

_childDocuments_.review: It has some cool ideas and a cool universe. There is some solid choices for sure. However, I find it very difficult to give it a third game session because it just isn't that fun of a game. The combat is fairly boring and the gameplay outside of it isn't great either. I didn't necessarily expect a Fallout experience, but I didn't expect it to be significantly lesser than Fallout as well. It could have compensated and have something more to have a more unique identity, but instead it's just a skeleton of what you would typically expect from these type of games. Because of this, you will find yourself comparing it to pretty much every other games of the same genre and it doesn't compare. All the weapons are too similar, all the quests feel more like errands than adventures, and the story is kinda boring. Again, the game's strength is so abundantly clear, it is a fascinating universe, but it doesn't really give it the stage it deserves. You see the universe, it's there, but you're not really a part of it, you're just a rodent sneaking around it. Maybe this changes later, but early on it's not the case. Also, the NPC AI is trash and inhuman. I do something and everyone pretends they don't like it, attack me, then the whole city attacks me for attacking them. Terrible. I really wanted to like this but it's missing an extra oomph it really needed.

_childDocuments_.review: “It’s not the best choice, it’s Spacer’s Choice!”Have you played the original release of The Outer Worlds? No? Go and do that. It’s approximately fifty-thousand times better than this half-cooked digital abortion.Why? Primarily, for three reasons:1. This broken ruin runs at the same speed as a jellyfish in a bucket. Got some seriously high-end hardware? Like to wave your e-peen around to impress the ladies? Good for you. It’s not going to help you here. Your game-play experience will still be about as satisfying as a pudding made of phlegm and broken glass.2. It looks objectively worse. I don’t know who decided to “enhance” the visuals, but they need to make an appointment with an optometrist ASAP. Everything looks washed out, and many of the “improvements” are things like “the volcano in the distance is no longer static... now it’s erupting”, and “let’s scatter random crap all over the place”. Look at the cantina sign in the original game. Now look at the cantina sign in this version. Were they drunk? Why?!3. It’s as buggy as a lice-ridden hobo. The scenery will flicker like a strobe light in a nightclub full of strobe lights, so I hope you’re not prone to seizures. Random T-poses are a thing, and occasionally NPCs will slide around the place like they’ve made a pact with Lucifer in exchange for the ability to levitate. And... it crashes, because of course it does.I take no pleasure in saying this, but this version of the game is awful. And that’s a crying shame because The Outer Worlds is a fantastic game. I own the original so this depressing expulsion only cost me $9, but had I known what it was like before paying for it, I’d have kept the $9 and spent it on a McDonald’s combo. I hope Private Division can patch it into a game that doesn’t make you want to douse your PC in kerosene and set it alight, but we’ve all been burned before, haven’t we kids?Buy this rickety embarrassment if you hate yourself, and/or enjoy throwing money in the bin. Not recommended.UPDATE:Okay, so they've patched the game to fix most of the performance issues, and a lot of the bugs. During testing, it didn't crash once, and while I was still getting some stutter here and there, it was nowhere near as bad as it was on launch. If you have the hardware to run it, it's now a functional product. Bear in mind it's significantly more demanding on your hardware than the original game, so if you're running a potato, give this a hard pass.I still think the original release looks better graphically, but that's personal preference and opinion is not the same thing as fact. If you don't own the game already and want a one-time purchase with all the DLC included (and an increased level-cap), the Spacer's Choice Edition is no longer the gaming equivalent of a malignant tumour. However, the thumbs down stays because releasing a crippled product and fixing it after the fact is shady behaviour and should be discouraged.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all a warning I needed a mod (The tweaked Outer Worlds on Nexus) to fix performance. Frame rate was sub 20 on ultra, improved to 60 after the mod fix. Motion blur rendered you almost blind on any form of movement, not just turning and the game stuttered on every kill, both of which the mod perfectly resolved. You may also want to consider a reshade mod, the game is very overpoweringly vibrant. It wasn't much of an issue, it just looked a bit rubbish particularly in settlements on planet.Base game was a bit meh. The story was extremely simple with no interesting or majorly disruptive twists or turns. They were also a bit too overt with their social/societal messaging they wanted to push. Not that I think having a message like that in your games is bad, just that they shared theirs poorly. The 'big corpo bad' narrative dumbed down the story and most dialogue interactions so there weren't really any hard choices to be made. The other message was a noble one of empowering women in positions of authority but the execution left much to be desired as it turned into 'all men are incompetent, all women are competent' with not a single exception to this. This one doesn't really effect the game all that much and can be overlooked easily enough, just a pity they couldn't do better.Gunplay was simple but fun enough, I used heavy weapons predominantly. Modding weapons and armour was pretty bare-bones but did the trick and I liked that the modifications altered the look of the weapon. The Eridanos DLC was also lacking. It had the same corpo bad sauce drizzled everywhere and the main objective of the DLC, investigate a murder, was done almost entirely for you via a handheld analyser, there was no opportunity to put your thinking cap on and solve it yourself.The Gorgon DLC was far better. It provided an interesting story of a failed experiment with disastrous consequences. This story is well discussed through environmental storytelling, dialogue and computer logs which surprised me as the logs were mostly a waste of time in the base game. If it wasn't clear in the setting of the base game it will become abundantly clear that this game and this DLC specifically is something of a love letter to  but in a way that is creative enough in its own right to not be a rip off of the source.Not recommended because while gorgon was great dlc the rest does not warrant spending money on.

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the quality of the original game, its very hard to recommend this "expanded" and "definitive" edition. The old definitive version (Non-Mandatory Corporate Sponsored) was going for $33-$38 last I checked. Now they are resetting the price to $48 on sale. They are charging preexisting owners $8 for a patch. So, this patch should be something substantial. Is it? Not really. First of all, the new graphical updates are not that impressive. If you're going to release a remaster 3 years after a game came out, the remaster should be making the game comparable to recent releases, and its not. The bigger issue is the performance. You charge $8 for a graphical remaster, and in 2023 we don't even get DLSS? For an Unreal Engine 4 game, which is one of the easiest engines to add DLSS to? No RTX either, obviously, not that this game could handle it. Sure, I managed to make it fairly smooth, by compromising the graphical settings in a large number of areas. It was not, by any means, an unplayable experience. But immersion-breaking stutters were fairly frequent. I'm rocking an RTX 3080, i7-12700kf, and 48 GB RAM, so make of that what you will. Personally, I don't think the game looks as good as Hogwarts: Legacy, Sony's Spider-Man ports, Hitman 3, maybe even Stray. The biggest change is the level cap (which is practically doubled), but Outer Worlds is... not really a game I can imagine grinding to that extent. Its not like any content was added with that increased level cap. Overall, this really feels quite greedy, and I pin it squarely on Private Division. They won't get to publish The Outer Worlds II, so they decided to squeeze some quick cash out of the game they did have control over (Outer Worlds) by putting out a cheap "remaster." Its really a shame; The Outer Worlds deserved better.Edit: More than a month latter, I come to back to check if the graphical issues have been fixed. They have not. I might just reinstall the old version I play that, tbh. Smooth FPS for good immersion is much more important than a minor change in visuals and a level cap increase, and at patch 1.2 this game is no better than at 1.0.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun and a great narrative experience from Obsidian, but not without its flaws. I'm hoping Outer Worlds 2 gives us some more moral ambiguity compared to the comically evil Board present here. There's really no justifiable reason for supporting the Board or their status quo unless you're intentionally playing an Evil route, and even then I'd imagine it'd be hard to stick with it given the sheer amount of cruelty they endorse. It would be less evil to simply murder everyone you come across.I also hope they drop the Tinkering system. It really just holds the player back and artificially increases the difficulty by forcing you to underperform, and disincentivizes using any rare or pristine mods you come across since anything that isn't the level 30+ version of an item is just going to be obsoleted and you won't be able to retrieve those mods unless you reach Engineering 150. This is made worse by the extended level cap in Spacer's Choice edition since later game content continues to scale up to you and at a certain point it can cost you tens of MILLIONS of bits to upgrade your gear, more than you could possibly legitimately earn in the entire game, and that's AFTER getting the upgrade that reduces Tinkering costs by 90%. You're essentially forced to use the Science Weapons on higher difficulty since they're the only thing with a capped Tinkering cost. It's a shame because the gunplay feels fairly balanced on Supernova difficulty when your weapons are at the appropriate level but you get priced out of that experience pretty quickly. This system only serves to annoy the player and I strongly encourage you to cheat money in to negate the issue.

_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Worlds is a great game that has it's downsides.  Here's some quick pros and cons:Pros: - The game has no chances in it, you'll always pass skill checks - The combat is simple and enjoyable with plenty of room for build options - The game has solid voice acting and dialogue writing - The RPG Skill system is straightforward and allows for cheap respecing from very early onCons: - The entire game is satirical, which can get old (I started skipping dialogue after about 40 hours) - There are no romances in the game (not a huge downside, just sad you can't get together with your favorite companion) - A Lot of the perks are uselessA few other points that you may like or dislike: - The game is really easy.  You may be able to make it harder by upping the difficulty, but the gameplay itself doesn't really lend itself to an interesting challenge, as the higher difficulty settings just make enemies spongier and harder hitting. - Supernova difficulty changes the way you play the game, but not necessarily in a better way. - The "Flaw" system is poorly balanced.  Essentially, once you take enough damage from a specific source (enemy type, element type, falling, etc) you'll be given the choice to take a "flaw" which will permenantly increase the damage you take from that source, but it will give you some sort of perk in return.  The issue is that the perk is usually an actual perk point, and the majority of perks in the game are worthless. - The Companions are fairly polarizing (Might just be me, but I didn't find any of the companions to be very compelling, I didn't really like any of them and I found there to be some much more interesting characters that didn't become companions)I don't really think there are any true negatives about this game, just some minor nit picks.

It's just too hard to say whether or not the improved graphics of Spacer Choice edition are worth the hassle unless you got it for like $9 USD like I did.  Like others have said, this update should have been free for everyone who already owned the game/DLC.  As someone who (happily) bought TOW twice, once on Epic, and again once it was released on Steam... having to pay even $9 more for this "update" felt... unjustifiable.  I hope that the more the gaming industry fumbles, the more it learns and perhaps improves... but it's crap like this cheap wax job that really forces me to have little faith.  Private Division should have known better than to release this mess... and no amount of updates are going to clean off the stink of an obvious cash grab.

_childDocuments_.review: Old review: "I'll write a thought out review when I'm done with this game, but every time the menu music gets going for a couple minutes I just can't help but think about how much I love this game and what a narrative masterpiece it is. I'd highly recommend this. New Vegas in space, 10/10."The Outer Worlds was a real pleasure for me. I wasn't really in the market for games when it was initially released, so I was never really excited for it and it only ended up in my library because of it's inclusion in a recent bundle. I went into it relatively blind, admittedly with some starfield hype though, and man was I shocked. This is an incredibly captivating space epic that has some real callbacks to Obsidian's previous works, and it's definitely worth your time if you're looking for a thick and culturally on-the-nose sci-fi narrative. It's really been too long since I've played New Vegas to give an adequate comparison between the two, but if I had to I would say Outer Worlds is better written, where New Vegas had more interesting and intentional environments and more combat versatility. While this game didn't necessarily overstay its welcome, I was definitely ready to be finished by the time credits rolled because of how dull the looting became and how over-powered I was. This would probably be offset by playing on a harder difficulty. Also, I haven't had any of the performance issues that were present on release. Overall I'd say this is a totally worthwhile purchase, even if you can't get it for crazy cheap. I probably spent a good 60-80 very enjoyable hours with this one and I'm sure to be thinking about it for much longer with such compelling writing.

_childDocuments_.review: Review:I'd describe this game as if Fallout and Cyberpunk had a monopoly baby in space. The game play, script, and voice acting is top notch. I especially love stealing from everyone, the goofy interactions, and finding items out in the world that later appear on my ship. There’s a big improvement with the graphics quality from the original. IT'S BEAUTIFUL! I understand some might find the story boring but I'm a fan of post-apocalyptic capitalistic dystopia IN SPACE so I don't mind listening to the NPCs and exploring every nook and cranny for fun interactions and lore. There's also a canon WLW romance and I am the captain of that cute ship.Advice:If you’re having trouble playing the game I suggest lowering your settings. I play with everything on medium and get an average of 80 FPS. I think there were a lot of issues at launch which contributed to the mixed reviews but it should be fixed by now. Also, a quick google search informed me that another common fix for game crashes is turning off screen space global illumination in the settings. I didn’t have this issue but a lot of people did. My specs: GPU: RTX 2060 CPU: Ryzen 7 3700XRAM: 32GBMobo: TUF GAMING X570-PLUS WIFICritiques: This game would be better if the RPG element was stronger. I feel like the recommended player choices tend to sway to the moderate side. Having actual romance options would be great too! Also, there needs to be more large planets/maps. A few planets are so small and only have 1 quest on them like Also I only get motion sickness from Obsidian games like this one or Fallout. The default sensitivity is very high. Thankfully, there’s adjustable settings that reduce my motion sickness unlike in Fallout New Vegas. I can’t play that game because of this so I’m glad that Obsidian added this into Outer Worlds!Settings adjustment to reduce motion sickness:Screen effects set to medium or lowReduce motion blur to 0%Increase FOV to 90-100Reduce mouse/controller sensitivity to 7-10%

_childDocuments_.review: Well, this was a disappointment.Fallout 1 (and 2) are some of my favourite games ever. There is a lot of Fallout here, superficially, but the game is so, so tame in most respects.First, there's the gameplay. The game is full of "busywork", of "stuff" that serves little purpose. I feel like I spent maybe 30-40% of my time just looting every highlighted item and occasionally going back to town, interrupting gameplay, to empty my bags.The game has a crafting system, stat-modifying consumables, and companions with skill trees - despite playing on Hard mode, I've had just about 0 need to take any of this into account. I did upgrade weapons, but mostly just levelling them up. I barely touched armor, and I didn't bother to really change the companions' gear, I felt no need. And the consumables - well, I occasionally used one that increased your backpack capacity for a minute, just so I could run to the nearest shop.Damage types, changing gear before facing certain enemies, thinking about how companions boost your stats - none of this mattered. Which makes the vast majority of systems (and looting) serve no point.It's just there because it's something that games have. Probably makes them sell, since players compulsively enjoy hoarding (I include myself in this), on a base level; still, it doesn't nourish and leaves you with an empty stomach (and head) by the end of the game.Second, while I was initially very pleasantly surprised about the role that "anarchism" seems to play in the game, that surprise was quickly turned into dismay, when the writing showed that it didn't understand anarchism at all.I didn't expect it to be a fair treatment - given that capitalism is taken in the most satirical and cynical possible way, anarchism could as well (even though anarchism has no "clear/serious" presence in most people's minds, so a satire of it doesn't help); but even when the game suggests that siding with the rebels is the "correct" action, it does so in the most tame possible way, and often ignores the anarchism aspect entirely.In fact, every anarchist character is revealed to be a "fake anarchist" and is actually just a self-interesting knucklehead.Of course, at the end of the game, you become the leader. Because why not? You don't even get a choice in the matter.In general, too, the writing was far to abstract and simplistic. You could almost not read the text at all and simply choose your answers based on stat checks. Plus, the solutions all follow the simple pattern: side with the capitalists (bad), side with the anarchists (worse), work out a compromise that leaves the capitalists mostly in power but slightly shifts the balance towards worker-fairness and so on (often provided by the anarchists).There is a lot more I could say about it, but it will take some time for me to organize my thoughts. So I'll end it here, for now, with the two or three most important points. Aside from that, the game can be beautiful (although the scenes are a bit too busy at times). Some of the writing can be very funny, and sharp. The advertisements are great. The clouds very beautiful.It is a polished AAA title, it plays well. But it adds almost nothing to the table, and it deeply screws up in the writing department, when it reveals that either the writers didn't know enough to take the subject seriously, or it didn't work for the gameplay and so whatever the original intent, it slept on Procrustes bed before being incorporated into the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Having finally and only beaten the the main story of this game, I have to say I'm pretty disappointed in the final outcome of the game. Not only does it feel like the game is half baked with its UI and perk system, the companions don't really feel great to play around with, and while their quests held my interest briefly, I was ultimately left wanting more development from each of them. I'm also pretty sad there really isn't a ton of music in the game, and the lack of immersion was definitely not adding to my enjoyment of the game. I guess what really ruins it all, is that your sense of progression just doesn't feel very obvious or fun at the end of the day. Having to choose from the exact same weapon with better stats is huge let down when you have the opportunity to go nuts with all sorts of wacky and whimsical weapons when you try to write a company that cuts corners wherever they can. The overall pay off for doing your companion's quest left me pretty high and dry, since most of them are only useful in pretty rare situations. I absolutely loved Parvati and the way she is written, but ultimately while there is a great framework for building on initially, there just isn't enough time in the main story to build out the characters the way they did. I hate to be yet another FO:NV fan boy, but the game, for being as old as it is, had a great depth, had far more time constraints AND limited resources with a clunky engine and STILL made it out to be a gem that I can't reccomend enough to play. So why am I still recommending it? I didn't pay full price. That, and some of the earlier writing is genuinely funny and interesting, but most of the NPCs in the game are just one dimensional and uninspired. I did get *my* money's worth for this game, but I wouldn't be terribly excited to play something Obsidian puts out any time soon. 4/10 Automags

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love this game. There's a lot of bad reviews, but I have had a great experience. I will speculate why people are struggling with this game. 1. It is going to hit your RAM pretty hard. I see a lot of reviews either not mentioning their RAM or saying they only have 16gb. This is simply not enough to run this game at the highest graphic setting. You can have a top of the line GPU and CPU but this game is RAM intensive. It loads A LOT of the world around you. I noticed that even though Edgewater requires a load screen, outside of the city you are loading in the billboard. Things like this seem simple, but they add up...the large volcano ever present in the background, the high quality water effects, etc. I also noticed it's loading in things like the water and billboard even in dialogue cutscenes. This is after the performance update. 2. A lot of reviews have very little hours in the game like 0.2 or 0.8. This is a problem because I'll admit the first load bit into the tutorial/outside Edgewater does have instances of frame drop. I don't know why, but it is not horrible or makes the game unplayable. However, if you look at the positive reviews, people are having many more hours and playtime experience. The ONLY other time I experience a frame drop was first loading Byzantium and it was 5 seconds.3. The reviews that do mention all of someone's specs do have a people combining Intel/AMD components, Does this work? Yes. But your PC is not going to run the smoothest and this game will really highlight why it's important to be consistent with your build. With that said, the one thing I don't like is the lighting on Monarch. This got messed up. The big trees casting shadows really screw with things, It gets dark, like REALLY dark. If you crank your gamme up at night, you're blinded during the day. In the wilderness of Monarch is the biggest offender, second to Fallbrook. I really haven't noticed major issues with lighting elsewhere except for small areas in like a staircase or something minor like that. I hope they fix this in the future.My specs are as follows:NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090Intel i9-12900K64GB RAM DD4-3600

_childDocuments_.review: So... I gave the original version a thumbs down. This version addresses enough of my complaints that this one gets a thumbs up. The graphics are better, less saturated---I can actually see the enemies usually rather than having them obscured behind garish colors. There are still issues with the lighting not being right (too dark or too light) and some other graphical issues but it's better. The increased level cap helps as well. I appreciate some of the choice to keep to a smaller system and the story overall better after playing Starfield. There is still a lot of load screens and I'd recommend having an SSD to play it. The load times seem shorter and less annoying than before.I do appreciate the anticorporate messages/jokes--anyone should but especially if you have worked in an office.  Overall, while I think Oblivion games are often overrated, this is now a good RPG and well worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: Many of the reviews I saw indicated this was a short game. I clocked in at a little over 43 hours, though much of that was exploring and looting. In true Obsidian fashion, there were many ways to solve most quests. There were many options for customization and player choice. The story was fun, including the DLCs, and I love that the end of the game gives a summary of how your choices and actions influenced what was to come. The companions were all different and felt unique. I only played through two of their side stories, so going through all of them probably would have added a good 10-20 more hours to the game. 40-60 hours is not a short game. To me, that is about the ideal length.If you like choice-driven RPGs, this was a fun one. 8/10.

_childDocuments_.review: At first this game released in absolutely terrible condition with insane requirements and constant shader and traversal stuttering. After many months they apparently fixed the game, and upon playing - yes, it performs better. Yet the graphics of the original have been stripped out for far more primitive visuals. While we get Global Illumination in shader form, what we lose is shadow draw distance, now long and even medium shadows are replaced with screenspace. Meaning you get abnormal looking distance shadows and the actual shadows draw in a few metres from the player. So in the area where you are meant to look at a large object in the middle distance, that object no longer casts shadows, so the entire game play area looks barren compared to the original outer worlds which had far better draw distance. This strips a lot of the game of its visual depth. And the global illumination looks terrible washing out the image dramatically. All around terrible decisions, and a baffling downgrade in visuals compared to the original game. Also, FSR 2 without any DLSS.

_childDocuments_.review: No intention to discount the experiences of others, but I will note up front that I had no technical issues whatsoever except for a severe frame drop the first time I started this game which seems likely to have been shader caching or some similar one time process. Otherwise? The gameplay makes for an extremely fun shooter, the levelling system is great (though perks leave something to be desired) and I loved the constant tongue in cheek tone. This is not a game that wants itself to be taken seriously—it is pretty much gallows humour from start to finish and makes no attempt to hide the fact that the scenarios and characters you are playing are ridiculous—while also being a solid RPG that lets you have a real impact on the world.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed the game. It was a little short, even with doing the DLC campaigns and doing the companion quests. However, the story was decent, and the game play was mostly good. A few complaints, I didn't feel like I needed to use the ability to slow down time more than maybe three or four times. Also I got armor and weapons so powerful early on everything else was lackluster, keeping most of the same weapons and armor throughout the game. Overall though It was good. I felt like a god by the end, which some people don't like, I get that. But I do like feeling like I'm actually getting more powerful as I play. _childDocuments_.review: Overview: Fun little bethesda-era Fallout-like in space. I like the fact that its hub-based rather than full sprawling open-world since the areas feel tailored to its quests and factions and feels more palatable to clear hubs rather than getting open-world fatigue (which has happened a lot to me personally in the last few years)Writing and Story: very tongue-in-cheek poking fun at a hyper-capitalist futuristic dystopia. Mood is overall light, Firefly-esque at times. Companions are relatively one-dimensional but have some interesting quest-lines and fun quips here and there. Its also fun to see them interact in random dialogue when you speak to other vendors and questgivers.Gameplay: I am playing a ranged-only character so can only comment on the shooty parts. Feels very polished and responsive and its cool to see different guns with cool abilities (shrink rays, charged up plasma weapons, grenade launchers, etc.)Difficulty: Kicked off in Supernova since I like survival-light elements. While its hard for the first hour or so of the game, if you have any experience with bethesda-style RPGs, it becomes pretty easy, especially once you acquire companions. It is slightly annoying that you can only sleep and/or save in your ship, feel like you should be able to sleep/save in inns/other safe areas but given that the hubs are relatively small and you can fast travel to ship, it is less of an issue than I imagined when I first started the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't played the original version and i'm not going to compare it directly to fallout:NV or Starfield, i'm going to review it based on its own merits.To quickly summarise It's not terrible or even a particularly bad game but it is frustratingly average.The gunplay is alright.the world and maps are alright.Majority of the quests are basic but alright.The graphics are alright.The RPG elements are pretty bare-bones, the perk system in particular felt like an afterthought.The companions, despite there only being 6 wildly vary between well written and interesting to have around like Eliie and Vicar Max to clearly added in the last minute such as Felix and SAM.The story for the main game and Peril on Gorgon can be summed up as "corporation bad", which while yes, late stage capitalism can indeed be very bad.  It's handled with all the nuance and depth of a terminally online 13 year old who gets all their world views from a Reddit thread.  Murder on Eridanos fairs much better as it's written like a B movie murder mystery and focuses on that.  Overall the writing is also a mixed bag, there is the odd interesting conversation but the vast majority is bland filler you'll forget almost instantly and I expected better from Obsidian.The Outer Worlds is in that awkward range where it isn't bad enough to be memorable but it also isn't good enough that I'd recommend it.  I just finished getting 100% before writing this and I guarantee within a couple days I'll forget playing it.6/10

_childDocuments_.review: This is not really the "next fallout new vegas" as advertisement and hype made us to believe. It is just too unserious to make me actually care about what is going on. That it is not serious is not necessarily a bad thing as I have no problem with a comedy space RPG. The problem is that it is just not very funny and tries way to hard to be goofy all the time. So hard that it harms the worldbuilding and story where they rather end on a bad joke than write something endearing.The graphics are good, but I really do not like the artstyle. It is too colorful but in like a corporate "look how fun we are" way instead of a vibrant fresh way. The retro future stuff is pretty neat though. Exploration is fine, but it is not that exciting to do and I struggle to feel motivated to go off the beaten path. What is good is the character building, combat and that there is quite a lot of choice within the different quests even though you may not care about the outcome (still not as impactful or percieved to be as impactful as NV, but more than any modern Bethesda game at least). Overall it is fun to play, but man it is disappointing.There was so much potential here to be a next gen New Vegas, but it was not realized. I hope they can fix a lot of the issues in the sequel that is in development, but I would not hold my hopes up. Hopefully Avowed is better at least.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Actually a decent improvement, but be prepared to wait 3-5 business days to launch (Around 90 minutes of my "play"time is just waiting for it to properly launch). Others have said the original with mods is the better alternative, so maybe give that a try.I completed this game on Xbox the week it launched and I absolutely loved it. I saw this on Humble Choice this month and decided to go for it. I was thrilled to play the game with updated graphics and a higher level cap as well as all of the DLC, which I never had a chance to play. I installed on my m.2 ssd because of reviews about launch time and crashes, just to give it the best chance of working. I launch the game and Steam says it's running, but nothing seems to be happening. About 5 minutes later I close it through Steam and try again. This time I wait about 7-8 minutes. Nothing. Then I remembered a review claiming it takes 10 minutes to launch, so I set a timer. 10 Minutes later still nothing. I decide to wait a bit more and around 15 minutes in, the GeForce Experience banner pops up and I begin to celebrate, but am greeted with a black screen. At this point it was 12:30 AM so I gave up and went to bed. The next evening I decided to launch the game and simply wait. I was not playing a game so it wouldn't interfere (obviously). I didn't set a stopwatch, so I'm not entirely sure how long it was, but I was watching a Top Gear Special (Burma) and around the 45 minute mark THE GAME ACTUALLY LAUNCHED. I played some and really did enjoy coming back to one of my favorite RPGs. Graphics improvements were actually very good imo, and face details were pretty nice. It really did look excellent in comparison to the original on Xbox One. If your rig is similar to mine, then it should work well with visual settings maxed. _childDocuments_.review: The first time I played the game, I was underwhelmed and I put it aside. When I returned to it, I forced myself to give it a chance and it was worth it!The game has many flaws. It is abominably optimised and the stutter is almost constant, at times nearly freezing. My game machine is no slouch, and it normally runs top games with high graphics detail. I had to turn nearly everything off to make this game barely playable. The game borrows A LOT from other games. Too much. In one location, the music and ambience were a flat out a clone of Borderlands. Homage or not, it was an exaggerated resemblance.The game play is okay. Combat is average. Not bad. Not spectacular. It's pretty much vanilla open world RPG in play style.And yet, I fell in love with the game. For all its flaws, once you get past the initial "introductory" missions, the game develops a charm and a personality all its own. And you start to discover subtleties that aren't explained or advertised. Your decisions have an impact on future events, sometimes even making progression impossible. It's not a bug. YOU screwed up. Normally, this would be frustrating, but it's done in a way that forces you to think things through instead of just randomly picking choices because it would be funny to do things a certain way. You CAN make enemies. You CAN lose allies. You CAN lose opportunities. Not by accident. By poor decision making. Because of this, the game is quite replayable. In fact, it's almost necessary to replay it at least once to correct the errors you made the first time and benefit from all the things you learned. It's a different experience the second time around.You can play the game without exploring, but if you do explore, you get rewarded. You might find a hidden side quest or unique armour or weapons that people who forego exploration will never even see. And even ignoring the rewards, there are cool things to discover that give more depth to the universe.They can clearly design a great game. Now if only they hired programmers who could make it run reasonably on a powerful gaming rig!

_childDocuments_.review: I was always interested in Outer Worlds, since I was a big fan of Fallout: New Vegas, the game that everyone seems to praise Obsidian for, and definitely one of the best RPGs I've ever played, despite its age. Humble Bundle Choice gave me the chance to play this game finally!The Outer Worlds manages to perfectly capture the things that made Fallout: New Vegas good. Decisions that really force you to  work the motor, a story that is serious yet doesn't mind cracking a few jokes along the way, and most importantly a story and main quest that truly keep you engaged throughout the game. Now I will say this:Outer Worlds is not as big as a Bethesda RPG necessarily, it's certainly smaller and less ambitious than Fallout: NV. But that doesn't stop me from liking it more than F:NV. The story is the perfect length, it isn't the traditional 100 hour game we have been conditioned to like. It's the right length, with the right stories, that are good in quality. It does what NV did, in a different yet similiar setting while also modernizing it. It's quite literally quality over quantity.Another thing I would like to praise Outer Worlds on is the companions. This game does companions very well, they are likeable, have their own respectable lines. You can have two at a time, and they will actually interact! It really beats the loneliness of these types of games. A true companion that isn't just a stone cold killer.Now that doesn't mean Outer Worlds doesn't lack in many parts, this is only the first game of this franchise, and I believe it will become a classic with enough work. Combat, like almost any other RPG out there sucks monkey b*lls. It's flat, the variety is synthetic, the weapons don't really make that big of a difference, nor does the enemy variety. The consumables piss me off, the amount of consumables that just do the same exact thing is freakish. Why can't there just be ONE item doing ONE thing. This has lead me to NEVER use consumables apart from healing ones that already come occupied. The wending machines, and traders almost never sell anything worth buying either. I've practically only bought ammo from them.I also think more life could be added to the open worlds, the cities are great in design, each area has great side quests that are worth going through. But one thing I've also hated in NV was the lack of action in the open world. Sometimes you will just be walking like a moron, for nothing to happen... No bystander events, not a lot of things that you need to overcome on your way, not a lot of breathtaking scenery even. Or music to distract you and let you get immersed. Maybe that's simply not the vibe the devs were going for, and that's fine. But I'm sure there is a billion ways to make the walk between point A and point B interesting. They could lean onto the looting aspect... If the things you loot actually are interesting! I practically found that the only things worth looting in this game are adreno and hacking tools.Speaking of hacking, I think a mini game to the hacking action would be great. I am definitely a sucker for how satisfying lockpicking mini games are. I understand that might be difficult with a hacking skill line... But if it could work, that would be great!Conclusion? I think Outer Worlds is still not there yet. It's a great RPG anyone familiar with the genre should try. But, I think the sequel will surpass this, and make this franchise truly shine. 8/10

_childDocuments_.review: Outer Worlds is a immersive, story-rich game with engaging characters. At least on Normal difficulty, it's not hard at all, but if you want more challenge, the difficulty can be turned up. It is possible to vary your playstyle and try to get different endings, but I enjoyed just playing it through once, and sticking with the ending I got.While the graphics are not gorgeous, they are effective in creating a distinct look and feel for each part of Halcyon. In short a great game for players looking for an accessible, fun game with a rich world. If you enjoyed this game, you are likely also going to like games like Fallout: New Vegas, which is in many ways a better game, but requires modding to really get the most out of it. Outer Worlds can be enjoyed as is, out of the box.I did not play the DLC but they simply add more content, so it's probably good if you want to extend your experience.
