_childDocuments_.review: I know, I know... I have played this game for a few hours, must not be so terrible aye?Well... It's not a bad game. Actually I did buy the first edition back in the day (didn't even remember it '_' )But I cannot recommend this new version over the "old one".Why? Cause it's been 4 years now (during which years they released many DLCs to make more money, but did not fix the bugs!!!), and now they released a 60$ edition, hoping to grab even more money (which they did), except they did not fix any bugs!Noticeable bugs:- First launch (after fresh install... subsequent launches are ok) takes about 1 minute of a black screen for a custom cursor to finally appear on it, and then again 20 more seconds for the title screen to appear (just an animated image), and even then, it's running at 1FPS (I really mean one single frame per second). It's absolutely unacceptable for a "gold edition" or whatever- Hair color during the character creation is not very noticeable, because of the weird lights (and light reflection) they use in this engine- In the inventory, helmets appear to have 4 mod-slots (small dots on the bottom left of an item in the inventory) but it's a bug in the inventory, helmets don't have slots... The mod-slots seem to stay in place when you change the inventory order- About the inventory order... It's a complete mess! First, the order is not "remembered" between two inventory openings. Which means you have to order it again to your liking every freaking time. Also, the ascending/descending order does not work properly, it shows items the other way around. Last, sometimes the "by name" order is displayed, but the inventory is not at all sorted by name, you have to sort it again to "refresh" the list. And it gets boring. Flawed File Explorer Simulator... Yeah, hard pass.- When you compare items, it is bugged as well. You can activate the "compare" option, but if you want to switch to another item to be compared to (typically you compare to your current armor to choose a better one and then you compare to your current helmet to choose a better one), then the comparison popup is completely broken. It's not comparing what it should. You have to fiddle with the comparison tool a few more times for the proper comparison popup to show.- You can't skip (or I didn't find how) the intro credits, which gets boring.- Worst of all: if you play with a sniper rifle, like I do, enemies pop up only below a certain distance, which makes the sniper scope... Well, not totally useless, but almost. The main goal of a sniper rifle is to stay far away. Not like 30 meters. But more like 300 or 500 meters or something.- Sometimes enemies walk/run past you without seeing you. Other times, enemies automatically know where you hide when they are in "hunt" mode, which breaks the "sneak" / "hide & seek" part of the game.- The light reflection on things is completely stupid- Current time is not displayed when you want to sleep in order to skip night time (because it is boring, obviously)- You don't have much freedom, after all, and not much to do except a few quests. It's sad that they did not deepened (is this a word??) the world, interactions, side quests like healing the so-called "plagued" citizens, etc. (or, for example, being able to repair the geothermal plant, and make everyone happy)- When you decide to pick up items, it's not specified whether they are junk... It should be.- Gravity is low, but for some reason you can't jump more than above your knees or something, this is stupid- I stop there because there are more where it comes from, but I have other things to tend to, and I think I made my point.All these bugs... BUT!!! Instead of fixing obvious bugs, they decided to spend (waste?) time making it harder for people to use a cheat engine. Seriously... In a single player game FFS! What's the point of wasting dev resources on this? Especially since it's pretty easy to break your lame cheat protections anyway. It's just a waste of time for both the devs and the players.It's the kind of game that I absolutely LOVE (Fallout-like RPG with a retro vibe).BUT seriously, it's completely RIDDLED with obvious bugs that they could have fixed in like a day or two. They really could have.And the fact that they did not fix them shows that they don't respect their player base an ounce.I despise that kind of greedy disrepectful behavior like nothing else!

_childDocuments_.review: Outer worlds is an odd game, It's basically firefly themed.I overall enjoyed my time playing through it, there are a reasonable amount of sidequests, a vast majority are not memorable. The main quest is surprisingly, laughably short, it is comparable in length or maybe shorter than the dlc main quest, which are the most enjoyable. I honestly don't know how the game was being sold before the dlc was released.The combat is passable, the stealth is not great, all of the enemy know your location if you engage a single target, and use a silencer, everyone seems to hear the silencer at distances that don't really make sense.The weaponry selection is good, the modification section came off a little half baked, you can find the majority of them early on and then that is kinda it, you just amass a giant inventory of mods that you don't really use.Repairing was tedious, and the tinkering was needlessly expensive with very low incremental impact, worst thing is you have to do it if you want to do any meaningful damage.The companion characters were probably the most enjoyable, I liked the conversations they had in the background, they had their own opinions on certain quests that you could ask about. Giving them a certain level of individuality.The NPCs were ok, Phineas Welles was I assume based off of Rick, from Rick and Morty. No where near as interesting though.The rest of them aside from the dlc were mainly static and forgettable.This goes the same for the factions, I had forgotten about all of them by the time they reappeared in the story, not fully grasping why they were suddenly showing up, as I never talked about my plans, they just happened to manifest in a very low impact sort of way, the disguise attachment you get close to the start made it low impact.The worlds you visit are reasonably different, the terrain was ok, the invisible walls on rocks were annoying. Most places didn't entice you to return much after your first visit, luckily fast travel helps with the tedium of backtracking.The main story is simple, short, they really should have hired a better writer, or at least a well read one, the whole story comes off as if from a writer that derives most inspiration from watching television media, it comes off a little juvenile. It'll only take you so far, read a book, read lots of books, get that imagination juice flowing, it will be a lot better.The leveling system was not very noticable, except for the dumb perk, my favorite part of the game, there numerous green moments with that perk!If you've made it this far, thanks for taking the time.Do I recommend this game, kinda, I did enjoy my playthrough, would I play it a second time? No.This game is old enough that there will be numerous deals available that give justification to pick it up, it's worth a playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts out pretty okay, and it does have it's moments, but the overall experience is quite bland. The combat is pretty basic, which can be okay but when there are 5 types of enemies it gets bothersome real quick. There are humans, robots, apes, lizards, and bugs, but apes, lizards, and bugs are pretty much the same in behavior and threat so it's actually 3 types of enemies with a reskinning. The companions were not working really either, they all feel like cookie-cutter characters that you have seen many times before, in a good roleplaying game this should never happen and I'm quite disappointed in Obsidian for this. The only companion or character in the world I could even remotely come to care for was SAM a cleaning robot, I think that speaks for itself regarding the NPCs.The story and quests are quite boring and feel predictable in a bad way, I believe they were going for "classic space adventure" but it's so safe and silly that it's boring. The quests are mostly "go here, go back" fetch quests are subpar but couple that with needing to go into several loading screens, and it gets insanely tedious.Final verdict, the game feels kinda of like a lackluster fallout alternative, without the interesting grim apocalyptic world and lacking all mystique. The RPG elements are there but without empathy for the cardboard characters you will disregard most outcomes, with only a few exceptions. If you want a better version of this game go play or replay New Vegas. If you want a better more fun experience without in-depth RPG elements but a way more interesting world, enemies, combat, and story go play Fallout 4.

_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Worlds: Spacer's Choice Edition is a must-have for any fan of science fiction and role-playing games. Developed by Obsidian Entertainment and published by Private Division, this game is set in an alternate future in which mega-corporations have taken over much of the universe.The game follows a character called the Stranger, who is taken to a corporate-run colony called Halcyon. Here, the player is presented with a choice: to help the locals survive or to help the corporations. This moral decision forms the basis of the game, and the player's decisions will have a direct impact on the story.Graphically, The Outer Worlds: Spacer's Choice Edition looks great. The game world is detailed and immersive, with a great soundtrack and sound effects helping to bring the game to life. _childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game, being made by Obsidian (famous for making Fallout: New Vegas and probably other things), feeling like this Fallout/Borderlands/almost Mass Effect hybrid. It has so many appealing looking locations and a lot of wacky designed people throughout the main game and dlcs. There's a good pool of odd weapons and armor that actually feel important as you'll meet and get to know all the factions and companies that make them. There's also a good amount of experimental weapons that have strange abilities like shrink rays and mind control guns, adding some unique and often hilarious fights. Some of Obsidian's humor and obscure cultural references also shine and will leave you chuckling or tipping your MoonMan Helmet to the writers. (The quest name "A Clockwork Mock Apple '' and Petunia the Plant really got me for some reason). There's a good perk and level progression system allowing for many types of playstyles. There's also several quests that actually show the consequences of your actions and change how some of the game is played. There's so many good things about this game, but there's too much wrong for it to be worth picking up, and I got this in a bundle for practically free. Bad things, so many bad things. The enemies are really cool at first, until you figure out there's like 12 enemies in the game and just different variants of them, you want worms, space dogs, space mantis, space gorilla, or crazy humans, take your pick. The loot, there's so much in this game, but the base game has waaaay more items that have to be stolen and arent just free to pick up. There's no consequences of stealing if no one sees you (take notes kids) so it's just a minor inconvenience that happens a lot. Though the dlc does fix this by making a majority of items free for all those grubby loot goblins. The dlcs, Peril on Gorgon specifically, might be the most boring and ugly add-on for a game I've seen, and I bought Oblivion horse armor. Peril on Gorgon is just soulless, there are practically no new enemies (drugged up marauders don't count, marauders are already drugged up, that's not stereotyping and I will die on this hill), the story is so unbelievably boring with some of the stiffest acting in the game, there are very few new weapons or even armor (one of them making you be able to run faster so you can get through the dlc asap), all of the locations are not any different from the main game, the dlc takes you to another planet for 1 mission and then decides you should never leave Gorgon again (even though you really want to leave). Moral of the story, I did not like Peril of Gorgon. Murder on Eridanos reminds you that experience with a game's engine really does show, this dlc is not great BUT there's features in it that make it a more memorable experience. A classic who dunnit mystery with some pretty good twists, but this dlc is so empty, they don't do much but what they do is pretty good. I spent more time walking around to get to locations than fighting or in buildings combined, and I had armor that made me move quicker. There's a lot of new weapons that are fun to use and pretty plentiful in the world (after you spend 5 minutes running there) but this is overshadowed by the very few enemies scattered throughout the map. The dlcs fixed the main game's problem of having way too many enemies scattered throughout the world, but instead of running into enemies every 10 seconds you have to play Woody's Roundup for a few minutes if you want to fight any large groups. Also I hope you like fetch quests and kill quests, because that's 90% of what you'll be doing, though the quests that do split from this formula are pretty good. There's no morality system but the factions reputation is affect based on who you kill and help, though if you want to be pure evil and pick the "worst" choices and kill everyone you're probably gonna be put on a speedrunning leaderboard with how fast you'll get through the game, the main game and dlcs are significantly shorter if you choose to be bad, but the extra missions for being good and helping everyone live is hardly worth the effort of never talking to the npcs you saved again. This game sometimes works very well in some spots and then absolutely tanks in performance in others, having the Space's Choice edition is supposed to make it look and run better, but I think the worse lighting helped hide the muddy look and frame drops more. There are some absolutely beautiful places in this game, like the space station the GroundBreaker, the luminescent Devil's Peak Caverns, and the massive bustling city of Byzantium, they would be even more awesome if they didn't cut my fps in half and send my gpu into an early retirement. There are so many things that should've been fixed with the Spacer's Choice edition, I mean they added an insane level cap of 99 that will be impossible to even get halfway to because that much xp does not exist outside of farming enemies for xp scraps. but adding that is much more important than fixing bugs like quest options not working for anyone still or being locked in your inventory screen because there were too many enemies leaping around when you needed a bottle of Purple Berry Juice. I also clipped through a few bridges in the game while spamming spacebar to go faster, which caused me more deaths than anything else in this game, so I guess look out for bridges. I wanted this to help feed my fallout addiction and give me another wacky sci-fi experience but all I did was put on a moon helmet, get addicted to drugs, and listen to the screams of my robot janitor committing genocide with acidic cleaner.6/10 - "It's not the best choice, it's Spacer's Choice!"

_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Worlds is an action RPG made by Obsidian Entertainment and then later "improved" by Private Division in Spacer's Choice Edition. I would love to blame all the problems on Private Division, but be honest for one second. In terms of story and gameplay The Outer Worlds is one of the worst games in Obsidian's portfolio. Spacer's Choice Edition did screw with the performance and created new issues, but the base game was already average at best.If I could, I would give it a mixed review, just for the expansions. There's some good stuff here, but it's hidden behind a bland main story, bugs, and joyless gameplay.Main StoryThe main story of The Outer Worlds is just plain and boring. Some weirdo scientist saves us from the hibernation chamber and then asks us to help him wake up the others. This is not easy and we need to do some other stuff beforehand. And that stuff is just... weak. There's no oomph, no emotions, and zero surprises. At least the choices matter - usually in small ways, but still.Side StoriesThere's some good and bad stuff here. The fetch quests aren't great, but you can find some gems with fun sub-stories. The faction quests are way better in terms of design and they entwine with the main story very nicely. I liked that we could quickly resolve some quests just by using our attributes during the conversation.WorldThe real "meat" of The Outer Worlds. The world created by Obsidian is a fascinating mix of sci-fi, post-apo, and cyberpunk. There are heartless corporations, cruel gangs, cults, weirdos - everyone that you would expect in a world like this.It's hard to exactly describe all the details and nuances - there are too many of them. Obsidian was able to create something fairly interesting and unique.CompanionsParvati was easily the best companion. Well written, well voice-acted, has some character development, and her companion quests are fun. It helps that we have lots of time to bond with her.Everyone else? Depends on what you like. Vicar Max has an interesting backstory, but his quest line is just meh. Nyoka and Ellie - they aren't bad, but they lack IT. SAM is fun for his one-liners. Felix is... not good.RomanceThere's no romance, only some flirting. Instead, you can help one of your companions to date another person. Interesting replacement, but I would prefer to have both things in the game.Peril on GorgonFirst story expansion. You can complete it in less than 10 hours (main story and all side quests).Unfortunately, the new planet feels like a rehash of what we already saw. There are some exceptions, but most of the new places felt dull. Too much walking and shooting the same enemies over and over.At least the story is intriguing. The new characters aren't bad either. I would even dare to say - both are more interesting than stuff from "vanilla" game.Murder on EridanosThe second story expansion and probably the biggest reason why someone would want to play The Outer Worlds. You can finish it in around 5 hours. Add ~4 hours if you want to complete all side quests.The new planet is medium-sized. It looks way prettier than most of the locations from the rest of the game. There are also lots of easter eggs and environmental storytelling.I especially liked the story of this expansion. It starts as a mystery, but very quickly everything gets weirder and sometimes unsettling. The plot twist near the end is also great.Unlike in the first expansion, the Murder on Eridanos adds a new gameplay element to the game - a tool that helps you find the clues.GameplayThe gameplay is very shallow. It feels like Obsidian wanted to create Skyrim/Fallout in their own universe, but they didn't have enough money to make it good. The foundations are solid and the ideas aren't bad, but the execution leaves much to be desired.We start with the character creation - it feels like in a classic RPG. A decent amount of options to choose from. Different faces, hairs, details, etc. You can also pick your attributes, skills, perks, and background story.Unfortunately, it doesn't take much to see the worst sides of this game. Small locations, repetitiveness, the world around us is pretty much dead, lack of balance, boring crafting, and much more.The melee combat is awful. The gunplay is not bad, but the lack of weapons variety is noticeable.There's a big problem with the enemies' variety. You'll fight humans, robots, and five or six types of animals. This is not enough to NOT make you bored after 15-20 hours of playing. It doesn't help that their AI is super dumb. They won't give you any challenge, no matter the difficulty level.The reputation system could be better. Besides discounts in shops and some different speech lines, it doesn't affect the gameplay at all.I appreciate the freedom to pick your playing style. The good guy, the bad guy, something in between - you can play however you want.VisualsThe game is just... ugly. There are worse-looking titles on the market, but I would expect something better from a game released in 2020. Besides some specific designs, most of the stuff looks dated. The models are too simple, the textures are often low quality, and the animations are extremely wooden. What's the point of the face close-ups, when the faces are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awful?AudioThere's nothing negative that I can tell about the audio. Everything is at least fine.The soundtrack fits the game well, but it's not particularly memorable. The sounds (guns, effects, etc.) and voice acting are solid. I wouldn't expect anything less from some well-known names that did the voice acting.It didn't bother me, but it may be a problem for some - the main character is not voiced.TechnicalitiesThe performance is bad. My FPS were never stable, even inside the buildings. They usually fluctuated between 100 and 144, but some bigger drops (below 70 FPS) also occurred.There are also tons of other problems. Crashes (two), a broken quest (Electric Fling from DLC), and an insane amount of small bugs (from flying corpses to getting stuck inside the objects).

The intricate web of choices and consequences allows for a truly personalized gameplay experience, with multiple branching paths and outcomes that encourage replayability and ensure that no two playthroughs are alike.What sets Spacer's Choice Edition apart is its impeccable blend of serious themes and irreverent humor. The writing is sharp, witty, and consistently entertaining, injecting a healthy dose of satire into the corporate-dominated world of Halcyon. From the quirky dialogue options to the amusing advertisements and product descriptions, the game embraces its darkly comedic tone with gusto, making every interaction a joyous and often hilarious experience. The memorable characters you meet along the way are brought to life with exceptional voice acting, further elevating the humor and injecting personality into every conversation.In addition to its stellar narrative, The Outer Worlds: Spacer's Choice Edition boasts immersive gameplay mechanics that keep you engaged throughout your journey. Whether you're exploring bustling cityscapes or venturing into the untamed wilderness, each location is a visual feast that adds depth and immersion to the game world.The Outer Worlds: Spacer's Choice Edition is a triumph in every sense of the word. _childDocuments_.review: This coming from Obsidian isn't as great as I expected it to be, but it is still a lot of fun to play and could be a strong franchise. This next part may be considered SPOILER, so stop reading if you don't want to know. The Story:At first I was annoyed feeling like there was an anti-capitalism sentiment running through this game. Instead, I think I have come to realize that it is more of a wake up call to the people to recognize that corporations don't care about you and that they will go to heinous ends just to make profits. It can also be a wake up call to corporations asking how ethical are your practices? Are you running your clientele into ground just so that you can milk them dry? What is the state of your soul if your goal is to make as much money as possible at the expense of others and your surroundings. Lot's of interesting questions presented throughout the game. The CompanionsThe companions were decent. I found myself running most of the time with Vicar Max and Nyoka. However, I did like the difference between each companion and the development of their personalities. Quite a rag tag team, but united in that they all stood for what was right. I couldn't stand Ellie at first because she was the most morally ambiguous to the point it was annoying at times. But, once I completed her side mission, it all made sense and made me grow fond of her more and more when I could get her to open up.Don't know why SAM was included, except maybe to provide an option for a non-sentient being??? I didn't use him at all, the only thing interesting about him was that he would cause ADA to become aroused periodically throughout the game. Pretty funny in an awkward sort of way.Game-playThe game play was a lot of fun. I appreciated that as you got stronger, so did the enemies. However, it did cause me to beg the question, what is the point of ranking up? It wasn't that I was bothered by it, but it did puzzle me that the whole point of ranking up your character and weapons is so that the enemy becomes easier to kill. Maybe it was just the way I encountered enemies in the game. I also liked that I was challenged to approach the enemy with some thought put into instead of just go in and "spray and pray" that you didn't spend too many bullets successfully killing the enemy. You also had to develop strategies in some situation. That was fun. Anyway, I am surprised more people aren't talking about this game as it is very similar to the Fallout/Elder Scrolls franchise with more of a Bioshock twist. If you like any of those games, give this a try.

People are experiencing stuttering and other bugs even on high end hardware.I have a Ryzen 9 5900x and an Nvidia RTX 3080 and my experience is that on ultra settings at 1440 the game is not nearly as optimized as I would like. _childDocuments_.review: Outer Worlds is simply put, a great time. (Presuming you do not have technical issues, I had the odd bug but my game ran perfectly on ultra throughout)Outer Worlds has you romping around a solar system as a recently defrosted human Popsicle. You'll typically be going from A-B doing a variety of quests, levelling up, gaining companions and raking in a bunch of loot and coin. Pretty par for the course of the genre and for Obsidian. One thing that I really appreciate about the game is that there's no fat to it. All of the skills have purpose and you can play however you want and approach the game however you want and make it work. None of the loot is useless junk and if it is useless junk, it's for selling. I love games that have systems that feed into one another and don't waste your time and Outer Worlds does that in spades. On an aesthetic level (I cannot speak in relation to the original version) but the game has a good variety of interesting and lovely looking locations. The various creatures and NPC's look decent (Though there could have done with being better variety for people's faces and voices as some looked/sounded very similar) One thing that particularly stood out to me with the game is that the companions aren't just there to be your bullet sponges. They engage in dialog, boost your stats and can even take over parts of quests for you. The dialog itself is solid throughout the game and having these characters with you works really well. Honestly I had a great time just gaining information and talking to folks and found myself picking up more dialog skills than I would usually. The overall story and world itself could have been a bit more interesting for me. It's not that it's bad overall but I just wish it gave a little more or that decisions felt more balanced as I typically found it much easier to go for one option with the other options just not feeling worthwhile. I will likely play a second play through down the line to see how things vary however. I do also wish there were more out there sci-for concepts in the game and different enemy variety too as I feel these elements were played somewhat safe. DLC'sThis version comes bundled with the DLC's which I'll do a section on. Peril On Gorgon:PoG sets you off onto an asteroid chasing a detective whom stumbled upon a variety of secrets from the labs on said asteroid. This DLC is largely combat and exploration focused and feeds into prior lore of the game. It feels like the rest of the game and rounds up well with some reasonable choices to be made and some neat locations. Some of the weapons of the DLC are rather fun but the location itself feels a bit bland. Murder on Eridanos:MoE has you recruited as a detective in a murder mystery at a wealthy hotspot set on some floating rocks which also houses one of the corporations factories. Unsurprisingly you are set to solve a murder of a famous actress whom was murdered at the hotel prior to a launch of a new drink. This DLC is more narrative focused but I enjoyed the areas within the DLC as it felt varied and the mystery aspect hooked me in. The outcome is rather interesting and there are some odd choices within the DLC but overall there's some fun encounters, some great weapons and an overall quirky fun murder mystery. Overall, I am happy to have gotten the game in the Humble Monthly and given it a shot. It's a solid game and I fully enjoyed my time with it and all that came with it. Aside from some repetitiveness and some minor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ here and there, it's a solid game and well worth the time I put into it!

_childDocuments_.review: Solid clone of Fallout, with a lot of similar mechanics and elements (and with VATS replaced with TTD). Story is definitely fine as well, its not the most original (evil companies, evil gangs, evil rich people, etc ...) but it managed to keep me entertained. Characters throughout the world, including your potential companions are a tad more interesting and some are very amusing. Which enhances the narrative a lot.The many different choices you can make, that actually have an impact, are probably the best element of this game. Half-way through you can betray the guy that sent you on this wild goose-chase and have for a completely different 1/3 of the game, so its definitely thought through. There is also 3 different endings, with each of the minor consequences of your choices laid out during the ending scene. All in all, there is some replayability if you're into that.Combat is also fine, essentially you point and shoot. Like I said it looks like Fallout a lot but with TTD being completely useless (perhaps on higher difficulties it has its uses). Aside from that: guns degrade, you find a better one every 10 minutes, you can upgrade guns and armor, there's different amunition types, you can melee if you want and you can try to stealth but that is very Unreliable :). Companions - which are optional - help you in combat and each one as a special attack you can use every x seconds. In most encounters they are capable enough so do not really need to micro-manage them, which is good. They also boost various skills, depening on their persona and the gear you assign them.Talking about skills, there is a slight RPG element in that you can upgrade skills at each level and assign a perk every 2 levels. Perks don't do a whole lot in my opinion, aside from backpack increases and Science damage you can pretty much select whatever. Skills allow for a bit of a variation, but 'supporting' things like Lockpick and Hack will gain you a whole lot more compared to leveling 'combat skills' like Long Guns for example. On top of this, there are also Flaws that give permanent debufs in exchange for a perk point. You do not need to accept them, but its not as annoying as it sounds so you can give it a shot. For example if you eat a lot of food you can be offered the Food Addict Flaw which will debuf some skills unless you eat every couple of minutes.Graphically the game is very very colorfull which is a nice change of pace. Technically it looks solid enough and runs smooth so nothing special to remark there. Which cannot be said for the amount of bugs that are still in this game, even in this SCE release. More then once could I not complete a certain choice - forcing me to a single outcome - because something was bugged. Some examples: In one of the worlds you can side with one of 2 factions or broker peace between them, I had everything lined up for the peace option but I simply could not select it (some of the NPC's even respawned later on in the 'peace location' because of this, having killed them earlier). In one of the DLC's a certain character is locked out if you meet him to soon. Assigning gear to companions randomly won't work until you open and close some screens. And on top of all this, the enemy AI is just plain dumb - probably not a bug but still noteworthy - and will always just rush you. I said earlier stealth is unreliable, to give you an idea; you can silently kill 2 enemies before everyone around you (regardless of floors) will know where you are and will just bumrush you. The only way to avoid this is to wait for a minute after every 2 kills, so guns blazing is usually the better choice.All in all, if you can pick this up in a sale I would still recommend it. The bugs are annoying, but not gamebreaking, and the rest of the game is actually pretty fun. Its also not annoyingly long, it tooke me about 32 hours to finish the main game and both DLC's and I definitely did some heavy exploring.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming from the original version (which I loved) this one is the version I recommend to both new players and the ones familiar with The Outer Worlds.First, I want to give my thoughts about the 2 main points of criticism:1) Look, I understand the point about paying 10 $ for better graphics and a raised level cap,  because for 10 bucks you could expect at least some content. That doesn't make any sense to me. If you own The Outer Worlds, just keep it. Why would anyone upgrade to this version and then leave a negative review for upgrading it?!If you don't own The Wouter Worlds, buy this package with all the DLCs included. Simple as that.2) After the initial release the performance was horrible. The developers since then released a patch, which solved all of the performance issues I experienced prior to that patch. I play on Ultra graphics and everything is fine.That out of the way, I want to say:I am a Fallout fan since 1997 and I'll always remember that thrill of exploring new worlds with a decent amount of freedom to go wherever you want and to do whatever you want to do. _childDocuments_.review: EDIT:: June 23 2023The devs have massively improved performance since my original (positive) review. They added AMD FSR, fixed lots of issues like stuttering the game had (I imagine by preloading shaders) and now I can 100% max the game out on 4k resolution even without AMD FSR turned on. However, I put AMD FSR on to "Quality" mode just to keep system temps a bit lower.Remember guys, support devs of your favorite games (even sub contracted ones) because all the cancel culture and hatred will only ruin the industry. Lots of women and men work hard on games like this. They don't work for free and also need to feed themselves like I keep trying to remind communities. It's easy to say "wah wah I am a crybaby with poopy pants and want free DLC and remasters"... but it isn't easy to remaster a game or make DLC for a game. It takes lots of time, patience, and support.__________________________________________________________________________It's good.Remember that the graphics have been enhanced, and therefore the graphics settings on the upper end (very high, ultra) require very beefy computers. That being said;Keep this in mind, the graphics setting "Visual Effects" and the "Screen Space Global Illumination" settings yield huge performance impacts. Set Visual Effects to "high" and Screen Space Global Illumination to "low" (which still looks GREAT). This alone will massively boost your FPS with MINIMAL visual impacts.The last thing to do is lower the "3D Resolution" from 100% in increments of 10% until you consistently get 60+FPS or whatever feels good. Just keep in mind, this is at 4k resolution. Upscaling technology by nature doesn't work the best for 1080P monitors/native resolution, but works decently at 1440p and incredibly for 4kOkay, all that being said just try not to jump onboard with all the modern "cancel culture". _childDocuments_.review: Scroll down for TL;DR +/- points.Really liked this game, I even liked stories of your crew mates even tho others may disagree with that. I would say difficulty of this game is similiar to other similiar games like Fallout 4/NV, Skyrim, Oblivion etc. meaning that on normal you probably will not have any difficulty in combat unless you screw up your build, or enter location that is way above your level. I would advice against picking Supernova difficulty on your first playthrough, not really because of the difficulty (which can be pretty hard if you dont know where to find good weapons, few tricks etc.).  One of those things is that you can fast travel only to your ship, it doesn't really matter during main quest (slows you little but it's bearable), but I couldn't imagine doing some of the side quests that require you to travel a lot.  Second one is that when your companions die, they die permanently, which will (obviously) lock you out of their questline.Third one is that you cannot manually save (only on your ship), so you are only left with autosaves which happen everytime you change location.Game offers some choices but it feels like in most of cases there are only opinions A and B, so basically see almost everything after two playthroughs. A little more in one DLC, but I would just advice saving before doing some more important choices and resume from there, rather than starting the game over.  Being able to choose dumb dialogue options when playing low int character is fun. Companions are fun, and often talk about what is happening, without being repetitive, sometime even talk with each other, definitely one of the aspects this game does better than most of games. At least on "normal" playthrough. When for example killing someone you had no reason to kill they will probably just comment something along "why?" and story will just go on.On the other side NPC's will sometimes repeat dialogues in combat but that doesn't seem to happen very often.  Performance wise I haven't noticed any problems even on my older system using RX 480 and some 10+ years old processor. Runs nice as well on my new system.I cannot really compare this version against the original since I haven't played that one.   I liked graphics even though I saw lot of reviews saying that it is either too cartoony, or that original version looks better. You should probably compare those two yourself.  Main quest was interesting enough to me and most of sidequests were interesting as well, one thing I really didn't like was how similiar the two endings were. .  Also game haven't really had many bossfights and those weren't really interesting in any way.The game also has science weapons, which have unique effects and can inflict various debuffs but I never felt like using those effects was more effective than just raw damage even on supernova difficulty.   I really enjoyed this game, played around 40h on my first playthrough, rest of the gametime was speedrunning second playthrough and collecting missed achiviements. Even tho I liked this game, it feels like it has little replayability after two playthroughs so I don't think I will be returning to it ever. Will pick up sequel when it comes out tho. TL;DR:+ Story was interesting, some of the side quests as well.+ Companions and their reactions to what was happening. (at least during regular playthrough)+ Dumb dialogue if playing low int character.+ Skill / perk / flaw system + Graphics (even though others may disagree)+- (non)Difficulty of combat.- Dumb restrictions for highest (supernova) difficultty.- Science weapon are nice concept but I felt most of them are not really usefull (except prismatic hammer which is my favourite weapon in this game.)- Low replayability (you have probably seen and tried most of things after 2 playthroughs).- Lack of boss fights and boss fights themselves.- Big similarities between the two endings.If I were to rate the game on scale of 10 I would probably rate it 7.5/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I am writing this because I was surprised by some of the negative reviews. Let me make my stance clear, if this game is boring or repetitive for you, you are not being creative enough. I have played through the entire game (almost) without getting into combat. I have played strictly melee, strictly ranged, the consummate diplomat, and the scientist among other less specialized characters. Skill options are hidden unless you are within a few skill points of the requirement, leaving most dialogue options hidden for an individual play through. There are no essential characters. Kill anyone you want and the game just...copes. Finally a world without "gamey" rules, just intuitive ones (as in, if you kill a member of the Board they look at you a little less fondly, and might try to kill you).You are an individual in dropped into a complex world. There are minimal boundaries, and more opportunity than 5 in-depth play-throughs can capture, let alone someone's review after 10 or 15 hours.This is worth it if you want a deep game that intensely fleshes out the lore, world, character choices, and honestly the different philosophies and cultures that inhabit These Here Outer World  -for those who take their time and those who lookIf you want a thoughtless shooter, buy something else.

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10When I first played this game back in 2019 I was disappointed because I was expecting another New Vegas. What I got was a lot smaller and the world was not as open as I expected it to be. This was before the DLC, Which adds about 15-20 hours of gameplay. I put this game away not expecting to return to it, but life happens and here I am. I know the Spacer's Choice had a lot of issues on launch, but Obsidian seemed to have fixed a lot of those issues. I had next to no issues, and when I did they were all visual glitches (Nothing game ending and no crashes). However, I am not speaking for everyone. The one thing I'd say, that is just as good as New Vegas is: the dialogue. You will meet many different characters with a lot to say, you can talk as much or as little as you want. The companions in this game are great. You can get them to join or leave you based on your choices. There are points where the story about corporate greed gets a little too obvious, but the writing and characterization remains intact throughout the game. My biggest complaints are the color palate being too saturated and no third person mode. However, I should not have judged this game against New Vegas. It is a much smaller experience and I am starting to enjoy these kind of games more and more. We don't need every game to be 100 hours. I think this will hit a sweet spot for a lot of RPG fans, just don't go in expecting New Vegas.

_childDocuments_.review: I planned to write this review a bit later, after I finish the game.But as the game is currently being included in the Humble Bundle this month - I decided to write the review early, to help people decide if this game is for them.This game was created by Obsidian entertainment, the creators of Fallout: New Vegas (and of course the original Fallout games).Which creates pretty high expectations of them from the get go.If we compare Fallout 3 (Bethesda) to New Vegas (Obsidian) - we see that Obsidian are much better in storytelling, side quests and humor.But on the other hand, F:NV had loading screens every time you switched locations - while F3 and F4 contained a huge open world.Looking at this game: it is also an open world RPG in a futuristic setting (which begs the comparison to F:NV), but this time it's also an original IP from Obsidian.And I must say, it fares pretty well.Not perfect - but still, pretty well...RPG elementsFirst of all weapons - there are 4 categories of weapons (melee, light, heavy, long), of each you have sub-divisions (for example: 1-handed & 2-handed melee weapons, light handguns, rifles and machineguns, etc.).In addition there are also 4 categories of damage (blast, plasma, corrosion, N-rays), which can be applies to any gun in the game.Each weapon starts with a basic version, and as the game progresses (and you level up) you can find additional (stronger) versions of the same weapon.In addition, there are "unique" versions of weapons, which you cannot mod, but have special mods already installed.And on top of that, there are completely unique (science) weapons which you find usually after doing special quests - which have unique death mechanics unlike any other weapons in the game.And on top of that - there are 3 mod categories for ranged weapons, 2 categories for melee weapons and 4 categories for armor.And speaking of armor - there too you have variety, with different bonuses and debuffs, and progression over the game.So weapon and armor-wise - you have an amazing variety of different and interesting weapons. And weapon-crafting in itself is a game-within-a-game.Skills-wise, you have several levels of skills distribution you can choose from, when creating your character.During the game, when you level up, you have both skill points and perks/bonuses you can choose from.And every 20 skill points, you can an additional perk/bonus to that skill.In addition, you are occasionally offered to take a debuff, in exchange for an extra perk/bonus point.And on top of that, you also have the ability to redistribute your points (for a small fee) during the game, if you discover you did not distribute well enough, or you decide to try a different build mid-game.So skills-wise, the game also offers a large and interesting variety.In addition, you have up to 2 followers you can take with you.And the followers have bonus points of their own for you to distribute, and weapons and armor they can use.And if you choose to go solo - there are perks that give bonuses to builds without followers.So overall, as you can see, the Role Playing element of this game is very well made, and is one of the strongest points of the game.Open WorldOne the one hand, in open world games you want a big map. And the game is pretty huge here.You have several planets you can visit - each with it's own biome. And each will building or even whole towns you can explore.And some planets you can land on different parts of the planet, and get different maps in each.Or sometimes land in different locations on the same (huge) planet map.On the other hand, many buildings and cities you visit, are not actually part of the same map (in-game) and require loading times when moving from/to them.Also on a less positive side: there is almost no diversity in creatures. Same creatures can be found on every planet.Over all the planets there are only 2 distinct species of creatures (ape-types and arachnid-types). (and 1 more in one of the DLCs) In addition to humans and robots, which can be found throughout the game, but besides being togher in late game (deadlier and harder to kill), they remain pretty much the same (same weapon types, same armor, same loot, etc.)Story / QuestsOn the positive side:This game epitomizes the cornerstone of any Open World RPG - (almost) every quest can be solved in few different ways.You can go in guns blazing.Or talk your way out of a fight.Or sneak in and do what is needed without being discovered.And as an added bonus: More often that not, you can negotiate your reward after finishing a quest (if you pass the required skill checks).And also, as was tradition in Fallout games - this game also has a sense of humor.There are plenty of easter eggs scattered about in the world.And in general - many of the quests have a funny side to them.Now to the less positive side, I've seen mentioned in other reviews as well.The plot/story here is simply weaker than Fallout. I'm not sure what's the reason. If the world is just less interesting because it's too much apart from ours.Or maybe the writing is not as engaging. Or the factions are not very thought out.But the bottom line is - as much as I enjoy the RPG-style gameplay of the game, the main story itself does not feel engaging to me.The factions all seem like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ - and don't make me want to help any of them.And there is simply too much text terminals. Every large rooms contains at least 1-2 terminals, and some even 5-6 terminals. And each terminal has several messages (half a page long on average) - so in an average location that's dozens of pages of text to read.And 95% of them are just superfluous text, that adds nothing to the plot.At some point I just stopped reading them altogether. I'm pretty sure I missed some jokes, and probably some dialog options for talking with people - but that's just too much text to read.Some additional nitpicking:At least in the original release - the graphics seem very cartoony. Even too much so.A serious Open world RPG, needs to have a serious look.You can't look like a $10 indie game, and expect to be taken seriously.Also stealing mechanic is not very well implemented.Stealing / Lockpicking / Hacking has almost zero repercussions, and are very easy to perform even if you're playing a completely non-stealthy character.It's so easy - it takes all the fun out of stealing :(After I already had around 20 hours in the regular edition, I upgraded to Spacer's choice edition - and can attest to the differences between the two.The new edition has much better graphics. Not just better resolution, but many graphical changes.The people look much more realistic (to the point that some have completely different faces), planets have additional huge structures in the background, which make them look much better. And other minor changes as well.It does come with a cost though. It definitely takes up more GPU resources than the original, and some people have reported bugs & crashes (although I must admit, in my 40+ hours I have not encountered any)In addition, the new edition has more/better Steam achievements.And the game itself is slightly more difficult - when playing the same difficulty level as the original.Overall I felt the new version was the better version, and having the choise - the one I prefer to be playing.But that may not be the case if you have an older/weeker GPU...The game has 2 DLCs (for which I will post reviews separately):Peril On Gorgon - Has a whole new map filled with enemies to kill. And an engaging story (better than the main plot of the game IMO). In addition, this DLC adds more skill levels, and more bonuses (for the higher levels).Murder on Eridanos - I have not finished it yet, but it's a kind of a detective mystery. With some new creatures and fun guns to try out.

_childDocuments_.review: The Outer Worlds is like a throwback to Knights of the Old Republic II (2004) and Fallout 3 but it doesn't feature the difficulty of the former and the novelty of the latter. In fact, it's kind of a been there, done that. The game isn't particularly difficult, even on hard, your crewmates will rip through most things and most fights are rather bland. There's a horrible time-slowing feature which is sort of this game's answer to Fallout's VATS but it isn't half as fun to use. Weapon upgrades aren't very well balanced, perks don't seem very interesting and it has one of those absolute skillcheck systems where if you don't have a whopping 150 points in one of your skills, you just won't ever be seeing that part of the game.Looting is kind of weird, there's tons of items you'll never want to use or need, the value of your lockpicks is often times higher than that of what it's inside the lootable box and for some reason, they created a lot of modifications for weapons but you won't ever see them unless you put 'm on yourself. All weapons and armour that you find almost always, with a few exceptions, come with no modifications.Unique items are often not useful because by the time you find them, you're probably already past the level they were intended for. And for some reason, the game's locations are littered with bodies (were they worried the player would get tired of killing things himself?) and every location feels a lot like a checklist. Do this, do that, check it off and leave for a new area with very little necessity to ever return to a previous location except to check off more things on your checklist. The locations don't change much if at all.There are some good things to the game: the crewmates are pretty neat, they have a lot of dialogue. The shooting isn't half bad and it's basically like playing Fallout 3 with a storyline that's a tad more intelligent by only by a very small margin.

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game a lot despite its flaws. I like the setting, worldbuilding, humor and dialogue, variety of playstyles and characters. Main story of main game,  DLCs and most side quests were designed and written well enough to keep me engaged with the game. There are a lot of choice and consequence situations that effect the environment and your end game slides. Actions of the player character create a convincing reactivity around the game. As for combat, shooting and killing stuff feels fine, some guns, especially science weapons were quite fun to use. Melee weapons are OK to use and time slow mechanic is fun to use. I noticed few bugs but they were very minimal and don't get in your way while playing.For flaws I have to say I didn't really find perks to be useful after some point in my playthrough. They didn't help me much and I didn't even notice their effect after let's say, 20th level on my long-heavy weapon oriented character. Also the the inventory system was difficult to use because every time before I was entering a combat, I had to open up the inventory look through all the names of my supplies and use the ones I needed that moment (e.g. a lotion for +10 armor rating or a drink that gives hp regen). This takes so much that it kills the momentum of the combat. Also, I didn't find the game too challenging despite playing on Hard difficulty. And I have to say the ending for the game felt a bit too rushed for me, as I was anticipating more activity on the last planet but the game ended fairly quicker than I expected. Another thing I noticed was that it's cool to have many different playstyles you can try each time you start the game but at the same I didn't find the main storyline to be fun and engaging enough to play the game 3-4 times but who knows maybe I'll play The Outer Worlds many more times...As for Spacer's Choice Edition, the game had a rocky launch but it runs OK on PCs right now. This edition has a different color pallete than the original too, and I wasn't a big fan of it so I had to download ReShade and apply filters to my game according to my taste. This made my experience much better, but still having to do this part is a flaw for the game. This just doesn't come down to personal taste because some parts of the game without Reshade just looks so bright and exposed.

_childDocuments_.review: First up, I've not experienced any performance issues whilst playing this game, bar a single crash caused by Windows deciding to go to sleep whilst the game was running. I did, however, wait until the 1.1 update was released before playing after reading other people's reviews, and I have a feeling that it would struggle to run on anything other than high-end graphics cards (like the 7900 XTX), so I'd advise anyone with older cards or entry-level ones to go and play the original game instead.That said, the graphical upgrades make an already beautiful game amazing, and it was the perfect excuse for me to replay this. Load times also seem to have been improved, though having a load screen every time you transition between areas does seem a bit archaic in the era of ultra-fast NVMe SSDs, particularly as the screens flash by too quick to read the often amusing notes on them!

_childDocuments_.review: Hands down, this game is incredible.  Its an open world game with more quests than you know what to do with and RPG elements where you can bond with your crewmates, and get to know them. The only bummer for me is that there wasn't any romance options which I feel would have amplified it. There's always more than one option to complete a quest, which I really loved getting to choose how you wanted to complete a certain mission, and equally enjoyed seeing how others did it, or even skipped over parts entirely.With being an achievement hunter, the supernova difficulty was a major pain in the ass, and made sense why there are so many food/drink options (Which I thought was super pointless, there is way too many) the great part is you can bum rush it pretty quickly after playing the game once thanks to multiple guides out there which made this way less daunting.With the Spacer's Choice edition you get two DLC, peril on gorgon, and murder on eridanos. I chose to do the Murder DLC first and my God- the mechanics behind solving this case, the very little combat involved, it was so refreshing to take a break from the main game and I absolutely loved it, the new world was so immersive where peril on gorgon was a lot more combat, a lot less immersive, and it didn't feel as fun as murder did. If you love these types of games, you'll definitely love this one. I cannot recommend it enough, and definitely would say to snag this one rather than the standard edition to get all of the benefits.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fine, but too repetitive even for its rather short runtime.The world building has one message ("Have you considered that hypercapitalism is bad."), which it reinforces by telling the same joke for 40 hours. Story is fine, but with a rather abrupt ending. Companion characters are likable overall, but not particularly memorable (and all other NPCs are utterly forgettable). Graphics look nice and are very colorful, but lack depth of field and facial animations look wooden. Loot is ubiquitous, but totally uninteresting and 99% of it is completely useless.I completed the main game + the first DLC, but skipped the second one because it started feeling like too much of a slog. Don't get me wrong, you can definitely be solidly entertained by this game for a while, but there are quite a number of more engaging RPGs out there.

_childDocuments_.review: [Lie] You play as Alex Hawthorne, a dashing gunslinger and captain a one of a kind ship, the Unreliable.It's really funny that you can actually assume his identity and basically RP as him for the entire game and with enough Charisma and Lie points you can gaslight even your companions into thinking that, which I did.Honestly, really good game. But overall still an amazing game.The game is gameplay wise very similar to Obsidian's other game, Fallout New Vegas, but an upgraded version of that, especially the combat. Some memorable characters, few gorgeous locations, interesting setting and humor, not much bugs, decent DLCs, but for a game aspiring to be something at least slightly comparable to the best action RPGs it does something absolutely unforgivable- it makes exploration and leveling up totally unsatisfying and boring. Perk system is a joke, 3/4 of choices is "X% more Y", literally zero creativity. After 1/2 of the game i didn't care about straying from the main path, because I knew that all locked chests will contain ammunition (ended the game with tens of thousands (!!!) bullets, on second hardest difficulty, using Long Weapons almost exclusivly), some credits (which are almost useless in this game) and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ weapons. Choices lack impact, we can end almost any situation with a compromise. Combat is acceptable at best (some players claim, that melee or science weapons builds are more fun, but IDK, I doubt i will start this game ever again). Very few enemy types with limited AI. Even the aforementioned humor is often used without moderation, too much irony and corporate stereotypes shoved straight into players mouth, over and over ("Haha, high chance of death at the workplace, but the welfare and well-being of the manager/corporation/planet is the highest value, and You, dear employer, shoud be proud of working here").ToW 2 is still one of my most anticipated game, I believe that bigger budget will help, the potential is here, but this one? _childDocuments_.review: After Obsidian Entertainment developed , they were inspired to create another role-playing game where the influence of one on another is unmistakable. Although the development of the theme is not entirely original, what is captivating is the world in which it emerges, taking place in the outer space. A soundtrack that is reminiscent of the compositions of Gustav Holst, or vibrant art on each planet, pull off to rivet the player's gaze once immersed in a haunting story about the fate of Halcyon.Similar to Fallout, the story takes place in a parallel world where the present-day US, William McKinley, is not murdered. Without his death, it paves the way to the beginning of the megacorporation that colonize most of the habitable planets in the solar system. In order to populate the planets, it's vital for the colonizers to go into a state of cryopreservation due to the long journey. Hope is a colony spacecraft that has been missing for many years, until 2355 is located and the scientist Phineas Vernon Welles, through some experiments, accomplishes to awaken only one inhabitant, who is the character we will take on. Phineas did not achieve to wake everyone up because many years had passed due to the freezing limit, in addition to the cumbersome bureaucracy of The Board, the group in charge of administering Earth-2, puts up too many red tape due to its urgent need of a permanent job. So the mission is to uncover what happened there as well as take the fate of the slumbering survivors like those now dwelling in the solar system, in order to discover what transpired on Earth-1.The story takes place in a world parallel to ours. Colonies are established on wild planets with vibrantly colourful landscapes. Each planet that together makes up the solar system is awe-inspiring with its flora and fauna. The plot is unfolding as the mission leads us from planet to planet. It is an open world, almost an open outer space, that the player explores alone or with someone. The world feels dynamically full of life but also in action due to its creatures and people, these divided into factions.However, the theme addresses the problem of food scarcity, as the inhabitants survive in infertile and dangerous worlds. It has the outline of the downside about megacorporation and their ethical stance. The theme fleshes out linearly, although it fosters the ambiance of journeying. Furthermore, it grows, or surfaces, itself according to the rhythm of the player. The plot attempts to convince the player to participate in the plot and find a suggested solution to the dilemma. Albeit the final episode is inconsistent, it doesn't bring about a satisfying climax after all the unravelling and quandaries averted. Fortunately, it is compensated by the variety of dialogues between the characters. There is a diversity of tones that conveys a narrative personalization to the protagonist, us, and the reaction, the interlocutors.In this role-playing game, the script is of utmost importance. It's noteworthy that each character possesses a sense of humour. Although the protagonist, we, due to the choice of responses or reactions in a dialogue, can acquire a personality in a given circumstance. This is a feature of the gameplay too. On the other hand, the script is serious but at the same time whimsical, hilarious and funny. That's quite reminiscent of  comedy. The variety of responses can be discerned when companions travel, interact and go along with the player. They also take part in some conversations and express their point of views. It improves the game in terms of storytelling dynamic and vivid, especially when it comes to making decisions. The game's script is fun and rich in language.As I touched on earlier,  is a role-playing game. This means that, firstly, the character is customizable (avatar, skills, and equipment). The character has attitudes that will assist us in certain moments, such as in combat or in conversations. For each level raised by performing missions or some activities (hacking, lying, using a skill or action) points are gained. And for each even level, we rack up points for the skill wall. However, when something dangerous happens to us repeatedly, for example falling, we gain points for skills but in exchange we sacrifice some other skill, this is called weakness. We can also recruit companions as the story progresses. Furthermore, our companions have the own skill sets that can be improved, and they also have special attacks. We can bring two of them with us. Needless to say, as , we have our team.Money moves the planets of the solar system. The missions also offer bits, which are the in-game currencies. The solar system is assembled of planets, space stations and asteroids to explore. Each of them has an open map. Despite the fact we don't see our ship move, it still simulates the feeling of voyaging through outer space (there are fast travel points on the map, but the ship enables us to navigate from planet to planet). There are quests in certain places. As we do primary, secondary, companion or faction missions, in the end our interaction with the characters and their contexts will have an effect. There is a reputation system that benefits or harms depending on our decisions. The character is like a paid mercenary.If you've played Fallout: New Vegas or Borderlands, this game will likely be familiar to you, with features such as repairing weapons and equipment or identifying weapons by their colour (corrosive, n-ray or science, for example). This game also features a V.A.T.S. mechanics, this is due to the cryogenic state of the character, and it can slow down time through Tactical Time Dilation with which we can analyse the enemy's statistics as well as deploy it in combat. So the decision of the gameplay depends on the player, it is not narrowed to just being a shooting game or mere action.The game is visually stunning, even though having design limitations due to the use of the Unreal Engine. Although this version requires a PC capable of running due to its demands.  The world is big, but far from becoming a solar system or universe. The story is gripping, although only the climax is planned, presuming that one day the developers will publish the second part. This version, Spacer's Choice Edition, is somewhat remastered and also bundled with two expansions. Both are inquisitive, but not the most promising. I admit that the way they are woven into the plot to lend it continuity is rather captivating. They are extensions that the game did not need, since it is complete from the beginning to the climax. In the rest, the design, the music, the script, are exciting but sometimes become slanted depending on how they are structured within the plot.The atmosphere of the setting is pleasant, the ambiance of working as a team is a clever novelty that turns out to be gratifying. It's like being part of a team with those who fight side by side in the galaxy. It borrows something of Fallout, but also something of its own, this is mainly reflected in the characters. There are many oddities in the game, so make your own verdict when considering this space RPG a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: So, for myself, the game runs flawlessly and I mean without a single hitch so far. I'm 8 hours into the game and I have yet to experience any of the so called "issues" people seem to be having. In fact, after updating my Nvidia drivers the game runs even BETTER. Graphics are extremely up-graded for this edition of the game. Everything POPS in all the good ways. Writing and signs are more extremely detailed and legible. The world's details were all given a solid layer of upscaling and paint. That includes everything from trees and bushes to flowers to homes to armor and guns. Lighting is extremely well done now with a LOT LESS shadowing down in foreground and background areas. Characters are more chiseled and have an eye shine. Lots of small improvement spread over everything that just makes it all look like a proper 4k texture pass without it being that. Now, it's been awhile since I played the OG version but aiming and shooting seem to be a LOT tighter now. Also, remember those god-awful loading screens? Man, they're almost gone now. Seriously. I'm counting less than 2-3 seconds whereas before those loading screens easily took upwards of 20-30 seconds. All in all, if you have never played Outer Worlds it is a fantastic game with great writing, great characters, great shooting and armaments, wonderful world building and amazing rpg depth. In all seriousness, if you're one of the many, many players that enjoyed Fallout: New Vegas like no one's business then welcome home. Outer Worlds is your NEW New Vegas.

_childDocuments_.review: An FPS RPG that is absolutely flooded with dialog and story. Seriously, if you're a "skip the story to get to the action" person, stop reading now. This game is not for you.The setting is Halcyon, a solar system far from Earth. You were aboard the Hope, twin ship of the Groundbreaker. Both ships were sent here from Earth to colonize this system. Thing is, the Hope didn't make it. However, you have been awaken from your cryosleep by a wanted criminal whose is tasking you with helping him save the system.I have to mention this now: This might not have been intended to be, but it is a scathing attack on unchecked capitalism. In Halcyon the corporations rule all, and working is considered living. The corporations aren't just your employer, they are your way of life. Work perfectly and you could even earn the ultra rare 15 minute break. If you die on the job, the corporation will charge you. People recite jingles and slogans like they are normal parts of speech. Meanwhile, the utopia is where the executives live and face absolutely no danger. Their lives are empty for other reasons so they turn to booze, drugs, splat races, and so on. The corporations are so focused on earning profit that they're hardly thinking about how they're killing the entire colony.Everything is very tongue in cheek, but also not. That might not make sense, but it will.The story is really solid and the dialogue is excellently written and voice acted. Some of the character you meet, as in any story, are unmemorable, but others are very memorable. There is a lot humor both overtly and hidden. I've played much funnier games, but the effort is appreciated.The game looks fantastic and the design behind the worlds is great, but can be a bit repetitive. The action parts play very nicely, but your companions will drive you nuts. The guns feel great, but there's a bit of overlap in them, imho. It did give more options, but I stuck with specific ones and never looked back. Plus, you have skills to improve your abilities, and you probably will only specialize in one, so multiple weapons becomes an unappealing option. They still work, but fights will get a lot tougher.The skill system is extremely varied. More so because of additional perks. Even your companions get perks. (More on them later.) I was able to "max" two skills being a completionist and finishing at lvl 48. I think I got every possible quest? There are probably 20 or so skills, and depending on what you choose, your game play will vary greatly from how others play.The companions come in six flavors and it's possible to not recruit any. All but one has a story line that can be played through. One of them is really short. Three are medium sized. The last one is large and involves running around all over, but it's for the most charming character, so it's enjoyable.Sound like something you wouldn't do? Don't. This is an RPG. Do whatever you want. There's a video out there of someone who, literally, killed every other human in Halcyon. You will always be given dialogue choices along the lines of honorable, honest, wise, and total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.Additionally, there are many choices to make within the story that will affect your ending. Don't worry, there are only two "core" endings, but the breakdown of your team, side quests, etc. change based on your choices.The ending I got was good, but there was a giant unanswered question that I hope is the plot of the sequel... Yes, I've heard a sequel is coming.

_childDocuments_.review: Obsidian, years ahead of Starfield, have made an excellent Spaceout: New Vegas. Many similarities exist. from quests to dialogue options to how progression can be altered or skipped through "efficient" means. It is an excellent FPS RPG, and absolutely worth the play. This game truly feels like a modern day incarnation of a simpler era. Whereas the upcoming Starfield seeks innovation through generating expansive universes with crawling but apparently shallow planets, the Outer Worlds has small but mighty open worlds with fantastic pathing and level design. I wouldn't go as far to call the game stunning, but the graphics and art style do well to highlight some of the martian terrain and foliage, as well as the occasionally gorgeous space skybox. Gameplay and gunplay are fantastic. The jankiness of the early Gamebryo/Creation Engine is gone, replaced with Unreal Engine 4. While, as mentioned, this doesn't lead to immense beauty, an RPG fan is going to enjoy the story and gameplay over graphics anyway - which is indicative of an Obsidian experience. Gun types are varied enough, with three main ammo types and about five damage types. I do find modification lacking and rather unincentivized; I do believe this is an area where the innovation of weapon modification in the likes of Fallout 4 feels better than the charm of an older-style title which is fleshed out in a modern engine. That being said, it is there, and it does add a mechanic to gunplay for those who don't mind irreversibly modifying a weapon scope, magazine, or barrel only for a better version of that item to be found on the next planet. The story is definitely not unique, but it presents interesting character choices throughout. There exist a plethora of defining dialogue options, as well as side quests and faction reputations that dictate outcomes along many main questlines. For completionists, this is a threat to achievement hunting, which requires multiple playthroughs (or well-timed save-scumming, but I recommend the former). Luckily, though, the replayability of this game is fantastic. My first time through saw choices that I would have made in our protaginist's situation, played on normal difficulty to balance story with some challenge. I then blitzed through the game on Supernova using speedrunning tactics and outcome optimization that Obsidian molds so well into games. A final playthrough was done on the easiest difficulty to become a world destroyer and enemy to everyone. It is seriously enjoyable no matter how many times through, or what personas and challenges you want to take on.Characters can be shallow at times, reacting to some decisions but not all, even instrumental ones that may see their previous hometown destroyed. That being said, all six have questlines, ranging from single-mission fetch quests to multiple-mission journeys that span different planets you end up on. It helps develop characters, but the lacking reputation with your own companions is noteworthy. I felt decisions were guided entirely by factions, rather than having more personal companions also be affected. While you do occasionally consult them, a reputation that extends to your crew and even individual crewmates (as they are all so different), would surely deepen character relationships and further complicate (in a good way) your choices.Any reviews reciting the infamous jingle, "It's not the best choice, it's Spacer's Choice!" are now overplayed and unrepresentative of this edition. Patches have solidified performance, and my midrange setup handled the game fantastically with minimal issues at 1440p. Also, FSR exists. If you already have Outer Worlds or have cheaper access to that game and its DLC (Which I do recommend, but don't find necessary), then ignore this edition. But if you have neither, the Spacer's Choice family might be the one to join.

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game when I first played it in 2019 when it was released on Xbox Games Pass but oddly, I didn't finish it. And wow! This gripped right to the end! The story and the characters - they got me really invested in this game. The story is fantastic - saving the colony from corporate greed and bureaucratic incompetence. The characters are fantastic - you just fall in love with Parvatti and co! The controls are pretty intuitive with combat being easy to master. The graphical aesthetic just suits this game perfectly - and the music... Just sublime!The game does use the encumbered mechanic and gear (weapons and armour) also get worn out. However, unlike in Starfield, you can break down your inventory for parts and fix your weapons and armour on the go so it's not really an issue.   One thing I would like to add, it was noted that 'The Spacer's Choice' edition was not as polished as the original game and was almost as buggy as Todd Howard's finest but apart from one crash, it was completely solid with a locked 72FPS (my monitor has a weird refresh rate...). Never stuttered or had any frame rate drops so your mileage may vary. For reference my system is an i5 13500 with 32GB RAM & an RTX 3060 so adequate but it played it at the highest settings albeit at 1080p.This game is one of my all time favourites and I'm glad that I got the Spacer's Choice Edition and replayed the game to completion.
