_childDocuments_.review: Before everything I must say that I'm not a fan of simulating games of any kind and at the moment of this review I don't have great specs on my pc, but I decided to try and bought it. After saying that, I must admit I'm surprised by this game. First of all, the atmosphere and the ambient are fantastic, capturing you while beating the wind at high speed. As I said, no big specs on my machine, but still the graphics is very well done even at low-medium settings, from the motorbike model to the damn piece of texture of the little stone wall where my bike crashed on!Now the gameplay: I feel the controls well made and I really liked the fact that the game isn't just for "who can really play simulative games" (that isn't me, for sure), because you can choose how much real physics the game has to apply to your game-style. Then you can choose what to do: you want just playing with bikes without much effort nor competition? Free-drive is for you; want to challenge yourself? There are various type of challenges: best-time-lap, simple races etc. and if you want to compete with friends or other people, you can get in the saddle and go hard!The maps are pretty big, and since last races I have found no bugs or glitches: I mean, I expected a little glitchy distorsion on the ragdoll when I crashed but still the game is so stable that crashing into trees and walls is not a problem... I mean not a bug one :) !But the thing that hit me the most are the configurations that you can apply on your motorbike: before racing there are some free-laps where you can adjust every, and I underline  little detail, from the hardness of the wheel to the elasticity of the bike springs, in order to give your best in the race. And with points that you earn by playing and winning you can buy new pieces and so new configurations.I think I've not said everything since there is a depth of things and combinations that I want to try in every aspect, but I hope that this first impression can help if you are in doubt.So if you enjoy racing with motorbikes, or just want to free-drive your bike in a relaxing rainy night after a bad work day, I really suggest that game.

_childDocuments_.review: I had the opportunity to try out the new motorcycle game, and I must say I was completely fascinated by the gaming experience it offers. From the very beginning, I was impressed by the incredibly detailed graphics and the realism that permeates every aspect of the game.The riding physics are exceptional.The game modes are varied and offer a wide range of challenges. Overall, it's an excellent product!
_childDocuments_.name: TT Isle Of Man: Ride on the Edge 3

_childDocuments_.review: Some things are improved over IOM TT2 and some things are considerably worse.I primarily wanted to try the new game, because I was hoping that they fixed some of the wierd inconsistencies with the handling of the old game. They did fix the funky slow speed handling (Ramsey Hairpin and Govenors are much easier to navigate now) and the wierd unstability over bumps that some bikes suffered from is gone. The bikes feel more heavy, stable and planted. Wheelies are also easier to maintain and not as prone to cause a crash.That's where the good stuff end. Unfortunately they have introduced a new big issue. The bikes are sluggish and unresponsive to turn and especially to transition from one side to the other. The actual return on a given controller input varies wildly, making it next to impossible to judge how much the bike will turn. Most of the time the bike simply does not turn and you will run wide into the botanicals... But suddenly every once in a while it suddenly turns like crazy and you crash because you hit the inside kerb. Put simply it feels like there's a huge elastic band between your inputs and the bikes handlebars. It is so extremely frustrating, that the controls seem like a vague guideline rather than a command.Other notes:The sounds are worse than in TT2. The cool swoosh noises when going past objects are not very pronounced anymore and the cool detail of the windnoise when sitting up while braking seems to be gone. Also the mixing of some of the engine sounds are downright awfull and there is some delay and significant stuttering between the engines' physics and its sounds.The graphics are much more detailed in the new game and there are more effects. It is considerably prettier. Unfortunately the clarity has suffered somewhat, so it was actually a little easier to spot distant turns coming up in the old game.The menus are annoying. You are dumped right into a freeroam mode and the only way I could find to practice on the actual TT Course, was to use the "Custom Event". Why, just why?The fictional England and Ireland courses are gone. Not a big loss... They are replaced with other fictional courses on the actual Isle of Man, including some new roads not part of the normal TT Course. This is cool, but not a big deal for me personally. I spend all of my time with the game trying to master the TT Course anyway, and that's plenty to remember...For me the dealbreaker is the sluggish and woolly handling. It's just not enjoyable as I do not feel in control of the bike at all. Refunded.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm happy to say that it's a solid game that I would recommend. If you enjoyed the previous games of the serie, you'll appreciate the improvements made in this one. The graphics have been upgraded to a more modern look, and the physics feel great without compromising the original game's difficulty.One aspect that stands out is the comprehensive history of the TT and the riders, adding depth to the overall experience. The open-world feature is also a fantastic addition, allowing you to freely explore the Isle of Man and its actual racing roads at your own pace. It's a unique opportunity to drive on different routes and test your bike and setups.Overall, TT Isle Of Man: Ride on the Edge 3 is abolutely a recommended buy

_childDocuments_.review: While playing TT, I was reminded of great memories from the Saturn console game set on the Isle of Man and my years creating racing and motorcycle games. The game immersed me with a strong sense of adrenaline and proved challenging to master. The control over the rider's weight introduced a fascinating mechanic. The graphics pay attention to detail in motorcycle models and environments, despite technological limitations. Each area has distinctive elements, even when bikes are stationary. The art direction adds character and substance without compromising realism, and the audio conveys emotions and adrenaline in every lap. I experienced micro-stuttering issues at full HD resolution, which I will investigate further. Overall, I'm delighted with this return to the island and highly recommend TT 3 to motorcycle enthusiasts and fans of extreme situations. It delivers convincingly.

_childDocuments_.review: They took so much away in this sequel. All the short tracks are gone. Yes, all of them. Time trials is gone (my favourite mode). They improved the graphics, but, seem to have based the game entirely on the Isle of Man only. It seems every sequel messes-up the UI. Great features like racing against the leader on the leaderboard has been removed. You can't download ghosts either. They've made it open world, but, it feels pointless. There are things that the first two games did right that have been stripped away. Even the audio seems to be so basic now. Where's the whooshing sounds gone? The devs need to go back to the drawing board and bring those features back. I think longtime fans will be disappointed. I will update my review as I spend more time with it. First impressions feels like this is a barebones graphical upgrade only.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, folks! Let me spill the beans about Isle of Man TT3, even though I'm more of a car game kind of guy. But let me tell you, this game left me absolutely gobsmacked!First things first, the graphics are out of this world! They've nailed every little detail, making you feel like you're right in the middle of the action on the Isle of Man's crazy 60-kilometer course. It's a wild ride, trust me!Now, I may not be a bike expert, but the selection of bikes, riders, and teams in this game is off the charts! The controls are so darn realistic that you'll find yourself leaning into those sharp corners without even realizing it. It's pure racing magic!But here's the real kicker—the open-world feature. You can explore the entire Isle of Man, discover different game modes, and take on mind-blowing challenges. Quick races, career mode, online multiplayer—it's a racer's dream come true!To sum it all up, Isle of Man TT3 delivers an immersive and heart-pounding racing experience that left me absolutely speechless. So, if you're like me, more of a four-wheel lover, trust me when I say this game is worth every second of your time. Rev your engines, conquer the Isle of Man TT championship, and prepare to have your socks knocked off!

_childDocuments_.review: Summary :Better then TTIOM 2 (the only one I played and was quite good at it). Physics are much more predictable and feel more "natural" than its predecessor. Still not the level of physics one gets from GP Bikes (best bike simulator in my opinion), however well above and will trash any milestone game physics, and love the vibration I get when threading the edge grip and the bike is on the edge of losing all of its grip and sending you into a wall. Positives and negatives:Some gripes I have with this game: - Sounds can be better - No the prettiest visually, especially when you slow things down.- No Forzaesque free roam, tho the new roads are pretty- Somewhat prefer the career in TTIOM 2 and the variety of tracks it has, this only has 8. - Less bike variety and sense of improvement. This links once again with why I prefer TTIOM2 career having your own rider and team Some general good points - Sense of speed 10/10 as always- While vistas can be better, the fidelity to the track and road bumps is amazing and immersive, watch any onboard and the games bumps are exactly where they are - Can finally drag a long ass wheelie - Much better physics, and got rid of the "wonkiness" that plagued the previous title. Conclusion:All in all, good improvement, though wish some elements from TTIOM 2 come back (career and Irish league and British tracks and having your own rider). However the most important element, that being the physics, are vastly improved and why I will keep on playing this game for hours..... Or until a proper IOMTT mod makes it to GP Bikes.

The Isle of Man Tourist Trophy is the most epic, most dangerous and most spectacular race in the world. It is a course of over 60 kms on the roads of the Isle of Man, includes 264 bends, and requires high-powered bikes specially prepared for the race. The riders who compete in it train their whole lives for the chance to win the ultimate accolade: being crowned champion of the Isle of Man TT.

name: Lil' Guardsman
detailed_description: In this deduction adventure, you play as Lil - an unlikely 12-year-old hero - covering your dad's shift at the guard shed and are tasked with deciding the fate of over 100 unique characters. You will question humans, elves, goblins, cyclopes, and other fantasy creatures using your powers of deduction to determine who to admit or deny based on how they respond to your questions and your trusty tools. Sending visitors to jail, inadvertently zapping them to smithereens, or letting them go on their merry way are all part of the job. But be careful: who you let through the castle gates will determine the kingdom's fate. See the Sprawl and its fantastical & quirky citizens through a royal wedding to one of two kingdoms vying for an alliance, and a subsequent siege by whoever you've angered in the process. Your decisions can determine the fate of the city and its people! Interrogate 100+ fully voiced characters in just the right way to earn a perfect score. Spend your hard earned gold wisely on powering up your guardsman toolkit, and strategically deploy these to admit or deny the right people or...goblins? Use your trusty Chronometer3000 to go back and get a higher score... but be careful not to break space and time in the process.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I don't even know where to begin. Things in Lil Guardsman start reasonably innocently. Lil is the daughter of Hamish, a guardsman who operates the gate at a kingdom called The Sprawl. He wants to bet on a Goblinball game and drafts his daughter to fill his position. As the days go by and the situation in the city changes, Lil ends up with increasingly strict restrictions from significant authorities in the kingdom, handling greater responsibilities and night shifts, and becomes a test subject for a Chronometer 3000 device that can let her rewind time.Much of the comedy in Lil Guardsman comes from the obvious and blatant silliness. That part of it is excellent and reminiscent of LucasArts classic titles. But I also appreciated when said humor involved critiques of modern society and issues stemming from corruption and intolerance. For example, the state of the working class and the nature of politicians are handled well and in genuinely funny ways. Speaking of those deeper issues, while Lil Guardsman is a humorous game, it also addresses them and allows players to make decisions to stand up to authority and for equality. For example, racism runs rampant. Species like Goblins are discriminated against, with specific "rules" on some days threatening punishments for Lil letting non-humans in or telling her she should treat them differently than human visitors. We also see firsthand how power struggles work and have moments during which we could be part of the problem rather than the solution. Those complexities can also be wholesome. There is way more heart to Lil Guardsman than I expected. The relationship between Lil and her father, Hamish, is absolutely exceptional. It pairs typical goofy dad humor with more serious moments between the two. Hamish constantly jokes with his daughter, but we also get asides that reveal precisely how much he's doing for her sake as a single parent. At another point, a choice that shapes the Sprawl involves Lil debating if she stays positive for him or is honest about how challenging the situation is for her. I hesitated because both sides could be the "right" answer or have "negative" consequences.As for the gameplay, it is a mix of Papers Please and classic point-and-click adventures. When Lil is at her post, there are certain daily restrictions and goals. She can talk to the person trying to get into The Sprawl, teasing, trusting, or doubting them to gain additional insight. Three advisors can be called to get an understanding or because it's part of the mandates for that shift. You can use a Bullwhip, Decoder Ring, Metal Detector, Truth Spray, or X-ray to analyze people further and handle the situation. It is also possible to confiscate items, then either use them later or sell them for money for the crystals needed to power and upgrade the tools you use each day. Of course, there's also the Chronometer 3000, a significant plot device that allows you to rewind at will or if you get a bad ending. After taking three "turns" investigating, you admit someone to the city, deny them entry, or even sometimes jail them.The only downside is that the array of tools only carries the same weight. The Decoder Ring, Truth Spray, and X-ray proved vital to me throughout the game, but I never needed the Bullwhip or Metal Detector. The Metal Detector was a backup item in case I'd spent my X-ray for the shift. However, I appreciate that the developers even realized this about specific tools, as it can come up cleverly depending on your approach in one encounter. However, since you choose how you invest Lil's paychecks into upgrades, you can… prioritize the equipment you see as crucial to you and focus on that throughout your run.I also appreciated that while the focus is on the guardsman shifts, occasional adventure elements involve logical reasoning or finding specific items. When these segments come up, they always keep their welcome and are well-integrated. There's a reason for Lil to be called upon to help make an important decision (adults are corrupt and incompetent)Lil Guardsman is one of those games that I took a chance on because the trailers made me smile, and I don't regret it. It's entertaining, sometimes touching, and even shocked me at specific points because of the immediate results of my decisions. Speaking of which, this is also a game during which you face the consequences of your actions, and I'm curious to go back and replay it to see how different choices will affect the city on another run.Imagine you're a 12-year-old, suddenly in charge of the guard shed at the castle gate, where you decide if elves, goblins, and 100+ other characters should be admitted. It's a combination of deduction, narrative, and puzzle games.Lil Guardsman's detail, depth, humor, and heart surprised me. I highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: Lil guardsman is an overall excellent game, even if it's advertisements are a bit misleading.Story: By far the best thing in the game is its story, with it's emotional core being the bond Lil shares with her dad.  The game perfectly balances Lil being a 12 year old who is put in a very stressful situation without them coming across as annoying.  I really liked how they SHOWED Lil missing her dad without ever having to directly state that.  Not only that but the world building is solid with different factions and people having their own desires and goals and you navigating the conflicts of said desires and goals is a huge part of the game.  Each main and supporting character feels fleshed out and by the end of the game you really do feel like you want to protect this town you've come to know and shape.Gameplay;  Okay so this is the misleading thing a lot of people get wrong.  A lot of people call this a "Paper's Please" game but with fantasy elements and I think that's an inaccurate statement.  To me a Paper's Please game is a test of your OCD; basically a test of your ability to notice small mistakes in a repetitive task while under pressure from a ticking clock.Lil Guardsman is not this; Lil Guardsman is more like Monkey Island with a Papers Please setting.  Yes you are working border security and checking people, but there's no time limit here and you also aren't given all of the information right away with every person having some kind of secret objective you need to perform to get a 4 star rating.  While you can logically deduce some of the secret objectives based on visual clues and hints from your info board, the game does strongly encourage you to just click your tools and see what happens.This doesn't make this a bad game, it's just not a Papers Please game if that's what you were hungry for.I do also want to state that the first level in particular is terrible from a gameplay perspective (it's great from a story perspective).  At no point does the tutorial tell you that there are MULTIPLE ways of getting a 4 star rating, as different tools and techniques can complete the secret objective.  Players will probably figure this out at some point when they realize they can't complete a 4 star rating because they used all of the charges for the needed tool up earlier in the run.But the game should really TELL the player this in the beginning as that majorly impacts decision making.  Also it's a very strange choice that the player doesn't unlock the ability to go back in time and redo their decisions in the first level.  Since that's when their most likely still experimenting and trying to figure out what each tool and option does.  Granted the first level is pretty much on safety rails and won't stop you from getting a bad ending but its still surprising nevertheless and leaves a bad first impression.Luckily the game does pick up from there and keeps going strong.  Managing your tools and upgrades and money is pretty fun although you can become quickly broken by mid game.  Hoarding items can be annoying at times since only a few are useless but since you don't know what will become useful later you end up keeping everything (especially since an item's use can be reveal hours after collecting the item).  Not that money is a big issue in-game since most levels rarely need you to use a single tool more than once in a level.  Still from a completionist standpoint it does feel weird to see so many items in my inventory collecting dust when I can sell them.I only played through the game once and got the best ending, so I can't speak on the game's choice system although it did feel like my choices were influencing events in the game.  Overall though I had a fun time and would recommend them game.
_childDocuments_.name: Lil' Guardsman

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so much more than what it seems. The Papers Please influence is incredibly apparent, but the tone and style of writing is so distinct from its inspiration that it's easy to forget that entirely. Lil Guardsman maintains a breezy vibe, but somehow manages to simultaneously establish genuine consequences for your actions as a gatekeeper, making for some genuinely tense moments. The puzzles are clever, the writing is consistently hilarious, and quite quickly I found myself caring a lot about the people I was interacting with. It became a personal mission to do the job right, to protect this cosy little community that was steadily growing around me.Lil Guardsman is so full of charm and sweetness, and handles its approach to branching paths in a fun, satisfying way. It's an easy recommendation!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is so underrated. Completely voiced dialogue by real actors, a wide range of humor, unexpected twists in writing, unique drawn art style. This game has made me gasp aloud and shout "oh no!" The game is worth the pricetag if anything for the length of playtime.I recommend streaming this game.The one drawback that I hope devs think of changing is to add a multiple fast-forwards option to speed up events--especially if we're replaying a chapter.Finally, everyone compares this to "Papers, Please". It's not. The only element is that you work in a guardshouse maybe 60% of the game. It's a fantasy story of a country where you uncover silly plots and your actions have impacts on the country's narrative. I haven't enjoyed a Point and Click game this much since Pillars of the Earth.

_childDocuments_.review: Many players must have given Papers, Please a chance at some point, and even more might have at least heard about the game. I see myself included in the first ones, and it was thanks to having experimented with its gameplay that Lil' Guardsman caught my attention when I was recommended its demo, which was a nice surprise. Now that I was able to play the full version, I can say that it captured me completely, with a very remarkable humor and characters and stories that range from cool to hilarious. It's a game where the decisions we make have repercussions throughout the kingdom, and while it turns out to be very relaxed in terms of difficulty, it feels very well executed and enjoyable, and I loved it as it is.Lil' Guardsman starts off by going straight for the humor, with a scene where Lil, our little protagonist who is only twelve years old, is dragged into the world of working adults to cover her father's guard shift, and decides who enters the kingdom of Srawpl. Understandable, since her father has to go place illegal bets on the goblin-bowl game, and that's a big deal! One thing leads to another, and our lovable character will acquire a magical contraption that will allow her to go back in time, as long as she is in her guard shed; and with this power, and too much responsibility for a girl her age, she will try to safeguard the kingdom from any imminent threat.It's a really entertaining story, both for the setting and for the number of characters and the humor they bring to the table, and the decision-making factor makes the situations feel dynamic because of the changes those choices bring. I saw different cast members end up in different outcomes on more than one occasion, and when I finished the game I got an achievement that told me something about having acquired the best ending (nice!), which makes it clear that there are several conclusions to the adventure! They put a lot of effort into the narrative and it shows.On the gameplay side, Lil' Guardsman offers a simple but interactive game experience. We'll be in charge of giving or denying entry to the kingdom, having several tools at our disposal to make our job more enjoyable. In addition, we'll have to follow some guidelines imposed each day by the trio of royal advisors, through the royal mandate that they will give us at the start of our shift. Some of these may be not allowing certain races to enter, or checking that visitors do not bring hidden contraband. However, following the rules to the letter could mean missing out on a fun event or situation, so sometimes you have to follow your heart, young guard!The most important thing is that we'll be able to perform a maximum of three actions per character, either talking to them, using tools on them, and other things that I will mention soon, and we’ll have to make our choices with this aspect in mind. It should be noted that we can always go back to the past a certain number of times per day, if we want to of course, to vindicate our "mistakes" and not stress too much about it.Regarding the tools I mentioned earlier, we'll have at our disposal some magical artifacts with which to evaluate the entrants. For example, a metal detector, an X-ray viewer and even a truth serum sprayer. It doesn’t sound very medieval, but it's a perfect comical addition to the mood of the game in general. These artifacts must be loaded with magic crystals every day, a limited resource at first, which provides some strategy when deciding which tool to use. Eventually we'll be able to upgrade the amount of uses and buy more crystals, thankfully. In addition to the gadgets, we'll be able to call one of the three royal advisors to ask their opinion on who we are examining, some being more helpful than others depending on the situation. Sometimes, we'll also be able to confiscate... ehem, acquire some items from visitors, and we can either sell them to buy crystals and upgrades, or keep them to give to other characters. I must admit that I was selling everything until I ran into a situation where I required one of these items... oops! There are several other things, some twists to the mechanics throughout the game, we can walk around the kingdom a bit after working, and interact with the various characters, but these are things I feel are more interesting to discover playing!Regarding the visuals, I think it goes without saying that Lil' Guardsman has a lot of adorableness, and the cartoonish style suits it wonderfully. The character designs are varied and very distinguishable, and while there aren't as many locations to admire the scenery, each one has a unique and detailed environment. There are references everywhere, even a very direct one to Monkey Island and Papers, Please, and I really like that kind of detail! In addition to the visuals, the soundtrack is a nice accompaniment, but what stands out most about the sound is that the title features voice acting almost entirely, and I must say that the actors did an exquisite job. In conclusion, Lil' Guardsman is a very fun game both for its comedy and its story; and I didn't only enjoy the humor, but also the more emotional moments such as those of Lil and her father, two characters I loved the most. The game gives us a varied cast of characters with their own plots and peculiarities, and the effort put into all its sections is noticeable, resulting in a very complete experience. It may seem "easy" on many occasions, mostly because of the mechanics of going back in time, but I think this is a point in favor as I enjoyed relaxing and being able to play without much complications, especially considering the replayability. Recommended is an understatement!

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: having played more, I think it's clear that the perfect rating is just for fun and you can still get the best endings through "good enough" ratings. It's still frustrating that the perfect ratings feel so luck-based/guess-based. I'd like to be rewarded for paying attention to the world and reacting accordingly, instead of just clicking every button.I'm giving this game a positive review because it has a great premise (fantasy Papers Please!) and I think full voice acting needs to be commended wherever it lays. But I don't think this game wants me to play it the way I want to.Each level is divided into a certain number of characters to interact with, using tools (more on these later), interrogation, or your superiors' help. You get a rating out of 4 based on your actions, and higher ratings require more specific actions. If you get a rating you don't like, you can retry the level (explained in the plot as time travel) to try again. You're told how you interact with the characters has consequences on the plot. You can infer that getting the best/most interesting endings are tied to getting a good rating.Okay cool. My instinct is, I want to get a perfect rating on each level before moving on to the next one. Then I can screw around. But if you play like that, the game gets in your way.For one, you can only use each tool a limited number of times per level. Your number of uses is based on how many power crystals you install in them at the beginning of the level, which begins capped at one. Already by level 2, you have to use every single power crystal at your disposal. If you realize you should've used your metal detector two characters ago, you need to rewind back to that character (which you can do limited times) or to the start of the level (which you can do unlimited times).Also, god forbid a tool you need uses one of the knockoff power crystals that fail 50% of the time. Even if you know what to do, that'll kill your run dead.Plus, the requirements for getting perfect ratings are vague (not necessarily a bad thing) and the hint system is not great (a bad thing). There are hints you get at the very beginning of the level that tell you more or less what to do for certain characters, and then you need to pay attention to characters' dialogue/actions for the rest of it. But if I'm playing Lil heroically, why do I need to confiscate ? Why should I use the truth serum on  and not ? You're not going to get it right the first, second, or maybe even fifth time.It all adds up to a lot of trial and error, and a lot of slow, tedious rewinding. And like, get this. If this were a game about playing imperfectly, making mistakes, and living with the consequences, I'd be totally into it. But the rewind mechanic tempts you. "Oh, you COULD get a perfect rating, learn hidden things about these fun characters, and influence the plot. But only if you're willing to get really, really bored first." Very mixed messages.

_childDocuments_.review: Lil Guardsman is a funny but not exactly lighthearted “choices matter” point and click adventure with puzzle-like dialogue encounters. You can make parallels to 3909 LLC’s “Papers, Please” or Crazy Rocks Studios’ “Contraband Police.” But saying that Lil Guardsman is “like” those games is a stretch, which I’ll get into. I would recommend Lil guardsman to those looking for a witty game with thoughtful choices and interesting characters. Lil Guardsman puts you in the boots of Lil, a bushy haired youngster from the Sprawl, the game’s protagonist city state. Lil’s father is a gate guard and after covering one shift for him, you are recruited to work the gate by a trio of characters that represent essentially a shadow government, making policy decisions without the knowledge of the Princess. The trio of shady characters use Lil to keep what they deem as undesirable characters out and let in people they approve of. Sometimes they will pressure you to do something that goes against what is “right,” and sometimes being the good guy costs you wages and approval rating. The dynamic is interesting, if a little underbaked. In between shifts at the guard gate, you can explore locations in the Sprawl, interact with NPCs, and shop. Typically, a level in the game involves a guard shift and then one if not multiple dialogue encounters in which the game’s story plays out. The player makes tons of little decisions that can have a big or small impact on the story, and I can easily see the interested gamer getting 3 playthroughs out of the game, especially with all its branching stories and encounter resolutions.The strength of the game is its writing and voice acting. I laughed out loud at some points. I liked many of the characters and the wit and humor is evident. I would not call the game lighthearted though, as much of the humor is very dark, people die because of the player’s actions and others are relegated to lives of misery. I enjoyed with fully voiced cast, and think it contributed much to the game. As I mentioned before, the game is different from “Papers, Please.” or “Contraband Police” because although the gate guard aspect is present, the game is much more than a bureaucracy sim. Unlike those games, you’re not looking for discrepancies in paperwork or searching cars for contraband, its more of a social puzzle. You can use certain items to gain information on a visitor and make decisions that impact the greater story. Each person that visits has a purpose and most impact the grand scheme in some way. There is also way more to do than just the guard gate, much of the game is spent away from the guard booth.My only gripe is that the game is tragically short. But for what you pay, I think it is a fair amount of content. I enjoyed my time with Lil Guardsman, and I think you will too.

_childDocuments_.review: Where Papers Please succeeds with its mechanical simplicity, Lil Guardsman falls down a dark hole and Game Overs.The issue is the 4-star grading system.In Papers Please you work for the state. Let someone in the country who is meant to come in, earn paycheck. Keep someone out who is meant to be out, earn paycheck. Mess either up? earn a fine. A very simple Pass/Fail system *graded by the state*. The narrative success comes from the player opposing the will of the state in order to accomplish what they believe is right.In Lil Guardsman you're graded on... the... success of the interrogation? or no, the juiciness of the secrets revealed. But also the 4th star is ONLY AVAILABLE if you do one very specific interaction that is unique to every character. Also the game doesn't illustrate what that is. At the beginning of the day you're given, much like Papers Please, the new rules/focuses for the day like: "No Goblins Allowed". If this were Papers Please and you let a Goblin in, you'd get fined. No further questions. In Lil Guardsman you can earn between 1 and 4 stars by letting Goblins in on the "No Goblin" day.And the game thinks not telling you how to succeed is good design, because save-scumming is an in-game mechanic. You're "meant" to play the same day over and over and over again, trial and erroring until you... you what? Get 4-stars, or get the story outcome you want? Lil' Guardsman doesn't know if it's a story-game or a mechanics-game, so it just lets them both fight over the same chair.It has a railroaded story, intentionally tedious gameplay, and is bloated with unneeded side-mechanics

_childDocuments_.review: To me this game is superficially humourous and not particularly entertaining beyond the scattered jokes that actually land; as both the gameplay and writing feel haphazardly designed.The production itself is relatively well rounded. The game feels polished enough, especially with the full voice-acting. Yet certain aspects of it do feel cheap still. The main character has a fully animated walk cycle but the movement of just about every other character is hidden by a fade to black, which blatantly cuts up the flow of scenes. A lot of emphasis is placed on the characters but their models do not actively change to reflect whether they are talking or not, which also creates a disconnect in the presentation. There are several other instances where the presentation and production seem abruptly budgetary as well. This standing out all the more when compared to the otherwise polished experience.The writing is distinctly superficial and lacks much immersive depth. The protagonist is meant to be a twelve year old child and the game description explicitly highlights their age, yet their behaviour is scarcely different from any of the surrounding adults in the story. The protagonist constantly makes inorganic, often self-aware and even fourth-wall breaking statements that seem to be intended as jokes; but their responses seldom mesh with the conversation and mostly derail the atmosphere. This alone makes it difficult to sink into the experience when the main character does not really sound like a person so much as a very transparent vehicle for generic funny remarks, which they constantly try to make. Many of the characters similarly feel very flat and are blatantly designed to fill a specific role in the current sequence. At best they come across as a one-trick joke and at worst a monotonous caricature desperately trying to be a one-trick joke, with various less exciting individuals in-between.The plot tries extremely hard to contrive the situations that the developers apparently wanted in the story, to such a degree that it's borderline frustrating to rationalize. Such as  or ; it just makes absolutely zero sense why various events unironically happen. No effort is made to cleverly establish or weave together a narrative that both allows and explains these otherwise fantastical occurrences, they just happen with complete seriousness in tow. Even if some grand twist does explain it all later in the story, which I cannot confirm or deny, this would still do nothing to resolve the immediate absurdity and lack of immersion that comes from these unbelievable events.The core gameplay appears to revolve around interacting with characters and choosing their fate at the guard station, with the player receiving a grade based on how many significantly unique interactions they successfully triggered with the character. Unfortunately most of the interaction systems operate on a finite resource economy, restricting how many options the player has. This creates a system of trial and error where players are ultimately forced to experiment and reset over and over if they actually want to get a better score and experience more facets of the game, as they are physically unable to explore every option in one organic instance. Yet the game places an overwhelming amount of emphasis on interacting with each character and building a progressive story; even though it also encourages the player to reset and engage in repetitious trial and error which breaks up the narrative flow.Apparently this experience also has game-overs which are triggered by completely innocuous choices and thus the player is randomly forced to repeat a sequence from scratch because they dared to pick a specific option that happened to have a lethal result. The game-over I experienced wasn't even particularly funny or interesting, and minimal production was even invested into the scene beyond yet another fourth-wall breaking joke line; otherwise it was essentially just a spontaneous nuisance.Players exclusively looking for a cartoon experience that makes them chuckle or maybe laugh every once in a while could be satisfied by this game, especially if they just ignore the rating mechanic and all things tethered to it. Otherwise the mechanical system isn't deep enough to be particularly interesting on its own, and encourages trial and error gameplay that looks more tedious than anything. The protagonist is a shallow, uninspired factory of contrived one-liners and most of the other characters sound like flat and forgettable props which only exist to fulfil the current scene. Meanwhile the overarching plot in its opening is an inane jumble of barely justified happenstances, that exclusively exist to setup the very specific story that the developers are trying to tell. All-together making the entire game world feel extremely scripted and inorganic.Nothing about this experience felt particularly meaningful or engaging in the first hour and half, nor did there seem to be any indication that the rest of the game would become anymore eventful beyond that. Between the sometimes high-effort and sometimes low-effort production, the superficial and contrived comedy, the shallow and flat character writing, the irrational plot points and the gameplay which simultaneously encourages and discourages experimentation; it does not feel like the developers really understood any of the conceptual elements they implemented into this game.If you're interested in finding some games that I do positively recommend they can be found on my curator page .

_childDocuments_.review: A lovely game that mashes up the premise of Papers, Please with a cutesy fantasy world that injects just enough unpredictably dark humor to keep you on your toes.Unlike Papers, Please, this plays more like a point and click adventure game rather than a "job simulator". There's no element of time management, and no NPC interactions are randomly generated. Plus, after every shift, you transition to point and click segments to wind down the day.For each NPC you assess, you can perform up to three of these actions before having to make your choice: Talk to them,  call one of three different advisors with their own agendas/biases, or use one of five tools such as your x-ray or truth serum, which are riskier as using them requires finite charges that play into the ingame economy.Unlike Papers Please, this game  ranks how well you do with each NPC on a 1-4 star rating, the fourth star requiring you to do everything right. It's not just about making the right final decision, it's about investigating the NPC well and having good grounds for your choice. I do believe there are still "choice" NPCs you can handle with a high/full star rating in different ways, so the system does a good job feeling like an optional bonus, not a slap on the wrist for being naughty- Though I admit, something is lost in  if you made the right call, and instead being told you for sure did a good job.If you make wrong/inoptimal choices, you can also rewind time during your shift. You can rewind to the beginning of a shift infinite times, or back to specific NPCs a limited number of times (usually, enough to retry every NPC once). It manages to balance empowering you to try goofy antics without making it feel like the job's free of tension.I don't think the guardpost gameplay is as ideal as it could've been, though. The truth serum, as might be expected, is overpowered and solves  more problems than most of the other tools, the game seems to be lacking a transcript feature to let me reread what people have said, and IMO the game should've been designed around at least some interrogation actions being "free actions", like how Hold It works in Ace Attorney. I just think that works better to make an investigation experience feel natural.Also,  line of dialogue in this game is fully voice acted, which really surprised me given how many possible NPC interactions exist. I'm not complaining, it hardly detracts from the game, I just hope the dev team and their budget are okay lmao.I think the overall content offering here is worthwhile for the price. This game doesn't seem to have a timeline branching system like Papers Please, which makes searching out all the different choices less convenient, but said choices, alternate dialogue, etc do certainly exist for solid replay value.While this game isn't  mechanically sound as Papers Please or  funny as Monkey Island, it does an excellent job of mashing the strengths of the two together into a unique package. Anyone interested in the border crossing hotseat or adventure game funnies should really give this a look.

_childDocuments_.review: A Papers Please style puzzle game where try and discern if a character is lying or hiding something. The aim is to get 4 stars by using different tools and information to find an item or have them tell you the truth. You can then decide if they should be let into the town, denied entry or be jailed. You also have a time machine so you can try again to get more dialogue or a better star rating.It has some of the funniest writing but could be missed if you are not selecting the "correct" tool and not trying it again. The game often breaks the fourth wall and does not take itself seriously at all. There was an instance where a character apparently died but then later I saw the character in town. Not sure if that was a bug or I missed something. Later you need to select characters that for a specific reason and you do not get much information to make a good decision to let them in or not. Ultimately this is not important or makes you fail but more information is often better for me to not feel cheated in some way.I would advise you to go in blind and play it yourself but if not you can watch me play it here:

_childDocuments_.review: Solid 8/10. It is NOT a fast-paced game like Papers, Please (which is the impression I got from other reviews). There's a specific order of people to evaluate and you can take your time. If you play it again you'll unlock some new scenarios and endings. Pros:- Its story is the best aspect of this game, even if it's pretty easy to predict who is the villain and what you should do. - Your choices actively affect the game's world state; there are multiple endings and unlockable scenes.- It doesn't solely focus on being a guardsman - there are mini-trivia games too. - Characters trying to enter are pretty creative, gets harder towards the end. But once you've figured out who is what, it's easy. Some cons: - It crashes sometimes then you have to redo everything from the previous autosave; sometimes there's a LONG wait between the autosaves. (I.e. it crashed right at the ending placards for me, I had to replay the level and skip a ♥♥♥♥ ton of dialogue.)- The dialogue gets tedious after awhile and while the voice acting is acceptable, once you've heard it once you DON'T want to hear it again. If there was a way to skip all the dialogue and just play as the guardsman, or an "unli-guard" mode where you'd just evaluate people, that'd be fun.- There's no higher difficulties after you're done with the game. It gets more difficult IN the game, although if you've played it once, it's not about getting it right anymore, it's about trying different story lines. Worth it on sale: Yes (but NOT if you're only in it for the strategy aspect. It's more visual novel than it is "letting-people-through-as-fast-as-possible-without-mistakes".)Full price: Yes IF you want a slower, more plotty, lighthearted version of Papers, Please.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic low-stakes fun! I downloaded Lil' Guardsman on a whim, and I'm so, so glad I did. It's an easy point and click interface structured around your shifts at the guard shack, where you will admit, deny, or even jail potential visitors to your city whilst juggling political intrigue behind the scenes. The writing and the humor of the game is where it really shines, though---the whole thing is very Discworld-flavored and is absolutely brimming with references to and parodies of other media (including but not limited to: Star Trek, Stardew Valley, various Disney movies, and Weird Al Yankovic). This game was an absolute joy to play.For me, the only drawbacks were the inability to save/pause mid-day, especially in late-game when the days are a lot longer, and some minor issues with trying to get the player character in the exact right position to get the dialogue options to trigger. But those are very, very minor quibbles---do yourself a favor and buy the game!

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the charming artstyle fool you, this game has a surprising amount of depth, where it touches now and again on deeper subject matter. Very good gameplay mechanics that are reused creatively. That is usually a common pitfall for point n click and puzzle games when they tend to introduce a game mechanic only to use it once and then never again. Lil Guardsman has it's arsenal of tools and mechanics that they stuck to which was a very good choice. It is spiced up sometimes but its always based on the same base mechanics. It also is quite comfortable to play as well since it gives you the freedom to explore several different options. Some things towards the end in act 2 doesn't get an obvious followup. Unsure if it's just in my own playthrough that simply missed it or if it's like that overall. Id like to see some sort of timeline tree or visualisation of all possible endings or choices added in an update but other than that the game has felt polished and fun through out.

_childDocuments_.review: From start to finish this game is funny, smart, and while a lot of the choices didn't seem very challenging when trying to get 4 stars they were all clever and deeper than you would expect. _childDocuments_.review: GOTY contender for me after finishing it. Utterly charming aesthetically, with the cartoonish character designs and storybook framing. The writing is fantastic and funny throughout, while quite emotionally engrossing too. The characters are all interesting and likeable, well-written and to have depth to them. Lil(ith) is a great teen girl protagonist, and it's hard to write a teen character who sounds like their age but isn't insufferable or predictable. She wants to live her childhood rather than do her dad's job, but also she gets stuck in when magic, politics, and consequences come about. She has a precocious and uplifting energy that carries through the plot and other characters. The investigation elements kept me on my toes, with obvious homages to Papers Please (Lil scolds the reference points for some meta humour) but the characters here are more involved and have arcs from start to finish, such as Mrs Abernathy, Tyronius, Chuck, Edward The Magician, Echo, and many more. Getting 4 stars on the levels is quite satisfying because you have to use most of your tools to get the best results. The consequences are also satisfying as you see the ripples of your actions play out with characters throughout, particularly to do with marriages and wars. I quite appreciated the anticapitalist commentary. There are no difficulty spikes and the ending is quite satisfying. Props to the writing team, I'm looking forward to what the developers and writers come up with in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: LIL' GUARDSMAN has the charm of a Lucasarts' point-n-click adventure with the gameplay mechanics of Papers, Please, and TIME TRAVEL (which was what piqued my interest). A fun, funny (and sometimes very sweet) romp that occasionally tested my patience with its time loop conceit.Time loops are core to the gameplay experience ("need to interrogate/search/WHIP that person a different way? REWIND TIME!") but there's a limit to the number of times you can do that in a single day, and after that you have to start the entire day over. It's a bit niggly but survivable.What's less fun: every time you do a time loop, you have to redo all the steps you'd done previously to reach the optimal outcome. There's no way to skip the (admittedly very funny) dialogue except for one line at a time (excepting one PARTICULAR instance that was TOO FUNNY to skip).In fact, there are a LOT of unskippable things: UI animations and scene transitions that won't speed up no matter how fast I mash the button to GET ON WITH IT because I'd seen it five times already thanks. They're mercifully short but having to see them over and over because I'm playing the game as intended (ie with time loops) is... not a whole lot fun.Basically, I wish there was a "skip" option a la a lot of visual novels that allow players to fast-forwards through all the dialogue that they'd already seen (VNs that don't have that option are dead to me). Fortunately, LIL' GUARDSMAN is still a very, very charming game in spite of this particular shortcoming, and meeting all the weird and wonderful characters of this world is incredibly rewardlng!

Im not dropping names for no spoilers sake but there are multiple instances of this and its quite jarring(Here is the spoilers edition: This plot is so painfully generic. _childDocuments_.review: I was hoping for something like Papers Please, but this is not it. The puzzles at the guard post cannot be figured out through logic. Rather, you're given a device that allows you to repeat people or the whole level and you need to experiment with different options in order to get 4 stars. It's completely arbitrary.For example, on level 2, there are two envoys that are coming to town. The instructions for that day say that you should "get them talking" which would mean that you need to interrogate them three times. That only works for one of them, though. The other requires you to phone someone who then tells you to confiscate their bugle. Another on level 2 is the painter. You have to use the metal detector and "confiscate" one of his cans of paint. There's nothing wrong with the paint and there's nothing wrong with the painter, but you can only get 4 stars if you steal his paint.If you're looking for a puzzle game, stay away.

_childDocuments_.review: Because of the numerous comparisons to Papers Please that I read in the reviews, when I started playing Lil' Guardsman the gameplay seemed to lack the dynamics and complexity of the first game. However, after some time I realized that Papers Please was just a loose inspiration, and the creators did not want to match its challenging gameplay. Lil' Guardsman allows the players to relax and enjoy the story without unnecessary stress and fear of failing to achieve a given goal. There is no need to worry too much about constantly upgrading the equipment or running out of crystals that allow certain actions, just let the history of the Sprawl unfold before your eyes. In the end, I really enjoyed the Lil' Guardsman, and do not regret buying it for almost the full price. I will certainly get back to this game in the future to try to get the other achievements and a different ending!

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I could recommend this. Lil Guardsman suffers from what I can only interpret as a lack of identity. It explicitly references Monkey Island and Papers Please - but the comedy often fell flat for me, puzzles felt lackluster at best... and obtuse or pointless at worst. On the other hand, the decisions felt weightless, and I didn't really care about any outcome from them, and the political commentary felt ham-fisted most of the time while the main character still made uncontrollable in-universe defacto racist remarks. By the end of my experience, I was just waiting for it to be over with. It's a strong premise with a good opening to be honest, but it never goes anywhere with it and the comedy couldn't figure out whether it was for kids or adults, and was inconsistent as a result. It also doesn't help my review that I had a few crashes, and the game's UI was extremely lacking at times. As an aspiring game designer I want to give kudos for the things that went right, namely the art, premise, and *some* chunks of the writing, but as a player I can't look past the flaws if I'm writing an honest review.

_childDocuments_.review: Very much worth the price of buying it-- a delightful, well-conceived choice-based game with unique mechanics!WEAKNESSES:1. Once you get a hang of it, the game gets to be unimaginably easy. (Make a challenge mode!)2. Some of my choices did NOT matter and it really grinded my gears. There seem to be multiple endings to the game, so I just wish the game did a better job of showing off the importance of your choices. On my first playthrough, it felt like the GLA would rise no matter what I did (I was trying to be evil, sorry). A goblin I freed from the big bad's thrall was somehow enslaved and calling him "master" in the war room. An old man who was said to have died from my choices was someone I bumped into on the docks later on. All these factors felt like a breach of trust. The fact that Chuck interrupted the wedding in part 1 despite the fact that I put him in JAIL made me think that my choices did not matter and I started to wonder if there was only one ending to the game. I also sniffed out issues with a certain group (you know the one) early on and for some reason that didn't seem to matter.3. For some reason, the game closes on its own if you leave your keyboard for 30 minutes. You'll have to redo the level from the start.4. (Related to weakness #2) Being loyal or unloyal to the three counseling you doesn't have any ramifications that I noticed. I expected a punishment for disobedience at some point-- which would have been a lot more fun.STRENGTHS:1. Wonderfully clever. A great murder-free mystery. You have ethical choices to make, story routes to choose, and strategic choices to make.2. Longer than I expected! I'm used to greedy pricing, but this is a REALLY, really appropriately priced game! So worth it, especially when it's on sale! Including all the story, each level times out around 30-40 minutes. There are twelve levels.3. Well, that's it. The game is fun and there's a lot of it. It's a story-based game, but the story is told through gameplay. If that sounds fun, then do it!

_childDocuments_.review: The story is really cool, the dialogue is great, and I love the gameplay. People compare the gameplay to Papers, Please a lot but the fact that it's more dialogue-oriented in this game really sets it apart from Papers, Please imo; you really have to pay attention to what people are saying so you can find inconsistencies and catch them out, and that can be challenging (in a good way) when you're distracted by somebody's funny gimmick or they talk a lot and you have to make sure you're not missing or losing details.My only big complaint isn't even against the content of the game, it's that it's oddly demanding on the computer. Sure I'm not playing on a big PC or even a purpose-built gaming laptop, but a point-and-click game shouldn't require anything like that. On my 2023 Macbook Pro with 36GB memory and an M3 chip (way above the recommended specs), this game completely drains the battery from 100% to like 10% in just under an hour, so I have to keep it on the charger to play more than like 40mins and it makes the computer run so hot it hurts to touch it. Other games I play on this computer are mainly the Stanley Parable Ultra Deluxe, Slime Rancher, Stardew Valley, and Sun Haven; none of these games put as much of a strain on my computer as Lil Guardsman does. I shudder thinking about how a computer with the minimum requirements would actually handle this game. The only game I play that drains the battery as fast as Lil Guardsman is Roblox and that still doesn't make it run as hot as Lil Guardsman doesI don't get me wrong, I really like this game and highly recommend it, just keep an eye on how your computer's doing while playing it especially if it's not particularly beefy or efficient at cooling.

_childDocuments_.review: Lil' Guardsman is a game by Hilltop Studios, published by Versus Evil and TinyBuild. It was released in January 2024 and follows the journey of Lil, a 12-year-old girl who takes on her Father's job as a guardsman, deciding who to allow or deny entry into the city of Sprawl. Over the course of the game you follow events taking place in Sprawl, The game has a total of 12 chapters with the plot progressing through each of them. Though most of them take place inside the same guard shed many of them manage to feel wholly different due to changes in some of the game mechanics and plot. Without getting into spoilers, If you think this game is just about letting people into the city, you're definitely wrong! That being said, the primary gameplay does pretty much stay the same, and after a while you get quite good at figuring out if something's not right. Which is the case for pretty much anybody passing through. So this game is really more of solving unique puzzles in form of people wanting to be let in rather than a more random challenge where you're trying to find mistakes in documents like 'Papers please' for example. Where I think Lil' Guardsman gets a little bit tedious is with its ample amounts of exposition and what sometimes feels like unnecessary dialogue. Obviously, since the main game mechanic revolves around figuring out who's lying etc., the game is going to have loads of dialogue. It is also set in a high fantasy setting, which is not exactly known for being easy and brief to understand. All things considered and even when taking these things into account, however, especially some of the scenes in between gameplay  felt way too long and I sometimes found myself quite frustrated and just wanting to  start the next shift.What should also be said is that though many points in the game emphasize how a choice you have made has an effect on the world around you, quite many of the decisions are things like cosmetic choices or don't really affect the story all that much, often just resulting in you getting different achievements. Obviously though, it is an indie game, so I'm not really bashing them for this. It just feels like something worth pointing out. In general I did find the writing pretty good and liked how the more mature topics and jokes contrasted with the otherwise bright almost child-like art style of the game. The story itself is also not bad. Maybe somewhat predictable but as is often the case, I think in this case it's just a result of good writing that foreshadows what's about to come.  Overall, it took me about 8 hours to finish a single playthrough and as a result of that playthrough and playing it a little bit afterwards, I would give this game a 3/5. I think it's a good game and manages to do some really fun things that kind of turn the high fantasy setting on its head while also managing to bring up real life topics and discussions. It is also clearly a product of much labour and love and is very polished, however, the copious amounts of exposition occasionally make it feel like a chore, which also eats away some of the replay ability which is not so ideal for a game all about making different decisions. If you want more reviews make sure to check out my YouTube or Tiktok @_gamesiplay_ or @_thegamesiplay_ respectively!

_childDocuments_.review: It's a... bit rich, but okay.Lil Guardsman is a Papers Please esque game where you play a 12 year old girl that's had a load of unwanted responsibilities thrust upon her... one of which being a border patrol officer ("Guardsman") for her home known as "The Sprawl."Unlike Papers Please, the tone is a lot more laid back. We have full voice acting for one thing, which gives my own vocal chords a chance to rest. Instead of checking papers you interrogate anybody who requests access to the Sprawl. You can talk to them, use one of you many tools (powered by crystals that you can buy with gold), or call one of the royal advisors for help (I found Stryker to be the most helpful). When you're not working the Guardshed, you're out in the hubworld speaking to the locals or performing a wealth of tasks to earn more gold or more crystals for the Guardshed.What sets this game apart from others like it is its approach to the "Choices Matter" format. Every single little thing you do has the chance to affect you or The Sprawl in the future. May it be letting in a potentially dangerous person via the guardshed, or by smart-mouthing a person in power in the hubworld. This FORCES you to think about every possible outcome when making decisions, no matter how stupid the decision might seem at first glance, or how stupid the outcome might be.Outside of gameplay, every character is charming as all hell. From Lil and the characters in the hubworld, to the extensive volume of crazies you meet at the Guardshed. Each character has a story to tell, an agenda to push, or someone to murder. I found myself walking away from a couple interactions audibly saying "Yeah, I like that guy" and getting really excited when I found them in the hubworld later on.Which brings us to my only problem with the game... the humor. Lil Guardsman knows what it is. It's a video game. And Lil Guardsman doesn't feel like keeping that fact to Lil Guardsman's self. There are SO MANY self-references, 4th wall jokes, and references to pop culture that it got genuinely distracting. To the point where in one cutscene it happened three separate times. You're not Deadpool, you're a little indie game that takes heavy inspiration from Monkey Island and Papers Please. I do NOT need you to tell me that.All in all, pretty good experience that I will definitely be adding to my recommendation repertoire.If you like Papers Please and wish it was less "gruff" and a lot more colorful, Lil Guardsman is the game for you.QAPLA!!!
_childDocuments_.name: Lil' Guardsman

_childDocuments_.review: Lil' Guardsman takes obvious inspiration from Papers, Please and the Monkey Island franchise, as evidenced by a sign in a game pointing to the directions "Arstotzka" and "Monkey Island." Although I have not played a Monkey Island game, I have played other point and click adventures in my past. I have played, and enjoyed Paper's Please.   Random TikToks introduced me to this game (yay for marketing) and compared it endlessly to Papers, Please, so I thought I would do a comparison. Lil' Guardsman is  to Papers, Please in that you:- decide who gets in, out, and thrown in jail at an entry point of a city/kingdom- discover the story vastly through dialogue- question those attempting entry- have updated rules to follow for who to let in/out/jail- have updated aspects to the guard station to vet each individual- choices have consequencesLil' Guardsman is  to Papers, Please in that:- the tone is much lighter, largely likely due to comedic dialogue and stylish, colorful design- the addition of magical items alongside questioning people with the aforementioned comedic dialogue, rather than meticulously checking IDs, makes Lil' Guardsman MUCH easier- the ability to travel to different locations throughout the kingdom via point and click is present within Lil' Guardsman, rather than sitting stationary at the border stationNow, onto the pros and cons. - wonderful, silly dialogue that really understands how a 12-year-old protagonist would process and present information- all characters are unique. I found myself looking forward to meeting a new individual every single  Chapter.- music is charming and fits each scene- there is SO MUCH voice acting, and it is all well-done. If you are dyslexic, i would argue that this might be a fun game to play despite it technically being a lot of reading because every piece of dialogue is read out loud to you. - choices genuinely impact the future of the game.- i want the game to be longer because of how good it is, but i also recognize that this is an indie studio. I really hope that there is a second game expanding on the cool elements of the night mode. - it scratches that Papers, Please itch in a new and interesting way- it is so clear how much love went into this game. It is nothing I could imagine a big studio greenlighting. - to talk to a person or interact with an object when walking, you need to click on a pop up icon. Even though it felt as though i clicked squarely on it, my character would walk past it, and i would have to click to walk back multiple times- there is a mode exclusive to night time that was very fun. With all of the things needed to know about the night time mode, you would expect there to be more of it. I wanted there to be more of it.- no fast travel means clicking constantly to walk. If you click the edge of the screen, you walk to the edge of the screen, which yes, makes sense. But constantly clicking in a long room, while trying to interact with objects/people and missing the interaction click bc your character walked a bit too far felt slightly tedious for an otherwise smooth game.   There is an area that can be immediately accessed from exiting a location and clicking on it to travel through the city, but if you enter the aforementioned area you cannot immediately exit it like you were to immediately enter it. You have to walk through an entire room to get out of it fully, and this aforementioned area is IMPORTANT to access. For those who want spoilers/ have already played the game and are reading reviews, I am referring to the .  I feel as though instantaneous fast travel would prove beneficial alongside  would be the fixes to this issue. - the game is about 8 hours long if you start with all of the dialogue being read out and then realize you want to click through dialogue because you can read a bit faster. i wish the game was longer.I really recommend this game!! I understand not wanting to pay $20 for a game that is technically only around 8 hours, but I feel like it is important to remind people that we are used to an industry overworking and underpaying talented, passionate individuals. However, if you are still thinking $20 is too much, which is totally fair with the state of the economy right now, I have seen it go on sale. Wishlist Lil' Guardsman, and I bet it will go on sale in the big Winter Sale at the end of the year. Or try and steam share (don't forget about steam sharing!!) with others if you can.

_childDocuments_.review: As of writing this review I just wrapped up with my first playthrough, and loved every second of it. This is a border agent game in  a similar vein to games like Papers Please and That's not my Neighbor. You handle deciding who gets into your city and who does not. You need to determine who means well and who means harm. And it is up to you to decide when the rules you have been given are wrong or right. With all of this in mind, I will now list my personal upsides and downsides to this game before concluding with some final thoughts.The Good:+ The Game is very simple to understand and play, and the game is super forgiving, letting you go back and fix mistakes at almost anytime. + The gameplay loop is simple but fun, requiring you to balance a finite number of resources with minimal income and ever changing rules. + If you ever feel lost there is likely a hint or two availabe to steer you in the right direction. + This game has LOADS of character and fun personalities. From kind old grannies to an actual incarnation of the devil, you will meet MANY different people and pretty much all of them are written well in my opinon. + VERY high quality voice acting. Every character is voice acted, and voice acted super well! Listening to the voice acting in this game reminded me of the quality seen in Baldur's Gate 3! Yeah it's that good! Honestly shoutout to the voice cast for some of the best performances I have ever heard! + The story is basic, but fun and interesting to enjoy. There are lots of moving parts and hidden secrets you can find all over the place that contribute to the story overall. + The game's visuals and artstyle is great, consistent, and used to lots of comedic effect. Visuals are easily one of the game's strong suits.+ The game's difficulty curve is not too intense, but it does allow for some genuine added challenge. You go from just handling random nobodies walking into to town, to dealing with night terrors, criminals, and more. + The game's quality stays about the same the whole way trough from start to end. At no point did I feel like the game hit a low, or was boring. It stayed the same the whole way through. The bad: - This game can feel REALLY short. Honestly my main complaint is that the game is only 14 chapters long. I would love to see this game continued, extended, or even get a sequel. - The game's default settings do not set the margins to fit the screen (at least in my case). So do not excpect the game to by default correct your resolution. Honestly that's my only pair of issues. I think this game is just good, and fun. With all this in mind my final thoughts are as follows: If you want a fun, simple, and short little puzzle game with loads of character and charm, then do I have a goldmine for you! This game is fun, funny, and overall an experience I would rate about 10/10.  I plan on returning to this game soon for some more fun guarding the Sprawl and fixing all kinds of mistakes. I hope you enjoy this game as much as I did!

_childDocuments_.review: Lil’ Guardsman takes the core concept of Papers, Please! and places it in an irreverent, colourful setting that oozes with charm and an endless amount of humour. If protagonist Lil, short for Lilith, was just a sarcastic little imp, it would not have worked as well as it does. But because she has heart–because the whole of Lil’ Guardsman has heart in spades–this game turns into one of the most earnest games I have played. It’s taken as its tonal inspirations such beloved LucasArts classics as Monkey Island. I come from a later generation and so haven’t played those classics, but from what I know about their sharp-as-nails writing, Hilltop Studios’ game would do those 90s titles proud.Humour is, of course, subjective. What is funny to me doesn’t have to be funny to you, yet there are some rules to comedy writing and Lil’ Guardsman keeps with them to produce a staggering amount of laugh-out-loud situations. Comedy works by juxtaposing what is normal with what is ludicrous; and from the get-go, the set-up is ridiculous. Your dad can’t make it to work today because he’s gone to bet all your money on the latest goblinball game, and you, a twelve-year-old girl, have to stand in for him. It’s not like you’ve ever substituted for Shamish either; it’s ridiculous, and you know it, and those travellers who come through the gates know it, and all of you acknowledge it. That’s the first stroke; the second is, after a single shift, it becomes clear to everyone you’re doing Shamish’s job better than he is. And because you’re a prepubescent girl, the trio of nutty councillors in charge of the Sprawl decide to make your position permanent because they think they can push you around, to look the other way whenever it suits them. Boy, are they about to be disappointed.Oh, and did I mention an archaeologist gives you a time machine to prototype under extremely specific conditions that have to do with your guard duties?I’ll say a little more about the plot in a minute but first, a few more thoughts on the comedic writing. Bad humour punches down; good humour punches up. In this respect, the most common targets Lil’ Guardsman picks are Disney and the heavy-hitting archetypes of the fantasy genre. The cast includes an impressive array of memorable and colourful characters, all of whom you’ll have to decide whether to let into the Sprawl or not. A few personal stand-outs include an ancient wizard who is a cross between Gandalf, Merlin, and the Dude from the Big Lebowski; a real, in-the-flesh singing Disney princess (are those red splatters on her sleeves? I’m sure it’s just paint), two goblins in a trenchcoat, and an elderly capitalist. Not one of these characters is played all the way straight–there’s always a twist, always the unexpected clue to be found, or the most ridiculous dialogue line suddenly injected into the conversation. What Lil’ Guardsman does is, it places the unexpected onto a pedestal and it makes sure that there’s all of us players benefit enormously from it.The game markets itself as having over a hundred memorable characters whose fates you can decide. Before playing it, I would’ve thought this hyperbolic; after finishing Lil’ Guardian, I know it to be the bare-faced truth.This is but a part of my review; you can find all of it on YouTube:

_childDocuments_.review: It's about supply chains! Economics!I first played this during Next Fest in 2023 and adored it. I even played the demo a few times for the different flavors (of tacos?) Lil' Guardsman is a fun and soul-refreshing mis-mash of light logic puzzles and a 4th-wall breaking fantasy-esque "save the world" tale. The game is incredibly forgiving and there are hints everywhere. Puzzles are not timed and neither is the story (much) and there are no pixel hunts. I'm also relieved that there are no collectibles. Rarely have a heard such a fun and "easy on the ears" soundtrack, which the developers enjoyed enough to put it on the juxebox. Speaking of sound, the voice acting is pretty much perfect. It's extremely well done - the characters "sound" like they are written and elevates even simple moments. There's no 'Echo".As for the game engine, it's smooth with clean, bright graphics. Unfortunately there is one pervasive bug, when in a room with multiple inter-actable objects, that you will occasionally need to walk back and forth to get the "triggers" to fire correctly. It's not game breaking, just a little annoying. I love this game - it's delightful, funny, relaxing and fun. Don't be turned away by the cartoon graphics - everything is well detailed and cleverly designed. I think all but the very youngest of gamers would (safely) enjoy it thanks to the multiple levels of humor.Even if it's not on sale, if you want a fun way to chill, "you should totally buy this!" as Lil would say. Have fun little sister!

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game. Play as a guardsman reminiscent of Papers Please without the looming threat of your family dying. Much more lighthearted, doesn't take itself too seriously, and has high quality voice acting, writing, and art.The biggest complaint I have is that, as a completionist who wants to get the highest score possible on every level, the game puts up some really annoying barriers that drag the experience down. Although the game features a rewind mechanic, its use is limited, and if you run out, you have to replay the  level, not just the part you are on. So you must spend a few minutes clicking through all the same dialogue making all the same choices just to get back to where you were.That wouldn't be much of a problem if it wasn't for my second complaint: some of the levels don't have intuitive ways of maxing out their score. Most of them do, even if the game kind of does a *wink* *wink* *nudge* *nudge* at you to get you to pick them, but some of them do require plain lucky guesses of what to do. So you will eventually have to use the rewind if you intend to get maximum scores.The majority of them are fine though, and figuring out the ideal solution without brute forcing does feel good.
