_childDocuments_.review: Video Review:Cookie cutter is a combat focused metroidvania featuring super cool character animation, turbo ultra chaotic combat and a humanoid robot protagonist named cherry who herself has got another robot companion called regina who looks like a…you know!While the game looks absolutely stunning, and the animations look incredibly detailed, it does have it’s share of flaws, some minor, and some fatal.For example, the opening cutscene and the tutorial that follows it are all fully voiced. But the rest of the game after the tutorial is just plain text. Is it some kind of a bug? Maybe? But the fact that it didn’t get FIXED even after a post launch patch, lead me to believe that it’s a feature; and a bizarre one at that. Okay so before I discuss further, let’s get the basics out of the way. You’re an android created by shinji, a scientist who apparently created you to have a romantic relationship with you. This marilyn manson looking evil corporation type guy kidnaps shinji and his two henchmen called ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ beat you to a pulp. a guy called Raz picks up your remains and fixes you, and now you must find your way to the evil corporation guy and rescue your creator slash lover, shinji. Beyond this, I didn’t really pay much attention to the story partly due to that glitch slash bug of voice acting vanishing out of nowhere, and partly cuz the game builds a lot of its world through texts readable in terminals you can find all over and I’m not a big fan of reading in games.It's a metroidvania so it has all the typical metroidvania stuff in it, like upgrades, switchable perks, hidden stashes, side quests with characters that eventually become merchants, bosses and what not. The only notable thing in the combat system is that it has a parry mechanic. The enemies flash a warning right before initiating a parryable strike and you have to press a dedicated parry button at the right moment, the usual affair. It’s fun, but the timing is kind of tricky and sometimes its hard to tell how far you have to stand from the enemy to be able to parry them succesfully. I actually liked that the game takes a rather safe approach in its design in that, it borrows pretty much every aspect of its traversal abilities, healing, level design, perks, upgrades etc. from other popular games of the genre. This is by no means a cheap-out though, as the developers have CLEARLY put some genuine effort into implementing all these in their game, which is why I didn’t mind it at all. I also kind of liked the fact that during about 90% of my playthrough the game felt kind of non-linear although the map always pointed to one singular objective that I’m supposed to go to. The overwhelming amount of optional areas to discover, hidden chests to find, never let the exploration get dull for me. But still, I wouldn’t call this game an exploration focused one, rather combat is very clearly its main focus. Even platforming challenges kind of take a backseat, only encountered sparingly; mostly in optional areas. That’s great! Because to me platforming here felt more frustrating than enjoyable.Combat, with its punchy sound design and super cool animation feels great…as long as you’re not locked in a room fighting hordes of enemies; Then, you’d really struggle to see what’s happening. This is caused by a number of design choices which I assume made it to the final game due to lack of enough playtesting. cherry is shorter than virtually every enemy, making it very difficult to see her when she’s swarmed by taller enemies; when she takes damage she blinks for too long, which in turn makes it very difficult to keep track of her position in the heat of the battle; when the enemies bleed, they bleed too much making the fighting area too noisy to read. All these, together with very detailed character models, attack and damage animations, and overdone VFX make you virtually blind during combat sections where you’re locked in a room and the only way to progress is to kill hordes of enemies that spawn in multiple rounds. These lockdown sessions happen very frequently in the game so dying repeatedly in these simply because you can’t see what you’re doing feels grossly unfair. The fact that the camera is generally very zoomed out only exasperates the problem.Keeping up with the amazing visual design of the rest of the game, the bosses are visually spectacular; but unfortunately they only have very predictable, small set of moves that they keep repeating in the same sequence, making the fights very easy. Moreover, I found that instead of hitting them with your regular kicks and other offensive abilities and damaging their health bar gradually, it’s much easier and faster to quickly learn their parry timing in a few attempts and just waiting till they try to strike you with a parryable attack and parrying them about three to four times to bring up the prompt for the finishing move and be done with it. This strategy, which felt more like a cheesing technique worked on every single boss, so overall, bossfights felt very underwhelming. It's a real shame because I actually really liked the game as a whole. Despite lack of any real innovation, The extremely eye catching animation, the adequete level design, and great music kept me engaged throughout my roughly 20 hours playthrough. Unfortunately the frustratingly over-animated combat significantly hurt my experience, but the simple yet visually pleasing level design kept me interested enough to want to overcome the somewhat unfair feeling combat zones. Would I still recommend it? Yes! Because despite all it’s drawbacks it’s still a good enough product for it’s price that I think you shouldn’t miss if you’re a fan of the genre.

I like the juggle combos a lot, but they're by far the least effective way to kill enemies, so I don't do them much. The most practical option is always parry. It's fast, it's low effort, it gains you resources instead of spending it. Sometimes I spam void wave to clear a group, then parry to get all my void back very quickly. I only hit the weapon button to amuse myself.(reading all the complaints about parries being too difficult makes me feel like I played a different game than everyone else. it's not that hard, folks. even if you miss it, you can tank the hit a couple times and get all your health back when you finally nail it. just take like 20 seconds to practice. _childDocuments_.review: Fantastic metroidvania that doesn't overstay it's welcome. Well written with some pretty funny banter and innuendo. The lore was easy enough to follow for my lizard brain, and it didn't dump a ton of it on you. Just enough to flesh out the story and build the world. Gorgeous hand-drawn art style with some awesome animations. Kept me engaged until I finished the game, which is rare. Glad it didn't end up another half-finished metroidvania in my Steam library. My only gripe is that it became impossible for me to 100% bc there is a breakable wall in the Denzel Factory, going to the Diesel Lagoon, that will permanently close off for some damn reason. You cannot break through that wall again, meaning if you go back to the Denzel Factory before grabbing the red crate collectible just ahead, there's no way to get it. It'll show up on the map taunting you, but you ain't getting it. So that was super frustrating. But honestly, I wouldn't recommend trying to 100% this game anyway, bc there are some really OP power ups that will completely trivialize the final boss. You have to do a bit of backtracking and side-questing to obtain them tho, and I kinda wish I wouldn't have, bc the difficulty was perfect throughout the majority of the game. Feel like I cheated myself out of a grand finale. Not that this is uncommon, my tendency to over-explore every nook and cranny and find every breakable wall and upgrade everything to the max has caused me to become too OP in many-a-game, and I never learn. Hopefully that "No Re-Entry" bug I mentioned will get patched tho, and I didn't run into any other bugs or glitches. All in all, a very good 8.5/10 metroidvania imo. I'll be looking out for the sequel for sure.

_childDocuments_.review: Thoughts so far:The animation and visual style are the standout here. The main character has a strong punk aesthetic that really brings her to life and everything is so fluidly animated. It won't be for everyone I feel but I really like it.Combat is melee based and is a little reminiscent of Guacamelee, beating the crap out of enemies and launching them into environmental traps. It's smooth and satisfying, with some comically brutal finishers, but does have some issues. Combat definitely contains too much visual noise, you can literally lose your character in the busier fights. You can get destroyed quite easily if you aren't careful and I found myself being stun-locked to death a couple of times. Finally, I'm not a fan of the parry, it doesn't feel reliable and is more risk/risk than risk/reward, especially on bosses. Nothing feels too punishing so far though and I've made steady progress without encountering any real difficulty spikes.I like the exploration so far and the map is suitably informative for backtracking. The abilities are standard fare (so far) and like most Metroidvanias traversal becomes more enjoyable the more you acquire.The story is a love/revenge narrative with cosmic overtones and questions about the nature of the soul (parts of it remind me of Lies of P's story). It's good enough to drive things forward and I'm interested to see what happens. I've seen reviews criticising some gaps in the story setup but if you play more than 0.2 hours you might find the answers you're looking for.Metroidvanias are ubiquitous these days and 2023 has seen a ton, but I feel Cookie Cutter is among the better ones and I'm having a great time with it so far.

_childDocuments_.review: With the expressive animation work of the characters, punk-like aesthetic, and over-the-top energy the game has, it’s easy to see that the devs had a clear vision with this game. This game is a labor of love. (which is why I'm still giving this a thumbs up. I think 300+ reviews are too low for this quality game)However, there are so many things that are unpolished, underdeveloped, and blatantly cheap.To talk about the technical department, I DO NOT recommend you play this game on Steam Deck for now. The game stutters like crazy when you get to the middle part of the game. Even with the Steam community’s discussion board’s help, I couldn’t bear the inconsistent animation frames and glitching, so I just finished the game on the Desktop instead.The option menu is also barebone, with no adjustable screen size, full screen/window mode switch, reduction option for the flashing light, or something like that.The structure as a metroidvania is alright. The mazes are designed tightly with the platforming sections that utilize unlockable moves, collectable that feel mostly meaningful for the player progression, and the frequent mixture of arenas -which is a welcomed addition, as the combat system is the main selling point here-.However, I think that, if the game is trying to sell the combat more, it should have had better enemies, which is my main gripe with this game. There are a few types of enemies, and here’s how I would describe them.Normal goons: Mono pattern fodder (sometimes they add a projectile move) and those attacks are arbitrarily hyperarmored (meaning that you can't stagger them consistently when they are in the attack-tell animation. Not a great feeling when you are playing a combo action game.)Big enemies: Twin pattern meatbag that flips like a card when players move around them. No collider prevents the player from going through the enemy so size rarely matters.Ranged enemies: Animations are just mere suggestions and the shooting point’s direction is always targeting you -meaning that the aiming animation never matches to the direction of the projectiles-. This aspect gets worse if the ranged enemy is a big enemy type too. (I’m looking at you, D!ckhead gunner.)Gimmick enemies: I’m talking about the flame shield guy and the bug-like robot that needs to be flipped before attacking. I don’t see any value in them as a combat chess piece.Bosses: 4-6 attack patterns with a barebone phase change. (Puanini and Final Boss were good though, even with this limitation.)And yes, I think the current pool of enemies wasn't enough to fill the combat section of this game. 2-3 new enemies per big area hardly give you an interesting discovery moment, and I would say almost all of them get palette-swapped so the surprise elements get diminished as the game goes on to the end part. The arena combat mixes up the enemies mentioned above pretty well (which is my favorite part of the game), but I think the dev should have put more thought into the Big enemy placements, as they sometimes just appear as a SOLE enemy without additional goons (meaning that they don’t even function as a space controller chess piece in the arena).I know making an enemy is hard for a frame-by-frame animation workflow, but considering that every enemy has their glory kill animation (I think it is pretty redundant to put too much effort into them), some man-power should have been allocated to different attack patterns or just entirely new enemies.It is obvious that there’s a sequel is planned as the ending credit appears at the urgent situation. I’m absolutely nothing when it comes to the developer’s direction (as I’m just a mere player) but my suggestion is that they should refine the strength they currently have (aesthetic, player toolset) and then put more effort into the enemies. Even though I think this game couldn’t nail down everything with its potential, I expect more good things from this developer.

_childDocuments_.review: Got this in a Humble Bundle and was drawn to try it because of the art style, the game itself is just... not that good.The combat is just plain unfun, to me. My biggest complaint is that the only way to do any meaningful damage is to use what is effectively your sub-weapons, your different weapons you can put on heavy attack. There's a whole combo system that you could easily and reliably get a 15 hit combo using your light attacks, but all of those hits are worth less than a single hit from your starting heavy attack weapon, all light attacks are good for is generating mana to use the heavy attack, but even then if you get an execute, which only triggers if you get enemies below a certain amount of health, you usually make back more mana than you used. Also, aside from the uppercut, which launched the enemies, the light attacks don't put any enemy type into hitstun, so if you open with a raw light attack you're usually going to be getting hit instead as the enemy just shrugs it off.Also, parries just don't feel right. I was practicing on the first enemy in the game, because he has a very obvious attack warning flash and it's easy to count when the attack should hit, to land the parry timing, but it honestly feels like the timing constantly changes. I think it's because the hitbox for the parry is VERY close to your body, perhaps just the size of your body's hurtbox, which means there's changes to the timings of every parry because slight distance changes can result in you getting hit at different times.Overall, in playing this game I just kept thinking back to Valdis Story and how, while not as a visually striking, it hits all of the things I hoped this game would have, but didn't.

_childDocuments_.review: After I had a slump with Metroidvania a while back, because of playing any I came across, I'm glad I've been able to return to the genre and continue enjoying what makes it unique. Cookie Cutter is a great example, as it employs mechanics that are familiar and beloved by gamers like me, from being able to re-explore areas after gaining new abilities, to discovering secret rooms that hold rewards, sometimes with its own twist. It’s a visual wonder, and the gameplay is super fun, although it can be frustrating at times due to the parry system, but it doesn't detract too much from the experience and ends up being a great adventure.Cookie Cutter places us in a dystopian world, where humanity has overcome the weakness of the flesh, and has achieved something that many mortals have dreamed of: to pass the consciousness of a living being to an android. But as greed is a human sin that always lurks around the corner, this dream come true turns into a nightmare when it’s used to train tireless workers, perfect to work forever; all at the hands of the INFONET organization.The story begins two hundred years after this revolution, focusing on Dr. Shinji, and her creation, Cherry; an android she created herself, and with whom she ended up falling in love. But misfortune knocks at the door, and one of the leaders of the organization kidnaps the doctor. It is then that Cherry begins a bloody and relentless mission, driven by love, and fueled by her fury. The plot itself is quite serious at its base, like most revenge odysseys, but it is constantly embellished by a particular and certainly not timid humor, which kept me quite entertained with how whacky it can get. It’s also complemented by a memory system, where we can see fragments of the past between Cherry and Shinji, although the NPC that helps us in this is a little buggy and at the moment you can’t see much. Despite this, I enjoyed the story without problems, and the devs are aware of the problem.As we follow our adventure, we'll explore post-apocalyptic terrains of the Megastructure, areas in decay and filled with dangerous creatures both living and robotic. To navigate these places, Cookie Cutter gives us a modest repertoire of exploration skills, from the iconic double jump that I love so much and that I never get tired of repeating, to combat tools that will also help us to make our way through doors or blockades.In combat we'll count first of all with our own fists and feet, which don’t do much damage but help us to generate void to use our other weapons. The void is what in other games would be mana or energy, and it can also be used to heal us gradually as long as we keep the assigned button pressed. This presents an additional challenge in the middle of fights, since it’s not instantaneous and we can be beaten to a pulp while trying to recover our health.To deal a bit with the healing issue, we'll have a parry skill, which allows us to avoid damage completely by timing it with enemy attacks, and that when successfully performed, it ends up triggering a bloody finisher that rewards us with health orbs. Some enemies are easier to parry than others, and we can only counter moves that show a flash before triggering. This part is what I found most frustrating about the game, but because I'm pretty bad at parrying, and I'm not sure if the bosses are affected by this mechanic; although I wouldn't be surprised if I had failed every attempt I had. Nevertheless, Cookie Cutter offers other ways to deal with fights, and finishers can also be executed on enemies with low health.As I mentioned before, we'll also have several weapons at our disposal, starting with a gauntlet that hits harder than our conventional attacks. Eventually we'll be able to have an electric guitar to defeat enemies in the most rock 'n' roll style, a device that shoots lasers, and a couple more that I'll keep to myself so as not to ruin the surprise. It's worth noting that this weaponry can be upgraded with certain NPCs, collecting money and materials, although they are not the only things that can be upgraded.Cherry also has a system of upgrades for her android body, and we can equip and modify components in certain stations scattered around the map, which also serve as teleporters, by the way. The components vary from health bonuses to even additional jumps, and require energy slots that we can find as we explore. This is what most motivates me to snoop around the nooks and crannies of the maps, as it is very rewarding to discover secret rooms, and make our robot grow in power with the loot. Moving away from the gameplay, Cookie Cutter offers hand-drawn and cartoonishly stylized visuals, radiating a somewhat grotesque and crimson-soaked charisma. The character design is very much in touch with the setting, starting with Cherry who I really liked, and with varied NPCs that bring to life a world that goes from colorful to dreary in just a few steps. The environments are complemented by posters and graffiti that add depth to the setting, along with references to other games that result in a nice touch. The animations are exquisite, especially the finishers that are different for each type of enemy in the game, and the soundtrack that accompanies the carnage is very cool! In conclusion, Cookie Cutter is a very particular Metroidvania, with fun mechanics, a fluid and frenetic combat, blood and guts everywhere. The story is the typical revenge story but it lends itself to enjoyment, especially thanks to the humor that accompanies it. Although I found some bugs, such as the NPC of memories or that the achievements do not work on Steam, I could finish it without issue and enjoyed the adventure a lot. If this was their debut game, imagine what they could scheme in the future, especially when the end of the game is somewhat open, but I'll end up not saying more than that.

_childDocuments_.review: Definitely not a bad game, yet absolutely not what I've expected of it to be. Artstyle is the key point for this game. First thing popped in my mind was Tank Girl, which I'm pretty sure was on the mood board here. Looks fun, quirky, colorful and great. Can't complain. Level design with the huge map, teleport points and savespots - very well done too. Enemies are... Well, fine, I guess?Music & sound- nothing particular caught my ear, but let's assume they are good too. What really ruined the game for me is the combat system. Basically you have two type of attacks - armed and unarmed, so to say.Unarmed are pretty weak kicks and punches that deal very low damage and aimed mostly to charge the "power bar".Armed attacks depend on what weapon you have active, do actual damage and deplete the "Power bar".In theory - sounds ok, on practice - I got reaaaaaly bored after just a couple of hours in game. Fighting loop is always the same - you see monsters -> you use everything you have to recede their numbers -> you use your kicks to replenish -> you finish the rest. Of course, there's a block & parry system that works well... if you're in 1vs1 fight. Mix another mob and you get chain striked attempting to block any attack aimed at you.Then you get to the boss fight and well... Forget everything you did above, as parry becomes your number one.Bosses are designed in such a weird way that they basically one/two shot you. So dodging all the way - is not an optimal strategy. What you want to do is block, parry, hit back and land couple of strikes just to circle around it again, waiting for next telegraph of an attack. I managed to kill 3 bosses and, sad to say, all the fight felt the same. So, yeah. The game has secrets, side quests, upgrades (yeah, I know you can level up your bare fight power - doesn't feel like much difference). There are also "trinket" system similar to that in HK. Also levels become varied, with lots of platforming and such. Maybe the game is good and I put my expectation bar too high after games like Guacamelee 1&2, yet I can't get through the boredom of the core fighting mechanic. :(

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; I have mixed feelings about this game. Parry system isn't well explained and there are a bunch of small issues throughout the gameplay experience that NEED to be ironed out. Overall I enjoyed it but it's also pretty rough, I say play the game but only if you are aware of what I'm about to explain:1) THE PARRY SYSTEM:The game will teach you how to parry but it doesn't do it well. Enemy attacks that can be parried will flash bright blue. The tutorial seems to teach you that you're supposed to parry the attack at the precise moment that it flashes blue. At the time of writing this review, that is NOT how you're meant to parry. The blue flash is NOT the parry window, it is simply an indication that the attack CAN be parried. It only works when you parry at the very END of the attack ANIMATION. This makes parrying feel really awkward and very inconsistent. That said, you can complete the entire game without parrying at all. It makes fights take longer but you can ignore it all together, which is unfortunate because parrying is a cool game mechanic and I wish it worked better in this game.2) THE VOICE ACTING:The voice acting is good, however it's only present in the first 20-ish minutes of the game or so. After that there is not voice acting for the entire game. It's a strange choice because it stops abruptly with no clear reason. It's okay to not have voice acting in a game, but when you stat with it but then  leave it out for the majority of the game it just feels like something precious was taken away and leaves you wondering why it was even there in the first place.5) ENEMY PROJECTILES:Enemy projectiles travel through walls. It is annoying. It is very annoying. The flying enemies can also travel through walls. It makes fighting them difficult and even more annoying. 0/10.6) MY STEAM DECK EXPERIENCE:Playable and smooth but there is lots of stuttering late game for some reason, especially in the least level. I have had my Steam Deck OLED for about 4 months so it runs well and no other game stutters for me expect this one. They are microstutters so they're manageable but it's still really irritating. Those are my biggest concerns. If I had to rate the game out of 10 it would be 6/10. Play the game, just be aware that it's in dire need of further polishing.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, Cookie Cutter is kind of a tough one. For those of you who don't like to read, for me this Game is a 6.5 out of 10. There you go.First off the Game started with problems. Had no sound in the intro at all, only after a restart did it work. In general I wasn't pleased with the Sound. I don't know if it was a bug or intentional but sometimes there was Voice Acting (mostly in the very beginning of the Game) and most of the time there was none. It felt akward to say the least.But also maybe it's for the best. Because I really didn't like the Voice Actress for the Main Character and also the Dialogue. It was way too cringey for me, I'm sorry...And while we're at the topic of the Main Character, I really hated the looks/design of her. What the heck are even those thick noodly spaghetti legs standing in an O-Form? At one point even the Main Character herself remarked that she looked stupid. Yeah, she's right.(Btw.: You can hate on me all you want for saying that, but this is my opinion!)So yeah, the Main Character paired with bad voice Acting and cringey lines almost made me wanna stop playing right at the start. Still glad I decided to give the Game a shot.So here is something positive. The animations and the visual style are really great. I liked this Underground Punk Rock Comic Vibe that was going on.The Movement at first was a mixed bag for me. At the beginning it felt like the movement and platforming were kind of floaty but after a while you get used to it and then it's smooth sailing. Still, there are better examples out there on how to do it tight and right from the get go.The Combat ranges from just okay to sometimes good to repetitive and annoying, but yeah, I don't want to be too harsh. It felt a little too button mashy for me.The parrying in the beginning really didn't feel good, the timing was very awkward. Sometimes I could parry 10 enemies in a row and sometimes I failed 3 times with the same enemy. (Also pretty sure that the tutorial said "parrying when it flashes blue" and I'm sure I am not color blind, so I was confused because I saw only purple flashes.) But yeah, you will get used to it also later on and for some enemies you just exclusively parry.  Short story: It got easier even though the timing for each enemy was very strict.Loading Times felt kind of long in the beginning, but later on it didn't seem to bother me at all. Maybe they were not as long as I thought?The Sound and Cutscenes sometimes were laggy, also in the Combat Sections here and there.This Game has a Castlevania knockback, that really sucked especially with the flying enemies that shoot at you through walls. I didn't die often but those shooty enemies paired with the knockback? Yeah, not my cup of tea, didn't like that one bit. Also flying enemies could fly through walls and sometimes be stuck in the wall which would make them not hittable, which of course feels cheap.Regarding the Combat, it also can get pretty chaotic at times and your character can get lost amidst the Chaos when 6 or more enemies are stacked on top of each other and you are in this bunch.It kind of grows on you but the chaoticness makes it a bit unrefined.But I have to say the finishers (they are different for each enemy type) are really satisfying to watch, even though they can get old after a while.The Game can be played in a non-linear way but also always gives you a clear path so that you never get lost and everything else - exploration wise - is optional.Exploration in this Metroidvania is competent but as I said before, I've played Games way better than this one.Controls in this Game kind of felt awkward, but same as with many things in this title, you get used to them.Music ranges from ok to kind of good in some areas, not bad but nothing to write home about.Some nice Easter Eggs here and there (Misfits, Blasphemous, NOFX, Mario and more).I finished the Game in 15.9 hours on my first playthrough, 28/36 Achievements. But even though I am missing a few, I can already say that it is easy to 100%. The missing Achievements for me would just mean that I have to grind for 2 and to just check a few areas again, but I have to admit I really didn't want to.So yeah, this Review is all over the place, but so was this Game. Kind of good, kind of bad in some places. But overall I can say I kind of enjoyed myself.Maybe some day in the far far future I complete the rest of the Achievements, but I don't think so.Still, barely a recommend from me.

_childDocuments_.review: "Cookie Cutter" is a fresh take on metroidvanias, set in a dystopian world. You've got Cherry, a tough android on a revenge quest, and it's all about breaking bones and smashing through the usual gaming norms.Cherry's on a blood-soaked spree, punching, smacking, and flattening everything in her way. Combat is brutal, with combos and a Void meter for epic moves. Customize Cherry's skills to fit your style – it's not just blood, it's your own symphony of destruction.Hold on tight; the Megastructure is huge and interconnected. Non-linear exploration, secrets, and challenging platforming – it's a metroidvania dream. The map is way bigger than you think, trust me.Visually, it's a feast. Hand-drawn animations, grotesque characters, and the most brutal finishing moves ever. The music? Combat gets heavy beats, and exploration has this sci-fi vibe. Cherry's quest has its own soundtrack.Real talk – the parry move is a pain, so I skipped it. No difficulty settings, but it's not a deal-breaker. Be ready for a bit of a challenge early on."Cookie Cutter" isn't just a game; it's an experience. After 18 hours, I was hooked. The world, the combat, the story – it all clicked. Sure, it has quirks, but Cherry's revenge journey is a ride you don't want to miss. If you're into metroidvanias and a bit of carnage, grab this one. It's a bloody good time in the Megastructure.

_childDocuments_.review: Edit note:I originally had issues with this game because of a few bugs that affected my playthrough. As of today, these issues have been reported as fixed so I wanted to immediately take down the non-recommendation for the game and the original paragraph targeting the issues.  The rest of this review (excluding the closing paragraph) is my original critique. Apart from those issues I had the rest of the game gripped me.  I have played a few metroid-vanias but none have kept me engaged as this one.  The combat you see in the trailers is as good as it looks.  The devs have landed on a great combat system that seems to take inspiration more from beat em' ups rather than the average metroid-vania.  This means the enemies have more health but you get to juggle and pull off some sick free-form combos.The next best thing about this game is the fact that the majority of the new abilities are weapons or attacks.  So if you got to the end of the last paragraph and thought "sounds repetitive", that's where they've got you covered.  So if you don't like something about the one you're using, depending on the situation you are in or because you have a cool idea for a combo, you can try out another weapon if you have it unlocked.and most importantly: there are minimal puzzles and skill based traversals. _childDocuments_.review: A fun and wonderfully stylized Metroidvania, I enjoyed my experience with Cookie Cutter throughout. I found the combat to be fun and consistently engaging (even though I could never figure out how to get the parry to work) and the character design, animations and general aesthetics did a lot to give the game personality. I loved exploring for secrets and discovering power-ups and power cells (needed to activate those power-ups). Interestingly, unlike most Metroidvanias you don't just increase your stats as you progress. You actually need to unlock the ability to upgrade particular stats then commit some of your very limited power cells into that stat. It's a unique system that led to me experimenting with a few different playstyles, something I often appreciate in games.It's not a perfect game by any means, though. The load times are terrible and the game can occasionally be a bit janky. At one point I had discovered a secret area and was fighting the enemies within when I suddenly saw a screen-filling explosion and found I had clipped through the floor to the area below. When I tried to go back, I found myself blocked by a door locked until I cleared all the enemies in the room I could no longer enter. It wasn't a big deal (I reloaded my last save and it worked fine the next time) but keep in mind things might go a little weird now and again.Still, the good outweighed the bad and I recommend Cookie Cutter to fans of Metroidvanias and hand-drawn animation.

_childDocuments_.review: + great artstyle+ fast and frenetic combat+ music is good if uncommon+ writing is great- lacks polish in many areas- lots and lots of bugs- map errors are frustratingFrom the moment I saw Cookie Cutter's announcement trailer, I was in awe of the hand-drawn artstyle. It's very Tank Girl-ish, very Mad Max-ish. Everything is gory and gross, especially the finishing moves. It's ugly, but in the best possible way, and I think it takes real skill to make something so ugly yet effective. It's perfect for the tone of the game.Gameplay, too, hits all the right notes for that atmosphere. It's fast and frenetic, frequently bouncing enemies off walls and each other, into spikes or other obstacles. And it can get quite bloody at times, especially in rooms that rush enemies at you. It's immensely satisfying plowing through enemies when you get in the flow, and it happens often during the course of the game.As with other metroidvanias, you incrementally upgrade your arsenal of weapons or abilities and often these tie into navigation. For example, finding a gun weapon allows you to shoot some switches to open doors; or a chainsaw that cuts away gem-encrusted doors that your other attacks do nothing against. The maps are large and are littered with opportunities like those where you need to revisit later once you've acquired the correct tools needed.A lot of early scenes are fully voiced, then most of the remaining dialog scenes in the game are unvoiced. Sometimes part of a conversation is voiced and the rest isn't. And when scenes are voiced, it doesn't always follow the script on screen. The voice acting is great so it's a shame it's not more consistent. The music is nice, though, what little there is of it. It's mostly ambience but occasionally you rock-out during a boss or enemy encounter.There's quite a few bugs: in several instances, objectives didn't spawn like the metal balls you push into sockets to open some doors, I have two rooms on my map with locked doors and sockets but no balls spawned. And sometimes when clearing an objective like a chest, the map still shows they're uncleared.A very annoying one is it's impossible to 100% the game because one of the checklist items is destroy flying robots that litter stages, but there's 2 or 3 areas where these respawn if you die or leave the level. I think the idea was you're supposed to slingshot these in sequence, so if you fall to spikes, they respawn, but even if you clear those passages, if you leave the level or die elsewhere, they also respawn.The game lacks a lot of polish. Cutscene transitions are abrupt and a little glitchy with frequently flickering; if you try to move the camera angle in some areas, you gain double vision as the screen vibrates; the script has numerous typo errors and even markup errors (newline symbols visible, text formatting markups, etc); I frequently got stuck on world geometry and especially on bounce pads. Stuff you might expect in an early access title.I'm of mixed mind on Cookie Cutter but generally lean to recommend. Just barely, though. I think the game is in sore need of bugfixing and general polish but these are more annoyances than anything that critically impacts the game. The gameplay, writing, music is great, and as a metroidvania, it's really well made. It just needs more time and possibly more eyes because a lot of the issues I encountered should have been seen with even basic playtesting.As low as 5w max TDP can keep 60fps. Load times are crazy long and I think it might be tied to wattage, too. At least for me, putting it at 5w gives 30-40 second loadscreens between level transitions and on game start, but raising it just slightly to 6w cuts it down by over half. It's very peculiar behavior.Besides that, it controls and plays well on Deck, although the game is just awfully zoomed out in areas. It's frequently difficult to see where Cherry is in the midst of action. Some kind of zoom-in feature would have been appreciated.

_childDocuments_.review: Focuses a little too hard on being "subversive" and not hard enough on being a good game.---First, a rant about the combat:Combat is very wonky. This game focuses very heavily on combat, but it's also very stingy with upgrades, moves, resources, and weapons and there is no leveling system or skill tree. You can install "components" to increase your power, but your capacity for components is extremely limited. You start with 100 HP and a basic combo that does 2 damage per hit, and you know what? You're never moving very far from those numbers. When you get new weapons, you're pretty much immediately discouraged from actually using them because every move that isn't your basic combo uses MP (a resource called Void), and every special weapon except for the Gauntlet you start with uses too much of it.Enemies, meanwhile, begin doing extremely high damage very quickly for some reason. Prepare to get chunked for 30, 40, 60, even 90 damage depending on what you get hit by. To avoid damage, you have a parry I don't recommend using, and a dodge roll. For healing, you have a channeled healing spell that roots you in place, or a Doom-style Glory Kill on enemies that are at low health. These don't quite make up for the enemy damage, since you take so much in a single hit and heal so slowly that it doesn't feel entirely fair. You have no post-hit invincibility until you hit the ground, and it wears off immediately upon getting back up, so you can easily be killed in one combo by some larger groups.Add in tons of ranged enemies without giving me any good ways of dealing with ranged enemies and yeah, I hate this combat system. I didn't die very often while playing, but every death I did accrue felt like BS. It's a weird system where the best strategy is to ignore most of my combat options and only use a few things because they're only the ones that work.---Other issues:- Several abilities need to be unlocked that, honestly, really should have been available at the start of the game. For example, you get an air dash after a few hours, but the air dash is actually your only defensive move if you're in the air, which you likely will be. It's also, frankly, not a very interesting power-up, so it's a really lame dungeon reward. For reference, think of Samus's ability to roll into a ball in Metroid... but if instead of unlocking it at the beginning, you didn't get it until the third section of the map.- Here's the thing about instant deaths: if you're going to use them in any platforming level, you better be very confident in both your platforming and your level design. Cookie Cutter uses a fixed-height jump, slightly-slidey movement, and attacks that physically move you around. The maps have infrequent checkpoints and VERY infrequent teleport points (which is fun when you also have no other way of warping back to the hub area or nearby teleports). As soon as I saw the pink spikes, I knew there was going to be a problem.- Oddly long loading times, at least on Steam Deck. I have no idea what that's about, since I've never seen loading times like this in a metroidvania. Each section of the map is separated by a loading screen, too, so the amount of time I spent just staring at a loading screen... gosh, I don't think I've seen it since the PS2 days.---Cookie Cutter isn't BAD, it's just... boring. It sucks, since the art and animation is actually pretty well done, but it's brought down by weird design decisions. If you aren't mesmerized by the robot-lesbian-trucker-vibe protagonist, you will realize that you're playing a mediocre experience and I think you can easily find better elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a strong combat-centered Metroidvania, with some niggling complaints that I'll mention at the end. I was hesitant about picking it up, but I'm really enjoying it now. Good pacing, some decent enemy variety, exploration and options (at least to a degree), and well-wrought controls contribute to the fun.The parry mechanic is solid- it's tight timing, but a high payoff for executing it well, even allowing you to take down mini-bosses if you're brave enough to land a few of them.Seems to be an interesting weapon variety- still more to come, and my sense is that it has a pretty good length, although that's based solely on pacing and intuition. There is no difficulty selection, which I think is fine- it's a solid challenge, and I've had to repeat a couple of fights, but the checkpoint system is well implemented and it hasn't been frustrating.There is a small complaint that I would make- there are basically no options beyond a volume slider. Doesn't even have resolution, which is bizarre (although it looks very good- I'm guessing it runs at 1080). I would REALLY welcome a couple of basic selections like damage numbers- damage numbers are on, which is definitely helpful at first, but I would like them off now:When you do a finisher on an enemy after breaking them with a parry/whittling down their health, it does a variety of very nifty and gory animations. It ALSO displays 9999 in big red numerals, which distracts the eye significantly from the great art. On the one hand, I can see that being a cartoon/stylistic choice, but I'd prefer to be able to turn it off.Overall though- strong entry with tight, enjoyable combat.

_childDocuments_.review: There is no redeeming qualities in this game aside from the fact that are is hand-drawn.  Even then, the art itself is not good, just slightly better than a fanfic drawn by a high school artist on a drawing tablet.  The character designs are lackluster, the backgrounds are poorly merged into the game, the enemies seem out of place, the game world simply feels disjointed. It's unclear whether it's supposed to be a city populated by aliens and robots or not, the art style and world-building simply lack coherence. Additionally, the game is filled with neon-colored visual noise that could potentially trigger seizures, so playing it in a well-lit area is advised. This is the first time in my time as a gamer telling players to play in a lit area.Combat and the metroidvania elements of the game are uninspired, with fatalities consisting of gory explosions that add to the neon visual clutter. Moreover, the gameplay experience is subpar. For example, small squishy organic enemies cannot be staggered easily with normal hits, requiring either an UpAir or a strong MP attack.  This contradicts the game's own logic:   A powerful android punk badass lady made of metal that wields colossal weapons should be able to destroy squishy enemies poise with quick attacks,  but it's actually the other way around.  I cannot overstate how horrible it feels to fight squishy enemies by kite and counter techniques, which should be reserved for strong mobs. The gameplay loop involving skills, MP, and healing lacks coherence as well, as healing during combat is useless due to slow self-healing and enemy rush tactics. Healing also consumes MP needed for strong attacks, which means you are going to heal out of combat, only to start the next fight with the MP you need to stagger even squishy enemies. It simply feels very bad to play.The game's controller mechanics exacerbate these issues. The character dies in  few ♥♥♥♥♥, which is fine, difficulty is always welcome.   However, the game's combat draws inspiration from anime fighters with combos and dashes but lacks the responsiveness of these 2D fighting games.   The Left Stick fails to register or queue commands correctly when you are in the middle of other moves, which leads to missed directional inputs and caused whiffed combos or rolling in the wrong direction. Just play the new Blaz Bluz metroidvania if you are considering this game due to combat, they got the combat right.Regarding the story and lore, even if this game was written by Saramago himself, fact is that the gameplay does not deliver, so quality of the story is a moot point.  However, the storyline, if any, is of low quality as well.  No matter how queer the main character is, she is still saving a damsel in distress.  The main character appears to be the lover or AI sex-doll of her creator, which gives incestuous vibes.  The game advertises itself as subversive, but this is not the case.  This is a "cookie-cutter" mediocre game plagued with bad design choices.Do not buy.

_childDocuments_.review: Cookie Cutter is a visually striking game, with an art style that immediately captivates. The hand-drawn characters and environments stand out with their quirky, detailed design, contributing to a unique aesthetic that's both charming and immersive. The world-building is just as impressive, offering a rich story that keeps you invested, blending narrative depth with engaging gameplay in a way that draws you in without overwhelming.However, while the game excels in its artistic and storytelling aspects, the difficulty curve is where things become less consistent. In some moments, the game feels rewarding and fair, especially during boss battles, where you can defeat a challenging foe with a well-timed parry. Yet, at other times, the game flips this expectation, with regular enemies that seem disproportionately difficult, requiring far more effort to overcome than the bosses themselves. This inconsistency in difficulty can be frustrating, as it feels like there’s a lack of balance in how different enemies are designed, making progression feel uneven at times.While the game is certainly enjoyable and has a lot to offer, it would benefit from a more consistent difficulty curve, ensuring that players don’t feel like they’re constantly at the mercy of unpredictable challenges.

_childDocuments_.review: **Review: "Cookie Cutter – Metal Arms, Broken Rules, and Zero Chill!"**  *Cookie Cutter* doesn’t just smash the mold—it rips it apart with a flaming chainsaw hand and throws the pieces in your face. This punk-fueled, side-scrolling beatdown of a game is a feral scream of rebellion wrapped in a neon-soaked, blood-splattered love letter to the genre.  You play as Cherry, a rage-powered android on a mission to find her creator, and let me tell you—she’s not taking the scenic route. The combat is blistering and brutal, with moves so over-the-top they practically slam through the screen. Every punch, slash, and explosion feels like an act of defiance against boring games everywhere.  The art? Gorgeous and anarchic, a riot of color and chaos that makes every frame pop like a punk rock album cover. And the music? Oh, it slaps hard—a furious, headbanging soundtrack that keeps your adrenaline spiked.  *Cookie Cutter* isn’t just a game; it’s a middle finger to the ordinary. 10/10—smash everything, feel everything, and rock out while doing it.

_childDocuments_.review: For someone who loves Metroidvania games and animation, Cookie Cutter was an absolute delight. The amount of love and care put into every attack and gory execution made the game incredibly fun and enjoyable (not to mention the hidden references to music, games, and cartoons!). The movement is fluid, and I never felt that the controls were unresponsive. In fact, they only improved with each new power. The combat were always challenging, with a tricky parry system that rewards you greatly when you learn the timming. Dying is common, but you revive in an instant .That said, the game does have a few issues. There are some bugs and glitches, and the parry timing signal doesn’t always match the animation for all enemies. From the midgame onward, enemies hit harder and have a lot of health, which sometimes made me skip the fights. Also, the instant-death spikes in certain areas felt more frustrating than challenging. One minor, more disappointing aspect is that the voice acting stops after the tutorial. With the amount of dialogue, it would have been nice to have more acting throughout the game.I’ve just finished playing, unlocked all the achievements, and despite its flaws, I highly recommend giving it a try. I’m crossing my fingers for a sequel or some DLC in the future!

Most of the negatives I see in other reviews really seem like matters of taste. The biggest thing is that parrying is so hard that I never used it. The risk / reward on them is just too low at that kind of success rate.The one other thing I do wish were a little different is the fast travel system and / or the map interface. In the latter part of the game it was really tedious to figure out how the places I needed to go to collect the various pieces and parts I still needed and then to actually get to those parts of the world. Being able to fast travel from save points rather than just Denzel Stations would have made that far less tedious, or even just being able to jump to previously visited Denzel stations from wherever I am would be great. Being able to drop pins on the map, or have a singular large map view would make coming back to places I couldn't reach previously much less tedious too. As it is, navigating in and out of local and world level map views over and over as I search for that one place where that that one thing was takes forever and is way harder than it needs to be.Overall though, great game. _childDocuments_.review: This was a very visually striking and enjoyable Metroidvania. It has it's quirks, both positive and negative, but overall a good game. The pros and cons as I found them are listed below;Pros:+ Good soundtrack, never found myself thinking that the soundtrack was boring or repetitive.+ Good mobility, as the movement in and out of combat feels snappy and responsive.+ Satisfying progression, as every upgrade you get makes every previous area more navigable and unlocks secrets that were previously unattainable.+ Collect-a-thon side-quests, which give the game a nice amount of padding that doesn't feel like a waste. + Lots of secrets and references, very rich background designs and NPCs which go to give the game a lot of brownie points for indie game enjoyers who take time to look around each playable area.+ Amazing art style, easily one of the most interesting and enjoyable looking metroidvania's I've played in a while. The art strikes an amazing balance between grime, horror and a teenage girls sketchbook.Personal Gripes:= Progression is very satisfying, but also incredibly slow. = Some enemy types are too easy/too difficult to fight depending on the area of the game you're in, with some late game enemies feeling incredibly simple to fight.= The parry mechanic is nigh useless against most bosses past the first 3.= There are a lot of bugs, both with progression and game-play. These are being patched out, but at the time of this review, the game is almost impossible to 100% on Steam due to achievement markers being placed incorrectly.= The weapons outside of the Gauntlet and Stratocaster seem quite under-tuned and borderline useless outside of progression. I never found myself using the gun outside of doors that require it's use to open them, and I feel as though the map isn't level enough to meaningfully use the Nitro Bunny for navigation.= Some people really don't like the humor in this game, as they say it's trying to hard to be edgy. I didn't mind it that much, as I think the games campy and off-putting dialogue fits the universe pretty well.Cons:- Simple combat. Most enemies in the game (with the exception of ONE SINGLE ENEMY TYPE) can be killed by doing nothing but basic attacks. And for this one enemy, the game references the fact (in universe with dialogue) that this is the only enemy type in the game that requires a unique action to be done to kill it. It came off as a bit tone deaf from the developers in my opinion.- Stage hazards. I know that this is a staple of the genre, but some of the rooms in this game are incredibly frustrating or boring to play through. Many rooms in the latter half of the game (Specifically the Mines and Golden Tower areas) are nothing but slow moving platforms and spikes. This wouldn't be an issue, but the hit-boxes on some of these stage hazards feel incredibly strict to avoid, making some of the platforming feel much less intuitive than it should be. There is also a big issue with being hit by an enemy that knocks you down and Cherry's hit-box barely touching a stage hazard, leading to either instant death or insane amounts of damage for failing to avoid a single attack.- Inconsistent level design. I can applaud this game for how unique each stage feels to play, however 2 of the areas are a SLOG to get through, especially if you're going for the 100%. The Denzel Factory and the Pnuema Chamber are incredibly large levels with only 1 and 2 fast travel points respectively. This wouldn't be an issue, but these areas also have the LEAST amount of shortcuts and the longest amounts of backtracking of all of the playable areas. It leaves a sour taste in my mouth as the other areas of the game feel just fine to explore and revisit! But these 2 areas made getting the 100% feel more like a chore than a fun sidequest.- Lack of voice acting. This struck me as very strange, as the first act of the game is all voice acted! But as soon as you finish the first quest, there is not a bit of voice acting for the rest of the game. I understand that it can be expensive and difficult, especially for an indie developer, to retain a VA crew for an entire game. But it takes away a lot of personality from the game as we only know what 3 of the characters sound like, and are left to guess for the rest of the cast. And finally, my biggest issue with the game: The final chapter. I'm not going to spoil the ending, as the story is fun while pretty basic. My issue comes from the room before you fight the final boss. There is an elevator that takes you to the top floor of the final area, and this elevator takes about a full minute to reach the top floor. This wouldn't be an issue, and is a pretty funny gag as you await the final boss with elevator music playing. The issue is if you die in the room next to the elevator, or go back to look for secrets and fall: The elevator ALWAYS takes a full minute, regardless of the direction it's going. This was so incredibly boring and frustrating to go through, as it just wastes an INSANE amount of time for a single gag that is only funny the first time and even then, barely so.All in all, I'd give Cookie Cutter a solid 6.5 out of 10. Very cool game visually, didn't mind the humor as much as some other people did. If this game got a couple of QoL patches and bug fixes, it would be up to a 7.5. I think the combat is a bit too basic, especially when compared to it's contemporaries. The game is quite easy, with most of the difficulty being in the platforming and exploring, but I don't mind that as it's quite refreshing in this genre to have a simple, fun game that doesn't take itself too seriously. Very much worth it on sale, if you really like the art style, buy it at full price.TLDR; Cool game with overly basic combat and a lot of QoL issues, but would be quite good with a couple of bug fix patches. The comedy isn't for everyone, and the story is quite simple, but the visual style is amazing and vibrant.

_childDocuments_.review: A real passion project of the game. The animation is weird and gross in the best way, starting strong with a grotesque "walk" cycle in the short prologue and continuing with strength from there. Combat is fast and aggressive, with enemies able to take big chunks of your health away but also being susceptible to juggle combos and wide attacks that can cut through whole crowds in one go. There's a focus on executing low health enemies, giving you both recharge of health and energy as well as a unique finisher for every type of foe.There's a bit of interesting world building to go alongside a reasonably simple story that sets up a potential sequel, and the game world was both fun to explore and offered up the occasional bit of tricky platforming. The main downsides are that the ending feels slightly abrupt and there's a touch of jank to the game, but nothing deal breaking. If you like the art style then it's a strong recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDRA seriously underrated game - you don't get one like this every three days - with a bit of metroidvania, but mostly good, fluid, fast, FUN! As Dmc comes from fighting games, the inspiration is felt here: combos, aggressiveness and reflexes are rewarded, and juggling enemies is a basic mechanic in this game. And it's quickly apparent: the art direction kicks ass, the characters the enemies the levels the weapons and the finishes are pushed to the limit, full of detail - each new adversary, even the swap color, is a pleasure just to see executed!In any case, it's a big yes, not a metroidvania, but a fun, nerve-racking Beat'em up that, despite a few shortcomings, remains accessible and easy enough, while being sufficiently challenging to renew yourself for the duration of a run.Btw flemme de refaire en français, j'ai les com' d'ouverts pour en discuter, y'a plein de trucs à dire dessus et c'est un vrai coup de coeur !

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried to like cookie cutter, and I can't give it a negative review. This is a clear case of "It's not you, it's me." The game looks gorgeous, and pulling off over the top finishing moves is fun. (About the first 20 times per enemy. Then it gets old.) But really my biggest gripe, getting back to me being the problem is: the game is hard for me. Ironic, coming from the og NES generation. I get that there is a demographic that loves that, and may even find the game too easy. But I am not part of that demographic. I'm old, have terrible reflexes, and do not enjoy dying 10 times in a row. My patience to learn (let alone master) a game system is limited. Which is my gatekeeper with cookie cutter.The parry system absolutely needs to be mastered, or you will have a bad time. (Either by constantly dying or upercutting the same enemy for a percieved eternity.)After almost 5 hours playing, it still does not work for me, making combat that is clearly designed around parrying frustrating for me. And judging by the achievement percentage I am not alone. You get an achievement for using one of your early upgrades (air dash) that only around 31% of players got at the time of writing. You can't progress without getting that achievement. This means that a lot of folks are nope-ing out of this game pretty early.Wait, maybe the problem isn't just me. Da*n you, cookie cutter for kickstarting my midlife crisis!Anyway, these accessibility issues are a real shame, because the world is fun and interesting, and full of eastereggs from Battletoads to Monkey Island. Cookie Cutter is a clear labor of love. An easy mode for the filthy casuals like me would have done wonders here.So while cookie cutter isn't for me, if you enjoy your games harder, you will probably love it. Just know what you're getting into.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is irreverent, violent, crass, a bit childish and I love every second of it. That’s your warning. I was originally going to call it uncultured too, but Cookie Cutter pays too much respect to its forebears for me to even joke about it. Everywhere you look, you’ll find references to NoFX albums or portraits of Not-Alucard, homages to the Metroidvanias and punk rock that inspired it - and none of it feels intrusive. If you didn’t recognize them, they just add to the awesome aesthetic of this game.Which is honestly my favorite thing about this game. I’ll get to the gameplay and story in due time, but where this game really shines is in its aesthetic. They had a vision, and it comes across so clearly. The grime and grossness, and the violence. Oh, boy, the VIOLENCE. This game has so much fun with its violence. Each frame of the brutalization animations are lovingly crafted to be equal parts gruesome and hysterical. I think my favorite is the one where she spiral-screws a collar on a monster so tight its head pops like a balloon. They’re so fast and flashy it can be hard to see the entire process, but they’re lovely. It was these animations that got me interested in the first place, and then seeing them in the context of this world made them that much better. The basic game is pretty fun puzzles without being impossible and the combat is fast paced and frenetic, both of which feel appropriate. Cherry is a character who has little patience for…well, anything, so it feels appropriate that none of the puzzles were ever too hard for me to figure out. That said, actually completing them was another matter entirely - that’s where the game’s challenge is. Figuring out what you got to do to get the Hyperdrive Void Power when you find it is easy enough - but you will be spending a hefty amount of time trying to physically do it. And for the most part, the game is really good at keeping its flow. The checkpoints are positioned in a way that you’re never too far from whatever it was that killed you, meaning that when you fail a challenge it’s usually a simple matter to hop right back into it, so you rarely get frustrated. The only place that bothered me was the Crystal Pits, but I almost feel like it was the intent that the Crystal Pits be extremely unpleasant - even more so than the Final Area. The Golden Tower is supposed to be a paradise maintained by a subjugated working class, while the Crystal Pit is an old abandoned mineshaft that is now swarming with hostile creatures. It feels appropriate, is what I’m saying. And that’s not to say the Golden Tower isn’t worthy of the final stretch, its difficulty is greater just…less frustrating? I’m getting side tracked. The point is the gameplay is fun and fast paced, and usually unfrustrating. Combat has a variety of options so there’s always new ways to fight enemies that are giving you a hard time. Timing is key, as is the balance between building and using void, and what you use it for. Do you save it to sneak in a heal? Or do you use it on a Void Power to kill enemies before they have the chance to do that damage in the first place? Good stuff!  I have two complaints, and both are pretty minor. The first one’s glitches. The game bugged out now and then. Nothing ever too game breaking - the checkpoint kept the time I glitched through a wall into a screaming purple void from losing me much, if any, progress - but definitely ones that make the game look…unfinished. At one point when I died I was respawned at a checkpoint I hadn’t ever been to. Thankfully, it was the next checkpoint I was likely to encounter but it was still weird. The game also didn’t record my destruction of the Chatter Bots in the Golden Tower or in the Diesel Swamp’s Nitrobunny course, even though I definitely did kill them, more than once. Also, either the thing from Poopah’s toilet is missable, or it bugs out if you forget about it too long after saying no.My only other complaint with the game is that it can sometimes be too irreverent. Which isn’t the sort of complaint you normally hear from me but here’s an example. There’s a part in the game where you run into Foby Tox, an obvious play on the Undertale creator. The guy wants to make friends with the wild monsters of the MegaStructure and shortly after you finish his side quest you find his dead mutilated body outside in the wilds and Cherry makes a joke about the monsters not having a spare option. This…would be absolutely hilarious, if it weren’t for the fact that this syncs up a bit too well with criticisms leveled at the game’s philosophy of non-violence. The kind that took the core thesis of “be kind” and reduced it to “lawal but what if someone is a Bad Guy, then you’ll just suffer and be taken advantage of” and ignore the fact that the game does in fact address that. It felt disrespectful to the work Toby did to make a joke like this, and it doesn’t feel like the creators actually believe that, just that they thought it would be funny to contrast their actual kill-or-be-killed world with the one in Undertale. Like they didn’t think it through all the way and just wanted to be crass. But then, that’s the point isn’t it? I don’t get to complain about how this particular thing in the game didn’t sit right with me when the rest of the game is committing warcrimes. The amount of “offensive” stuff in this game is ridiculous. I’m pretty sure every main character’s name is a NSFW joke and the only reason I’m not committed to that statement is that my ace brain doesn’t know that many of them. One of the downsides of an “offend everyone” mindset is that you will, eventually, offend everyone. They could’ve thought some of their crassness through better but the game would take longer than the universe has existed to come out. There’s no deep secret message here. The game touches on a few themes about love, grief and duty, but it is not here to be Shakespeare. It’s here to be a fun, violent, crass hell of a good time and in this endeavor, it succeeds. The game ends pretty solidly pointing to a second one so I hope to play it. If you can handle the game’s attitude and spunk, and you love Metroidvanias, you’ll love it. If you love hyper violent robots on a rampage of revenge for their lover and creator killing their enemies by spiking them to death with a mohawk of raw energy you’ll love it. If you don’t think you can handle that, steer clear.

_childDocuments_.review: NOTE TO DEVELOPER: I initially played this on the Lenovo Legion Go. I had a TON of save issues where the teleport save would freeze in this pink bloom when accessing the teleport that would require restart. Some areas I couldn't leave at all because it was freezing every single time. I updated drivers, waiting for your big update, no improvement. I almost gave this a thumbs down after reading some others had the issue but when I switched to Steamdeck or desktop no issues at all.  Maybe its the 7840u chipset. In any case try yto address it so a glitch doesn't  ruin your reviews.  Overall great work. Also, why did ur update turn off bootup audio during ur logo screens and the thunderclap audio when using teleport?  I missed those after the update.REVIEW: 7.5/10 graphics: 8/10mood/ style: 9/10art design: 6/10 (but only for samey backgrounds otherwise 8/10 if not for lack of variety)level combat: 7/10boss combat: 8/10 and very fairplatforming: 8/10  precise and at rare times more precision demanding than fun but very fairBeat the game. Awesome art. Nice feel and vibe that you u won't see in any other game I'm aware of. Many other reviewers say the levels feel samey and I hate to admit I felt the same. I really liked the game but a metroidvania has to have a feel of discovering vast areas with different vibes that evoke wonder and mystery.  Too many places just look subterranean and need set piece background that immediately tell you where you are and why this area is different.  Like the Diesel Lagoon has no lagoon or body of oil or oil anything really except some pipes, but it has this cool oil spill coloration in places that I loved, just give me an oil lake in the background or something. Blasphemous  had a level inside a giant bell and you collapse it and the level shifts. The foreground has nothing bell related really but you never forget the scale of that massive bell. It makes u ask "wtf happened here?".The parry is broken, even after an update and it should be fixed or removed.  Is it that hard to fix? I found it uselessly unreliable but enjoyed the game pretending it wasn't there. I saw another review that said the air dash should come sooner, I couldn't agree more. Give me air dash and double jump early to improve the combat. I loved the combat once movement opened up.  I felt battles were fair. Boss battles had clear but quick telegraphs for their moves that you had to learn but usually kicked ur ass initially.  U can't spam ur way through bosses. Never thought bosses or platforming was unfair even when challenging. I will say there were some short tedious platforming sections that made me better in combat when I realized I could string movement together that way.  There's a few basic puzzles, all of which I liked. I wan't using the psychic punch right until a silly little puzzle forced me to see it. I almost wish there was some DLC or expert endgame to replay with everything unlocked cause once its wide open movement is really fun and well done.\Some have said other games do everything better.  I would argue none do it with this style and vibe and it has very few weaknesses apart from the parry that you don't need. I'd say if the art seems to appeal to you you'll enjoy it.  I really did.  I'd ask the developers to address the parry, and open up the air dash and double jump earlier and make sure saves are never an issue and this will be more accessible to the people who try it.  I'm hoping for a sequel.

_childDocuments_.review: It is mostly good. got it in a humble bundleIf you told me this was an early access I would believe you.the game somehow feels unfinished(not due to its length to be clear. ending notwithstanding)weird theming in the story.(also somewhat light on the story as well) but kind of humorous. The game play is interesting but kind of unintuitive at times. At least for me it felt like at any stage of the game's progression there was always an optimal way to handle combat and that a lot of the options were either not great or lacked opportunities to shine. I like the animation style but as a person with a MASSIVE flicker fusion threshold combat can sometimes feel like a flip book and I found myself needing to learn the enemy patterns and feeling out combat rather than actually watching what the enemies are doing and reacting. (long nitpick short, I wish the animations had more frames.) Also the game is kind of zoomed out which I appreciated at times(mostly platforming) but sometimes made combat during the traversal part of the game hard to execute with fines. Even when you get good at the game it sort of does not feel like it. I am not looking to be overpowered or anything, I reached a point where the game felt easy but I felt a lack of control and deliberateness due to everything I mentioned above. Also having a dialog volume option after the opening scene confused me as there seemed to be no voice acting after the beginning of the game(was this a glitch?)Some things feel super hard to find. This would not bother me so much if the name of the game did not make researching anything about it difficult. It is way worse than when I was playing control. It was mostly a problem because on a couple of puzzles I could not tell if I was just not good enough or if I was missing abilities that would make it impossible to complete some challenges. Additionally there is a weird bug right now on handhelds that use the 7840U/Z1 extreme that causes the game to glitch out and go completely purple on teleporters but only sometimes and it can ♥♥♥♥ up the flow of the game. part way through I just had to resign myself to the fact I could not play it on my portables. Also sometimes some of my map exploration would be reset which would make trying to collect everything or solve the overarching puzzle that is a metroidvania more tedious. I think it takes some interesting risks and tries to iterate but it is hard to ignore the feeling that the game was not out of early access.(this is not helped by the ending) anyway I give this punk scifi sapphic holoknight like game an A for style, effort and vision but a c for execution. All the 2d art seemed like a labor of love. however It can be hard at times to tell what is the result of bad design decisions and what is the result of a failure to execute(whatever the cause of that failure might be; time, resources etc.)My next thought is more an expression of how the game made me feel than an actual educated supposition about the games development. The background art and references were cute/amusing but after a point I started to worry if the team might(baseless speculation) have allocated their focus inefficiently when making this game given the state of some of its elements. My review might sound harsh for a positive one but I am mostly trying to express how I feel like the game was enjoyable to me but can see so many ways I think it could improve(mostly in execution).

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever seen the movie Heavy Metal? It's an anthology film comprised of a violent, schlocky animated scifi/fantasy shorts that is more about putting weird, cool, and gross stuff on the screen than telling any kind of coherent story. Like Disney's Fantasia but with bewbs and guts and a soundtrack of the music your Boomer dad listened to rather than classical symphony. That's basically Cookie Cutter- a game that feels like a scrapped adult animation concept that was repurposed into a metroidvania. It drips with visual style. It's a very decent metrodvania, and one that I totally understand why it will be absolutely loved by many.Yet I do not. I don't hate it, but after spending close to five hours with it, I can tell that it is meant to be played in a way that I simply don't like playing. Cookie Cutter is a combat-focused metroidvania. Cherry, the player character, navigates the maze-like environs of a cyber-punk dystopia fighting mutants and insane robots along the way. A lot of them. I don't think I have seen a metroidvania map this packed with enemies before. You start out with a power glove to deliver a flurry of kicks and punches. Even with this single starting weapon, you actually have a lot of moves available. From here you pummel the enemies into submission and if you wear them down enough, you can execute an over the top, gory finisher that makes them explode into coins, health, and loot.Here is where the problems for me start. Cherry's basic attack might throw the enemies around like ragdolls but the damage output is like if your grandma took up prize-fighting at the retirement home. She hits like a limp noodle, and it takes forever to wear down these damage sponges. It's clear the devs really wanted you to have to use all the cool moves in the arsenal, and they wanted you to use the parry system, as that almost always results in breaking them down to the point you can unleash the execution super moves. I hate parrying, in this game and any game. I actively avoid any game where parrying is mandatory rather than something that will make your life easier in certain circumstances. I am a dedicated member of the the Dodge Roll Lovers club. I cannot seem to get the timing right, and that makes combat pretty miserable. I did find that you can solve the problem somewhat because the zones are full of traps: lasers, furnaces, electric floors and ceilings, and inexplicably placed buzz-saws. Just throw them into a trap and Bob's your uncle. But you can't always depend on traps because not every room has them, and eventually you will run into kill-box rooms where you get sealed in and have to battles waves of enemies before you can proceed. I'm in the mid-game, and I can already see the enemy hordes on the map getting tougher, denser, faster, and even spongier. Since I don't really like the combat system, and I can already see that there is just going to be increasingly more of it as the game wears on. I guess I could push on to the end, as it is a decent metroidvania at it's core, but it's a game I can already tell I will like less and less the deeper I get into it. And the bosses are not very good either from a visual design or fight-quality standpoint which surprised me considering how this game focuses on combat and style.
