_childDocuments_.review: Arzette serves as a tongue-in-cheek homage to the old CDI era of games. However, it ventured too close to the sun, replicating flawed mechanics and design choices instead of properly refining them. This approach resulted in a lackluster experience that feels too simplistic for its good and lacking in redeeming qualities. However, for those seeking a niche nostalgia trip, the game's quirky visuals and cutscenes might hold some appeal despite the janky gameplay. A decade of peace in Faramore is shattered with the return of the malevolent Daimur, threatening the kingdom's very existence. Princess Arzette, blessed with unique powers from her lineage, emerges as the kingdom's hope. She sets out on a perilous journey through varied landscapes, encountering relentless challenges as she moves towards confronting Daimur and restoring peace. The narrative is incredibly cliché, leading to a forgettable and underwhelming story. However, its few redeeming qualities come from the diverse array of characters encountered and interacted with along the way. These moments significantly enhance the story's appeal through their distinct and enjoyable interactions. The gameplay is disappointingly barebones, consisting of bland platforming, one-dimensional combat mechanics, and a series of unengaging minigames scattered throughout the experience. Despite gradually introducing new abilities, unfortunately, the gameplay quickly becomes repetitive, lacking the necessary variety to stand out.The combat is dreadfully dull, with such simplicity that one can mindlessly button-mash through encounters without any need for strategy or logic, especially considering the lack of enemy type, most of which have the same attack pattern. You have two offensive buttons: you can either attack with your sword or gun, that's it. Additionally, you have a shield that reflects all enemy projectiles with no cooldown, making the enemies, heck, even bosses, trivial challenges. As you progress, you unlock items and skills, but they ultimately have minimal impact on combat, primarily affecting exploration.  The platforming is, at best, adequate. It suffers from being overly simplistic, which hampers its potential for engaging movement; it first becomes passable once you acquire the double jump, where the experience takes a considerable turn for the better, albeit too late. Despite these shortcomings, surprisingly, the highlight still is its exploration; this is due to the charisma of the characters you encounter along the way, each interaction feeling refreshingly unique.  Despite its prevalence, backtracking is surprisingly enjoyable. The accessibility of the map, coupled with some quality-of-life additions and the gradual acquisition of items that aid you in unlocking access to new content, ensure that revisiting areas remains engaging, especially considering the levels themselves are well designed. Every return trip serves a purpose, whether it's uncovering hidden secrets, fulfilling quests, or exploring previously unreachable regions to progress your journey. This depth and intrigue add layers to the world.Once you've completed the story, the content doesn't quite come to an end. You have a couple of options to extend your experience: Collect the remaining collectibles and complete the various minigames, or try the more demanding Hero mode difficulty, which presents tougher enemies and eliminates health drops, or for those who somehow enjoyed the boss fights, there's a boss rush mode, which pits you against a series of bosses without the need of going through levels.  The visuals suffer from conflicting styles, resulting in jarring transitions between the two aesthetics; the cutscenes and character sprites perfectly capture the essence of the CDI-era whimsy and pixel aesthetics, paying a fitting tribute to its goofiness and retro charm, and is incredibly amusing seeing their quirky liveliness. Whereas the backgrounds clash with a more drawn aesthetic that feels at times blurred or smoothed out as opposed to the hard outlines the sprites and UI have. The sound effects and soundtrack effectively tap into nostalgic essence and seamlessly integrate with the fantasy setting, leaving an impactful initial impression. However, they quickly become repetitive, lacking diversity and standout tracks. The voice acting is notably unique due to intentionally being bad but in a silly yet charming, over-the-top way. It may not appeal to everyone, but I found the peculiar dialogue and execution quite enjoyable. It strikes a balance between being fun to listen to without becoming annoying or boring.
_childDocuments_.name: Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore

_childDocuments_.review: Arzette took what the 2D Legend of Zelda games on the catastrophic failure that was the Philips CDI did wrong (And Hotel Mario as a bonus!), and did them very well. Sure, it isn't a perfect game. I thought that some of the backtracking could be tedious, but I almost feel as if most of this games shortcomings add to the charm. For instance, all of the bosses are complete pushovers, much like in the CDI games. You can literally defeat the final boss in seconds if you traverse right (If you are fully upgraded, that is!)Getting the Blue magic felt like it came a bit too late, but other than that, the progression was quite good. Much like those CDI games, easily the best part is the music. Legit, very well composed, very well put together, and fits the game very well. I thought it was great, even at it's worst! I would love to get this OST as a DLC for the game.Of course, though, the main draw of the game is the cut-scenes. Everyone knows the OGs, everyone loves them, and to this day, I see memes which have "Dinner" and every single Morshu quote in them. This game, once again, doesn't quite reach the heights of the Zelda CDI games, but if you were expecting that, All I can say is that lightening is hard to capture in a bottle once: CDI games managed to do it 3 times if you include Hotel Mario. The cut-scenes are nearly as good, and I really enjoyed watching them. They were awkward, uncanny, and funny as hell.The gameplay itself is very fun. It controls well, almost like playing as Zero in the Megaman X/Zero games. It's a simple metroidvania, filled with collectables and backtracking. I really enjoyed going back and collecting all of the items, which made a game that started out reletively tricky, into one that was a breeze.Overall, would recommend if you haven't played it yet! There is more to this than the cut-scenes, which is much better than Zelda CDI to boot!So please, take your time and buy this game!Wait, you don't have 20 bucks?

_childDocuments_.review: NO, you do not need to know anything about CD-i Zelda or anything Nintendo-related to play this game. While it is a spiritual successor to Faces of Evil / Wand of Gamelon, it takes place in its own world with its own characters. Doing some fun research adds to the experience since you're able to recognize motifs, but it is a separate story entirely and you won't miss anything if you play it without research.On its own, it's a fun and simple Metroidvania with hilarious over-the-top cutscenes and electronic music set up in graphics which resemble a 32-bit system. As you explore with a simple jump and a sword, you will eventually find upgrades for your weapon as well as upgrades to break open certain areas and finding secrets. Backtracking levels is REQUIRED for progression, though certain cutscenes and extra areas may open up when visiting older levels. It is a game for any skill-level, and the game even features a casual mode which gives the player health drops as well as weaker enemies. There is also a Hero Mode, a harder mode for expert players who beat the game on Classic.As far as the gameplay is concerned, it's fun enough, but it's nothing to write home about. It's fun to play and maybe beat for 4 to 5 hours, but nothing concerning gameplay is innovative in any way as ideas found in this game are found elsewhere. The best parts of the game are the colorful painting-style graphics, the catchy music, and the cartoon cutscenes, which are my absolute favorite part of the game. They're something akin to a Saturday Morning cartoon: they're in-your-face, over the top, and hilariously corny. It is a clear parody of media in the 90s marketed for kids and younger teens, as what was rampant back then is now something for us to mock and laugh at today. See for yourself in the trailer, and if that is something you see yourself enjoying, this game could be an instant purchase for you, as the purchase of this game also supports the artists. Other than that, it's great for Steam deck and you can even buy it digitally on Nintendo Switch.The choice is yours if you feel this purchase warrants $20, but if you're still unsure, wishlist the game and wait for a sale. If you feel that you have enough money to spend, might I suggest going to Limited Run Game's website, as they offer a physical edition ($35) as well as a collector's edition ($90) with artwork, a physical CD of the soundtrack, and a faux-controller straight from the system it was inspired from. The developer name "Dopply" may be familiar to you. Or maybe it isn't, I'm not you. Regardless, he remastered the Zelda: Wand of Gamelon and Faces of Evil sometime in 2020 for Gamemaker Studios. It was a game which took a lot of the problems the original games had and made it much smoother. This included loadtimes, the ability to pick up items without swinging your sword, and faster movement speed. Why would anyone do that? Because as awful as these games were, they had many great ideas. Two of which we would never see again, the first being that it was a mainline Legend of Zelda platformer. Zelda II was the first and only time Nintendo themselves took this venture. The other is that it was the only other mainline Zelda game (besides Spirit Tracks) in which we would get the chance to play as Zelda. For many people, it was a lot more fun seeing the roles reversed, where you are the princess off to save the kingdom.Dopply later founded the development team Seedy-Eye (lol) Software to create a spiritual successor to those games with its own world, characters, and levels. It also features completely original artists and voice actors from different backgrounds to create the cutscenes. You might even recognize a few of them. I'm happy to say that a lot of it holds up and carries over, even if it's all for the sake of parody. The writing feels like you would expect from a Zelda CD-i game, from the shopkeeper going "These wares aren't elsewhere!" to the guard girl going "It's a nice surprise, if you have the supplies!" or even the strong and buff bartender saying he is frail and weak and needs a strong, muscular hero to find object for him (all that while he's FLEXING).If you enjoy the music and the graphics of the original games like I have, these ones hold up just as well. The graphics are an excellent blend of spritework and painted backgrounds. The best part is you will never be confused of where to go next or what to jump on because the game is actually well designed: anything that you may jump on clearly pops out and uses different colors. You are also not required to press up to jump, though that mode may be turned on if you wish.The music is EXCELLENT. It is reminiscent of the smooth electronica music that the original game uses but does not feel nearly chaotic and has a musical direction for each level. If you're one of those people that loves to put the Zelda CD-i music on in the background as I did, then I would highly recommend visiting the game's Bandcamp and purchasing the soundtrack.There's a lot more control to this game than you might think. While you can play with a keyboard, I highly recommend playing on a controller with a centered d-pad like a Dualshock controller or an 8-BitDo Pro controller. You will be using all of the face buttons as well as the shoulder buttons to play, as this game features dedicated buttons for certain items. It goes without saying that the gameplay is much more polished than its inspiration. However, there may be some situations in which enemies turn around too soon, or jumps may be a bit too far, and it is somewhat frustrating to not be able to jump high enough without a double jump. These are minor complaints, and they don't impede progress in any way. You could very easily beat this game at any skill level.So far, this is the quintessential CD-i game. There are tons of inside jokes to the original games as well as other games like Hotel Mario. Yes, the tutorial does teach you how to duckwalk, and yes, there is a shopkeeper just like Morshu. There are tons of motifs and injokes that you'll definitely get, but I won't spoil them. If any of this sounds interesting, I highly recommend purchasing this game. And yes, you can even purchase this on Nintendo Switch of all things if that's more convenient. You can even purchase a physical copy on Limited Run's website ($35), or even a Collector's Edition box set with tons of artwork, a world map poster, an audio CD, and even a CD-i remote controller. It's obviously not practical to use, but it is fully functional and looks great on a shelf. The whole collection is $90.

_childDocuments_.review: "Arzette - The Jewel of Faramore" is a faithful reimagining of the atrociously bad Zelda CD-i Games "Wand of Gamelon" and "Faces of Evil" that received cult-status for their unplayableness and the wacky character-interaction-animations. You play the spellsword-princess Arzette on her quest to defeat the demon-lord Daimur (again), traversing the different locations that present themselves in the typical CD-i "hand-drawn" style, changing levels via a nice-looking overworld, slashing derpy foes, collecting rubies and items and talking to various oddballs. Objectively it is just a decent sidescrolling action-adventure with metroidvania-style gameplay and with a lot of fetch quests and backtracking, that has weird item-usage limits and a slippery power-curve and can be leisurely 100% in around 4-5 h.But it is (as you have guessed) more about the homage: While I never played the originals I am well aware of their uncannyness and the developers of "Arzette" really embraced this - the combat, while modernised and well executable, feels intentionally sloppy sometimes, spritework is cohesive, but also off, bosses are not killabe in one hit, but are laughable nonetheless. They wanted to make an enjoyable game that is as "bad" as its roots. And they did quite well. While the characters and their interaction-animation may not be as memorable as in the originals, they nonetheless pulled off a great job: Everyone seems charmingly demented and the voice acting adds a lot to it. Music is also funky! They even managed to bring a serious tone in all the goofyness around halfway in the game, which I did not expect.Sadly there a few scenes where you can see that they used a 3D-model and animated over them (the beacons and the second scene in the palace), they feel out of place and not in a good way.Overall "Arzette" is a great "bad" title, that is not just a meme-experience, but also has a lot of heart! Go for it, if you are not pulled off by the price tag (which I find reasonable enough)!

_childDocuments_.review: A little history to kick off this review: I have history with Youtube Poop. I spent all of my high school years and a small chunk of my college years watching, enjoying, or being involved with YTP in some capacity. It wasn't a perfect community, but I still hold those memories near and dear to my heart, and it wouldn't surprise me if I know/knew a lot of folks listed in the credits. (And if any of those old acquaintances end up reading this, I hope you're all living your best lives! :U )But when I say "Arzette is good", I mean that even beyond my own bias. Because while Arzette is a wonderful tribute to its interactive animated inspirations, it's also just a really good, solid, fun-to-play game in general. You can tell right from the start that this is a labor of love, and I can't stress enough how strongly that shines through in the final product. It looks great, sounds great, plays great, and is just the right length to make replaying it feel completely natural, even if you aren't the type of person to do multiple back-to-back runs of a game.First off: visually, the game is fantastic. The painterly maps and backgrounds all look distinct and full of little touches, but it's also balanced and drawn in a way that makes the platforming easy to parse. It's not very often that you go "wait, is this a platform or...?", and the few times it does happen, it's in safe areas that won't punish you for making sure. The spritework is also richly-detailed, and that does a lot to elevate the whole experience. Weird of a comparison as it is, it reminded me of playing Rayman, where characters and enemies alike are full of personality.Next: there's a lot of stuff to do here. Much like its inspirations, Arzette's world is very "Metroid-vania"-like, with a lot of visiting and revisiting, finding new items or abilities as you go. If you want to blitz through the game lickety-split, then you can certainly do that (and there's even certain tricks to make doing so easier!). But if you want to take your time and just vibe in the world, there's a lot of goodies and things to hunt for. Some of them are pretty well-hidden, but most areas have some small environmental hint to clue you in - and the few areas that don't are usually easy enough to find via your own intuition. (Pro-Tip: make sure you put that duck-walk to good use!)Lastly: all the animated sequences are, of course, wonderful. They're goofy, whimsical, sometimes bizarre, but it's all played in a straightforward, earnest manner - just like the game's inspirations. It's weird, but it's not riffing on itself, nor is it deliberately playing itself up. The weirdness is simply one small part of the charm. It's a fun little world with a fun little cast of characters, and it feels like an old Saturday morning cartoon come to life.Arzette is just... fun. It's good, earnest, wholehearted fun. It doesn't overstay its welcome, but it's also got enough stuff on offer to keep you occupied and satisfied. It takes what Faces of Evil and Wand of Gamelon did, expands on what those games did right, and shores up the areas that those games faltered in. And, in fact, I think I might very well go right now and play it through again!

_childDocuments_.review: I had a look through the other negative reviews to see if my main problem was addressed, and it wasn't, so here's my general impressions.Arzette does what it says on the tin, it plays like if a CDI game controlled well. This does unfortunately mean the game plays kinda basic, but that's not necessarily a bad thing.Cutscenes are the same sort of CDI jank you expect, voice work is good and "accurate" to what they're trying to emulate.Some cutscenes are rotoscoped 3D models which don't look very good, but I appreciate animation is very time consuming.Music is good, not very CDI, but pretty catchy. Reused music for a couple of stages which is disappointing.My biggest problem however is in the progression, unless you have photographic memory and remember exactly which one of 3 colours the progression-barriers are, you'll be playing the same levels from the start over and over looking for one place to try and progress.Levels are supposedly marked with a red "!" to show points of interest, but I had these show up maybe 3 times in my time with the game. Is this a bug? Who knows, because I was still progressing and unlocked almost all the areas. Either way, I could have done with a lot more signposting mainly because it's not fun playing the same easy levels over and over just trying to find the one place I need to go to progress the game.You could say "but the Zelda CDI games were like that!", but isn't this supposed to be "CDI game but good"?It fixes a lot of problems the Zelda CDI games had, but other aspects of their design were not looked at with enough scrutiny and feel like they're this way just because the old games were this way. The gameplay wasn't the only problem of the old CDI games.A sad thumbs down from me. I tried to really like it, and did for at least half my playtime, but it is so close to the source material it'd be akin to recommending people play CDI games. Which nobody should ever do.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic love-letter to the ill-remembered The Legend of Zelda CDI games. I just finished this game with 100% completion just a short while ago, and I couldn't begin to say how awesome this game is. This game corrects everything that was wrong with the Zelda CDI games, and adds its own flair, and personality to its overarching storyline. The game isn't particularly long, and it isn't very difficult either on its base difficulty level, but the overall quality of the entire game is both nostalgic and feels fresh at the same time. _childDocuments_.review: The weirdest part about creating a spiritual successor to those old Zelda Cdi games is that nobody actually played them. The Wand of Gamelon and The Faces of Evil explicitly were not classics, that’s the whole bit. They’re goofy software locked to goofier hardware, and what little spot they take up in the video game zeitgeist is owed to memes, not their actual content.Enter Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore; a 2D adventure platformer with that same expressive memey style but with substance that can satisfy more than just a cutaway in a YouTube video. Arzette infuses its platforming missions with heavy backtracking and powerful unlocks—almost like a metroidvania without the interconnected world. It doesn’t quite stick its landing: the campaign ends on a deflatingly short final boss, but otherwise Arzette delivers absurdist fun in a breezy retro package.Publisher Limited Run Games and developer “Seedy Eye Software” (pronounced C. D. I.) are early clues into the kind of experience that’s in store for you. Even if you don’t splurge on the boutique physical collectors versions, Arzette is still a game that worships retro hardware. On startup you get Seedy Eye’s production logo animation which is disk insertion into a fake console.Once you actually start playing it feels so effortlessly old. It recreates so many gaming sensations that would otherwise feel like antiquity if it didn’t pull them together so well. You harshly transition between movement and combat states: weapon swings bring you to a complete stop rather than giving you a little nudge forward as has become the industry standard.All conversations with Arzettes memorable cast of characters are initiated by hitting them with your sword, which suddenly drops the background music channel before bringing in the dialogue.It’s more than just a fun visual novelty, too. You’ll need to reach back to folds you haven’t used in a while and remember how to do those weird little hop-attacks at the edge of an enemies hit box to offset your lack of mid-swing mobility. You’ll also find a lot of success in cheesing their simple left and right movements on whatever platform they’re locked on and peppering them with ranged attacks from safety.It all sells the illusion that you’re not just playing a throwback, but playing something that throwbacks are throwing back to. With one key exception: difficulty.Arzette is not a punishing game. Checkpoints are frequent, lives are infinite, and an average playthrough will only take three to four hours. It’s an enjoyable little journey that teleports all but the frustration from booting up a game from last century.It’s also a worthy homage to those old goofy CDi games as much as it is to Zelda more generally. You’ve got an evil porcine wizard trying to take over the land, magical triangular macguffins you gotta collect, and booting up the game actually starts its logo zoom out from the “Z E” in Arzette, subconsciously filling your gamer brain with the name “Zelda” before you’ve even touched the controller.The writing is self aware without going overboard. It's a pleasure interacting with every NPC and seeing what ridiculous way they will express themselves and finding out whatever task they will have for you.What’s surprising is how well Arzette nails an adventure fantasy in such a small and silly package. The elevator pitch makes it sound like it’s here to sell a vibe with the ‘game’ as an afterthought, but there’s more to it than that.On top of its simple and enjoyable combat, there’s a tangible progression system befitting Greek heroes and Hylians alike. Magical boots, protective cloaks, and enchanted swords are but a few of the unlocks you can expect. Some are mandatory, some are optional, but all make a significant impact on your traversal and combat.You weave in and out of levels via a menu but still need to take those mental notes of locks whose keys you don’t have yet. It gives that adventuring sensation but doesn’t let its reach exceed its grasp, and I found myself drawn to finding as many of these powers and extra hearts as I could.Maybe too many of them. By the time I got to the final boss it was over in seconds, with its challenge so invalidated that I didn’t get to experience all those wonderful mid-fight combat animations they built for the encounter. Otherwise the handful of boss battles that do exist are an enjoyable challenge that play with the absurdity of the character designs.Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore isn’t just an animation project in a gaming framework, but a worthwhile retro adventure in its own right. Its blend of snappy platforming levels combined with non-linear exploration give it meat without being too exhaustive. Its unmistakable style captures a phantom nostalgia for something I’ve never even played. Arzette may be based on a meme, but it certainly isn’t one.

_childDocuments_.review: If you've only heard about this game because of the memetic works that inspired it, you might be surprised to find it's a fairly competent, enjoyable, and charming (if a little short) side-scrolling Zelda-style game. Despite the aesthetic inspirations clearly being the CDi, the gameplay feels like a refinement of the best parts of NES Zelda 2 mixed with the slightest levels of intentional technical jank that facilitates some amount of sequence breaking and speedrunning. The music is really catchy, and you already know from the trailer if this style of cutscene and voice acting is for you or not. And if it is for you, it is *very* for you. I kinda freaking love this game. It didn't ask too much of me. It didn't outstay its welcome. It isn't a marvelous game, but there's really very few other titles to satisfyingly scratch the vibe and style itches that this game is designed for, and I will absolutely be picking up any followup games it has if they hold up to this as the baseline standard of quality.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a brilliant, well-made game, and a lot of fun!The controls are smooth and responsive, so it never feels frustrating to play. Whenever I died in the game it was only because I myself had misjudged a jump or mistimed an attack or something like that, so the difficulty almost always felt very fair.Speaking of difficulty, there is a good variety of difficulty settings here. Whether you want a more laid-back, easy-going casual experience, or a more intense and challenging experience, this game can provide it.Each level has a lot of places to go through and explore, but the levels are so well-designed that you never feel lost or confused about what you have to do.There is also a good variety of enemies. Each have creative, distinctive designs, and their strengths and attack patterns are different enough to stop the gameplay from ever getting monotonous or boring.I loved finding new items, both to move the story along and to help me get stronger/get new fun abilities. It felt very satisfying to gradually get stronger and learn new skills. There are also plenty of optional items, and optional side-quests, to keep the game interesting, and to keep completionists happy!The music is absolutely wonderful. It does a really good job at emulating the sound of the old Zelda CD-i games, and is also just really nice to listen to by itself. The tunes here are very varied, but all fun.And, of course, this is a very well-observed and very loving homage to the CD-i games, which is clearly made by people with a deep knowledge of these games and a great respect and reverence for them, and I really appreciate that. I've watched hilarious YouTube Poops and memes based on these games for years, and being able to play a game based on them, which is actually WELL-MADE and FUN TO PLAY - well, it's a dream come true!But as well as being a great, reference-filled homage, this game does a great job at telling its own compelling story and creating its own interesting world, with its own humour and its own characters. Even though everything is deliberately goofy and cheesy, I still ended up feeling a great amount of affection and connection to the characters and the story, even when I was laughing at them. This is a great testament to how much care, thought and sincerity the creators clearly put into this game, even though it's largely tongue-in-cheek.The only serious criticism I have is this - it is impossible to finish this game without finding a secret, hidden item. It's fine to hide away items if you don't strictly need them to beat the game and they just provide an extra advantage, but when you hide away items that you outright NEED, that seems a bit frustrating and unfair (Admittedly, I easily looked up where to find this secret item, but even so, I don't think it should have been hidden in the first place).Overall, this is a great game, a lot of fun and a very satisfying, light-hearted experience, as well as a homage that manages to be very loving and respectful of what it's paying homage to, while still being goofy and humourous. I hope that more games like this, in this series, will be made soon!

_childDocuments_.review: Now that pixel art and low polygon 3D styles are mined out, developers are having to dig deep to find novel art styles for their retro games. Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore is for all those people who had a Philips CDi... or at least spent time watching meme compilations of the Zelda CDi games with the bizarre, meme-able animations. The game nails the uncanny faces, butt-ugly character designs, cheap MS paint animation with janky movement in those Zelda adventures Nintendo wishes we'd all forget. As for how it plays, Arzette is a decent RPG/platformer. The game is stage-based and non-linear, meaning that to move forward you will have to complete quests for NPCs to find tools and items you need to progress, a bit like the Shantae games. This means you'll be revisiting stages multiple times as you gain progression abilities to get through that one obstacle that blocked your path last time to get the thing you need to get the other thing in another stage. A fast travel system would have been nice since each time you revisit a stage you start from the beginning, but at least the stages aren't too long. It's an enjoyable game, but there are literally dozens of games that do what Arzette does just as good or better. I think a large part of how much you will like this game comes down how much you want a playable parody of The Legend of Zelda: Wand of Gammalon.

_childDocuments_.review: It's always a bit of a balancing act when you're making something that's a spiritual or literal successor to something bad. It can be tempting to take advantage of your inspiration's bad reputation to peddle a subpar product under the guise of being "deliberately bad", which misses the point that the original product tried to be good and failed.Arzette thankfully ignores that entire balancing act, instead delivering a solidly made adventure game that hearkens to its influences through its presentation and style, plumbing the Zelda CD-i games' most infamous yet most memorable aspect - those weird cutscenes that I think were animated by some Russian studio for not a lot of money and I assume without much quality control. In some regards, because the most memorable part of the games has nothing to do with the gameplay, it's a lot easier to deliver a well-made game since no one remembers the CD-i or that it was really more designed for edutainment and FMV game show adaptations rather than real games. Hell, there's so few people invested there isn't even a good emulator for it.But that's beside the point. Arzette's gameplay is solid 2D action platformer fare, bolstered by lovely visuals, fun music, and a good sense of humor. If you have any nostalgia for Youtube Poops (or the CD-i, I guess) then Arzette is a pretty easy purchase for a game that pastiches and homages. You even get a good game out of it.

_childDocuments_.review: bought and installed within the first minute of availability, which idk i will ever do for a game again, so feel free to take my autism with a grain of salt. but this is an exceedingly, endlessly lovable piece of art, one which reaffirms just about everything ive grown to believe about art in the first place. the source material , once uncomplicatedly loathed, has been slowly chipped away at by years of collective intimacy...sentences heard as groups of syllables, individual frames of animation immortalized, control quirks forced to be grappled with, npc requests and locations forced to be stored away in memory. this is to say nothing of the dedication it took to create an entire fan remaster, which leads directly into arzette via its lead developer. the result is a combination of nostalgic warmth, a grasp of what is compelling and memorable and striking about those games, and a melancholy stare at the parts that could have been better...a melancholy that could only be sated Through creation.arzette will be described by many people as "the cdi zeldas but good." having enjoyed the remasters of those games, its more the final step in a process of escalation towards "the cdi zeldas, but there is less in the way of the good." the ultra-memorable quirk and expressiveness of the animation and voice acting are more widely acknowledged as boons now, but arzette also runs with the gorgeous background art, the lush and memorable music, and the miniature zelda experience via an interlocking spread of bite sized metroidvania maps. since its no longer on the cdi, individual screens are much meatier, which does make it slightly longer to recheck places (and rechecking places is what youre doing a Lot in all of these games, but especially this one with its more complex item progression), but it also allows for much more deliberate and satisfying level and encounter design. tricks from the cdi games have their most unpleasant edges sanded off, yet still retain their character. its by any measure an improvement on its inspirations, yet it never once feels judgemental or callous...instead it feels freed and joyus, the result of passion and time and effort and improved technology, chipping away at a dream created almost accidentally by people working with a bad console under tight time pressure.and more then anything, even with some fun and dry meta jokes, i may not play a game more full of shamelessly earnest love this year. its close proximity with its source material allows it to share a bunch of discoveries its made that its so bubblingly excited about...yet its also an individual and distinctive piece of art carrying with it all the best sensibilities of contemporary metamodern media engagement, a plea to look closely at things that are dismissed and create beauty out of them. its most singular advancements are not its polishing up of rough gameplay ideas, but are in its disarmingly heartfelt and kind story and general tone. i know many people are cynical about pastiche, esp in a world where the same ideas are endlessly recycled over and over...but art should be about the free exchange of ideas, putting them out in the world for other people to respond to, feel about, and create on top of. it certainly cant be dismissed out of hand if it produces results like this even occasionally. hot moose man.

_childDocuments_.review: A spiritual successor to a CDi game but a little MMMMMM RICHER!Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore is a action adventure 2D platformer game heavily inspired by the videogame masterpieces that are Link: The Faces of Evil, and Zelda: The Wand of Gamelon. Two infamous Legend of Zelda games that were released for the Philips CDi and notable for a multitude reasons. The plot of the game has the Evil Daimur return from a parallel of the two CDi games and it's up to Arzette to "do this" and collect all the Jewels of Faramore to banish Daimur once again. Arzette is basically "What if we took the vibe and mechcanics of those game but actually made it well designed" and they did exactly that. It's a true love letter to this iconic part of early internet and YouTube history that despite all odds has remade relevant to this day. Gameplay of Arzette is as similar to the original CDi as much as possible while playing and running a million times better. You're given access to a overworld map and tasked with finding all the pieces of the Jewel of Faramore featuring a colorful cast of NPCs and enemies. Each area of the game is presented like a 2D Sidescroller, much like Zelda II or of couse the CDi games. While each level does have a end or a level boss you typically can't get to the end on your first run, you'll have to enter and exit multiple levels at different points to be able to collect powerups and items to complete quests. It's faintly a Metrodvania-like set up just between levels and not one giant map. As such Arzette gains more and more upgrades as her journey progresses, such as more health, movement options, and deadlier weaponry. As you unlock more and more levels by activating the game's beacons within certain level, eventually you'll get to the game's boss fights which are nothing mindblowing but are fairly fun. Honestly the biggest loop of the game is collecting items and cross referencing them with NPCs you've met to get even more items to continue. Since the levels are fairly short and you getting upgraded every so often you'll find that the repeat trips get easier and eases down the tedious factor of revisiting levels. Style wise, Arzette is a absolute love letter to Faces of Evil and Wand of Gamelon from nearly every aspect on how it looks but with it's own spin. Firstly with the levels, the background combined with the detailed pixelart for the enemies, Arzette, etc is absolutely on brand to imitate that CDi style. Though with the background art specifically, an effort has been made to make it clear what's a platform and what's the background, As this was a issue with the original CDi games. As for the cutscenes, the original CDi games are highly regarded for their bizarre, jank, and often weirdly charming cutscenes. Arzette obviously being a homage to those games, does this. But without just coping Animation Magic's artstyle but by having multiple people work on the animation at once. This means that not only do you have no idea what the cutscenes will be about, more often than not it'll be animated completely differently from other cutscenes. It also helps that the game genuinely has amazing character designs. Everyone from the major bosses to the random NPCs you interact with have designs that look really good with the game's base artstyle. It's amazing how good the designs are considering how little screentime a lot of the character have. Overall, Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore is what you get when you have a bunch of passionate fans taking a game, making it their own thing, and fixing basically all the gameplay issues the original game had while also being as faithful as possible. If you're a fan of 2D Action Adventure Platformers or simply love the pure chaos that is the Zelda CD-i game I would highly recommend this game. It's just a pure love letter to the best part of a terrible game and then taking that game into something that the original game truly strived for!

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who grew up with, and genuinely likes, Link: Faces of Evil, Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore is so, so much fun. It's a competent 2D platformer that doesn't overstay it's welcome. Music is good. Controls are good. There are light Metroidvania elements in that, as you gain new powers, you'll likely backtrack to areas you've been to open up new paths. Levels are relatively short, so backtracking never felt too bad.Now, if you've played the Zelda CD-I games, you'll, undoubtedly, see and hear a lot of references to those games in this one. For example, sound effects were, basically, lifted straight from the CD-I games and dropped in here. The sounds of picking up items, shooting the sword, bombs exploding, and projectiles reflecting off your shield are all from the Zelda CD-I games, just to name a few. There are more you'll likely catch. You can talk to a wide variety of NPCs with your Smart Sword! Cool, huh?! Most of the time, when you talk to them, you'll trigger a short cutscene animated in that unique Animation Magic style (Animation Magic was the company behind the CD-I games). Similarly, the NPCs are voiced in a deliberately imperfect way to emulate the voice work from the original CD-I games. Love permeates this game and it might be in these cutscenes where it shines through the most. The animators and voice actors hit the nail on the head and if you had told me these were from the CD-I, I would have believed you. Something I just learned was that Rob Dunlavey contributed to some of the backgrounds for Arzette. Rob did most, if not all, of the backgrounds in Link: Faces of Evil. So much care went into this game that it's almost unbelievable. I feel very positive about Arzette and a lot of that is due to the references, big and small, to the Zelda CD-I games. I can say that, had I not had a history with those games, I probably wouldn't like Arzette as much as I do. Regardless, it's a fun time and an easy recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: After completing this game, I have to say that I very much liked this game.While its a retro based game that revolves around the style of the CD-i Zelda games, the game is very well made. The animation style of the cutscenes, while intentionally being bad in the animation department to mimic that style alot of us are used to in this day and age thanks to youtube poops, were also good in telling what the story is about. Which is Daimur (Ganon expy) is sealed inside a book (sounds familiar?) 10 years ago with his compatriot Duke Nodelki (Duke Onkled expy) being sentenced to scrub all the floors in Faramore. But after 10 years, Nodelki somehow got the book and released Daimur. So its up to Princess Arzette to collect the shards of the jewel to stop Daimur once again.If my expy drops are to go by, this game is technically a loose sequel to Zelda Wand of Gamelon. Just with names and setting completely changed. But unlike that game, this game is far more well done. Enemy placement is far more fair but still challenging (they don't spawn endlessly like in WoG), there is mercy invincibility to help you get back on your feet (Arzette even has a hurt sprite), and the most mundane thing in the game, opening the menu, does not require you to crouch and hit the jump button. Arzette herself plays as you'd expect from a character in an action platformer. You run, jump, slash and do the duck walk (cool huh?!). And again, in comparison to WoG, she's not at all slugish or a pain to control. The controls are very smooth and responsive. I should mention i used a controller to play this, but i imagine it isn't hard to play either with a keyboard or the cd-i styled spoon controller. Talking to npcs still requires you to cut at them though. But much like WoG, Arzette brought her smart sword. So it won't hurt anyone friendly. As odd as this sounds, it kinda threw me off as at this point in time, i'm used to just hitting up to talk to npcs in action platformers. You also get upgrades. Akin to actual Zelda games and Metroidvanias. Perhaps a downside I have with this game is bosses are too easy. While I know the bosses in Wand of Gamelon weren't that tough either (they all die in one hit), the bosses here could've been more challenging. Especially later bosses where Arzette is extremely op (at least assuming you got the upgrades). Given, they're not pushovers either as they do put up a bit of a good fight so you can't just mindlessly run up to them and cut them until they die.The map, while being a bit reminicent to Wand of Gamelon and Faces of Evil, feels more in line with Wanderers of Ys and Order of Eclessia. Ala you pick via a map icon and proceed by hitting whatever button you have for confirm. And much like those games, Arzette has a town hub where you can restock on items and speak to npcs. The town itself is pretty big for a CD-i tribute game. As are the levels. Many of the level designs are pretty big and are akin to those seen in metroidvanias. They're neither unfair or braindead easy. While there are a couple instadeath pits, you can easily avoid them by paying attention to the terrain. And the enemy placement, as I said, are not unfair compared to the games its a tribute of. And they don't endlessly respawn so you have some breathing room once you kill them. Overall, the game is a fun tribute to the CD-i Zeldas, but obviously doing something way better than them. Gameplay is great and some of the cooky characters are charming and amusing. With many of them being expies on several CD-i characters you might be familiar with. But the game can range from being manageable to a little too easy. I should mention that a certain streamer does have a voicing role in this. I ain't spoiling what character he is, but you might recognize him once you get to him.tl;dr, great game. fun characters and animation. but could be a little challenging (i'm aware of a mode unlocking, but i'll keep my review spoiler free so i'm not mentioning it besides what i just said). Would recommended to those that like metroidvanias, action platformers, and/or youtube poops. If you're for some reason expecting this to play like the actual zelda CD-i games (i hope you're not), then you'll be disappointed with how much better this one plays.

_childDocuments_.review: I will preface this by saying if you're not a fan of late-2000's "YouTube Poop" culture, or the infamous cutscenes of the CD-i Zelda games, you might not get much out of this. Having grown up watching the aforementioned media, I enjoyed what Arzette offered. Past that appeal to internet nostalgia however, may not be something that stands on its own much.What I believe seperates Arzette from most games today, nostalgia aside, is how it imitates a "cheaply-made" game. Purposely, enemies pace and fly around with no smooth transition in their speed nor their animations, giving no warning for when they switch direction, as they move in an unnatural, yet familiar way. Projectiles can also pop out without warning too, or so quickly, it'd be harder to defend yourself if it weren't for a tool you get early on. It sounds like the makings of a very unfair game, but it's designed with these in mind. The player character moves slow enough for impatient people like me to become wary and observant before taking another step, and your "Smart Sword" can nullify most projectiles. Naturally, bosses are designed like this too, and they're kinda intense... at least without the reflector ring. Perhaps a big highlight with the gameplay, Though, in execution, it's still rather basic. Once you get past those funny quirks, what you have is a pretty straightforward adventure game. No puzzles, no unique mechanics; just simple exploration to find important items and enemies blocking the way. Maybe that can work in its favor for some, being a non-complex, relaxing game where consistent progress can be made. Yet, progress is annoying to make with this one, cause there's a lot of times where you could find a hidden path, only to need another tool to actually nab your reward. Of course, there's also fetch quests to really extend your playtime. Just a lot of backtracking that probably wouldn't exist had there not been as many blockades or upgrades. I guess you wouldn't expect much complexity or innovation from a game like this anyhow.Cutscenes aren't as iconic as what you'd find in CD-i Zelda, since they, understandably, can't quite get as much uncanny detail with the animation or as accidentally hilarious with the voicework and script. What it delivers right is the feeling like it was made in older times, and of course, leaving many possibilities as to what video editors can create by messing with the material (which is generously given to you in the local files, backgrounds omitted). Old-styled sounds, lower frame rate, and lines delivered with varying amounts of... expression? These certainly have the charm that shows they care, but without my love for Arzette's inspirations, these aspects could've fallen a bit flat for me.It's hard to recommend this game to others without the level of context its general audience would have, but I also think it'd be unfair for me to label this with a thumbs down. As far as I can tell, the game only set out to be a love letter to all the beloved works people have cherished since their earlier years, and to maybe even be a new source for future YouTube Poop videos to borrow from. It accomplished those things the best it could, and I like it for validating my niche interest in a bygone era that feels more distant as time passes and our culture's internet humor changes.Definitely get it sometime if you're into those same things and want one more thing to remember them by. Otherwise, well, I hope you know what to expect now.

_childDocuments_.review: It is, of course, drawing heavily off of the Zelda CDI games, but it still manages to have its own identity. I love how the characters and cutscenes are outright the same style and type as the CDI games, with Arzette herself acting like a normal person would to all of this insanity, being annoyed, weirded out, angry, etc. having to deal with the more whacky characters. The game play is really fun.I only have minor gripes like the collision boxes seem to be noticeably bigger than the sprites themselves, where a lot of projectiles clearly should've went over my head or something, but it was only minor where I only had trouble as I initially got used to the game playing it the first time, as you do any game.One of the best parts was how the game's final battle was a throwback to the "boss battles" with Ganon in the CDI games, except it's actually the hardest boss in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore

_childDocuments_.review: Arzette is a nice hommage that is better than its blueprint... and also somehow worse.To take Wand of Gamelon Remastered as a comparison (and for the record I like that game), combat and movement feels more snappy in Arzette, and platforming is more clear, as both WoG & FoE had really rich and detailed visuals that didn't make what was platforms very obvious sometimes.Unfortunately, while Arzette is longer than WoG & FoE, it's longer in the worst way it could've been. There are way too many back & forths between zones, more than the CD-I games, sometimes you redo a whole zone for 2-3 minutes only to unlock 30 seconds worth of level design to be stopped again, then back out to look for another item in a zone you've already done, then back into that first zone again to give that item to an NPC... granted, I might've been playing it in a suboptimal way, but if I have to backtrack more than 4 times in a level that isn't the main HUB, then in my opinion, it's already doing something worse.Progression is simply smoother in the Zelda CD-I games. They might be shorter games, but I never felt like they dragged. Arzette drags, despite being only about 2h30 long for the main quest.Backtracking is the biggest drawback of this game, on top of boss fights in general being way too easy (then again it wasn't the Zelda CD-I games' strong point either), and the lack of consequences to dying (at least in Normal mode, I haven't tried the unlockable Hero mode yet) which makes potions completely worthless, risking of being a game running on auto-pilot for more skilled players where being reckless and damage boosting is too validated. That last one also the CD-I games didn't suffer from.Otherwise, the game accomplishes everything else it sets out to do, it's fun, it's charming as hell. Goes well with a CRT filter through Reshade. I don't feel done with the game, but after awhile, it felt tedious in a way I never felt like Wand of Gamelon Remastered was.For a potential sequel, I'd want at least the backtracking to be lessened & streamlined, even if it means making more shorter levels, or making less levels but longer.
_childDocuments_.name: Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore

_childDocuments_.review: The cutscenes in this game are spot on and are absolutely worth the price of admission. The game itself is fun, it's just like the remastered CDI link and zelda games but much more grounded, but the cutscenes and character interactions absolutely are the best part and so many easily match the corny and completely insane style of Faces of Evil and Wand of Gamelon. Arzette herself is also a complete bab and I am so happy to play as her.My actual biggest criticism is that the game forgot about the infamous boss-teaser cut-scenes that your assistant would show you at the start of their designated level, and that the game relies on text-boxes instead of cutscenes after you've helped certain people, but they ask for more help anyways for certain upgrades. That said I am very happy with what I got! Don't get me wrong, it was just a little disheartening I couldn't see more of a lot of my favorite characters.If you want a good idea of if you would like this game or not, find and play FoE or WoG Remastered and give it a spin. Arzette is that but MUCH more polished. There's still some frustraiting bits, especially the volcano where your inability to look down REALLY bites you, but I can absolutely say I had a lot of fun with this and will be replaying it soon!

_childDocuments_.review: A great experience that can be a bit bogged down by some awkward level design and enemy placement. I bought this because I enjoyed watching people play the original CD-I games years ago, but I really think this is also a great standalone title for anyone who is into action-platformers with some puzzles mixed in.There is an overwhelming amount of backtracking, but the game also has some neat intentional sequence breaks that can clear up the monotony and rewards replayability. But my other major gripe comes from the unlocks in the game, as you have to:1. Beat 'Classic/Normal' Difficulty to unlock 'Hero' Difficulty and 'Boss Rush'2. Beat Hero to unlock 'Classic' Difficulty3. Beat Classic to unlock 'Oneshot' Mode4. Beat Oneshot to unlock 'Cheats', with one of the cheat codes (found online) including another mode called 'Seedy Eye Mode'and you need to clear Steps 1-3 to even have a chance to unlock all the achievements in the game, meaning a minimum of 3 playthoughs with minimal changes other than more damage received, new enemy placements, and a 'continue' system for Classic.Other than all of that, I really enjoyed the music and visuals, even though the visuals could sometimes make platforming a little awkward. But I still recommend this game, just maybe not 100% completing it.

_childDocuments_.review: Mah Boi, or girl, or whatever, this game is what ALL true gamers strive for.I couldn't be happier than say this was the BEST $20 I ever spent on it. The fact that it was sprouted from an idea to remaster the old CDI Zelda games for PC and make this game as charming and fun as possible.This has to be one of the best indie 2D games I've played so far!First off, the art, spritework, music and cutscenes really well made. Arzette controls extremely well and even better when you actually hunt for the upgrades in her health, armor and movement.The game is always fair and gives you a decent amount of clues to find nearly all the hidden collectibles and treasures.The only thing I didn't like too much is that when you leave a level, you're always teleported to the beginning of the level even though the magic scrolls that are at the end and middle part can lead you back to the map. I assumed you could teleport to those locations, but nope, you're always teleported back to the beginning of the level.And although the levels aren't THAT huge and don't take too long to get from point A to point B, I still felt kinda annoyed that I had to keep doing the same thing every time I returned to the level.Also even though again, there's no need to complain too much about the level since it's not that huge, I would've liked to have a map to show what collectibles I've haven't gotten yet, but since on the map it shows you what you are missing I guess it's a compromise~Overall, I HIGHLY recommend this game. It doesn't take too long to beat, the cutscenes are full of cheese and charm much like the YTP's everyone grew up watching, and I commend the entire team for doing a wonderful job on this. Cheesy cutscenes and all.My only hope is that we get a sequel that improves on this even more~

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to know how to review a game that's intentionally mimicking bad games, but I think they do a good job achieving what they set out to accomplish. There seem to be plenty of side quests and upgrades to get for people who are looking for some extra mileage out of it, but I felt there's already already borderline too much backtracking in a normal playthrough for my taste, so I probably won't bother getting everything. That said, I thought it was the perfect length and it didn't overstay its welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: I started playing Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore expecting a full on parody or a funny-bad game or a ‘so bad it is good’ game….. but instead found a plainly good game!  I understand it makes homage to Zelda: The Wand of Gamelon,  not as a parody but a really a full improvement over the source material. If Arzette had come out 27-30 years ago it would undoubtedly have been a console seller and a game we would have had several sequels of over the years!There are of course many funny references in the making of this game but the gameplay is overall sober while the animated cut-scenes, from the very first one, convey most of the most of the specific nods. The developer’s name ‘Seedy Eye Software’ makes of course reference to the Philips CD-i; the mystic console with which Nintendo had partnered to try to counter the Sony PlayStation on the optical medias nearly 30 years ago. The developer I feel made a very eloquent interpretation of all the memorable and amusing peculiarities of the CD-i Nintendo games art in the cut-scenes. It is a form of animated naive art that I hadn’t seen before nor since. I am certain not have missed a lot of references but there was more than enough for me to be amused about with the presentation. I understood that one of the type of bonus level for closing doors is an homage to Hotel Mario which also came out on the CD-i.I played Arzette on my Steam Deck and found it fitted the form factor perfectly. The length of this game is the longest I have used my Steam Deck since I have owned it. The visual pop in the art direction really made great use of the 7 inches of display and the controls are responsive. My only remapping had been to remap the trigger (to change the spell category) to a more 'clicky' button. I did have some rare hard freezes initially on the Steam Deck but an update that came out just after seems to have fixed the issue. Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore is a fun metroidvania (meeting a basic adventure game) with a forgiving difficulty (at least until harder modes are unlocked), frequent auto-saves, plenty of hidden secrets and a really nice art in the painted levels and a really catchy and memorable soundtrack that feels truly authentic (kudos to Button Masher !).I enjoyed the responsive controls: Arzette initially might feel like it plays like a bit like a classic game but with a few unlock it quickly shifts and starts to feel like a more modern platformer. The succinct but very varied level design has a very forgiving interpretation of what can be a ‘platform’ you can walk on (as opposed to the classic games in the same style). Going through levels is rather quick once we understand the layout, which is a boon because of how often one has to in order to find all the secrets.I received this game as a gift and to do this gift honor of at least trying it I started playing this game with little expectations … but before I knew it, I was hunting down all the secrets replaying the same levels repeatedly to get a 100% completion. I intend to play more to unlock all the achievements of this game … and that is saying a lot because I have felt compelled to complete maybe 0.5% of my Steam library (if I round up).Azrette doesn’t overstay her welcome: I finished the game in about 4h30 in the normal difficulty (I expect it should take most people longer). I enjoyed the time playing it as a condensed quality experience, unlike the kind of padding in difficulty and repetition a classic game in the same genre would have had. After completing it once, as one might expect in the genre, a harder game difficulty and a boss rush mode were unlocked.For anyone in the target audience for this game understanding the nostalgia/homage it proposes with good humor through a short and sweet platformer experience: you can’t possibly be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: First of all: I haven't finished the game yet (I'm at about 50%), so my review can change later on.Not many can pull off deliberately making something "so bad that it's good" without making it "so bad that it's bad", and at several points, Arzette tries a bit too hard. Also, some cutscenes ooze with this "14 year old girl on tumblr" vibe. That being said, you can really see the love and effort they poured into it. They clearly know their source material, and it's fun guessing which character is based in which CD-i/YTP character. I also noticed they use a lot of the sound effects also found in the CD-i cutscenes.On top of that, the game plays and controls quite well - unlike the original games. And I speak from experience since I'm the (more or less) proud owner of a CD-i and a formidable library of games, among them Hotel Mario and all three Zelda games (even the elusive Zelda's Adventure, which I have yet to play).It's also longer than the originals. The remastered versions of FoE and WoG by Dopply took me about two hours each to finish. In this game, I'm four hours in, and not even halfway through.As so often, I wish there was a "mixed feelings" option. But all in all, I think I will give this game a favourable review.

_childDocuments_.review: Memes – that was the legacy of the infamous Nintendo licensed Zelda titles on the Philips CD-i. Not surprising, really, since both Link: The Faces of Evil and Zelda: The Wand of Gamelon were not very good games. But they did have bizarre and unconventional visual style, especially for their animated cutscenes, all of which became a popular source of the “YouTube poop” videos that used to be insanely popular in the late 2000s. So it’s interesting, how many people grew up knowing these titles, without ever playing them. Back in 2020 Seth Fulkerson (also known as Dopply) created unofficial remasters of both games running on GameMaker and featuring a lot of improvements that turned those titles into something that was at least playable and less frustrating. Those remasters, for legal reasons, are not available anymore so instead Dopply decided to create a game that would serve as a spiritual successor to those bizarre titles. And in doing so, managed to create a game that is genuinely enjoyable.Since most people know the CD-i Zelda games only for their cutscenes, most do not know that the titles played as 2D side scrolling platformer action adventures. You usually have access to one or more locations you can run and jump around, killing enemies, and in those locations you might come around certain blockers. Some could require a use of an item one can buy from a shop with the currency dropped by killed enemies. Some require finding specific permanent upgrades. And some items are used as, essentially, quest items that NPCs on levels may want, who, in turn, provide progress. Due to this structure, the ability to “fully finish” the level isn’t guaranteed on your first visit and you would regularly need to go in and out of levels in search of the “correct” progression. Which is a fun concept for an exploration focused game if the main gameplay is good, but that’s where the CD-i games horribly failed as playing them was miserable.Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore takes the exact same approach with how it builds its progression, but on top of that makes the core gameplay actually fun. Not great by any means – this game cannot compete with any competent action platformers with its combat or character controls. But it makes everything “good enough” to be enjoyable, and let the process of exploring the world and doing quests for bizarre characters really fun.Meeting said characters leads to the fantastically odd animated cutscenes in the style of the CD-i games. That still somewhat remind of the works of Robert Sahakyants, except done with Paint. And it’s glorious. Visual presentation in general manages to perfectly evoke the vibe of an strange cheap “plug and play” console with unlicensed games, but unlike those it manages to look good and not ugly, just slightly off in an endearing way. Same can be said about a very simple, yet really charming soundtrack that might not land into your casual playlist after playing, but fits the style of the game perfectly and is instantly hummable.The game does have a few odd decisions and weaker levels that start reminding of its main inspirations in a bad way for a little bit. And it may have moments from time to time where it’s hard to remember or figure out what your next destination should be. The PC settings are also somewhat limited and I can only hope that this won’t lead to some potential issues with the future hardware. But in general the title is highly enjoyable and extremely fun to explore. If you like games that focus on exploration, you’ll probably like Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore. And if you’re here just for the memes, there is an easier difficulty that might be enough to get you through the game providing a good dose of laughter and smiles.

_childDocuments_.review: They really did revive the CD-I Zelda games, didnt they?In all seriousness, this game so far is actually pretty good. They managed to keep all the goofy charm those old games had but cut out the annoying stuff, and then they turned it into a proper metroidvania??? There's...a lot of backtracking, like there's maybe less fast travel than there should be, but that comes with the genre I guess. I still feel like I was progressing even after replaying areas with new items and abilities, and it's actually really fun too.I don't even know how to describe it, but the writing in this game is also really good? Like they kept the comedic atmosphere for most of the game but then actually made the characters likeable and even a bit emotional at times, it's actually kinda wild how I actually felt invested in these characters that are supposed to be a parody. I'm not even sure how much more there is, apparently I'm only 38% done with the game as of writing this and I'm genuinely interested to see what new faces Arzette talks to next (perhaps faces of evil, hmm?).This game is a love letter to the most infamous games in Nintendo history, but it's also just a really solid metroidvania with a very competent story that's fun to play even if you haven't even heard of the games it's based on. I can't recommend this enough. Buy this game if you're interested, as long as you have enough rubies of course.

_childDocuments_.review: A parody game paying homage to the Zelda games on CD-i isn't something I ever thought I needed in my life, but after seeing Deceased Crab play a little of this game I could tell just how much care went into making this game.The visuals and animations are very, very close to the ones found in games like Wand of Gamelon, but ultimately have a charm all their own.  The soundtrack also brings back a lot of fond memories of gaming in the 90s, and the fact that the .ogg files are packed right into the game and readily accessible was a very pleasant surprise.  However, the real improvement over the games that inspired Arzette is found in the gameplay.  The controls are intuitive and responsive, and Arzette's movement feels like something out of Symphony of the Night rather than Wand of Gamelon.Really, the only complaint I have about this game is that there isn't more of it — and if that's the worst complaint I can make about a game, then the developers did a good job.  I hope we see more of Arzette and Seedy Eye software in the future!

_childDocuments_.review: An affectionate homage to the compellingly awful CD-i Zelda games that succeeds largely on the strength of its art direction and humor. I think projects that set out to be "so bad it's good" rarely succeed, but more often than not I found myself laughing along with Arzette. The tone throughout is delightfully goofy, and the writing isn't overcrowded with memes. The hand-drawn level backgrounds and animated sequences are very effective. Arzette thankfully plays closer to a Shantae game than the games that most directly inspired it, but the enemy AI is very simplistic (there are a whole lot of them that just pace back and forth, occasionally throwing projectiles), and almost all the boss fights are trivially easy. Still, the level design is at least decent, and the game is so densely packed with secrets that I didn't mind all the backtracking. I feel that this could and should have been a much longer and more substantial game—you're given so many items and upgrades in so short a period of time, with so little space to make use of them, that they don't really feel meaningful.Consider this a recommendation, but not a strong recommendation, I guess.
_childDocuments_.name: Arzette: The Jewel of Faramore

_childDocuments_.review: Arzette is an easy buy IF you were ever into Zelda CD-I youtube poops and want to experience those weird cutscenes again. It's too  well made to be called a joke game but also falls a bit short for me to recommend it to people who are only looking for a good platformer metroidvania. It's quite short (first playthrough took me under three hours, with a fair amount of side content done) and pretty easy.With that said, i think this game achieves what it sets out out to do: pay homage to those awful Philips CD-I Zelda games while still being fun to play. The cutscenes are very cheesy and entertaining, some of them are a bit "still" but others play with perspective and weird facial expressions in a way that made me feel like i was watching a YTP for the first time again.Gameplay is basic but fun; Music is catchy; Story has an oddly out of place tonal shift in the middle but otherwise remains goofy and lighthearted.

_childDocuments_.review: THIS [Game] IS WHAT ALL TRUE WARRIORS STRIVE FORarzette is great. on its own merits its still a fun little metroidvania with some good replay value. if youre in the know about the cdi games and ytp/animation magic jokes and like games like this though, this is a no brainer. the game is very forgiving and doesnt feel too frustrating due to a healthy amount of checkpoints and qol stuff, but it never feels too easy either, even though i played on casual mode. really good balance. could use few quality of life tweaks though: 1) being able to fast travel to any teleportation map in a level and not just the entrance one 2) finding progression on a blind playthrough during the more open ended sections can be a BIT disorienting (though this is just something that happens in Any metroidvania) 3) you cant switch items on the fly, which isnt too bad but would be useful to have 4) no level map for the individual levels, would be EXTREMELY useful to have a map similar to metroid fusion/prime to know what you can use new items on. itd also would be nice to have a sound test/ cutscene gallery, and maybe a better side quest tracker. other than that though i would definitely recommend this game if you like ytp and cdi bits, this game is both such an earnest love letter to the zelda cdi duology and an actual proper evolution of the cool parts about those games even outside of the jokes people make about them.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm only an hour in, but I'm ready to sing this game's praises. In an age where AAA game developers rely so heavily on cheap nostalgia to sell their titles, Arzette stands out as a diamond in the landfill, because it not only calls back to our childhoods, it legitimately understands /why/ it was so special to us to begin with.It's a love letter to a simpler time when memes were the reigning power on the internet, and making Nintendo characters say swear words was the funniest thing in the world. It's a game that -- let's be honest -- nobody really asked for, and yet, was exactly what we wanted: a project born out of passion.Booting up Arzette for the first time made me feel like a kid again, rushing home from Blockbuster Video to play the new game I picked out because it had a cool cover on it. Best of all? The game is actually quite well-designed. Even if you aren't in on the joke, Seedy Eye has breathed so much life and personality into every character design, cutscene, song, etc. It's just pure charm all-throughout. The voice acting -- which is supposed to sound hammy and strange -- is very genuine and cute. I especially love Arzette as a character and seeing how she reacts to the strange people of Faramore. The janky controls of the original CD-I games have been totally revised in exchange for snappy, fast-paced movement. An overall joy to play in every facet.I can't offer a rating quite until I've completed the game, but so far, Arzette has offered me the most genuine, wholesome gaming experience I've had in a long time. I would recommend this game!

I 100%'d this game over the course of about 8 hours, so it's not too much of a commitment. Would highly recommend to any Metroidvania fans or CD-i fans alike... as long as you have enough rubies.

_childDocuments_.review: Its essentially a just okay Meme game. It parodies the CDI titles, more specifically the CDI Zelda Games and does a good job doing so but the actual gameplay suffers for it. The gameplay is incredibly barebones and calling this a metroidvania does a disservice to the genre. You also break any form of challenge as soon as you pick up the reflecting shield which even turns bosses into a game of standing in one spot and holding the shield button while you wait for the boss to kill itself on you. I also can't help but feel that they didnt fully commit to the meme by trying to make the story come off as somewhat more serious and taking shortcuts in some departments like voice quality or using cg for some cutscenes and just drawing over it (The last one in particular was jarring to me as you can clearly tell the difference from other cutscenes).As it stands i wouldn't say its awful but i also wouldn't recommend to someone looking for an actual game to play. It's a Meme Game, you're either in on the meme and play it or you have no clue and won't get the appeal. So if we're judging this on its on merrits without context of the memes and purely as a game then i'd say move on from this one. But even with the context i wouldnt say its worth almost 20 Bucks when you can get an actual great Metroidvania like Hollow Knight or other great indie titles for that instead.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard one, once again, steam needs a "meh" rating. The game controls fine, it gets the style of the old CDI games down pat and some of the songs in it are actually pretty catchy. But the gameplay is just.....boring, now I know there isn't really much you can do if you're going for a 1 for 1 with a game that's historically known for being bad but still, copying a bad game still means you're gonna make a bad game. The game's cutscenes were of course made to be ugly and cheesy to copy the style once again, but its just not really funny, it's more just cringy, after all if someone tries their hardest and fails it can be kind of funny, but if someone tries to make something look crap then all they do is create something that is just crap.The real biggest issue is 2 fold: 1. the game is just too short and too easy for the asking price. 3 ish hrs for this price? With basically no replayability unless you like getting a few achievements? No thanks2. this game behaves like a castlevania game where you find a new power up and can access areas you couldn't previously, although good luck remembering where the areas were that you needed that, which means going through basically every (boring) level like 5 times over just to progress.Overall I give it a thumbs up only because I respect what they attempted to do and for better (but mostly worse) they succeeded.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the CDI Games, while not good games on their own, their cutscenes and influence on the internet, YouTube and YouTube Poops mean so much to me and many others that it’s safe to say I or others wouldn’t be the people we are today.Arzette is a love letter to not only the CDI Game’s Cutscenes and their wonderful weirdness, but also drastically improving the core gameplay of the 2 infamous Zelda games, which were decent on their own at base, but poorly executed due to the CDI Console itself, oversights from the Developers and more.The game’s cast of characters are wonderful, every single character is memorable with whacky and creative designs, some of my favourites are the Princess herself Arzette, Dail The Bard, and Odie, there’s a lot more and I’d be here all day listing them!The voice acting is super cheesy and brings a smile to my faceThe music is absolutely excellent with some real banging tunesThe controls are solid, all of the problems I had with the game are with my skill and not the game itself.Graphics are beautiful and I love the pixel art, and the cutscenes are just *french kiss* perfect.The game is very funnyAnd it’s just a ton of fun to play, it’s one of the most fun games I’ve played in a while.This game is a 10/10, if you have any curiosity about this game, please play it, you will not regret it.Also if anyone is curious as I watched CDI YTPs since their early days, some of my personal favourites when I was younger were from The Morshu ShowWhile the more “modern” CDI YTPs, without contest this is my favourite.Yea the humour might outdated and offensive but I don’t care I still find them funny!
