_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting and unique language based puzzle game.Controls:- Locked camera angle and position, which might move if you get close to the edge of your screen,or briefly fades when you enter a loading zone- With mouse and keyboard, you click were to move- With a controller you can also move around with analog controlsGameplay:- You see glyphs in certain contexts (e.g. in walls or in speech bubbles from native speakers)- You try to guess their meaning- You can take notes of what you think it might mean- At certain key locations the game gives you the option to validate them by connecting them to images or glyphs of other languages in the game
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: There aren’t many video games for writers. Why would there be? They have farming simulators and power washing simulators and lawn mowing simulators and truck driving simulators and goat simulators. But it’s hard to make a video game for the creative community. There have been some attempts, like Elegy For a Dead World, but that’s really a “write this thing here and we’ll spit it back out to you later”. Like Mad-Libs. Ultimately, you have to have something like Dungeons and Dragons where it’s basically your character versus someone else’s narrative, which creates a story. (Maybe that’s something positive AI can be used for.) But then I found "Chants of Sennar". Chants of Sennar is a short indie game where you play a hooded figure trying to get from point A to point B. The problem is that you can’t understand what people are saying. They talk in foreign glyphs and the core gameplay comes from figuring out what those glyphs mean. You have to piece it together through context clues and labels placed through the environment. (And there’s a few stealth segments, but they’re easy.)And every language has its own grammar. In one, plurals are indicated by repeating the noun twice. In another, you use the indicative glyph before the noun. In another, it goes after. And there’s all kinds of little things like that to make this a unique puzzle-solving game. It’s not flashy and I wish there was a sprint button, but it’s intriguing and the art style has kind of a French art deco thing going. The difficulty is only based on your own logical thinking and reasoning (and besides, you can find walkthroughs for anything).
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: First off: Amazing Game. If you like puzzle games where you figure things out, try to define rules and explore for hints and solutions.I recommend you try this game.If you like puzzle games where you have clearly defined rules and a clear goal to work toward,Don't expect these elements in this game, it very much requires exploration, guessing and connecting the dots.As for my opinions about the game: (If you want to play, I suggest not reading stuff in the spoiler tags or in any guides.)Wonderful atmosphere and music.Solving the puzzles and deciphering the glyphs is fun.Also, as a language puzzle game, it was forgiving enough to not be frustrating but still be challenging.I loved the ending and, in general, the little stories throughout the game.Sometimes the walking gets tiresome when you just want to go somewhere, and you know how to get there, but you can only walk somewhat slowly. But all in all, most areas are compact enough to not require too much walking.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I beat the game in a little over 9 hours, getting every achievement in a single playthrough. I used a controller to play, and found it quite easy to navigate around for the most part. None of the puzzles are too difficult, though one part required doing math in a foreign numbering system, which did take a bit of thinking. There are stealth mechanics during some parts, but they aren't overly challenging. A few times when identifying certain words you can simply brute force the solution, which makes identifying some words even easier. If you make a mistake and something 'kills' you, there is no real penalty. It usually just puts you back to the beginning of the room you're in. Game didn't crash even once, and I don't recall encountering any bug/problems that caused frustrations.If I had one complaint about the game it would be that I can only play it once. My memory is good enough that I am able to recall a significant number of the symbols used in the first 4 languages, which would prevent me from getting the same experience a second time. Maybe I'll return in a year, see if I've forgotten enough to play again.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is a fun puzzle game, with beautiful artistic direction and interesting mechanics. But what will stick with me most is the ending scene, which managed incredible poignancy with just a few moments.If you like the art style, the idea of decoding simplified languages, and/or just well made, moderate-challenge puzzle games, I think this one is worth the time and money.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Relaxing and very beautiful puzzle game. The sound design and music is very good! The linguistic take keeps it interesting but can also be challenging for a dum-dum like me who for one tends to forget words, and second tends to read in too much and complicate things. My #1 thing in the game are the cats (love u devs). Also the magpies makes me weirdly happy.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Vibrant, wholesome, and a terrific experience of a puzzle game. The more I played Chants of Sennaar and learned about the various peoples and their cultures in it the more invested I got in the slowly-snowballing story line. The mystery of trying to figure out the language of each level becoming either more complex or varied kept my interest and gave several "a-ha!" moments as well. The way the environments *pop* with each level progression was a great progression indicator as well as the noticeable difference in background (like climbing the tower in the 2nd region of the Warriors). The only downside I'd have with this is that it does make the brain tired for a bit so I played about 1 area/level per day, but still thoroughly enjoyed the experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: The story was sweet and pretty interesting, learning the languages were amazing, and there were both hard and not so hard puzzles. Now, i didn't like how the perspective changed every time you went from one area to another. it made it very hard for me to navigate. Traversing made sense, but could also be very slow at times. An ingame map that you fill out as you go would've helped tremendously, and even fast travel to points of interest, though i understand why they did it the way they did. I also wasn't a big fan of the chase/stealth sections.All in all i really enjoyed my time with it!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful point-and-click game with the most unique and compelling puzzle system I've come across. While most of the puzzles in the game aren't too hard (Barring the 2nd to last area, be prepared for some maths), the challenge comes from trying to figure out just what the puzzle is asking of you.It's a nicely bite-sized game at 8-9 hours long and it keeps the energy and pace up the whole way through. I couldn't put it down and burned through it in just a few days.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Very nice little puzzle adventure game well worth your time and money. The languge based puzzles are satisifying and neatly tie into the themes and strong worldbuilding of the game. The artstyle is striking with bright color pallets that differ in each major area as well as music and instruments that also reflect the people living there.The downside in this otherwise focused game is the occational stealth and chase segments that to me felt unneccesary. The character movement can also at times be a bit slow, especially when you have to backtrack. These are however minor gripes and didn't substract much from an otherwise great, thoughtful and relaxing time.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a lovely game with great visuals and a lovely score. Puzzles increase in difficulty as the game goes on but never feel unfair or impossible. Fewer and fewer language puzzles towards the end of the game (instead more stealth and spatial reasoning) which I personally found disappointing. Storyline is a bit simplistic but that's not why anyone plays this game. I had a lot of fun and I really enjoyed myself.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I had such a fun time I played it non-stop and finished it in one setting! Chants of Sennaar is a beautiful game with a unique and colourful design. It is full of puzzles that were fun to solve, although sometimes I was at a loss because I couldn't figure out what I had to do next. Make sure to explore every corner, and I mean every corner, of the maps! Unraveling the story was a treat as well, not spoiling anything but I enjoyed it very much.In any case, this game is for you if:- You love puzzles- You love learning languages- You love games that have a charming design, where everything has a meaningI hope that if you decide to embark on the journey of this game's Traveller, you enjoy this game as much as I did c:
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is a cute adventure game. It tells a fairly compelling story about cultural barriers between societies that don't share a language. And how a lack of curiosity, compassion, and understanding can lead to xenophobia, hatred, and isolationism where everybody is worse off for it. While that general message resonates with me, particularly in recent times, from a gameplay perspective I found Chants of Sennaar to be short, shallow, and far less stimulating than I thought a puzzle game about language would be. For that reason I don't feel like I can recommend this game.My main complaint about Chants of Sennaar is that it is very easy. There is little challenge in translating the game's languages due to , , and . What challenge could remain is essentially eliminated by the glyph validation feature -- which would be interesting to try and avoid using but that also means you would deliberately skip some of the game's achievements. I can understand the developers want people to finish the game but without some more challenging side puzzles the game is just too handholdy for me.Aside from these issues with the core puzzling system I think other game mechanics and aspects of the UX are mildly annoying (playing on steam deck). In particular, I found navigating the game's various stealth sequences to be a clunky slog which I wish were completely absent instead. They, again, pose no real challenge and the controls on a gamepad are rather frustrating in my opinion.I definitely didn't hate this game. But as someone who cares most about engaging gameplay over presentation and story I don't think Chants of Sennaar sticks out as a game puzzle enjoyers need to check out. People interested in a colorful and interesting story that isn't too physically or mentally taxing can definitely enjoy the ~8 hour journey though.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is an S tier game through and through. The balancing and absolutely perfect automatic note-taking system (among other things, like the insane progression and ending) makes this puzzle game one of the best I've ever played. On the note taking, multiple times I had physically taken a note or two and then immediately after exiting that menu my in-game character took that exact same note but better. The ability to match these notes with your own guesses for what words might mean leaves room for personalization within the notes (I know I'm talking about the notes a lot but nothing is better than writing in that my best guess for a word is "ballerness-scepter" or "coolsh*t" and, i mean, I basically got it. And you don't have to perfectly get it, as long as you get the idea. God I love this game.) Great googly moogly please play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, my experience with the game can be counted as being positive.More specifically, while the game is an interesting puzzle game, the puzzles themselves aren't that hard, at times frustrating.There is a lot of slow backtracking you can't speed up.Translating each language becomes at time just boring, there is no reason to try to even think about the logic behind the different codes.  The story is a bit simplistic, but for a puzzle game I'd say it's good enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is overall a good game. Decryption every single symbols as well as grammar rules were so much fun, especially when my guesses made sense in an actual sentence. It is also great that some of the puzzles requires the understanding of the language to, for example, obtain certain item or follow certain instructions.That said, I have also had great frustration on the other elements of the game. For a puzzle game of language, I did not expect the emphasis on stealth; let alone being chased or jump scared. These are rather detached with the overall gameplay, and they serve very little purpose other than minor story-telling features. Considering the passive screen scrolls, stealth through certain sections were absolutely torturous, and I had nearly given up the whole game because of stealth levels being so punishing. Another example of how the game design punishes the player was how its interactives were layed out. For example, For the language puzzle such engaging, I am willing to let go of my grudge of all else.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun adventure, and extremely fun for those interested in linguistics.The low-poly graphics are very pleasant, and the usage of colours adds to the atmosphere. Only if you're photosensitive I'd be careful with the last levels. Amazing soundtrack. The way that camera works sometimes can be a little tricky, but the angles are worth it. The world of The Tower is worth exploring for the variety of its architecture alone.Does it earn its memed name of Dark Souls of Duolingo? I'd say the difficulty is easy to balanced but this is not a bad thing.The game doesn't punish You for mistakes, so it makes for a relaxed weekend play.That being said, it also doesn't lead you forward in any way. The minimalistic style works to its advantage, but also, sometimes you may get stuck. Keep an eye out for concealed passages!It's not too long (that's expected of an adventure game), and the plot is quite simple, but the mechanics and aestetics provide enough entertainment to make up for that.I think this game knows what it wants to be, and executes it very well.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar deserves all the hype it gets. I can't think of a single bad thing to say about it.You may have heard there are puzzles and infiltration sequences, and like me you might have thought you're not good enough for that.Forget it.This is a translation game, first and foremost. And it has everything people may love about translation. Finding out what glyphs mean and being able to follow conversation is incredibly rewarding, but by understanding a language you are also understanding the culture of each people.They may have different words to say the same thing because they don't see the world the same way, they might lack some words, there are so many things specific to each culture ! The attention to detail is incredible.And you not only have to understand each language, but also translate from one to the other, which is both a linguistic and cultural exercise. This is such a nice feeling.And it's not just the language. Each people has a distinct architecture, fashion, colour palette and music. You are completely immersed in the world and it's such a pleasure to stroll around and look at the scenery and appreciate the music. I have rarely seen a video game environment have such personality.And it's just so beautiful. Visually it is reminiscent of Monument Valley. And I have been listening to the soundtrack on loop since finishing the game.The gameplay is impeccable. You might feel lost in the vast levels, but you will never miss a place. The pace at which you see new glyphs is just right, and the timing for decoding them is perfect to help you progress. The puzzles ask you to think a little but instructions are very clear so it's quite easy. Infiltration is extremely forgiving and does not distract from your main objective.And this could have been it, but the game also has a complete story with a satisfying end ! There is an actual narrative, and it wasn't even needed, so it's such a nice touch.There are also sub-stories within each levels and between the people which makes your progression feel even better.Honestly, no matter what kind of game you usually prefer, give Chants of Sennaar a chance.This is definitely the best game I've played in 2024.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Oh, how I am regretful that I cannot make sentences in the language of this game in this little box. The fun I would have!------ The Short Version ------Listen. If you are the sort of person who sat down one day and learned cryptography because codes and mysteries are fascinating, this is absolutely the game for you.If you are the sort of person who treats words NOT as parallels to one another, but rather as another culture's attempt to personify a concept that you must take the time to grasp, this is absolutely the game for you. (The English "Hello" to the Hawaiian "Aloha", as but the most bare-bones of examples, comparing grapes to raspberry fields.)If you are! The sort of person! Who was fascinated with Egyptian Hieroglyphics NOT necessarily because of any interest in actually speaking the language of the pharaohs, but rather because the symbols connected the ideas in every range from extremely literal to supremely hyperbolic, this is absolutely the game for you.If you spent a profound number of hours in the game TUNIC, taking the time to really read the manual, this is the game for you.------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The Long Version ------Chants of Sennaar is a fascinating game about language, culture, and differences.The earliest example of the depth of this game comes near the very start, when you approach a locked door guarded by a small platoon of men in tall helmets, who speak in symbols that you have not come across.And at this stage, you still don't even know the first language you're hearing.The game is fascinating. Every language denotes its culture, every language is framed around the main focus of its people.I could write such a paper on this game.I could write it largely IN the languages of this game, because they are so well designed.And because, truly? All languages are just our best attempt at using the symbols to convey the world.This game captures this factor. It captures so elegantly what language really is, and how it is decided.Have you ever sat down to invent a language? It's honestly not complicated to do; To make a WHOLE language is complicated, but to start is very simple. You just have to pick a word, and a way to write it.And honestly? The way to write it is the easy part.What do you pick? What word comes first?Is your language by the religious? Is it centered around god, or belief?Is your language scientific? Is your first choice a number system? Or perhaps a way to write formulas?Is your language for the artistic? Do you express theater? Or perhaps beauty?What comes first, and why? What is the second word you need?This game is all about learning languages, and discerning their cause and their meanings off their structure.Listen. I have something for you. A note, a point, a joy purely from myself to you.The First Language of the game has a word for the concept "Fortress". It is never asked for in the game, and you can never use it. It appears in exactly one place, half-torn away: But the rules are clear. You know the whole picture if you understand the rules.If you have found that symbol, then you have enjoyed the game more than most.If you have deduced that symbol, you have had as much fun as I have. (It's not a difficult task, but I hypothesize only those who love the game will put that amount of thought into it.)Enjoy.10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a brilliant game about exploring and learning to translate languages. Based loosely on the story of the tower of babel, the puzzles get more complex the further you get in a wonderful way. And, the 'true' ending includes an incredible ending sequence and final section - I have never before seen a puzzle game that legitimately felt like it had a final boss.Like any puzzle game, sometimes puzzles aren't super clear, and the game could *really* use a map, but these are small issues in a much larger work that is really excellent.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I really loved this game. It reminded me of another favorite of mine, Return of the Obra Dinn, but with a totally different aesthetic and narrative style. I wasn't completely sold on it early on - there are some stealth sections that I found annoying, even though they were not difficult at all, and very forgiving when you mess up. However, by the end it had fully won me over with its charm. I was incredibly touched by the final reveal right before the credits. Would recommend this to anyone who likes narrative-driven puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I really adore this game. The atmosphere is brilliant and the chosen artstyle works really well.There are a few gripes with the length and sometimes the movement is a bit annoying, but overall a very smooth experience that I can only recommend to people that like a neat little puzzle gem with a nice coherent story. The only true caveat would be the price tag, since for people that wolf it down like me 25$ are a bit much. On sale I definitely recommend checking it out.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, this game reminds me of Moebius' (Jean Giraud) art. Gameplay-wise, Sennaar reminds me of Outer Wilds and Fez. The pacing is nice and relaxing while the puzzles are just difficult enough to make you scratch your head a couple of times.Loosely based on the story of the Tower of Babel, the premise is good enough to carry you through this rather short game.All in all, I loved it
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely loved this game! It's essentially a puzzle-solving game built on linguistic anthropology - you explore the tower and interact with people and their writings in order to slowly form an understanding of how the various peoples' languages work. It's also one of those games that's really rewarding to those of us who love to explore all the nooks and crannies of the game worlds we play in. I highly recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: along with the even more accessible The Forgotten City, this is likely what i would rec to those interested in this new, difficult-to-define wave of "knowledge based games", or "world-based puzzle adventures" or "things u would recommend to ppl who liked outer wilds" or whatever we end up calling it. chants of sennaar nails everything that is lovely and engrossing and satisfying about these games, which for me is two primary things. (1) the framing of puzzles first and foremost as about understanding the worldbuilding, puzzles as something that bring you closer into the places and people around you rather then purely abstract logic or test of real-world knowledge. (2) the underappreciated Power Fantasy of knowledge, of using abstracted and approachable versions of intimidating real things for a series of satisfying game puzzles that provide an unbelievable amount of satisfaction relative to their actual complexity, which even at their trickiest tends to be Quite Low In The Grand Scheme Of  other words, chants of sennaar uses language learning in the same way outer wilds uses space flight and astrophysics, or how obra dinn uses forensic crime scene analysis. few will defend the non-puzzle gameplay sections, but theyre too short and easy to make a dent in the experience. what rly pushes it over the top for me is the starry-eyed optimism that it pulls thru by the end...combined with the biblical slant, its even slightly heretical
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: The ending part is spectacularly good.However: the learning curve of this game is extremely steep. Like in section 1, each glyph is illustrated by 3-4 examples, and you encounter only 1-2 new glyphs each time; come the beginning of section 3, you are faced with a dozen new glyphs all at the same time and the illustrations are sparse.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a beautifully crafted game visually, and the soft melodies will complete the atmosphere. The linguistic elements and patterns are so well crafted that it gives you a satisfying sense of accomplishment when you've discovered what the glyph commonalities are before the game confirms it. A shorter game, but completely worth it. Grab this game at full price if you can; we should support developers with vision like this when the final product is this good.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I half expected this to be sort of like Outer Wilds, it's not, and it's not bad.I loved the visuals and soundtrack, the overall atmosphere. Was fun to run around and explore all the nooks and crannies. The game ran well, controls were good, didn't have to bust out the notepad for puzzles.I didn't like that some sections and puzzles were tedious. More importantly, I think towards the end, the way they did some stuff sort of cheapened the entire experience to some extent.Overall, they focused on telling a story, and they did it well. But there were shapes of much different game, one of being lost in translation, misunderstandings, travelling and learning, I kinda wished they fully leaned on that instead.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Really fun PnC adventure. If you are interested in etymology and language, a really interesting puzzle game. I never felt insurpassably stuck. It is really interesting how the different groups languages differ. I loved the art and music, really set the tone for each level of the tower you were on. Highly recommend. Spoilers:
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: You ever played Doom and thought 'If only I could talk to these monsters'? Well this is only tangentially like that, but you have no gun and the monsters are concepts like xenophobia, fear of death, the idea of god, and hierarchical power structures. Even with a hoity toity idea of that driving the core of the game it's satisfying to 100% in just a little under 10 hours with the occasional use of a guide because some of the syntax of the different languages is tricky.Buy it even if it's not on sale if you like puzzle games.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: The ones complaining about the bad stealth gameplay is over-reacting IMO. It's not *that* bad and it's not a huge part of the game.I think I'm about 1/2 - 2/3 through now and it's a very well-made game. The graphics, feel, and overall difficulty is good. I'd wish there was a way to cancel "replays" (but it's not a large part of the game) and maybe a "hardcore mode" which prevented the mapping "checkpoints" from being available? (or reduced the number of tries to N)It would been nice if it was possible to rearrange the symbols in the "code book" and if you could attach longer notes to each symbols in addition to the length-limited guess.Tip (very minor spoiler?): As with almost all games like this - the walk/run speed could been even higher (or a speed-mode toggle), though this game is by no means the worst "offender" here.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is a puzzle/adventure/stealth/linguistics/platformer, earning immediate credit for novelty. Unfortunately, the puzzle/linguistics elements are the only ones that really work. The "platforming" happens exactly once and is trivial, the stealth is mostly an annoyance, and the story that builds up over the course of your adventure never really comes together. The secondary aspects (graphics, audio, controls, etc.) are all good enough, but you wouldn't play the game for them.Given all this, the puzzle/linguistics elements really need to carry this game. They do. In fact, this is my favorite game of the last few years -- the quality of the experience is almost continually phenomenal. I wish there was a "hard mode" where less was given away, but that's really my only complaint. The game is beautifully crafted, deeply engaging, and harnesses parts of the brain rarely used in gaming.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This was a fun, quick language/translation puzzle game.  It's not particularly difficult except for a few unexpected quirks with translation here and there.  The graphics are nice and fit the game well.  I normally play games with the music off but decided to give this a chance, and it came through there as well.  The only downside is that it was very fast, 100% in 11 hours without really trying.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I had an absolutely fantastic time with this game! Language nerds will really have a blast - the different languages in the game have not only different notation systems and vocabulary, but also different syntax, which is very cool. There's a little bit of platforming (a very little bit), and a bit of stealthing/running, but not so much that I got frustrated. Speaking of frustration, though, I thought I'd finished the game and it just said "The End." and reset me to the beginning. But don't give up! Walk into the scene, and you'll see what happens.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, i did like the game, linguistics and all. However i am left feeling bit mixed due to the mechanics of the game. The amount of walking was insane - trying to find places, people to check what they actually said and what not. I was walking all over the place and in certain levels i was lost 70% of the time. Annoying and ultimately fairly boring, when something like things going into your journal would have helped. I also didnt enjoy the jumping or sneaking parts.Besides these complaints though i did enjoy the game and loved the language aspect of it. I just kinda feel the walking etc was just pointless padding - i would have preferred to just walk around once and after that teleporting and having the things in my journal. Or at least a map.Other than that, rewarding experience, i really enjoyed the story as well. I had to check couple of things, since they where obscure to me (or i was just fed up with the walking)
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: An amazing puzzle game all about deciphering languages, thoroughly enjoyed everything, . Puzzles are definitely a bit taxing but you'll figure them out eventually. Great little notebook system in the game too when you think you've figured out that a symbol definitely must mean "Hello" to find out that everyone's actually been calling you an idiot. Amazing art style, decent soundtrack. 10/10Definitely pick this up whatever the price. Really can't wait to see whats next!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I like to tell people that everyone should get a chance to take the Defense Language Aptitude Battery (DLAB) once in their life, because it's the trippiest test I've ever taken and you'll be randomly having epiphanies about one question or another for years afterwards. Chants of Sennaar is the DLAB in game form.First, all the roses. The artwork and music is beautiful. The language constructs and character meanings are diverse and thoughtful. The non-language puzzles, including figuring out the order of steps to take in each level, nicely complement the core language decoding challenge. The intertwining narratives between groups was very clever, and the overarching goal of bringing them together was super wholesome.I can't think of a game I've played in the past few years where I've had such a high density of "wow that is really well done and clever/cool" moments. Three stand-out memories are , , and . Thank you to the developers, artists, and everyone else on the team for making this game! I strongly recommend it.I hesitate to include a thorn in this review, call it personal preference or polite disagreement about the endgame.Once again, thanks to Rundisc for a phenomenal game!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: There is some game that once you completed the story, you just wish that you can be forget, so you can play again as a fresh player. This game definitely matchs this description, as the gameplay was so impressive and original. I've never played a game (for now?) where the language is the center of the puzzles, where you need to learn them from your surrounding, match the right words with the right symbols, and links them to the others languages! This game was really well thought-out, and not just for his gameplay, but also for his main story, and all of the people's story too! You're just flabbergasted, and you forget for hours that you are in a game, since you seems to live with these people too...I recommend to you to try and explore every levels of this game, a 100% here worth totally the effort. I just hope to play others games like this one now!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is delightful.  If you love puzzles and deciphering messages this is a great time. I loved how the game allows you to begin understanding before you have the answers, and then offers further clarity when you find them.  I didn't find the puzzles to be repetitive despite being very similar though the whole game, and the revelations felt very satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my first Steam review, but I just had to come praise this game.It's very unique, at its core, it's about giving you the joys of language learning in small, manageable chunks (multiple simple languages of a few dozen symbols; 1 symbol ~= 1 word/concept) - You come to a new location, people speak to you in plain gibberish, then you start to figure out meaning of different signs from different contexts, so you start understanding the people, which allows you to fill in the blanks, until eventually, you master the language, understand the speakers and figure out that the mysterious text was solution to the puzzle you needed to solve all along. It really reminded me of linguistics competition I took part in during my high school years, which inspired me to give language learning another go after I already got tired of cramming vocabulary in traditional language subjects in school. So I feel like this game might be a great language learning motivator to some people.I've heard some reviewers complaining about mixing in some stealth sections. I personally really enjoy stealth genre, and these sections were not difficult either way, but I guess it's something worth mentioning if someone really dislikes stealth.The graphics are pretty simplistic, but really nice, and together with the soundtrack, they make for a pretty relaxing atmosphere. The environments are interesting, with each culture's location having different feel and color palette. Having the journal with pictures representing the different signs as a validation tool was pretty creative design decision, making sure the players mostly cannot brute force the solutions, and giving additional clues in case the other ones don't suffice. I tried to not look at the journal too much (as suggested in one YouTube review), trying to figure out the meanings first from the environment and really only using the journal for validation. I think if I didn't do that, the clues in the journal sometimes were a bit too helpful, giving the players information their character wouldn't have gathered. Also, when getting close to figuring out the whole language, you can brute-force the last few meanings (if you can limit yourself to only a handful of signs to brute-force), I almost did that when I knew the set of symbols was of the same category and the specific assignment felt a bit arbitrary, before stopping myself. Also, I was able to assign some of the last symbols of a language correctly to validate them, only to find out I got the meaning completely wrong. I wish this was avoided by providing me with more contexts to explain the word, but not sure if that's possible with some of the more abstract words.Towards completing each of the cultures' regions, there was a bit of running around aimlessly, searching for the last few meanings to solve a puzzle to get to the next region. Before everything clicks, you're not really sure what are the puzzles, and what are the clues for it. For those stages of gameplay, the individual regions are maybe a bit too big, forcing you to spend more time wandering around confused then actually figuring something out. Still, eventually I was able to figure out these puzzles without the game holding my hand, which is pretty impressive game design feat, and while I feel like this stage didn't feel ideal, it never got to a point where I was frustrated. Similarly to the late stage of learning each language, I feel like the last stage of the whole game suffers a bit from this running around. By this time, you're running around the WHOLE map, which was cleverly handled by supporting fast travel. I was still a bit confused at this point, because I still had gaps in my knowledge of 3/5 languages at this point. That meant I would sometimes start trying to solve one puzzle, only to realize I still cannot figure it out, keeping it for later. One of the inventory items served as . Maybe it would have been helpful to . Also I feel like the map  didn't communicate very clearly which connections I already rebuilt and which not, and where they are, so I kept revisiting locations where I didn't need to go anymore.I enjoyed the final stage of the game when you already have most of the languages figured out, and there are two new types of puzzles - . I enjoyed these puzzles, as you couldn't just rely on the vocabulary you already validated here, but still had to know the different grammars of each of the languages. Also I liked how the symbols were not completely arbitrary, sometimes you could tell the category of the symbol from its shape. I kind of wish there were even more different grammar features in the languages but that's pretty difficult to do while trying to keep the languages simple. If there's any sequel or another game of this new genre to push this further, I definitely look forward to it.Also it was a good design choice to not have your inventory appear in the other regions than it could be applied in, so when players get stuck, they will not try to run around the whole map needlessly, but will stay focused on the current region. It was pretty impressive how the game communicates visually without words to a large extent and doesn't use pretty much any texts in English to guide you, unless the original text is in one of the in-game languages, that you already figured out the meaning of yourself, in that case it will give you a tooltip with the translated sentence. That takes away some of the hard work of figuring out each text yourself, but I think that's mostly a good thing. I liked how for one of the languages, the tooltips , thus making reading easier for players but not taking away what makes the language unique.One of the languages doesn't give you too many contexts to work with, instead you mostly solve it with your knowledge of the other languages. I don't like this decision very much, as I didn't have that strong relationship with that language as the other ones. I guess this shows you how far you've come in your knowledge, but the last section of the game does this as well. Also the rebuilt connections of this culture aren't as interesting. Maybe it was a simplification that came from budget running out? But the language still had some pretty interesting features.There were two instances where I got stuck because I didn't figure out some trivial puzzles (not related to languages), one involving  and one involving . I didn't end up solving those puzzles (only looked up later and solved for an achievement), I was still able to finish the game regardless. However, this meant I didn't understand some of the symbols until the end of the game or had to do some guessing. The clues for these symbols didn't get added to my journal for validation as I managed to avoid solving these puzzles. Maybe there could have been a bit more clues how to solve these puzzles (something that would more explicitly tell you ) or when you obviously already figured out a different puzzle with same solution or completed a region, the clues could get added to the journal regardless.I liked the games overall message and liked that each of the rebuilt connections made sense in the game's lore. Cool how different cultures have different vocabularies. The above are largely nitpicks, again, I overall really enjoyed the game.

_childDocuments_.review: As a linguistics major, Chants of Sennaar  scratches my brain the right way. The distinct architecture of each level of the tower. As a point and click puzzle game itself, the aesthetics of Chants of Sennaar had already caught my attention long before I found out that it revolved around language deciphering. Having just taken a class on cryptography and Egyptology and learning about Champollion and how Egyptian glyphs were deciphered, i was incredibly surprised to find that the core of this game was language translation, and boy oh boy did that get me excited. The best part? Each group even had their own sentence structure, with the bards speaking like Yoda and warriors speaking like a typical meathead. I had an immense amount of fun figuring out the languages of all of the groups of people living in the tower, and the icing on the came comes with the quests you have to undertake to unlock the true ending. No spoilers here, but the results of these quests made me smile. If you've made it this far, thanks for reading and I hope you consider playing this wonderful game.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like translating languages?Do you like stylized point-and-click adventure?Do you like good music and good art in your video game?Then I recommend Chants of Sennaar! Incredibly rewarding to solve yourself.The bad:While not strictly linear, the game has points where you need to complete X or you're stuck (there were times I consulted the internet for help). CoS could use a map feature, especially when certain environments room-to-room get very confusing. If you skip a puzzle or a point of interaction, chances are you need to complete that area, so do it now or do it later.The game does reward mastery of its puzzle systems, and does have a great learning curve that I felt challenged the player appropriately. I wish it was longer, and I wish certain puzzles took less time. I also wish there was more language, and there are certain words that I hated translating. A mixed bag of mostly good; go get your journal, your quill, and get translating!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm glad that the answer lock-in mechanic popularized by Return of the Obra Dinn is gaining a foothold. It's a nice way to feel like you're making progress in a puzzle, without being too easy to brute force. That being said, it is still possible to brute force the answers on a given Journal page if you're certain about all but one of the glyphs. If you're planning on making a sequel in the future, I'd like to suggest an extra wrinkle to make the Journal system more robust.Once you fill in all the glyphs on a given page, the game should not immediately make the check to see if you got them all correct. Instead, once you fill a page, you must re-read three unique instances of a glyph on that page (instances can be in conversations or written material). Once you find three unique instances, if the glyph is correct, it becomes locked in; otherwise, it's removed from the page. This simulates the process of going back and putting your hypotheses to the test. The player may also realize their error before finding three unique instances of the glyph, simply by noticing that the proposed meaning doesn't fit the context. In any case, if a glyph is removed or changed before a glyph is fully checked, the counter for all unconfirmed glyphs on the page is reset.Would this be an annoying feature that wears on players' patience and does more harm than good to the overall experience? Well maybe, unless there were more NPCs and written material scattered about so that you always had enough unique instances of a glyph close at hand to check against. I did feel that this game could use a lot more NPCs to chat with, so that's something worth considering for a sequel.Anyway, I know this was more of a suggestion for future games than an actual review, but I don't type up these sorts of things for games I dislike; on the contrary, it means I got so invested in the game that I want to make it even better than it already is. The game's great, is what I'm saying.

_childDocuments_.review: fantastic point n click adventure gamethe aesthetic is strong throughout but with enough variety to remain interesting and a sense of environmental themeing that communicates the attitudes of a community immediately (which plays an important role in deciphering the language of an area). very nice to look at in general and used extremely well from a gameplay perspectivethere is a story, and while its arguably a background element, its intriguing and enjoyable. clearly very well made and carefully considered the puzzles are great. theres plenty of standard and well made point n click affairs- space puzzles, riddles, fetch quests, etc etc. to add some variety, but of course where it shines in the language puzzles. theyre well made, challenging without feeling unfair, and satisfying in a way that i can only attribute to the fact that they are about learning communication within the world- some innately human desire fueling the fun. the languages become harder to decipher as you progress (any good puzzle should), but it never feels as if its because the languages themselves have become more complex- just that each one requires a different way of thinking and the observation of the environment around you to learn. this keeps what might have otherwise been a progressively boring and repetitive experience fresh and excitingthe game is absolutely worth your time and its price- honestly, its worth more. very enjoyable

_childDocuments_.review: I'm writing this review after just finishing the game, for real (iykyk).I cannot express how beautifully well-made this piece of art is. My partner and I started this game last night, and couldn't stop playing it until 4am which we then collapsed, got up at noon and then continued the game until the end. This game, is one of those real gems that will enchant you with its absolutely unique gameplay.My partner and I are both kinda language nerds. We LOVED the whole game. The story is rich, made-up languages are well structured, there's not just vocabulary, but also grammatical and conceptual differences between the way different nations/races see the world and the events.The architecture, color palette, cultural norms, outfits, speaking tones, gestures, etc. of each level / nation, is vastly different from one-another; you'll never run short of "sense of discovery". You have to be on the look out for visual cues, environmental clues, and cultural symbols to piece together enough information to form a sort of a bridge between yourself and the natives of this new world that you're exploring.Game never runs out of sense of novelty. I have felt excitement, scared, proud, happy, sad, pity, anger, and I had so many "aha!" during my playtime. As I'm writing this review, I'm still high on all of these hormones and emotional journeys.Saying thank you with all my heart is an understatement of how grateful I feel. I sincerely don't know how to express my gratitude and admiration for the developers of this absolute masterpiece of modern indie games.

_childDocuments_.review: In short: Beautiful game about language, culture, and bonds between people. Fun puzzles, good music, and good visuals.In Chants of Sennaar, you are a traveler going up the tower and learning the language and culture of each of the 5 groups. You have to piece together the meaning of all of the symbols you see with a combination of pictures, conversations, and rosetta stone-like objects (same thing written in multiple languages). Sounds intimidating, but they have mechanics built in to keep you on track. This mechanic takes the form of a journal entry, which will appear when you have enough information to deduce the meaning of a number of symbols. Once you get all symbols correct for that entry, you will permanently confirm the meaning of all of the symbols in it. It's a great way of making the game feel challenging without feeling overwhelming.

_childDocuments_.review: The language decoding is very satisfying, with plenty of opportunities to have little "aha" moments where you feel like you're ahead of the game and identifying patterns beyond what's being directly asked of you, whilst having enough structure to keep you from going off the rails completely. The game also looks great: clean and minimal, but in a distinct style with plenty of character.I'm only part-way through, but it would take something pretty drastic to sour me on it by the end. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I recommend this, but it's a bit of a recommendation with caveats.Visually, it's a lovely game, nice and clear, colourful, but everything is distinct. I also love the premise; the game getting you to piece together all these languages is a really interesting idea, and I think that it's for the most part done really well.I wasn't as sold on the ending sections, though, which was disappointing. For the Exiles level, constructing the language felt like an afterthought, something I was being rushed through because surely I was bored of it already. It started to feel like a pretty standard logic puzzle, a brute-force connect-the-pieces puzzle that I could find in any game, rather than having that flavour that I was really enjoying from other levels.Then, in the final section of the game, connecting all the people together, I felt like it was all busywork. I would have been totally happy to finish all the terminals -- was planning to anyway! -- if they were secret, extra pieces for 100% completion or something, but having them be the actual gameplay for a while was unfulfilling. I wanted the gameplay to be linguistics puzzles with optional extras, not suddenly become a fetch quest.I do honestly recommend the game -- for the first levels, and while the devs seemed to still be interested in the actual draw of the game, the world is interesting, the puzzles feel good to solve, and the linguistics puzzles are fun and cool. But the ending was a real let-down, for me, and if I were rating this game, I think I'd have to give it a 7/10 because of that.Also, this is entirely personal, and I realise why this wasn't in the game, but I do kind of wish there was a Hard Mode where I could turn off filling out the words in the diary thing. I would have Loved an option where the game never confirmed my translations and made me work out whether I was accurate or not from whether the puzzles were solved or not. I think the game already has enough feedback in the in-world text and the puzzle solutions to make it work, and it would have been a fun little bonus. As it was, I found the diary was a bit hand-hold-y, though not enough to affect my enjoyment of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: My feelings about Chants of Sennaar were mixed, and the recommendation I'm giving with this review is somewhat tentative. The visual design, world-building, and story were excellent and distinctive, but the puzzle mechanics, and sometimes even the language-learning theme that drew me to the game in the first place, were underwhelming.In Chants of Sennaar, you play a mysterious robed wanderer exploring a tower inspired by the Tower of Babel, interacting with the cultures who live on its various levels. The different cultures speak different languages, each built up from a set of simple glyphs which you learn meanings for as the game proceeds. As you translate the glyphs, you gradually learn details of the setting and unlock the information needed to complete point-and-click adventure game puzzles that allow you to proceed up through the tower and learn your purpose there. Also, every once in a while, it turns into a stealth game out of nowhere; more on that later.The neat thing about language-learning as a puzzle mechanic is that it feels organic in a way that allows for a well-integrated story without displacing the puzzles. This is normally really hard to do! Because a really good puzzle mechanic is often simple and abstract, it's difficult to weave a story that feels natural into a game based on that mechanic. (For example, I love Portal 2, but the number of times the game needs to find a reason to put you through a sequence of puzzle chambers begins to strain my immersion in the story.)By contrast, language learning is already a pretty good puzzle in real life, and language is what stories are made of, making it an ideal basis for a puzzle game. And I really enjoyed the way Chants of Sennaar interwove gameplay and story. Because the story is told entirely through the game's invented languages, each of which has only a few dozen glyphs, it has a feeling of fairytale simplicity, and the developers lean into this with both the clean, appealing visuals and the mythological feeling of the Babel-like setting. But despite that simplicity, the story still found ways to create a variety of fantasy cultures, and to subvert my expectations and surprise me. The language puzzles play a role here too, gradually revealing the story at a pace gated by the process of learning new words. At one point, a seemingly beautiful level began to turn sour as I learned a certain glyph that meant something unpleasant, and then realized how often people around me were using it. The distinct visual styles of different alphabets and the way certain glyphs resemble the concepts they represent or each other both work to make the languages feel natural despite the limitations of their small lexicons.That said, the language puzzles were occasionally disappointing, for one big reason: the game often feels too eager to tell you what its glyphs mean. As you encounter glyphs in the game, you're prompted to place them next to pictures in a book, and filling out two pages (which generally only requires 3 - 4 glyphs) explicitly confirms those glyphs' meaning. While this approach does keep your vocabulary expanding at a steady pace, I had a few problems with it. First, this just isn't a very high bar to clear. Since you're asked to match glyphs with pictures, but the glyphs are also often introduced with visual examples, translation sometimes felt like it boiled down to matching pictures with other pictures of the same thing. Near the end of each level, there's few enough unsolved glyphs that filling out the book comes down to a process of elimination. And it's easy to brute-force guess a glyph by just trying all the options in the last slot on a page -- which felt like it went against the spirit of the game, but which I occasionally resorted to in frustration.The second issue is that, when you complete pages and are shown the official translations of glyphs, they may not agree with your own idea of what the glyphs mean, which is jarring. While mistaken assumptions are a necessary part of any language-learning puzzle, the frequency with which this game provides that feedback makes it feel like a tutor is leaning over your shoulder and correcting you as you go. And this links into my fundamental problem with the book mechanic:  When you unlock new pages of the book and see a picture of a person screaming, it gives you context that you might not get from your interactions with the world. You now know that, at some point, you're going to learn a glyph that means "fear" or "screaming", short-circuiting the work of deducing this from seeing the language in use. The experience of checking items off a list and being told "This means 'silver'!" is a less satisfying puzzle payoff than using the language to say or interpret something -- and while this game has plenty of the latter as well, it feels diluted.Admittedly, learning a language purely through context clues is difficult, and designing a well-balanced puzzle game around this seems even harder. So I shouldn't be too harsh about the game's language mechanics, which I still enjoyed, and which had lots of interesting details. The languages have subtly different syntax (a concept it would have been nice to see the designers go further with) and late in the game, you are tasked with translating between them, putting your understanding of their grammar to the test. The basic interface of the game, allowing you to mark glyphs with their potential meanings and then see automatic translations based on these guesses whenever hovering over text, worked great. And while the game leaned fairly easy, it still had a clear difficulty curve: each level felt like it presented new challenges and mysteries.What I did not enjoy were the game's other mechanics. A substantial amount of gameplay is in the classic point-and-click adventure game mold: meander around until you find the metaphorical key that goes in a metaphorical door, open the door, proceed and repeat. This isn't very interesting, and it's made frustrating by the fact that the game lacks a map, which resulted in me walking around in circles hunting for unseen rooms. But this still led to a few neat puzzles. What drove me crazy was the game's truly baffling (and thankfully infrequent) stealth sections. At various points, you're prompted to crouch down to avoid watchers, dart between cover spots, and occasionally throw a distracting object. But there's no reason this game should have stealth mechanics: they have nothing to do with language learning and very little to do with the setting in general. And the stealth feels half-baked: there's no visual indication of what enemies can or can't see, and they're only able to hear when it's necessary for you to throw a distracting object. The game's Wikipedia page claims that its designers originally envisioned a game about stealth, and its presence in the finished product indeed feels like a weird remnant that doesn't belong.But as much as I might gripe about this game's mechanics, any game that spurs me to write this much about it can't be all that bad. And I came away from Chants of Sennaar feeling more positive than negative, because of the unique setting, beautiful visuals, intriguing story, and often innovative language mechanics. It didn't have the level of challenge I had hoped for, but it still got me to feel invested. And if this inspires others to create more complex language-puzzle games, all the better.

_childDocuments_.review: CHANTS OF SENNAAR scratches the same itch Obra Dinn's puzzles did, only with linguistics rather than a murder diary! With five different languages to translate, the game nevertheless manages to deftly guides the player with subtle hints that lead to those wonderful EUREKA realisations.That said: I did consult a guide a couple of times because I missed a particular rosetta stone for a section or two, leaving me with a whole swath of "???" words and getting bombarded with increasingly complex sentences that I didn't even know where to BEGIN translating.One section IN PARTICULAR mixes up the subject-verb-object order and I found that VERY confusing. It also didn't help that two words I'd translated as "scientist" and "servant" turned out to be "you" and "I" instead. Can't even BEGIN to tell you how much THAT cleared things up.Also, when you lock in the translation for words they are represented as pictures: which works well for stuff like "pot", "fire" or "warrior", breaks down a bit for abstract stuff like "transformation", "question", or "be". Only guessed "be" because it was the last word not matched to a picture.There were also some (fortunately very short-lived) stealth and run sections that I found inoffensive, but I wouldn't say they were a highlight in a game about navigating a world and learning its languages. Could consider it a brief diversion from the main gameplay loop? Eh.In any case, had a really good time with CHANTS OF SENNAAR! It marks my first game completed in 2024, and I got all the acheivos to boot too, woo!

_childDocuments_.review: If I had one pound for every time I played a game with a simplistic, cel-shaded graphical style, which was about a lone traveller with a red hooded cloak exploring a strange world that blended ancient architecture with elements of sci-fi tech, and meeting diverse factions that don't see eye-to-eye, I'd have two pounds.It's not a lot but it's weird that there are two of them.Sable jokes aside, this game is honestly pretty great on its own merit. It's not a long game (I completed it and got all steam achievements in about 10h 30m of gameplay, without external help), but it makes up for that by having a pretty rich experience throughout, with a lot of atmospheric story-telling and intrigue throughout the world. It's a "quality over quantity" kind of deal, and it's very evident that a lot of thought and care was put into the world design and languages.I would say however that the stealth sections aren't really a bright spot in the game's favour, BUT it does make logical sense that, as an unknown traveller wandering through another faction's territory, there are going to be times where you might need to traverse through an area where you're not welcome. So while stealth sections make sense logically, they don't really gel well with the themes and objectives of the game, though that's far from a game-breaker.Personally, I'm a big fan, but I feel like this game is probably not for everyone - I suspect many people wouldn't really "get" it or vibe with it in general. Nevertheless I hope that more people try this game out simply for how creative and original it is. Language interpretation & translation being the central mechanic of the gameplay in this way is, as far as I'm aware, unique and very untapped territory. It's absolutely worth trying because there isn't really anything else quite like it at the moment.

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is one of the slickest, coolest puzzle games I've ever played. The loop of learning words and discovering their meaning is truly addictive. The art, music, and overall world are all beautiful. The story is simple, but told in an interesting fashion. I have a few gripes: the stealth and chase sequences are kinda poorly done, but thankfully few and far between. The drawings are sometimes *really* difficult to interpret. Sometimes, the function that shows all usable objects doesn't show all of them. Finally, But don't let these nitpicks prevent you from enjoying the game! It's a lovely experience. I've let several friends play through on my computer already, and it's fun watching them put the pieces together!

_childDocuments_.review: This review will contain spoilers, marked as such.While I had a few qualms, I loved the game overall, so I'll start with the cons, so that I can end with the pros.- Some of the glyphs did not make sense to me, especially the . I especially struggled with  from that section and spent a lot of time going back and forth. Unfortunately, guessing one or two glyphs wrong can lead you down a very long rabbit hole that's a pain to back out of.- The movement and camera were a little clunky. I often found myself struggling to click the right spot to get where I wanted to go, or figuring out where I wanted to go because it was way off screen. You also have no control over your movement speed, which can be a pain during the .- On that same note, it was difficult seeing places that you could go sometimes. A few times, I got stuck not knowing where to go, only to find that there were stairs just off-camera. The only way to know is walking to the extremities of every room, which isn't fun gameplay.- The  were just 'eh' to me. I don't really feel like they added much, other than just an obstacle to slow you down a little.Okay! Onto the pros!- The music, gorgeous. Not much more to say than than!- The scenery, beautiful in some places , atmospheric in others . Each area had its own feel to it, its own style and its own culture.- Likewise the art style, really interesting! I think 3D renders will cell shading and line work to look like 2D illustration is a really interesting style all its own.- The main gameplay mechanic, the translations! This was what drew me in initially, when I played the demo. While it does get tough with some of the more esoteric words that can't be easily shown as an image, it is overall a very fun mechanic and really enjoyable to try and figure out what's being said.- Assigning glyphs to words is fairly forgiving as well, I want to say it was . For the most part, I thought the substitutions were fair and usually had the same general feeling. - This game scratches a lot of the same itches as "Journey". Don't get me wrong - they are very different games! But both have this feeling of isolation (even though Sennaarr has people in it, and you feel it less once you learn the languages) and this drive forward and upward, even though you're not  sure what it is you're heading towards. You don't know who you are or what your goal is, and that's the primary driving force -- to find that out.If you're into 'Journey' and word games, give this game a try! At least try out the demo. And if you find yourself spinning your wheels, don't be afraid to look up a walk through to see what you might have missed. I can't believe I forgot the most important aspect of the game -- you CAN pet the cat!

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who is very interested in linguistics and conlanging, i.e. constructing languages, I really recommend this game. The work with the languages is just as beautiful as the graphics and message of the game -- I am happy on all fronts.(slight spoilers about the languages)My one critique is that it did feel like the language acquisition drastically accelerated towards the end of the game. For me it felt like three first languages took more time, effort and exploration, so with eleven glyphs in the fourth one simply being for digits and the fifth one hastily figured out through the Rosetta machines, I was a bit disappointed.As the game progressed, it felt like the focus shifted from languages to story telling, which is not necessarily good or bad. While the joy of getting to experience a slice of what it is to be a field linguist mapping out a hitherto unknown language slowly dwindled, the joy and pride of the worth in language and communication grew.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: IMO, this game is a total masterpiece.The central game mechanic is about learning alien languages by deduction, by talking to people and examining clues in the environment (e.g. statues, artwork, graffiti). It is a highly unique idea for a game and IMO it works extremely well.The puzzles are challenging but never frustrating, because there are many clues scattered around the world, and there are many different ways to deduce the meaning of the words. The gameplay loop is very satisfying and addictive, because learning new words has a snowball effect that accelerates progress and demystifies the world.Not only is the core game idea great, but the implementation is flawless. It has a beautiful art style and everything about the gameplay and the user interface is very polished.If you're the type of person that likes challenging puzzle games, I highly recommend giving this a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Good puzzle game where the challenge is in finding the rules/instructions to the puzzles.  Sounds and visuals are great and serve as a good separator between instances where you are figuring out or taking inventory of the languages you have to learn or map.  At least for me, the developers did a great job in leading the player's hypotheses to be vaguely certain so that when the times comes for the game to verify them they often felt satisfying instead of repetitive.Most of the challenge in this game is in figuring out how to read or recognize written symbols within the context the are used.  The game is very good at this when it is doing it.  You tolerance may vary with the quality of time between these language puzzles, but I never found it too wasteful of my time and often pleasant breaks.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played through this game twice, and naturally I have some critiques. The stealth aspects can at times feel relentless, out of place, or like they alter the pacing of the game, and some parts of levels can be a bit annoying to navigate (Gardens Sewers I'm looking at you).But despite those things, the game is immensely enjoyable and just the right amount of challenge and difficulty escalation.Were there moments that I got a bit frustrated? Sure, but the game never felt unfairly difficult and at the end of both of my playthroughs I felt a deep sense of satisfaction.I thought this game was going to be a one and done title for me, but the challenge of translating each language combined with the breathtaking art style and phenomenal music, all wrapped up in a fascinating story based around the concept of The Tower of Babel makes this a game I'm proud to give a permanent spot on my desktop for whenever I've got that puzzle solving itch.

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished the game tonight. Playing it was such a delightful experience all the way from the beginning to the end. This game is for you if you like exploring and discovering new areas and completing puzzles. I had to take notes and draw maps on paper, as the game has no map system you can reference, but I enjoyed that aspect of it.There are some stealth and chase sequences in the game, but they are very forgiving if you fail, starting you up not far from where you failed. This made what otherwise might be very frustrating parts of this game pretty bearable.The whole endgame was fantastic, taking all the skills and languages you learned to the test. And last, but not least, the soundtrack is superb. I'd recommend purchasing it separately, but in game, it does a great job conveying the mood of the different areas.This game came recommended from someone who said it was similar to the language decoding in Tunic. While I love Tunic, there is definitely much less focus on combat in this game, and way more focus on exploration and puzzles, and of course the language aspect is front-and-center. If all those are your jam, definitely pick up this game and play it!

_childDocuments_.review: Thank you for making this game. I don't ever want to play an RPG anymore that doesn't involve deducing the meaning of an unknown language or script. I sincerely hope the functionality sticks around, in the genre or why not in any games that involve exploring and deducing.Just imagine this for Baldur's Gate 3, or Tomb Raider, or Phasmophobia. Imagine Skyrim or Starfield with a ledger that you fill with texts and riddles you find throughout the world, on weathered gravestones, in a mage's library, on an abandoned space station, or in the deepest dungeons, and you slowly piece together their meaning - until finally, they lead you to a treasure chest, a secret quest, reveal something about the world, etc.EDIT:I'm almost at the end now, and I really would like to play more of this game. Please devs, make a sequel, or ten while you're at it. I want to share all the possibilities for a sequel that came to my mind today:-An interstellar pirate-turned-goodguy reconnecting the peoples of a fallen multi-system-republic (maybe including planets with desert outposts, jungle cities, cloud ships, etc.)-A sailor visiting the peoples on the coast of the ancient eastern Mediterranean (maybe including Egypt, Tyre, and Minoan Crete, before or after(!) the Thera eruption 1600 BCE)-A Sumerian boatman meeting peoples on the river banks of the ancient Euphrates (I'm thinking Ur-III period)-Waking up in a quaint little town by the sea, full of people who you don't understand (and maybe they don't understand each other either)-A plot visiting the mythical places of The Odyssey / The Argonauts (like Circe's island, the Lotus-Eaters, Nestor's palace, and many more)-Or simply additional levels to the tower (in vast caverns with underground lakes, and on floating islands and sky ships)-Expanding the idea of lore secrets (think: )-A (space) ship that belongs to the player, that can be filled with trophies won and companions met along the way-Languages take longer to complete, due to sheer quantity of expressions, or due to complexity of syntax, or due to the circumstance of encountering them making it harder (think: someone's journal found in the attic, a short novel, a law text)
