_childDocuments_.review: This game really feeds my love of languages and the puzzles were just difficult enough that I looked up a couple hints, but not so difficult that a more stubborn person could complete it without them! There are a few times when you need to sneak or run away, but that's a very small part of the game so my poor reflexes weren't an issue.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A surprisingly good adventure/puzzle game based on learning languages, with a side of stealth game. None of those parts felt too hard, though the stealth bits were definitely more challenging than the puzzle bits. Somewhat expensive for the length of the game, but I don't regret paying the asking price.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Original concept with lots of smart puzzles. Well-executed and looks great.Doesn't quiiiiiiite live up to the potential shown in the demo, but pretty good. Perhaps a little too keen to tell you the answers, rather than letting you live with uncertainty. Also doesn't seem to be very long, since I'm 4 hours in and apparently over 50% of the way through.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Really fantastic game concept and well executed. I'd love even more ambiguity in the word definitions, and translation problems between languages. I mean, it's already challenging enough, I just think its fascinating when concepts don't quite translate between different culture's languages. Been having fun playing with a friend and debating the meaning of newly discovered words. Often we have different takes, and one or the other of us turns out to be more correct upon gathering more clues.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting game, with a wonderful premise and beautiful art style. Get ready to take notes though xDPROs:- As stated, beautiful.- The language aspect was VERY cool.- Story narrative was also cool, if a bit generic. Taking things at face value in the beginning only to slowly uncover the secrets of each level of the tower (and the tower overall) felt just as good as slowly deciphering the language.CONs:- I do wish we had some sort of map function for those of us who are directionally challenged in video games. I missed content and spent a lot of time wandering around in circles trying to get where I was going to go.- Some of the puzzles are pretty obtuse unless you did things in the exact right order... which I rarely did, since I tend to try and explore everything instead of following the obvious directed path.- Inability to skip glyph scenes even during a replay of the scene. (Worst part was accidentally hitting a rewatch of the play and sitting there for like 5 minutes.)OTHER NOTES:- Not a con for me, but could be for some -- this game is very difficult unless you're taking notes / referencing screenshots as you play to solve the puzzles. I enjoy making 'game journals' so this game was great for me in this aspect, actually, but some might find it frustrating.- The controls... they're not terrible, but they're not great either. I played with controller but several of the puzzles required me to switch to mouse.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is an incredible game. The story is good, the gameplay is engaging, the puzzles are interesting, the music is incredible and the lore is fascinating. That said, with a run time of less than 10 hours, no/very little replay value, and some janky movement controls in certain sections, I really don't feel like it's worth full price. Buy it when it's on sale, but don't shell out the full $20 like I did.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this, I really did... The linguistic puzzles are too few and far between. The art is dope but not cool enough to justify entire segments of just walking across the screen through several empty set pieces for the sake of walking through empty set pieces. Don't get me started on the (*multiple*!!!) stealth "challenges" in this game. Sucked all of the joy and enthusiasm out of me, dropped this game faster than a hot pan after the 3rd one in 3 hours (a crime!!!!! might as well thrown in a couple underwater levels why don't ya). On a final note, some of these non-linguistic 'puzzles' are just poorly designed in parts. A good game subtly leads the player along the path it wants you to take, it doesn't just hide disjointed interactive elements in empty rooms and hopes you click on a random pillar after steps X Y Z as the one way to move forward. Just not for me, I guess?
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I was immediately excited when I saw that a language game was coming out! The whole concept of deciphering languages through interactions and clues and translating to other languages within the game was so fascinating to me I found the puzzles manageable, coming from a puzzle game enjoyer, and the languages did get harder to decipher as I went up the different worlds (Alchemist world took me three days). The only thing I would've liked having was a mini map to show the layout to keep track where I've been, only because every game I've played has a minimap of sorts. The only time I needed to consult a walkthrough page was towards the last stage (Exile) because it got a little confusing as to what I was supposed to do. Overall, though, it was truly a satisfying game that tickled my brain for it being so affordable!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is a language deciphering/translation game, in the same vein as Heavens Vault. In contrast to Heavens Vault I really liked that the player can guess at what the words mean. Although it does not really affect gameplay since the language deciphering does not ask for the correct translation, but only the correct symbol.This can lead to player getting frustrated (maybe because they missed a clue somewhere or they misunderstood a symbol/word for something else) and just brute forcing the deciphering. This happened to me a few times, but I recommend the game regardless. When the game works (which is nearly 100% of the time) it works perfectly. The language deciphering is satisfying and the small revelations about the different cultures in game give a sense of a bigger world/story. Truly the dark souls of language deciphering games.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: One of the more unique games I've played. It's visuals and music are beautiful, while the game play is can be challenging but fun.While I did find myself "guess and checking" my answers from time to time, the puzzles aren't too difficult. Each language has slightly different mechanics that make learning each fun and unique. It's so satisfying to be able to determine the meaning of a word and be able to go back and fully understand conversations that were previously unintelligible. Definitely a game I would recommend for anyone that loves puzzles.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVED THIS GAME! I could play 100 more levels. I'm a big word=puzzler, so this was right up my alley, along with the cool story, it made for many fun hours. I hope there is a sequel or another variation, maybe with another ancient fable or location, such as the Gardens of Babylon or Atlantis or some such.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most gorgeous game I've ever played. Incredibly atmospheric, fantastic music, visually delicious, calm pace but yet challenging... I wished it lasted longer, I could have spent many more hours in this intriguing yet relaxing world. It's really one of a kind that doesn't resemble anything else. I wish there were more games like that! 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty amazing puzzle / detective game in the Obra Dinn / Golden Idol mold with one major flaw. The biggest issue that keeps this game from being truly amazing is that it has quite a few forced stealth sections. Everything about piecing together the languages of this game are amazing, even when it's almost just a little too obtuse. The fact you can write in what you think the words mean and see the sentences translate that way really helps things along. All in all it's definitely worthwhile to get as the only linguistic puzzle game that's really out there, just prepare for a few dips when the forced stealth comes along.There's also one thing I need to nitpick, one of the languages can't seem to choose its word order. Sometimes it was VSO and others it was SOV. It's tough because it's really great to see them include something that's not SVO (like English is) but even if this is something that occurs in real world languages, I'm sure linguistics majors could give a handful of examples but I couldn't find any, it was a bit annoying to have to guess at the grammar because it kept seeming to change. Maybe there's a context where it changes but I wasn't able to catch on to it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Play it if you want to be pleasantly surprised. Some of the languages follow different syntax than straight translation, so I enjoyed having to think in a different order sometimes when translating. Could be very frustrating, but also very rewarding when you finally got it. And the story, graphics, music, ending, all really lovely. Worth the play.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I can't really put how much I enjoy this game into words very well. The story was great and fun to follow along, and the languages were all so intuitive and creative, it was an absolute blast to solve them all! If only there were more, amazing game, the true ending was incredibly pretty, and so was the rest of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: I'd like to add after finishing the game, that ending sequence was so simple but so well executed.Top quality experienceAs someone who really liked translating Tunic, it's real nice to have an entire game dedicated to translating fictional languages- especially as Sennaar's languages each have different structures & maintain patterns between words like all verbs using the same symbol and so on. Keeps you on your toes while also feeling like a genuine language that could exist and not some mumbled garbage blanketing over generic English
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: First off, I don't know what possessed me to get this game - I STRUGGLE with languages.Second off, this is a really good puzzle game where most of it I didn't need a walkthrough. For me it was the 3rd language being backwards to my normal language that I struggled figuring out the order the words should be in. I missed a few things the first time through but I went back before the final end to get the rest of the achievements.This game isn't too long, as it took me 11.1 hours to do, probably would be quicker if I was better at languages and didn't have to go back for certain bits.But if you want a game which can tell you what it's like to learn languages at times, has a few extra puzzles and a good story then this is the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what an excellent puzzle game. They don't make them as good as this everyday and if you like puzzle games, put this one right at the top of your list, because it is such a treat. I almost wish there were 3 different ranking systems on steam, a thumbs down, a thumbs up and a two thumbs up. Because there are a lot of good games that I have given a thumbs up to, but that doesn't mean they are on the same level.  Just want a way to give the extra accolades, Its beautiful, extremely satisfying, perfect difficulty (Minus that one puzzle that needed me to figure out math, I did use the walkthrough on that lol) but as far as solving the languages, translating between languages, what fun, what a treat.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a lot of fun, mostly puzzles but there is some timed stealth and a chase scene which was the only part I didn't like. Luckily it wasn't to hard and I think most people with some game knowledge should be able to play it. The graphics are really pretty and the whole thing is a delight to look at and explore. I know I will play through the game again.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty simple and smooth puzzle game experience. Thanks to the unique language mechanics, it's a lot of fun to play despite its simplicity.The best part of the game is how everything is tied together. There are a lot of usual Point&Click-style puzzles, like finding an item and bringing it somewhere else or pushing buttons in the correct order, but to find the solution to these simple tasks, you'll have to learn the fictional languages, which requires observation of the world you're exploring, its people and their history. It creates a pretty natural loop where none of the core elements are left out.However, I wouldn't expect complex puzzles or a deep story from this. The game is overall quite simple, but not in a bad way. It's pretty clever and focused in its simplicity, without really having any redundant elements.The only part I had issues with was the ending of the game,
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game, for me it could have gone on another ten hours, but I am glad to have experienced it.I'm a sucker for learning about languages and the little ways they develop, about etymology and more, and the way you can spot connections but also differences in these little languages, the way certain words are used for certain groups, the grammar, the understanding of things.. it's just very nice.And more than about language it's about connection and understanding :) It's our little reverse tower of Babel.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is more of a MIXED review, despite the core of the game being amazing.If you're interested in conlangs or language learning in general, download the demo and give it a try.Great concept, but several QoL features are missing:- There is no mapThis is especially problematic, since most of your time will be spent exploring 5 layers of a convoluted tower, looking for items and glyphs.- Misleading puzzlesSome puzzles cannot prompt you to interact with them, but cannot be solved without first finding a specific item. Once you do find the item, it basically solves the puzzle for you.- The languages become LESS important in the late gameOnce you decipher a language the game gives you complete translations of any sentence as soon as you hover over it. Additionally there's barely any chance to actually engage with the final language, you just interact with 3 objects and get the full vocabulary.It would be much better if hovering over individual characters would only give you a translation of that character, and instead clicking on the speech bubble/sign would translate the whole thing.Overall the core of the game is amazing, but be prepared to waste a lot of time running around similar looking corridors and confusing levels, with no map or guidance as to where you should be going.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful if you enjoy language puzzles! Each language has its own quirks and syntax -- translating from one language to another is tricky and incredibly rewarding. The world is so interesting that you want to explore every nook you can! It's a much bigger game than I expected and well worth the pricetag.Unfortunately, not very replayable. When the game ended I felt very satisfied -- and ready to uninstall. Because I already had all the answers and I don't feel like there's much left to discover.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: It's a fantastic puzzle game that unfortunately has some really awful stealth segments attached to it. They're not bad enough that I wouldn't recommend the game to anyone that likes puzzles, especially people hoping to scratch that deductive puzzle itch that games like Obra Dinn and Golden Idol manage to do.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Somehow, it has the feel of an old school Sierra adventure game (in a good way), through an art filter reminiscent of The Incal and Evan Dahm's art (every time I saw it advertised, I thought it was his work, because of its top notch colors and surreal qualities), all put in a 2.5D environment that begs for exploration and discovery, and of course the linguistic puzzles are really enjoyable to decode (don't forget to pay attention to nuances of grammar!).  I'm not strong with a controller, so I predominantly played on PC, but I also played a bit on Steam Deck.  I think the stealth puzzles are easier on a computer than with a controller, but that may be a me problem.  I appreciated the relatively forgiving fail-mechanics/auto-save which didn't penalize me when I inevitably screwed up somewhere. Beautiful, addicting (I rushed through it in a few days - in retrospect, taking time to map out some of the more confusing areas would have been a good idea to avoid going around in circles as much as I did in parts); I hope to see more from these game-makers because it was a truly enjoyable experience and I loved how the story unfolded.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: What a lovely game. It's all about language and communication, and it's so satisfying to correctly decipher something from context. The clean, bright art style fits the gameplay perfectly. It's brief, <10 hours, but that means it stays focused and doesn't overstay its welcome. There's a few stealth sequences, but they're not too hard. The majority of gameplay is talking to people and exploring. Nothing wrong with games about punching or slashing, of course, but it's nice to see games branch out and take a different approach. Minor negatives are that there's no map, so I got turned around sometimes or had trouble finding things, but the world isn't huge and each area is self-contained, so that's not a big deal. Also the last area uses Rosetta Stone puzzles instead of having you figure things out through conversation, which isn't quite as fun.Definitely recommended for anyone with an interest in languages, or really, for anyone. You can really tell the developers put their hearts into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I loved this game so much, I powered through 12 hours of it. I pulled an all nighter yesterday and now just finished it. The puzzles are great and trying to figure out the different languages are super fun! I also love how you can figure out what is happening for different groups of people just by observing and just guessing when you are limited on knowledge of the language. There were a couple of moments I wish I got a more clear clue for puzzles but I either eventually figured it out or went to the Google haha. I had a blast! Unless you have an insane memory, I can see the replay-ability to figure out the language again. I found that part the best thing. Al the cute little achievements were great too. I was so close to getting all of them. Just missed one. Maybe my next playthrough?
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I play a lot of puzzle games and I really loved this one. It was fun without being too hard, but still challenging enough that I got out a pen and paper a few times. They even play around with the conjugations, and you have to translate stuff from one language to another quite frequently. If you love puzzles and linguistics I highly recommend this game!!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing puzzle game. Not too difficult, but does make you feel really smart at many moments. LOVE how intuitive the languages are; there was clearly a lot of thought put into building them.Do not worry about missing other endings or achievements. No miss-able achievements so you can fully go back and do everything. This gets rid of the need for guides! (If you missed an achievement tied to getting one of the endings, this has been patched. Just get the current ending you are able to get and it will automatically grant it to you)
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Great visual style and atmosphere, puzzles are fun and varied if not overly challenging. I love figuring out the glyphs and then going back to talk to everyone to get the translated lines.Edit: Now that I've finished the game I'll pad out my review a bit. I like how the challenge level gradually builds as you go along, and building connections between the languages gets more and more intuitive as you get into the rhythm of it.Spoilers for ending: All in all I found it a memorable and enjoyable game, and very much worth experiencing. I look forward to seeing what the developer Rundisc comes up with next.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I majorly geeked out on the linguistic variances in each depicted language they integrated in the game, which gave depth on the puzzles. If you're into linguistics and languages, this is the game for you.On top of that, you also get wonderful ambient music and striking artwork and game design. Oh, and did I mention that you can pet the cat? Just a few hiccups for me:
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend if you're a relaxed puzzle gamer who enjoys beautiful colouring and visuals and moving music throughout. The game moves at a good pace and goals and objectives are easy to figure out and don't leave you running around trying to work out what to do. Learning the languages at the beginning is challenging but once you get the hang of it you really start to flow, especially by the end. The note book was a life saver, and I must admit I had the notes app open also (especially when trying to remember syntax). Feel very big brain after playing this - might play again when i've forgotten the languages.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Solid adventure game with some unique gameplay mechanics, stylish art and nice, even if cliche, story. Execution is slightly flawed due to implementation of some of the gameplay mechanics being a bit clumsy(from what I can tell, it's a 2nd game made by this studio and their first adventure game), but it's not detrimental to the enjoyment of the game. May lean a bit on the easy side of the adventure game spectrum, so hardcore adventure & logical puzzle gem fans may find very little challenge. At the same time, this makes the game friendly to more casual players.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Setting aside the wonderful atmosphere, music, design, setting, etc. Chants of Sennaar is one of the few games that really pushes what *games* can do as art rather than another medium such as film, animation etc. It elegantly uses its mechanics to get across ideas very Wittgenstein ideas of language and understanding. (At one particularly tutorialized point it straight up gives you the brick-laying language game). Then as the game unfolds we get to see how precisely the language has influenced culture, and culture influence language. (ex. The bard race don't have a word for their servant class, they just use the term "idiot"). All of this is done with incredible elegance in its core design and creates wonderful understandings and anecdotes in the player that I personally found comparable to my actual experience learning and misunderstanding language. Minor gripes include distaste for some of the stealth segments, more optional translation puzzles/questlines, not being able to communicate to NPCs in their own tongue to relate matters of interest (Preacher, Sewer Man, etc.), and the game beginning with the main character implicitly already having an understanding of the concept of language (there is a lore reason), but the artistry shines through and the grin on my face as I connected the dots (literally and metaphorically) truly outweigh all of these issues substantially. Absolutely phenomenal work and the best puzzle game I've played since perhaps The Outer Wilds. Peak ludo and honestly tops Hi Fi Rush for GOTY 2023
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game I'd recommend most everyone play. And that expands beyond 'gamers' - I'd love to see kids playing this in schools as a demonstration of what can be so interesting in linguistics. Chants of Sennaar is a puzzle game which reminded me of all those pretend languages I invented as a kid but never carried through on. Developer Rundisc - Moya and Panuel specifically - saw to the end what I can only imagine is a linguistic fascination and knowledge to create a videogame that feels like it's pushing the envelope of what constitutes videogame fun, relying on the innate human need to recognise patterns, while wrapping it in a very nice aesthetic package to boot. Structured around a story which emphasises connection via communication, Chants of Sennaar is visually crisp, satisfyingly challenging, and cleverly composed - both in game design and OST. It wrapped up for me at just under 10 hours, which felt just about right (with some very light help from walkthroughs here and there, because I am impatient rather than excessive complexity). Any puzzling frustration was quickly averted by the satisfaction of the solution, which more often than not has you marvelling at the construction of the puzzle in the first place.Any genuine criticisms I have are mild - I would have loved a map, and / or a faster way to navigate. The ability to capture my own diagrams and notes would have been nice, too, but in both cases, these have little to no impact on my enjoyment of the game.I can only hope for a sequel because I need more of this.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This game's innovative idea and its excellent implementation combine into one of the best games I've played. At times esspecially when you enter a new region you can feel a bit overwhelmed but despite that you steadily progress and learn more about the interesting world you found yourself in.tldr: good game, buy it!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Brain usage:If you haven't ever tried to learn another language, (even in school) skip this one.Graphics:Wow this is really nice and looks goodStory:Kinda basic but enjoyable (there are a bunch of guys and they don't get along)Replayability:You won'tScore:If you like puzzles that make ur brain hurt and don't want something too long. Also a very unique sort of challenge. Would recommend on sale for puzzle enthusiasts.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: The language decoding gimmick of this game is absolutely fantastic, and I'm hungry for more.  This game does require some patience though, as much of the time spent playing is clicking something on your screen and watching your character slowly jog there.  There's also some stealth sections which feel out of place and unnecessary, but they're well done and forgiving so I can't really complain.I'm really hoping for a sequel with more challenging solutions.  The difficulty of the puzzles really got interesting when I missed something in the level and had to work with incomplete information, whereas it often felt a little too easy if I find all the 'hints' in the level.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is a great game that combines linguistic & numeric logic puzzles & stealth-lite elements in a chromatic-minimalist art style with excellent mood music. The languages themselves serve as the puzzle pieces & there's a lot of satisfaction in combing out the clues of the citadel for pieces of vocabulary to assemble an understanding of the language, then weaving the pieces between languages together to progress further through the world. It felt like a good way to stretch the brain over a weekend. You can also pet the cat.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is pretty fantastic.  The whole "deciphering alien languages" aspect is new to me and it's well done.  I found it deeply engaging.  My primary complaint with the game is lack of a map to tell when you are, and the often kind of long walking around you have to do to find things.  However this is a minor annoyance in an otherwise stellar game.  I kind of wish that the art was more developed and detailed, but again.  A minor complaint in a game that I thoroughly enjoyed.  I kind of wish the deciphering stuff was a bit harder, as it's pretty minimal right now.  Maybe the dev could think of a way to get more symbols onto one page, as it's pretty trivial to cheese it right now.  If you like puzzle games with novel twists (which are enjoyable) this is one.  You will not be disappointed with it.  It's definitely an 8/10 for me, closer to 9 than 7.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A great puzzle game with a unique concept and a good soundtrack. The concept of gradually discovering languages is a great idea. As a player, you discover symbol after symbol, trying to discern their meaning by their usage in dialogue and writing or by the similarities to other words. Each language has its own system of building words and sentences. Apart from language puzzles, the game includes other puzzles and quick-time events so it never gets boring.The game tells the story of the peoples living inside a tower, that progresses as the player climbs the tower. Some puzzle games suffer from a too linear progression. This game has regions with different paths and secrets to explore. Also, the regions progress with the story. The player can visit again to see how they changed. I really enjoyed playing this game and recommend it to anyone who likes puzzles. And in case you ever get stuck, their is a feature to highlight objects you can interact with.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who has a major interest in language and has studied Linguistics formally, this game was very enjoyable. Of course, it is not as in depth as one might think, you get maybe 40-50 symbols per language, but it still created a very engaging story using language as its major puzzle. I had so much fun with this game that I made sure to get 100%, which was rather easy given that all of the achievements can be unlocked within one playthrough. I am especially impressed with the usage of multiple word orders, I half expected languages to only be SVO (subject verb object) but many of them used different forms. There is also a good representation of strategies to make plural things, how to negate sentences, and how language is used.As someone who loves language and someone who enjoys seeing well made and acurrate representations of real forms. Play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: provides a very enjoyable deciphering puzzle, with a striking visual style, and is enticing enough to remain engaging from beginning to end, despite a rather shallow plot with some tacked-on endgame content and a glaring gap in quality-of-life features.The game provides a very fun puzzle, and I think this has a lot to do with the type of puzzle that it is.  It's just immensely satisfying to piece together an understanding of languages - and the relationships between them - through interpretation of dialog and found writing, and then to answer with the appropriate actions once you become fluent.The difficulty ramps steadily but never gets too difficult to manage.  A sequence of new words might leave a player stumped for a short while, but the game frequently presents the player with illustrations to which to match glyphs by meaning.  This is simultaneously a challenge and a pretty big hint; more than once I found that the illustrations provided a bit too strong of a clue, but overall I didn't find this to be too much of a problem.  The game is a suitable challenge for a pretty casual puzzle-lover, and won't be boring for an aficionado.The game's story is not particularly deep.  I think you'll find yourself engaged more by the puzzle itself than by the story.  There is a marked absence of any particularly interesting characters, but there is still joy in seeing the interactions between characters, especially when you're able to facilitate their cooperation by acting as a translator, a brilliant feature that ties the game's sections up nicely.  The game's environments are varied enough, crisp and nice to look at, and the visual aspect of the glyphs that players must translate is very well done - each language has a distinct design, different words are easily distinguishable, and the relationships between words with similar meanings are clever (and make the player feel clever for noticing them).The game provides a solid interface - the Journal - for tracking the meanings of words (including being able to type your own custom note prior to confirming the true meaning, a great feature).  But the game's greatest flaw is the lack of comprehensive logging.  I was extremely dismayed to see that the only way to review previously-seen dialog or text is to , which can become quite tedious.  There are some cases where the game will add some extra notes to the Journal for you automatically, but I was truly surprised that the game doesn't simply provide  text for review, at least as a simple log.  This, and perhaps the story, is where this game compares very unfavourably to , a similar game which provides extensive ability to review past text, a feature which I think ought to be mandatory for the genre.  Its absence is a significant annoyance, but hopefully short of game-breaking for most players; consider taking some notes and screenshots of your own as you play.I've not seen too many games of this kind (deciphering languages); as such, almost every game like this is a must-play for me, given my interest in the genre.  If  had the language logging features of , it would have done wonders to improve the experience.  Regardless, even without,  easily clears the bar for a strong recommendation to anyone interested.(I feel the need to make one final note regarding comparison to , which has issues of its own - due to the truly awful navigation that plagues that game, I would give the overall edge slightly to  if forced to choose between the two.  I'd certainly play this game first - if you still hunger for translation puzzles afterward, and you can stomach extreme clunkiness in a general sense, then move on to .)

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very interesting puzzle game based around languages. If you like to learn languages like I do, then take a look - Chants of Sennaar has essentially taken the language-learning process and gamified it. What results is a puzzle game that has a sense of satisfaction to it like no other when you get the answer right.The basic premise of Chants of Sennaar is based on the Tower of Babel. There are 5 distinct peoples with 5 distinct languages who cannot communicate with each other. You start from nothing and over the course of the game you gradually learn each of the different languages and eventually use that knowledge to help translate conversations between different peoples to unite them. It's very satisfying to have started from nothing and end up using one language to translate another.The in-game languages are all fictional and it's entirely text-based. You start off simple by using clues like signs on buildings and watching what people do when commands are ordered to figure out what different symbols mean. While there are some grammar differences between languages, such as different word orders, it's mostly vocabulary-based. Learn the words for "move", "box", "carry" etc to figure out what someone is asking you to do and then complete the task. Filling out your own personal dictionary involves identifying 3/4 symbols on a page and associating them with a drawing of an action or object. My gripe here is that sometimes the meaning of the drawings isn't clear. Things like 'Sun' and 'Key' are easy and obvious enough but I thought the drawing for the word 'Call' was referring to an angel or something. It sucks when you are not sure of a word but you don't even know what word you're trying to define. However, when you DO get the answer correct, there's a satisfaction that is unlike any other puzzle game, as it follows the same sort of process you'd use when trying to understand a new language in real life and you get that same "aha!" moment.Graphically the game is pretty basic and I'm not a fan of the simple geometric structures and backgrounds. The environments are kind of abstract, which suits the game, and each people of the tower has their own distinct identity, but it wasn't a very visually interesting game. It felt like programmer art, or something like computer art from the 90s. The buildings felt like 3D representations of an architect's blueprint rather than an actual building, for example.The worst bits are when the game strays from its strengths. It's a language-based puzzle game, but for some reason the developers felt the need to include some light stealth and platforming sections where you have to time your movements or run away from something. I guess they felt the need to provide some more variety to the gameplay but these were my least favourite bits. They're not terrible and they're meant to provide some sense of danger but I don't think they really gel well with the rest of the game.Fundamentally, this is a solid puzzle game that will appeal to language nerds. It's a very niche game but if that niche suits you then you'll probably enjoy Chants of Sennaar.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a unique game where you try to decipher symbols to find out what words they correlate to. You do this by observing the environment and speaking to characters in the world. After finding a symbol in the world, you can type in what you think the word is. It's totally free form. You also have a journal that shows you some pictures and each picture has a place for a symbol. If you place all of the correct symbols on the same page, it tells you what the symbols mean. Then if you encounter that symbol in the world or if you talk to someone, the words are inserted into the conversation whereas before it would just be "..." for each word or the "..." would be replaced temporarily by whatever you had guessed the word to be. You can change your guess at any time for all of the symbols. It's fairly difficult, but it feels rewarding when you solve a puzzle. I've never played anything like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Quite a fun little puzzle game, easily worth the money. I liked the visual style: simple but with enough depth, shadow, and variation to keep things interesting. The gameplay weaves the cryptograms, exploration, and environmental puzzles together in a way that is mostly tight though not always perfect. Near the very end of the game, a few puzzles are highly simplified in a way that seems intended to speed up that part of the game. It needs to be sped up because that part of that chapter of the game doesn't have enough environmental or story complexity to sustain the explore-learn-solve loop you enjoyed in the rest of the game. I would have enjoyed the game more if it had managed to have that complexity and maintained the same gameplay feel. Instead, the game starts to focus on wrapping up its story and the gameplay feels less dense, less tightly designed. I wouldn't call the ending of the game unsatisfying, but it does feel like it didn't get to incubate as long as the other parts of the game. Overall, the game presented me with a good variety of environments and puzzles and languages, held my interest until the end, and is worth recommending to anyone who likes the idea of being dropped into a strange world where you have to figure out a series of strange languages as well as where everything is and how everything works.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very charming game that does a lot with a little in every aspect of it's design.  The ways in which the story is told through making connections between different languages and the ways cultures do or don't interact is really cool and it's easy to recommend for most puzzle game fans, though this comes with more caveats than most Steam reviews and this won't interest players looking for something difficult.The early language puzzles felt too linear and susceptible to brute forcing over the organic logical deduction I enjoyed near the end, the game can often suffer from old adventure-era backtracking to check for information or trigger certain events, and the story often lacked intrigue until near the end where it then struggles with some poor use of cliches that threaten the much stronger narrative arc it has.The game ends strong though, and it's still just a really cool and interesting piece all round.

_childDocuments_.review: the game would've benefited a lot from focusing more on the linguistics and less on everything else.the premise is simple. you go up the proverbial tower of babel and learn languages. there's 5 languages across the game, but the language difficulty counter-intuitively kinda peaks at the third one. the fifth language is a joke and it takes only like 3 minutes to figure out all of the words in it once you get over the initial hump.the languages are all very simple. there are no grammatical cases or prepositions. the sentences never grow in complexity beyond "you give me tool" or "i not like you". this makes the game very accessible to anyone without any sort of linguistic experience but it also makes the core mechanic of the game - linguistics - lack any real depth. it barely educates the player on how different real languages work, and the core puzzle mechanic - figuring out words - remains a gimmick. each language's vocabulary is very limited as well.the languages don't have any obvious connection to each other. as you move from one area to the next one, anything you learned from the previous language has no bearing on the new one, aside from an occasional plaque where you will see the same phrase written in two languages.all the words are single glyphs, meaning its much harder to actually remember the words just based on the way they look, which makes you want to rely a lot more on the in-game dictionary and auto-translation feature. you can go through the whole game without really learning any of the languages in it.there are non-linguistics sequences that basically amount to clunky stealth sections that really break the flow of the game and feel very out of place. they can also get really frustrating. there's a lot of walking. a lot. of. walking.admittedly, figuring out a language feels satisfying in the moment, but ultimately it left me wanting for a lot more than what was in the game. if you're looking for a game that really goes hard on linguistics - this is not it.the visual design was really strong. the story was kinda mid. feels like the devs themselves kinda gave up near the end. game could've been a lot more.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: fantastic game. I can't remember the last time I marathoned a single-player game from start to finish, but Chants of Sennaar just reset the timer.- The language decoding is genuinely fun, and both the logograms and the grammars are clearly loving nods to some real-life natural languages—e.g., there are real languages that have distinct plural markers or use reduplication to mean "many", one of the writing systems is an obvious wink to Devanagari script, so on. They're pretty simple overall, but it's a good balance—any more complicated and it would probably turn off a lot of people who don't have a special interest in linguistics. (No I totally don't have a fixation on linguistics, why do you ask?)- It's a pretty game, in its own way. It's not super detailed graphically, but it doesn't need to be; it's economical and thoughtful about how it uses shape and color, and that pays off. Even with a limited palette and fairly uncomplicated line art, each area is carefully put together and has its own very distinct visual vibe. It also means it'll run on a potato with integrated graphics crudely glued on, and I think this game deserves to have a wide swath of people who can play it. (That said, some of the illustrations in the journal are unexpectedly beautiful—make sure to spend a few minutes admiring them.)- Good balance on difficulty. I like puzzle and stealth games a lot, and there was a section or two that stumped me for a few minutes. Only a few minutes, though—someone who isn't used to puzzles or stealth might find some sections challenging, but I don't think it'll be so challenging as to put them off the game. The puzzles are also clever as hell but still feel approachable; they depend more on being observant and a little bit of logic.- The plot is definitely there, but leaves some room for interpretation; it does a lot of showing instead of telling. I like this and don't mind plots being a little vague or leaving some open questions, but this could be a downside for some people, so bear it in mind.- Good at explaining the basics of what it wants you to do without actually explaining it. Good guidance, no handholding.- The fast travel system is helpful, but it's still kind of a pain in the butt to get around sometimes, and no map means you gotta do a lot of backtracking and getting lost until you have the area roughly mapped out in your head. That definitely has some appeal for an exploration vibe, but even then it can be frustrating at times. It'd actually be easily solved by making the player character run just a tiny little bit faster when out of danger.- Does not feel good to play with mouse and keyboard. It's  improved by using a controller, to the point that I'd say a controller is basically a requirement for getting the most out of the game.- The auto-positioning for the stealth sections is really annoying, and the explanation for how to switch to free movement took me a minute to find again. I understand why it's there and it's probably a big help for some people, but if you're experienced with stealth games, you will probably find it irritating.- Too short. Gimme like 3 more floors I wanna keep playing kthx :)Again, overall, fabulous game, and frankly I'd have paid double the price and still thought it was a good deal.

_childDocuments_.review: *I was not paid for this game, but received it for free as part of a Dare Drop campaign.*Having said that, after playing for 8 hours straight I have to say I highly, highly recommend. The game works in such a way as to maintain a sense of progress and movement, whilst not feeling hand-holdy or simple. There are puzzles, and secrets to be found, and unknowns that you will have to just accept as unknown until later on. The process of discovery and understanding is captured so well in the game, and the game managed to continually pique my curiosity. Further, the setting of the game, and the stuff you find out as the game plays on just makes the whole thing come together really nicely. I'm not done with the game; I am maybe around 40-50% through.There are plenty of shortcuts and connecting paths in the world design to help reward exploration, without ruining the sense of feeling lost in a new world. (Also very helpful if trying to go back to an unsolved puzzle, for example.) There was some slight backtracking I had to do, which felt slow, but in part this was because I hadn't fully explored a given area - once that was solved it fixed that feeling. I for sure am looking forward to playing some more. Definite recommend from me, especially given the fact there's a demo available currently.Pleasant surprise, this one!

_childDocuments_.review: I tried the demo and it convinced me to buy the game, which I finished in around 8 hours.The principles are rather simple, but also clever and quite strong. I really appreciated that each language you need to discover have different grammars (to handle plural, negation...) but without going into smaller tedious details (tenses, conjugation, declination, the touchy topic of articles, genders...) : it remains a game not a linguistic exercice.The world (lore and art) is sober and colorful, simple, but with enough relevant details to make it memorable and likable.There are a few levels where you need some back and forth to handle the puzzles, but I felt the design did a good job guiding me and helping me understand what was expected (even though, to be frank, I sometimes had to try some combination several times before finding the solution).Overall, I recommend this game if you are attracted to the theme. If you are hesitant, I really recommend the free demo that will help you figure out if this game is for you or not.

_childDocuments_.review: The art in Chants of Sennaar is amazing, hands down. The game is so artistically unique. The strong yellows and reds help the game stand out, but depending on the area the game is not afraid to stray away from its yellow color palette for cooler blues and whites. No issues there.Obviously a game like this is going to struggle in the story department, and I have to agree that the story is not exactly ground breaking. Smart people made a tower, others came to the tower, height-based hierarchies formed, racism ensued. No one before you has had the ability to translate between the languages, or if they did it was forgotten a long time ago.Chants of Sennaar relies heavily on the language mechanics and exploration. The issue I have is that the exploration feels far too similar to a traditional point and click adventure. I had hoped that the game would lean heavier on having to use the languages I’ve learned to gain access to new locations. The game shines brightest in its language learning theme, but it relies too heavily on key-door style mechanics to reward the player for learning the intricacies of the varied languages the game has on offer.Some counterexamples are the higher level translation puzzles that is revealed to the player early on, but are only solvable later in the playthrough. These puzzles are stimulating and engaging. They make me wish the languages were more homogenized throughout the world in order to allow for basic translation to act as a progression mechanic on a smaller scale.Even worse are the games stealth sections. Mandatory stealth sections are a horse that was beaten to death years ago. The game has mandatory stealth sections, and their inclusion feels silly and awkward.Is Chants of Sennar good? Yes absolutely. The game clocks in at about 13 hours for me, and it has an absurdly high finish rate of about 55.5% according to steam achievements. Considering most games have a completion rate of about 13% or lower I’d say this game is very worth your time!If you do play Chants of Sennar, you should turn off achievement notifications because there is an early game spoiler that gets revealed from them *wipes tears from face*.

_childDocuments_.review: A phenomenal experience, bittersweet only in that it is so complete that I can't imagine a Chants 2 ever being made. It is a whole experience, a completely contained story, and that is extremely refreshing and a little sad.This game really gets everything right: the Moebius inspired art style conveys beauty and simplicity, the level design that communicates so much about the peoples of each level of the tower, the game design involved in teaching languages to the player, the complexity of the puzzles is never too overbearing, the many simple mysteries that invite the player into the setting, the moving soundtrack that fills the game with emotion, even travel is easy with several fast travel locations strategically placed for maximum convenience. It is, put simply, a work of art.On more than one occasion this game brought me back to Myst. Each of the new peoples' I met told a different story and showed a different way of living in this world. Their words told me stories beyond what they actually said which were reflected in the meanings they ascribed to them. Each puzzle or device had a kind of tactility to it where you could just play around and figure out more about the machine... there is one machine in particular that teaches you how one of the peoples count just by fiddling around with it! The game lets you guess at words based on your own interpretations, but also provides a journal which lets you confirm your understanding for each new symbol discovered. You don't HAVE to use the journal, but once you do it provides a new layer of contextual understanding to the language in question.None of the languages are overly complex: the game doesn't delve into tenses and verb conjugation, and it is all the better for it. It is great that some of the languages are syntactically different without the extremely complex differences many real life languages have. This allows the player to translate more easily than they would be able to do with real languages, but still with some assumptions or deductions needing to be made to truly make those translations work. The stealth was fine. It didn't make me stop playing. I understand that it was probably included in order to break up the pacing and add some tension, and it did that, and it was fine. There should generally be ups and downs in player tension throughout a game, but really I could have done without them. Myst never needed parts where a bad guy chases you and honestly, neither did Sennaar. This is a phenomenal game. It has all the best parts of Heaven's Vault without the very sudden and unpredictable scene transitions you can't come back from and the stupid glider travel mechanic. It has a lot of the best parts of Myst including fiddly puzzles and simple mysteries that are really pared down to their most essential elements. It has an excellent story and a moving soundtrack and gorgeous art... what more could you want?! Go buy it right now!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A really phenomenal game! It has an absolutely gorgeous art style, and it felt incredibly rewarding to learn the words, grammar, and linguistics of different languages and explore the Tower's different societies. I really admire the linguistic logic in each language, and the commitment to teaching about the world in a very natural feeling way. This recommendation does come with an asterisk, though: I first tried playing this game in Latino Spanish, and found I had to brute force through one of the areas, where the translation (provided to the player) and the original words (the physical untranslated words in-universe) didn't translate in a way that made any sense. I could discover individual words, but couldn't understand its reading order or translate from language to language. Frustrated, I switched the game language to English, and found that the sentence structure was changed in a way that didn't reflect in the slightest in the Latino Spanish translation. Otherwise, the Latino Spanish translation was extremely well done! I also realize that translating changing sentence structure is difficult (many languages don't even facilitate that!) but its a little disappointing that a game all about translation doesn't work in one area if you're playing in some languages.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is the first game in a few years that's grabbed me enough to keep me up late into the night because I don't want to stop playing. But I've absolutely loved everything about this game - it's full of character, the art is gorgeous (and whoever did the camera work deserves an award), the language puzzles are tough but also keep you feeling like you're making progress, and the logic/stealth puzzles add enough variety to keep the game from feeling like it has one note to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: It's like if Duolingo was a puzzle game, and for a bunch of (really neat) fictional languages instead of real ones. I almost didn't realize how good I was getting at understanding these made-up languages until I stumbled upon the meta-puzzle around mid-way through the game (several hours in) and realized I could already confidently translate between three of the languages without even looking at the in-game reference book.The languages are all really interesting too, and each of them have their own unique vocabulary based on the speakers' culture, different pluralization rules, different word order (SVO/OSV etc.), punctuation rules, compounding rules, etc. Translating between them is real fun too, since there are several instances where the target language doesn't quite have the same vocabulary as the source language, and you're forced to improvise a bit. Would've been a great game to have around while I was taking linguistics classes lol.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who doesn't have a lot of time to sit down and play a game, this was a refreshing change of pace. _childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: It's exactly what it's meant to be: a linguistic puzzle game. It's a nice brain teaser, there's always enough hints to go on, but it still requires some thought to go through, especially in the later parts of the game. Once you have enough clues, you can also do some brute forcing to solve some puzzles (notably validating glyphs) but at some point cheating just a bit is fine. The only other notable gameplay mechanic is the stealth, which is serviceable. All in all it's a pleasant game to go through, although obviously as a puzzle game there's not much replay to do.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A nice, mostly relaxed puzzle game that might make you think for a while!You spend much of your time trying to translate the glyphs (or words) of other languages whilst solving a variety of puzzles as you climb the tower. The 'threats' in this game are fun, but have little consequence, ultimately meaning you can learn at your own pace, yet they still give the impression of tension. Checkpoints are very generous, rarely getting in the way of actual progress.Chants of Sennaar spends it's time wisely, at first luring you into thinking that core is just a matter of translation, but it's far more than what it seems. Without giving too much away, do make sure you don't skip any puzzles you find, as the proper ending is wonderfully meaningful without saying a word.A clever, well thought design, with a vibrant and deeply unique aesthetic. Well worth a purchase!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: The dark souls of duolingo. You gotta learn various languages inferring their syntaxes and words by seeing people talk and act or just plain signs in the world. While you advance, new languages shows up with different symbols and syntaxes. Making this game a compelling learning curve.Progress is saved in a journal; matching symbols with depictions of concepts, once you get a page correctly: english words now appear over their in-game symbol counterpart. The problem with this is that you can easily brute force it, trying all the permutations of the symbols over the concepts. I hope nobody will do it like this. My major issue with this game are the stealth sections: they seem off and doesnt feel aligned with the purpose of the game. For me, they just hinder the progression in a non compelling way. Another problem this game has is the pacing, once you get the hang of the gimmick and the innovation wears off, you have seem everything, now its just doing the same over and over.Despite its flaws, this game is innovative enough to provide a worthwhile experience that i recommend everyone to enjoy.

_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: What a brilliant game. The execution of the language puzzles is so unique and it feels so satisfying. As you discover glyphs, you can write down notes of your guesses as to what they mean, and periodically, you will associate them with pictures in your journal, upon which the game will validate their meanings. But it's not just about learning the languages. You will then use them, both to solve other puzzles and to translate between the different cultures that inhabit the tower. Once you've validated glyphs, the game will automatically translate them when you see them, but it's a special kind of satisfying when you realize you can read them even before the translation pops up.The visual design is impeccable, the soundtrack is gorgeous, and the UI is unobtrusive and functional. One of the best games I've ever played. I wish I could wipe my memory of it and do it all over again.

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is a second person linguistic puzzle game with a minimalist but enchanting artstyle.The game is a masterpiece, the second person camera charm reminded me of flash puzzle games like Steppenwolf and especially Chasm.Figuring out glyphs of different languages, you can learn by context and assign custom placeholders for glyphs you encounter, which leads to many humorous encounters with dodgy translations as they use your placeholders. Learning these fictional languages is extremely fun and you'll notice having the languages "click" for you as you proceed.Syntax, context, translations, deduction will be your tools in decoding languages and the difficulty ramps up in a satisfying way.The stealth sections are not bad at all and are well executed and sparse.If you like a game where youre dropped into a world you need to figure out to proceed (like Obduction or Outer Wilds), or if you even remotely enjoy languages and symbolism, you will love Chants of Sennaar.Best to go in blind, so take care with looking to much into the game before playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting puzzle game that has you navigate a series of environments and cultures, trying to decipher the languages and grammar patterns use that knowledge to complete further puzzles to progress. Whilst the premise can sound daunting, it gives you enough help to get by, and the game is paced well so that when you start to hit a stumbling block, you'll inevitably find a clue that can help solve the issue. The languages each have their own distinct grammar patterns as seen in real languages that keep sentence formation varied, even when you know the words, and stop it devolving into a checkbox exercise. There's also some clues as to the origin of the symbols, and the root of more complex or precise words can be seen in the symbols used, something explored more in the latter chapters.The only potential note of improvement would be an option to sort your currently learned glyphs, which would greatly help with the translation challengesWith that being the only note, and a minor one at that, I cannot recommend this enough, especially with the demo to let you see how you get on with the early stages

_childDocuments_.review: I guess that's another French game I play without knowing its background and discovering at the end that it was created by a wooping 5 persons. Congratulations to them, just a word to Thomas : Quitte ton boulot pour le prochain, dormir 3 heures par nuit, ça tue la santé.The logic of the game makes it easier for you to eventually categorize the glyphes and guess what they mean depending on the glyphe aspect and the place in the sentence. The Devotee language is quite simple and the style allow you to approach the game feeling like you can actually understand what is said and when you're wrong, you're not that far off. As you progress, it's impossible to deny the prejudice between the various inhabitants of the tower, the simple facts the warriors think that the devotee are impure is enough to have you sitting for a few minutes and ponder what could have happened that made them think that way. Language isn't only about communicating about the weather, but also opinion. The fact that the word devotee doesn't exist in the warrior language and is replaced by impure mirrors our own prejudices implied in our own language. I think that besides the terrible infiltration parts (for which I was forced to switch from controller to mouse every single time), this game is rewarding and push you to think of yourself and the languages you know.If there is an advice to give to people who only know their native language, it would be to play this game and maybe consider spending time learning a new language. This will open your mind as you'll notice how your own language can be derogatory regarding a topic while another language wouldn't and vice versa.To end this lenghty review, I'll just say that I did appreciate freeing the "workers" and finding them back discussing with the Devotee. This part of the game made me uncomfortable until I could act on it. A reminder that slavery was a thing and still is in some part of the world is important, getting uncomfortable regarding this topic is important. Passivity and acceptation of things as they are because "what can I do about that anyway" isn't how we should consider anything uncomfortable.

_childDocuments_.review: A great knowledge-based game marred by QoL annoyances and questionable design choices.For QoL, there is a lot of running around and backtracking in order to solve puzzles. Unfortunately, the run speed is slow and you often need to move the character past the edge of the screen to make the camera reveal the whole scene, meaning you have to first click the edge, then move the character past, then finally to where you want to go. Not to mention, the character stops briefly every time you click a new spot, so the process becomes even slower. In addition, there are teleport points, but you have to walk all the way to the specific rooms they're in to teleport to another one. This makes backtracking even more time-wasting, and made me want to quit several times. It would make much more sense to be able to teleport to those points from anywhere.As for design choices, I feel that the interesting and main part of the game, decoding language, is made too easy while the uninteresting parts, like finding items and solving non-language puzzles, are unintuitive and obscure. For the language part, the fact that pages in the notebook show up only after it can be solved with the current known vocabulary (i.e. after that page's words have been seen) makes it way too obvious which words belong on that page. As a fake example, say you find a new word "Z" on a sign with no context, and then immediately after, you open your notebook to a page with 3 types of food. Without any actual language decoding, you now know that Z is a type of food, and that 2 other known words are also types of food, completely ruining any attempts to figure it out yourself. The uninteresting parts are the complete opposite of this. A lot of the puzzles rely on obscure items or sequences that are not given any hints at all, making progressing frustrating. Ironically, the puzzle design is anti-language; words can be ambiguous and still convey meaning, while the puzzles can only be solved in one exact way.All in all, Chants of Sennaar scratched the itch for knowledge-based gaming similar to Outer Wilds and Tunic, but it could have been much better.

_childDocuments_.review: More language-based puzzle games please! This gave me a lot of Heaven's Vault vibes (one of my favorites) and I had a lot of fun with it. I sometimes found it a bit too easy to get all of the glyphs for a specific language especially as the game progressed. In a game like this, I do like when there's still some mystery after the first playthrough, but on the other hand it also made the whole experience feel very tight and intentional (props to the designer there). The devs also did a really great job differentiating the different biomes/factions and their associated set of glyphs. There is also a bit more linguistic complexity in this game than I'm used to seeing. For example, different languages have different word order or even specific question  markers. This elevates the puzzles above simple word-for-word translations and adds a bit of naturalism to the game that language nerds will really appreciate.Biggest wishes for a sequel or another game in this style:- More of the translation puzzles between two in-game languages; these were really fun and required that you really understood the rules- More "useless" words in the languages to increase the mystery/easter eggs and deepen the world-buildingAll that being said, congrats to the two-person dev team. This is a 2023 gem and I hope more people experience it

_childDocuments_.review: First off, do not play this game if you don't like jumpscares or flashes of the screen. This occurs if you get caught by an enemy character during stealth moments. It really put me off the game as I couldn't turn this off and it can be very scary!Overall, this is a solid game and I can see why it has such positive reviews. I have been eager to experience all the hype and took my time to fully complete all the achievements the game has to offer (this took me 10.9 hours). The art is incredible, truly absolutely outstanding. The animations are smooth, the music a delight, and the premise of collecting the words and matching up their meanings works refreshingly well. However, the stealth aspects are very lacking and the jumpscares really ruined the experience for me. When I got to the final language I felt like things had got a little rushed and the language discovery wasn't as satisfying. There were a number of points towards the end where I became reliant on a walkthrough guide as I had, unknowingly, been completing the game out of sequence. I love the flexibility you have in exploring each area at your own pace, but the frustration of having a page missing and a language therefore unable to be "completed" clouded this. The narratives that appear at the end of the game seem to go a bit off topic and I felt like I was playing a different game entirely.In summary, this is one of the most beautiful games you can play and listen to, if you can put aside the stealth sections and jumpscares.

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy games like Myst or Quern: Undying Thoughts you will likely love this game.  The art and sound design are fantastic and the puzzles (while not super challenging) are enough to keep a puzzler fan interested.It's a bit short at only 9 hours to completion, but most puzzlers aren't really expected to be long games.  The translation mechanic is well thought out (mostly) but there are a few points that are targeted for solving when there is (in my opinion) insufficient context to figure out the meaning without using meta knowledge like process of elimination and brute-force solving.  This becomes more and more pronounced in the latter half of the game.  I'd love to see this studio give another go at a sequel but try to make the whole game have the quality of the first half!

_childDocuments_.review: For years i am now regularly scouring the depths of the internet for those little indie gems, that feel fresh and innovative, the ones with the little extra. With Chants of Sennaar I might have found one of the most amazing games in a long time. The amount of thought that must have went into building the game world is mind boggling. Basically it is a simulation of the tower of babel, inhabited by multiple peoples with different customs and languages that grow increasingly hostile against each other. Your task at first sounds unsurmountable: Without any previous knowledge at all, learn all the different languages from scratch, including their glyphs and grammar and then use them to befriend and interconnect all the peoples.But the way the developers have constructed the gameflow is so genius and the story so gripping, that i could barely stop. So you run around with your little notebook, collecting context clues for the various glyphs, solving puzzles, trying to make sense of it all, piecing it all together, step by step. Figuring out the meaning of a new glyph or finally realizing what that one guy in the sewers wanted to tell you, is so satisfying and rewarding, that you will feel like a language genius. There are also many twists and turns that will keep you on your toes until the very end. I am still totally blown away, this is truly something special and will go into my all-time-top 10 indie games. So if you have only the slightest interest in puzzlesolving, exploring strange worlds or languages, you should give it a try!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not a fan of exploration type games but this is gorgeous and engaging. I heard about the premise of the game from Instagram. _childDocuments_.review: Very fun game. I would recommend if you want a casual puzzle game with a simple story. Not super difficult but does require some thought and effort. The game was longer then I thought it would be which was nice, It took me about 12hrs I think but I am a generally slower player lol. The story is simple but interesting still, and well communicated despite the limited vocab used throughout the game. The final message is nice but overall not the draw of the game. The puzzles were pretty good. The fake languages are interesting and each unique while still being similar enough to translate between. Outside of the language part there is still some interesting puzzles, and even after you translate everything there is puzzle to be had, although the deciphering is the big one. The game was occasionally confusing on what was next if you missed something but generally I'd say it was on the easier side. If you want an exceptionally challenging puzzle this is probably not the right fit but I would not say it was too easy to ever be boring. The deciphering part becomes easier and easier as you do it more and learn the general theme of the game but even the last ones (there is about 200) had their own little twists to be interesting.  There is a lot of time spent waiting for the character to walk across the screen, which can get tiring if you are stuck and need to go back and forth looking for things but I never found myself annoyed with it (I got stuck at one point trying to find something for a bit and that was the closest I got to bored while playing). The rune check system can also sometimes give the answer away or allow you to brute force it but that is mostly up to your own actions. Overall I would say the game was a good buy - I bought it on sale and would say it was worth the price.
