_childDocuments_.review: Gotta say this game is great. Chants of Sennaar is an extremely fun puzzle game that is very immersive and thrilling to play. This review does contain spoilers and there are tons of things to commend so I’d recommend getting the game and experiencing it yourself. The music in the game is absolutely stunning. The score swoops and soars with new discoveries, stellar views, and tense chases. It always perfectly accented the mood and really gave life to the many areas of the Tower.—---------- Minor SpoilersSpeaking of the Tower, the level design was extremely fun to play through. I played this game with my partner and most of her comments about the game were about how massive and elaborate the area’s felt. The colour choices in the different layers of the Tower were excellent at evoking the feeling of the people that inhabit it and what they do. Pastel yellows and oranges fill the grounds of the Abbey, stoic blues and reds adore the ways of the Fortress, pale white and yellows accented by sharp reds accentuate the opulence of the Garden, the curious oranges and purples of the Laboratories, and finally the other worldly yellows and purples of Exile. I’d say my personal favorite area was Exile. The regal almost alien purples with sharp ascending yellows gives a very unique and semi-off putting vibe to the final stage of the game. In the beginning each area felt dead, with the people being miserable and trying to venture further up the Tower. (Except for the bards, but I’ll go over that later). As you continue to play and connect the people through the terminals the area’s begin to become more alive with people crossing into different layers of the Tower. Another design aspect that I liked was the people in the Tower. The clothes of the Devotees in the Abbey strongly resembled burqa with adorning headwear to represent their position in their faith. The washed out seafoam green of their robes helped them to stand out against the oranges of the Abbey. The armour of the Warriors complimented the blues of the Fortress with maroon red robes and very distinct helmets. They were my personal favourite design. The roman aesthetic of the Bard’s robes fit well with the ancient Greek and Roman styles of the Garden. As well, the mask emblematic of the Comedy and Tragedy masks opposing the drab blue grey masks of the idiot Bards highlight their caste system very well. I do feel that the designs of the Alchemists were a bit bland, but they are very recognisable with masks that somewhat resemble a flattened version of the classic plague doctor mask. Their robes also stand out well against the background with strong bold colours. The final design was a bit perturbing being for the Anchorites. They seem to wear pure white masks with black tear tracks wearing odd coloured clothing in floating hunched chairs. I believe the off putting design is to accentuate the impacts that Exile has had on the people. =========== Major Spoilers	I really enjoyed the puzzles, especially those that involved the different languages. There were plenty of non-language based puzzles, but the language ones were the most unique and intriguing. The puzzles never felt too difficult, but also sometimes were the easiest. The developers definitely found a good balance of difficulty. But I can’t talk about the best puzzles without talking about the languages that are the game's calling card.I loved the concept of basically walking through the tower of Babel and trying to learn your way to the top. Most langues felt very unique with only two that felt a little too similar. A few of my favourite quirks of the languages were: In the Abbey, they would signify plurality by doubling their nouns, the verb noun sentence structure in the Garden, the overlapping runes building further ideas in Exile (Like German, but superimposing instead of adding a million tailing words), and the numbering system of the Alchemists. Each language had ways of showing whether a glyph was a person noun, a verb, an object, or a location each of which was very interesting to figure out. The one language that, in retrospect, I felt wasn’t very unique was the Warriors language. Compared to all the things I exemplified above it felt very bland, and scarily similar to that of the Alchemists. Not to say I don’t like it, it was just the least unique which is ok. Clearly a lot of thought and care went into the construction of each language into making them function and believable in the story.Story wise this game is a bit of a mystery. You begin the game waking up from a sarcophagus in the Abbey learning that each layer of the Tower is segregated and try to ascend to the top. Once you reach Exile you find what’s happened to the Tower. An AI called Exile trapped all the Anchorites in virtual realities causing the Tower to lose its ability to communicate between its different peoples. You eventually find an Anchorite that tells you that they created us to fight Exile, free the Anchorites, and restore the Tower to its former glory. After turning off a few of Exiles stations you eventually reach the top of the Tower where it seems you couldn’t unite the Tower. It then seems as if the game resets starting back at the beginning, but the areas are devoid of the people that once inhabited them. You can find glitching text from exile trying to rewrite the Tower to keep you from escaping. You eventually break free from your virtual reality Exile trapped you in and finally turn it off saving the Tower with the final cutscene showing that the glyphs that represent each people's core beliefs all derive from the same core idea atop the Tower ending with the people from different parts of the Tower talking to each other finally able to communicate. It’s not explained why Exile was created, but it can be speculated it was to keep the Anchorites safe or to make their life easier. This led it to trap all the people in virtual reality so they never need to worry about the outside world leading to the Tower deteriorating in their absence. >>>>>>>>> Spoiler’s Over	Overall this game was a very enjoyable experience and is well deserving of its best indie game award in 2024. Take all my rubles.

_childDocuments_.review: I would absolutely recommend this game to everyone who doesn't mind taking their time and thinking things through. A literal Tower of Babel experience, Chants of Sennaar puts you into a world without any cultural or social understanding, and then you piece together languages by interacting with locals and recognising contexts. I can't say I was every truly stuck in this game, never had a moment I wanted to Google an answer, and felt supremely rewarded by understanding a word after a while of thinking. I cannot recommend it more strongly to people who enjoy games like The Witness, Myst, or even someone who may have enjoyed some puzzle aspects of Tunic. Give it a go, you'll have a good time.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game about reuniting those who are closer than they think.Beautiful yet simple graphics, even simpler controls, and designs that show the different roles and personalities between communities. The ending music genuinely gave me goosebumps.Admittedly, I did have to look up solutions at parts (although I highly suspect that's just user error), and there's a fair amount of backtracking, especially if you want all the achievements- but the storytelling and puzzles make up for it, 100%.All in all, would definitely recommend Chants of Sennaar for those who enjoy casual puzzle games.

_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a wonderful little game about linguistics. You are in a tower (of Babel) trying to puzzle out the speech patterns of five different languages from five distinct cultures. You pour over their alphabets and try to figure out how they do their plurals and how they say no. You have to use a lot of context clues and the game can be pretty generous with hints at times, but it's still a wonderful experience. It's quite rewarding to go from being completely clueless about what is going on around you as you build a vocabulary and gain more and more understanding of the story. I played this doing couch co-op with my wife, who knows 9 languages and attacked these linguistic problems with terrifying efficiency. On my own I would have probably had a lot of trouble with parts of this thing, but it wasn't too difficult for two intellects to tackle. I think that's the best way to play the game personally, but that's just me. There aren't many (or any?) other games like this and if the basic idea of playing a game about language is not enough to deter you, then I think you will find a great deal of enjoyment here.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I  enjoyed this gem of a game! (It's so good, I even recommended it to strangers at a party, lol.)It's a very satisfying puzzle experience. You get to decipher the languages of the different character factions and piece together the story of why they're there and their relationships with one another.There are a lot of different puzzle types, keeping it engaging throughout, with none of the puzzle solutions being overly obscure or too complicated to solve. Most things were very intuitive. I only needed to look at a walkthrough video twice for a couple of minor things.If there's  to nitpick (and I mean really  nitpicks)...

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is the perfect pickup for a weekend of gaming.  It blends its storytelling with its puzzles to keep you engaged and active from start to finish.I think greatest triumph of this game is how well paced the language puzzles were.  The game starts you off with a very simple, photographic language that you can quickly discern from the shapes alone.  As you progress, the languages begin abstracting away from pictures and into more complicated, but still structured lexicons.  .   I loved how each layer of the tower had its own personality.  The denizens of each layer are given character not only by their environment, but also by how their lexicon looks, how it is structured, and how you learn it.  The greatest example of this being the bards and alchemists.  The bards are chatty, expressive, and artistic.  Their script is calligraphic, flowing, and places a focus on objects rather than subjects.  You will learn many of your bardic words from chatting with them and viewing their works of art.  Conversely, the alchemists are research driven and data focused.  Their language is geometric with shapes indicating parts of speech and obvious patterns that allow you to puzzle words together from the ones you already know.  You won't learn as much chatting with an alchemist compared to a bard. Instead you should look at their research and conduct your own using their tools.  Putting yourself in their shoes helps you make the discoveries needed to progress.The story itself is cute and simple, but in a charming way.  It's certainly not the meat of the game, but it's a nice side dish that comes with each word you learn and room you explore.  Given the nature of the game, I applaud the fact that there was an easily understood story at all, so you'll find no complaints from me here.What I will complain about is the amount of backtracking.  How streamlined your experience is can vary greatly based on how well you remember where key items are.  Someone may be able to 100% the game and backtrack only once or twice if they play as efficiently as possible.  That someone certainly isn't me, as I must have spent at least 20% of the game running through places I had already been, searching for something I found an hour ago but didn't know how to use yet. There was also a stealth section very early on that frustrated me.  A guard off screen kept spotting me and sending me back to the start. I had no clue how to progress, but I did eventually brute-force my way past him.Those are minor, forgivable flaws for a puzzle game that does so much in so little time.  I highly recommend picking this one up if you've got the money to spare and a weekend with no plans.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. It's designed to be a wonderful experience from start to finish. The illustration and animation art is great and goes well with the personalities and languages every different group of people have. I recommend playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit apprehensive about playing this game at first. It's been ages since I last played an adventure game which heavily relies on puzzles as its core mechanic. Normally, The genres I'm more familiar with would be roguelike, adventure, strategy or FPS. This game turned out to be a very pleasant surprise. What intrigued me the most about the game was its setting, from the title alone (the Koine Greek rendition of the Hebrew Shin'ar) you can deduce that the game draws inspiration from Biblical narratives, in this case the Tower of Babel (which was located in the land of Shin'ar).The story takes you on a quest to reach the top of the tower, and without spoiling too much of the story much of it consists in deciphering the different languages spoken on the tower's different levels. Having a background in linguistics, the puzzles were quite enjoyable to me as the drive to decipher alien-looking scripts comes naturally to me, I am however well aware that I might be an exception here and some of you could end up discovering that what I deem to be an entertaining pastime is a form of mental torture.The puzzles are not overly complex, that's not to say they're easy and at times you might really want to pause and return to this game when you're more rested, with a fresher aptitude to think out of the box as there are some "stumbling blocks" along the way to the top so to speak. Tellingly, I did not consult a guide throughout my playthrough, so again the puzzles are all manageable.The design and graphics are alright, the art style is original and every level has its own peculiar atmosphere and distinct set of colours. The stealth mechanic is a bit iffy but I've seen worse (including in stealth games), thankfully there's not a lot of sneaking around in this game. The soundtrack isn't particularly striking or memorable, I certainly won't be listening it to it in my free time, but at the very least it isn't annoying which in my view is a much more essential point. The story is OK, remastering Biblical themes is no easy task and I think the developers managed to pull it off as gracefully as could be hoped for. In terms of replayability, this game has low potential considering that it is a very linear one.Verdict: If you like adventure, puzzles, intrigue and/or have a thing for Biblical narratives (regardless of whether you're a religious person), I would definitely recommend giving this game a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A dream game for any linguist, anthropologist, or autistic person (me)I can't really put how much I love this game into words, its an incredible example of modern video games evolving. It has incredible design that utilizes cultural influences, color palettes, and architecture to define and differentiate all the civilizations. It immediately explains the lifestyle and culture of the characters before you are able to understand them through language.AND THE LANGUAGE ASPECT, THE FEATURE THAT REELED ME IN, IS STUNNING!!!! Oh I could write a thesis on how cool this is! Each language has it's own syntax and grammar which makes translation into a fun puzzle of sorts. Each language has a unique written style that conveys the history and culture of the world around you and it is a dream.SPOILERS KIND OF - NOT FOR THE STORY The devotees are on the lowest level, they're very simple and their lives revolve mostly around religion. Their language reflects this perfectly. There are very few words, no formal plural form, and consist of easy and small strokes. Compare this to the bards, a more complex civilization that centers around art and leisure. Their language consists of very painterly and detailed strokes. They have words to indicate tone and plural forms. There are more words, they span beyond religion and cover places and activities which indicates their wealthy and indulgent lifestyles. Don't hesitate just buy it

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game, an indie masterpiece! I really enjoyed the way the game develops and the main mechanic of learning these mysterious languages through the clues and context as you play is creative and well thought. _childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I had fun with this game - languages were different from each other despite using similar building blocks, the story that was there might not be the greatest but it was engaging enough and the score complemented the simple visuals nicely.The only thing I didn't really like in this game is stealth mechanics and some more faster-paced sections - I'd rather have some cutscenes instead of these - instead of tension I felt frustration battling against the (lack of) controls.It took me about 7hours to complete the game 100%.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I was blown away by this game. The ending had me with tears in my eyes! If you like the linguistics gameplay of Heaven's Vault, the detective gameplay of Return of the Obra Dinn, anthropology, religion, and/or philology, this is a game for you!My one (minor) gripe is the stealth sections. They don't overstay their welcome, and they aren't so difficult that they presented any real blocker for me, but they aren't as fun or fleshed out as the puzzles or the linguistic gameplay. For example, there's no real way to evade pursuers if you get spotted, which I think should be standard for a stealth game. Still, they're pretty straightforward sections and the autosave is very forgiving, so I can't complain too much. I just want more linguistic goodness!Overall, I can't recommend this game enough. _childDocuments_.review: "Chants of Sennaar" is a visually stunning puzzle game full of great ideas - but ultimately fails to offer a comprehensive and meaningful set of mechanics to decipher, learn and understand its languages.The game actually makes a strong first impression. Overall presentation and quality is fantastic, whether it's the unique and colorful visual style, the great soundtrack and sound design, or even the user interface. The idea is incredible as well. Using the learning of languages not only as a puzzle mechanic but also as part of an overarching storyline to reunite different groups of people and cultures? Sounds intriguing, count me in.There's just one problem: The main puzzle mechanic - learning languages - barely works.In the rare moments it does, the game is fun and engaging. Often you're able decipher the meaning of symbols from imagery, gestures, or locations. Comparing different sentences to each other can be a good strategy to discover common symbols or symbol placement. Occasionally you can even translate from previously learned languages. And every time you think you understand what a symbol means you can write it down in your journal, in your own words (free text).All solid mechanics - if it weren't for the fact that you're only really able to figure out a few of the many symbols within each language. The game simply fails to provide sufficient information and source material for the rest. The only way forward? Guessing. And the game mechanics, intentional or not, even seem to enforce this behaviour. A chat log is nowhere to bee seen, you'd need to constantly backtrack to actual locations. The journal comes with drawings next to symbols, and all of the sudden you're playing a game of (often painfully ambiguous) image matching rather than actually deciphering a language. The game - regularly! - turns into plain trial-and-error and tedious bruteforcing. Once you finally "figure out" a group of symbols, their true meaning is revealed - and with that your own definitions are gone. The results can be mind boggling; a "rock" is actually "carbon", another randomly guessed symbol is meant to be "duty".I may have been able to overlook the variety of smaller issues this game has, such as the long and confusing ending, the regular backtracking and unnecessary stealth sections, or the weird and limited controller implementation. But the undercooked puzzle mechanics turn this game into a very unsatisfying and often frustrating experience.I cannot recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Great puzzles, great story, I hope there will be more games like this. Discovering the languages bit by bit is very fun, some words are more obvious then others, and sometimes the actual meaning is surprising. The languages don't just have different words for the same things, but also different (simple) grammar and special words depending on their speaker's needs.Not much explanation is needed, the game design is very visual, highlighting the important objects.10/10Minor things I would have wished for:- longer story- ability to reorder words ()- faster travel/skip to the doors, some paths are very long and require waiting for a different camera angle, which can become tedious if you have to travel around a lot or get lost

_childDocuments_.review: Very qualified amazing game.  It's an indie puzzle game.The good, it has a unique puzzle element that is a lot of fun to figure out, specifically, learning symbolic languages.  It has a interesting story, that uses the different races fairly well.  It isn't pure puzzle, and there is an interesting sprinkle of very easy game play.  It uses limited point and click actions very well.  You probably won't have played anything quite like it.The bad.  If you want great graphics or action, this doesn't offer either.  There is too much pointless walking around and backtracking for my taste, particularly if you want to complete all achievements.  A couple of the puzzles are ridiculously hard, and basically just require you to guess, however, most of them can be figured out by paying attention.  I hate the sewers - it's a maze you have to navigate while walking around for no reason - just terrible and frustrating design.I'd give it a 10 or 10 for it's intended audience, if not for the bad, which take a point away for just being annoying.  I still highly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely buy and play this game.Do you like Obra Dinn? Do you want more silent high-contrast environments to explore, so you can piece together a wide web of puzzles? Then Chants of Sennaar is for you. The conceit of the game is you go through several different cultures, learning their written languages from context clues. What was amazing about this experience to me, besides being a fun puzzle game, is that it totally activated the language learning center of my brain. I'm currently on a 60 day duolingo streak learning Japanese, and the amount of symbols that I saw and mapped to their Japanese word equivalents surprised me.Each culture has their own distinct personality, that directly ties into the structure of their language. 10/10 would climb the tower of babel again.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: If you've heard of this game, it's probably for its clever language puzzles and slowly piecing together new cultures by picking up words. While that's still there, nobody brings up its heart-touching story about compassion and understanding. HARD recommend if you enjoy emotional investment and gaining mastery of a space through curiosity.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a well-crafted and delightful little puzzle game that demonstrates an excellent understanding of how to make art style and game design work to make the gameplay experience maximally enjoyable. Everything about the visual presentation and the moment-to-moment interfacing and interaction with the world is right on the money, and it does a lot to help deliver a really solid experience -- allowing us to better enjoy the world created for us. The nature of the puzzles, storyline, linear game structure, and NPC interactions are highly creative and it's implemented in a way that feels very intuitive and takes very little explanation... thanks to these successes, it's easy to become immersed in the game's world not in spite of its minimalism, but because of it.Around 8-10hrs of puzzle gameplay in total. I would recommend this at its base price to avid puzzle gamers who enjoyed titles like Journey (2012), Myst (1993), Gorogoa (2018) and Return of the Obra Dinn (2018). I would recommend this at a discounted price to ANYONE.

_childDocuments_.review: It's an intriguing and beautiful game that puts your curiosity and skill to the test while entertaining you with its beautiful soundtrack and landscapes. _childDocuments_.review: TL:DR; Fun low impact puzzle game, but if you're in it for the language deciphering, try Heaven's Vault instead. I played the demo first, which is basically the first chapter and gives you a good idea of what this game is. If you're on the fence, try that first. It's a point and click game that's mostly without time pressure. There is one chapter where there are a couple of jump scares, and one chapter that is time sensitive. However, both have rules built in that give you some breathing space so it's not an impossible mad dash. If you do end up dying at any point, you just respawn and there are save points built in in the puzzles themselves, so you don't need to endlessly start over the same puzzle, I rather liked that. The languages themselves are basically also just puzzles, and the game is good at making you find the solutions. Some people consider that too much handholding, I thought it was fine as I wasn't looking for a big challenge. The languages do seem to each follow certain rules, but the system is nowhere near as intricate and coherent as, for instance, Heaven's Vault. If you're in it for the language element, try that one instead. Replayability is basically zero, at least for me. There is no 'start+' option, the story is static. You solve the puzzles, the end. But if that's what you're going for, then yes, it's engaging and easy enough to keep you occupied for some hours without it becoming grinding or demanding.

Reaching a culmination of understanding of the different languages to the point where I could  felt so organically rewarding. Very soulful and rewarding. Highly recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: In the spectrum of "I wanted more" to "I looked up the answers," Chants of Sennaar sits in the "I wanted more" camp. I you want a puzzle game that offers a unique challenge then you have found your game. However, I will warn that this game is not for the puzzler die-hard. Often I would finish a language (world) and wish that there were a few more puzzles to test my linguistic wit. This is not to say that Chants is easy, but very rarely do you use causal reasoning to figure out the meaning of words. The last language offers the hope of a linguists dream, but the little circle matching mini game at the end ruined all hope of this. I recommend this game because you will enjoy it, but will leave you wishing for more.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredible game. This is exactly what I wanted a game about languages to be: drop in with little instruction and try to learn the language by reading signs, talking to people, making educated guesses, and paying close attention! I really felt the lack of a map (I spent way too much time getting lost and walking in circles and being frustrated), and I think the otherwise lovely ending was . _childDocuments_.review: I cannot recommend this game enough. On a mechanical level, the puzzles are immaculate and everything you manage to decrypt feels earned. Each puzzle feels distinct, but there's enough common ground from what you know to what you're trying to figure out that you can intuit what you need. _childDocuments_.review: ----SPOILER ALERT-----This text-based puzzle game is a gentle introduction to linguistics and hieroglyphic alphabet systems. The illustration of five different peoples under the same tower separated by languages was very exquisite, and every shade of detail that one experiences in a single playthrough engenders a vivid characterization of this world, as if we unravel the mysteries behind a people while leaning their language. The design of the game Finale in connecting the link between every pair of people to reach a union was also very illuminating, emphasizing the importance of communication. As for the bread and butter of the game, the game puzzles have moderate difficulty, and with decent guidance the game itself provides, it shouldn't be hard to reach the true end of the game. The most interesting design of the language system would be the way parts of a glyph potentially represent the partial meaning of the glyph as a whole, and similar glyphs may share a component (in technical terms, the glyph alphabets are ideograms). If you practice languages that have this feature (i.e. Chinese) then many features of the game would be unimaginably explicit and natural. Now to the critical part. The game puzzles opened up a lot of interesting ideas, such as the derivation from conventional English SVO structure (as in the Bard's language) and the formation of glyphs based on the composition of simpler ones (as in the Anchorites' language). However, the extent to which these ideas are developed in the puzzles is mildly unsatisfying. In the alphabet systems, the sets of vocabulary are mostly the same, and the way glyphs are constructed is roughly the same (i.e. verbs possessing a specific characteristic). At the last stage--the exiles--the language with the most exquisite writing system, but the puzzle-solving experience is significantly diminished. There are no more dialogues or text logs the player refers to. Instead, the glyphs are translated completely from prior languages, and specifically the way the puzzles in this level are designed makes the process of learning this language brainless and even boring.  Most of the puzzles simply require one or two layers of cross-reference, sometimes with a few brain twists. Notably, the pictures the main character drew confused me at times. Components of the game other than puzzle-solving, such as stealth, are much less interesting compared to the actual puzzles. Replacing them with more thought-provoking puzzles that develop the ideas to a greater extent would significantly improve the game experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely charming game, had a great time playing it. The game makes you feel really clever for working out the puzzles, though they're not especially difficult. I think some of the pure puzzler game was lost in aid of the story telling, which is fine, it was clearly the priority for the studio, though I do wish the languages had been a little deeper/harder. _childDocuments_.review: I never leave reviews on Steam games, but this is a work of art.I know it sounds hyperbolic but finishing this game caused a physical reaction to me that has never occurred in my years of gaming - my hands began to shake and my head felt like it was bursting, I stood up to walk it off and had to sit down again after getting short of breath, I'm dying out here and I love it. I almost NEVER talk games up this much - there's a handful of games I've had somewhat similar experiences to, but this is the first time I actually felt PHYSICALLY ILL in suspense as the end credits started rolling. Plot twist after plot twist, the game absolutely bombards you rapid-fire with jaw-dropping realizations and intricate callbacks, tying in everything from the very first shot to the final chapter and everything else in between. That's the thing about Chants of Sennar - it doesn't waste your time. So many other games would spend HOURS and HOURS slapping you with new systems and extra features, cutscenes after cutscenes until the awe has faded and you're just waiting for everyone to stop screwing around and get to the final boss already. But CoS condenses as much excitement, creativity, and wonder as it can into a single stretch of gameplay, and then just when your intrigue starts to dip, it moves on to another chapter absolutely dripping with inspiration. In just 21 hours of gameplay it invoked more astonishment than all the time I put into Tears of the Kingdom and Breath of the Wild combined.At its core, the theme of the game is the concept of language barriers and an attempt to bridge cultural gaps between peoples who can't even communicate with each other - after spending hours soaking up all the information a nation has about their neighbors you ascend to the next city and understand that your friends were wrong. Not COMPLETELY wrong, just...OFF. Missing context perhaps. You'll meet characters late in the game who are responsible for the actions which occurred earlier on, although at the time it was interpreted as something else; citizens from opposing nations will describe their relationships in such completely opposite ways, oblivious to who the others truly are.Chants of Sennar is the prime example of gameplay mechanics being a thousand times more important than graphics - not to insult the obvious attention to detail put into these simplistic, nearly monocolor set pieces. Whether complex and detailed, rigid and militaristic, simple and repetitive, the glyphs you read tell so much more about the people speaking them than just the words themselves. Each language feels so REAL and USED, even if we're only introduced to around thirty words or so, because each has its own recognizable patterns and systems - some cultures put the subject first, some the verb - some have a symbol for "plural" other designate it by putting the same word twice, if the word for "human" is a lowercase j, then you can bet the word for any occupation will be some variant of that. At one point I got so used to these glyphs and sentence structure that I completely stopped seeing them as glyphs to decode and started reading them as...well, words. I saw "  " and said "One book, comin' right up!" with no hesitation.There ARE some pointless stealth/math puzzles that bordered on tedium, but in reality I cannot honestly call this game anything short of breathtaking. The only thing stopping me from recommending this to every single person I know is how much of my enjoyment probably came from my personal preferences - I can't say this is the best game ever made, but I CAN say that this is the game that feels the most like it was made for me specifically. Everything I look for in a game, everything that gets me hype, this hit all of it just right to create this endless river of amazement as I played. I don't know how anyone else feels, but for me this is a solid 5/5. The replay value seems shallow as I've already memorized huge portions of all the languages, but it's not out of the question that I might just go through and do it all over again five minutes from now.

_childDocuments_.review: And the whole earth was of one language, and of one speech.And it came to pass, as they journeyed from the east, that they found a plain in the land of Shinar; and they dwelt there.And they said one to another, Go to, let us make brick, and burn them throughly. And they had brick for stone, and slime had they for morter.And they said, Go to, let us build us a city and a tower, whose top may reach unto heaven; and let us make us a name, lest we be scattered abroad upon the face of the whole earth.And the Lord came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men builded.And the LORD said, Behold, the people is one, and they have all one language; and this they begin to do: and now nothing will be restrained from them, which they have imagined to do.Go to, let us go down, and there confound their language, that they may not understand one another's speech.So the LORD scattered them abroad from thence upon the face of all the earth: and they left off to build the city.Therefore is the name of it called Babel; because the LORD did there confound the language of all the earth: and from thence did the LORD scatter them abroad upon the face of all the earth.

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is just a wonderful game of deduction and logic; a point and click adventure that is fantastic at occasionally making you feel really stupid, followed immediately by you feeling like an absolute genius. the "AHA" moments on this one can be really strong. The real meat of this game though is definitely the further you go in, as it goes from letting you learn a language piece by piece to absolutely overloading you with information and letting you solve your way around it, it can occasionally be intimidating but I never found it frustrating. Yes the "stealth" stuff isn't amazing, but it's simple and quick and does add some occasional flavour that I do think adds some good world-building so I get why it's there, I actually have more issue with a "cart-moving" puzzle in the early game if anything because I think it gives the wrong impression that the language stuff is going to be surrounded by filler.... it isn't. The further you go in the more every puzzle is defined by language and by the end all the puzzles are solely language based and it's so good and satisfying and fun.Seriously this is a great puzzle game that only gets more investing the further you get in; I cannot recommend it enough, I loved it!

_childDocuments_.review: While Heaven's Vault is focused on one language in depth, Chants of Sennaar, true to the Biblical tale (Gen 11:1-9), is focused on multiple languages, as well as the relations between them.  Not everything is straightforward and English-like either, as sometimes you might have your typical SVO ordering, but other times it might be SOV or OSV, just like in natural languages found around the world!  But fear not, for this is not a difficult game, and no linguistic experience is necessary to enjoy this game.That said, Chants of Sennaar is a somewhat short game, with around 8-10 hours to 100% the game (6-8 hours to simply beat it), and so each of the languages is not explored in depth, nor are there many of them.  Still, games like this are important for fleshing out a genre of sorts.  Language itself is part of storytelling, and so let us never forget of the  of ways it can be done (including whether spoken, or written in alphabet, abjad, abugida, syllabry, and/or ideographic/logographic)!  Yes, there is so much untapped potential when it comes to language — more so than music or art — and who else but the freer-than-AAA indie devs to break into these barriers first. In fact, what I just said above is the main reason I'm nominating this game for the "Most Innovative Gameplay" award.The artstyle reminds me of Journey, Sable, Heaven's Vault (albeit mildly), and Monument Valley (mostly in the isometric perspective, but also the point-and-click way of moving); and the music reminds me a little bit of what Austin Wintory composed for The Pathless.  All in all, I'd say it's worth its full $20 price.

_childDocuments_.review: Simple but intriguing gameplay that ends just a moment too soon.Chants of Sennaar is a delightful and visually gorgeous game centered around language translation. The premise is rather simple: you are a wanderer in a tower with no understanding of the words and symbols around you, and through context clues, visual puzzles, and general knowledge of how people communicate, you can gradually begin to understand what people are saying to you. Of course, once you've figured out one language, there's suddenly another group with another language to learn. This is the core gameplay loop: working through how one language is constructed via puzzles, determining what you must do to further ascend the tower, encountering a new group, and starting over again. Each of these groups is visually distinct, has their own set of priorities and values, and constructs their language in a different way, requiring the player to think about how we communicate things like sentence order, negation, and plurality.Over the course of a few languages, the game presents numerous puzzles that challenge not only what the player thinks each symbol means, but how they are used in a myriad of settings. For example, a simple card game early on demonstrates not just what those words mean, but how the things represented form a sort of hierarchy, which comes back later in a number of ways. It's also fascinating to see objects and concepts change between groups, adding to the different ways these groups see not only the world, but also each other. Though simple, the game manages the balance between exploring the tower's languages and learning about the world quite well, such that the player never feels like they are sliding backwards just because there's a new unfamiliar language. In short, the strong thematic differences and ways of challenging the player keep the core gameplay loop compelling throughout the experience.My only complaints are that 1) I would have loved to have seen more puzzles about translating between one language and another, and 2) I genuinely wish the game was longer. On the first point, the vast majority of the game is about learning languages for yourself, and the only puzzles that require you to translate from one language to another arrive pretty late into the game, they're small, and there aren't that many. For a game centered around figuring out languages, moving between them feels like a natural evolution that I wish had more room to grow. Leading into the second point, I want more game! My own journey took just under 7 hours from start to finish, and while I enjoyed every second of it, it does feel like certain things weren't fleshed out as much as I would like. Along with the translation puzzles, it's only really once you reach the last language that the game introduces more complex ideas, like how logographic languages differ from syllabic or alphabetic ones. Suddenly, language is vastly more complex! I can see how these different symbols were formed, and how prior languages do something similar! It's bold, it's exciting, I'm all ready for some puzzles that will test my knowledge, and... the game is over. I would not change a thing about the first six hours, but they do set up one final push at the end that doesn't fully materialize.I would be overjoyed to see more of this world and dive deep into the power of language. Even still, Chants of Sennaar is a wonderful experience for anyone interested in language and/or puzzle games, and I recommend it wholeheartedly!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Beautifully atmospheric puzzle game. I really enjoyed the variety of translation tools you were required to use. Some were straightforward logic or observation, but many required more complex understanding of the structure of the languages, the cultures they are representative of, and even the nature of the script itself.Later areas and puzzle concepts felt underdeveloped however, and the difficulty and complexity ramps up for the first 3 areas and then plateaus disappointingly. Rather than exploring a mystery, constructing an idea in your head, and measuring it against reality, it feels like you're simply being given the answers towards the end. Still a strong recommendation based on the first three areas but I am left yearning for more.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Very gripping gameplay! You work your way up a gigantic tower, while discovering different cultures in the process. And for about 9 hours of gameplay (inlcuding all achievements) 20 bucks seem a little excessive - but hey, it's a small developer.Play the demo and see for yourself if this is worth your time. (It was in my case.)

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game giving it the benefit of the doubt but it ended up really disappointing me. The premise of the game is amazing but it was squandered. My negative feelings started in the tutorial when they give you the definitive answer to the meaning of the symbols right after introducing them, taking out all the fun of figuring it out myself. Then they just never stopped giving me the answer. The only actual puzzles once the devs removed the puzzle of building the language felt like those artificial game lengthener puzzles that don't require solving so much as clicking around until the game give you a code to a door. Then they stuck terrible stealth gameplay into it and I couldn't do it anymore. Are we really waiting for guards to walk back and forth in a linguistic puzzle game?I don't know why everybody likes this game aside from the good premise. The game Tunic does linguistic mystery much better while also being a fun game. I'm not mad, I'm just disappointed...
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is everything I love about puzzle games that don't hold your hand (ie, Witness, even though these are not Witness style puzzles).  It also has a classic point and click adventure game vibe with some of the exploring.  And one of those games that tells a story with gradual reveals of lore and a changing world.  Do yourself a favor and try really hard not to look hints or spoilers up.  If you get stuck, take a break, come back later.  Explore, back track, look for things you may have missed or clues you may not have put together.  It's worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: only issue I have is how the game immediately confirms and give the correct answer once you have correctly placed the glyphs in a single page, this takes away any suspicion and doubt you might still have on the meaning of the glyph and makes it too hand-holdyother than that what a great game, 9/10 would recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe 40% of this is an interesting language puzzle game about determining glyph meanings from context and across glyph sets. There's some execution here I could critique (meanings are rigidly "unlocked", the final language is a cop-out that feels like they ran out of time) but the rest of the game is the greater issue.Another 40% is a mixed bag split between stock adventure game puzzles in the vein of "find the widget in room A that must be used in room Z" and unfun stealth segments.The last 20%, I swear to god, is just walking around. Either you're fighting the slow player movement and the player character pathing issues or you're backtracking through half a dozen empty rooms at a time. The game is also inconsistent about what information goes into your journal automatically, so for certain puzzles this compounds the backtracking issues. By the final stretch of the game I had lost patience completely and looked up the solutions for the last few puzzles to see if the finale would turn my opinion around any. It didn't: it felt like they had an idea they were building up to organically in earlier sections but they second-guessed whether it would land and hamfistedly emphasized it with final-stretch elements.It's unfortunate because I really enjoy language and knowledge-based puzzles, and the mood of the first four segments was engaging enough to keep me going in spite of the control flaws, but I just didn't care for Chants of Sennaar as a whole and would not recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Once again jewel recomended by Steam discovery queue (it works yay!).Last few days I was completly submerged to lingvistic adventure in the Tower. Sometimes I was afraid geting stuck but everything in this game make sense and it's just about observing and deducting. For once I hardly find something to complain. Maybe this is it...one of those mythical 10/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is a stylistic linguistic puzzle game that challenges the player to explore a crumbing city while piecing together the inhabitants' language from context clues, artefacts, and one-sided conversations.If you have any interest in linguistics, puzzles, or strong art direction, to play the demo now - it's a good taste for the rest of the game, save for some light-ish action sequences that appear in the full game.  A few of those are a bit overtuned for what is otherwise an extremely accessibility-friendly game, but they're thankfully rare, and retries are quick.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A super creative and satisfying puzzle game! If you're interested in language and linguistics, I think that this game will be especially interesting for you. And if you're not into language/linguistics, but are into environmental storytelling (as in - a lot of what you learn about the world of the game is directly related to you interacting and being in the world) and creative puzzles, I think you'll enjoy this too! The art direction is absolutely stunning, from the character design, to the environmental design and to the music of the game. The feeling of 'it's all coming together' when you start figuring out how translate the glyphs is super satisfying.My only feedback is that, mechanically, I wish that there was a way to rearrange the glyphs after discovering them. However, this is more of a 'something extra that would be nice' - not being able to rearrange the glyphs does not make the gameplay any less compelling.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is a well rounded, short, yet profound experience. The puzzles in this game convey the feeling of deciphering a foreign language very convincingly, and for the most part do not get boring as the game progresses over roughly 9 hours. Only the puzzles of the last chapter fall a bit flat.I have rarely seen a puzzle game in which narrative and mechanics are so tightly interwoven as they are in Chants of Sennaar. Over and over again I found myself in awe as the pieces of a puzzle, and thus a sentence, came together and revealed the next beat of the story. The artstyle is beautifully minimalistic and very coherent, lending each nation of the tower its own color scheme. The soundtrack appears scarcely, but makes a great impact when it takes the place of the eerie silence otherwise present in the game.Definetely recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: The puzzles were just difficult enough to be interesting and challenging without being frustrating.  As a former linguistics student, it was also cool to see the patterns in the languages, and I'm glad they had different sentence order for the bard language, as well as different plural locations/ways of communicating pluralisation.  It's also a visually stunning game with great shape and colour language.  Phenomenal!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: It was so good but I don't know damn what to say. Try not to see the tips but you may need some in case you lose the way. I did haha. Love it and I look forward to play similar type of game in the future. _childDocuments_.review: Extremely cool game!!!!!The best and the only game I played about language, feels like Duolingou.Fantastic and cute storytelling, the setting where warriors like music is so cute. _childDocuments_.review: I'm really enjoying the way the language discovery is unveiling the plot of this game. The way that the different groups identify themselves and the unique grammar structures are delightful. Being able to make any notes you would like about words/characters based on design, context, or even vibes can be so rewarding and sometimes funny!
