_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful language point and click puzzle game where the main challenge of the puzzle is figuring out what the puzzle is asking you to solve! It's extremely rewarding seeing your guesses of foreign hieroglyphs you've presumed based off context clues be verified. Main critique was that the "action moments" eg: the avoiding rocks section/being chased - don't have any real consequences other than just setting you back 3 seconds so they never really invoked any kind of sense of fear and ultimately just felt out of place for the game...and maybe the character walks a little slow for my liking.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: thank you developers, art designers, and everyone else who worked on making, funding, & promoting this game. it is one of, if not, the most interesting, unique, and thoughtful game i have ever played. as soon as i heard of it and played the demo i instantly knew i needed to buy it and play it through. i sincerely hope and would urge you to make another game like this in one capacity or another. be it a sequel/prequel type thing with other towers to climb and unite through language deciphering/translation and puzzles, a dlc, or a totally different take with the same language and journal aspect. if you create another game like this or dlc, i would gladly buy it and play it again. thanks again, and i hope to see more things like this from the chants of sennaar team so i can continue to buy, support, and play masterpieces like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Has the worst sort of adventure game logic going on. The game actively enourages you to just spam choices until something clicks--if you are honest with yourself about when you do and don't understand something, you might leave a bunch of pages open in your journal and have to sort things out later. On the other hand, if you just brute force each journal page as soon as you can, you're a lot less likely to be confused. This isn't helped by the fact that the layout of the world is part of the "mystery" or something, so there's no map or obvious guideposts--I traversed most screens several times just making sure I didn't miss anything or nothing had changed since I last was there, and movement in this game is so tedious.It's basically about as good as any mediocre point-and-click. You're not here for the logic, you're here to click on things until the game tells you that you're a genius boy. Good job, you.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fantastic idea for a game that is executed pretty well! I especially enjoyed how each language's ideograms had different structures and combinations of shapes to denote its grammatical context - for example, a square surrounding an ideogram in one language indicates it is a physical place, while another might use a dot under one to do so. Every language only uses a few dozen of these, but it makes translations much less tedious. The only negative that I can think of is the forced stealth sections, which should honestly be removed or reworked. Overall though, a 9/10 for me!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Intriguing world, smooth gameplay experience, only got stuck and had to check a FAQ twice (if I'd been playing with someone else on the couch I bet I'd have had more patience). I have a few quibbles with some story beats but it's a solid, beautiful experience! Highly recommend it to anyone interested in linguistics, minimalist storytelling, or relatively easy puzzles. A bit like Heaven's Vault, Unpacking, and Strange Horticulture, in those ways respectively.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: So... I played this one beginning to end on a day off. And just wow. SUCH a great game! One of the best, to be sure. The art style is delightfully clean, the colors are lush, and I got a really immersive feeling despite the fact that it's POV and line art. The music and atmospheric sounds are flawless. They create a really still, quiet, but comforting feel. The story has way more heart and beauty than I'd expected, given the quiet and calm of this game. And the language based game play was just as intuitive and also tricky as The Witness at times. It's such a unique idea, and I want more games like this! Makes me feel so smart to learn a new language so fast lol. But I actually started to just read some of the glyphs without the subtitles, which was very ego-boosting.  It took me about 8.5 hours to complete the game in one sitting (excluding snack and bathroom breaks) but I just didn't want to leave the cozy vibes. The puzzles weren't extremely hard, but some got me stuck for a few minutes so it was fun to get a steady stream of little breakthroughs. The hardest part for me were the time-based puzzles, but those were also VERY forgiving with quick saves at multiple steps which kept it from getting frustrating. Honestly, no complaints. Even with an 8 hour play time, I think the price is quite fair given the sheer quality, fun, coziness, and beauty of this game. Treat yourself! This one's worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Phenomenal puzzle game held back by some very mediocre stealth/action sections. I think its still worth playing, the language discovery is very cool, but I had some moments of genuine frustration when I was pulled out my puzzle solving enjoyment to engage with the mediocre stealth systems or action segments.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I significantly preferred this to the other language translation game I’ve played, Heaven’s Vault. I loved that with Chants of Sennaar, I could type in my estimate translations, and continue to work from those hypotheses as I met other characters and found other puzzles. Translations can be brute forced if you wish, but the gameplay does not require it, and you can delay validating your translations until you feel sure of them. Heaven’s Vault’s translation mechanic was far less appealing to me, much as I loved the language design. Ultimately Heaven’s Vault is primarily a narrative game and Chants of Sennaar primarily a puzzle game (though still with a meaningful story). The language translation satisfyingly integrates with the other styles of puzzles in the game. It is also beautiful to look at.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic little game, I can really tell the love which has gone into it. I went in expecting this to be a pretty short and simple experience, but it just keeps on giving!! Plus it has real cat voice actors so that's just purrrrfect. Revisit the game in future, definitely I shall."ME WORSHIP COME TOWER" is probably the best mistake I made.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I saw that Northernlion was playing this game and knew within seconds that I had to play myself. I absolutely loved this game and it has now become one of my favorites. I have wanted a fictional language puzzle game for years and this one delivered in every way. The art style is breathtaking and the languages are well thought out. The puzzles are challenging enough to be satisfying when you solve them, without them becoming overwhelming or impossible. I am eagerly awaiting a sequel!!!If you're on the fence, get it! I cannot recommend it enough!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Rare nowadays to come across something you've never seen before. The language decoding system is completely unique and very fun. Enough stuff is automated for you so that it isn't a pain or have to keep a word document on the side monitor.Stealth sections are meh. When are they ever not.Also you're a chad if you know 3/4 of the words and then just guess every possible combination for the last.Editing after 100%: Stealth actually isn't an issue. Not nearly as prevalent as it seems. But the puzzles in the 4th level & epilogue get pretty insane that's my only gripe.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. I finished it in only 2 days, and I loved learning how the sentences are constructed in every language and seeing how they used different terms for the same concepts. The last floor felt a bit rushed, as you didn't really have to think about the language, but I still really enjoyed the last reveal and the ending.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This game f*** rocks! It's a game about translation & exploration. Closest comparison is The Return of the Obra Din. The way you learn a language and decypher puzzles feels super rewarding and the devs actually trust that their players are smart and can make their own deductions.As a bonus the artstyle is gorgous and there are so many lovely little touches that make the world come alive.I you have any love for explorative puzzle games do yourself a favour and give this gem a try <3 Good job Devs :-)
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fun but only about 10 hours long, so maybe wait for the price to drop.The story is extremely simple, consider how the entire game uses a pool of 30 words for each level, you can't do much with that. The ending is also not very compelling. By the halfway point, you've seen everything and there's nothing new the game can show you.Similarly, the more you play and the more the magic of exploring wears off, you notice how there really isn't much beyond a pretty face. It does look very nice though, the world building is top notch.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Game design is very interesting and novice, and the visual is one of the best I have seen. The difficulty of the game is not too high and there are a lot of hints that the game itself provides. Definitely would recommend for people who are as nerdy and interested in languages as I am, or just anyone who likes to have a bit of brain-teasing in general.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is a puzzle game, where you play as an individual who doesn't understand the (fictional) languages of those they encounter. You progress through the game by deducing the information you need, and especially by deciphering the language. I think the concept is very clever, and nearly all elements of the game feel very impressive, from the visuals to the music and audio cues. The gameplay is simple, consisting mostly of point-and-click movement around different areas of the map. However, the puzzles are challenging, mostly because you have to first learn enough of the language to be able to understand it, and I think that extra layer of complexity really adds positively to the experience. I really enjoyed this game, and would highly recommend it. It's definitely a game I'd recommend reading as little of the plot as possible as well. Additionally, I'd encourage you to try challenging yourself to get through the language deciphering bits! I was surprised at how quickly I was able to snowball into intuiting many of the words. However, if you need assistance, there are several community guides available, and I found them to be very helpful when I got stuck at a couple key points.Overall, great game that I think puzzle enthusiasts will enjoy!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely clever puzzle design, very strongly designed visuals, just enough variation across the story to avoid feeling repetitive but with enough consistency to feel extremely cohesive. Stealth sections can be a little finicky, and the run up to the ending felt a little odd, but they stuck the landing and the rest of the game I honestly can't say a bad word about. Really just a fantastic experience
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful game - I love the art and music, I love the puzzles and I love its message. There are so many small heureka moments when you finally understand something about one of the languages. It really encourages you to think about the symbols and their meaning and how they connect to the people and their culture. Sure, if you think about it, a library could just be a "house of finding"! The puzzles aren't too easy which makes them rewarding to crack but strangely I never got stuck for long periods of time. I especially liked the conclusion of the game. It beautifully spells out something that you already intuitively learned from studying these people and their languages. It's one of those games where you wish you could play it again as if it was the first time and I really recommend you give it a shot.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good, it's fun and has an interesting and unique premise. Though a slight down side, some parts of the game-play aren't well explained and aren't intuitive enough to be easily understood. And sometimes the images used don't match the words very well making it more annoying than challenging.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Great take on the Obra Dinn formula, refocusing it on the idea of translation instead of investigation. Babel's tower is a great setting for this cocept and is used well for the game's plot and themes.One of Chants' worse, however, is it's system for verifying translated words. It allows for a fair bit of guesswork and suffers from a little bit too much hand-holding, which Obra Dinn managed to almost completely avoid.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Probably one of the best games that came out in 2023. As someone who is passioned about languages and linguistics I dare say it's very smart. The story is beautiful and I loved the ending very much. The overall morale is kind and is well entertwined with the whole concept of discovering the glyphs.Maybe the saturation is a tad bit too much for me but the design I liked a lot. 't was not only easy but also beautiful. And the soundrack is really on point.Easy gameplay, nice controls, difficulty was okay (very easy if you're more than a casual gamer). It's a win.If you're still wondering, go for it! You'll not be disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer for the things I find fun: I'm a linguistics student, so language is the thing I am most passionate about in the world.Beautiful little adventure game about language and the connections we make. Piecing together the different languages of the Tower is a deeply enjoyable challenge, linguistically they're pretty simple but each of the languages are unique in their own ways, one might show plurals through reduplication and another might have an OSV word order, and they all have different and really quite visually appealing writing systems. The feeling of using the knowledge you accumulate to connect the People of the Tower and backtracking to see what has changed because of your actions is pretty special. One day adventure game devs will realize that this is not the genre for stealth segments but today is not that day, and this is not that game. That part is frustrating but the segments are short and rare enough that it doesn't make to much of a dent in my enjoyment. The soundtrack is also great.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: funny enough, no words can describe how beautiful, artistically designed and well made this game is. It is a to play this game to experience its splendor.Do not let the point and click deter you though, as well as the seemingly intimidating linguistics problem solving either. Perseverance and curiosity will be your greatest ally and believe me, it is beyond your expectations.Amazing game, 7 hours and a worth every second. I look forward to the next masterpiece the devs will make next.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those few games where I sat through the credits in awe. I loved it. It started off a little slow, but as soon as I figured out where it was going, I couldn't put it away. Slowly deciphering the languages through puzzles was a lot of fun, having to use those languages to translate for characters was even better. The (real) ending blew me away, too. I wish I could play this again.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Puzzle/adventure game based on deciphering simple languages.It's fun. You climb tower of not-babel, each floor inhabited by a different tribe using their own language.Each language is glyph based and they use different syntax. You must decipher the meanings of glyphs to solve puzzles and sometimes translate from one language to another. Don't expect anything robust, it's just several dozen words, the very basics.The game allows to type your guessed translation for each glyph, and it displays those in-world, It also uses system similar to the Return of Obra Dinn. When we "collect" enough glyphs, it shows us a page with some drawings representing the meanings. You can assign glyph to those images. If all images on the page are paired correctly, the game acknowledges it and provides "official" translations. This is optional, you can try to finish the game using only guesses. There are also some simple stealth sections here and there. They are not difficult and can be also considered as puzzles of sorts.I like the visuals, they are simple but elegant. And the music is nice too. It's just a pleasant experience. And the length is just right.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great experience. Would definitely recommend to anyone that enjoys puzzle games with some story. Doesn't take a crazy amount of time either. If you take your time and search every spot you can, all but 2 of the achievements will be unlocked to you. I spent 9 hours on it and got 100% including achievements. Amazingly fun for a relatively short game. User be warned though, this game is one that will quickly suck you in until you finish it.0.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is an engaging puzzle and exploration game where you play a stranger trying to climb a tower inhabited by different groups of people on each level who speak different languages. In order to solve the puzzles required to open the way to the next level, you have to talk to people and learn how to understand their language. You do this by observing your surroundings and talking to people in order to gain clues as to what each symbol in their writing system means. Along the way you learn a bit about the different cultures that live in the tower and the history behind it, as well as what your own purpose it. You might want to have some notepaper handy when you play this game, although several important parts are automatically entered into your character's notebook. Some of the puzzles can be challenging but all of them are solvable with careful observation. There are also a few areas of the game that require stealth movement, which can be annoying, but none of these sequences are that hard to get past. A great game for people who like atmospheric environments and minimal storytelling that is mostly unlocked through your own observation.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Unique experience, highly recommended!Pros:* clever game concept of progressively learning languages* for all ages* pretty ost, variety of immersive locations* variety of different puzzles* full completion very possible in your first playthrough without guidesneutral - your opinion* very short (I played 10 hours for full completion)* puzzles are easy, it's not about the challenge but moreso the experience* only small variations in grammar for the languages, I'd have hoped for more (to emphasize differences). Does it make easier to learn sentence structure* once you discover a certain set of words, you get to match words to pictures or translations - this "unlocks" words with full reliability. So at a certain point, you'll be able to know each word's meaning for 100% sureCons:* I really can't think of any. You could put some of the "neutrals" in here, if you believe so.Worth playing for the unique experience!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: My hours are off, I left the game idle at work. My actual save file took exactly ten hours on the dot (plus five minutes for me to go back and snag the two achievements I missed).Saying that, this is one of the best puzzle games I've ever played, it gave me similar a-ha moments to that of Obra-Dinn (albeit this one is quite a bit easier IMO).The stealth sections are mediocre but short. They serve the purpose of breaking up and book-ending the language puzzles pretty well.If you like puzzles and find the concept interesting, pick up this game now.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Very good game. One of the best I've played recently. Play the demo and if you like it, get the full game. I probably wouldn't have bought it if it wasn't for the demo. I played 5 hours in my first sitting and finished the game the day after.The puzzles are at a good level. Just challenging enough that you feel smart solving them, but not hard enough to be frustrating. Not sure how hard the language parts would be if you don't like learning new languages, but they were not too hard. I got some words wrong, but most were very close or exactly what the game wanted.Go in blind. Half the joy is discovering the game mechanics. Most are very intuitive.You can't automatically continue from where you left off in the demo, but it's very quick to reach the same point in the full game after you've played it once (most time is spent learning how the game works).A thorough play-through is about 10 hours. Plays well on the Steam Deck. I played maybe 40% on the Deck's screen and 60% on an external monitor with a controller.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful little puzzle game where you try to understand people who speak different languages, and can be completed in about 10 hours.Keeping your whits about you, clutching your trusty notebook filled to the brim with strange symbols and scrawled guesses, you travel through an absolutely gorgeous game full of distinct societies and cunning puzzles. You feel really clever when you (finally) work out what the people around them are saying and how it relates to the world around them!Chants of Sennaar was well worth what I paid for it, and I'd highly recommend it to anyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best game I played in years! Challenging and very intelligent puzzles that require some out-of-the-box thinking, but not in a frustrating, undoable way. This game has stunning visuals, great storytelling and immersive worldbuilding. Also, I loved that the languages had their own grammatical features! These languages really stole the show for me.The stealth mode sections were mostly surprisingly doable and fun, although for the 2 hardest ones I asked someone else to do them (usually I don't like that kind of gameplay, because I have to react too fast, so that I mostly liked them was surprising). I love point-and-click puzzle games, but this one was outstanding in every way. I really enjoyed it and I am hoping this team makes/made more games.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: There's something incredibly satisfying about making discoveries. It leaves a lot to the player to decide, and learning the rules of each language is its own puzzle to figuring out what terms mean. Walking around and getting lost in the worlds and languages felt like it was intended, and while it was annoying to walk around in circles for a bit, eventually each area and language becomes so familiar that it's easy to navigate and communicate. That thrill of discovery is what drives this game forward, so if you're looking for that and are willing to make mistakes while exploring, this is the game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: has among the most creative gameplay of any game I've played in recent memory. You start the game by awakening on one of the lower floors of "The Tower" (inspired by the Tower of Babel, as the game's description says), knowing nothing of the language spoken by the denizens. Through observation and context clues, you have to decipher the language as you go, as well as the four other languages of the distinct peoples higher up the tower. It's a clever and well-executed concept, and at its best it does what every puzzle game should: challenges your brain and makes you feel smart when you succeed, without being so esoteric as to be frustrating.There are a few areas of the game that I didn't love:These complaints are relatively minor, though, and the game is great overall. Once I started playing, I was barely able to put it down and ended up finishing it in just two sittings (for a total gameplay time of around 8 hours). These days, it's rare for a game to be able to hold my attention for that long. I really enjoyed , and I hope to see more games like it in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennar is an excellent addition to the genre of "its sort of like Obra Dinn" that have cropped up over the last four years. Should we start calling them Dinn-Likes?Much like Obra-Dinn, Case of the Golden Idol, Heaven's Vault, Forgotten City, and Outer Wilds; Chants of Senaar is very much worth your while, if you enjoy being thrown into the deep end of archeology without a hint of how to start progressing. Senaar is the only one of these lot where you have to construct a whole language from absolute scratch, and mixing and matching not just one but numerous languages (which you may yourself not fully have translated by the time you reach later areas where that knowledge is very much required), is Senaar's main triumph over its contemporaries. You're going to be doing five times or more the amount of grunt work as any of these other titles and I loved discovering every single word. A brief aside; the game's control scheme is absolutely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ horrid. You'll just have to get used to it. Physically typing things on a gamepad is asinine and a waste of your time, and physically walking around the gameworld with a mouse and keyboard is just as bad. The best way to play is to have both and mix and match as needed. I'd also like to briefly mention that the steam cards have ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ spoilers for puzzles on them, so dont look at them.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly fun and engaing, definitely recommend!Puzzles are fun although i had two instances of not knowing how to comeplete a language without a guide bc i missed something easily overseen but it didn't ruin the experience at all (just mildly annoying lol) as some wise person once said:I I need more game game like this!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I can't speak for the accuracy of the linguistics, but as a puzzle game, this is incredibly beautiful and fun to play! Most of the puzzles are pretty straightforward, but I felt very smart while solving them (especially when it came to deciphering the languages!). I really enjoyed playing and exploring, though I do have a couple of gripes:1) I wish there was a map! I kept getting turned around and it made it very hard to get to certain places, especially Chapter 3. 2) I wish the journal pages would be given to you if you had all of the symbols for it instead of having to trigger a specific event. With three of the languages, I had all of the symbols but needed to look up how to find one page because I missed one sign early on (or similar). And that's it! If you like puzzles, languages, and/or pretty graphics, this is a pretty good game for you! It's pretty short and low-stakes, and the controls are very simple (all you need is a mouse). The soundtrack is really nice as well, very calm and definitely something I want to listen to while drawing or reading.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A very interesting game, a combination of understanding puzzles and language learning, there are many small details need to find each map, to run a lot of roads. The scene at the top of the tower together at the end moved me very much. The kid who started out playing hide-and-seek with me turned out to be the one who woke me up.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game with loads of puzzles. Here and there I got a bit stuck but never for long and never felt any frustration when I couldn't figure out some words - just moved forwards to collect more and then had a second look at the hints. Several times I thought I am close to the end of the game but no, I couldn't have been more wrong :D Definitely recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful, thoughtful experience of translating language and culture to bring about understanding. There's a very rewarding sense to feel new words fall into place, though some of the needed symbols are hard to locate. Each new culture was a wonderful new micro-world to explore, and seeing new views on common words was great, as was trying to translate between languages which highlights what elements of culture are untranslatable.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Lovely puzzle game with a simple but really sweet message about the importance of talking to those who are different from us. Getting to play a character that facilitates those conversations was very satisfying to me. Occasionally obtuse to play--the stealth mechanism is awful (though fortunately only regularly relevant on one level), and something about the level layouts frequently involved me getting lost and crossing the same ground more times than I would have liked. I also found the final language a bit anticlimatic--I didn't feel I really "learned" the glyphs to the same extent I had everything else.But gorgeous art, lovely music, good story, good puzzles. Really enjoyed my time.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: The first chapter of this game is simply amazing. You're immediately puzzled and interested in your character and their relationship with the world. The first characters you meet talk to you in simple phrases, which fits the situation and helps you learn how the game's language works. You'll find lovely parallels to real languages, for example, such as finding the same character at the beginning and the end of a sentence, making you deduce that this character is most likely a question mark.However, the game loses its focus quickly. While even the first chapter had its issues (slow walking speed, tons of long corridors or sets of stairs that needlessly elongates the time spent exploring the world), it was at the very least focused on language learning. Alas, the next chapters include stealth sections, chase sections, quick thinking actions, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ labyrinths.. It loses itself.The biggest hurdle this game faces is how it discourages its player base from trying things out. It takes time to go to any location, and the map is needlessly big. I often found myself wanting to check the internet for hints and then immediately regretting not having done so sooner. For example, some sections cannot be done because your character hasn't put together what you have, and in one section in particular, I had to go through the 2 mins stealth section THREE TIMES, to click on something I had already clicked on, but in the wrong order. Soured the experience.I'd purchase a sequel of this game, that's how good the potential is here. If only that one could focus on language and culture learning. </3 Maybe something that focuses on one language too. Say you meet a cute foreign girl and want to wife 'er up? It would be cute and charming. And not having you learn 4 languages, each time expecting you to dismiss previously obtained knowledge.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting concept for a puzzle game. Explore a tower, figure out different languages to solve puzzles.I got by with a lot of mashing combinations of glyphs into the journal, to tell me the translations. A smarter person might have done it properly by making use of notes/screenshots regarding the way sentences were structured to make better guesses. But a) I'm a lazy git and b) I only think of that after the fact.... Not a big fan of the few stealth sections that got thrown in, I believe they are there to create a bit more tension. Fair enough, they aren't too difficult or a huge focus of the game, so not a problem.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is exactly the kind of game that appeals to me, though I think it won't be for everybody. It's fundamentally a puzzle adventure game, but with an unusual twist: the core puzzle mechanic is deciphering the multiple languages spoken by the inhabitants of the game. The storyline is obviously strongly inspired by the Tower of Babel, and the game is stronger for it. None of the puzzles are too difficult (there's a strong sense of fairness about the game), but also not too easy. Highly recommended if you like this kind of thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic little indie game about decoding and translating languages. God-tier environmental story-telling. Art style is clean and simple but immensely well-crafted. The music and sound design is so so good, every little sound from the players' footsteps to the water dripping from a leaky ceiling are on beat, blending into the soundtrack. Overall it's a really well polished puzzle game of moderate difficultly. The only bad things I could say are that I had like three moments where I wasn't sure what I was supposed to do next that were mildly annoying. Super well done, worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: What an incredible game. It more than deserves a place next to other great narrative puzzlers like Return of the Obra Dinn and The Case of the Golden Idol. It brings a unique twist in that you don't only have to figure out the story, but also the language in which it's told. It's such a perfect mechanic for a narrative puzzle game that, in hindsight, I'm surprised no-one has done it before.While AAA studios are trying to make games like movies where the player is mostly just along for the ride, this game shows what is possible when you use gameplay mechanics to tell the story. The result is an incredibly engaging experience. I cannot recommend this game enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Short ~10 hour puzzle game that is really beautifully made. It's clear that each of the languages you decipher was carefully crafted to reflect something about the culture of the people who use it, and it's really a treat to see the "story" develop through understanding the glyphs. Soundtrack is also great.The changing camera angles when you go from room to room can sometimes be very disorienting, which I think is intentional, and definitely easier to comprehend after it's happened a few times.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I watched someone play this game on YouTube and it got me so involved I stopped watching after 5-10 minutes and downloaded this game myself. At first it seemed fun to 'just translate glyphs', but soon it became so much more. It exceeded all of my expectations. The artwork! The gradually increasing complexity! The hidden details and achievements! I really, REALLY liked this one. Will gladly recommend it to anyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Worth the money spent. I really enjoyed all the puzzles and trying to figure out the languages. I also have an appreciation to all the small details involved, especially seen in the last part.I've read some would have liked a map, but I just considered it an additional puzzle, considering how labyrinthine the floors could be. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This one's a real gem. I had lots of fun appreciating the cultural and linguistic differences of the people. The visuals and art direction are superb.The main thing that brings the experience down is the gameplay and puzzle design. The mechanic that bothers me is the way that you "confirm" glyphs, by matching them to drawings in your notebook. It's nice that you can establish some glyphs as known and not have to worry about their meaning, but the process of doing so brings down the fun of figuring them out in two ways.First, the pictures are often not very good at suggesting the concept to match. Specific example: (very minor spoilers ahead)- there's a sequence where you have to avoid being caught by a person. Almost immediately after that sequence, you get the opportunity to confirm some glyphs. One of the pictures depicts that person(or one very similar to him) wagging his finger at you. I assumed that this meant "catch", so I matched it with the symbol that later turned out to be "find". Instead, the picture is *actually* supposed to depict "not/negative". This came up a few times for me, and was by far the most frustrating part of the game.And second, I think it's a little bit too simple. The fact that there's relatively few glyphs and that grammar is very bare-bones means that most of the glyph confirmation/investigation can be solved by just guessing. I suppose I should have stopped myself from guessing glyphs that I only half-knew, but a lack of consequences and the previously mentioned unclear pictures make me think that a large majority of players solved some of the glyphs by just guessing.I'd like to see another game like this in the future, with maybe a little more depth in the languages themselves.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful puzzle game that's perfectly paced and priced. It fits into a similar vein as The Case of the Golden Idol and Return of the Obra Dinn where you are given a notebook containing blank spaces to fill out with clues. This formula seems to be a cheat code because there hasn't been a game I didn't like in this genre and Chants is no exception. That being said, Chants still manages to find its own unique take through its wonderful and varied world and its clever focus on language as the puzzle.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: soooooo.... i realize i did not review this game exactly when i finished it. however, it was recent enough that i will still write my review. i first found this game on tik tok (one of those accounts that talked about upcoming games) and saw that it was already out. so i decided, hey, why not give it a try? the premise seems really odd and unique.what i wouldn't give to experience playing this game for the first time again. the vibes? immaculate. the music? beautiful. the gameplay? funky, fresh, and super fun. the ending?...... insane. i was baffled. flabbergasted, even. needless to say, i highly recommend to anyone wanting a short and sweet game to get into.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Very interesting game. It's straightforward but in a way that lets you explore the world/languages in your own time/pace. Good puzzles that are the right level of difficulty & interest where it didn't get frustrating. The game gives adequate clues to guide your understanding. Tackled language in a very ingenious way.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is a perfect piece of art.It gives the full condensed experience of (language) learning: the sense of discovery, gradually deepening understanding, and connecting. Beautiful (in many ways: music, visuals, concepts), inspiring and kind. Gentle in the sense that it is not required to remember everything (because you take notes in-game), or to do a big part at once, so not too hard but surprisingly satisfying.It put me in the mood for learning stuff. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. It's full of great puzzles that are just the right difficulty, and a very satisfying progression loop. I used it to help me study Japanese, and the gradual deciphering of in-game languages paced well with the real language that it was automatically translated into. I don't know if the developers had considered using this as a learning game as a possibility, but I'd absolutely recommend it, even if some of my new vocabulary is taken up with talk about caste, bells, alchemy, exile, and the occasional saw.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I went into this game rather blindly, I'd seen a short video introducing the game very broadly and then read two or three short reviews here on steam. I love puzzle games so I thought I'd give it a try.My poor friends and family have had to endure my excited rants about learning fictional languages and their grammar, and understanding the mentality behind them. Once you get started the system of a language begin to make sense, and every "aha" moment is glorious. This game made me struggle just the right amount, not so much that it got frustrating but also enough that progress felt like a real accomplishment.I finished the game in just over 9 hours, I missed five achievements so lets assume it takes somewhere between 8 and 10 hours to complete depending on how well you solve the puzzles. There isn't much replay value, which is understandable, and I would absolutely love to see a sequel to this in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful game.  Puzzles were challenging enough to be stimulating but I never felt really stumped.  The puzzles are designed to let you experiment and tinker with them in order to figure out what you're intended to do.  Highly recommend checking this out if you're even a little curious.  Reminds me a lot of Fez and Oneshot to give a few comparisons.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked this!The gameplay is very straightforward, with you moving around and interacting with things with just your mouse. The translation mechanics were very well made. The puzzles aren't overly difficult, but just enough to make you go "aha!" when you come up with the solution. There's also a nice story in the background and the game's graphical style makes it look really pretty!The pacing is good and there's enough variety so that at no point did I feel like "ugh, I have to do that one thing again".I definitely give this a recommend if you're at all into puzzle-solving games!
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I even start - this a masterpiece.The initial premise of a language-riddle game intrigued me, but what was in store for me I could never have imagined. The sheer beauty of this game in its visuals, music and themes is immense. And though throughout the entire game not one word is actually spoken, the languages are all fascinatingly different - from sentence structure to vocabulary, the detail is perfect. Accompanying these linguistic themes are beautiful vistas, gorgeous music and a story that genuinely surprised me several times - especially the very final scene brought tears to my eyes. This game, ironically, spoke to something very deep within me like very few games or even any pieces of media have. In my eyes, this is a masterpiece through and through and should you give it a try I promise you, you will not regret embarking upon this journey to Senaar.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the best games I've played recently and It got me completely hooked. It's been quite some time since I was so eager to continue playing. I loved the idea with translating languages - most of those puzzles were not very difficult but still fun and interesting. It was also really great that those puzzles were so connected with whole story, it made everything more immersive. And last but not least, this game is so beautiful... I loved the designs of each of the levels and how they corresponded with people living there. Overall, really amazing game.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I can't say I've encountered many reverse tower of babel games, but this one makes me want more of them. Picking apart a new and unfamiliar language, filling in what I think the words mean and slowly making sense of what I'm being told is supremely satisfying. Of course, when you're struggling to make sense of it, it's a blind stumble though puzzles you can't understand. Still, easy recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: AVOID | LACKING | MAYBE | WORTHWHILE | COMPELLING | Chants of Sennaar is a puzzle and exploration adventure game at its core. It's been a hot minute since I've been pulled into a game right at the onset, but this game immediately grabbed my interest and kept me engrossed until the very end. I can't speak highly enough for how well designed the puzzles are - everything you need to solve them is in the game, so you never need to guess at an answer. Everything is logical and consistent, leading to very satisfying conclusions. If you run into a problem trying to solve a problem, you likely simply need to explore a bit more and/or think creatively to get the answer. This game feels like it gently prods you in the right direction, but given the need to explore to get answers, the devs aren't holding your hand as you do so. The puzzles require some thinking, but you don't need to be a genius to get it. Again, I can't speak highly enough about this aspect of the game; it is simply incredibly  well done.The game is also beautiful to look at. It reminds me quite a bit of Monument Valley in its scenery. By that I mean that both games feature colorful and simple yet also labyrinthine-like landscapes. I've seen some reviews mention the stealth sections negatively. While they weren't my favorite part of the game, they also only comprise maybe 20-30ish minutes of the entire game. These sections felt well-implemented and neatly fit the narrative, so I'm not entirely sure I understand the complaints beyond the fact that they're a departure from a strictly puzzle-driven game (but again, considering how little stealth features in the game, it feels a bit like nitpicking to me). The game took me ~13 hours to complete, with an additional ~30 minutes to do some achievement cleanup. I got stuck on one section which led to probably an additional hour or so of gametime than what might normally be expected. Overall, If you have any inclination whatsoever for puzzle games, you owe it to yourself to try this game. This is one of the best puzzle games to have come out in recent memory (if it's not actually just straight-up the best). Also, if you enjoy language/linguistics/deciphering, I'm sure this would be a delight for you to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a masterpiece of storytelling and embodies all the best aspects of why it is that I fell in love with linguistics as a discipline. Please play this game.There are aspects that could be improved and pacing that could be tightened - some of the longer wandering outlook segments were a bit annoying to backtrack through - but overall this was so genuinely wonderful from start to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: This game is one of my new favourites. If you like religious themes in your puzzle game, this is definitely for you. The repeating puzzle elements with recurring solution rules made progression feel natural. My only gripe in this game is that you don't have a map that you can reference easily which can sometimes be frustrating if you're playing the game in multiple disconnected sessions and you forget where things are.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chant of Sennaar is a fantastic indie game with a very unique concept.Imagine not understanding anybody, and you have to build your own dictionary of multiple languages to navigate through puzzles, logic, and the story. It might sound weird, but it's really rewarding when you start to understand how the language works.Overall, the concept is super cool and innovative – definitely worth a shot!Some parts could definitely use some quality of life improvements, but overall, it's a smooth experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Don't get me wrong, it is smooth, beautifully drawn and has a good idea behind it. But.. It is not the game of the year. I wouldn't pay what it costs now. It is A LOT of walking, boring music, easy puzzles and a lot of hand-holding. I am 2 hours in, I will finish it and revisit this comment. But for now, don't think this is anywhere close to talos principle or portal kind of a puzzle game.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: Chants of Sennaar is high up on my recommendation list for anyone who likes puzzle games, linguistics, or old legends. The game is hands down one of the most enjoyable games I have ever played. The puzzles were challenging, but doable with a little time and detective work, without becoming too frustrating as a player. One piece of advice for your play-through is to avoid verifying your glyphs with brute force. Try and guess each glyph until you organically confirm what each one means for a more authentic game-play experience. The visuals are pleasing and the soundtrack is wonderful, but can get a bit repetitive for the amount of time you spend in each area. While the main draw to the game is the linguistic style puzzles, the writing is very good. The underlying story is shrouded in mystery that you as a player must unravel and discover as you climb the tower. I felt the design/story for one of the areas was somewhat weak and off putting, but it all come together nicely by the end of the story and didn't distract from the overall experience. There isn't much replay value to the game, but the initial play-through is worth it. It took me about 12hrs to 100% the game which isn't too challenging or frustrating to do. I could see myself replaying the game down the road when my memory of it gets fuzzy. I did not encounter any bugs while playing this game. As stated before, I highly recommend this game for anyone that is curious about it.
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review: I liked it overall but it's not the flawless indie darling puzzler a lot of people make it out to be, it's great, but not perfect.Pros- Generally really fun language puzzling, the book system clearly taken hints from Obra Dinn which was a good choice- Absolutely great art and music, the landscapes are simplistic but very stylish, and the soundtrack does a good job carrying the themeCon:- This seems to be a me thing but I thought the story was really basic, there's two twists as part of the true ending and I guessed the big finale one in my first hour of playing, but ymmv- While the language puzzling is fun, it's also really shallow for what it could be, some cultures mess with sentence order or small things, but none of them do any big weird things, again though, depends how hard you want your puzzles to beFor casual puzzle players I can see this going down really well, for people looking for something to drinke your teeth into, it's a good way to spend an evening or two but won't be massively challenging8/10
_childDocuments_.name: Chants of Sennaar

_childDocuments_.review:
Divided since the dawn of time, the Peoples of the Tower no longer speak to each other. But it is said that one day, a Traveler will find the wisdom to break down the walls and restore the Balance.

Explore and discover an enthralling world in a colorful, poetic setting inspired by the myth of Babel, where men have forgotten their past. Travel the endless steps of a prodigious labyrinth, uncover an ominous truth and unveil the mysteries of this fascinating universe where ancient languages are both the lock and the key.

Embark on a captivating journey with ancient languages to decipher.

name: The Caligula Effect 2
detailed_description: ●STORY Redo - a world without regrets. Regret - a mysterious virtuadoll. Those who hear her songs find themselves transported into another world. The world of Redo is a virtual world built from the regrets of many people. 'If only I'd done things differently...' This is a world where everyone's secret desire to redo their lives can come true. A place where they can become the person they would have been had they chosen differently... Redo - a dull world with no regrets, where anyone can experience a life redone. Another Songstress and the Go-Home Club Another virtuadoll exists - χ. She seeks to destroy the false world of Redo. She gives strength to the protagonist - who is slowly awakening to reality - as her chosen partner. They form the Go-Home Club, gathering other members who have also found out about the world outside Redo. Thus begins their arduous task of making it home against the will of the creator of the world. Go-Home Club's True Selves In Redo, members of the club are in their 'redone' forms, which they have obtained by ignoring reality and undoing past regrets. Their true selves are secret forms only the player can deal with. Tread carefully and choose actions that will leave no regrets... 　 ●CHARACTER STORIES In the world of Redo, Go-Home Club members are in their 'redone' forms - manifestations of past regrets that have been undone. Each member is trapped in a situation dreadful enough to cause them to turn away from reality. What happened to them? And why are they trying so hard to return to that painful reality? These are only some of the mysteries the player must unravel. There is a chance you may find the members' true selves unacceptable. So tread carefully and choose actions that will leave no regrets... 　 ●BATTLES Imaginary Chain Chain combos in the battle system while predicting the future! The battled system is turn-based. Once an action is selected, you can peer into the future and see what it looks like successfully executed. Use this ability wisely to coordinate attacks with allies or cover them during bad situations. χ-Jack When certain conditions are met in battle, a χ-Jack is activated, in which χ's singing voice hijacks the battlefield and powers up the Go-Home Club. The effects differ according to the song chosen. This move is powerful enough to completely turn the tide of battle. Develop χ's abilities to improve the effects of a χ-Jack.​ 　 ●OTHER FEATURES WIRE Use WIRE's group chat function to discuss club goals or ask allies questions on private chat. You may be surprised by what you can learn from their replies.​ Some special questions can only be obtained with high affinity or via quests. CAUSALITY LINK Even residents of the ideal world Redo have minor gripes and problems to contend with.​ Perhaps these stem from their true selves or personal relationships in reality...? Complete quests from townsfolk to gather more information and uncover hidden truths.​

short_description: Redo is a world without sorrow created by the virtuadoll Regret. Virtuadoll songs give Redo residents respite from their struggles. Our protagonists discover the truth and form the Go-Home Club to return to reality. Make your way home with companions bearing heavy burdens in this school-themed RPG.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game.It's a Matrix inspired JRPG made by some of the old Persona (as in Persona 1/2) developers. You lead a happy-go-lucky existence in a virtual world, then a rebel AI program force-feeds you red pills. Now your goal is to destroy this world and wake up. However, there's one more twist. Everyone's virtual avatars are idealized versions of themselves and can differ greatly both in personality and looks from their IRL selves, so exploring each character's motives and backstory is a big element of the narrative. Many of them will turn out to be depressed, broken people. Despite the high school setting, the game seems to be aimed at an older audience, and the writing is more mature than in many other JRPGs. The game is low on anime tropes, and only fantastic characters have brightly colored hair or outrageous designs, everyone else looks like your everyday East Asian.To get the obvious out of the way, this is not an AAA production. The graphics are just okay, and many animations are wooden. But this is still a pretty high effort game and it has such cool features as completely seamless battle transitions and a really amazing dynamic soundtrack. Here's  from the first dungeon, to give you a taste. The voice acting is very good too, but there's no English dub.The combat is pretty innovative. It's turn-based, but the outcomes play out in real-time, and the main gimmick is previewing your turn and using a slider to time your actions to counter or block enemy attacks, dash out of harm's way etc. E.g. the enemy is just running forward and attacking 3x this turn, you set one of your characters to intercept the enemy, parry and hit him a bunch to send him flying, while another character can be set to start shooting the moment the enemy is in the air for extra damage. You can even juggle enemies by chaining aerial attacks. It's a very cool system and there are NO QTE's, everything is manual, it's just that it's not as snappy as regular JPRG combat, as fiddling with the slider can take some time.The PC port is excellent. The game is using Unreal Engine 4, and it's very well optimized. No stutter or hitching of any kind, very low GPU load. I haven't encountered any crashes or other technical issues.Overall, an easy recommendation for any JRPG fan.
_childDocuments_.name: The Caligula Effect 2

_childDocuments_.review: I will admit, I did not go into this game with high expectations. I played the first and was not a fan. So with the sequel, I expected more of the same – but got something actually kinda better?It plays almost identical to the first game, but with one major change: χ-Jack. This is a special ability that is charged over time and can be activated to reset your entire party to the front of the timeline and boost their abilities at the same time. It is mega handy for boss fights and can even be upgraded using a special currency to increase its effectiveness – an excellent change to an already excellent combat system.I had a lot of fun figuring out different combos, trying out each party member, and generally just trying to dissect this massive thing that is Caligula’s combat.I also like what they did with character equipment. Now, instead of just giving straight stat upgrades, you’re able to level up individual “stigmas” to unlock passive abilities that usually grant the same effect as the equipped stigma. It’s basically a way to “teach” your party members certain upgrades that can then be equipped in a separate menu.It’s a cool system, but it does unfortunately introduce a good chunk of micromanagement, as you’ll need to constantly shuffle around these stigmas to make sure you’re not wasting potential stat upgrades. So a bit of good, a bit of bad with this new system.The sidequests were absolutely terrible in the first game and unfortunately just as bad here, just with a nicer coat of paint on them. NPC dialogue does not seem to be as recycled, but the quests that they give you are the usual JRPG garbage. “Go here, talk to this guy, buy this for me, give me this item,” there is nothing really noteworthy about any of these quests and they felt more like filler than actual game content. Unfortunats, as they are a massive chunk to the game.The first game's story had some good points, but was ultimately a disappointment. Caligula 2, on the other hand, makes notable improvements across the board. The structure is mostly the same – you got your virtual world full of people with their own mental issues that are uncovered as the story progresses – but more time is spent exploring these issues and giving characters proper time to develop.The pacing is managed better, the tone doesn’t jarringly shift as much, and the dialogue just flows better, even if it may still be a bit wordy. Granted, it is helped out A LOT from its increased length – around 30-40 hours long, which is roughly 40% longer than it took me to clear the first.Of course, this means there’s a lot more dialogue. The game often goes off on 20, 30, sometimes 40 minute story scenes and I won’t deny some of them can drag a bit.The musicians – the bad guys, basically – are also a notable downside. They are not given the same time to develop like the main cast and some of their stories are just dumped on you during their introduction, leaving their motivations as these simple, surface-level things.All of that said though, the story is still quite interesting. It’s not perfect, but again, much better than the first game.Just like the first game, Caligula 2 uses a bunch of vocal tracks sung by the in-game AI, and pretty much all of them slap – definitely something I’ll be listening to outside of the game. That said, the music carries over the same problem from the first game – the fact that there’s little variety. You get your one vocal track per dungeon and that’s it, so you’ll be listening to that same track on repeat for upwards of a couple hours or so.Graphically, I can’t really say I noticed a difference between this one and the original Caligula. Neither of them looked bad, so I guess not too much of a complaint, but it’s definitely a PS4 game and the graphics reflect that.I haven’t noticed any specific content changes compared to the PS version (whcih I have already played through), but I can report that the game itself runs much better. PS5 version was 1080p 60fps and here I am roughly half a year later playing the same game at 1440p 144 fps with no technical issues to speak of during my time testing it. Options-wise, you get resolution, a window/fullscreen toggle, and 3D scaling, texture quality, post-processing, and anti-aliasing sliders. Nothing too crazy, but definitely not bad.I also tested it on the Steam Deck and had no issues there either. The PC version is optimized well and has some surprisingly solid keyboard and mouse controls on top of that. I still prefer a controller for a game like this, but I would have no problem using keyboard and mouse, it’s intuitive and works much better than some of the other JRPG ports we have been getting. Granted, it could still use some improvement by way of mouse input in menus.The Caligula Effect 2 is a notable improvement over its predecessor, with better writing, better characters, and – to a lesser extent – better combat. Still, it does continue some of the same faults from that first game, like its completely garbage side quest system and lack of decent quality of life features. And while the story has improved, it still has its issues, like the occasional bad character and the overuse of meaningless choices. Regardless, I’m glad I gave the sequel a shot in spite of my problems with the first.Follow my  for more reviews + videos!

_childDocuments_.review: Please play The Caligula Effect 2.PLEASE play this game.I already played through this game twice on PS4 and, good god, I'll probably play through this game twice on Steam too. The Caligula Effect isn't just a Persona clone, it's a Persona clone with a pedigree. Namely, Tadashi Satomi, the writer of the first three Persona games (that is, Persona 1, 2, and 2 again), wrote these games as well (well kinda. he was involved at any rate). And man, I really like The Caligula Effect 2's writing. I'll get there.Let's start withThe immediate elevator pitch of the gameplay is that it's Devil May Cry on the active time battle system. Maybe not entiiiiirely accurate, but what I basically mean is that it's if you took the gameplay of a character action game and somehow reworked it into an RPG. It's focused a lot on juggling enemies in the air and countering their moves with your own attacks. It takes a while to figure out what  the game is asking from you, but once you get it, it's a blast from start to finish. It's great holding opponents up in the air and slaughtering them before moving onto the next. Just, a really good time.Look, I'm gonna be atom bomb blunt here. The Caligula Effect 2 is only a  prettier than the first game. But it's still very much a lower budget game. Character animation is stiff and awkward, it looks like an early PS3 game at the best of times, it's not really a game you look at and go "damn!!" But at the least, the UI is nice and clean, it's easy to tell what's actually going on, and the character art you see in dialogue scenes and the pause menu are really nice. The music, though, is the big standout piece of the game. The Caligula Effect is a series about Vocaloids, after all, and to go above the call of duty, they actually got a list of different Vocaloid producers from creators I really love like cosMo to creators that, gotta fold here, I never heard of. But every single track is great, it's very close to being a flawless soundtrack. The one issue I have that the final boss theme is just a remix of the main theme of the game which is just kinda... underwhelming I guess.You could probably criticize the localization of this game for relying on modern meme culture and while that's not UNEARNED, it's still definitely there. Chi calls a character a simp, she says we live in a society, another character calls her a yolo swagster. Okay most of it comes from Chi but where this  be read as incredibly grating, I honestly read it as really endearing. Like it feels a bit more real without ever giving the sense that this game will be completely incomprehensible in like 5 years. Outside of the memes, though, it's a really well written game. Usually in RPGs there's always a character in the main party where I'm like "uuughh THIS fuggin guy," but that didn't really happen with Caligula Effect 2. The first two party members you get, Gin and Sasara, immediately set the tone for the rest of the game. Gin not seeming that wild at first, kind of reading like Caligula's own version of Masao from Persona 1, but as you go through his character arc. Well his reveals matter to  dammit. Sasara meanwhile is just an impossibly kind creature that has no idea what a phone is and I treasure her more than anything on the planet. And it just gets better from there. Shota, the strict dweeb, Kiriko, the lax dweeb, Niko, who is just perfect in every single way. I love the whole cast. I won't talk more here just because I don't want to spoil anything, just trust me, it's good.This part is where I get controversial, in that I think what makes The Caligula Effect 2 so much better than 1 is that it has  going on. The first game had 500 different NPCs, all with their own quests, that made the idea of 100%ing the game or even really doing any of the quests feel like a frustrating nightmare. Its combat allowed party members to put in 3 different moves at a time, making battles feel really chaotic and yet kind of abrupt and empty feeling. In other notes, the localization was kind of a mess, with some quests being completely incomprehensible, and boy. Sweet-P. Jeez, Sweet-P. Judging by this game's attitude I think the approach to trans characters is less hateful and more just confused, but it's still pretty rough! But this game doesn't have any of these issues, it was all toned down or changed so that the whole product feels much more focused and complete, where the first game felt like a lot of interesting ideas strung loosely in a vacuum. Good ideas, sure, but this is where those ideas really get to flourish.As for if you need to know what  in the first game. Once upon a time a lady named Thorn used a Virtuadoll (Vocaloid) named Mu to make the Matrix and Mu's best friend (yep that's really all they are uh-huh) Aria helped the party turn it back to normal also someone named Marie is there, there now you're ready for this game.Not that the first game is bad, per se, I just think this one is better.Wh. YES. YES. PLAY IT. DUDE, WHY WOULD YOU READ ALL OF THAT AND THINK I'D SAY NO? PLAY IT YOU JERK, PLAY IT.

_childDocuments_.review: Caligula Effect 2... Oh wow! I had no idea there was a sequel to Caligula Effect: Overdose, so imagine my surprise when this title appeared on my Steam recommendation. And I had to play Caligula Effect 2 because I love trying out new JRPGs on Steam. However, like its prequel, the overall experience left me with mixed feelings – again! But I definitely enjoyed this one much better compared to the prequel, though.I'm just going to give it to you straight; the story is not the strongest aspect of this game. It's decent at best. If anything, the developer did a better job at the story presentation, and they also did a pretty well-executed introduction; it showcased your daily life as a high schooler before χ suddenly shows up and drops a bomb about the truth of this world. Now, why have I heard that story before? Oh right! That's cause it's the exact same premise as the first game, that's why! After the event of the first game, some no-name songstress shows up and, with the help of her underlings, creates a world that is supposedly better than Mobius while trapping people again! In the process. That's called lazy writing! While it's not a complete carbon copy, the core story is basically the same.Honestly, localization is the next biggest issue I have with this game. Some lines were just cringeworthy and dumb. Somehow, they made χ even more grating than the developers probably had intended.The only saving grace of the story aspect is the bad ending, which I think is miles better than the regular ending. And individual character stories, for which I think they did an excellent job. You can also learn more about each boss's backstories during post-game cleanup. That deserves a thumbs up in my book. First, props to the devs for doing a major overhaul to the combat system. If you're here after playing the prequel, here's some good news! You can kiss goodbye to those days of spamming soul surge to keep your DPS up because they add natural MP recovery to each character. Additionally, they add recovery items into the mix, which means you have more freedom playing around with the party roster since you don't have to reserve that one spot for a healer or character with resurrection skill. In a nutshell, what they did is a complete quality of life improvement to the combat mechanics.Another thing I adore about the combat in this game is how dynamic the visual and audio is. The dev went all out with the songstress theme; as you explore the overworld, all you'll hear is the instrumental version of each boss OST. But when you encounter an enemy, the song lyric hits, and a mini music video plays in the background, which is a real feast for the eyes! When you think it can't get any better, during a boss fight, the beat drops, and the remix version of the OST plays, which is awesome! Caligula Effect 2 combat system has two main features; imaginary chain and χ-Jack. Imaginary chain is a feature that lets you see into the future and adjust the timing of your move to deliver the best outcome, whether it's a counter move or repositioning your character. There's a slight difference with the imaginary chain in this game; unlike the prequel, each character can only use one action per turn instead of three, which means you'll have to think twice before ending each turn.The χ-Jack is a get-out-of-jail-free card feature that allows you to move instantly and grants your entire party plenty of buffs. As you march against mobs, you'll slowly fill the voltage bar, which allows you to use χ-Jack and overdose bar, again, same stuff, only this time it's to use finisher move. So, the general rule of thumb is to fill those bars before each boss fight. Do that, and you're pretty much in the clear for most bosses.It's refreshing to see the songstress actively participate in combat instead of nagging and complaining but not contributing like the one in the previous game. There is some good and bad news about the causality link (the infamous bonding system the game has); before I get into it, here's a piece of advice: make sure to max out all your party member bond levels. By doing so, you'll unlock that character's ultimate move, which sometimes can be a make or break during certain situations. Here's the thing about the causality link, it's a feature that rewards you for bonding to almost every NPC you find throughout the overworld. In the prequel, the developer went over the top and let you bond with over 500 NPC, which is an overkill if you ask me.The good news is in Caligula Effect 2, the developer took the smart decision and downsized the amount of bondable NPC to 193 – yay! Not only that, it's now easier to track down specific NPC because they added the general location information in the causality link menu, which means less running around and hoping for some random NPC to wander in your direction. While you will still have to run around to find some of them, this is a vast improvement over the original game and a huge plus in my book because the last one was just godawful.Another small but helpful improvement that is related to the causality link feature is the sidequest system. You can now do multiple quests simultaneously, which means less backtracking! That is another plus in my book. Last but not least, a frickin quest indicator – no, I'm not kidding, that new addition is like a godsend for clearing them. However, there is an issue with the sidequest system. It is divided into two groups, solo quests and group quests; while the latter had a clear indicator on the mini-map, the first one didn't. That means extra effort to find those quest givers.Another good news is that the quests are relatively easy to do, so long as you keep smashing crystals scattered throughout the overworld. The bad news is that some quests require you to spend lottery tickets, which is a limited resource. Spoiler alert! You'll need 40 tissue packs for 100% completion. Caligula Effect 2 was an okay sequel, and I enjoyed the game despite its flaws. If you're looking for a JRPG with a high school fantasy setting and banger soundtrack, then you're in the right place! A bit of advice, I highly recommend playing the prequel first because the game mentions many events and characters from the previous game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not doing an essay for this one, and plus I'm lazy so I'm just gonna make a pros and cons list. If you're more of a video game music lover (specifically weeb or J-Pop stuff) over other aspects of a video game, I highly recommend this game, as it's whole gimmick is revolving around music to uplift a society of people ()-Acting three times like in Overdose is replaced by χ-Jack, which gets significantly better as you unlock skills for it-They cut down the Causality Link to a comfy 150+ people compared to the 500+ in Overdose, and it's easier to find and do their quests. Sadly, you can't recruit them like in the first game-They upgraded how the equipment works compared to the first game, which is great!Cons:-EXP multiplier caps at 1.5x (For completionists, it's gonna take some time to be a certain level for a side quest lol)-No run button-The localization team () had way too much fun with the translations, and let me say it's not gonna be for everyone LMAO-(Purely subjective) Can't act three times like in Overdose, not necessary but I do miss that a bit-The lead up to the true ending was very... something else-The bad end is barely as emotionally impactful as the prequel's bad end-Conclusion:Solid 9/10, as this is a must-buy for turn-based/dungeon-crawler/persona-esque enjoyers who like buying games no one knows (at least in the west). And if you like it alot, consider suffering through the prequel like me! I really, really would like a Caligula Effect 3, I won't lie to you.

_childDocuments_.review: This game shot up to become one of my favorite games, maybe even my personal favorite. Not only are the themes and ideas tackled here interesting and unique in themselves, but the way they're handled is something I really appreciated. The story is something I greatly enjoyed, especially the aspects of it that connected to the previous game. But more than that, I love how thematically cohesive the game is-- from the character design, to the songs, to how each party member's class/playstyle (and even their skill names) are a reflection of who they are, to how the foils are setup for each party member, the meaning behind the flowers assigned to each character, what their Catharsis Effect looks like, and a lot more other stuff that would take way too much space if I list them all down.It's abundantly clear to me that there's a really strong sense of direction and intent from the writer/director in how every little thing is laid out in the game, especially the message they want to convey to the player/audience. So yeah, I highly recommend this game, especially if the stuff I mentioned above are things you also value, especially in rpgs....Oh right, and you can also juggle and combo a wheelchair in mid-air.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, I prefer this game's combat mechanic over Persona hands down. Strategizing turn-based with time simulation is just brilliant, and to top it off, it was very well-balanced, every combo hits are satisfying, and the OST are top tier. I am the type who easily gets bored grinding for JRPGs when it's the same sh*t all over(I still do it, but with pain), but grinding here doesn't feel grueling at all. Once you get used to its combat, you could fight much higher-leveled enemies with well-timed combos and the possibilities are endless.The progress of the story feels natural and there is apparent character development throughout the story. All characters are lovely and they have their own struggles to relate to. Not to mention, chatting with them through WIRE was so much fun. Other than the main story and character episodes, I just wish there were more places where the protagonist could interact more with the characters, maybe as a hangout/side event or sth.But I would still give this game 9.8/10 for all the effort the amazing devs put into this game.
