_childDocuments_.review: First off, this game is a direct sequel set 5 years after the first game and if you're wondering if you're required to play those first (original on vita or the remake, Overdose), you aren't but I would very much recommend at least Overdose because it's a very great game on it's own.From the synopsis and first look on the game, it's hard to not get the impression that it's going to be the same as the first one but that is shaken early on and even more as you progress the game and notice their big differences. Things like the virtual setting of both games, Mobius and Redo, being completely different in every aspect despite being similar in concept. Or the battle system, while still called Imaginary Chain, is largely adjusted mechanically and has new and great functions added. There is also the music being more consistent quality-wise than the last game, both with the character tracks by various artists (Kemu, Ayase from YOASOBI, KairikiBear, etc.) and Tsukasa Masuko for the rest of the OST. All these elements come together to make old fans feel a completely fresh experience and give newcomers a very unique one.The characters and plot this time around take an overall more serious tone. While the entire main cast is written in a way that not a lot of people will directly relate to, players will still be able to empathize with them as they get to know them more and find out the circumstances that put them in Redo and their regrets, which is the main theme of the game. A theme that isn't uncommon but, to me, isn't something that has been tackled this masterfully in a way that would definitely leave something for all players to reflect on as they go through and ultimately finish the game.To end the review, I feel the game has set a gold standard for sequels and JRPGs as a whole for me. Caligula 2 is not only a game that improved on the first games but went over and beyond all expectations for me with how it managed to feel so much like the previous games while being completely different at the same time. A game that will definitely make everyone feel something they will never experience again with any other franchise. I highly recommend the game to anyone interested.

_childDocuments_.review: Okay, I'll just say that I think this is better than its prequel The Caligula Effect Overdose in almost every way possible.What I meant by almost it's still not perfect, I would say they spent a greater amount of time making this game, but it still feels very low budget in most parts, but other than that it improved significantly.Now would I need to play the first installment before this? I would say the events happen after whatever transpired in the first game. So it's safe to say it's nice to know, but you can easily just look it up on youtube or some ♥♥♥♥ because I DO NOT recommend that game.Now the story basically is that a new Mobius called Redo is made by a virtuadoll named "Regret". And again like the first game, we start a new 'Go-Home club' where we recruit new members to destroy the virtual world, kill regret, and escape back to reality. The ending is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ trip let me tell you that first, honestly I'm fine with that because of how unexpected it is. But of course I ain't spoiling ♥♥♥♥.Character-wise, I prefer these to the first Caligula effect. They're more unique, more stylized, have better backstories, and are more useful in combat. Besides, we have best Okkaasan in the group Sasara.The soundtrack as I stated in the first is very good. This time I think is even better. I think damn that the soundtrack is my favorite part of the game, not even lying.As for the combat in the game, it's a lot more simple really. This time you only get one turn to use whatever ability you choose then that's it as it moves to another character. Honestly, I think it's a step in the right direction so I wouldn't have to button-mash my way to finish my turn like in the first installment.The dungeon crawling is also simpler too. There are a lot less enemies around than in the first game, which I also think is good. That way you don't get too overwhelmed and want to rush through the game (just like in the first installment again).The casuality link is also dumbed down since there are a lot less people you can befriend and its side quests are actually a little more interesting, but still not the best. I just quit doing side quests halfway through the game.I feel the atmosphere in this game is a lot more vibrant and colorful. I didn't like the bright white everywhere in the first game (again) so that was good too.If I were you, I'd just skip over the first game and head straight over to this one. Though I also would read more about the overall plot of what happened in the first installment before heading on through.

_childDocuments_.review: I was honestly surprised that 1/Overdose even got a sequel, and since the first trailer, I was hesitant about this game for a number of reasons and had lowish expectations. However, I was graciously gifted a copy, and was able to try it out. Overall, I feel that it is a . If you enjoyed the first game and want more, then I would recommend picking it up.I was initially concerned about the reduction of the Imaginary Chain from 3 (12) to 1 (4) moves, but it wasn't as bad as I expected. The combat starts off slow but once you get more party members it gets faster and more fun. Once you get X-Jack () you can just steamroll on any difficulty and ignore boss/enemy gimmicks should you so chose. I was playing on Hard but honestly I would recommend either Hard with no X-Jack, or Extreme, even for a first playthrough, because I ended up killing bosses in a single combo without them being able to even queue up their first move.Each character is about equally as viable (without level modifications) and you won't be at any real disadvantage by playing with certain characters outside of extreme outlier situations. That said, there is an "Izuru" character in this game and some characters end up just offering more to a team than others. One issue I had by the end is that you are given too much choice - each character has a lot of skills to pick from but you will only ever end up realistically using a handful of them (which is sad because I'm pretty sure that like 25% of the game's budget went into animating 700,000-Millenia-Miracle). I think that sometimes too much choice/freedom can be a bad thing, and despite having so many different characters to choose from, I ended up not swapping them out very often after getting the last party member.In terms of the more general gameplay loop, it is the same as before and I have no complaints other than that some of the dungeons feel slightly too long/repetitive (but not all of them), and having to return to the X-express to go to another area is a little tedious. However overall, I have no major complaints, although I do wish that X-Jack had some more customisability, for example you being able to pick both the song and the effect independently from each other.Unlike Overdose, it doesn't seem like you can rebind multiple keys to the same action within the game. I have done it and talk about this later.The story is better but questionable. I started out by thinking it was much more well constructed than the first game, and it is - all the characters feel like they contribute more and aren't relegated to a single chapter and then forgotten. The party member characters and their interactions between each other are consistent and more convincing than the first game. As well as this, their designs and behaviours have subtle traits that hint at their traumas and backstories, which is a very nice touch when compared to the first games. (for example, the Musicians , or later ), and in one particular case, I felt that a certain character backstory/justification was just simply pathetic/disrespectful (in particular, the Musician ). I felt that all their arcs were NOT resolved during the story, and the (ending spoilers) .You are able to learn more about the Musicians through postgame challenge fights, but despite people assuring me that things would be explained well, I feel like they didn't really provide much - they gave only a surface level overview of a Musician's backstory rather than a proper "deep-dive" into their way of thinking, leaving a lot to be desired.There are some funny localisation moments but none of it detracts from the story and all of it is in character, so if you are concerned about that, don't be.I like some songs more than others. The remixes are nice, and it is cool that X can sing them too. However depending on your playstyle you might not hear much of the boss remixes. I don't have much more to say than that, despite music being an integral part to the game. The songs are relevant to the character they are paired to, and each is distinct with meaningful lyrics. Outside of the primary songs though, I prefer the music from the first game.Improvement over the first game but still some odd looking models. Not a major concern, but whenever I saw certain things I would always be consciously reminded of how strange it looked, particularly when characters showed their teeth.I really don't know whether the call the Causality Link better or worse. In terms of "story/world-building", it is leagues better than 1/Overdose. It feels like a proper affinity chart/network of people - each character and interaction actually feels like you are accomplishing something tangible within the world, instead of just being 500 tedious quests with randoms and grindy repeated tasks that you'll forget instantly (although I still remember you, Nozomi Hara and your double poison).However, it is still tedious and clunky to complete - the displayed locations for NPCs to hand in quests is often wrong or inaccurate, there is no function like in 1/Overdose to summon them to your location, and despite the minimap texture files having the icon for it, the map does not show you if there is someone near you who you can hand a completed quest into, and despite being able to "master" a skill, you still have to manually equip it for quests.That said, on a single casual playthrough I talked to 91% of them and cleared 60% of the quests, so it is much less taxing than it used to be, although still inconvenient.TLDR: Do NOT do the postgame, it is NOT worth your time, the game does NOT respect you or your time, and the postgame content is tedious, frustrating (due to tedium and bugs), and offers no real incentive either story or challenge wise. Highly recommend not doing it: much better for your mental health not to spend 90 minutes on an Extreme +100 fight when the Imaginary Chain decides to break and every enemy is already taking actions before your characters have drawn their weapons. I played Tower of Prometheus on Hard, then Extreme, and then Extreme +100. Like the first game, accuracy tends to become a big issue when underlevelled (level 80~90 party vs. level 200 enemies with exponentially increased HP), and the fights tend to end up being puzzles of Dashing/Emergency Barrier while waiting for short burst windows to deal damage. You can clear it with any party you want, but it just takes so long to do, and you aren't given anything to justify it other than a short-lived sense of pride and accomplishment.Don't be an idiot. Bring Niko as your fourth (the other 3 you should already know who to use).I do think that overall, this game is an improvement over the first game, and if you've played that or are looking to get into the series I would give the go-ahead. That said, there are some story elements that may mean a lot more if you had played the first game and done the required reading ().Edits:Fixed instance of punctuation.I also want to clarify that while it states that I received a key, I did not: I was graciously  this game and the DLC.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent game. While I do prefer the first one overall, you can clearly see where it takes after the preceding title. It does things a bit differently, but it makes for a game that is still very interesting and fun to play. Without going too in depth:The story works well . The characters, much like the in the first game, are well-written, likable, and relatable. You'll probably have a favorite by the end of the game. The graphics, well, honestly, I don't care in this department, but the game looks fine to me. The 3D models look a little off from some angles, but generally speaking the presentation of the game is fairly attractive. The theme of music being used to represent characters and express their emotions is still prevalent. The OST is solid across the board. Do yourself a favor and look up the lyrics to each musician's song as you play through the game. I absolutely love the how the soundtracks of the 2 games were composed. An attention to detail and creative implementation that I personally appreciated. "Designed Desires" is the best song, btw.Overall, the game is pretty great. My main criticisms come from my personal preferences and some areas that I feel the first game did better. Namely, the progression system and the character episodes. I won't go into detail on character episodes, but I will say they are far better written and better paced in the first game. They are far too brief and abrupt in he second one. It doesn't give you as good an understanding of each character, which is a shame. Progression-- this has been simplified and streamlined compared to the first game. Now, this is not necessarily bad. It works very well, with characters learning abilities as they level up. I personally just preferred the more freeform style of the first game. I wouldn't even hold it against Caligula Effect 2. It's totally fine. Also, a certain someone returns in this game, and I was hoping to learn more about that someone than what I ultimately got from the game. A shame, really. There is a new game+ after you clear it, but I do not yet know what that entails. Maybe I'll get my wish.Battle system is dynamic and frankly very engaging. At first it felt slow(because it was-- slow as balls), but as you develop more abilities and fill out your party, it gets much faster and rewards good strategy. I used every party member in rotation and had a blast doing so. Again, the game is different from the first one, but the departure, I feel, was still well done. It feels like a sequel while still setting itself apart. As a side note, it's a rather easy game. I recommend playing on Hard at least. I played blindly through on Extreme, and I feel it provided a fair challenge.In conclusion, I'm thrilled that Furyu/Historia was able to get a second game out, as I thought The Caligula Effect was one of the most refreshing games I've played in a while. The Caligula Effect 2 delivers. It's a fine sequel, even if it's not my preferred game. If I give the first game a 9, this is easily an 8-8.5. I would absolutely recommend this. I look forward to replaying it one day,Also, enough with the "persona clone" ♥♥♥♥. It's far past the point where it's gotten old.
_childDocuments_.name: The Caligula Effect 2

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, there's no doubt in my mind that this game is far better than it's predecessor. It's a lot better visually even if it's not outstanding compared to other JRPGs released within the same time span. The combat system has been updated and refined in various different ways, slightly new mechanics that improve the flow of battle such as voltage and being limited to one input instead of three per turn which gives you a larger incentive to really consider your choices. Furthermore, if you're not grinding a billion levels or trying to find the most optimal stigmas or whatever, then the difficulty is relatively fair. The main story this time in comparison to the previous, is considerably better, still nothing special though. Moving onto the characters, the characters in this game are very well fleshed out, some characters have backstories that I didn't really find that interesting but their personalities made it up for that, there are also some very crazy things you can learn about these characters once you dive deep into them. In terms of designs, I think I prefer the older art style for sprites more, the portraits of characters sitting in chairs striking poses as you went into their status info page was a nice stylistic addition and this game does not have that. It has the same sprites for characters in formation and inside the status info pages. Designs are still quite nice, at least to me, since art like that is preferential. Enemy variation is just as lack luster as the game prior, you're either fighting the same mobs or fighting the bosses and their summoned minions. Music is once again, composed by the well known vocaloid composers and sung by two different virtuadolls instead of one now. I kind of hope there's a self cover album later in the future, because without going into spoilers one of the bosses' is voiced by Takehito Koyasu, DIO's voice actor. Lastly, while it is indeed a sequel, the connections to the first game are minimal and if you played the first one, good on you, the game will certainly feel better, but even if you haven't it does not hinder your experience or will explain those connections to you in a digestible fashion, Overall, very solid 7.9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: is possibly one of my favorite game of all time despite it flaws in the first game, the same can also be said about  which I've cleared numerous times on Switch. I've bought the limited edition before on the Switch, then once again on the Steam to support this series. I will try my best to write my own personal impression on this game, pros, neutral and cons.- The music is, without a doubt, one of the best aspect of the series. Both The Caligula Effect: Overdose and The Caligula Effect 2 absolutely perfected in the meaning of each song from the Musicians in both games. While Overdose's Ostinato Musicians music contains more emotion and power, the Obbligato Musicians have a far more catchy theme.- The battle system have returned to a far more tactical style of The Caligula Effect (Ps Vita) rather than the Overdose's version. For me, it makes the combat both more challenging and more engaging than the prequel and with the addition of χ-Jack meter, the drawback of long cool-down have disappeared completely once you upgraded all χ upgrades.- The Go-Home Club's in The Caligula Effect 2 members are far more likable and relatable than the first games. Unlike the first game, all members have their own trauma and reason to not get out of Redo, this make their Character Episode far more rewarding, getting to learn and help them overcome their own trauma is genuinely one of the best feeling I ever had. Not only that, but the Go-Home Club in this game felt really close to each other like a group rather than a band of people with the same objective in the prequel.- The hospital section is my favorite arc of the game. Doktor and Kranke, despite their limited screen time and being an Obbligato Musicians, are two of the best character in the game. Their personalities and bitter-sweet relationship have set them apart from all other Musicians and might be on par with both Kuchinashi and Thorn from the first game in my opinion.- The pacing in the story is far better than The Caligula Effect: Overdose, every flows in the story felt more natural instead of rushing through the main quest in the first game.- The addition of jukebox in χ's train is possibly one of the best thing ever, you can now replay the music of your own choice, either Regret's version, χ's version or even the remix version.- Both ending are pretty good, although not as great as Overdose's true ending. While the bad ending is short, it is emotional. The Easter Egg in True Ending from the anime make me smile though.- This might be a personal take but the battle track from the first game doesn't fit with χ's upbeat singing at all. Aside from Orbit, I can't imagine χ sang any of the song in the first game at all, whereas I could imagine μ sang every song from this game and it would fit perfectly.- The Chamber of Memories is just... alright. This is a special place that you can unlock after clearing the game and achieve a True Ending which focus on The Obbligato Musician's backstory. Instead of learning by interacting with the musicians, you are given a book with the summarized of their past and how they come to Redo. This make me like MU-Kun and Kudan a little more though. - The protagonists and χ, while played perfectly in the story, cut off one of the best aspect in The Caligula Effect: Overdose. Because their body have been shared with χ, this mean you can't (and won't) be able to play as a Musician ever without having to re-write the story completely which is weird, considering The Ostinato Musicians are the strong point of the first game. This brings me to my next point:- The Obbligato Musicians (with the exception of Doktor and Kranke) are disappointing when compared to The Ostinato Musicians. The Ostinato Musicians's motive to abandoned reality to live in Mobius felt strong and make you empathize with them. And because of the protagonist's situation that make them unable to become one of the musicians, you don't get to spend time or expand on their personality or backstory either.Despite having more flaws than the first game (for me), I still loved and enjoyed The Caligula Effect 2. It is far from a perfect sequel but it isn't bad either. Just don't put your expectation too high for this game and if you can look past the animation and graphics then you will enjoy your time!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is indeed a step up from the original Caligula Effect, but still miles away from me actually recommending it to anybody. While it doesn't do anything massively wrong, it tends to fumble the ball on everything it does right. The two high points of this game are the music and the concepts of the combat. It's about the "Prediction Engine" where you can watch the battle unfold for ~15 seconds into the future, place your actions into the timeline and using frame data to guide your choices.This means you'll be precisely timing your jumping attack so flip over the shooting enemy, or guarding the precise moment to block an attack without losing too much time, or choosing the right counter for a scary attack. This is the kind of game that throws a level 50 enemy into your level 20 dungeon... and with skill you can win this instead of returning to the dungeon later. The first boss is a difficulty spike because they require you to master these systems. It's tense and its exciting and its a brain-burner... and its all downhill from there. By the second boss you've unlocked counters for all the basic actions and multiple types of limit breaks so you can one shot everything in the future. The high point of the combat was the very first battle and then its just added systems to break the game even more.  Outside of the combat, this game is a persona-wannabe that for the most-part works if shallow. There is a hundred something NPCs that you can meet, perform a sidequest for and turn into best friends. This raises your main character's stats and nets useful items. It's less tedious than the first game and while I'd prefer a small well-written cast of characters this didn't hurt the experience. That said... if I hear one more person say "My world is falling apart do you have any superglue?" when they meet me again... I might hurt something.Now, for the writing. I don't know if its the localization or the original developers, but it didn't leave a good impression on me. A game that deals with trauma, and regret and psychological issues is walking a really thin tightrope and requires a very high level expertise that these writers lacked.The story was passable enough that I'd shrug it off in most JRPGs, but when it deal with mental issues puts it in a different light for me. Some sidequests made me uncomfortable, and many of the positive quest resolutions ranged from "stupid" to "dangerously unhealthy". God I wish I was just complaining about the cringey writing (#YoloSwag4Life) but [spoilers] maaan.There is a great start to a game here and its enough of a step up from the original game that I'll look into the third as well. If they can better balance the combat and trim some of the excessively OP systems I could see it being one of my favorite JRPG series.

_childDocuments_.review: Regret - a mysterious virtuadoll.Those who hear her songs find themselves transported into another world called "Redo".The world of Redo is a virtual world built from the regrets of many people."If only I'd done things differently..."This is a world where everyone's secret desire to redo their lives can come true.A place where they can become the person they would have been had they chosen differently...Redo - a dull world with no regrets, where anyone can experience a life redone.The Caligula Effect 2 is a JRPG that implements a matrix "future-seeing" battle system similar to its predecessor called an "Imaginery Chain" that allows you to see the future of how events plays out. This allows you to correct any actions such as your timing for abilities to hit or dodging an enemies strike frame perfectly. Given the nature of this game, it's relatively easy to progress through the game even in the hardest difficulties with no issues. Now I'm no fan of this game, I came in blind. I saw this game on sale and was looking for something to play for when I'm at home and when I'm out and about on my Steam Deck. I can say that I was pleasantly surprised, from the characters to the music itself.While the game itself isn't really great in terms of animation and expressing emotions, the positives being more focused on a decent background of the individual Go-Home Club Members, Fleshed out enemies and the music makes up for such a minor issue. Seeing the Go-Home Club Members and their respective Musician rival interactions is an interesting idea and it's well executed in the game.As a sequel to the first game, we are introduced to a new cast of the Go-Home Club. They are all unique in their own rights and all hold some form of regret, hence the reason why they are in Redo. Seeing their daily struggles in normal school life when they're not trying to fight is pretty nice. I can't really say much as it'll spoil a lot of things but just remember that in Redo, everyone is a facade as who they are in Redo is a projection of their ideal person in the Real World.I particularly enjoyed each and everyone of them. Although you are technically using 4 members at a time for exploration and not using certain members to some extent, they still bring forth diversity in the group. What I did not like however was the amount of skills everyone learnt throughout the game, you get a lot of skills through a few levels only and you usually use about 30% of their entire skillset and it's ridiculous so I wish they would cut down the number of skills.The Musicians are a bunch of group antagonists of the game, each with their own unique style of music. Ranging from a funky groovy beat to a hardcore literal rap fiesta. The songs are composed by the Musicians and is sang by Regret, who is the supposed main antagonist in this game. The music plays an important role as everyone hears it in-universe and it also acts as the dungeon music for the respective musicians we are exploring. The music itself is a representation of the Musicians as the lyrics of all the Musician songs are a reflection of their personality. Upon beating the bosses, X (who is the partner of the main character and also known as a Virtualdoll - Virtual Idol in short) is able to sing the songs of who we beat. She will be able to sing with the ability known as X-Jack (activated via Voltage); an in-game mechanic with a meter on the right side when full; instantly allows all party members to instantly act again, cancelling wait time and providing additional bonuses such as Defense, Increased Duration of Voltage and Increased Voltage via Kills, Aerial Attack, etc..; Using this ability allows X to sing whatever songs we pick and different songs provides different bonuses such as an increased in attack, defense, critical rates or all stats depending on the song.The battle system is your generic turn based combat, but it borrows a few aspect from other games and create its own unique style of gameplay. It acts as a real time combat system with the ability to time your attacks or dodge according to the "Imaginery Chain". It's acts like a timeline battle system with a bit of Final Fantasy 7's ATB system.Going a bit more deeper in the battle system, the "Imaginery Chain" is an in-game mechanic where you're able to see how the battle progresses without actually doing anything. It means that you're able to adapt to any situation as according to what the enemies are doing. You also have to take into account the delay after your attacks as some attacks either has a short delay or long delay after performing said attack. While the battle system itself is very technical, it isn't really difficult to get used to it.And can I also say the transition of the music is absolutely fantastic? It reminds me a bit of the idea of Fire Emblem: Three Houses with their battle music transitions of Rain and Thunder. This game does a bit of the same but it's from instrumentals when exploring and then the vocals kicking in when you enter a battle. Even if it gets hella repetitive as the same song plays through the dungeon for like 5 hours, it's still a gawddang bop.. Still wished that you are able to change the music somehow for variety but that's just me being nitpicky.Main Story was relatively linear, you get introduced to a boss, enter their dungeon, explore said dungeon, you beat a boss, take a break, do side quests, character episodes, go back to sleep and prepare for the next dungeon. The story itself is fine, I didn't particularly enjoy the Good Ending as I felt it was a bit lackluster for what the main characters were fighting for and the Bad Ending is a big spoiler by itself though so I won't really dive too deep into it..Although it is a sequel to the first game, you do not need to play the first game to enjoy this. The Caligula Effect 2 does a bit of referencing of the first game here and there though. I would heavily suggest playing the first game then the second to get the full enjoyment as if you've started playing the second game first then onto the first game, you'll be aware of certain characters names and existence of certain characters already such as  and especially Side Quest is a hit or miss for everyone, I felt like it was meh.. in general. In order to progress through the side quests, you will need specific "Stigmas" which are equippable accessories you get in Soul Remnants (Chest). Some of these Side Quest literally drag on till the end of the game and if you missed a Stigma, you cannot retrieve it if you progressed too far, thus making it impossible to complete the side quest.Similar to the first game, both Causality Link Chart and WIRE makes a return. Talking to NPCs and completing their quest levels up the Causality Link Chart. When you talk with NPCs with a "?" on their head, you automatically add them on your WIRE app and once you maxed a bond with someone, you're able to see the details of the real world of the people you have maxed bonds with. Upon clearing certain Side Quests and playing the lottery, you're able to get additional conversation messages to use to interact with people through WIRE.The Caligula Effect 2 is a game that definitely won't satisfy every people, but if you are looking for an interesting game to play and waste time on, you might want to consider The Caligula Effect 2 and its predecessor; The Caligula Effect: Overdose. [7.2/10] Game is decent and music is on-point and also don't forget... よこそう, あたらしの世界. PS: The game took me about 100 hours to beat for a total of 3 playthroughs.Edit: Grammar Mistakes, Additional Notes and Minor Nitpicks.

_childDocuments_.review: is a very interesting and unique RPG about realizing that you're in a idyllic virtual world and trying to escape it. While I think many people look at its surface and say 'Persona clone', that's doing it an injustice. I think if you're a fan of Persona because of its story and characters, you would probably also enjoy this game, but there's a lot more to appreciate here.I won't go into much detail about the story - the general gist is covered nicely by the description at the top of the page. Overall, though, it's a very fun ride. The strongest aspect of the story, in my opinion, are the characters.A lot of love was put into both the members of the Go-Home Club and their rivals, the Obbligato Musicians, who serve as antagonists. They all have very well defined personalities, as well as a good amount of depth (for an anime game), and watching them interact is great. I had a lot of fun pulling back the layers on each of them over my playthrough of the game.In addition to their obvious presence in the main story scenes, you also do this through 'character episodes', which are basically mini-chapters dedicated to that character's personal story. You could compare these to 'social links' if you want to go down the Persona route, and that'll give you a good idea of what they're like. However, you can also talk to these characters via WIRE (basically text messaging) by asking them a question; you unlock new questions through quests, finding them around town, and so on. There are well over 100 of these, which lets you get into these character's heads even more by asking 'what animal are you?', 'what do you look for in a relationship?'. You will bombard these characters  and love every second of it.In summary, the story is solid, and the characters are excellent. I guess if I had to name a negative, it would be that at times, the localization goes heavy on the memes, but it's not unbearably often. The positives greatly outweigh the negatives here.Lastly, if you want to know if you need to know the first game's story; no, not really. There are some elements that are referenced, but you won't be lost if you haven't played it. It will probably enhance your experience though, so feel free to play it, or watch a let's play, if you want.You can expect the usual RPG patterns - main story sequences where there's dialogue, then going into 'dungeons' and fighting enemies. There are also optional side quests you'll find everywhere, and I mean everywhere - I'll get to that. But first, I want to talk about the battle system.The battle system in this game is probably not like any other game you've played. It's like a fusion of Active Time Battles from FF, with some rock-paper-scissors, some fighting game-ish elements, and some comboing. It's hard to explain, but I'll try my best.Basically, battles operate in 'real time'. Characters get their turn and you choose an action - that action has some 'startup' before it attack comes out, and then some recovery time after. Once the action is fully recovered, they get their turn again. You can also choose to delay this action on the timeline by moving it left and right in something called the 'Imaginary Chain'. This lets you see a preview of the next X seconds of the battle - you can see what your characters will do, and what the enemies will do, before you commit to an action.This means that if an enemy is using a big attack, you can opt to have your character perform a defensive action, or run out of the way. If one of your party members knocks an enemy into the air, you can combo your attacks together to juggle them - the Imaginary Chain takes out the guess work because you'll see exactly what is going to happen. Having your characters coordinate to pull off cool combos is -really- fun.It does require a little patience as you plan your moves, however - if you're someone who just likes to mash one button when playing games, this might not be your cup of tea. Speaking of patience, let's talk about the quests in this game.There's, like... 70% of a good quest system. You will get a lot of basic requests which are simple 'bring me this item' or 'do this thing', which is fine. But when you go to turn these in, you might not remember where the NPC is and only have a vague location to go by (Hospital 4F Dayroom, for example). Icons for these solo quests, as the game calls them, don't show up on the minimap, so you might find yourself getting lost.They do show up for the 'group quests', though, which are more story focused. They all boil down to 'talk to this person with a specific item equipped'. I won't get too in-depth about this, but it's just a little bit more hassle than it needs to be.The soundtrack is superb, in particular the music used for battles and boss fights. The dynamic transition from instrumentals while out of battle, to vocals when you enter battle, really gets your blood pumping. The battle music also exists in-universe - it's why the antagonists are called 'Musicians', and each piece reflects the personality of the character it's made by, which is kind of a cool story detail.There's no dub, so all of the voice acting is in Japanese, but it's all done well. About 95% of the dialogue has voice acting for the main cast, and cutscenes have subtitles. Battle commentary is not subbed, though, so your experience will be enhanced if you know a little Japanese.I have a pretty average gaming PC and it ran perfectly well for me. I experienced 1 'fatal error' crash in my entire playthrough, and it may have been my fault. I doubt this game is going to push anyone's specs too hard.I loved my time with this game, and I hope it gets more attention (and another sequel). It's an easy recommend for anyone who likes anime and/or RPGs in general. It's a solid 7/10 or 8/10 and very much worth playing.

_childDocuments_.review: The original Caligula Effect: Overdose was a neat game and a great foundation for an ongoing franchise.  It had a number of gameplay issues, but many of them just needed a bit more work to get everything right.  And since it was originally a 2016 Vita game, there was a lot of room for overall polish when moving up to home consoles/PC.  So when I heard about The Caligula Effect 2, I was excited to see what they'd do to improve things.Turns out, they didn't.  This is just the first game again.  In fact, the character models and animations are on the same level as the 2016 Vita game.  But let me be clear, I liked the first game, so I enjoyed doing it all over again (even if I felt sort of let down by the missed potential).My recommendation: play The Caligula Effect: Overdose, and if you want more, you'll enjoy this as well.

_childDocuments_.review: This game improves on Many parts of the Original. From a more fluid combat system to a smaller but much more well written cast, this game is a testament on how to learn from the mistakes you made. Now, the game's not perfect, with the models looking like its from early PS3 era often, but the visual style alongside a bopping soundtrack does well to mask it when you're in combat. I highly recommend this game should you be able to grab it on a sale.P.S: If you are worried about the DLCs, none of them are mandatory so feel free to skip them as you wish. They're mostly stat buffs that will quickly be tossed aside and the OSTs while great remixes of the first game, I can't really say you need them, and they're mainly fanservice for fans of the original.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid enough game. You don't need to have played the first to understand anything taking place here and honestly if you had then one of the plot points kinda got spoiled before even beginning this title, which is a little odd. I honestly prefer the cast and party system featured in Overdose in addition to the general story but mechanically speaking, this game is better on all fronts and probably a great way to get into Caligula. The OST is incredible and probably the best part about the entire experience. I'm not too big on χ's covers but they aren't terrible by any means. The DLC also does DLC things when it comes to RPGs but once you reach a certain point you will have outscaled the DLC boosts anyway.Combat system is super interesting and pretty innovative but rather jank and a bit boring once you stat-check everything typical RPG style. Fortunately there is an autobattle for the grindier sections later but up until you reach that point, finding creative uses and timing for combinations does feel really rewarding. The main cast has some hit or miss characters but overall, I liked them all and it's a bit clear who gets the most development and screentime by the later stages, but ultimately enough is there to supplement anything you'd desire to know/see concerning them. Lastly, the endgame is fine enough. No spoilers on it, but there is a postgame with difficult content to complete and 100%-ing the game does require 2 playthroughs if that's what you're looking for. The game isn't terribly long if you just do the core story, but it has enough immersive elements to make you want to pursue the side content to a degree.... though finding every freaking NPC AND doing all relevant sidequests associated with them got really old REALLY fast.Overall 7/10, can recommend. Lacks polish but is innovative enough and does not mince words nor discussion about real topics.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a damn good album that comes with a free JRPG game.A lot of people compare the Caligula franchise to Persona, and it's hard not to make that connection. But instead of looking at it like a bargain brand Persona, I see it more like an under-loved cousin trying to do it's own thing while taking some inspiration. If you go into this game looking for an exact replica of Persona, you'll likely be disappointed.I nearly 100%'d the game on PS4 and was very excited to see it release on PC. The port runs really well so far. The franchise itself is way too underrated for what it is and deserves a lot more attention. Not perfect, but it makes me very excited for the future and it was overall an enjoyable and unforgettable experience. I've been listening to the soundtrack for months.Pros:-Massive improvement over the first game.-Fun, satisfying, and unique combat. A lot of ways to experiment with party members and strategies.-Excellent voice acting.-Top-tier soundtrack.-Very well-written characters. Your party goes through some well-deserved character development. Some antagonists actually push them to grow.-Great art design and style-New Game Plus and Post-Game Options that can be challenging.-Entertaining Dialogue-Hard-hitting, relatable, and profound themes. It balances tone very well.-A psychology nerd's wet dream.Cons-Mediocre dungeons-Less-than-desirable side quests-Combat can get a bit too easy in the mid-game/late-game (you're just simply given way too many options -- though it is fun to juggle an enemy like it's DevilMayCry). I recommend playing on hard or extreme. If you're new to the franchise, you might want to think about playing the first game (remastered version: The Caligula Effect: Overdose on Steam), though it can be a drag to get through.  There's also a mediocre anime as an alternative. The story in Caligula 2 will be a lot less impactful without the knowledge gained in the first one, but it's not strictly necessary to have; They properly bring you up to speed in this one.Try this game. You won't  it.

Took me 58h (IG time) for all achievements on Hard : 20h for the story, 30 h for the casuality links quests + explored all areas, 4h for the lvl 60 grind quest and 4h for the extra stories of each musicians + second playthrough for the bad ending. i didnt do the optional Tower because it wasnt that appealing and there is no story/achievement behind it.Score : 7.5/10The Goods :-Interresting sets of characters, friends or musicians. Each one got a different personality and trauma.-The OST, mostly dungeons musics is a banger. One of the best i have r heard those last years .-Combat is good and doesnt feels static even if it's turn based. You can counter attacks or guard them when you cant counter. Positionning is important too and risk management is one of the best way to do damage. The game is better played at high difficulty where most of the combat system must be used.-Better level design than the first game.-The optimisation/port on PC is very good, never dropped below 120fps and got 0 crashs.The Bads :-The game need an option to speed up the pre-visualisation of the "round" when you validate an attack. _childDocuments_.review: I didn't get the first review like I wanted...what a tragedy....In any case, hello there! Remember me? Probably not! I'm the one jackhole from the overdose review section AND I'M BACK AGAIN FOR ROUND 2 TO    REVIEW THE GREATEST SEQUEL EVER MADE. I'll leave comments open this time I'm already satisfied with the positive praise and discussions so far and hell it'd be fun to be socially awkward with some of you perhaps.TL;DR version on what makes this amazing and an instant buy:MarieAmazing and varied music(Mostly) likable characters, like MarieLively and beautiful scenery that is complimented by the musicMarieUnique and T A C T I C A L battle systemIt's the greatest sequel ever madeM A R I EMiniature college essay version I had to rewrite a lot:So obviously I already own this game (I pre ordered LE day 1 for PS4). Yes I bought this game twice. Yes it was well worth it. I bought the first game 3 times technically. That should be enough in of itself to sell you on this really.I 100%'d this once and am well prepared to do it a second time because I have a crippling addiction to the Caligraphy Effect and MARIEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE Amabuki.But how does this compare to the first game? Honestly it plays considerably different and with the overall higher production value if for some unthinkable reason you DIDN'T like the first game then you should absolutely park your assback here and give this NEW masterpiece a shot because apparently the creators of this series are gifted by higher powers or something. The battle system itself as far as pacing and other things go has been changed to be slower and more tactical. Gone are the 3 move spam chains to obliterate all who stand in your way and now has come the era of stacking triple buffs on everybody and one shotting them after 6 minutes of setup time (unless you use the same chad off meta team as Seth, Kobato FTW). This is good and bad in its own ways really and even now I don't necessarily have a total preference over one or the other but its more up to preference than anything if you're coming from Overdose.The "soul" of the first game is very well still present and in absolute abundance I might add. As much as I adore Mobius, the wonderful world of Redo has so much more life and activity to it all around. I am completely content at times just idling in the station while SINGI blares through my ears. The soundtrack in general honestly has no bad songs, AGAIN. I'd even dare say all around the music is even better overall (with some outliers from the first game still being some of my favorites). It's actually beyond my comprehension. And even if it DOES have a "bad" song in your eyes frankly it's a lot more diverse compared to the first game which means I almost guarantee there's a song in here for everyone to enjoy. The short loops of the first game are gone with the wind (as they admittedly should've been with the remake really) and you are now graced with the full version of each song as you traverse some equally diverse locations this time around that beautifully fit them.(Mostly) new crew of characters this time around on both sides. They are all around as remarkable give or take as the first though I would maybe dare say the first game's cast was overall superior. Unfortunately though even the ones here I initially despised we're magically written into good characters in a matter of 2 scenes which is just blatantly unfair honestly.This should honestly be the REAL definition of the "Caligula Effect", because it had to have taken some other worldly power to go from making me want to kick Ryuto off a moving train and then make me not want to do it *as* much by the end of it. In some cases for this to occur you will have to do SOME extra digging but the point remains. Everyone in this virtual world has their own problems. Some you'll understand, some you won't, but it's what makes us all human in the end.I think I touched on all my major points here from before. Thank you for coming to my TED-talk. If we get Caligula 3 I'll be sure to make that one even longer and more outrageous. This series as a whole has literally changed my life for the better by playing it so you better be damn sure I'm gonna want other people to play it. That reminds me, everyone buy this game 3 more times so we can get Caligula 3. Do it for Seth.Did I mention Marie?

_childDocuments_.review: The thing I liked most about the first game was that you could essentially play out the entirety of a fight in the first move, essentially creating your own fight from start to end, but I understand the change from giving the player freedom to "create your own fight" to limiting them to 1 action at a time. Caligula 1 wasn't for everybody and came with a very overwhelming battle system that allowed for players to either do one action at a time and ease themselves into the full potential of the system or allow the more ambitious players (people like me) to go all the way from start to finish. Caligula 2 offers a more accessible battle system by essentially introducing a more nerfed version of the system in Caligula 1. Instead of feeling overwhelmed, you can now do 1 action at a time. The devs could have just doubled down on Caligula 1's system, but they opted for this and I'd say it was a good move. It was just a bit of a disappointment for me personally going from mastering Caligula 1's freedom to Caligula 2's restrictive version. I was personally hoping to do even more nutty and batsh!t insane timelines in Caligula 2. But that's just me being spoiled by how creative you could be in fights with Caligula 1. This series has been the most unique RPG and is fighting for first place with Legend of Legaia for me. These games are worth playing and beating. A step up in many aspects from 1 but subjectively a more neutered and boring combat experience with an objectively better and more accessible combat system. I hope if they ever make a third (DO IT. YOU BETTER DO IT! If you need a reason, make it out to be like X getting corrupted by hacker groups that want to escape reality and the people in the new world fight to forever end the whole virtual world from ever being realized again), they reuse Caligula 1's system now that more people have experience with 2's system. The full potential of the system is so much more fun. It almost makes you want to start with Caligula 2 and then go back to Caligula 1. JUST GIVE ME MORE OF THIS SERIES!!!!!

_childDocuments_.review: The game is interesting, and I score it negatively because the cons outweight the pros of my experience.So rather than stating the game is not worth playing I will say this - if someone enjoyed Caligula Effect: Overdose, then they will play this part, as the concept of the series as a whole carries on.The port is done well, and I had no issues, so the negative aspects are tied to the core of the game.My advice would be to wait till the game is heavily discounted, as it has its merits, but not at this price tag.Pros:- No more aimless running around: so my main issue with the Overdose part was the Causality Link "trips" to npcs scattered around maps to fix their trauma. I am a completionist and going through it all really snuffed the enjoyment part. In Caligula 2 you get information where to find the npc, and for group quests you even get a tag on a map.- The unlocking of new links is less cringy: another issue that showed while playing Overdose is the way the npcs introduced themselves. So there were over 500 people there and majority had the same line "I am shy so I did not talk to you" (guys) and "I am suspicious so I did not talk to you" (girls). At first I was confused, and then just wanted to run through the text because there was nothing new. Here while texts are repeated, they are not on that lazy level, and I can see a mild bit of interest shown for it.- No more "3 steps ahead" : the combat is now more reactive. Instead of planning 3 steps ahead, you get one which is a large improvement in terms of reacting to the flow of the battle. It also allows less waiting time for delay corrections.- Group quests: Instead of a plethora of single quests we get introduced to "mini plots" that allow us to complete the links more efficiently. Most of them are interesting, and would love to see an improvement of allowing the player to steer the outcome, without having just one single road to take.Cons:- The graphics are mediocre: So this is a 2021 release on consoles using Unreal Engine. Yet the game itself feels like from 2012 or earlier. The characters have look like a cutout copy of one basis body, with features slapped on it. There is also no distinct facial animation - sure eyebrows move and the mouth while talking (in a repetative patterns not fitting the voice). On top of that the protagonists looks like they were fed with lemons via slingshot since early childhood. They lack the ability to show facial emotions and it makes hard to enjoy playing as such.- The issues that victims of Redo have are meh: the people in Redo are all brought with a specific regret. That much is understandable, but at the same time it does not make sense as a plot, because of how shallow it can be. I get the fact that those are life regrets, and wanting to change, but the whole idea did not stick with me. Maybe because everyone has some regrets during their life it makes for a numbing effect in regards to the issue, but I really could not get into caring for the people in the plot.- The antagonists are shallow: so the stories of each antagonists is very brief, and the interactions the player has with them is minimal. While I enjoyed their plots in Overdose, here I am indifferent. And the whole idea that they were "handpicked" makes it even more difficult to follow up, since each of them have a different goal. I really would not be surprised to fight an angsty teen who regreted not having milk for breakfast, and the fights would be include a cereal bowl and bottle of milk as adds. The general feel was that the plot was done very poorly from the "bad guys" perspective, and needs way more attention.- The music lacks the "oomph": So one of the main feature for the antagonists is that they are musicians. Well it seems to me that in this part they are just getting a track made by someone else and slapping the "musician" title. The boss music is ok, but before I reach them I had to listen to the normal "theme". Now I am not hating on the songs as they are good. But repeative listening to it made me shut down the BGM and instead listen to Spotify. In addition the tracks are more mellow and lack the spark that is associated with battle. Instead of being hyped I was chilled and that got boring real fast. Maybe an option to have 2-3 tracks being played could solve this.- The combat background: So another issue that I had is the siezure invoking background that while interesting at first, was later on more and more annoying. I undestand that this is a part of "brainwashing".- No drawn animations: So in the animation department there must have been some layoffs, because this title is missing drewn animations. It is a huge layoff for me as I was hoping for more of them than in Overdose.- "Tissue issue": Whoever came up with a decision that this will be a good idea should not work in game development. It is an RNG element that has nothing to do but artificially extend the game time or cause people to reload saves to complete. I really am beyond understanding how this is part of a game that should be enjoyable.- Character episodes are not well done: So each character has episodes for their plot, but they are really limited to a bit of talk, one or two choices and that is it. People responsible for writing the plot of the game really need to step up their game, as I was not impressed by the content given me with this.- The ending is the "real Regret": So when I reached the ending I was really hit by how bland and low-effort it was. Seriously all the time spent and the players are served "this". I am beyond words on how dissapointed I was, and the time leading towards it suddenly lost meaning.Overall the game has a lot of flaws which steer me from recommending it. Fans of the series will still play it, but the game is a rushed heavily that is suffering from the "sequel syndrome" and is delivering less.I really hope that if there is Caligula 3 (I wish that be the case), then it will be more polished in terms of enjoying not only the gameplay but plot.And also if you are using Unreal Engine please utilize its functions rather than using stock models.

_childDocuments_.review: 10x better than the first game, there's no question about it.The story is miles better, it has no comparison, I got very immersed in it and I actively wanted to interact with the choices that were given to me. The dungeon crawling doesn't feel like a chore anymore (although I still recurred to Normal for dungeons and Extreme for bossfights), and the combat system has been refined a bit (but imo the concept was already promising, it just needed some improvements). This game feels easier though, some abilities and characters are completely busted if built and used correctly which I didn't immediately see in the first game.The characters are no longer cardboard cut-outs, their stories are very interesting and original (especially if we compare it to the first game), my favorites personally were Niko and Gin. Also one of the few eastern games to openly talk about gender and openly position themselves in favor of LGBT communities, which I can only name a few that do this, like the Yakuza series or the NieR franchise.Imo the music in this game is a lot better than the 1st one, it's so full of bangers I have trouble deciding in a top 10 lol.As for the negatives: The graphics are pretty much unchanged, but it's understandable since it's a low budget production.While it received a lot of QoL improvements, it still needs a lot more, the quest system has been improved a lot and completing a quest is a lot more meaningful than before, but it's still a bit tedious having to look for a specific NPC in a specific location every time you want to accept/continue/finish a quest, and they took out the Wire option to TP them to the starting area where you're in too.Same goes for the combat, while the premise is interesting, it still feels slow, especially when you have to play with tight timings, and not being able to switch characters when 2 turns come simultaneously is still a major pain, because you can't coordinate attacks effectively.Still, this is a very fun and interesting game to play, I recommend it 100%

_childDocuments_.review: I will start off with the bad, the graphics are very very VERY dated, which should be obvious at one look of game play clips, but I am not someone that cares too much about graphics. That is probably due to AAA games prioritizing graphics over everything else, but I digress. I also don't like how quest givers move around constantly from zone to zone because it makes turning in quests a quest line all on its own. I would have liked to have the option of English voice acting too but  the Japanese voice acting is phenomenal, like easily some of the best voice acting I have heard in a while especially Chi's voice actor. I have not progressed too far in the story yet but the general premise is promising and interesting enough that I want to know more. The characters have a distinct personality and I like that they are not defined by stereotypical tropes. The combat takes some getting used to but when you pull off consecutive combos, it feels very rewarding. But I will admit that the combat feels pretty bad when you only have one or two usable characters. All in all, I am looking forward to continuing this game when I finish Trails into Reverie and I highly recommend it for anyone who wants a good JRPG experience. Side note : I did get this game while it was on sale for about 20 dollars and  I think that is a good price to get this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sorry guys, i'm gonna have to be the one guy among a sea of loving fans that doesn't recommend this game. People are right to praise this game for it's writing and characters.  My problem is the rest of the game. CE2 is easily one of the most unbalanced, boring, and unvaried gameplay experiences i've ever had in an rpg.Combat and DifficultyThe combat system in CE2 is extremely unique, and FULL of potential. There's a lot too it, so i won't try and explain it in detail, if you're curious, looking up a gameplay video or watching the trailer on the store page gives you a very general idea. This system had SO MUCH potential to be an incredibly unique and fun experience. But it is balanced so poorly it feels like that no testing was done at all. The poor balance is actually a symptom of a few specific mechanics though.Seeing into the futureThe combat in this game is a mix of turn based, and real time. On your turn you're able to see exactly what each enemy is going to do on this turn. It is so detailed, that you can basically tell the exact frame an enemy is going to hit your character on. This is an incredibly powerful  ability, so the developer must have done some pretty hefty balancing to keep the combat engaging and challenging...right? No, they didn't. Enemies will never change their tactics, nor will they ever react to what you're doing. It creates a scenario where the gameplay is stale and bland. When you get to your turn, you eithera. attack the enemy, because they're not doing anything (or blocking, which you can guard break)b. React to the enemies attack with a block, counter or other toolc. The most effective, and most boring option, you delay your turn until the enemy attacks so that you can land a counter attack Combat becomes incredibly reactionary, it feels like you're just wailing on training dummies half the time. This is a problem at the heart of CE2's combat. One that should've been addressed from the start. However, it isn't even the biggest issue.JugglingThe ability to juggle enemies is probably the biggest problem plaguing the game's combat.All characters have a counter attack in CE2, if you hit an enemy with this while they are attacking, they launched into the air. The enemy cannot do anything while in the air, and many attacks do additional damage to them. This is cool as ♥♥♥♥, and a lot of fun to do. However, if an enemy is hit by ANY attack while in the air, they get RELAUNCHED. There is no limit to how often they can be relaunched. I think the effect this has on gameplay is best shown rather then described.(minor spoilers I guess)In this video, i am 20 levels under the enemy im fighting. In a normal JRPG, it would be impossible for me to defeat this enemy. However, in this game, he only gets to attack me once, and then is helplessly floating in the air for the rest of the encounter. Juggling enemies completely removes all the challenge of the game, it is always the best choice in any scenario to attempt to counter an enemy and launch them into the air. Once they're in the air it's easy to keep them there, and even if they do land they stay on the ground for a bit before standing back up. Even with multiple enemies, it's not hard to counter all of the enemies since each character has one or more counter attacks. There aren't any enemies in the game that are immune to this either. Bosses will be hyped up in a cutscene only to be immediately tossed around like a rag doll as you air combo them to deathAll of this results in combat, against normal enemies and bosses, that is extremely easy. Even on the hardest difficulty combat is easy, bland, and one sided. Something that should not be, when combat is the majority of the gameplay.Side quests If 75% of the game is story and combat, then the remaining 25% of content is side quests. I'm just gonna get straight to the point, these are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, easily the worst part of the game. Side quests are exclusively running around social areas and speaking to npcs, who's then dump a wall of text on you and then send you to the next npc. Rinse and repeat. There is a mechanic where you have to equip the right skill to progress, but the skills all come from the main missions, so they serve as a meaningless progress blocker and nothing more. The stories are often well written, but gameplay wise it's such a chore it can barely be called gameplay. They also take a tremendous amount of time, and reward you with....stats?One of my pet peeves in games is when there are stats you can view as a player, but the game refuses to tell you what they do. Well doing side quests increases your stats, but the stats don't have conventional names, and the game has no explanation on what each stat does. You also have no choice in which stats you get, so it doesn't feel good to get them, and you have no idea what you're getting anyway.Honestly, i could write so much more. About how character levels don't matter, about how tanking is completely pointless and healers are a joke, about how there are only 3 enemy types but I don't think I really need to.The Caligua Effect 2 was so close to being a masterpiece. It has deep, masterfully crafted character stories. Its world and writing are so interesting, the game is worth it alone if that's all you want.But I absolutely cannot recommend this as a game. The gameplay is so unbalanced, the side quests are so uninteresting, it just ruins the actual "game" part. It's pretty clear to me that the developers ran out of time making this game, and had to skip some parts of the QA process. The games mechanics just needed more work, and it's a shame that this game, so obviously filled with passion from its creators, just wasn't quite the masterpiece it had the potential to be.

_childDocuments_.review: It's insane how much better this is compared to the first game, almost incomprehensible that a game can go from a massive hit or miss to an insane improvement overall.Turn based gameplay with reactionary combat is the best way to explain it. You select a skill and the turn plays out in a preview known as the Imaginary Chain. Some attacks can counter certain other types (ranged counter, melee counter) which launches enemies up. The gameplay loop pretty much involves planning out your timeline to counter as many enemy attacks as possible and finish them off with style, gaining bonuses if you fought well. I would like to emphasise the reactionary aspect of the combat as you're actually able to actively dodge moves by timing your attacks or movement commands properly. If you're smart you can actually get through the entire game with 0 guarding too. On top of this there has been a ton of additions such as equippable passives that enhance your skills, increases stats and other things to help customize your characters. You also get access to a new mechanic x-jack which lets x sing a cover of a song sung by Regret (or covers of songs from Overdose from the DLCs) which buffs your entire party. I love this mechanic cuz it's basically the "why do I hear boss music" meme.Aside from that in between chapters there's an infinite amount of time to spend on character episodes and extra grinding. Side quests are much better handled this time round as well with much better rewards. Doing side quests develops your personality chart which increases your stat growth. Some side quests also have mini side stories (some are good some are meh) that are nice to go through. Enemies roam around the dungeons and you can either gain advantage by hitting them there or avoid them entirely depending on your pathing.Story is much better, characters are more well fleshed out and unique. If you care about representation there's a small but nice bit of it similar to the previous game though I won't spoil any of it. The story is almost one to one in terms of plot details compared to the previous games but is much better handled. There are also 2 endings this time as well.Graphics are eh but the music is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing. Caligula Overdose had great songs as well and this game doesn't disappoint either, maybe a little worse in some aspects but still overall amazing. Just like Overdose the game's music is composed by some pretty major vocaloid composers so if you're into those composers give this game's OST a shot. Songs also play a massive part into the character, personality and backstory of the musician that composed it in lore, having lyrics that relate to those aspects (nice thing to look up once you've finished the game).Otherwise, game's kind of styled like a VN with character stills showing emotion. Models have no real facial rigging and basic animation but it does the job. Gameplay has way better presentation than the story though, constantly juggling enemies and good set pieces for the story.High difficulties aren't super hard but there's tons of postgame options to give you a challenge. Do note that cuz this is a JRPG the difficulty varies with leveling more than anything (skill does play a part into it thanks to the style though) Looking at about 30 or so hours for main game without going out of your way to do side quests or postgame content.After clearing the game (entirely not the shorter ending) you unlock an option to add x amount of levels to the base levels of all enemies in the game which is good if you want longer fights that will challenge you more.Boss rematches that unlock the best character unique stigmatas (equips) with the highest(?) stats which also unlocks extra backstory for said bosses that you can read. They're pretty much just mini novels, would've been nice if they were flashbacks with voice acting but they're nice to have.Extra dungeon with challenges as well. This game's worth the money, highly recommend it if you don't mind a little bit of jank and eh graphics. Amazing soundtrack, good gameplay and overall an insane improvement over their previous title. You don't even need to play the first game to understand any callbacks (though it will help a decent bit with some core aspects like how the musician's music are related to their own personality and turmoil since that wasn't explained this time round).
_childDocuments_.name: The Caligula Effect 2

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly a great game from start to finish, I really enjoyed the story and the combat in this game. I never played the first game (probably won't). I found this game in my search of finding hidden gems and I could tell you this one is. Also can I just mention that the music in this game are an absolute banger? (also the full album is on Spotify if you ever want to listen to the music again) I wouldn't recommend doing a 100% playthrough of this game as it adds at least 20+ more hours of the game and a lot of side quest are a pain in the butt to complete (like grinding until you reach level 60) or a lot of them or just really hard to know what you have to do and finding guides for this game is impossible as there are none. Anyway if you're looking for a great time, I would recommend this game
_childDocuments_.name: The Caligula Effect 2

_childDocuments_.review: It's massively improved from the first game. Battles are more enjoyable, levels feel like they're more than just mazes. More thought was put into the writing of each characters problems too, even with that being one of the most important parts of the first game. Sidequests are still pretty uninteresting, but that's a pretty minor part of the game
_childDocuments_.name: The Caligula Effect 2

_childDocuments_.review: I think in the full landscape of JRPGs this game is a solid Medium but overall I really enjoyed it. It's a massive improvement over the first game in the series and the combat, if you enjoy it at all, stays fresh all the way into the postgame. Ex+100 bosses were a ton of fun. Most of the characters and their scenarios are engaging and and I liked interacting with the party. There's a lot of references to the first game, but its not necessary to have finished the other game first.I have some minor gripes; a couple of the characters fall flat, the sidequesting is confusing(I have completed 100% of them, some of the earliest quest chains you get can't be completed until just before the final dungeon for example), and the enemy variety could have used even just 2-3 more types, visually if nothing else. The enemies look the same all game.I think the most important thing to know upfront is that on hard+ the combat is really unforgiving, so you can't just turn your brain off and watch shows to grind mobs. You get to see the future so if you get hit or die it's 100% always your fault, it's entirely fair, but even 10-20 levels up the autobattle can sometimes create disasters. At level parity, using it is probably just going to kill you. You have to plan your moves *every single fight*. I think the combat system is the game's best feature, but if that sounds tedious, I'm not sure the rest of the game holds up well enough to plow through it on easy for the story.I'm really looking forward to historia's next game after this one. The jump in quality from 1 to 2 is awesome.
_childDocuments_.name: The Caligula Effect 2

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend this to anyone who enjoy reading the story. I really love all the characters from Go Home Club; they are very well made. The character designs are superb as well. The combat system is good, the flow is smooth and I think it's not so boring. The only thing that irks me are the monsters that's very plain until the end. I just wished there are more new types of monster. And kinda wish for the boss to be not so easy to defeat. I played in hard mode, but once you gear up all the equipment, the last stage is too easy to beat, almost close to no thoughts head empty.But yep definitely recommend this game, the story is good, but the character's stories are very exciting and fun to read. I especially love Ryuto.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played the first game and you liked it, your gonna like this one, if you didn't play the first game, you're probably still gonna like this one, it has a interesting combat system, a lot of good characters, a interesting story with a intriguing mystery, and for those who persist, a lot of twists and turns,  playing the first game is recommended as there area lot of tie ins here, TLDR, you should probably get this unless you really, really... REALLY hate anime, spoilers aheadbut personally I found the first one to be more enjoyable, and it comes down to the vilalinsslight spoiler but in the first game you get to actually go undercover and meet the villains, it adds a lot ofemotion to the story, you get to really relate to them, to understand them, and in this one, while there are some memorable villains, you also have... mu, whose the most dirtbag and annoying villain ever, and pandora was kinda lame too, and machina didn't do all that much, and qp was qute sort of but... meh,  the go home club as well, I found Ryota to be just a less interesting version of izuru, the rest ranged from OK, to holy sh!t this was a ride and a half,I also found the story to be more interesting than the first game, but less engaging, what made the story in the first so good for me was how it intertwined with the story of the characters and how everything sorta weaved together <again, the musicians story added so much more to the game> , in this one its more like you have the story and then you have the side stories for all the characters, which while both good feel a bit disconnectedin terms of gameplay it's fine, the combat system is more or less the same, it's a very interesting take, and it's really engaging, but when you have to do it over, and over, and over, it kinda gets to you, hence why a auto resolve option would be nice or some way to fast forward it, there is also a lot here between all the side stories so you won't run out of content tho I do feel like there's less side stories but they are better overall, kind of a quantity over quality also quick TLDR, the game does use modern terminology and pop culture jokes and mimis, someone calls someone else woke except instead of talking about politics they talk about how much they love trains, it's kinda funny, there's a lot of PC stuff here so to speak except I didn't feel that the devs were trying to force feed me ♥♥♥♥ or try to make the story about it, it's sprinkled into the world, organically, characters aren't just a one note trope of oh look at my sexuality or gender or whatever, they are defined by the things they do not the things they are, and there was a lot of that in the first game too and i didn't mind it there either hope this helpes
