_childDocuments_.review: This is the best entry in the Total War Franchise in a long time.==========TL;DR:==========- Absolutely amazing entry, the best one I've played in a long time- An amazing mix of everything I love about past Total Wars, with huge improvements to things like the user interface, which takes some learning but is brilliant and intuitive in the end, and insane customizeability, plus tons of new flavor/RPG additions that scratch and itch I have been wanting TWs to for years.- If you're okay with the colorful aesthetic [some call it cartoonish, I call it accurate to the colorful civilizations and armies of the past] it's absolutely gorgeous- More than accurate enough to scratch my historiographer itch (I am obsessed with history and love the bronze age)- Can be as insanely challenging or as comfortable and easy as you want it to be (try the Hittites/Supiluliuma, tons of fun, crazy tough at first)I am legitimately too obsessed with TWs, and when I have one of those artful, goosebumps moments, where I think "Whoa, I care about this campaign, these characters, this plot and journey... I feel transported back to history", this is when Total War is at its best to me, and Pharaoh has given me several of those moments already in its first weekend out.==========Extended review/rant==========I say all of this as a die hard fan of the historicals. Started with Shogun and Rome way back when, but for many years been playing basically just, in order of play time, rome 2 + DeI, attila + mk1212, and thrones + shieldwall. Sure, I am not unwilling to play anything since they messed with collision--i'm not THAT hardcore/hipster about it. Rome 2 and DeI is an incredible experience, and more than plenty to make up for what the later installments removed that the early ones did well.And they absolutely nailed it this time. The game is a wonderful mix of total war with a variety of Paradox/CK3 style flavor added into the mix, which has been missing for years. A ton of RPG flavor, insane customizeability to a level I did not even begin to grasp at first (there are SO MANY options I am seeing where I am like YES, they have needed this UI option for YEARS!!! FINALLY!!), and perhaps equally as important as anything, the UI itself is ACTUALLY CLEAR and intuitive such that I am seeing and learning all of my options and capabilities within the game interface, on campaign and on battle views.Now here's the thing--like any total war game, or any game of any complexity, the UI can seem clunky or bad at first--and there are definitely things they need to work out. But in just one weekend of playtime, I have learned how it all works--which is at LEAST as good, or better, than any other total war game I remember learning. I think that if anyone says otherwise, they have simply been playing them too long to remember how much they had to learn at first.I stress the UI and campaign-level RPG features so much because they turn out to be hugely important when you play a game that overwhelmingly takes place on the campaign map. But, onto the gameplay itself--there are issues, but there are also great things. The collision could use some work, the stickiness could DEFINITELY use some work. You have to fight to get your money's worth out of your chariots, they will stick very easily, and change direction/start moving extremely sluggishly. Which, to an extent, is not unrealistic, but when your foot traps insta-pivot and run rapidly to their destination, and chariots have to fight out of sludge not matter how you apply them, it's an issue. Still, they are useful enough in a cavalry role (flank cycle charging, distraction/diversion, taking out missile troops, etc) to be worth having at least one.That said, the battles are awesome and gorgeous--again, they take a bit of getting used to, but again, no more than any TW game. At first I was really annoyed at the forestry obstructing the hell out of so many of my battles (I started as Hittites in Anatolia, which is no desert/darker and foresty) but quickly realized I can turn off foliage to see more clearly. This has been in a lot of past TWs, but it was made more clear here after being an issue at first, because of, again, great UI.I really love this game already, so I want to do it justice, and want to account for all the great things and the things that need improvement, so this review is a work in progress.Okay, now some details and list items to try to get more juicy detail.Pros:- Gorgeous aesthetic, accurate enough to the time period to satisfy my history obsession- Super fun RPG/Paradox-style flavor additions, like Court, Ambitions, ancient Legacies, a Shemshu Hor cycle, honoring gods, leader/general customizeability [even more if you are the high king/pharaoh]- You can now simply directly click on siege ladders to get your troops to use them (!), with the cursor turning into a ladder to indicate as such- [WIP]Cons:- Chariots are not great. They stick, are even slower to move than i think real chariots would be, altho they would be sluggish and awkward--but it is not realistic relative to foot troop movement. Still useful, but not great.- Showing/hiding the army panel no longer seems to have a shortcut hotkey (I could be missing it, but I am a huge hotkey fanboy, and could not find it in the controls settings) and when I did it repeatedly in a battle by clicking the show/hide arrow in the bottom right of the army panel, it actually bugged out such that the panel slowly moved more up the screen each time i did it, hahaha, so clearly a bug or two to work out here and there, but this was the only actual one i found.[will finish this review when I am more able to put together thoughts cohesively/write down all the detailed stuff i love about this game, but for now wanted to get a positive review out there to try to balance out all the negative reviews from people who didn't seem to play it more than an hour or two]

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great. To me, the campaign feels more complex than it ever has, but it also trims some of the fat, making each decision matter more. Court positions give meaningful bonuses, outposts offer an interesting variety to settlement management, and the five resource economy drives players to conquer lands that provide what they lack, even if those lands are held by stronger neighbors or are more exposed to raiders. As for the combat, the unit variety is more limited than other titles, but the weather and terrain systems, as well a unit formations, make the distinction between light and heavy units dramatic, a far cry from previous Total War titles with more units (of which only the heaviest 10% were actually recruited).Overall, the game looks good and feels good. I would recommend it to any fan of ancient history, as well as anyone that enjoys Total War or strategy games in general. :)

_childDocuments_.review: My thoughts on this game are complex, so I'll take a stab at it through the separate, but linked lenses of a history buff and a gamer.As a history buff, I'm glad that this interesting setting - Ancient Egypt, Canaan, and Hatti on the eve of the Late Bronze Age collapse - was explored with a "Total War" game. I don't mind the relative lack of unit variety (no cavalry, battles mostly being infantry affairs), as I enjoy watching battles fought between historically-authentic armies. That being said, I would have liked to see a more fleshed-out map. The anti-"Troy" mob seemingly annoyed CA into decreasing the number of settlements on the map, as the developers said in as many words during one of their interviews. While those only into the gaming aspect of "Pharaoh" may be glad to not see many reskinned faction clones (like the non-Trojan Anatolian factions in "Troy"), I honestly wish that Canaan had far more cities and cultures, such as the conspicuously absent Ammonites, Moabites, and Israelites, as the region should feel a bit more chaotic and fractured than it appears in the main game. I also wish that the greyed-out areas of Libya and western Anatolia were immediately available, as it would be fun to play as the Libyans or the Mycenaean Greek colonists of Asia Minor. I understand that Mesopotamia is probably a big ask for a game centered around Egypt, but the hype around "Pharaoh" being "the ultimate Bronze Age game" just doesn't fit a game centered around a zoomed-in, yet occasionally sparse part of the world. Otherwise, I really enjoyed battling the threats of the Sea Peoples and the migratory Libu, Kaska, and Phrygian peoples, as I got a sense of other parts of the world experiencing a similar collapse, and the refugees of these disasters bringing the collapse with them as they search for new homes and plunder. My two last criticisms of "Pharaoh" from a historical perspective are Merneptah and Setnakhte. I firmly believe that Setnakhte should have been playable, as the one faction bordering the Libyan desert, and as the only adult Pharaoh in the game not to be playable (despite having played far more important of a role in the civil wars than Ramesses). Secondly, the cutscene for Merneptah's death showed up in c. 1203 BC, only for Merneptah to still be alive and well in the next turn, and to battle me (as Ramesses) for a few turns before the cutscene replayed and Merneptah truly died. Merneptah should stay dead once the first cutscene plays, rather than force me to roleplay betraying a Pharaoh I thought dead.From a gameplay perspective, I enjoyed the Sea Peoples "wave mechanics", campaign customization was a major improvement to the series, and I enjoyed the stress of having to manage and trade resources at a time when international trade was threatened by the collapse. I don't have many complaints with the day-to-day of the game, from the historically-accurate battles to the campaign mechanics. However, a criticism involving both history and gaming is the developers' decision to once again feature immortal characters. Historically, Amenmesse died in 1198 BC, Seti in 1197 BC, Bay in 1192 BC, and Tausret in 1189 BC. Even old Kurunta would have likely died before 1190 BC. That said, it is wildly disconcerting to be playing as Pharaoh Ramesses III in the 1180s BC and seeing these people still alive. It's totally ahistorial, and, while I understand that "Pharaoh" is a sandbox in which history can be altered, I'm sure that - if these characters were as mortal as any other general - most of them would likely be dead by the 1180s BC, whether from battles or plots. Honestly, I would rather have had competing family trees (with Seti and Tausret as one faction, Amenmesse as his own, and Setnakhte and Ramesses as one faction) to give me the sense that I'm forging a dynasty, not just playing as one invincible character. I can already imagine reaching the ingame year 1100 BC and playing as a 100+-year-old Ramesses, who still has yet to cut his lock of youth.Overall, I enjoyed the gameplay and the setting, though the "invincible heroes", CA's decision to cut the number of settlements due to fan pressure (when this actually sabotaged the game), the limited scope of the "ultimate Bronze Age game", the lack of family trees, and the Troy-style graphics verging on cartoons tempered my excitement. I'd still recommend the game for those who don't mind the historical inaccuracies (including having years displayed above the turns, but the years meaning nothing to characters' ages) and for those who want to finally play as Ancient Egypt in a Bronze Age game, but I have many reservations about recommending this game to history buffs or even Bible readers who may expect a larger scope and more historical details in a game set in such an exciting, yet under-portrayed region of the world.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. Take the TW community with a grain of salt when you hear them complain about balance, glitches etc. This is not a reskin of a game - it is a pretty in-depth journey into ancient Egypt. Of course there are elements from other games, and that should be the case - why wouldn't you keep great features across your titles? If you are into historical TW titles - this is one of the best ones. The only game IMO that still outshines this (and by a longshot) is a Shogun 2 - but that is a universally acclaimed jewel. I'm not a fan of the Warhammer nerd series - apologies - so I am not including the fantasy garbage that TW succumbs to - I only am interested in historical titles. What I love: Unique research tree; unique buildling and city trees (to the point where I feel like I am relearning the game (in a positive way)Unique units and progression - the battles are very different as well, of course there are similarities but the balance is entirely different between units, and the desert environment has some really interesting opportunities. This game is entirely challenging even on normal - and not in the computer cheats type of challenging that other titles have had, but rather complex diplomacy and repurcussions for invading a neighbor - or neighbors that may trade with you but will attack when they sense opportunity. In fact, cascading diplomacy repurcussions is a really interesting part of the game - something lacking in prior titles IMO. Graphics are really nice - and the game is beautifully optimized. Loading times are 10% of prior titles which is a boon for those old harddrives.  Issues:I mean sure there are glitches. The god I created was named something "debug" LOL. They will work it out in time I'm sure.A few crashes here and there - typical on most TW titles especially if you "alt-tab" into a work meeting like I occasionally do :) Balance issues - yes there are a few specific cases where I can see balance still needing optimization - but you can't expect this on release in any TW title. Recommendation: Easily worth purchasing. I bought for $30 because I've been burned by TW in the past - but having played the game, I would buy it full price and have recommended to my friends.

_childDocuments_.review: I've played most TW titles since 2001, including Medieval 1 (yes, as well as 2).Pharoah is VERY GOOD in my view. Sure, its maybe a bit overpriced, but that is my only significant criticism.There are loads of enjoyable mechanics to get to grips with and if there's one you don't like there will probably be a way of minimising it in the optionsThe customisation screens for the start of each campaign are a major step forward for replayabilityMany You Tuber criticisms are weak - for example "no cav" - that's easily fixed by moddersfor example "unbalanced" - this is often the case for any game of this type and is patchable - If you follow Warhammer over the last 7 years, the relative strength of each faction goes up and down with each patchThe game design is quoted as aiming for deeper tactical battles rather than the crazy clickfest that characterises other TW titles - this is more satisfying play for me, you may feel differently of course, so go play an FPS or whatever.The development of TW with this game is way better than some other new titles by other developers - for example Age Of Empires IV (no change in graphics or UI and not much extra value)After 7 years of WH1 WH2 and WH3 its refreshing to go old school for a change, and anyway you can still get into Deities for the magical realism angleEnjoy, if you have the spare cash :)

_childDocuments_.review: Overall, very good TW game, but future support for the game is brought into question due to excessive hate/ review bombing the game causing the game to have a poor release (although CA really could have done better marketing tbh) all seemingly because the game isn't Medieval 3, which is an... interesting thing to complain about, because there are numerous other games coming out that aren't Medieval 3 but oh well i guess.I think it's so cool to finally have a bronze age focused grand strategy game, especially a TW game. I've always been interested in playing Egyptians or Hittites from the period. The scope of the campaign focuses on Egypt, Anatolia and the Levant to great detail and is very cool imo. I also really enjoy the outpost system which is similar to the building system in games like Empire but also having provincial building systems more in line with modern TW games using the workforce system (which is like population in Rome 2/ Attila). The way each region has its own native Unit roster is really cool. The game accurately depicts the warfare of the bronze age by putting focus on chariots making the period feel more unique as a TW title along with Troy as true Bronze Age strategy games. The only real downsides are the relatively small selection of playable factions and not having the Iraq area as part of the default campaign, although this does make sense considering the conflict this game is based on. Overall I'm looking forward to playing more of this game and seeing what CA brings to this game in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game for £25 from a CD keys website, rather than the £49.99 for the Standard Edition on here. I would not have bought it at full price as I knew it was effectively a re-branded Total War Saga, with all the connotations that brings regarding lack of faction variation and historic/geographic breadth.I tried the campaign as Ramesses III and its enjoyable enough, though lacking in replay-ability. The economy is pretty identical to Troy with food, wood, stone, bronze and gold as the resources respectively. I do quite like the resource system as it requires a bit more thought than just acquiring one currency type and also it means your settlements tend to have vastly different building setups. The Sea People invasion stacks as well as the constant stream of tribal invasions(Libyans, Kaskians or Phrygians depending on where you are on the map) take up a lot of your attention for the bulk of the game. You are expected to fight these invasions simultaneously alongside expanding your empire through wars with traditional settled factions. The tribal invasions become irritating rather than a genuine threat rather quickly, and unless you are willing to leave large expensive armies near the areas they spawn i.e. the Western Desert for Libyans; then you are forced to focus the settlements in these zones on garrison buildings & outposts.The religious element of the game is fun and it allows you to mix-and-match different Egyptian/Canaanite/Hittite deities to suit your play style. I didn't find the Egyptian Court political mini-game very enjoyable or purposeful, it felt like more of an after thought.The battles are fine even if armies all play rather similarly. At present there are no ranged artillery which sounds historically plausible and cavalry are entirely chariot based. Archers are deadly but even the most heavily armoured archers are extremely vulnerable if engaged even by a tier 1 melee unit. The return of sappers in sieges is a welcome move, though the holes they make in the walls appear at the very beginning of the battle. Constructing siege equipment such as ladders/towers is a necessity as units no longer come with in-built ladders like in some other Total War releases. However, melee can still miraculously destroy gates without a battering ram even if slowly.I think like most people i'm disappointed by the pricing and the narrow geographic coverage - I'm in camp of desiring a Bronze Age Total War with Assyrians, Babylonians, Mitanni, Mycenaean's etc. The frequency of the tribal attacks should be reduced and the Sea People's should perhaps come a little later but in stronger waves. I suspect future DLC's will feature over-the-top new faction leaders with a 'cool' a-historical aesthetic but only slightly different unit rosters to the current factions; rather than new cultures and expansion of the map to other parts of the Levant.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been waiting for another historical title for ages and I must say the campaign of this one does not disappoint. Building slots out of settlements can help your economy and add additional garrison units to your fort but they are vulnerable to field armies. Also they add great maneuverability to your armies on the campaign map. I am currently playing as Ramesses and boy oh boy did I need the movement bonus to move my armies from Canaan to Egypt and the coast to protect from other Egyptian factions or the Sea People who just won't let me be at peace. And of course the Court mechanics add more depth as you can get sweet sweet bonuses to help with some aspects (cheaper buildings, gold, legitimacy to name a few).For some negatives I must say I do not like the immortal characters, nor that the caravan system (a sort of international trade system which is good to have for and immersive for the time) is restricted to Pharaoh Legacies rather than being a core mechanic for all factions. Also, a larger map covering the other parts of the map (Greece/Mesopotamia/Elam) would be nice.As for battles they are close to Troy as they are infantry dominated but the rebalancing of units plus more dynamic terrain and chariots being actually useful albeit fragile makes for a very fun experience during combat. All systems in combat have their use. Advance and fall back commands can be used to maneuver units during combat (even pointing the direction this should be done) while shield walls [an old mechanic] and setting the environment on fire (which actually deals damage) spice things up. And of course weather, dynamic weather can really hurt or assist you according to your army comp (for example sandstorms reduce range and accuracy of missile units). For being based on the warhammer engine an A for effort must be  given to Team CA Sofia for providing such a smooth and fun experience.Price aside (which it is very steep) this is a very worthwhile and enjoyable Total War title :)

_childDocuments_.review: Sadly, a Huge DisappointmentA big fan of the Bronze Age and long time fan of CA but this title is disappointing on so many levels.The game is set at the end of the 13th Century BCE, at a time when historically the 18th Egyptian Dynasty came to an end, and Bronze Age civilisation began to collapse. It's a time when the world witnessed re-emergent and nascent powers (Neo-Assyrians, Israel, Edom, Moab, Ammon, etc)The period is a prime setting for all the grandeur, glory, grit, gore and gruesome politics and diplomacy of this interesting part of human history. Rameses III held off a massive invasion of ‘Sea Peoples’ only to be murdered by an ambitious second wife.Alas, you won’t find any of that here.  What CA have offered is an over simplistic, over saturated cartoonish  depiction with so many developmental shortcuts, generic lifeless depictions and frustrating 'features' that render the game quickly repetitive and dull. There's negligible trade or diplomacy, but the memory leak associated with both UI screens persists. Don’t get me started on how long the AI turn cycles take.  Add to this the developer’s apathy in historical fidelity (needless 'artistic license' when historical reality was sexier, chariots not depicted historically accurate, etc) and fixated political priorities, and the title soon looses it’s lustre even for the most die-hard historical fan. One of the most notable examples is the decision to remove Israel as an extant faction within the game. This decision was taken, despite the game’s starting Pharaoh (Merneptah) having made a big deal about fighting them in the period and the “Yaweh worshipping Hebrews” having come to dominate Canaan from the 12th Century BCE (Professor Eric Cline, 'After 1177 BC'). These and these alone have been white washed from the historic setting. Not only did the developer see the need to remove the faction but they rendered the territory that was then held by that faction as impassable blobs in the middle of the map. What the developer has offered, is a plethora of generic 'cultural' factions, some of which are quasi-mythical or anachronistic (400-500 years before their time), factions who often have little differentiation or dept and an endless sea of generic (lacking geo-cultural nuance) settlements to conquer.The developer has offered the Dynasty Edition, with some extra free content, but in reality it's just more of the same / 'lipstick on a pig'. I desperately wanted to love this title but after 200+ hours of gameplay, I've refunded the product.Is it worth it?:If you’re a Total War fan or history nerd, you’ll soon find the game lacking in any substance, devoid of ambience or immersion and full of copy paste adversaries. If a casual gamer new to the franchise, you may be entertained for a period, but your hard earned dollar may find better service elsewhere.Imho

_childDocuments_.review: Pharaoh is a breath of fresh Nile air for the Total War series. It takes a bold step forward with:Visually stunning battlefields: Witness the clash of chariots and the glint of swords under the Egyptian sun.Improved AI: Your enemies will put up a more brilliant fight, keeping you on your toes and engaged.Matched combat animations: No more awkward conga lines! Soldiers now duel like true warriors, adding a visceral thrill to every battle.However, the sands of time haven't wholly eroded all flaws:Limited faction variety: Compared to the array of cultures in Rome: Total War, Pharaoh's menu feels a bit...sparse. More historical rivals would add some extra spice.Bloodshed light? While the combat is undeniably cool, some players might crave more limb-lopping action.Overall, Pharaoh is a promising oasis in the Total War desert. It could be better, but its strengths shine brightly. If you're a fan of the series or love ancient Egypt, it's worth a visit. Just wait to expect a full-blown feast for the senses.

_childDocuments_.review: The lukewarm reviews probably came at the time when Creative Assembly was under a great deal of controversy.The game itself is great. Fantastic historical ambience set in the Bronze Age, with lots of innovations in systems and features that deviate from the standard historical titles and the Warhammer ones.Many of those innovations were present in Total War: Troy, but Pharaoh takes them further and adds many quality of life features. The ability to fully customize your campaign experience by tweaking both new and traditional features of Total War in general gives this quite a bit more replayability than it would appear.Not to mention, with the incoming (at the time of this review) update that will include Greece and Mesopotamia, thus evolving this into a nearly full blown Bronze Age Total War that so many have hoped for, Pharaoh might really become a sparkling hidden gem, sadly overshadowed by controversy and bad timing.

name: Shadows Over Loathing
detailed_description: Mobsters, monsters, and mysteries — welcome to Shadows Over Loathing , the shady side of an already black-and-white world, and a follow-up to the award-winning West of Loathing. Your Uncle Murray has requested your aid at his antique shop in Ocean City, but upon your arrival the old man is nowhere to be found. Your investigation into his disappearance and the artifacts he’s been collecting takes a turn when you stumble across some shadowy plots (and a bunch of squirming eldritch tentacles) that threaten to bring about the end of the world. Explore a sprawling open world chock full of danger, quests, puzzles, and stick figures in this single-player comedy adventure/RPG set in the prohibition era of the Loathing universe. See how many enemies you can stuff into a phone booth as the athletic Pig Skinner, control the curds and whey of the cosmos as the cunning Cheese Wizard, or march to the beat of your own inscrutable purposes as the hip Jazz Agent. _childDocuments_.review: If you're familiar with Asymmetric's other Loathing titles then you'll be right at home with this game. For the uninitiated, this series of games is the king of false first impressions. What appears to be a simple RPG adventure game with stick figure art and stupid gags hides a complex world with diverse locations and hidden secrets that contain... more stupid gags.Shadows Over Loathing makes massive leaps when it comes to atmosphere and worldbuilding. The game is split into multiple areas and each area is filled with all sorts of mysteries and they all try to do something unique. The overarching story is simple, but very well told and I found the build-up to the ending genuinely exciting and intense despite the more comedic approach of the Loathing games.New players will find themselves more comfortable with the character-building, stats, and combat in Shadows Over Loathing as it's been massively slimmed down. I do think this hurts the game's combat in the long-run as it becomes too easy and boring, but it might've been worth it to avoid the clutter than West of Loathing thew at players.I think Asymmetric outdid themselves with this game and I loved being able to get absorbed into their silly little stick-world all over again. Heavily recommend to anyone who likes RPGs or loads of solid writing.

_childDocuments_.review: A former on-again, off-again player of the original browser-based MMO(ish)RPG Kingdom of Loathing, I enjoyed the single player spin-off RPG West of Loathing, and found it an agreeable experience with serviceable gameplay functioning as a bedrock for the true experience of the game: the writing. Well, with my first playthrough of Shadows Over Loathing clocking in at 21 hours, I can say with confidence that it's a worthy follow-up. It features the same degree of wit and absurdist humor as its predecessor -- and the namesake Kingdom of Loathing browser game -- and in many ways gameplay that serves once again as a purely functional vehicle to deliver the story and experience. That is to say, if you're looking for an extremely in-depth and challenging RPG experience, this isn't your game. It's a class-based, turn-based party system where your custom character, a familiar, one of multiple party members, and whatever guests and summonable creatures you can muster square up against the dark forces of the world. There's generally no end-state resulting from a loss in combat (in fact, losing can beneficial when not meaningless, with either temporary buffs granted upon defeat, or easily-removed penalties), and you start out with a dearth of combat options before gradually becoming so overpowered in combat you can steamroll through standard mobs, and it becomes more like a chore to get dragged into a fight than an engaging experience. It's telling that the game can be played completely without undergoing a single fight (there's even an achievement for it), although for the sake of "the experience", I still suggest at least one combat playthrough: the various enemies, weapons, and effects can be amusing all their own and elicit a chuckle or two on occasion.  The story and script are the true stars of the show. Inspired by the works of H.P. Lovecraft (look at the title!) and the early 20th century in which he lived,  but with that unmistakable Loathing-charm that makes even the eldritch more absurd than frightening - although there is the occasional moment where even this world can be unnerving, if never outright scary. The world also takes myriad cues from science fiction, fantasy, and just the right splash of contemporary pop culture -- basically the same wonderfully-done mishmash that KoL and its spin-offs have always excelled in. It's also worth pointing out that the game does take some elements from point-and-click adventure games with its quest design, with puzzles to match. Rarely (if ever) as esoteric as early Sierra titles, but some of them can be headscratchers - just look at the forums for evidence of such. To wrap this up, Shadows Over Loathing is a brilliant, absurd game with brilliant, absurd writing and a brilliant, absurd world. Just don't expect the greatest combat system ever, and you'll definitely enjoy yourself. 8/10 - as much as number scores matter.

_childDocuments_.review: Cons:Combat has same problem as first game, which is where main character gets leveled up to God and the companions get out paced and are just fodder.  Can be fairly mean in locking out certain achievements by just selecting a wrong random dialogue choice.  Bad item management, but at least better than first game.Pros:Should be called Sidequests over Loathing. Has 10 million of them, and the game is basically an excuse for them.  Which would be annoying if they weren't the best side quests in the RPG world.  They are so fun.Laugh out loud funny writing.  Jokes just flying around everywhere.  Fun graphics style, if you like black and white stick figures (which I DO).Debatable:Some of the puzzles in this game are REALLY hard, which seems a bit out of place in a comedy game.  But, that's more of a completionist thing, the ones to actually finish the game are pretty light.  There are a million items to get, and although they are all kind of charming, 90% are completely worthless.  Replayability: The game requires multiple playthroughs to get everything you can get.  You miss so much in just one go through.  Some people like that in a game, I personally don't like to replay games at all.  So, debatable.  Overall, the game gets an A for sure.  I give it, and it's predecessor, my highest recommendation.  Don't let the look of this fool you into thinking it's some cheap little thing, this is a fully fleshed (well, if you can call a stick figure fully fleshed) RPG.  Underappreciated gaming gems.

_childDocuments_.review: So hey, let's talk from two points here. First, the point of this game just as it's own thing. It's great. The combat's tight, the items are useful enough that you are thankful for them, and scarce enough that the battles aren't on easy street. The comedy is on point, the characters are fun, and the puzzles are satisfying. All in all, an easy 9/10.Now, the second point. How this game compares to it's predecessor, West of Loathing. It's much harder in the nitty gritty. You don't get multiple food, potion, and booze buffs dependent on stat levels, you get one of each that is replaced rather than stacked when you use another. The leveling system is entirely different; no more Asheron's Call spend ye XP how thee wish, but instead there are skills for purchase that raise your stats up to a certain point (not much), with the rest being obtained through a variation of temporary buffs, permanent buffs, accessories, clothing, food, booze, potions, and cats (yes, really). Getting to 15 in all stats is considered a grand achievement in this game. Everything has been, for lack of a better term, "nerfed". This is not (in my opinion) a negative, as the entire game has been build around this new, lower power tier. There is also the matter of the story; West of Loathing had a premise, this game has a story. There are characters, acts, and a definite ending. Whether you like that or not is up to you. I rather enjoyed it for what it was, but on the whole I prefer West of Loathing's method of "go, explore" better. Then there is the humor, which is admittedly a truly subjective thing. I personally found this game to be far less "haha" funny than the last, most likely because the framing device of Cthulu Mythos meets Prohibition is not as fertile ground for jokes as the Wild West is. There were some things that made me laugh out loud, but overall the laugh factor was down from West of Loathing. The quirkiness and surrealism was up though, which I found to be an acceptable substitute. That being said... I honestly feel that the addition of the story and chapter structure was an overall bad choice for this game, as it just sort of... ends. The "finale", as it is, isn't that great. The companions aren't that well fleshed out (no Susie Cochrane levels of pathos here, guys), and the characters in general are kind of bare bones. To be fair, they are not the focus of this game by any means, but given that they went with a story structure it does feel like some things are lacking. The last complaint i have is that the puzzles in this game are not all winners. Some seem to literally be based on "go brute force this solution". A bit walkthrough-itis-y.Despite all my gripes, I still cannot recommend this game enough. It has consumed my life from moment one and I suggest all who really enjoy turn based combat to go give it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: West Of Loathing was fun, but it's fair to say this transcends it.Honestly, this is a top tier lovecraftian rpg, and the writing sometimes forgets that it's supposed to be quippy Kingdom Of Loathing Phantom-Tollbooth-With-A Hangover material and hits immensely good surreal or cosmic horror notes.Not that the Phantom-Tollbooth-With-A-Hangover stuff is missing or bad. The elaborate puns and wordplay are still present, but there's *so much else* going on that they're not the central selling point if you don't want them to be.There's meaningful choices. Branching endings. The combat is somehow good. The setting feels vibrant and not just zany. The puzzles are fun and complex and there's a wealth of easter eggs, but they don't block the critical path through the game.Also the dang thing's huge. I've put ten hours in and I'm at about the halfway mark.I'll update this review if I run into anything that revises my opinion, but as it stands Shadows Over Loathing is a gem. If you need your lovecraftian fiction to be tonally serious, probably check out Stygian instead (it's rad too,) but if you like horror-comedy and crpgs, give this a go.Edit: Game cleared, I guess I got the bad ending for missing...something? All side quests dried up by the time I was in the final chapter, and I'm pretty sure I closed all the rifts, and I had maxed stats, so I'm not 100% sure what was required here. There's a *huge* amount of variation in the game's ending, and likewise in the path you take through the game, so this thing's replayable... but I'm not sure I would make any different decisions, so I don't feel personally compelled to replay it. Overall, this is a heck of a crpg, a fantastic puzzle game, and honestly a solid pulp cosmic horror title. If anything I've said here sounds even a little compelling, get this at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who adores West of Loathing, and considers it one of the funniest games I’ve ever played, I admit I went into Shadows over Loathing with pretty lofty expectations. Sadly, while my experience was overall positive, my praise for Asymmetric’s latest isn’t quite as effusive. It’s very clear that the same level of polish and care has carried over from WoL. The art design, lore, and period detail have been given plenty of attention here. It’s Lovecraftian inspired world is well…lovingly crafted. Shadows never fails to feel like the work of a very talented (and demented) dev team. I would be remiss if i didn’t mention the musical score as well, which is superb throughout. Many of the tracks will be stuck in your head for a while.It’s a shame that, as the game goes on, things never quite seem to gel as much as you’d hope. The narrative pacing is often slack, and isn’t helped by several rather tedious puzzles whose humorous welcome wears out fast. Some of the puzzles tend to rely on trial and error, busywork, and other mechanics that often felt like chores. I’ll admit that I put the game down a couple times and was not excited to pick it back up again after taking breaks for days. Asymmetric is known for their comedic bent, and there is certainly a lot of effort put in here. There’s sight gags, references, and deadpan lines galore. A lot of the humour does land, but oftentimes many conversations felt very extraneous, with the semi-serious quirk of each interaction quickly becoming one-note. West of Loathing had me in stitches, and with a lot more brevity in the wit.There’s also a fair amount of combat here. It’s quite enjoyable initially (I played through the game with a friendly spider companion that you can enable from the settings menu), but with the exception of some pretty fun weapons and offhand items, it felt like I was simply using the same strategy each time after a while. Shooting Parmesan cheese missiles at people shouldn’t feel as rote as it ended up being.I don’t want to come across as overwhelmingly negative. Many sequences in the game proved quite memorable, and there’s a lot of satisfaction to be had after completing an especially involved side quest. I just wish that, with this expansive and creative vision, I had more fun.Overall, I’d rate it a 6/10.

Quite frankly I just do not get this change, nothing would have been damaged nor lost if instead of putting places in individual maps the developers rather placed it on one large city map2) The Number 1 reason I believe I do not like this game is the main story, The West of Loathing story was nothing short of beautiful, a complete lack of one, rather just a broad directive "get to 'frisco" but here your not allowed to do anything without advancing the main story, all I wanted to do was immerse myself into the silly world but again that map comes into play with me being unable to play further until I finish the main story which quite frankly I found quite boring as a concept, with assisting in the banishing of evil spirits from objects a relatively boring concept and not one worthy nor holding up to the promised cthulu esc lovecraftian dark horror with that classic loathing humour that i was waiting for, instead i got Ghostbusters straight to DVD stickfigure edition 3) Some of the achievements are just not fun to do, and require my most hated task, reloading, and since you cant really save nor reload your kinda screwed having to replay large chunks of the game, granted this was an issue with west of loathing as well, but at least that game had the mechanics to back it up4) Similar to 2, however the game does not feel lovecratfian, it feels lost and jumbled, like a prohibition mixed with again ghostbusters! Something I genuinely do not appreciate after I played west of loathing which I believe is a genuinely good portrayal of western atmosphere and vibe, I felt like a rootin' tootin' cowboy bootin' bean slingin' wizard man where as now I feel like a guy that talks like a guy and acts like a guy, which quite frankly makes playing have no atmosphere5) I am going to keep this brief because talking about mechanics is boring to me but combat is simply terrible, in comparison to again a game they created years prior. Every time I start an act I feel incredibly weak, as if all that previous work was useless and I found myself just hating combat and actively avoiding it6) The new puzzles are actually so bad its crazy, the amount of backtracking and walking and travelling and yada yada. What happened to those great self contained puzzles in the first game? Remember the pickle puzzle? or the necromancer tower fluid puzzle, or any of those other puzzles that managed to work and be fun whilst not requiring me to run across half the map whilst getting attacked just to get one thing and go right back, well the only puzzle like that in the game was the one right in the beginning under the park area with the valves, and that was so quick it could literally be done by brute forcing itIn the end I suppose all that i have left is disappointment for an instalment that could have been fantastic, I hope they improve the franchise in the next game, however I would be lying if I said that if such a game came out I would try it out after the sheer garbage I forced myself to play for nearly 6 Hours

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows Over Loathing is a unique, imaginative little gem that takes a worthy stab at the herculean task of combining cosmic horror with comedy. I'm going to list what I didn't like before I list what I do, simply because the former list is significantly shorter.The Bad: -The game is very easy to break combat-wise, and it doesn't take much effort or thought to assemble a build that can snap the game like a twig. This turns combat less into actual challenge and more into busywork that you'll need to do while wandering around each map. This problem is made more egregious by the fact that the game features a surprisingly robust crafting system that would have lended itself well to more depth, especially concerning the game's elemental damage and resistance systems.-The writing is good. This is bad because the writer sometimes forget that he's writing for a comedy RPG first and a cosmic horror story second. I admit this point is subjective, but some of the dialogue concerning the game's tentacular side made me wish the game was more of a straight-laced cosmic horror RPG. This is because the writing is good enough that snapping back to cheese magic and jazz agents gave me whiplash due to the tonal shift.-Wandering around takes up more time than it should. Either wandering around the map or going to a specific destination guarantees a combat encounter or a random encounter that might give you some loot or XP. This isn't the problem; the problem is that your character needs to physically cross the map instead of simply getting the encounter immediately, taking up to four or five seconds of time every time you need to go somewhere. Needless to say, this quickly stacks up.Now on to the good: -The game's soundtrack was composed by Ryan Ike, a man who seems absolutely incapable of missing. His style of variable mixes and differing instrumentation works wonderfully with the game's generally off-beat atmosphere and mood. Somehow, it still maintains enough classical grandeur and mournful energy to match the game's horror-oriented elements like a glove.-There's a lot of content on offer, and the writing, as mentioned above, is good. Since much of the side content is only tangentially related to the overarching comesmic horror storyline, anyone who just wants more Kingdom/West Of Loathing style absurdity won't walk away unsatisfied. -While combat is easy, the real enjoyment in fighting comes less from actually thinking your strategy through and more from seeing what kind of ridiculous abilities the game's going to give you next. Meteors made of stinky cheese, weaponized pianos-on-the-head, aggressive saxophone music, and literal instruments of murder are just a few of the available options. With three separate classes for each of the game's three main stats, there's a good deal of replayability.-I've admitted before that I'm a sucker for historical fiction, and the Roaring 20s are really a period that deserves more love from modern game developers. Even in a game with deliberately irreverent writing, the cast of whimsical hobos, bootleggers, mobsters and flappers are a welcome deviation from the usual cast of characters in anything that's even Lovecraft-adjacent. This is ironic, since the time period depicted is contemporary with Lovecraft himself.

_childDocuments_.review: Very similar to West of Loathing, almost everything that can be said about one title can be said about the other. The main selling points are the humor, storytelling, and the puzzles, with many scenarios and quests being solvable without combat. The new setting is enough to keep everything fresh. There are some mechanical changes to how stats and buffs work I think are a slight improvement, but the combat is almost unchanged.It doesn't go as far as the previous game to give you multiple solutions to each situation (so far each step of the main quest has had one combat solution and one noncombat solution, and only about half the sidequests have multiple solutions), so I think that makes it a slightly worse game overall. But if you liked one game you'll like the other one.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute joy to play. I thought it would be West of Loathing but with a prohibition-era H.P. Lovecraft setting, but it feels very different in many ways. Firstly, it's a lot more "immersive" or whatever you call it; even simply creating a character isn't just assigning a look and name in the main menu, but going through the prologue and making your character creation choices through various interactions. The game's polish also really helps with the immersion, despite stickfigure graphics and grayscale colors the game does it's best to present the world through small details, effects, and nice parallax backgrounds.I got curious and went back to West of Loathing just to revisit some areas, and Shadows over Loathing feels much "cleaner" than it's predecessor.Second, you're not just exploring a western map to your heart's content, but rather, multiple small-scale maps that you get access to one-at-a-time every chapter of the story you complete. Yeah you could say that West of Loathing's map expands as you play too because the railroad extends with each part of the main quest gets completed, but it just feels like more of the same map to roam and explore, whereas Shadows over Loathing's maps are entirely different locations (at least the 3 that I have unlocked because I've not finished the game yet).Lastly, I like the UI more here, it's much less cluttered than it's predecessor's and displays a perk's effects without needing to do anything to show it.Side note, the music in this game is really cool, often it's orchestral stuff but in some areas there are multiple sources of instruments playing and you can walk between them and hear the balance of the sounds change but they all go together to create a whole song.Apart from the comparison, some criticism that I have for the game is that you'll be doing quite some backtracking because of time-travelling mechanic stuff. The time-travelling stuff is cool, but I wish I could strap a doorway to my back so I could change between past and present wherever. The combat isn't too much better, or hasn't hooked me yet because I still feel confused as to what the point is to half of my abilities/items.Anyways, some final thoughts are that this game is now one of my favorites. I already loved the first game and I love this one even more. It has already made me laugh many times in my ongoing playthrough and dialogue has not been more entertaining. I can already see myself playing this game again but making different decisions, because I have a feeling that there's still so much that I haven't seen. It might look like a simple game at first, but it's far more sophisticated than you'll expect. 10/10 Would kiss my future self on the lips again.

_childDocuments_.review: That's it. there's not much I can tell you. Again, like other reviewers giving this a negative, I gotta say: . I'm being serious. The first one is absolutely charming, chock-full of silly humor, and while some spooky things happened there which was neat (the talking doll & the Necromancer quest), it's still overall a lighthearted fun adventure.While in this game... they lean toward a Lovecraftian horror setting, nullifying whatever funny absurdism they could have written. But on the horror aspect, it did not give me enough thrills to succeed at being one. It does give a handful of clever jokes in the beginning, but by the time I reached the University chapter I just zoned out and wanted to finish the game as soon as possible. At this point I lost motivation to complete the game.When I first heard of this game being released and news of it came out, I thought it could have worked great. I thought they could craft .  What would a location called , seemingly having tentacles sprout in every direction would have the narrator say, joke-wise? You'd think they'd describe wriggling, writhing tentacles doing funny things in an overly-described fashion like the Spittoons in the first game, or maybe there could be one tentacle doing something peculiarly weird. In the end, the narrator just judges you for choosing to go to the tentacle house upon first encounter (), and then you get a bunch of boring fights against the tentacles, and the house gets clean from them. that's it. It's just a slight wink towards hentai, and even that is not executed well. They didn't riff on it any longer after you arrived.But other than the narrative, I do have some gripes with the other game mechanics:: I've met three interchangeable companions so far. Goblin Lady, Mobster Lady, and Gator man. None appeal to me. Not only because they don't have any motives or aspirations, you simply don't talk as much to them. Remember how it worked in West of Loathing, where you can arrive at a comically large cactus and the characters provide slightly entertaining commentary acknowledging it? or Susie telling you about poisonous mushrooms that turned a pig inside out in one specific location? That's memorably funny, and makes you want to talk with your companion a lot, since they provide unique dialogue a lot. Even when arriving at churches where each companion has reasons to not enter made me smile.That does not happen here.  like WoL. Instead, the chapter system lets you discover new "areas", groups of locations that consist of like 12-20 locations. But in every location, when you try to talk to your companion, they will only say, at best, 5 pieces of dialogue consisting of 4-liners about the general area, irrespective of your actual location. So when I go to the absolutely creepy, entirely  Frathouse (possibly petrified from a curse), the companion says f*ckin NOTHING. The alligator just says he hates math or science or whatever, and in another dialogue just says he wants to eat people or kill people basically. It gets old super fast, and kills the potential for either creepy stories or funny stories. And you can't really connect or know much about your companion when this opportunity is lost.. Lots to unpack here. Starting with combat items, . WoL was arguably grindy if you play on hard and requires you to stack up on combat items, but it feels rewarding being able to bypass fights when you've put enough time into it. Instead, this game mitigates any need to grind by making your losses give you stat increases. Which is a nice feature, I have to admit, but it gives us a weird paradox:  Instead I have to experience "losses", which is never fun, no matter how much it doesn't affect me negatively. (Oh yeah, forgot to tell you, , which feels even worse. You can change it by eating/drinking something else, which is a waste, but it makes the food system feel simple where in the first game you can have specific combinations feel like a "build".)Also the AP system feels boring, it regenerates too slowly compared to the first game, 1 per turn even if you start combat with 5. , but maybe I misremembered things. The "AP-giving item" can again, only be used once per turn since it's a combat item. It's better to make some combat moves once-per-turn instead of combat items imo, but I digress. Both suck.. The effort in music-selection just gone. Unlike in the first game where changing places among those small locations can change music and give you a different-but-fitting vibe, this game is, again, having a more area-centric mindset. . Also the devs are kind of a d*ck when I asked as to why the soundtrack does not have the "Speakessy/First Bar" music, which is arguably the best track I've heard in the game. Just on account of being "composed of a lot of smaller parts, including your footsteps depending on which shoe you're equipping while walking around" (granted, the instrument volume changes when you get close to where the sound is coming from). They say there's not a "definitive" version in that case. which is stupid. SFX is a different matter entirely, and the definitive version would be all instruments playing at the same time on max volume. Even fans on youtube have uploaded it already because the official soundtrack will not list it. All in all, I lost motivation to complete this game by the time I reached the 4th non-prologue area and already felt it since exploring the 3rd one. As other negative-reviewers are saying: Just buy West of Loathing, it's better. Alternatively, you could opt to play this sequel first: to save the best for last, by ending on West of Loathing. Just be prepared to wonder why is this called a sequel and why it has 90% positive reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate giving this a negative review. I loved West of Loathing, it was one of my favorite games. But Shadows just . . . falls so much shorter than West.There are two major issues: it isn't funny, and the combat is awful.First, the combat. It's tedious. In West, combat was snappy if you knew what you were doing. In Shadows, even when you have maxed stats/gear/buffs, the battles take forever because every enemy is an HP sponge (and a common enemy has a 5-damage limit when it has 40 hp). To add to it, your character's health does not remotely scale to the amount of damage the enemies do, so it quickly becomes necessary to defeat everything in 1-2 turns. This is difficult given your companion is useless (doing 9 damage to 40+ hp enemies in mid-game) and the pets are even more useless.The only way I've found of reliably getting through battles is maxing AP -- somewhere around 10 at late game-- and just chipping enemies down. This is both tedious and boring. Yes, I can beat a group of 4 enemies with 40+ hp in one turn, but it takes forever and frankly isn't fun.Second, the humor. I get that Loathing is a satire game. West was a satire game--of Westerns mostly--and Shadows is Lovecraft+1920's. But in both it falls flat. The Lovecraft parts are just not clever--oh, you go to the house from The Colors Out of Space, and have to--survey it for bank repossession! Sure? The political parts of the game are grating at best and are everywhere. Most of the satire is basically political -- oh, isnt it terrible we allowed smoking, oh, isn't the government corrupt and a joke, oh, isn't the 1920's so full of nonsense? It isn't even a matter of agreeing or not, its just annoying after awhile. It feels like the author has an axe to grind, and it just makes the satire more preachy than funny.And overall the game just isn't that fun. Of the six areas -- 1920's City, Time-Travel Lake, Didn't College Suck? , Swamp, Lovecraft References, and Dystopian City; only one of them I liked--the beginning chapter. Time-Travel Lake is lots of backtracking and with the battle system tedious as hell; I know college sucks I don't need to relive the reasons I hated it; the swamp is just--whats the joke? Its a swamp; the lovecraft references are just not clever or funny; and the dystopian city was so grating with 'look, the government is evil!!!!!!!!!1111!!' that I just stopped played. Yep. I quit the game in the final chapter.I just don't CARE. The shadowy villains don't interest me like the el vibrato or hell cows or the necromancer did in West; and the plot is thin at best. Find your mysterious uncle . . . who is basically ignored for most of the game. Like, we find cursed stuff yes, but is he referenced? Not really.I know this is long but I am just *frustrated*. West was amazing. Shadows just misses the mark so badly. If the battle system was better I might ignore the preachiness; and if the preachiness was gone I might ignorethe battle system; but both being bad and nothing really being good means I just. Don't care. And probably will never finish the game, nor 100% the achievements like I did in West.Let's hope the next game is better.

_childDocuments_.review: Always very sad to finish an Asymmetric game, cause there's nothing quite like them. Shadows Over Loathing is an endlessly funny game that's also shockingly deep. It's like a really good book that you never want to put down, with the added bonus of turn-based combat and inventory management (which can be overwhelming at times). There are so many opportunities and routes to play, I'm convinced the developers have become part-machine. There is SO MUCH to explore and you will miss so much on your first playthrough. Overall I'd give it a 9/10, it's exactly what I wanted out of a West of Loathing sequel plus a little more.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:+Relentlessly joke-filled.  Even if not every joke is laugh-out-loud-funny, some are, and there's still something to be said for a consistently funny tone.+Charming art style and presentation, which is often used and subverted to great effect+Easy on the computer.  It starts up and loads games instantly, instant loading times, and runs smoothly.  I can't stress enough how much this makes the game enjoyable to jump into and play.+Some encounters / scenarios really wowed me with the cleverness of their design.+Heavily rewards approaching the game thoughtfully.  There are lots of interactions that the devs accounted for.  Cons: -If you're a completionist like me, some things can be frustrating; such as how easy it is to miss large chunks of content because of a choice that seemed inconsequential.  Note, this could also be considered a positive of the game!  I admit, it does have a certain charm to it, despite the frustration it can cause. -Can be a little grindy.  ==============Final Thoughts:While the actual roleplaying elements aren't that high, there are tons of situations which really require you to think about the characters in it, and their relationships with one another.  You can brute-force the entire game, but there are lots of times when you are rewarded for carefully thinking things through, which is immensely satisfying.Yet, it's still got a consistently lighthearted tone that makes playing it so fun.The ease with which the game starts up, and how you can load your game immediately, makes it a joy pick up and put down whenever you want.  I definitely recommend it if you are looking for a game that surprisingly rewards a thoughtful approach to its setting, while subverting and parodying various lovecraftian tropes, and other horror tropes as well.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this is the most funny game of all time. It doesn’t necessarily include the funniest thing in a video game, but it has the largest amount of funny moments in any game. Except for the games with really high replayability, that could potentially continue to be funny for thousands of hours, which isn’t even really a fair comparison. Out of all the finite single player games, this game has the most funny moments. But even this statement doesn’t accurately represent the funniness present in this game, the number of funny moments is only half of it, the average magnitude of each funny moment is great too. This game has the largest average magnitude funniness of all video games, in addition to having the largest funnies per minute of any video game. Except, even this statement, is an inaccurate portrayal. There are games with very infrequent but incredibly funny moments that have an average funniness higher than the jokes present in West of Loathing, and there are games that sacrifice the average funniness of its funny moments for the sake of having many more slightly funny moments. What Shadows over Loathing does that is special is balance out these two factors. Imagining a graph where one axis is funny frequency and one axis is funny magnitude, Shadows over Loathing’s coordinates on this graph functioning as the vertex on a rectangle which also had a vertex at 0,0 would have the largest area of any game.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted this game to be good. I loved West of Loathing, so I thought that this would be a fun time. Instead, I received a game full of overly complicated and unrewarding puzzles, a combat system that is either incredibly easy or just tedious, and an ending that they didn't even both animating (I did the companion one, so it might be different in other cases). By FAR my biggest complaint with this game is that it feels incredibly bloated. West of Loathing didn't have a ton of locations, but each one felt unique and purposeful. In SoL, most locations are for side quests that you solve with ridiculous puzzles that make you groan when you find the answer. I mean, I'm starting to think that the devs were going for complexity rather than actual fun in most cases. The sheer amount of forgettable side quests (I'm not exaggerating when I say that I dreaded talking to new NPCs because I knew they would give me 20 minutes of busywork) was so tiring that I stopped doing them entirely near the end of the game, with the exception of the more interesting storylines like the mob or that one cool NPC in the S.I.T. basement.Another huge problem is the dialogue. SoL feels the need to write a paragraph for what WoL could do in one sentence. I found myself skipping through battle introductions, side quests, and even skimming through main story text because there was just so much of it. And to be honest, most of it wasn't funny. I understand that they were going for a spooky lovecraftian theme, but trying to merge a horror game with the WoL engine and style isn't going to work no matter what. Especially coming from the really funny humor of WoL, this game was a disappointment. I could forgive the humor if it wasn't one of the main reasons the game interested me.I could go on and on about how the game massively drops off in quality after S.I.T., how the companions are worthless in combat and don't react to the environment, the story feels like an afterthought, how a LOT of achievements and content is very missable/requires multiple playthroughs (which only happened like once in WoL and still irked me, and how the game would have been so much more comprehensible if they dropped the lovecraftian theming and just went with a 1920's prohibition theme. To put it simply...TLDR: The game is chore. Gary by himself is better than this game. Go play WoL (or replay it) instead of this.-My friend through family sharing

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows Over Loathing is the next instalment in the "Loathing" line of games. And while these games may look incredibly simple, with the simple black and white stick figures looking low effort on a first glance, this game is incredible. The art style may be mistaken as lazy, but they manage to do so much with the simple art style and aesthetic that you can't help but fall in love with it. Despite the lack of detail, the characters manage to all stick out and feel memorable, the environments manage to set the mood of every scenario flawlessly, and the game manages to get you engrossed and invested in spite of the simple graphics. The antithesis to style over substance, Shadows over loathing is overflowing with content and wit.The gameplay is pretty simple turn based RPG combat, but with all of the options and customisation, it manages to feel fresh throughout the journey, and with different class options and tons of different skills and partners, replayability is heavily encouraged. Want to make the combat more chaotic? Add a bunch of random spiders to both sides of the battlefield! Hate spiders? You can toggle the same setting to remove them from the game outright. Hate combat altogether somehow? You can actually play the whole game without fighting! There are options for everyone out there, not matter how into RPGs you are. And while the combat is pretty fun, I would argue it's heavily overshadowed by the best part of this game. The writing.The writing is this game is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ perfect. In an ocean of terrible games with the same awful fourth-wall shattering garbage, or shudder worthy, out of touch pandering, Shadows Over Loathing shines above them all with it's genuine witty writing oozing with personality. Despite being a text only game with no vocals to deliver the jokes, the humor still manages to catch me off guard and audibly chuckle in a way most modern games just don't seem to be able to. It doesn't have to constantly reference pop culture, or drop bottom of the barrel vulgarities to shock you, its charming characters and confidence in it's writing carries it from beginning to end, and manages to leave a lasting impact that makes me feel nostalgic for a time when humor didn't feel so saturated and terrible.I loved the original West of Loathing when I played it however many years ago it was now, and this game took what West of Loathing excelled at and knocked it out of the park. If you like fun world building and great writing, with a little bit of cosmic lovecraftian horror mixed in for good measure, I can't recommend this game to you highly enough. 9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows Over Loathing is very difficult game to write a summary on (or maybe I'm just bad at writing reviews. Probably that, to be honest.). It's a very  RPG with a weird meta-slapstick-parody humor to it. (Read the description, that'll give you a somewhat good idea. Despite it's black and white stick figure art and ridiculous puns, it somehow manages to have a lot of dark and compelling storylines to it. It has a ridiculous amount of side-content including side-plots that are kinda bigger than the main ones, Running jokes, and I'm running out of things to write I feel like this is a college essay. God, I was thinking about this review the whole time I play the game and this garbage is what I come up with?The Good:- Hilarious- Somehow, an original interpretation of time travel and paradoxes- A unique type of puzzles quite different from any other video game- Filled with easter eggs, references, and  attention to detail. Like, RDR2 level attention to detail.- Great soundtrackThe Bad: (This section is quite long, but don't get me wrong, this game is amazing. Criticism is easier to write than praise.)- Repetitive combat system that I was totally tired of by the time the game was over- Progression system that leaves a lot to be desired, with basically nothing to spend XP by the time you reach the end of the game besides... ...hot armor. I guess. And then you proceed to use it exactly nowhere.- Somehow manages to make fetch quests worse by instead telling you to find an object or a person that can do something...  in the world, with little to no guidance on where. Usually it's a dinky building you were in for 2 minutes once, or an NPC you did a side quest for 10 gameplay hours ago.- In the game's defense regarding the above point, if it weren't for these quests making me search the whole map, I wouldn't have found a couple cool little details and side quests.- Difficulty system that is very artificial and lazily done, with the default being far too easy and higher difficulties simply turning them into sponges.The Subjective:- Story(ies) take a much darker turn compared to the previous game. There's still humor, but less of it.- The lead developer (Zack Johnson) abused his ex-wife. She claims it was both emotional and physical, but Johnson only confessed to the emotional abuse and denied the physical abuse. She also claims that a prominent community member (Randy Mack) raped her, and that a third member (Kevin Simmons) knew this but never really did anything about it. On top of that, she claims a 4th member (Josh Nite) gave an underage player of Asyemmetric's first game (an online website MMO called Kingdom of Loathing) vodka. At the time of writing, most of this happened about 18 years ago. Of the 4 developers mentioned in this paragraph, all but Nite are listed in this game's credits. Mack didn't develop the 1st two games in the franchise. More information can be found here: Advice for the player:- Try to avoid fights whenever possible. At many points there are puzzles, stat checks, or callbacks to characters you've done side quests for that allow you to skip them. These feel much more rewarding to accomplish.- Search . If you haven't learned this from West of Loathing because you haven't played it (you should), Asymmetric has a tendency to hide their coolest, most clever questlines behind 30 yards of red tape and secrets upon secrets that only 2% of players would ever find blind. Read every item description, walk next to every object, press every button, talk to NPC's 20 times, because there's wild stuff hidden everywhere (and no matter how much you do this, you'll never find even 50% of the game).- You need a pencil and paper for many puzzles.Overall: 8/10 (if you can ignore the whole scandal. I get it if you can't. It's... it's a lot.)

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very humorous RPG. I like it. Shadows over Loathing is part of the series but can be played completely separately. It's very lighthearted, whimsical, and tries to be funny consistently. It's impressive. When nothing funny is happening you are still entertained: every object description, every line of dialogue tries to do some language joke or a reference. Most of the time it wants a sensible chuckle or approving nod from you, not all-out laughing. It might even get exhausting, because my English wasn't good enough to comprehend everything in the game without a dictionary, not to mention missing references to something unknown to me. Writing is the main attraction there, so if this doesn't sound appealing to you don't try this game. Graphics are non-existent, RPG mechanics are fine but not enough to keep you through the game, it's not a short one. Also, the music is good too, with some inventive implementations.It's kinda based on Lovecraftian horror, but it's much broader than that - it plays on themes of the Interwar period, so you got Prohibition, Mafia, mad scientists, and genius detectives. And beyond that, everything else is referenced more subtly. RPG mechanics are more complex than what you'd expect from a game like that. There's JRPG-style combat that requires some preparation. There's character progression that gives you various ways to solve problems outside of combat. Even on max difficulty, it doesn't become too complex, but the systems are not just a distraction. It's a little strange the main progression ends long before the end and you have to invest in equipment and books to improve your character, but it helps the game remain challenging up to the end. There are also many puzzles and they're good too.One thing that surprised me was the game is bold enough to let me miss a lot of the game. On the path I've chosen, there were very elaborate and completely missable puzzles (like a series of trials for robot that you had to program Zachtronix-for-babies style). I've missed major quest lines by not finding them or refusing to do them. I especially loved how one location allowed me to instantly wipe it out of existence by not understanding what is it about instead of exploring it. It is not a light RPG, it goes all the way.I struggle to name a better comedy game. I can see someone not liking if they hate fun, or someone having issues with it if they're not comfortable with English. Otherwise, get this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Possibly even funnier game than Asymmetric's first Steam stickman romp. Shadows Over Loathing is the 2022 followup to West of Loathing, taking place during the prohibition era United States, in which you're yet another aspiring youth, but this time looking for your missing uncle. While both games use the same turn-based RPG combat and exploration mechanics, Shadows takes a slightly slower pace in item and skill progression. It opts for a more episodic approach, locking separate large maps between chapters, instead of discovering them one-by-one like in West. It expands the gameplay with a higher focus on crafting and using a variety of items and upgrades, as well as a broader subclass system. As usual, at the start of the game you get to pick your main class between melee, ranged and magic, but you can also spec into elemental equipment like poison, bleed, fire, etc. This time around you can even upgrade weapons with multiple modifiers, so even if you don't get an elemental weapon drop, you can still customize an ordinary one with upgrade items. The map's just as interesting and varied this time as in the original, maybe a bit more, with several unique areas you'll unlock as you progress the story. Writing is slapstick and punchy, and the jokes are a combination of excruciating puns and observational humor.  It's entertaining, witty, and it'll probably keep you invested the whole run. If you take your time, you'll clock in at least over 20 hours, or at my pace, 40-ish. Buy at full price.

It kept me entertained for hours and wanting more every time I hopped out. The writing is perfect and the music is fantastic! It kept the West and Kingdom of Loathing spirit I loved so much and raised its Moxie by eleven. I would quite honestly have paid double the price to play this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you haven't played the previous game in the series, West of Loathing, first, then I recommend that, because it's cheaper and shorter and you'll have a good idea of whether you'll enjoy the game style before jumping into this one. If you have played WoL and enjoyed it, then go right ahead and purchase this because gameplay-wise it's very similar. It's set during the Prohibition rather than the Wild West era, although honestly the plot is a bit less thematically cohesive than WoL's (with the main antagonists being eldritch shadow creatures, and most of the sub-areas not really relating to the Prohibition setting at all). It's still pretty fun.At 20 hours' playtime, I've completed my first playthrough. It takes a minimum of three runs to get all the achievements, a lot of which are very finicky or just obscure and easy to lock yourself out of if you don't know about them in advance and plan. In fact, this is really another disjointed thing about the game – it really wants to be the kind of game where you stumble about and Just Try Things and make discoveries and successes on your own, but this is not how you get many achievements. Maybe it makes sense to have your first run be a walkthrough-free experience, and then do more runs where you use guides and walkthroughs to hit up more side content and strive for achievements if you liked the game enough after that first run. Or you could be like me, who looked up guides in my first run and feel no shame.Also, note: there are a lot more than three "defeated the game with [companion]" achievements, but after you beat the game, you can re-enter your save and get deposited back immediately before the final confrontation, so you can switch companions to any others who you've qualified for the endings for and redo the final confrontation. No problem!
