_childDocuments_.review: While I like the game, I'm not a huge fan of the price considering the amount of content and difficulty in puzzles (especially the combination locks...there's a horrible one for the longerfellow ship, an optional area in one of the later chapters). You could beat the game without a guide, but man, they seriously need more hints and explanations for certain things. Like you can choose a starter perk but you don't have a clear idea what it is until you actually choose it, unable to change your mind later without resetting. Even some of these perks aren't clear in their description, apparently some of them give unique dialogue choices but you only figure that out much later. While a guide isn't strictly necessary, I still ended up scouring reddit and steam discussion section more often than I would like.Personally I decided to get shadow tainted to see what would happen, I didn't know they would lock me out of several quests though, especially ones I had already started when I wasn't shadow tainted. That's such a stupid mechanic that punishes players for being curious, like at least give me an option to reverse what I did without bricking my save and forcing me to reset (I was too far in so I didn't). Technically there are some benefits to being shadow tainted but I feel like there were more cool interactions if you weren't otherwise. It feels like the mechanic was implemented as a subtle way to make fun of the player, even the ending was garbage compared to other endings (without spoiling things, the "evil" ending is literally repeating things like "ha ha ha" and "rejoice"; this screams such low-effort on their part when you compare it with other possible endings). Saying my character is "shadow tainted" sounds bad ass with Cthulhian undertones spread around, yet my character felt more like a loser by the end of the game.The combat system is more or less the same as West of Loathing, though I did unintentionally have a ton more combat items in the end. My inventory was becoming cluttered and increasingly difficult to manage even with their "filter" system that's obviously more geared for consumables vs equipment. My biggest pet peeve though was the inability to discard items. There's one area in the game that allows you to get as many copies of a gun you want, so of course I got several copies hoping to sell them. I tried later but none of them showed up in the shop to sell even though my inventory had a ton of them...with no ability to discard them, they're stuck in my inventory. Why offer the player the ability to loot a specific object multiple times if there's no utility in doing so other than cluttering up the inventory? This is dumb. Maybe it was a bug, specifically it was a car in the future you are able to loot with a wire coat hanger though the accursed key allows you to loot it as many times as you would like. I could see the inventory issue not being a big deal for a lot of folks, my build prioritized item drop though (and if your game allows that then the inventory should be designed in a way to help accommodate that).There are a few more issues, some of them technical like the sound bugging out in certain areas (final region in particular). I think if you're a fan of the loathing universe and enjoyed West of Loathing then you'll likely enjoy this game, I'll probably replay it as a different class several months from now. I had a decent experience despite my grievances since it pretty much played like West of Loathing. That game kind of serves like a prequel though and is more polished with DLC. If you're new to the series then play that instead of this game, it's cheaper even with DLC included.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is just as hilarious as its predecessors, and it manages to be extremely creative despite the art being made up of simple stick figures. It encapsulates the idea of less is more by somehow being intricate despite its surface level simplicity. The only con is that the game has a lot of text and it's sometimes hard for me to not zone out and miss important information. I recognize this is a me problem and not everyone will feel this way. However, if you aren't a fan of reading a lot in games then keep this in mind when deciding to purchase it. I still recommend it though. The humor is great, and the story is creative. If you loved other games by this developer, then I believe you will love this game too.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: The game is fine. On a scale of 1 to 10, it's like a 6? No where near as good as West of Loathing, far too simplified, the charm of the previous game where you never feel like you have to skip anything is just... gone. Everything is so much slower, the game is a lot less open-ended, it's lost a lot, and honestly I just... I made it through the end of the game once already and I don't think I could play through again, because it just takes so looooonnnnngggg, and the progression system is awful. Hope you like 16 basic skills and a few ones that you can invest in again (that all give variants of the same thing, that being resistances or health). Honestly, if you loved West of Loathing, I'd say you could get a playthrough or two with this, but if that one was a bit iffy for you, just don't bother. I mean, I recommend this game only for the fact its a fun playthrough for the first time, but honestly this game feels like a massive step back. Its just... its no West of Loathing.

_childDocuments_.review: West of Loathing was an absolute gem, and ever since I finished it (and then finished it again, and then again on hard mode, and then...) one of my biggest gaming wishes was to forget all about it just so I could experience it again.Shadows makes that wish come as close to true as I can get without severe brain injury. _childDocuments_.review: If you enjoy humorous RPG adventures, give this one a whirl. For a taste of the style and comedic sensibilities involved, check out the free Kingdom of Loathing game - the mechanics are a bit different than that 20+ yr old RPG, but it's the same company.I've completed a run as a Jazz Agent, Cheese Wizard, and Pig Skinner and had a really good time with each playthrough.When I started I was a little worried that it might be a little too point-and-click adventure in the sense that resources might be quite limited and puzzle-dependent, but that's not the case. There are random encounters - combat and otherwise - but only when travelling between locations and one of the interesting wrinkles is that combat is entirely optional. Use those consumables and combat items, buy those oddball items, and don't worry too much about not being able to replace them later.The only real caution I would give is be at least a little careful with your choices. The game is designed around the idea of multiple playthroughs, so if you do make a plot or achievement-related decision, there may not be any way to undo it. So no reloading an old save to undo a decision you thought better of later. It's an entertaining game with a lot of replayability, just don't be too careless about things.I'm deliberately avoiding spoilers, but I will state the final showdown is repeatable, so if you were looking at the achievement list thinking it designers would be just going insane with the multiple-run mechanic, you can relax. You'll be able to finish off stray side-quests, attempt new approaches to the final conflict or just keep noodling around in that run.Just take it easy, enjoy the jokes and puzzles - if you get in over your head in a fight,  there is no penalty for losing, and sometimes you might even get a buff out of it. The game's creators seem to really want you to have a good time, why not take them up on it?
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: The number of games I've played to completion lately is extremely low, but this is one of them.  The humor is great.  I regularly found myself laughing out loud at some of the gags.  Some genuinely clever stuff here.  The music has no right to be this good.  Musical abilities even integrate with the sound track, it's wonderful.  The puzzles are a good mix of different elements with many different solutions to them.  I will absolutely be playing this at least one more time to try some of the other paths.  Story is mostly forgettable, but good enough to keep things moving.  Overall, it's an excellent game that will keep you entertained and an actual serious contender for my GOTY
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Game is amazing, just like the original West of Loathing. If you haven't played West of Loathing these games are just very silly, fun addicting turn based rpg style games with silly stick figures and dialogue. They also have replay-ability with different classes and choice options and different solutions to puzzles. I recommend this game to any lover of the original and any newcomer. This isn't a direct sequel so the first game isn't needed to be played, however there are a few nods to the original during some dialogue. I'm so glad they finally made a sequel and hope this developer continues to make games because they are a genius.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: It feels like I'm in the 00's with a pizza on the way and a competent DM who can navigate through my terrible decisions. Maybe they should call games like these "Role-Playing Games"?My spacebaring affinity faded away when I (re)discovered how these HDR words would massage my tired eyeballs, long neglected of wit and soul. There's also something about KOL's art style which has always jived with my imagination. (Some might call it "cost-effective" ... Let's compromise and call it "eco-friendly")The humor is less over the top than West (not a bad thing) and so far it hasn't even been that spooky, but admittedly I'm too afraid to turn spiders all the way up, so maybe the fear is more of a subconscious sort of thing. Alas, I have not yet found a way to be reunited with the depths of a spittoon. I have no desire to look up anything in a wiki/guide yet, it's just fun finding stuff. I have no idea when the story will end, but I've had great time so far. I'm looking forward to a pacifist run afterwards!

_childDocuments_.review: To say this is a fun game with good humor would be an understatement of how fun this is. It's hours of consistently funny content, wrapped around a solid game. The story is solid, the gameplay and jokes are both consistently good, and the art style is consistent and clear.But I'd be remiss if I didn't mention the downsides. There's a lot of missable content. Like, maybe 20% of the game is either easily missed or designed to be mutually exclusive with something else. If you want to aim for the achievements you have to beat the game a bare minimum of three times, or maybe a lot more depending on the in-game choices you make. And while the game is fun... it's not so fun the sixth playthrough when you have to play six hours for one missed achievement.In other words, play it once - but it's not at all worth the trouble to complete.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows Over Loathing is the perfect sequel to West of Loathing and Kingdom of Loathing. The developers have done an amazing job carrying over the same refreshing creativity and witty writing as well as expanding on fun game mechanics. I can and will play and replay this game for many, many hours.EDIT: After going back and playing West of Loathing (again) then playing Shadows Over Loathing (again), I am even more impressed by the details! It's clear that the battles, the inventory menu, and the character menu were fine-tuned to be formatted more clearly and intuitively. The references to the past characters are great. I appreciate that the game's puzzles are difficult while still very solvable (to other players, not me, I am horrible at them but respect them nonetheless).
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game. Simple mechanics, easy to catch on, but the story is rich and the world is layered and full of witty humor and references. _childDocuments_.review: Did you like West of Loathing? If yes, you're probably going to enjoy this. _childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not one for verbal loudness, but this game had me in helpless stitches less than five minutes in. I had family members come in and ask if I was alright. That's how you know it's a good game; you get so invested your personality changes because of it. No, I swear I'm not cursed. If you need reasons to get this game, here's a few; a cursed lumberjack who speaks in Olde English and investigates a murdered tree; more silly walks than you can shake a fedora at; tips of the hat to their previous games and other famous titles; there is at least one spittoon; cheese wizard -- CHEESE WIZARD; pets, you get pets that level up like Pokemon; and a wide variety in humor both clever and dumb. Sound fun? Come join the dark side and investigate the shadows hanging over Loathing.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked West of Loathing as much as I did, I'm sure you already bought this game. This was a good decision on your part, I'm sure you weren't disappointed.For everyone else who didn't play that game but want to play this one, absolutely go for it. Compared to West of Loathing this game is significantly trimmed, in a way that will likely make it very approachable to those unfamiliar with the games that came before it. Not that that's particularly *necessary* mind you, these games have always been very simple and more about being a vehicle for jokes than anything else. Regardless, this one is very approachable. Generally speaking I'm opposed to simplifying things just for the sake of broader appeal, but here its clearly a very deliberate choice made early in development that rippled throughout the design of the entire game and I honestly respect it.Give this one a try. And if you weren't a huge fan of West of Loathing, I'd still say give this one a try. Its very much designed in a fundamentally different way that there's a decent shout your gripes will have been addressed in some way.This game gets full marks from me. A hearty well done to everyone who worked on it.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: When it comes to games with odd humor and simplistic graphics, West of Loathing and Tux and Fanny are my favourites. _childDocuments_.review: Did you like West of Loathing? Good news, Shadows over Loathing is both more and better content. This game has gotten more genuine laughs out of me than any game since West of Loathing, the comedic writing is top notch. The story feels more grounded in the characters, the stakes are higher, and the soundtrack is more intense to match. Great game. My familiar is a giant mosquito and my lesbian mobster companion calls me "kitty".
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, this is another one of those "muh event badge" reviews.Nevertheless, Shadows Over Loathing is a great game if you're in the mood for a slapstick (emphasis on the stick) comedy RPG. When it comes to combat its nothing groundbreaking mechanically, just your relatively standard turn-based system with a few spins here and there - but the game's humour, quests, locations, the narrator, interactions with NPCs nail it for me. Its a game that knows it doesn't want to take itself seriously and does so really well - it doesn't overdo it and keeps the experience interesting the entire time. If you want something to chill out in and have a laugh about, this game is a good choice - and so is West of Loathing, the previous game released in this series.

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic expansion to the Loathing universe. It builds on the combat system from West of Loathing while creating a more condensed story. Combining the goofy comedy of the Loathing world with lovecraftian horror makes it one of the few games i've played to actually get me laughing out loud.Fantastic.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: The game balance and overall plot isn't perfect, but the intense attention to detail, the sheer quantity of hilarious sidequests, and the delicately struck balance between the slapstick humor and the darker tones of the overarching plot is worthy of respect; I've clearly still got a few more runs to get through before I can say I've experienced it all! _childDocuments_.review: An excellent follow up to West of loathing. Expanded in every way it is full of things to do. _childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: This game is the sequel to an almost equally amazing game, West of Loathing. The main difference is that this game has better story, better combat, better game play, better characters, better puzzles... I could go on and on. You are set in the 1940-50's, and are sent to Ocean City when your uncle sends you a letter. But when you get there, everything is a lot different than what you expected! I give this game 9/10 stars. One deducted because I had to look up how to pass Chemistry class.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Just finished my first playthrough, took me about 30 hours to get through the main story plus all of the optional content I felt I could reasonably complete. I had a lot of fun!One thing I should note though is that Shadows doesn't have the same "pick a pardner" system and so the partners you do get feel thinner, less significant. They're still generally pretty fun and entertaining, but you definitely won't get as attached, especially since you can swap them out whenever you feel like it.On a gameplay level I'd say the combat is improved and the puzzles are interesting. I haven't replayed West in a bit so I can't make a direct comparison, but it sure FELT like there was a hell of a lot more to do, just on a "number of places to go and things to do there" scale. And what is there is indeed FUN, I had a good time with all of the puzzles and mysteries I came across, smiled a lot, laughed out loud here and there. The game definitely takes advantage of the fact that it's supposed to be comedic in order to set up interesting puzzles and such that it couldn't get away with if it was playing things more straight.I definitely recommend this game to enjoyers of West Of Loathing, unless your absolute favorite part was the Pardner thing and you feel like the game just simply won't compare without it. But in my case I think the quantity and quality of content in the Humor and Gameplay departments made up for that! Like, for example, there was a good deal more jokes with very elaborate set-ups, which is something that I love to see.I hope Asymmetric can keep up the good work on these games! If we get another Loathing game in this style I hope we can get a return to the "one partner that sticks with you through the whole game" thing that West had going for it, but aside from that I don't really have any big changes to the formula I'd want to see.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Regular audio bugs. Especially in battle sequences where the music cuts out entirely.Supremely disappointing as reviews said the music was a strong point and I enjoyed in in their previous title.Refunded.[edit] Lack of audio looks to be deliberate choice? _childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: I never finished the game. I didn't think it was funny or charming enough to keep playing, since that's really all the game has going for it. 3 hours in and the story is pretty boring and the fights are basically just using your best attack constantly, so the humor is really doing the heavy lifting but the quantity is honestly lighter than I expected. Just overall boring.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: I'm someone who loves West of Loathing and Kingdom of Loathing. I've been playing this game all day since it released and so far it's at least as good as those games. The writing team at Asymmetric are masters of their craft, and their games remain some of the only ones I think you could say are strongly in the genre of comedy (and they're good comedy, at that!). The puzzles and RPG elements are clever and well done. I strongly recommend this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: West of Loathing was one of the funniest, most cleverly written games I've ever played with an awesome soundtrack, and Shadows over Loathing is a step up in almost every way.The world is bigger, there's more gags to find, the combat system is more interesting, the story is more engaging and intriguing, and the soundtrack by Ryan Ike is WAY better than it has any right to be for a comedic game about stick figures.The only part of Shadows over Loathing that isn't a complete step-up from West of Loathing is how comedic it is. The story takes itself more seriously than West of Loathing did, but I suppose that's to be expected. Lovecraft-style cosmic horror in the roaring 20's doesn't have as much inherent comedic potential as the wild west.But don't get me wrong. Shadows over Loathing is still a VERY funny game and 1,000 times more worth your time than $70 AAA slop like Forspoken.Buy this game. You won't regret it.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best day ever, christmas really came early this year. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I thought this game was going to be better. I'm a huge fan of another title in the series, West of Loathing, but I think this game doesn't even remotely come close. This game is much, much more linear and confining than I expected; in order to unlock pieces of the map, you need to progress through a specifically cultivated narritive. Each 'piece' that you unlock is pretty small, and again- everything is laid out in a linear path without too much room for deviation. _childDocuments_.review: It's good, but not as good as West of Loathing.It's pretty much the same rhythm, go to new location, discover its gag/jokes, fight/solve a puzzle, do some excellent dialogue/choice, repeat. All that stuff's still here again, and it's great, but it doesn't hit as well as the first time around. Maybe it's the premise that does it, as when I saw the title "Shadows over Loathing", I could immediately tell what the game's theme was going to be about: cosmic/Lovecraftian horror. I anticipated much of the content of the game before I encountered it, such as . Contrast this with West of Loathing, who in addition to the expected Western genre fare has , for its three major sub-plotlines. Shadows over Loathing's more detailed setting definitely hinders it more than helps. It's main story is more linear than West of Loathing's was, and worse, I would argue. Another point of subjectivity was that the game felt far too long, and the game systems themselves didn't support the length. It's very easy to get overleveled in this game, with many disguised grinding points, some of which are gags themselves, which was funny, and your initial list of skills doesn't expand, leaving you with tons of XP but nowhere to spend it.I had great moments of surprise and literally laughing out loud, but I guess the experience was lessened by the fact of me having played West of Loathing before, and with this game now expecting crazy turns out of left field. Combat's as serviceable as ever, that's not really the focus of these games, but it is more of a downgrade this time I feel, although this is more of a subjective taste thing.

_childDocuments_.review: I LOVED the original West of Loathing - not only does it deliver with interesting characters and an engaging story, but it is chock-full of some of the most ridiculously funny comedy writing I've ever seen, and I consider it to be the funniest game I've ever played. I was beyond excited to try out Shadows Over Loathing when I heard about its release. And while this sequel is able to imitate and build upon West of Loathing's style and mechanics, it fails to capture its predecessor's spirit, with a distinct lack of the charming humor that characterized the West of Loathing experience.In the original West of Loathing, there are lots of options in dialogue menus that will leave the player with ENTIRE PAGES of dialogue to read at a time. In any other game, this would be a major pain in the ass and a huge disconnect from actual "fun", but West of Loathing has such ridiculously funny dialogue that every sentence is a joy to read. In this sequel, though, there's much less of a commitment to actual jokes and self-contained gags, with much more emphasis put into the Victorian, 1920s-era atmosphere and combat/perk mechanics. There's just as much dialogue as West of Loathing, but without much of the comedy that would have made the dialogue interesting, leading me to skip sometimes entire paragraphs of dialogue at a time. Sometimes Shadows Over Loathing opts to reference something goofy in the original game without actually explaining it OR making any kind of joke about it at all, rather than build its own catalog of goofy characters and fun gags. And the constant barrage of side quests and expository dialogue being thrown at the player for the entire duration of the game leads to a ton of information that the player has to swallow - without enough humor to wash it down with.All of the little mechanical aspects of character perks and combat (the weak point of the original West of Loathing) have been expanded and brought to the forefront in this sequel, with a more convoluted perk system and unnecessary amounts of combat items that feel like they all do the same thing - and this approach carries over into other systems and mechanics in the game that never needed to be changed. Perks have to be upgraded through books and a specific leveling system, instead of just putting skill points into three character traits. Puzzles can range from mindlessly easy to absurdly tedious and annoying - the biggest offenders in my opinion being the sickle curse puzzle and the robotronics course. Some puzzles ARE ridiculously easy, but require an item or location that's frustratingly hard to find. Character classes are less distinct. The map is bigger than WoL but split into completely different sections that retain their own characters and atmosphere, making the world feel more disjointed - which works against the consistent atmosphere that this sequel is trying to build.This game is a sequel to WoL in style, but not in spirit. Everything that worked just fine in WoL (like the map system) or was a little boring but wasn't a big deal (like the combat and perks) has been expanded and compounded upon in this sequel to the point of being confusing. The puzzles are often tedious, the world feels disjointed, and the constant side quests vary in quality. Meanwhile, the charming humor has been replaced with a spooky Victorian atmosphere that's sometimes serious and sometimes funny, but never settles into one groove for long enough to feel authentic. I didn't hate this game by any means and was still engaged enough to finish it, but due to its lack of engaging humor, Shadows over Loathing feels less like a barrage of jokes and more like a barrage of annoying systems and mechanics, making it... well, an average RPG. 5/10

_childDocuments_.review: The missile knows where it is at all times. It knows this because it knows where it isn't. By subtracting where it is from where it isn't, or where it isn't from where it is (whichever is greater), it obtains a difference, or deviation. The guidance subsystem uses deviations to generate corrective commands to drive the missile from a position where it is to a position where it isn't, and arriving at a position where it wasn't, it now is. Consequently, the position where it is, is now the position that it wasn't, and it follows that the position that it was, is now the position that it isn't.In the event that the position that it is in is not the position that it wasn't, the system has acquired a variation, the variation being the difference between where the missile is, and where it wasn't. If variation is considered to be a significant factor, it too may be corrected by the GEA. However, the missile must also know where it was.The missile guidance computer scenario works as follows. Because a variation has modified some of the information the missile has obtained, it is not sure just where it is. However, it is sure where it isn't, within reason, and it knows where it was. It now subtracts where it should be from where it wasn't, or vice-versa, and by differentiating this from the algebraic sum of where it shouldn't be, and where it was, it is able to obtain the deviation and its variation, which is called error.

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyably consistent successor to West of Loathing, which itself is a fantastic experience.The game is overwhelmingly similar to West of Loathing in most regards, enough that it barely feels like any time has passed since the previous iteration was released. The environments are slightly more complex and dynamic, while the combat has some new features. But otherwise the experience remains largely propelled by that exact same gratifying collect-a-thon esque gameplay; and comical, text heavy narration.The new setting manages to be reasonably distinctive. There's quite a lot of interesting elements and little stories woven into this world, although how much of it is derived from what the game was seemingly based off may be questionable. Regardless the writing is great and does a fantastic job of comfortably narrating this story, balancing its more comedic and surreal aspects with relative ease. The combat is still overly simple and repetitive much of the time, but it's not a major problem. The statistic upgrading system is definitely less interesting than in the previous game though, which was more open ended and variable. There's hardly even enough unique unlocks to get players through half or even a third of the game too. Meanwhile some puzzles are overly cryptic and dry but at least they're sparse; and optional.Quite possibly the worst part of this experience is just one of the endings, which is horrifically short and empty of substance. Thus I would suggest you avoid  to not get locked into such. Like the previous game it has some obnoxiously restrictive mechanics where players can get locked out of entire endings, achievements or pieces of content all because of arbitrary choices.This game isn't particularly innovative or impressive compared to its predecessor. As mentioned these games are so similar it almost feels like they were both made within adjacent time frames. However the previous game was phenomenal so by extension this game is too, and there's loads of content to explore. Although I would hope that future Loathing games might shake things up a bit more.If you're interested in finding more games like this I've probably reviewed quite a few on my curator page .

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved West of Loathing (WOL) like I did, there’s really no reason to not buy Shadows over Loathing (SOL) as well. It’s more content in the same vein as what you’re used to.If you liked WOL but didn’t love it, maybe wait for SOL to go on sale.If you never played WOL, go play that game before buying this one. That’s the first game in the series, it’s half the price, and you’ll probably like it more, anyway.Above is really all you need to know if you’re on the fence about buying SOL. Below, I’ll go much more in-depth about my thoughts (which are mostly feedback for the devs).I’ve got 60 hours in the game and 34/37 achievements, so I think I’m knowledgeable enough to start dissecting the game.Undoubtedly, the production quality has greatly improved compared to WOL. There are many more effects, sprites are more detailed, backgrounds are fuller, they added spatial audio, and overall the world feels much more fleshed out. It feels a bit jarring to go back to WOL after taking things in SOL for granted.Another main improvement from the previous game is the story. WOL’s overarching “story”  was basically just wanting to reach Frisco. It worked fine, but it doesn’t compare to SOL. I was actually engaged in what was going on and wanted to learn more about all these characters with various motives and backgrounds. I’m pretty sure I gasped a few times. Now, this ain’t no Pixar movie, don’t get me wrong. It just was a really pleasant surprise on top of the humor that I was expecting. I also really like how a couple of threads were left open for future Loathing content to tie up.Finally, SOL provides much more total content than WOL did. Even after 50 hours in the game and multiple playthroughs, I was still finding new characters, areas, and questlines here and there.Unfortunately, not everything was a step forward. The first things that come to mind are class identity, build customizability, and character progression, which all work together to make combat worse. It doesn't ruin the game or anything; it’s just a lot less fun than it was in WOL and I think it’s worth discussing so that this stuff might be better in the future of Loathing.A number of changes were made for the sake of balance. While they succeeded to a certain degree, I think it came at too high a price.Each of the 3 classes plays very similarly to one another. Many abilities are practically copied and pasted. (For example, each one has an ability that deals 5 damage, one that increases the class stat by 5, one that doubles the damage of the next class-stat-based attack, one that deals damage equal to an enemy stat, etc.) That definitely brings classes closer to each other, but it also just kinda defeats the purpose of choosing a class. The solution to a class having a weakness is not for the devs to neuter class differentiation, but for the player to plan around it. In SOL, you can have both a pet and a companion. Let the player choose allies that cover the main class’s weaknesses. It’s much more fun as a player to feel like you are outsmarting the game by solving a problem than for the devs to never present the player with a problem in the first place. SOL is much more forgiving of the player for losing a fight than WOL was, so it’s fine to let the player possibly lose a few fights, learn, and adapt. If you fainted enough times in WOL, the next day would start, which would remove all the potions, food, and booze buffs your character had. Certain buffs could only be gained once per playthrough, so you really didn’t want to lose all of those. The same doesn’t happen in SOL, however (which I think was a good call). Other than a handful of story or quest-related fights, there aren’t major consequences for losing.Side note on classes: I don’t think they fit SOL nearly as much as WOL’s classes did. What the heck does a pig skinner have to do with 1920s mobs and prohibition? Or a cheese wizard? Jazz agent was the only good one. I would have made the muscle-based class a boxer, as boxing was apparently very popular in that time period. The magic class could have been more of an illusionist since Houdini was on stage in the 1920s. But, I digress.On top of the classes not having very different kits, players are limited in how they can craft builds. There are 3 gear slots that can alter stats (like +2 moxie), a weapon slot that changes your main attack, 1 that gives you an ability once per fight, and a ring slot that can have varying effects. WOL, on the other hand, gave you 8 gear slots that could affect stats, which includes the weapon and ring slot doing what they do in SOL as well as giving stats. WOL’s gear system simply offered more to the player that let them customize their build.Gear is just half the story, though. The character page lets players spend xp on increasing stats, upgrading combat abilities, passives, and more. Each passive and active in WOL could be upgraded to level 3, 5, or 7. Muscle/mysticality/moxie could also be upgraded indefinitely. SOL, however, only lets you upgrade actives once and muscle/mysticality/moxie are limited in supply. SOL’s xp spending is more like choosing in what order to fill out a checklist rather than an opportunity to make a build.This lack of upward movement leads me to my next gripe with SOL: character progression. My combined muscle/mysticality/moxie for an average endgame character in WOL is 200-300 compared to only 30-40 in SOL. Unlike WOL, SOL refuses to give more than 1 of the same stat from any piece of gear or buff. You may get +1 to all 3 stats, but you’ll never see +2 or more to the same one in a description. That makes late-game stuff only marginally better than early-game stuff. This, in turn, means it’s very unexciting to get loot. I may have worked on a quest for 20 minutes straight and been rewarded with a hat that’s a straight downgrade from what I equipped hours ago. I think I only changed my hat 1-2 times in each SOL playthrough compared to 5-10 times in an average WOL playthrough. All of this further exacerbates the lack of build customizability in addition to not letting the player feel like they are getting stronger.Ability scaling, or lack thereof, is another large problem with character progression. In WOL, spell damage and muscle/mysticality/moxie increased the damage of spells. SOL threw away both of those. You have the base ability, you can upgrade it once, and that’s it. That’s the strongest it will ever be. When the base ability deals 5 damage, the upgrade adds an extra 2 damage, and the final boss has health in the hundreds, that ability is utterly useless in late-game and weak in mid-game. Sadly, that’s the situation for almost every ability in SOL. That sucks in and of itself, but it also further weakens class identity. It doesn’t feel like your class plays very differently from others when most of your class-specific skills don’t even get used because they are so unviable.Now, I know that was a lot to write on my part so I’m sure it also was a lot to take in on yours. I’ll recap to make sure the main points are clear: SOL took large steps backward from WOL in terms of how different each class is, freedom to create builds, and progression. While all of this standardization somewhat made the game more balanced, it had the severe side effect of making combat much less satisfying. I think with the right changes, we don’t have to make such large sacrifices in future Loathing games.So what would I do if I was in charge? Firstly, go back to how WOL handled spells/abilities. _childDocuments_.review: Well I can't refund the game because I was one hour over, so I'll do the next best thing and make it clear why this game isn't worth your money.It's like they took West of Loathing and everything that made it unique, and just went back like three steps. The companions aren't as useful, combat is even more messy with item management hell, and while the IDEA of a focused main quest sounds nice, it still comes off as a confusing mess I'm barely following. Starting off with Combat, it blows chunks. The combat in West was already flawed in how many useless combat items they tossed at you and expected you to use, here in Shadow it's like a warehouse full of useless junk YOU WILL NEVER TOUCH EVER. Worse off there's no more Stomach, Liver, or Spleen, so you can't enjoy stacking food and potion bonuses to pass the harder challenges and deal with the tougher fights. You just have to hope for the best and lean in on your class's main stat. Also item crafting just feels tacked on compared to the first time where there were some really useful things to make. Here it's just making stuff like bombs that do 10 damage to all enemies, which sounds good, until they have like 30-50 health and you either use more, or just pray you can kill them in a few rounds before they overpower you.The writing also takes a downturn, and instead of a bunch of fun gags, it's alot of info dumps that either lead to punchlines that aren't funny, or just plain word dumps that take up your time. It's made worse by quests that involve alot of back and forth between areas, to a point where I just ignored the dialoge to get the quest over with. THE KEY ELEMENT TO A COMEDY GAME, AND I'M IGNORING IT BECAUSE IT'S DRAGGING IT'S HEELS.Despite the idea of a focused main quest, I don't feel focus at all. The game just kinda throws things your way and you're expected to kinda get the idea. I'm kinda just in a car getting car sickness praying we stop somewhere to get fresh air soon. Instead we just keep going to zones that have visual character, but no meat on the bones. The City, The Lake, Porkham, etc, they don't have alot of deep character beyond what you're there for and whatever else they could think to put in those areas. If we're making jokes with Lovecraft, just keep Porkham and expand on it, REALLY lean into the Lovecraft influence. But the thing that got me to just say, I quit? Throw my hands up in frustration and just say that's it I'm writing this scathing review?THEY BROUGHT BACK THAT HORRIBLE PUZZLE FROM GHOSTWOOD IN WEST. Where you go BACK AND FORTH, BACK AND FORTH, BACK AND FORTH, for a big long "haha red tape am I right?" gag. This is after already doing that Cursed Sickle items that just drags on and on and on. I was overjoyed when I heard there was a sequel after playing West of Loathing, and after watching Tomato and Markiplier play that, I was estatic to get my hands on this. Now I wish I didn't, I could have bought some quality food with this, or anything else.If the developers are reading this. I'm sorry to be so scathing, but I was really expecting more of what I liked from West but in Lovecraft form. Why you did things like remove Stomach/Spleen/Liver mechanics I can't fathom, that was the best and only way to actually play West of Loathing; from boosting your stats so hard you can kick Cthulhu in his 15 testes. Instead it's one food item and one potion, nothing else.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is hysterical.  I laughed out loud multiple times while playing this and the writers never ceased to come up with new and creative ways to make jokes. _childDocuments_.review: Steam only allows us to thumbs up or down a game. This game is a Thumbs up from me. IF that's all you want to know you can stop reading here.Now, for the proper review. This game is good, but in my opinion is neither as good, nor as funny as it's predecessor, West of Loathing. I'm not saying this game is bad, it's just that the previous game was significantly better.For one, the previous game was funny. Shadows over Loathing on the other hand is not. Or at least I do not find it funny. The first game had me laughing within a few seconds thanks to it's silly walk system you uncover at the very start of the game. No such moment in this game. That's not to say the writing is bad, it's just that the first game felt like what the writers wanted to write, while this one felt like what the writers felt was expected of them.That last statement has multiple meaning. For one this game is a lot more "progressive" than the last. And by that I mean there are a few times where SoL does something progressive that's expected from a more modern game without actually doing anything with it. Pronoun selection being one of those things. In the same vain there's a point where a character refers to a woman as a Jezebel and is called out on that... weird thing is that he's not called out immediately, but a few sentences after. We have a chat, he does the biblical reference, we continue the chat, then our character - unprompted by the player - calls him out on his sexism and the guy suddenly folds like a house of cards. In the first game two of our Pardner's were female, and several female NPCs had thriving businesses. This game is no more or less progressive than the previous, yet, there are a few - very, very few - moments of shoehorned "progressivism" that just don't feel like they're actually part of the story. The Jezebel example really felt like someone came after that dialogue branch was written and added it in. But hey, that's just ONE very small problem some people might not even notice. The real problem comes from the writing not being funny. After I finished this game I reinstalled West of Loathing so I could check is that game was really that much funnier that Shadows over Loathing and having just finished a full play though of West of Loathing my impressions of SoL have only been confirmed. Thankfully the writing is strong enough, and decent enough that even if you don't find most of it funny, you can still enjoy the game and it's story. Unfortunately this games comes after West of Loathing, a game lauded for it's humor.As if this wasn't enough, the gameplay has also suffered greatly. The original game had 3 regions and 7 zones plus a prologue and a tutorial zone. This game has a tutorial zone, a prologue zone and 5 more or less independent zones. But here's the thing, in the original game it was very hard, and required a lot of mindless grinding to get most stats to the max, and it was literally impossible to unlock all stats before the final region and final 2 zones were unlocked - or at least before you could unlock them. In SoL it's impossible to fully explore the first two regions and not max out your character class stats. Skills, perks and effects are given a better interface than they were in WoL, but the gameplay is also a lot more shallow. To make matters worse, when we select out class we do so in a dream under the form of a collage degree we finished, only for chapter 3 to take us to a university to get a 3 hour degree. Why is that worse? Because by chapter 3 it's impossible for pretty much anyone playing to not have maxed their starting class. Some of the perks and skills we get should have really been reworked here to allow us to effectively double class. That would have at least made it feel like we were progressing as a character as opposed to basically soft locking any power from chapter 3 onward behind gear. It literally feels like they starter designing the game to be an improvement on the first one, replacing levels with class perks only to give up early on and move to an item based system.But hey, that's not all. Oh no it keeps getting worse. This is a lovecraftian game. That means the writers probably do not enjoy Lovecraft's work, but because a few highly influential writers like his work, the man has become famous with certain crowds and some exec want to cash in on that. Now, I know, you're going to accuse be of being a bit too cynical. So here's my evidence. Chapter 1, tentacles sprouting from the ground start attacking us. The Finale, after slowly adding an ever increasing number of world specific "shadow" monster that make sense to be in the game, at the very end of the game, we start seeing Lovecraft inspired monsters joined the enemy roster. Enemies that based on their design wouldn't be allied with either one another or our current enemy. That's the thing about Lovecraft, tentacles for him was a short hand for inhuman. If something had tentacles that was shorthand to tell the readers of how weird, and strange these creatures were.  But not all, not even most of his creatures have tentacles. Yet when anyone who has only a superficial knowledge of him does cosmic horror, that horror is more often than not tentacles. The monsters that start joining the lines of the enemy at the end are inspired by various species from Lovecraft's mythos, creatures that were not only at times at odds with one another, but at odds wit the Old Ones and the Outer Gods. For all intents and purpose, the lovecraftian inspiration is more like a thin veneer than an actual inspiration. One of the main reasons why there are no good lovecraftian games is because all game devs go for style over substance. Lovecraft is all about man's insignificance in the grand scheme of things, about the indifference of those with actual power to the plight of human beings. That's what cosmic horror is all about. But to people that don't read Lovecraft, it's all about them tentacles!If in WoL we had ample opportunity to make use of our non combat skills or class in the form of dialogue choices, that mechanic is almost completely absent in SoL. Worse of all is probably the significantly longer dialogue trees. It might just be me but it feels like in WoL dialogues were a lot shorter. For every reply you selected you only got a bit of text then you had to reply to that or go down another branch. Rarely did you get a page or more. In SoL on the other hand it feels like you don't get to choose your replies, you select a topic, and then your character and the interlocutor just go at it without any more input from you. There's this old Obsidian RPG called Fallout New Vegas in which you can chose to side with Caesar's Legion - a group that is a literal patriarchal slavers where all women are slaves and all men are legionaries. Pretty much all other factions have you dismantling the legion. But you can still chose to join the legion. In SoL I can chose to be evil, to literally consume my nemesis and the Shadow President, the main antagonist of the game, AND actually take their place in their universe controlling scheme but I don't get to chose if my character get's upset if a woman get's called a Jezebel? My character will do world damning evil but not be sexists? really? In case someone was wondering why I think the game was pandering as opposed to that being organic writing I just didn't like, this is why.It's 2024, what game doesn't have shoehorned in progressive BS? Ok, we'll get past those pain point. It's 2024, what RPG doesn't limit player interaction and hide massive choices behind sentences that don't even begin to describe what the PC will say? It's a lovecraftian game that's not scary, and a comedy game that's not funny... But hey, it's actually above average, so by that metric this is technically a good game, and under Steam's simplistic system, this does in fact earn a thumbs up from me. I just hope that the next game will actually be better.

_childDocuments_.review: Sometimes you reach the end of a game and feel satisfied from the adventure you experienced. Sometimes you reach the end and jump right back in. Sometimes, as with Shadows Over Loathing, you rush to the end just to get it over with.I figure I might as well recommend the game, because while it's weaker than West of Loathing (WoL), also by Asymmetric, it's still enjoyable. If you're reading this you're probably already interested in this sort of game. Every review above and below this will likely wax on and on about what's good about the game. So let's go into the problems, since if you can get around the issues I bring up, this will be well worth your money.There's two, only two, which is good and bad. It's good because there isn't actually much to take issue with for this game. It's bad because the two issues have a ripple-effect that sours much of the rest of the experience.If you've played WoL, you'll probably remember two things about that game. Aside from being really really great, funny, and unique, it was also short and the combat wasn't very polished. Well, Asymmetric tried to fix those two issues, but wound up making it worse.I wonder why combat even is in these games aside from the obvious fact that the original Kingdoms of Loathing (KoL) was a surrealist satirical take on fantasy RPGs, and so needed random combat encounters. You could excuse those encounters in WoL as well, since wild-west tabletop RPGs has a lot of content to lampoon as well. SoL though, with it's similarities to the Call of Cthulhu RPG and Cthulhu mythos in general doesn't *need* combat encounters. In fact, most game-related Cthulhu mythos content generally makes a point of having players *avoid* combat, espousing survival tactics instead.Mechanically, the combat system is pretty simple. Characters take turns attacking one another, there's hit points and status effects. The good news is if you lose or surrender in a fight you don't really face any kind of real issue aside from being prevented from continuing the story or taking a stat increase/decrease (that's right, sometimes you get bonuses to stats when you lose).Unfortunately, the combat isn't balanced at all. It now takes you a little bit longer to get overpowered, but overpowered you will naturally become. You'll also wind up with hundreds of items and combat abilities. It isn't even a case of hoarding "in case you encounter a tough fight", but more like fights only last 2-3 rounds, and enemies either one-hit kill you and your comrades or you one-hit kill them. I had so many healing items at the end because I had no use for them. Also, there's a bug at the time of writing where some items say you can use multiple items per turn, but don't actually let you do that.You'll pick from three classes which vaguely map to fighter, rogue, and wizard, but they're all mechanically similar. There isn't too much different from any of them, but the wizard (the "cheese mage") is the standout overpowered one. The jazz player (rogue) tends to give you slightly more Moxie early on, which can help resolve certain puzzles, but overall none are particularly interesting to play, just read about as you make class-based quips or do jazz hands to amp up damage.BTW, highly suggest turning combat speed to the highest setting. Characters will walk at a snail's pace ten feet to bop an enemy and then walk all the way back. If I had done this earlier, I feel like you could take 4 hours off of my total playtime.One last issue with combat, the game expects you to grind. There are several grind spots you'll find here and there, and if you *don't* grind, you will hit a wall and wonder why enemies are suddenly so powerful. There's also, technically, a pacifist achievement, but it's not the sort of thing you can do on your first playthrough by being clever, rather you'll probably catch it on a subsequent run, and with the help of a guide.More egregious of the two issues is the game's length. Despite only taking 20 hours to beat the game (including several sidequests and added content), the game feels very long. A lot of the punchy jokes from WoL have been painfully stretched out across a vast game full of puzzles that take time to solve, not because they're particularly difficult, but because you have to deal with the arcane UI to pull out the exact stat boosting item to solve a puzzle you mentally solved 10 minutes ago.That's right, this is one of those games full of puzzles where you'll figure out the answer long before the systems of the game lets you resolve it. You'll have to backtrack through different rooms, manipulate items or the environment, and swap out food, drink, and cat blessings to get the stats correct so you can solve the puzzle.And some puzzles require multiple playthroughs. This game follows the old-school method of hard-locking content because you made one mistake, and there's no save-scumming, the game is quick to auto-save when you beef it. Just daring you to play again so you can... read the same jokes you've already seen before?The third area, the SIT campus is the real kicker. All momentum and interest really hit a wall at that point and never really recovered, which is a shame since the areas after it are all very interesting, and some of the best locations in the Loathing franchise.It's also a shame because a lot of the actual horror/cthulhu mythos aesthetics and tropes are hidden away in the late game as well. It's true that most mythos stories save the wild horror for the back half, but at least there's a growing thread of dread and mystery as the story goes on to propel you deeper. SoL just has 5 level setpieces with a different story of the day, and a final chapter that quickly wraps up the scraps of lore it clumsily drops between chapters.There's also several endings, each based on helping a companion or getting a "bad" end. The endings are each gated by a long ending sequence where, aside from 2 sentences at the start of the ending slideshow, repeats THE SAME STUFF you've already read five times. There's no way to skip it or make your life easier, and there are no new animations or descriptions of things when you engage one of the endings. They just sorta happen.Cool...Despite all that, I did enjoy SoL, I just might... think twice the next time Asymmetric releases a game. Read a few reviews first. Knowing them, it'll either be sci-fi, wuxia, or modern fantasy. We'll see.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a lot of bugs (and some features) that make certain content unobtainable on playthroughs. This coupled with the lack of save files and compounded by the fact that you need to do multiple playthroughs to unlock everything anyway with certain branching criteria means that if you're a completionist like me, this game is frustrating and tedious and I can't recommend it.E.g. you need to do all 9 of a certain thing I won't spoil, and you can only do 3 per playthrough. That's a minimum of a 3 playthroughs already. In some playthroughs maybe you find out a toilet is arbitrarily locked forever because an npc randomly despawns from her own house after you finish her quest. Perhaps you find out a hobo you met at the start of the game didn't register for whatever reason. Both these situations essentially necessitate full near 100% playthroughs to rectify and the game is LOUSY with arbitrarily gated content from innocuous dialogue that will cause you to miss things like this through no fault of your own.It's not the worst game if you don't care about that stuff, nothing special but competent and funny at times, I'm at 20 hours or so at the time of writing this review and I've finished all the content. I feel the need to point this out because by the time I've done enough playthroughs to pop all the achievements I'm assuming it will bloat the playtime. 15-20 hours of play is what you can reasonably expect.

_childDocuments_.review: My playtime is because I left the game open for a couple weeks.It's a lot of reading.  A LOT.  If that's what you want in a game, fine.  But I don't.  I skipped a huge amount of the reading (more than 80% I'd say) and still "won" because there aren't that many dialogue options.  The writing isn't bad.  But it's not like it's as good as, say, a Terry Pratchett novel, which has a similar overall tone.  If you want to experience that kind of feeling, skip this game and read one, and you don't have to deal with the painful mechanics.And the "art"--well, what you see is what you get.  It's rudimentary.  The same is true of the audio.  I got and played this game hoping it would be good *despite* the awful art.  Not so.Mechanically, there are way too many items, and way too few ways to navigate the inventory in various circumstances.  Just endless lists of visually undifferentiated items.  No way to tag them or group them.  No way to hide them while keeping them in your inventory (which you need to do in case some event needs the item later on.  There's no indication of where "stores" are in the maps.  There's no way to speed up combat animations.  I Deliberately used only ranged weapons so I didn't have to watch a stick figure cross the screen 100 times.Can't really recommend this.  I don't understand the overwhelmingly positive rating.

_childDocuments_.review: You start with a pointless sidequest to find gas so you can continue your trip. This is the only narrative tool in the entire game. If you picked the wrong roleplay dialogue options at the start, it might be impossible to progress in the optional beginning dungeon due to lack of good stats. Which is a great introduction to the game's general feel of being overall bad.  The game tells you at the start that you can use WASD to move, and that also works in menus. But in a fight, you cannot use keyboard-only to target enemies or select moves. This baffles the mind. Why not support keyboard fully? Nothing in the battle system is hard to make work with WASD movement and space for selection. I guess the developer thought keyboards are only for typing out pointless text, which 99% isn't even attempting to be a joke. Wait, I'm getting ahead of myself. Humour in this game. Oh boy. The game begins with a great visual gag, and plays it out competently. It gives you this oasis of humour, then throws you out to a desert of essays with a line or two of "haha random" sprinkled in. The game's dialogue screens are barrages of fire-and-forget missiles. One-liners of "haha random". Don't get me wrong, some visual gags still exist in the desert, but stuff like a mirror to change your expression in-game is humorous, was it not a PARS 3 LR Anti-tank guided missile. There's other mirrors before and after it, and none which I saw acted like the one specific mirror in one specific bathroom. Running gags are inherently more funny than "haha random", even if they start out as the latter.  The game has a positive fanbase. That is great. You really have to try to make something this bad, and I can understand the fandom surrounding such dedication. But with such a drive to create and such an understanding of good and bad choices, this developer could easily make a good game if he focused next time on making the good choices.

_childDocuments_.review: I played Kingdom of Loathing many years ago, so when this game came across my discovery queue one day after years later, saying I was thrilled would be an understatement. As I'm working on my final achievement for this game, I figured I should finally write a review.Shadows Over Loathing is one of my favorite games. You can play it to your own strengths as it offers different difficulties and puzzles. You can choose to be very combative, not fight at all, or something in between. You can spend hours finding every side quest and story, or you can focus on the main objective. You have so many options, all of which are likely to impact your ending. I'm a bit sad I'm almost finished with over 100 hours put into this game and have enjoyed sharing it with friends as well.I hope to see another game from Asymmetric in the future as wonderful as KoL, WoL, and SoL.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a good game, and I recommend it for anyone who enjoys: West of Loathing, Lovecraftian themes and horror, to a limited extent the New Weird genre, text-based RPG's, or surreal humourWhat is this game? It is a cosmic horror tongue-in-cheek sidescrolling RPG set in the 1920's-1930's (not sure which). Does that sound like a tough line to walk? The game does, and it does it easily with room to spare. I enjoyed this game for three reasons: 1. I enjoy RPG's, story reactivity, and choices—This game breathes this; 2. I love cosmic horror—This game has to be one of the most complete treatments of the genre, with many hours of content and endless references, and; 3. I love the kind of humour this game is peddling (surreal humour, with appropriate levels of parody and satire where required). The West of Loathing and Shadows Over Loathing games come from the same developers as the Kingdom of Loathing browser-game. It's not something I was able to get into, but it's here in case you're looking for something more.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I would recommend this game ONLY if it's on sale for about $5, otherwise I wouldn't recommend it.Let me preface this by saying that I greatly enjoyed West of Loathing. So much so that immediately after finishing it back-to-back, I decided to pay full sticker price for the new one in the series - Shadows of Loathing. I had high expectations, they were not fully met.Shadows of Loathing still has some of the humor elements of its predecessor, but they come off as much more forced and they lose that organic characteristic that helped land the humor in West of Loathing. The writing seems less inventive and the situations and characters seem less off-the-wall and wacky. Not good news for a game that relies almost completely on its humor as its selling point. There's also significantly more hand-holding in Shadows of Loathing versus West of Loathing, which, again, draws away from some of the charm of the game. In West of Loathing, you'd be unaware that saying a specific thing, picking up a certain object, etc., would initiate yet another string of quests and goals. And that randomness made the game enjoyable and fun. A seemingly unimportant act like letting a bird out of a cage at the very start can ultimately shift the whole ending of the game. This (in my opinion) is not the case with Shadows of Loathing. The game will be very upfront and tell you "Hey, heads up, this is another little quest" or "Wow, that looks kind of important *hint hint*, I wonder if you should hang on to that?" Again, that draws the player out of the randomness and funny chaotic nature this game 100% survives on. Ultimately, I'm disappointed. It's a decently fun small studio game and I'm sure I'll play it, have fun, and finish the game. But the studio failed at making something that lives up to the previous title.Is this a fun game? Sure. I'd recommend it to almost anyone assuming it's on sale. It's one of the better small studio games I've played. Is it a good *Loathing* game? sadly, I feel it isn't.

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy sequel to West of Loathing.Same wonderfully funny atmosphere, and interesting world to ♥♥♥♥ around inMy only real gripes are how they changed Leveling and Combat. Leveling is now far more restricted, with you spending EXP to get a fixed number of upgrades to your stats and abilities as well as a few books with minor buffs and resistances to sink extra exp into. This massive change from the much more free form leveling system severely limits the creativity in builds you could make for the last game. In WoL, every beanslinger looked at least a little different, usually with different stats or skills prioritized. Now, each class has the exact same progression. Stat ups, and buffing your sideclass. Its kinda really boring. Leveling no longer becomes an active choice, and putting hard caps on how high main stats can get makes it not fun for me. This bleeds into combat too. Combat in WoL wasn't the highlight necessarily, but it was fun, and I enjoyed each classes' playstyle. You would have a few different choices for each scenario, there wasn't ever a one size beats all solution. Granted, you could level yourself so hard combat became really easy, but that takes a LOT of extra effort. in SoL, every combat is Buff yourself, one shot each enemy. Its really really repetitive. And its not like you can easily do a different approach, as most skills are just more buffs, and enemies are a lot more deadly, especially in large numbers. When it was hard, it was frustratingly hard, and when it was anything else, it was boring

_childDocuments_.review: In mathematics, non-Euclidean geometry consists of two geometries based on axioms closely related to those that specify Euclidean geometry. As Euclidean geometry lies at the intersection of metric geometry and affine geometry, non-Euclidean geometry arises by either replacing the parallel postulate with an alternative, or relaxing the metric requirement. In the former case, one obtains hyperbolic geometry and elliptic geometry, the traditional non-Euclidean geometries. When the metric requirement is relaxed, then there are affine planes associated with the planar algebras, which give rise to kinematic geometries that have also been called non-Euclidean geometry. _childDocuments_.review: I recommend this game as it's good, but West of Loathing was better.Shadows Over Loathing has an interesting core premise, which is that you're an adventurer during the Prohibition in the 1920's, set in the same world from West of Loathing. There's evil cursed relics out in the world that you're tracking down in order to de-curse them to find more leads to find your missing relic-hunting uncle. However, it fails to juggle the serious and the silly as well as West of Loathing did.A lot of the jokes in West of Loathing I remember either were lengthy or recurring, absurd concepts taken seriously, or were just plain silly. West of Loathing told a story of an adventurer heading out west doing things along the way, changing the world either for the better or for the worse, wrapped in a silly and absurd package.Shadows Over Loathing's tone is more serious, from the setting being the Prohibition to the soundtrack being more dramatic and even ominous. A lot of the times the jokes feel rather brief or one-note; there wasn't anything that made me laugh as much as West of Loathing or even Kingdom of Loathing. However, even taking that into account, Shadows Over Loathing somewhat disappointed me from the quality of the gameplay.In West of Loathing, the game is effectively split up into 3 sections, clearly shown on the map. It makes it so that travelling from a late-game area to an early-game area is as easy as going to the map and clicking on said location. However, Shadows Over Loathing is split up into chapters, with a new area being introduced per chapter. The game's way of going between these areas is by selecting the area through a menu on the map screen, which makes it feel clunkier than West of Loathing's traversal. Add onto the fact that if you're going from one location to another, but they're in different areas, you have to go through 2 random encounters as well. It makes traversal between locations just annoying when they're in different areas, which is something that wasn't a problem in West of Loathing given that the map was one whole thing. You just had 1 encounter per trip, not 2 encounters and a menu in between.The game also has issues with puzzles and progression, where there's a good handful of encounters and events in-game that will be permanently missable if you do them incorrectly, such as looking left in the Borge House, showing a specific newspaper in the Old Ham Mill, battling Dean Wormwood, missing out on an amazing cat boon if you don't do certain things in the prologue or skip the prologue in future runs, the shadow rift in Hans Zimmer's house, or turning down the mob's offer. It makes the game feel more restrictive than it should be, which is a shame because of how fun and free West of Loathing felt to play. There's also the occasional bug that requires you to manually go through your save file to correct a flag.In spite of all of what I've said above, I still recommend this game. I believe it should've been kept in development for longer, because it really feels like they rushed a good amount of the game just to hit the 11/11/2022 release date due to how special the number 11 is to the Loathing series of games.Shadows Over Loathing still has solid rewarding puzzle sequences that involve digging up the in-world history thanks to your access to both a defunct newspaper agency and a university. There's a good handful of side quests that feel great to do, such as working for Rufus at the S.I.T, working for the verbose Don Toblerone, learning the hobo code from hobos and building up the hobo camp, and various other small tidbits throughout the game. The combat is still great and practically unchanged from West of Loathing. The soundtrack especially is SUPERB, and for a fun treat involving it, try out special moves as the Jazz Agent class.I'd give it a 6/10. It's good enough, a passing grade. I just wish that they kept it in development for another year to hit 11/11/23 and refine the rough edges it has.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Lots and lots of small problems that add up towards a rather disappointing sequel.First off, the amount of backtracking and spending time in an area that you have to do makes the progression feel insanely sluggish, and it's easy to get bored of one area before you're even fully done with it and saw everything. It's almost reminiscent of the Breadwood joke quest from West of Loathing where you're sent on a long winded string of fetch quests going back and forth between the same two areas.Secondly, the balance of the game is waaaay too easy to break. With the right build and very little effort you can one shot almost every enemy in the game, FROM EARLY GAME. If you count items, you can also do it without taking a lick of damage! The pets are a cool mechanic and all but I've yet to find one that comes close to the power of the bird you get at the beginning. Getting +3 to all stats every turn with the move that triggers your pet's ability 3 times might just be a little dumb. No stakes to combat combined with the slowness of the progression just makes doing the quests feel less like fun exploration and more like a chore.And not to mention the theming. I'm of the opinion that the early 1930's setting is too grounded for the wackiness expected of this series. No ridiculous supernatural phenomenon like Cows, no abundance of the undead, no bizarre race of Clowns, just Shadow beings. Like who cares.If you liked the silly walks from West, youre in for a treat. You can only have one at a time with the new shoes equip slot. This wouldn't be so bad if all of them didn't make a repetitive noise that gets reaaally annoying after the first 10 seconds. There's a lot of walking in this game.Overall, this is still a decent game, but it's always going to be living in the 'shadow' of its older brother West of Loathing for me. Get it if you're a superfan like me, but be prepared for an inferior experience.

You get a lot of different dialogue choices and you can resolve situations depending on your skills which offer a lot of variety (and possible consequences) down the line.There is also more replayability due to certain sections only being accessible depending on your previous choices. The only arguably bad things are that you may need to backtrack and go to the same locations sometimes for quests and that it gets a bit samey after a while, some random events do get repeated often while exploring the overworld. _childDocuments_.review: Quick little heads up, you don't need to play West of Loathing to understand the story. A couple of nods here and there, but nothing note worthy.West of Loathing was a shockingly funny and quirky RPG that's been in my backlog for quite sometime. After beating it i wanted more, after beating Shadows Over Loathing i want even MORE. If you played the first Loathing game, the core experience is pretty much identical. Writing is top notch as is expected from these devs. Even something as mundane as a rock is turned into a paragraph of ridiculous dialogue. Combat is what you expect from any turn based RPG, but with the signature Loathing charm. Fish into a toilet and get a wad of greasy hair, throw it at an enemy to amp up fire attacks, obviously it works because its GREASY hair.The main difference between West and Shadows is the theme. West was more of a spaghetti western and all the cliches that come with that. Shadows is more about mystery solving and story telling. Both are great, but Shadows is a little more "puzzley" in some of its quests, at least in comparison to the main quests in West. West can also be picked up whenever, even if you haven't played in a while the story is very simplistic and not much of the focus. Shadows is a bit more story driven, so you might need a small recap if you haven't played in a month. Another banger in the Loathing series, I respect the change in theme and the effort put into the story this time around. If you liked West, you'll like Shadows just as much. Highly recommended.

_childDocuments_.review: Just like West of Loathing before it, Shadows Over Loathing is filled to the brim with content content and some more content. There is a lot more than I've seen during my 18 hours of playtime, and the choices to see that content begin with the prologue. So if you want something different for your playthroughs, there's a lot to choose form, not even mentioning the random chance of stumbling upon some of it. Even if you're not a completionist, the story and the sidequests are compelling enough to keep you playing, and if you don't like the combat you can turn it off. There is nothing wrong with combat, and it does that RPG thing where you can stack up numbers so high you can kill most enemies before they make a move or find some other way of cheesing the combat (sometimes literally [it makes sense in context]).The atmosphere of the game is amazing - it's the fine blend of supernatural vs the mundane, like having a college course named "Spiders" played completely straight, or having the mob fight vampires in the city because it's just another gang to them. And fittingly for the 1920s there's this atmosphere of new and exciting creations just being dropped into the world, letting you encounter something new every chapter. The one thing I'd say I disliked was the music at some parts, especially in the latter chapters - not that it's bad, it just becomes too intense when compared you going though corn mazes and just wandering around farms, with this feel of urgency, which is not fitting the overworld exploration. It's like having boss fight music 100% of the time, so it stands out too much and becomes tiring. Overall a solid recommend if you like adventure games. Bring out pen and paper (or Steam notes) as you'll need to think and remember things more than once!

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game immediately after someone informed me that it existed. The original provided about 5 hours of fun, comedy-rich content, and I was looking quite forward to a new experience. The game that met me blew my expectations out of the water. Excellent use of theme, refinement of mood and combat mechanics to the highest level, and - my goodness - the music surprised me wonderfully to the point that I listen to the soundtrack in the background as my go-to driving music. The jokes are still funny. The mechanics are still enjoyable. The story is still interesting. In every way, this is a refinement of West of Loathing, and is my genuine pick for the Game of the Year for 2022. I paid $22.00 for 66 hours of gameplay (I went for 100% completion), but even the initial playthrough is rich enough to offer at least 5 hours, which would cost $35.00 at minimum wage. For this price, you get a classic Lovecraftian Noire tale that is filled with unmatched comedy, great music, and a lovely take on RPG mechanics. Asymmetric has really outdone themselves, and I cannot recommend this product enough.
