_childDocuments_.review: If you're familiar with the Loathing games, this is another one. It's nearly twice the size of West of Loathing with much more emphasis on interconnected quests and overall narrative. Like WoL (and KoL) it's viciously funny and consistently clever in a way few games are, but at times that cleverness gets in the way of the clarity. Also, the combat in this game is sluggish and omnipresent. Your core stats are extremely limited, so even by the end of the game it's unlikely that you'll be able to efficiently clear out mooks without leaning heavily on items or your familiar. This isn't a huge deal unless you're spending a lot of time trying to find all the content, but if you are trying to find all the content it becomes a slog incredibly quickly. In the vein of 'all the content', compared to WoL this game feels like it has a lot more sidequests and interactions that can be missed, failed, or are otherwise incompatible with other choices. While this is great for replayabilty and gives real weight to choices, combined with the occasional lack of clarity due to the jokes and it's easy to miss out on companions, factions, or entire facets of the game without noticing. One of the funniest jokes in the game takes 20 hours to get to the punchline, and due to the byzantine nature of specific choices that have to be made to actualize it only 4% of players have seen it. The Loathing games have always been made with a clarity of vision and a full-throated willingness to have puzzles and interactions that are too hard or too opaque for most people to get without a guide. I deeply respect that decision, but it does have costs.Overall, at this point you know what you're in for. If you liked West of Loathing, this is more of it. If you didn't, this won't convince you. Great game either way.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're already a fan of the Loathing series know that this is more of the same with a distinctly Lovecraftian/horror twist!If you've not played the Loathing games before, Shadows over Loathing is a fun, irreverent romp through a world filled with esoteric (and not-so-esoteric) mysteries. The strength of the game is it's sense of humor and genuinely intriguing puzzles, some of which are fairly easily solved, other of which are...not. There are plenty of locations to explore, random encounters to encounter, and toilets to fish in. The writing is delivered with tongue firmly in cheek and a narrator that occasionally seems to have a personal stake in punishing the player for making the silliest (or grossest) possible decisions. The combat is pretty basic (as in all Loathing games) with three classes to choose from where damage is calculated based on personal stats (Muscle, Mysticality, or Moxie). It can end up getting a bit repetitive as the game goes on. However, the good news is that Shadows of Loathing gives you PLENTY of ways of resolving conflicts that don't involve combat, and even has a "Pacifist Mode" that prevents you from engaging in combat. To a large extent, the combat is an entirely optional part of the game, which makes it a lot more tolerable. There's also a fairly significant amount of replayability potential, with several decision-locked companions, personal nemeses for each class, and decisions to make about exactly how comfortable you are with the forces of darkness. It is impossible to see all of the content in the game in one play through, which makes replaying a must if you want to see everything the game has to offer. It's also quite forgiving in that it allows you to continue from just before the final act of the game so that if you left anything undone or discover something new in one of your next playthroughs you can load up an old character and keep playing. All in all a fun, silly, and surprisingly challenging narrative and puzzle driven game!

_childDocuments_.review: Much like its predecessor, Shadows over Loathing combines Point-and-Click style riddles with Rpg fights and gameplay aspects.While the graphics may appear lacklustre at first, they do provide a very unique charme and fit in well with the general wackiness of the game. Combined with some good tunes they set the stage for this very fun adventure.And fun is the main aspect of this game. There is a joke at every opportunity, lots of silly things happen and silly items are waiting for you to find them. This game pretty much never takes itself seriously, but can seriously make you laugh.Compared to West of Loathing, this time there is a more coherent storyline for you to follow, giving the game more structure. In addition to that, Shadows over Loathing implements some quality of life changes that make it easier to play and navigate. With this it manages to be an even better experience than the last game.All in all I can only recommend this game. With Shadows over Loathing you are in for a great time and a lot of laughs.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: - Honestly, the game isn't much to look at, but impressive visuals have never been the focus of KoL properties. That said, I've enjoyed the visual design since playing the original browser game back in high school in the early 00s- It's actually impressive how much character and personality the devs were able to infuse into the game despite the simplistic visuals- Music is pretty good. Nothing spectacular, but there was a decent variety that kept the game from sounding too stale- True to the all entries in the series, the writing is once again creative, witty, and very amusing- In that same vein, don't expect the game to take itself very seriously. The overall tone is intended to be humorous- The story is very simple but serves as a nice framework for the rest of the game's writing. Just sit back and enjoy the ride. You're going to be doing a lot of reading- The mechanics of the game will feel familiar to anyone who has played Kingdom of Loathing or West of Loathing. For those who haven't, it's a simplified 3-class turn-based JRPG- There's also a lot of puzzles. Like A LOT of them. Some of them are pretty fiendishly difficult, but very satisfying to complete- I'm definitely smelling a replay in the future, mostly because there's so much depth in the game in terms of exploration and hidden side quests. I feel like I touched on 60% of the game in my 20+ hour playthrough. Hell, I didn't even get an achievement until hour 14- The only real knock on this game I can think of is the combat. It's shallow even by JRPG standards and begins to feel very stale even a few hours into the game. Enemies aren't spongy and I feel like the encounters are well-scaled (even skewing a bit easy), but all you'll ever be doing is spamming your most powerful skill and attacking to end your turn- If you feel like solving some challenging puzzles and chuckling at your computer screen the whole time, this is definitly a game to put on your radar- Playing this has really gotten me eager to go back and replay West of Loathing- The "Deck Verified" rating is well-earned. It ran flawlessly the whole way through, but this shouldn't be surprising giventhe game's very light system requirements- . The humorous writing, devilish puzzles, and seemingly endless depth make this a game well-worth paying full price for. If the combat weren't such a chore, I would be recommending Shadows Over Loathing to everyone who likes RPGs. If you're a KoL fan or liked West of Loathing, buy with confidence
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Very good writing, cool gags, music-tastic music and whatnot, definetly would recommend it to anyone as well as the other Loathing games.To compare it to WoL, it's a bit less replayable, but the main questline is a lot more interesting, and everything comes together very neatly at the end. _childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: There's nothing from West of Loathing that Shadows Over Loathing didn't improve on. Clever, funny, and with one of the BEST pay-offs for a joke in gaming history, Shadows Over Loathing has near-infinite re-playability. In 37 hours I've gotten to the end of the game 3 times and still have achievements to unlock and mysteries to explore. SoL also carries a bit more subtlety, requiring the player to pay attention and think about the dialogue options they're choosing. It's just so good. Please play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: As always with this series, the game is incredibly funny and well written. I think in many ways, the mystery element present in this game suits the style of the series very well, with Shadows over Loathing having a lot of intriguing and hilarious new mechanics for a good laugh or a genuinley clever execution of a concept. I'm definitely enjoying my time spent in the game, and for anyone who is already a fan of the loathing series, I can definitely recommend it. For newcomers, I think this would be a fine introduction to the wacky, off the walls experience that is the universe of Loathing.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: I just started playing this game, and I love it already! The witty and silly humour, the beautiful graphics, easy-to-listen music, and a big story to unfold. The upgrading system uses a new mechanic in which you can't just ingest many different meals, drinks, and potions at the same time to improve your character like in West of Loathing, but I don't think of it as a flaw but more of a challenge to learn from. If you're looking for an RPG that seriously doesn't take itself too seriously, and/or you want to something different from anime-style (J)RPGs or semi-realistic first-person RPGs, then this is for you.

_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: The adventure game that keeps on giving.  A really nice refinement on West of Loathing.  Felt a bit directionless on my first go (why am I going on these quests again??), and individual chapters didn't feel as cohesive as I would have liked.  I played through the whole game fairly thoroughly (about 25 hours), and then made a new character and on my second play through I found so many things I missed in the first run.  Another 25 hours later, my third character still keeps finding things I missed.  There's so many hidden gems - sometimes an entire zone is hidden behind a tiny encounter.  It takes some risks that don't always pay off but I really appreciate the team keeps experimenting and overall this REALLY worked for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to really get into what's special about the game without spoiling it,  but I'll try and sell to someone who isn't familiar with KoL/WoL.It's very casual sidescrolling with turn based combat. There are some nifty tricks and strategies you can learn but the game itself is not difficult to progress in no matter what your play style or imagination and ingenuity are. You might have to grind a little at times to get to the point where your character can reach certain areas or beat certain enemies. It can be a little tedious at times and some of the jokes can get old as you encounter them again (and again and again), but the amount of random stuff to do, random opportunities make grinding a rewarding experience that can even lead to other quests. Speaking of ingenuity, imagination, and rewards, this game will reward you for being a little creative, cunning and clever, so get your thinking cap on when playing. Likewise, you'll want to be well versed in some tropes, this game will reward you for your knowledge of tropes. You'll also want to bring along a fairly weird, dirty, twisted, morbid or some other sense of humor that comes out of left field. Oh, this game is very funny, that's the real appeal of it. Yes, the gameplay is very satisfying and enjoyable and you can waste a lot of your time on this game (you'll get your money's worth if you can appreciate that this plays like a 2000s flash game, gee) but it's very very funny. And pretty deep at times too. If you appreciate that sort of thing.SO BUY THE GAME, GEEK!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Good game, however not as enjoyable as West of Loathing. The game is less comedy focused, more linear, and longer compared to West of Loathing. The requirements for 100% feel a lot more grindey because of this. Having to play through the game 3 times in a month sucked most of the fun out, especially because of the longer game length from the linear storyline.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Do you like the Kingdom of Loathing web game?  How about West of Loathing?  This is a mystery/horror-themed game with the same humor and similar mechanics. There's plenty of hidden references and obscure puzzles and even more obscure achievements to add to replayability to a certain extent. Great stuff, so long as you like that style of humor.You should give the web game (Kingdom of Loathing) a whirl anyways since it's interesting and free, but that's the easiest way to determine if you like the graphical and storytelling style for this game assuming you haven't played West of Loathing already.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows Over Loathing is an amazing rpg with a great sense of humor, but it has some flaws.PROS:- Nice inclusivity, I appreciate the game letting you be referred as he, she, or they.- Lots of exploration. You can easily go in only doing the main line quests and barely discover any new areas, but doing side quests and wandering let's you unlock so many more areas to explore.- The combat is very simple to grasp, but still is able to provide a challenge later on.- There's ton of dialogue with tons of jokes, you can easily go throughout the game skipping through dialogue or you can pay attention it and enjoy the jokes.- There's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of things to do, I tried doing (almost) as many side quests as I could, and many of them didn't feel tedious nor annoying.But regardless, there's still flaws.CONS:- Puzzles can be extremely difficult, with some not even making sense. CHAPTER 6 SPOILERS - The game just kinda...ends. Like CHAPTER 6 SPOILERS - Though the game has tons of dialogue, the game makes almost no effort actually explaining the main conflict or the bad guys in the game. You're told very vague things about them and then are given a vague  and that's about all you'll get until near the ending where you're given a brief lore dump and that's it.All and all I'd give the game about an 8/10, but the game felt so rushed near the end. Such a horrible ending to an overall masterpiece of a game.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommended.After I spend many hours in 'West of Loathing', I decided to give 'Shadows' a try. After I finished one playthrough of it, I can honestly say that it is amazing. My first run is not perfect, there are a lot of things that I didn't explore to the fullest, but even so I had a lot of fun. If you come from 'West of Loathing', you won't be disappointed.Just keep in mind, for some locations you would need a guide. I got lost a few times and for one companion I messed up a bit. It's not game-breaking, just part of the fun for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor to the West of Loathing (WoL) game. This time however, it has a darker and a more serious undertone, combining elements of Lovecraftian nightmares with conspiracy theories on a verge of the Great Depression and during Prohibition. This all leads to a subdued tone of the game compared to the WoL in terms of humor but still delivers a very nice story, puzzles and atmosphere.Pros:If you loved WoL, you'll love this game, tooWriting is impeccable.Tons of content for people who are invested in the story.Enjoyable gameplay (it's easier than in WoL IMO).The bespoke atmosphere of the game is there.Cons:Less humor which is understandable given the choice of the game's time period and influences. While WoL jokes are over the top sometimes, in this game they are more subdued and witty which will not appeal to everybody.Puzzles are sometimes grindy (in a bad way): while you can deduce some of them via logic or attentiveness, a few others seem almost chance-based or extremely vague which was annoying. To be fair, most puzzles were quite satisfuing to solve.Character stats are now more important than weapons, and buffs are easy to come by (I presume this is done to make it possible to finish the game without any combat).ps fingers crossed we get a similar adventure in 80s retro style
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure how much the humor of Shadows Over Loathing will appeal to someone who hasn't played Kingdom of Loathing or West of Loathing, but I've enjoyed it a lot. They really built on the companion and pet systems of the previous games and I really like all the Lovecraftian references in the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I just love the Loathing games.  I played as much of West of Loathing as one possibly could, unlocking every possible thing across several playthroughs on the PC and Switch.  Much like its predecessor, Shadows Over Loathing is a a game taking place in a specific time period - this time the early 1900's.  While it's similar in aesthetic and humor, SOL is an entirely different experience from WOL.  It's a game where the story, plot, game mechanics, and so on all exist as a catalyst for its best quality: the writing.  The writing in this game is just *so* good.  Nothing feels flat or one-dimensional.  Dialogue, descriptions, events - everything is just a treat to read. Everything in this game has character - even the characters who don't talk more than a mumble or two have you wondering "What's this person's story?" The writing manages to be charming, flowing, and nearly flawless (I have only seen one typo so far between both games, and that was in the resolution for a random encounter later on in the game, involving the Death's Head Moth.)The game mechanics, which are entirely customizable, let you play how you like. Want really challenging battles?  Got it.  Don't want battles at all?  That's an option too.  Can't decide between no spiders and a bunch of extra spiders?  Somehow, the folks at Asymmetric thought of that too.New this time around is more character customization, at least with the face, and a chance to give preferred pronouns.  Character classes appear to have sub-classes now, and combined with backstories, offer a unique experience depending on your choices. The level up system feels much less like an automatic thing that does the work for you; this time it's a slower, more deliberate process.  Familiars accompany you in combat, acting as a little boost, and companions can be swapped with relative ease.As far as critiques of the game, I will say that the prologue was a little frantic, as I'd watched a Youtuber play it ahead of time and thus knew there was a very deliberate way to approach the tasks.  But not getting them all didn't negatively impact my experience with the rest of the game, and if anything it just gives incentive to try some different things next time around.I often get the free "Game of the week" or whatever on other platforms, and regret wasting my hard drive space with them after an hour or two of play.  Shadows over Loathing, on the other hand, was completely worth both the money I spent and the space it took up, and I look forward to many more hours with it.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a decent enough game, but if you are considering buying specifically because of West of Loathing, lower your expectations. The game delivers on several aspects presented in WOL but fails to recapture its spirit. This game feels more like a mess of a bunch of new concepts that felt more like trying to be new for the sake of being new. WOL also had lots of strange concepts but each of them was given so much dedication that they ended up forming a concrete amazing experience. The character customization and freedom to explore in WOL are not found as much here, and there is a more linear streamlined experience which I feel takes away from the wild world that is being created. Additionally, there are points where the game just feels like a slog of trying to equip random stuff to try to scrape up enough stats to clear a check while experience is pushed to the side and used for useless combat upgrades. It can't be played over and over again like WOL because there is an inherent lack of nuance to every location. Whereas WOL inspired you to travel around, find new items, go back to locations, discover mysteries, etc, this game just gives locations where you finish the isolated storyline and move on with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ item that doesn't help. I will give it credit as the story itself is amazing. The main and sidequests do deliver but just not in a way that aligns with WOL. Honestly, I'd get it if it were on sale, but a larger price for an arguably smaller game is not justified here.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't say this often about games, but this one is worth full price. If you get it on sale, it's a steal even at a dollar off. I didn't play West of Loathing, but I watched my favorite Let's Players when they did. And I kind of felt like I missed out by not just playing it myself first and then watching them. But when this gem came out, and I started watching, and time went on between play-through uploads, I decided to take the dive and play it myself first and then go back to watch someone else play for lawls.I have to say, if you miss a solid, but simple, turn based rpg format with a good story and a whole lot of humor, this is the game for you. It does not take itself seriously, even a little bit. I personally feel the reason it's so good is because this game specializes in very few things really well. A lot of newer rpgs like to load you up with stuff like pets and crafting, ect. The Loathing series does none of that. It's focused on combat with a few small extras (like cooking and potion making in this game). I don't need to worry about feeding, petting, or cleaning my helper pets. I don't need to hang out with my companions unless I just want to chat them up for fun; it won't raise their skills or give them bonuses. This game does not spread itself thin with all of that. And I'm not saying that those things are bad. But it's refreshing and fun to play a game that doesn't have all that, where you don't NEED it, to fully play the game and kick some butt and engage with the story.Sometimes less is more, ya'll.So if you want to play a fun game with some serious laughs, decent headteachers for puzzles, and a touch of tentacle horror, this is it. I lost hours of time in it and regret none of it.

_childDocuments_.review: The Loathing series is known for being extremely funny and intricate, so obviously you don’t need much push to purchase. So instead I’m going to use this review to state the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ parts of the game.For starters, for such an intricate and complicated game, there is next to no forgiveness. If you don’t choose precisely the correct dialogue options, you can be locked out of entire sections of the game. Not to even begin to mention the achievements, some of which require restarting the entire game to attempt a second time. All due to a single misinput. Mind you all of this is usually unexplained, so unless you consult a guide (for a lot of the game there simply isn’t one online), you’re pretty much screwed. This is by far my biggest gripe with the game, the lack of forgiveness for these mistakes is incredibly upsetting.Secondly, the difficulty. I played through the game my first time on the hardest difficulty, 11, and found it a breeze. Expect little to no challenge in the combat areas. You’ll be playing mostly for the humour, writing, and puzzles anyway.Thirdly: the items. There’s thousands of useless items. And I really mean useless, we’re talking 10 different items with the exact same effect, all of which being useless because one item you have outclasses them all. Food and potion items are extremely common, but are effectively useless since you can only use one at a time each, meaning the 1000 meals in your inventory are useless since you only need around 10 per playthrough.These things are the only gripes I have with this game. Those aside it’s one of the most well structured and complex games I’ve gotten the pleasure to play since West of Loathing.

Now I have seen gameplay for the game that confirms that if you start the quest on unlocking the location you get dialogue that explains the rule and you at least get a closer to reasonable chance to not lock yourself out of the quest (btw the failure condition isn't even in view because it is obscured by the dialogue box lmao).Now if you do what I did and left the area and then came back later, if you break the rule as you enter, you won't get any dialogue at all, you will be met with a black screen before you are dumped back into the location, having the quest locked off.While my experience is a bug, the fact that on a TYPICAL playthrough it is very easy to miss the entire questline all because of a keystroke does leave a sour taste to the design of this specific quest.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, it's a very text-heavy game. If you need a TL;DR because you can't be bothered to read more than one paragraph at a time, then this game isn't for you, and that's all there is to say about it. A pretty decent game that suffered a virtually invisible release. If you're not familiar with the Loathing series, it's a stick figure RPG heavily driven by an off-the-wall, pun-based sense of humor. Basically, imagine if someone took the old Xanth novels and made them into a video game. (And if you don't know what Xanth is either, I'm afraid there's nothing I can say to help you.)If you are familiar with the Loathing series, then you probably already know whether you want this or not, but I'll tell you a little more about it anyway.Compared to West of Loathing, the combat system has been revamped. The main change was keeping numbers smaller, with a soft cap of about 15 in each stat, as opposed to WoL where they could reach triple digits easily with enough grinding. I'd say the combat is better, though that may depend on your own taste. It's also been made entirely optional; it is possible to beat the entire game in "Pacifist Mode" without entering combat at all, and you even get an achievement for doing so. That said, you can't do *everything* without fighting. Some content will be impossible to do, but not much.The writing is also changed a little bit from West of Loathing. Compared to West, Shadows is a much more linear storyline, and split into chapters rather than the wide-open-sandbox that was WoL. It's also generally better at actually following through on storylines. (See The Stearns Ranch for an example of WoL's tendency to create intriguing story arcs that just go nowhere.)On the other hand, I didn't find Shadows to be quite as funny as West. It's also much more preachy, with two moments in particular late in the game that just straight up stop the story so the writer can pull out a sock filled with quarters and with "Liberal Democrat" embroidered on it, and bludgeon you to death with it. () So if that sounds like it's going to bother you... well, you've been warned.In all, I'd recommend it in spite of its flaws, especially to anyone who is already a fan of the other games in the series, West of Loathing and Kingdom of Loathing.

_childDocuments_.review: Tentacles!  Paradoxesisis’ses!  Double jump!9/10 – short main game but lots to get involved in.  I remember the refreshing first play through of West of Loathing.  I had never played Kingdom of Loathing, but it is something which I should probably do.  WOL is one of the most inventive RPGs I have ever played.  It is let down by feeling a bit unfinished in places – but oddly is very replayable due to the character classes and hidden bits of the game.  SOL brings itself up by having a lot more to do and uncover.  It is still packed with the same sense of humour – sarcastic and drawing on fantasy archetypes.  In this case Lovecraftian horror (without the hate crimes).  Amongst all the silliness, there is a odd warmth that comes out of both SOL and WOL.  SOL has a rather good main plot of trying to uncurse items linked to the story – and the subgames/puzzles in this branch of the game is very well done.  You will behold:Tentacles.The terror of the Borge house.Bureaucracy.Junior witchfinders.…and more.  Improvements to WOL mechanics are welcome too.  There is no game breaking of being able to use combat items until you run out of them.The Familiar buddies are great – giving a compliment to your own combat style.  Allied groups also step in to help with combat and open up bits of the game.  A notes section is also present (1990s style) to build on your SOL lore.  On the downside, similar to WOL, SOLs lack of save slots means you have to redo large sections of the game to get back to your pre-redo point.  (PLEASE say I haven’t missed something crucial here).Also, some quests and puzzles do not log on side quests and need swift writing/typing to record - and the main quest is really quite short.  In summary, SOL is sarcastic, inane and somehow touching in places.  Unless you are made of stone, some of the quest conclusions will have you laughing your bits off also.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows over Loathing is a sprawling RPG that tasks you with tracking down a bunch of cursed objects (it reminded me of the old Friday the 13th TV show) that are wreaking havoc in it's bizarre, comedic America-in-the-roaring-20's-adjacent setting. It sells itself as a Lovecraft-inspired game, but while there are a lot (A LOT) of Cthulhu jokes the setting takes aim at the weird horror genre. It's fairly consistent in its worldbuilding, ridiculously inventive in its stories, and mind-bogglingly generous with its jokes. Every description, every line, will probably contain a pun, a double entendre, a small joke or a bit of wordplay. The stories will often be deeply ridiculous and hold a punchline in store should you decide to pursue the many, many quests and mysteries dangled in front of you. Not all the humour is laugh-out-loud funny, but... well, a lot of it is. And all of it is goofy fun. To cap it off, while it's definitely got a jokes-first ethos, the stories are still interesting. The overall plot may not be all that, but you can tackle it in a number of ways, and it's always surprising you with neat tidbits or weird developments. And there's always a sense of joy in the writing, as if everyone involved in making this was revelling in coming up with all these stupid vignettes and descriptions and snippets of dialog. It's definitely a joy to read. And the game itself is good, too! You'll spend your time mostly wandering small, blocky rooms, talking to folks and interacting with the environment. There are a few mazes (boo!) and a quite a bit of JRPG-style turn-based combat, though there's a pleasing almost puzzle-like nature to battles this time around. Everything is depicted using a current of the Naïf artistic style that the studio has been developing for years now which could be described as line drawings. But then again, aren't all drawings line drawings? Just... buy it already. Or buy West of Loathing, which  is a similarly good (if a bit crunchier and less polished) version of this. Then come back and buy this one.

_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

Also highly recommended if you have finished West of Loathing, as there are plenty of returning characters and references to the previous game that you will surely enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Fairly short, but with good replay value. The graphics are charming and the story and humor and enjoyable. Some of the puzzles are great (I highly recommend engaging with the time loop puzzle, it's was my one of my favorites). Others were not particularly enjoyable (Mudhenge). Combat has the potential to be interesting, but most of the time isn't. There are also a handful of degenerate strategies, but those can be left to the player as an exercise because breaking the combat is somewhat fun, at least for the fighting encounters that are supposed to be difficult. I know it sounds like I'm complaining, but these are incredibly minor nitpicks to what is overall a really good game. Even at full price, it's good value.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game. I really enjoyed West of Loathing, so when this was dropped unexpectedly I was ecstatic. I've played through it twice and can safely say that this game was totally worth the wait. The writing is witty and sharp while also managing to tell a compelling story. The characters are so much fun; my current favorite being the unsinkable Molly Buttons. The combat in this game also felt a lot more balanced to me that in the last one.   My only gripe is that I wish the companions had a little more to them. I miss your companions having something to say about each location like they did in the first game. It would've been a good opportunity for them to have even more development and comedic moments. Also, while this game is certainly not lacking for content, I definitely would've enjoyed more of it!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely fantastic. It takes all the humour from West of Loathing and throws it into a whole new and wicked scene. The characters are great, the combat system works really well, the silly art style is kept to very well, and the newer occult theme works very well in the game's favour. And, for those that like side quests, there is so much bonus optional content for you to enjoy. It is absolutely a phenomenal game and it is wholly worth buying especially if you enjoyed West of Loathing.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: If you love games with branching paths and incredibly funny scenarios that are well written; then this game is for you. I found myself drawn in by the first game in the series. West of Loathing. And this game absolutely improves upon each and every factor from the first. From the intractable environment and simplistic combat, to the over all graphic overhaul and ear soothing music. This game has such a depth that the first did not, and i'm completely happy with my experience with it. At first I was concerned about the setting, seeing as the first game had you toting around as a bean slinging cowboy. But the care and attention to detail put into the era really make it feel like i'm interacting with things that would actually be prevalent in the games era. The in-depth mechanics with boons really struck me as interesting and how much it actually effects things is inviting. In the settings there is modes for individuals who do not wish to do combat as well which I think is intelligent to include, but then there is Spider mode... I was just clicking around and ended up happily surprised. It spawned in extra spiders on your and the enemy side each combat encounter. It was so much more fun that I even left it on the entire rest of the time I played. Overall: Is it worth the price?: Absolutely with how much you're getting out of this hilarious experience and the replay-ability. Not to mention the accessibility. I think it's safe to say this game lives up and surpasses the expectations I had.  Especially since I thought the first game was never getting a sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Its very funny. The only thing that's frustrating is that its so long. Normally that wouldnt be a complaint, but in a game like this where 1 misclick can ruin your entire perfect run or whatever you're going for, that's frustrating. West of Loathing was frustrating too, but you could beat the whole thing in like 3 hours. This game even a quick run takes me around 6, but most my runs end closer to 8 or 9 hours. Im hoping to platinum it so I'll be playing many more hours to come, but I do wish there was a checkpoint system or something that you could reload to earlier if youre ok with losing the progress you made between checkpoints.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: I loved West of Loathing and I absolutely loved this too. When this released it was the most excited I have been about a game in years and it absolutely delivered. Full to the brim with delightful comedy and puzzles that are both very funny and decently challenging, this is everything I could have wanted and more. I love this game so dearly, thank you everyone who worked on it for giving us this game. A wonderful experience from start to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows over Loathing. The humour is sometimes great, sometimes a bit too... american. They're not great at it, as you might know.All the puzzling is often solvable in very creative ways, you really have to think out of the box!Usually the idea is that pacifist solutions require thought and work. You can always fight, but that's the easy way!And the solutions can be.. punny. :)
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: One of the most fun games I have played, for multiple reasons!The humor is solid the entire way through, but it doesn't take away from the story and what is at stake. Mechanically, the RPG elements are solid with 3 classes each with different skill trees that fit into the world both logically and thematically. For instance, at one point in the game I found a mouse who wants cheese, and you get items for each type of cheese delivered, which is already funny, however my class was Cheese Wizard so I had a special option to summon cheese for the mouse. These kinds of examples are all throughout the game and are always a joy to see.There's so much of the game that is better experienced than read or watched, both big and small details in main quests, side jobs, and even just incidental details revealed through just being aware, everything in this game is gold as far as I am concerned.

_childDocuments_.review: Love this game, on my fifth playthrough. This is a turn based rpg. Each playthrough you get to choose a different class, specialty and 3 of 9 school classes, as well as different pets and followers. It's easy to get locked out of specific questlines and there can be multiple solutions to solve puzzles, so every time you play you may get see different things, get different items, even get different endings. There is so much fun writing in this game and so many different ways to play. Don't like fighting? Try pacifist mode. Like spiders? Try spiders mode. Hate spiders? Try no spiders mode. Want to go full on evil? Give that a try. Want to conjure cheese and beat your enemies with it? That's a choice as well. Want to adjust the difficulty to easy? Easy. Want to turn it up to eleven? You can do that too. I find myself playing again and again to learn more of the stories and see if I can't find a better ending next time. The devs are extremely diligent, patching a bug that I reported within a day, you can tell this game is a labor of love. My first playthrough took me about 20 hours. One thing to note is that the game autosaves. So if you make the wrong choice, you may be locked out of a questline until your next playthrough. I take notes as I play so I can try a different path the next time. I really enjoyed the puzzles in this game, a lot of them are very clever, a few of them were quite difficult but the community has done a good job helping each other solve them.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an awesome combination of RPG and old-school point-and-click adventure game, with a great story, multiple endings, and more humor that you should stuff into any one place at any one time.  Its love language is clearly snark, and if you like sarcasm, irreverent humor, or just absolute nonsense, this game is a must buy!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: The horror segments of West of Loathing were some of my personal favorite parts of the game, so to see a sequel game based around horror was a welcome surprise! There's so much content in this game that it's definitely worth the price imo(as an edit I forgot to add how weirdly amazing the soundtrack is)
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: I don't have a lot to write here. If you loved West of Loathing, then this will scratch more of that itch. This is probably the first game I've purchased upon its release (which came out of nowhere) in ten years and I've not been disappointed with that risky decision. Comments below reflect changes from my review of WoL - I'm not going to retype all the praise I had for the original.+Five difficulty settings (Normal is pretty casual)+Primary companion can be swapped out at will+Up to 8 simultaneous combat companions+Still many areas to grind XP if you want to+More room decorations+More character customizations+Even more replayability+Dynamic changes to music are a nice touch+Combat is slightly more strategic since you can now see opponents' moves ahead of time, and attempt to prepare/counter.~There is a sort of level cap and stats are harder to raise~Menus and inventory are still a pain to get through~Ran into a few gameplay bugs, though I guess that's to be expected~Silly walking is still in the game, but works a little differently-The programming lab was tedious for a number of reasons-The sickle "puzzle" was 30 minutes of RNG torture. Change or remove it.-Some missing sound effects

_childDocuments_.review: As I'm writing this review I haven't yet completed the entire story, but this is already just as easy of a recommendation as West of Loathing was. The visual style is the same, and as charming as ever. Again, very befitting. The story is obviously the main point of interest in such a heavily narrative-driven title, and at least in my opinion (and given how far I've gotten into the story) Shadows Over Loathing delivers! The story has a similar charm to it that West of Loathing has, and at least in my opinion has been very well written. Again, an easy recommendation!

_childDocuments_.review: Can you improve on a masterpiece?Yes. Yes you can. And they have.Asymmetric is my favorite Dev/Pub but no bias here. Few games make me laugh out loud like the "Loathing" series does. The mix of dialogue and characters are unmatched. Much too unique and well-written to have competition. Lovecraft, jazz, classic LucasArts-style adventures (and a reference or two), meat, and all other things good in life, get this game. If you already got the game, we are best friends. _childDocuments_.review: Tons of fun, I love seeing all the little hints and nods towards West of Loathing, and the countless gimmicks and gags they throw in. Definitely worth getting especially if you're a fan of West of Loathing.As for which is better, West of Loathing or Shadows Over Loathing? I honestly don't think either one is definitively better. In West of Loathing it definitely feels like you have more freedom and choices in how fast/slow you want your run to be. As well as what kind of quests you do and don't want to do. Though in Shadows Over Loathing it feels a lot bigger and you get truly immersed in the game, as if you're actually traveling throughout a whole world and then some. While the quests and side quests intersect at some points requiring you to unlock/grab an item in a totally unrelated area expanding upon the immersion. It does also make it feel a lot more strict and as if you have to do things in order instead of the totally free wandering and advancement West of Loathing offers.Nonetheless while it may feel a little more restrictive in the adventuring/advancement I still highly recommend checking out this game (as well as West of Loathing if you haven't done so already).
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Having played both West of Loathing and Kingdom of Loathing, I do enjoy the route they took in this game. I love the characters, the story, and the humor. It definetly is a step in the right direction.However it does feel a bit limited in a couple of ways:1) Unlike WoL and KoL, its basically impossible to get your main stats above 20 and while the stat checks match the cap, I do like the idea of making a number absurdly large. Though that is just me being picky, it makes no difference either way.2) I am not a big fan of the perk/buff system in this game. It is the only game in the franchise where you can only have 1 food/booze/potion buff at a time. I enjoyed that in the other 2 games you could have multiple food/booze/potion buffs depending on your level and what not.3) The game uses KoL elemental armor instead of WoL elemental resistance, which I kind of dislike. I enjoyed being able to make myself completely resistant to elements in WoL and feel that the armor limits what you can do. While yes armor limits damage, it doenst completely migate it, so it makes armor a bit pointless.Then again, that is just me being picky. It is a great game and I definelty enjoy it, I hope they release a wacky DLC like they did for WoL.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Gender neutral pronouns :)That aside, this game has some amazing humor, and a story that can be enjoyed both ironically and unironically - a rare feat! The only big issue I have is with the combat balancing, as one particular familiar that I got made every combat way too easy, to the point where it was essentially just "press this button to win". I found myself surrendering in combats that I could have easily won, just to not have to go through yet another forty seconds of familiar attacks.Where the game especially shines is in its exploration and puzzles. It was a treat picking through each of the locations for hidden secrets, both mechanically useful and just funny, and I felt rewarded for my completionist instincts (though I do wish it were possible to take the remaining classes in a single playthrough).Overall, this game was far from perfect, but it was still a blast. There will likely be one or two moments where the game gets in the way of your fun, but it's just oozing with character (and, at times, with ooze) at every corner, and it's especially fun to stream with friends. 9/10!

_childDocuments_.review: Yes. I love these games and this dev.The only thing about them I don't like is how if you make a single misclick or you progress faster than you want to (such as uncursing something you didn't want to uncurse or missing something inside the uncursing areas), then you have to start over from scratch, which honestly sucks a lot.And this game has a LOT of chances to mess up.Also, you don't get to rename your pets if you skip the prologue unless you have the ability and knowledge on how to edit the .json save files.So while I love this game, it's got a fair amount of drawbacks making the game more stressful and less enjoyable overall.

_childDocuments_.review: Asymmetric Publications has been mostly making the same game since 2004, but fortunately for them it's a very good one and they've nailed down the core concept of the satire adventure game. Shadows over Loathing takes the Loathing formula previously used in Kingdom of- (a browser-based satire of the fantasy adventure genre) and West of- (satire of Old West/spaghetti-Western adventuring) and applies it now to 1920s Lovecraft. As before, it's a sendup of the base genre, done in hand-ish drawn stick figures, with a heavy emphasis on impenetrable 1920s slang. All sorts of dumb things happen and as in the best adventure games, you are encouraged to get into the stupidity of it for the sake of the punchline. Somewhat more seriously, the game builds to its ending with better pacing than in West of Loathing, where the end can sneak up on you without sufficient warning that you're going into the finale. The franchise keeps getting better at telling the same sorts of jokes, so if you enjoyed what they've done before, you'll love Shadows over Loathing. If you're new to it but like comedic gaming that both does and doesn't take itself seriously in the places where each is called for, checking it out will likely prove rewarding.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: If you like text-based comedy, and you can stand words upon words upon words, this game is perfect for you. A lot of games try to be quirky with their humor and end up falling flat on their face, yet this game tries to go in the opposite direction. Instead of trying to be quirkywacky, it is pure stupidwacky. Have you ever wanted to fish up gobs of water? Have a magic contest against an evil Christmas themed wizard? Or even attend a college class about spiders? It's possible.If you've played West of Loathing, you know what to expect from combat. It's still rather lackluster as the game progresses, but that's not the point. The point is that you can summon cheese golems.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows over Loathing takes the whimsical insanity of its predecessor and improves on every front. From an eerily realistic visual art style to touching character arcs, and from petting cute cats to battling Lovecraftian horrors beyond human comprehension, this game has got it all. A truly life-changing experience, with huge replay value to boot.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: A quality Asymmetric game, all around. The art is what drew me to play West of Loathing, my first experience with this game series, and Shadows Over Loathing heightens that style further. It's just so visually *enjoyable.* (A weird statement, but fight a duck enemy and tell me it doesn't make you laugh.)The puzzles range from simple ones to real head-scratchers, but none are completely esoteric or impossible. The music is phenomenal and adds so much to the atmosphere of the game. The game feels extremely replayable, as well, given all the different options and endings. I'm 26 hours in, and on my second playthrough. Can verify that Pig Skinner and Jazz Agent are hella fun.Best of luck on the end battle, buddies!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Same old loathing. Puzzles that should be tedious and annoying keep throwing some kind of oddball humor to keep me interested. I can't count how often I laughed out loud. Kingdom of Loathing didn't age too well (don't get me wrong, it was awesome when it was new), but West of Loathing was great, and this just refines that formula.So if you're familiar with the Loathing series, and you like their style, this is that but a lot less obtuse. There's no looking up some obscure meat-paste recipe on a wiki; I've found so many secrets just by trying random stuff or thinking about what kind of pun would be funniest, or, you know, solving puzzles that kind of make sense. They're not always easy, but they make sense in the world of Loathing. You get in its headspace after a while. I solved a puzzle yesterday by imagining what would be the stupidest answer. I've completed a *lot* of sidequests and I haven't looked at a guide yet. But the game did make me work for it.My only complaint is I never got an achievement for managing to get that stupid rifle off the wall.Edit: Never mind, I just had to wait for it. Well played.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked WoL, there's plenty to love here, and a few things to yearn for (Where are the spittoons? I am so sad. Spittoon DLC? Name your price, Asymmetric Games!! I can't believe there was just a single one I could admire from afar...)Anyway. I love it! There are definitely a couple of things I'd improve and a couple of things I preferred in West of Loathing, but this has been an absolute joy! And to be clear, I think this also improved on WoL in some ways. It's funny, surprising, challenging (puzzle-wize). I particularly loved the music and the incorporation of my attacks into the music (I played the Jazz....class). Surprises like that really make the game for me. The references to WoL were great too. It was rough doing it without any wiki, which I also enjoyed and recommend. I loved how much of the game seemed just...fun for fun's sake. I never knew if something was important to the plot, or when it was just there to surprise and delight. Or horrify! I also love that the devs mock you a bit when you're making bad decisions but generally don't stop you (Unless it's smoking, apparently?)
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

Worth playing but was a bit disappointed.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: It's good but I'm not sure if it's as good as the first. It beats it in some ways and not in others. I really don't feel like I had a class choice this time? Which could be good or bad once again. I can swap weapons at anytime from guns, to magic, to melee. There seems to be a level cap also and you can't get any stronger past that point. Overall my character is pretty weak even built as far as I could towards ranged damage. The sad part is my pet bacame my strongest trump card. With the mosquito and a fully upgraded attack command he usually clears the field before I have to do anything. He attacks once, then each additional AP I spend he attacks 3 more times. I have 4 or 5 AP.... Plus pets don't seem to have a level cap so you can keep boosting his damage/health further. I wish pets had equipment too? An annoying amount of stat checks for puzzles too, constantly in my inventory trying to get 1 more point of Strength, or 4 more points of Stench armor, etc. Overall still fun though and worth a buy full price IMO.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Highlights - I'm a flavor text junkie and as always, so are Asymmetric's devs. They also put effort into giving you just enough information to focus on the right parts of the mysteries they want you to solve. There is a whole lot of "this will reward you later down the road" experiences within this game, and they often have a few creative approaches to solving the same puzzle. Every time a new section of the map opens up, especially unexpectedly, it leads to a unique, often hilarious, setting.Things to consider: You need to be willing to investigate things a few times, sometimes without being prompted, in order to advance some storylines. In some games it's tedious to keep going back to the same places over and over; but I feel like it's just so rewarding in this game (as in, unlocking additional entire worlds on the map or characters to travel with). They don't tend to handhold with their in-game clues.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: This game came out of nowhere. I was so excited when I saw Asymmetric tweeting about it. _childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: I beat the game not too long ago and I'm already half way through a new save. The comedy of the game is pretty funny, albeit funny due to the large amounts of absurdity and surrealism it uses. The puzzles will range from easy to mind boggling hard, but those are generally for puzzles that are achievement oriented (Trust me you will need a guide for some, if not a majority). The rpg combat is fun if not a bit slow, (which can be remedied by making it faster in the options menu) it changes the enemies up to have you use tactics you may have otherwise not use. For example having enemies that have a cap on their physical damage so you have to use other elemental based damage on them for combat. Being a point and click game as well you have to keep a sharp eye out for anything and everything ontop of weighing all your options before making a decision, as they may tend to be final. It had been frustrating at times missing a key item somewhere you hadn't paying mind to or to miss a key piece of information in a wall of text (the irony isn't list on me). However, for the most part it's a very enjoyable game and I'd say for thr price tag, worth the 20 bucks I paid for it. Overall I'd give it a 8/10, but might put it at a 5 if the humor and puzzles aren't your thing.

_childDocuments_.review: i'm a huge fan of west of loathing and i was super exited when i saw there was going to be another game in the series. i haven't been playing it long but its what you might imagine. its basically west of loathing but during around prohibition times. i love how there is still the same kind humor and the same silly locations to explore. my only complaint this far is how small the map is.

_childDocuments_.review: I have the first game West of Loathing on the Switch and I recommend that game heavily but this one is different. _childDocuments_.review: Rarely am I compelled to write review on Steam, but since this game seems to have dropped without much fanfare, I want to take the opportunity to urge anyone with an interest in CRPG type games to give it a try. Similar to its predecessor West of Loathing, this is a much bigger and more ambitious game. Everything from the writing to the art direction to the music has been given far more attention. For those unfamiliar, the game allows you to build your character and places them in a bizarre world which, while light-hearted, never strays into some of the more "cringey" trappings of some indie games. I can't praise the writing enough for towing the line between ridiculous gags and genuinely telling a story worth seeing through. Charming and compelling from start to finish, and with loads of optional content for completionists. The game feels even more open ended than the last. I'm honestly just very glad these kinds of games are still being released. Might be my GOTY

_childDocuments_.review: I CANNOT recommend this game and West of Loathing enough. They are their own category of games that are filled with everything you could ever want from a game. _childDocuments_.review: I mean...it's more of West of Loathing, one of my surprise favorite games over the last few years. I rarely finish most of the games I own, but I played fully through WoL FOUR TIMES. This is pretty much the same game in a 1920's Prohibition/pseudo-lovecraftian/flapper girl setting.I'm only to Chapter 2 while really taking my time looking for secrets etc, but so far I'd put WoL slightly ahead of Shadows as far as how entertaining it is. This is mostly due to the setting being a little all over the place. With a Western it's easy to make things feel weird and goofy without trying too hard. The 1920's, while a whole other pile of material to work with, just aren't as interesting as a backdrop. The writing still delivers, it just has less to work with. Character creation is a little different, where you play through a prologue before gaining access to a small skill tree of sorts, mostly for stat boosts. A lot of things I've encountered so far have been stat checks, but the numbers have been really low so I'm not sure if I should be specializing or not just yet. Again, only in Chapter 2 at this point so who knows. And this is the kind of game that will randomly unlock mechanics out of nowhere, so maybe there's more to this I just haven't seen yet.In any case, I'd say pick this up no problem if you enjoyed West. If you haven't played it, go do that one first!
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time fan of the Loathing games starting with West (Thanks Mark) and then Kingdom, this game is a true Loathing experience no doubt. With my 30+ hour first play through i'm still wanting to go back in for more, as there is so much to discover and enjoy that one single run will never be enough to find it all. _childDocuments_.review: Okay I've played it all the way through twice at this point, once as a jazz agent and once as a cheese wizard, and I like how some of the storyline actually changes based on what character class you choose. There's also significantly more locations in this game than in West of Loathing, so there's more, objectively, to do. That being said, I think WoL has more interesting side quests in general, and there's more humorous aspects to WoL that SoL doesn't have. There's nothing like the spittoons in this game (the closest we have is fishing, I'd say, and that's not really funny, more just to get the items), and I've yet to find any storylines like the clowns or necromancers or anything along those lines. That's not to say they don't exist, but I personally haven't seen anything like that yet, and I'm 30 hours into playing. I think the puzzles in general are more fun, some of them are really difficult, but even the difficult ones are fun (except mudhenge, that was a pain and I still haven't solved it because I don't have the patience). Overall, I'm very happy with this game but I don't think it'll be replacing WoL as my favorite.

_childDocuments_.review: Review from having completed a first playthrough: I am planning a second and third playthrough to try all the variations, as well as some time getting to 100% completion. So it is good enough to keep going.The strength of the game is in the vignettes. The main story is basically a frame to hang a lot of little stories and location-based events on. It works because the little bits work. If you don't like a little bit, leave that side quest, and there will be a dozen more available. There are some really great moments in the main story, but its greater purpose is to push you to the little stories that abound in the game. (Shout-out to content involving the President. That is great, both in the moments and in the story arc.)The humor is great. It is an Asymmetric game. You see a new one and you buy it, whether or not there is a sale, because they have earned your trust as a development team. If you have enjoyed the somewhat absurdist humor of their previous games, you will also like this one.The combat is not amazing in this one. You can optimize and defeat anything without letting the enemy get an attack in. It is not the most interesting way to fight, but it is the way to win. I will be trying a pacifist run next, which looks more interesting just because I will not be able to brute force my way through.For at least my first class, the classes do not seem that dynamic. My Jazz abilities seemed to amount to adding a sound effect to some abilities. I did not feel that uniqueness that Kingdom of Loathing has in its classes. That may help balance, but it felt like whether you were Muscle, Mysticality, or Moxie-focused just set a key stat for damage and whether your attacks were classified as melee, magic, or ranged. And then you can either break combat or avoid it entirely, so that does not matter much.The graphics are surprisingly good, even if you know from their previous games that the graphics are surprisingly good. You can still be surprised by the better pieces of art.The loading times are amazing. I have so many other games that are poorly optimized trash in terms of using computer resources. Shadows Over Loathing loads quickly and closes more quickly. There is something to be said for stick figure art rather than AAA 3-D rendering that adds little to the game. I have games that freeze for 15 seconds the first time you open inventory as it makes some poorly implemented database query, while Loathing games instantly and deftly handle large inventories of complex and customizable items.I was so happy to see McMillicancuddy's ducks.Some of the puzzles are annoying or opaque. Which those are will probably vary based on what you consider intuitive. Good news! Spoilers exist and you can skip those ones. Some puzzles also have in-game hints that can help you out without explicit spoilers. I do not think you should feel any shame for asking the internet "what am I missing here?" and learning that you needed to go back and talk to a guy two locations over. You effectively set your own level of difficulty. Please do not pay for puzzles and then just look up the answers, because you will be cheating yourself out of fun, but also do not feel the need to pound your head against a wall if something is just not clicking for you.Shadows Over Loathing is fun. I am glad I bought and played it. I am going to play more.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: If you were a fan of West of Loathing then you are going to love Shadows Over Loathing just as much if not more. _childDocuments_.review: Hell yeah, a sequel to one of my favorite games just drops out of nowhere. _childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing, completed the prologue and a handful of side quests. TLDR is that it's West of Loathing, but improved. The art style and dialogue/comedy are the same but in a 1920s Prohibition Era theme. The story follows a Lovecraftian and Eldritch horror theme. Turn based combat makes a return but it tweaked to be smoother. You can't cheese fights anymore with unlimited items, but so far, it feels fair. Classes have been redesigned to offer more freedom. Classes aren't focused on a specific attribute anymore (Muscle, Moxie, and Mysticism), but rather every class is broken down by the special spells and abilities it offers you. If you want to play the Cheese Wizard and beat people helplessly, you can build towards muscle and do that. If you want to be a Jazz Agent with magic, you can do that. If you don't feel like skinning pigs but shoot them instead, you can do that. You aren't trapped into pumping a certain attribute to the max because of your character class. There's also perks now instead of dumping infinite skill points into boosting stats. There are 4 lines of 3 perks each that I call the Muscle line, Moxie line, Mysticism line, and the Environment line. Each line (except for Environment) gives you +1 to that attribute, plus other bonuses like added armor, more XP, increased weapon damage, etc. The Environment line gives you things like your class' version of persuasion, increased loot drop %, etc. There's also a crafting system to make potions and whatnot. Not a lot else to say right now other than "It's basically West of Loathing with Cthulu stuff and mobsters." If you like West of Loathing, you'll like this too.More extensive play time edit: Yup, game is good
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Did you play and like West of Loathing?Then you will love Shadows over Loathing. It has a completely new view on the Loathing universe, and shifted from the Wild West to the roaring 1920s.  The humour is still excellently weird, and fans of strange combat techniques and even stranger character classes (e.g. "Pig Skinner") will find this game suitable to play for hours and hours.And the best for casual gamers like myself: You can adjust the gaming difficulty, and you have to do combat only if you want to. The hilarious humour keeps the same. Even better: If you never played West of Loathing, this is your game, too. You don't need to play WoL before playing SoL, because all the characters and places are brand-new. So give yourself a kick, give Steam the money, and give yourself an excellent game.If you only buy one game a month, or a year, or your whole life - Shadows over loathing would be one of the best choices.Get it. Now !

_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Everything West of Loathing was + more! They really have perfected their style/humor, and the combat is much improved!! Stories are compelling + memorable, and the game's reward system is extremely generous. There is so much attention to detail. My only complaint is that the ending feels a little rushed compared to the rest of the game. _childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed West of Loathing this is an insta-buy. It's WoL, but more. Longer, more content, more branching, etc. I think WoL probably had a greater density of laugh-out-loud moment, but SoL is very funny, a great experience, and doesn't overstay it's welcome at 15 - 20 hours for your first playthrough depending on how obsessive you are with side quests. _childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really good.It is more Loathing, which is always a fun time.I would say that the game is significantly longer than West of Loathing (without DLC) and the puzzle crafting in here is a bit stronger than WoL (which had a tendency to work with moon logic and with giving minimal info) as it does give hints and rough tips on how to do things.I would also say that the difficulty is improved significantly.WoL had the issue of combat essentially ceasing to exist after a certain point, because you wiped every enemy off the map pretty much instantly.now however, the game does a really good job with preventing stat-bloat and is surprisingly balanced.Sure, it isn't darksouls level of difficulty, but almost every fight at the very end, I felt at the least partially as if I "could" die if I messed up... (Where as in WoL was every fight a single button press away from instant destruction)NOTE: This time the game has a difficulty setting, and I was playing on normal. There are two easier difficulties and two harder ones, so... I think there can be a fair challenge here.The music is overall good, however it is a BIT repetetive... as the game consists of multiple "mini maps" that you can walk around in (essentially imagine that the overworld in WoL was squared off in multiple pieces and you can move from farm to farm in said piece, each farm being a mini area) with each "Mini-map" overall having the same music. (With a few exceptions)The story is... well SoL at the least HAS a story, where as WoL didn't really have a story... at all. XDIt isn't fantastic or anything but it does deliver the Loathing comedy quite well. I have however say that the atmosphere of SoL is a bit weaker than WoL...The cowboy theme was stronger, and more consistant... as SoL essentially goes after "Lovecraftian Cosmic horror" and... kinda misses? It isn't as strong is what I am saying. Not bad, not even mediocre or meh, I would say good...but not as strong.Overall, I would 100% recommend Shadows over Loathing It is good stuff, enjoyable and with some really good puzzles that actually did require me to get a pen and paper at times to remember details or write down patterns.
_childDocuments_.name: Shadows Over Loathing

_childDocuments_.review: Been a fan since Kingdom of Loathing and I loved West of Loathing. Shadows Over Loathing has been a blast to play so far, lots of exploration, and on my first playthrough already seeing what I want to explore differently with another build next time.Highly recommend and hoping it comes to Switch in the future as well.

_childDocuments_.review: Shadows Over Loathing is a titanic improvement over West of Loathing in every way imaginable. It features a more robust plot, more distinctive design, more quests that are easier to find (if not necessarily easier to solve), and more to do in general. If you played WoL, then you should play this too - period.Shadows brings a lot to the table, but maybe the most praiseworthy element is the setting. This isn't some generic Lovecraft knockoff with cheesy jokes, nor a simple mystery with ghosts. The world of SoL is surreal in a way that forces the player to keep going, if only to see how far into the dread cosmic it might go.If you've read this, then go play it already. You wouldn't have wasted the time to read this if you weren't interested, and if you're interested, then you're probably going to like it.

name: Nobody Wants to Die
detailed_description: Lose yourself in the world of New York, 2329, where immortality comes at a price that someone has to pay. Following a near-death experience, Detective James Karra takes an off-the-books case from his chief with only the help of a young police liaison, Sara Kai, to assist him. Time reveals all as they risk everything in pursuit of a killer, uncovering the dark secrets of the city's elite. Experience a noir adventure in an alternate future of New York City in 2329; technology has advanced to offer humans eternal life, allowing consciousness to be stored in memory banks or transferred from one body to another. That is, if you can afford the subscription. See through the eyes of Mortality Department Detective James Karra on his hunt for a serial killer who targets the city’s elite citizens. Investigate crime scenes using his time manipulation augmentation and advanced technology to reconstruct events leading up to each murder and uncover clues that lead to the horrifying truth behind the murders. Lose yourself in a dystopian future through this meaningful and original interactive detective story, that explores the dangers of transhumanism and immortality. In a world of eternal life and vanishing morality, you, a hardened detective, must navigate the lines of right and wrong in a society where death is a distant memory. Utilising the power of Unreal Engine 5, Nobody Wants to Die pushes the boundaries of storytelling, combining photorealistic graphics and a distinctly unique narrative experience.

_childDocuments_.review: The only way that I can properly describe Nobody Wants to Die is by calling it a dystopian masterpiece that is heavily influenced by so many gems (Blade Runner, The Fifth Element, Cyberpunk 2077, and L.A. Noire, for example), but manages to tell a unique, compelling story through excellent gameplay, phenomenal voice acting, gorgeous visuals, and interesting characters. From the first few moments, I was hooked, and it only got better with every additional moment. While I've still only scratched the surface, this is already one of the best games I've played this year.So far, the only criticism I have is regarding some light spelling errors in the subtitles and some in-game text. With that being the only fault I can find a few hours in, Nobody Wants to Die isn't far from perfection whatsoever. It's a unique experience that I could not recommend enough and definitely deserves significant praise. I cannot wait to progress further and I will definitely be following this developer closely in the future.

Also aside from the ending which for my taste feels a bit rushed at the end,its a solid 8/10 game and you will likely remember it if you are a fan of stories á la Altered Carbon or Cyperpunk.- Should you buy the game? Probably yes- Is it the best noir detective game i have ever played? no not really- If i could rewind time and forget the game would i buy it again from what i know right now? definitely yes- is it worth the 24$ish (atm) pricetag? absolutely

_childDocuments_.review: There are many reviews out there which sum up this game quite nicely. It’s got a great retro-futuristic atmosphere, probably the best I’ve seen in any piece of media to date, and the voice acting/soundtrack are both phenomenal, with a couple of exceptions. As the kids might say, it is absolutely dripping swag. The performance ranges from smooth as butter to a peak of 25fps, depending on the level, and there’s no way to disable the god-awful upscaling, but you do get somewhat used to it after awhile. As far as gameplay goes, it’s like if you took Cyberpunk’s braindances (Which in my opinion are probably the worst part of the game by a landslide), then made them infinitely better and got rid of pretty much every other facet of gameplay.The game’s heavily scripted, so you can’t really do anything your own way; most of the evidence is only accessible after uncovering other pieces of evidence, and the game will walk you through finding every piece needed in a very linear fashion. You need to find pretty much every piece of evidence in order to close the case, and you’ll come to the same conclusion every time as crucial pieces of evidence can’t be missed. Even if you figure out what transpired ten minutes before reaching the end of the level, you’ll still need to follow the path set out by the devs in order to move on.It says that decisions matter, but as far as I can tell, there’re only one or two options which actually affect the ending. Every other choice you make just unlocks lines of dialogue you’re able to use during specific conversations. Either that or there’s some kind of paragon/renegade system, in which case it’s more determined by getting x amount of points towards whichever ending you want and less about individual actions.On the topic of endings, I didn’t find either of them to be particularly satisfying. In the bad ending, which seems to be the one most people get on their first try, the game pretty much just skips directly to the credits without giving any sort of closure. In the good ending, the explanation you’re given essentially disregards everything you’ve done in the story up until that point. It kinda felt like the writers either didn’t know how to bring everything together in the end or ran out of time/money and had to come up with something on the spot. Either way, it’s like that one photorealistic horse drawing where the final bit is done by a toddler. It’s not the worst ending out there, but it’s far from the ending this game deserved.TL;DR - It’s a linear walking sim with a pretty solid yet somewhat muddled story absolutely drenched head-to-toe in vibes.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing game full of terrific ambiance, themes, and a terrific story that is best experienced twice.Very on the rails and more of a cinematic experience than any real deductive game like Ace Attorney or Layton, but a very enjoyable experience, and I truly hope that we see something of this universe again, it is just dripping with dark charm.

_childDocuments_.review: The game takes you through some genuinely interesting story-building and lore-building, doing detective work on a series of related incidents, while also doing a lot of character development for the protagonists. The game mechanics during the main body of the game are excellent. It then ends abruptly with one of 3 endings, which themselves feel rushed and refuse to elaborate on or conclude the actual case you were working on. The endings focus more on the protagonists than what's really been taking most of your attention for the last 5 hours and are pretty underwhelming. Overall feels almost like the devs ran out of time to finish the story and had to put a final scene together to conclude itThere's just enough info scattered around the story to figure out what was actually happening, but you'll probably get it from a comment somewhere rather than figure it out for yourself, because it's really not well tied together by the game itself or any of the case conclusions you were doing in-gameIt's a unique experience, and I would give it a neutral review if I could
