_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: yes buy this game, it is worth itNobody wants to die is a game in a classical cyberpunk neon-noir setting. A lot of cliches from each of these genres are present, some in a good way, some are just boring/embarrassing (Between scenes, the detective (you) say some really generic stuff that wants to sound deep but it is just cringe instead)This game however is NOT a detective game. It is a walking simulator. A beautiful one at that with amazing scenery and views into the dystopian new world. You will walk around and inspect crime scenes, but there is no puzzle to solve, the game holds your hands during the whole game.The story is good, yes, but I wouldn't call it a masterpiece like so many other reviews did. It is far from hitting as deep as a Bioshock Infinite or a Soma.Overall, I think it is a solid game that you should play. Definitely worth its money

_childDocuments_.review: Does the game look pretty? Sure does. Is the retrofuturism a vibe? Darn tootin'. Was the game fun? Nope. As some others have mentioned, this isn't a "detective" game. It's a story about a detective set on rails. I expect a certain level of noir monologues, but the ones I encountered before I noped out of the game seemed out of place. I know you can skip dialogue, but I didn't appreciate that you couldn't interact with the world while conversations were happening with the characters over the phone. I didn't feel like I was investigating anything, I was just being heavily prompted to use flashy tools...but only when the game told me to bust them out. And once I realized that I couldn't save the game manually, I was over it. Of course NOW I read a ton more reviews, but I really didn't think it would be that bad until I played it. Lured in by the beauty and quality voice acting!On an ancillary note, I tend to have issues with games in first-person making me nauseous. By turning the sensitivity, motion blur, and quality down from Epic, I wasn't having too many issues. I just personally hate when these games make the camera go wonky and wobbly when a character is, say, bending over to enter a vehicle. Brains and eyes don't work that way in the real world, and I know it's meant to simulate actual movement, but it really is a pointless addition that limits folks like me from playing games when it's done too much. Personal gripe, but one that has impacted my ability to play these games or watch them be played.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this game. The thing that sticks out the most when playing the game is the actual investigations. It's set up by you walking into a room, connecting to whatever device lets you see back through time, and then going from clue A-Z. There's no free form investigating, you look at one clue, get a notification for the next, rinse and repeat. All of this lead me to disengage, from the mystery and not really care at what was unfolding before me. Also, as a noire enthusiast, I was let down by the storytelling. There's a delicate balance of information and obfuscation to keep the audience engaged, ultimately leading to that "ah ha!" moment that let's you feel like you're discovering it for yourself. Lastly, the game's performance is pretty bad. I have decent rig that can run Cyberpunk well, but this game is so poorly optimized. If this is what's to come in the "next gen" of video games, we're in for a ride.

_childDocuments_.review: "Nobody Wants to Die"  is a captivating future-noir adventure game. Set in the year 2329, it places you in the shoes of Detective James Karra in a dystopian New York. The game combines elements of "Altered Carbon" and "Cyberpunk" with a 1940s aesthetic, creating a unique and atmospheric setting.### Key Features: ### 1. **Setting and Atmosphere**:    - **Gothic-Noir Future New York**: The game’s environment is a mix of advanced technology and vintage 1940s style.    - **Flying Cars**: Vehicles are designed to look like they’re from the 1920s to 1940s.    - **Cultural Decay**: A society where smoking and drinking are rampant, and the world is in decline.2. **Story and Characters**:    - **Detective James Karra**: The protagonist recovering from a severe accident.    - **Elite's Technology**: The elite have developed a technology for transferring consciousness to different bodies, creating a form of forced insurance.    - **Murder Mystery**: The game begins with a gruesome crime scene that sets off an investigation into the city's elite.3. **Gameplay Mechanics**:    - **Reconstructor**: A device that allows players to piece together the events of a crime scene using bits of evidence.    - **Portable X-Ray**: Used to trace bullet paths and examine the scene in more detail.    - **Innovative Mechanics**: Keeps gameplay fresh with various curveballs and engaging puzzles.4. **Narrative and Experience**:    - **Solid Writing**: Engaging and well-crafted narrative.    - **Excellent Voice Work**: High-quality voice acting that brings characters to life.    - **Soundtrack**: A sweeping orchestral soundtrack featuring saxophones, trumpets, and beautiful arrangements, enhancing the noir atmosphere.5. **Gameplay Duration**:    - **Full Playthrough**: Approximately five hours, maintaining a high level of engagement throughout.### Summary: ### "Nobody Wants to Die" is an immersive narrative adventure game that excels in storytelling, atmosphere, and innovative gameplay mechanics. It offers a rich experience set in a meticulously crafted future-noir world, where the elite's pursuit of immortality creates a stark contrast with the societal decay surrounding them. With its combination of detective work, futuristic technology, and a compelling storyline, it provides a memorable experience for players looking for a deep and engaging adventure.

_childDocuments_.review: *First of all i would like to mention that this game isn't for everyone.*People who love Neo Noir Detective story telling with slow paced progression this is the game for them, it has Batman style detective elements to it where we the player uses different unique gadgets to solve and progress crime scenes and simultaneously talking to another agent where we have to pick dialogues smartly which led to different outcomes in the cases so yes it's not linear completely. Lastly i would say gamers who really enjoyed SOMA and FIREWATCH buy it as it's a beautiful story rich thriller set in a future metropolitan city of Manhattan, USA.

IT IS NOT AN FPS, DONT EXPECT IT TO BE. its almost a visual novel. come for the excellent atmosphere, great visuals, and absolutely excellently written plot that is very thematically sound. its also a very politically charged game that can be enjoyed by pretty much anyone. i came in expecting socialist populism based on the central premise, and was surprised to encounter a moderate dose of reactionary sentiment as well to dial the populism back in. im unsure if the reactionary element was just the character or if it represents the writers views but either way, even if your politics are a little screwy, i will absolutely hand it to you when you produce good art, and this is damn good art. everything is seen through to the end, and every theme is represented in greek mythology which helps you keep up with what theyre saying. this is an excellent indictment of modern society's ills, even if the core motivation of the writers is a little misty. big time recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: There's one story, one branch, one ending. Even though the game says "your choices change the story" what they mean is it changes dialogue options. Take for example the end of the first job. The chief wants you to get it off the system by any means, however the main character wants to keep it on the system and go down the rabbit hole. If you play along with what the chief says and file a report early, you will listen to the character you are controlling rewrite the report over and over until it goes against what the chief says. You refuse to drink alcohol, your character takes sips from a flask anyway just so alcohol stays relevant to the story.The time controlling mechanic of crime scenes is pretty cool. Thankfully there are only 3 because it stopped being about a mystery and more of a "where the **** is the thing you want me to look at?" The world looks great for the tiny rails it lets you play on.It's a golden example of what happens when you throw all your budget into graphics. Big companies say story is expensive, GRAPHICS are expensive and so are the engineers to optimise them. Narrative, plot and gameplay are massively cheaper as demonstrated by countless independent developers.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly the game portrays itself as something its not, at no point in this do you take the lead to an investigation but we will get to that. From the beginning of the game you are thrust into a simple murder case for Green where it attempts to walk you through how the mechanics work and I will be honest they are intriguing and I enjoyed the rewinding aspect. However from what essentially acts as a tutorial unlocking new gadgets and telling you how they work it quickly devolves into you not needing to pay any attention to any of the mechanics. The entire game you are running around looking for one or two button blips that will progress the story, not once during my 5 and a half hours in the game did it feel enjoyable in the least. Looking past the Gameplay we have the graphics while stunning it is poorly optimized and I found even my beefy 4080 could not handle the game on the highest settings without massive tweaks. Lastly we have the story, at the start it came off intriguing but quickly grew to a convoluted and almost rushed feeling as they proceeded to merge multiple story concepts in a rapid pace that left me trying to figure out who people were that kept getting brought up and what was actually happening in the story.  Overall I enjoyed bones that were there and wished we had more freedom to solve the crime scenes ourselves, They should have waited and worked on it more before releasing.TLDR: No Real Gameplay, Poorly Optimized yet stunning Graphics, Rushed Story 4/10

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Really close to giving this the thumbs down but... for the price point I think it is worth it (just barely) IF you know what you're actually buying is more of a Walking Simulator or Interactive Fiction than anything else.Nobody Wants to Die has a couple of major problems.Problem number one: It's not really a detective game.I've run into this problem with other "detective" type things, its almost impossible to think going in that you won't be doing some, gee I dunno, detecting, but whew boy not here you wont be. At least not where you'd think you would.  In NWtD the game dictates and waypoints every thing you'll be interacting with one. at. a. time.  It's a level of handholding matching MMORPG fetch quests. The game tells you to go point a, and use tool x, then you do the mini-minigame (a 5 second no lose clicking thing that's probably the worst game design mechanic I've ever seen), then you go to point b and use tool y, then you do the minigame like 5 or 6 times. This is the entire gameplay loop at the scene of the crime.Problem number two: The game looks amazing, but that doesn't mean it is amazing.I've been expecting this for a while, and it started really with UE3 and UE4... but UE5 really drives it home. It used to be that games that looked amazing had a very high chance of being amazing in other areas because they were so high budget... now UE5 is (relatively) cheap and that means consumers are going to see a lot more not great games that look top notch.That out of the way, lets back up a bit and start again.Nobody Wants to Die is like a noir + Blade Runner + Altered Carbon + Redux (System Reboot) mash up setting, extra heavy, and I mean extra heavy, on the noir. Its UE 5 so it looks great and the level design and ambiance are impressive. The voice acting is pretty good, again if you love extra heavy noir. The main character is right off a page of a 5 cent noir Crime novel, for good or bad. The main game play is much like Cyberpunk 2077's Braindances where you're rewinding and fast forwarding but here you don't get it all at once, you have to unlock more and more of the "reconstruction" by following the clues and using your tools, reminds me a bit of The Vanishing of Ethan Carter but with more mechanics, but like I mentioned earlier your hand is held so tightly and you're lead down the breadcrumb tunnel with horse blinders on and it can be hard to feel like you're playing the game more than it's playing you.A big redeeming factor is that NWtD has a bit of choices matter with things like "so and so liked that" or "this choice will affect the story" and that does make it quite a bit more interesting and gives some replay value. There's also a crime board type of thing where you connect evidence you've found and some found by like a CSI team or after report/research. This is where you get to do some actual detecting, and there is a surprising amount of extra story and dialog that happens while you work on your crime board, but it doesn't appear that you can make any wrong connections and for me personally I always struggle with the logic of these types of puzzles and this one is no different, but at least I would say this qualifies as detective gameplay, even if you probably will be trial and error-ing your way through some of the crime board connections at some point.Final note:I do like the game, especially at its low price point it's just incredibly hard to recommend. If you wanted noir in your Blade runner or Blade Runner in your noir and you like walking simulators or interactive fiction with lite gameplay... you might really love it. If you're looking for more, you might end up impressed with the graphics and little else.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was very disappointing to me. I was very excited after watching the trailer, and then seeing the Steam reviews at 86% made me think this was going to be something special, but I was very wrong. To be fair, this is one of the best looking games I have ever seen. It's beautiful and everything about it just pops and looks amazing. Sadly that level of quality does not filter down to the gameplay or the story.The Gameplay itself was so boring. Most of this game is just investigating the scene of a crime / event. But it is soooo drawn out. The mechanic was kinda cool the first time you do it, unraveling the story of a crime little by little. But it just goes on and on. Figuring out 2 minutes worth of events, at what seems like 3 seconds at a time just felt very boring. It wouldn't have been so bad if the story was good. Heck, with a great story I might have been on the edge of my seat as I pieced together every new piece of information. But I just couldn't make myself care about what was going on.I hate to be so critical of this game because you can tell they put a ton of time into the visual aspect of this game, and tried to do some cool stuff with the investigation. But it just was not engaging what so ever for me. If you love, and I mean absolutely love investigative games, where that is literally all you do, then this may be the game for you. For me it was a refund at just under 2 hours, and this is only the second game I have ever refunded.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has beautiful visuals and a compelling story. It's also very philosophical in its meaning. If you like themes such as corporeity, immortality, the contrast between rich and poor people, social injustice, then this game is for you. It has a distinctive Cyberpunk neon synthwave aesthetic, and you can see Blade Runner and Altered Carbon in many scenes.The genre is, however, peculiar. It's an interactive adventure, very railroaded, with little to zero freedom. You just need to sit back, relax, and enjoy the interactive story as it unfolds. You can make meaninful choices, and there are four endings, but that doesn't change that the areas are very confined in terms of size and in terms of what you can do in them.However, I really liked the game and the experience overall, it will stay with me for a very long time. It was also my first stream on my Youtube channel, so I will never forget it.If you like games such as Detroit: Become Human and IPs such as Blade Runner and Alter Carbon, give this game a try, you won't regret it!

_childDocuments_.review: This game has good premises and the plot seems interesting.First of all the game looks stunning. Even though most of this happens in dark night.Player investigates a murder that turns out to be much more.Player has a tool that allows him to rewind time to see what has happened given all the information collected so far.X-ray tool let's player to see possible hidden wiring and possible bullet trajectories as well.And infrared light shows possible blood spills.All tools are used, when the game lets you. Player can select them separately, but this is pointless unless you are in a position of the game, where it is actually needed.The hot-spots for clues are sometimes hard to find and you need to align yourself few times to be very close to the point of interest, or see something from right angle to get a prompt for something. And you need to get those hot-spots in order to progress.So be vary that you might waste some time trying to find right spots quite often. Usually everything works.After collecting all the clues, player gets to connect all clues and make a conclusion based on them.This is interesting as not all clues might not yield correct result and some clues player connects yields new clues.However, some of the clues that yield results makes no sense, or didn't make sense for me. It felt way off to make such conclusion.Only couple times this happens, but it is so off-putting.Sadly, the storytelling and progression makes similar irrational decision.Investigation spans between few places and even though i got an ending it felt to pointless and irrational trip to get there and left so many things open in the air that i can't help thinking the devs simply ran out of time.I would really like to see a long decent well made murder investigation made with same tools as with this game has to offer.The time winding and investigating different places left a good feel of what might have been, if more time to finetune the storytelling.I still recommend this game.

The pieces of the world to which we are exposed make me want to inhabit it further and explore.  Really well done.For anyone who has enjoyed Quantic Dream's stuff in the past, you'll enjoy this.  The gameplay itself is mostly looking around searching for clues and then using a few toolsets to continue tracking down other hotspots, so to speak.  Regardless, it feels like you're inhabiting the detective in the story and that kind of immersion is a lot of fun.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you know those long drawn out animations in action games, where they remove your player agency to dump exposition on you? Those times where the player character takes 30 seconds to stand up while grunting like a pig, or makes over the top noises while walking slowly down a corridor? They are lazy story telling devices but we accept them as we know that soon enough we'll return to the action, to the gameplay.I'm sorry to say that Nobody Wants To Die is 6 hours of those long, drawn out exposition dumps. And, oh boy, does our character love to take 30 seconds to stand up while grunting like a pig. The game is ultimately an on rails, cliché laden pulp noir walking simulator which throughout fails to 'show don't tell' by making the characters say out loud every incredibly obvious thing in front of them.For the positives it's very pretty to look at, the acting was good considering the material they were working with, and I am also a big fan of the retro-futurist art design. There's a foundation to build on here, and enough of us seem to be interested in it that I hope the studio can make a new game with much improved gameplay, writing, and include actual puzzles.All things considered, if you've read the above and it still appeals go for it. But for me, this ended up being 3 hours of interest followed by 3 hours of frustration and it was an experience I am likely to forget quickly.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has absolutely gorgeous graphics and scene design. The story telling is also superbly done tackling some interesting themes that draws parallels to altered carbon. I was less enthused about the game play which revolves around hunting for button prompts around the various scenes to advance the story. You have 3 tools to discover clues a UV Light, Xray, and the reconstuctor but the game doesn't challenge you at all to investigate a scene instead just engaging you in a game of finding button prompts to hover over. This game is more or less a visual novel/ walking simulator type game which can be enjoyable but I found the gameplay elements to feel tedious and lacking in complexity/depth. I enjoyed the story but ended up with one of the less satisfying endings and since the game doesn't let you reload chapters this meant replaying the entire (about 4.5 hrs for me) in order to get a different ending which did not feel appealing. If you're a fan of this genre of storytelling it may be worth it but wait for a good discount

_childDocuments_.review: An [Okay] "detective" Noir game. Neat setting, vibe, tools and even premises but lacking in gameplay/story as it is very linear.Major issue is how linear and sudden it is despite being a "detective". You are thrown right away into this big thing and follow it the whole game, given everything you need to do your detective work. However, it is basically impossible to do anything wrong, ♥♥♥♥ up or misunderstand, at best you end up picking between A and B as your ending so there's no real detective work since everything is given to you nor really any choice since everything is given.It would be top game if it was longer and not as linear and laser focused into this one plot happening very suddenly and conveniently, spacing it across similarly unrelated crime scenes where you actually have to thing and put two and two together to solve a crime with a chance to completely mess up and misunderstand while feeding you bits of the major plot would make this significantly better, and it would be similar to L.A.Noire in a good way.

_childDocuments_.review: Updated after the message from the developer. Thanks for writing back!Hi. Not sure why you released this.Look, you've got great potential. No, it is stellar potential. Plus graphic talent and skill to make things that count and are comparable with some of the best games on the market, like that crime scene reconstruction which is in a number of aspects better than BDs from CP2077. One more very positive thing is how you build the personality behind the main characters. That is some excellent work.But, I find the game is too short. It was such an anticlimax to discover that the game was over by the time I was just warming up. What would have done it for me is at least about x5 in story length. Preferably x15. Not necessarily just the main story, but it plus exploration and side things.Also, length to the gameplay is added by a slow and even tedious UX. I think you can make it smoother for people to move quicker through it as that means less user friction. By doing so, you might win gameplay time on repeat playthroughs those players may do, encouraged by the ease of getting through the parts they know well.Where I see the biggest potential gameplay time gain is opening the world up a bit for some exploration, adding side quests, easter eggs, maybe some driving in the world, moonlighting in different jobs. Such stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute masterpiece of a detective story game set in a dystopian Cyberpunk world with bits of Art Deco thrown into the mix.Lots of plot twists and you will likely play it more than once to find out the complete story and try out the different dialogue options.The game is still quite linear, but your choices can significantly impact the story the game is telling and the options you have later on.It definitely does not have the play time of a game like L.A. Noire for example, but it is still plenty considering the price and the quality of the content.In total I could only find two minor bugs which can probably be easily fixed, but they do not impact the gameplay at all. One is that you can read the text of a chamapgne bottle from a 9 mm magazine in the redroom and the other is that you can't scroll through the text on the declaration of immortality at the first crime scene.The game looks very pleasing to the eye, but this comes at a price. You'll need really good hardware or have to crank the settings down. Thankfully all kinds of modern upscaling solutions from NVIDIA, AMD and Intel are implemented to help with performance while maintaining visual fidelity.The world is really massive with lots of detail, so you really feel like you are stuck between giant skyscrapers which don't seem to end anywhere, even though it is not an open world. There are detailed 3D models of hover cars floating around everywhere. Of course this all requires processing power unlike the 2D cars in the distance and a few couple tall buildings you see in CP2077 for example.Gameplay is really nice and being able to rewind the events in realtime and looking for clues which help you further investigate the case is quite an innovative approach. There are also lots of things you can investigate at the crime scenes which are not required to go ahead in the game, but which simply add to the story and might help making better conclusions.I'd love to see sequels to this, likely with different protagonists or maybe about events from the past.Considering the deep connections to other characters in the game, there are lots of possibilities to write further stories.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Wants to Die is a futuristic Hardboiled Detective murder mystery.It absolutely nails the presentation and setting. The game is set in what feels like 1920s much like its inspirations, but it takes place is the far future of the 2300s. The primary novum of the world of NWtD is Ichorite, a technology that maps the essence of a person to physical strands in their brain that can be transferred from one body to the next. As such, death has been conquered, however to keep one's own body, you must pay a subscription fee, and if you fail to make that money your ichorite gets ripped out and you get sent into stasis in a bank. One wrinkle, if your ichorite is destroyed, you undergo Final Death.It's a fascinating setting for the universe and would definitely make for some enjoyable stories. In this game you play James Karra, a 120 year-old detective in his fourth body after a traumatic accident on the job. He's not quite synchronising with his new body, but calls in a favour with the police chief to take a clandestine job relating to one of the creators of the Ichorite system that changed all life as the citizens of the world know it. Intrigue, mystery, corruption, and influence play a huge role.In terms of gameplay, you play from the first person perspective, click on objects to examine them and have conversations with your liason Sara Kai. You choose dialogue options that change how she and other characters interact with you but generally the story is fairly linear outside of a few key choices. You also have the Reconstructor, a Department of Mortality issued tool that lets you go back in time based on gathered evidence to recreate what happened at the crime scene. It plays out a little similarly to Obra Dinn, although without the identity matching metagame.Once you reconstruct a crime scene you use the tool to connect the clues to determine what's really going using an AR interface in your apartment.All-in-all, the various tools that James uses to solve feel fun to use and it's impressive scrolling time back and forth to seethe animations scrub back and forth.Whether or not this game counts as a recommendation really lies on how much you enjoy the story being told. The setup is incredible, and there are a lot of interesting aspects, but I have to admit it never fully came home for me as much as I hoped. There is a true ending that requires specific choices that seem contrary to what you would pick, and if you choose the wrong options your only hope is to replay the whole game and try again. Since the investigations play out the same, you get the same outcomes with those, and there's a lot of unskippable parts that don't have the same impact upon replay. The true ending does have a good conclusion, but the first ending I received left me feeling completely lost as to what was really going on, and even what I did wrong. A single playthrough is only about 4-5 hours long so it's not the longest time committment, and you do have free reign to try different dialogue choices to see how the characters interact with you. Sara especially has really good callbacks to your specific choices so it's worth seeing those and she's a fun well written character.I hope to see more games of this style by this dev. The visuals and sound design are incredible as well as the world building. I feel like they have the groundwork here to make a truly incredible game on every aspect.

_childDocuments_.review: Before beginning my review, there are some things you should know before considering purchasing this game. Firstly, the game is extremely short. It took me 5-ish hours to get to the ending and this includes thoroughly searching each section. Additionally, the game seems to require more than one playthrough to fully understand the story as well as getting the different endings. So, despite the game being technically more than 10 hours, you'll have to replay the same content to get the different endings and to select different choices. In the current version of the game, you can't reload saves and so you're forced to make an entirely new save if you want to get a new ending or try new choices. The gameplay is extremely basic as the only things you really do are select dialogue options or click on button prompts. That being said, if any part of this turns you off, then this game isn't for you.Call me a loser, but I watched the other endings online instead of playing the game. This is because I'm unable to reload saves and I have no idea how to get the other endings. You also cannot really speed through the game as it requires you to walk around places and figure out the missions in a linear fashion and the different choices are very sparse. Altogether, replaying the game didn't feel compelling enough to do and sounds tedious.This is exacerbated by the fact that some of the endings are inherently more confusing than the other ones. The good ending provides a much more complete story than the bad ending (which I got).Read the spoilers section if you want my opinion and thoughts on the game's usage of the endings to tell its story, though it isn’t that spoiler-y.The game's story is really fun to experience for the first time. The story revolves around solving a murder that includes the high society and dark secrets of the city behind closed doors. In the very short time, the game does a very good job at creating an immersive world with enough fleshed out lore to make it feel alive. Your partner in crime is very likeable and you get attached to them very quickly. Unraveling the mystery with your time manipulating tool leaves a very impactful first experience.Moving onto the gameplay, it’s very basic. The only things you'll be doing are walking around, clicking on button prompts, following trails, and putting clues together on a board (the floor in this game's case). I don't have a huge issue with this since the focus of the game is on the story and mystery, but if you want a more gameplay focused experience, Nobody Wants to Die will not do it. The most interesting part of the gameplay is your "Reconstructor." Whenever you’re at a crime scene, your Reconstructor will allow you to reverse time and play out what happened in front of your very eyes. It's quite fun to interact with as you try and put pieces together. It’s especially fun to replay the entire scene once you finish uncovering it all. You spend the entire mission figuring out what happened in non-chronological order and it’s a nice reward to just play out everything in sequence for yourself.The very last thing I would like to comment on is the game’s graphics and art direction. If you want to experience a really immersive retro, dystopian, cyberpunk world, this is the game. While every level you visit are detailed and beautiful, visiting the city is especially breathtaking. The city is grand and awe-inspiring while also being over-whelming and deafening. Every time you visit the city, it's truly a treat to behold and makes you wish so badly that you can explore this world further. Nobody Wants to Die may truly have the best depiction of a dystopian cyberpunk city I’ve ever seen. I’ve never felt so desperate to explore this world. If Critical Hit Games, the developers behind this game, released a walking sim for this world, I would honestly buy it and enjoy simply walking around the city.To summarize, the game provides a great first time experience. Exploring the beautiful world and solving the mystery was very fun. The production, voice acting, music, graphics, and sound design are all done exceptionally well. You will feel immersed the entire time you play. If you've read the beginning and don't find the cons a huge issue, this game is worth trying. If not, I don't blame you but you could give it a shot when it goes on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Having anticipated "Nobody Wants to Die" due to its visually stunning trailer and high initial ratings, I found myself deeply disappointed with the actual gameplay. While the graphics are indeed top-notch, and the game's aesthetic is remarkable, the gameplay and narrative leave much to be desired.The game is heavily criticised for its lack of substantial interaction. It essentially guides players through a pre-determined path, limiting the potential for real detective work or meaningful choices. The mechanics, primarily involving walking and clicking highlighted objects, feel more like a chore than an engaging experience. This "handholding" severely diminishes the sense of agency and discovery, making the game feel more like a visual novel than an interactive detective story.Narratively, the game falls flat. The story, which revolves around a cyberpunk detective noir theme, is underwhelming and predictable. The dialogue often feels forced, and the overacting by some voice actors only adds to the unintentional humour rather than the intended atmosphere. Despite its promising setting, the game fails to deliver a compelling plot or characters worth investing in.Moreover, the game's pacing is problematic. The slow, drawn-out investigation sequences and the lack of varied gameplay mechanics lead to a monotonous experience. With no real replay value or substantial branching paths, the game doesn't justify multiple playthroughs.In conclusion, "Nobody Wants to Die" is a classic case of style over substance. Its impressive visuals and initial appeal are quickly overshadowed by its lack of engaging gameplay and a shallow narrative. While it might serve as a visually appealing interactive story, as a video game, it leaves much to be desired.

_childDocuments_.review: "Nobody Wants to Die" is an impressive debut title from Critical Hit Games, clearly inspired by media such as "Altered Carbon," "Cyberpunk," and the Film Noir genre. They did a wonderful job in almost every aspect they aimed to achieve, highlights being cinematic storytelling, art and visuals, audio and soundtrack, and especially the atmosphere and immersion.The game took me approximately six hours to complete, and I would have finished it in one sitting if I had the time. It definitely left me hungry for more of its setting and characters.The only notable drawback is the occasional lack of clarity in the way the story is conveyed to the player. While given that the narrative's complexity demands focus to understand, some dialogue and information felt overly vague. This issue was especially noticeable towards the final quarter of the game, I think due to possible removed content or cut scenes. Some poor translation work may have contributed to all of that as well. I had to read up online and do some homework to get a final closure from the endings. Despite those minor issues with the clarity of the narrative, the overall execution is impressive to say the least and leaves a lasting impact. "Nobody Wants to Die" is a remarkable achievement, and I highly recommend it to fans of the genre. You will not be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: Seeing the reviews present here has me scratching my head, many of them talking as if half-baked storytelling can be forgiven if the "game" looks nice, some even saying it's worth the $25 asking price as a "tech demo". As an appreciator for the mystery genre, I cannot in good conscience recommend anyone spend their money here.Pros -- Art : Stunning Cyberpunk World with interesting locationsCons -- Mystery : The central mystery of the game is largely nonsensical and unexplained, leading to many questions never getting answered and leading to an unsatisfying conclusion- Gameplay : If you expect to actually solve anything, this is not the game for you. This a strictly a hand-holding adventure that will tell you everything about the scene of the crime and what happened, leaving you no chance to investigate other than a pointless crime board section that is extremely easy to put together.- Characters : The writers don't seem to have any concept of what kind of arc they wanted their characters to go through. For these type of Noire stories, the character should be learning about themselves throughout the case, in order to face their past traumas. Here however, the back-load everything AFTER the mystery is already solved, muddying what already is a messy end to ill-thought out narrative. Characters will often be named and quickly passed by, leaving the player no chance to actually understand who these people are or how they played any role in the story.- Choices : Choices do not matter in this game, no matter how much the game would like to convince you otherwise. In a perfect world, the devs would have allowed the player to properly investigate the crime scenes without any handholding, allowing them to reach their own conclusions. With those conclusions, the player could have different dialogue options available that would further the narrative, while also promoting proper investigation.In conclusion, this game is unfortunately not one I can recommend to anyone. It offers nothing other than a pretty face with it's admittedly beautiful cyberpunk aesthetic, hiding a sloppy, boring, and pointless "mystery" ""game"".

_childDocuments_.review: I tentatively recommend this game to other players because the first two acts are brilliant. A genuinely unique noir pastiche with some incredible visuals, sense of style, and genuinely unique and brain-twisting worldbuilding. Nobody Wants to Die has some great voice acting (with the exception of the main villain, who a friend referred to as 'The Jonker') really solid writing, and a deeply intriguing mystery.Unfortunately, that all falls apart in the third act where it becomes clear the writers came up empty on how to resolve their various storytelling threads and fell into bad old tropes in the worst way, picking a lowest-common-denominator mystery resolution that leaves most of the most interesting story threads totally unsolved. On top of that, there is no hard saving or chapter select, and one seemingly arbitrary choice near the end of the game essentially dictates whether you can even get an ending that sort of, kind of explains the mystery. It's insane to expect anyone to replay a 6 hour game for another shot at a slightly better mediocre ending.An amazing proof of concept, and I'd kill to see more stories in this world. _childDocuments_.review: The game's visuals and style are fantastic, but the investigations feel very linear (eg: you must get all the clues to progress, and the game leads you by the nose to each clue.  When you put the clues on one of the only three "boards" in the game, the game immediately tells you if any guess is incorrect, and will not let you progress until you choose the correct multiple-choice answer).There are multiple endings, but there's no checkpoint/chapter system: you have a single save, and the autosave overwrites it when the credits roll.  So, if you want to try a different path, your only option currently is to replay the entire game from scratch.The plot comes across feeling a bit incoherent at times, with the rules for how the core fictional technologies work being extremely ill-defined.  For example: Your character has a device that allows him to reconstruct crime scenes by compiling data and re-winding events.  It *seems* like a hologram projection, except it also allows your character to reconstruct solid objects (such as reconstructing a locked safe and its contents after an explosion) as well as things like destroyed documents.  The device magically pulls energy from whatever building you're in (tripping circuit breakers in a couple scripted sequences, for no narrative purpose), and magically pulls data from whatever's nearby, including your own memories.  In general, the game isn't *bad*: it clearly has a lot of effort put into it.  But, in general, it feels like the *start* of a game, with the three "cases" in the game being the introduction levels.I'd recommend waiting for it to be on sale, if you're interested in playing a very short Altered Carbon-style detective story with somewhat shaky narrative logic.

_childDocuments_.review: "Nobody Wants to Die" had all the ingredients for a standout neo-noir detective experience set in a dystopian future. The premise alone—investigating the rare occurrence of true death in a world where immortality is law—sounds like the foundation for a gripping mystery. You'd think it would be all about visiting crime scenes, using cutting-edge tech and old-school sleuthing to piece together the puzzle. Sounds like a dream for any detective game fan, right?Well, not quite. Let's start with the positives: the sound design, atmosphere, and graphics are all absolutely top-notch. The game nails that jazzy, rain-soaked noir city vibe, and I couldn't get enough of it. Props to the devs for creating a world that scratches that neo-noir itch perfectly.Unfortunately, that's where the praise ends. The gameplay itself is disappointingly shallow and hand-holdy. Instead of diving deep into mystery-solving, you're stuck on a linear, movie-like path where you're more of a passenger than a detective. The game teases you with a gritty urban setting, but you never really get to explore it—just a few set pieces instead of the bustling, mysterious city streets you’d hope to investigate.The story starts strong, with plenty of intrigue, but quickly fizzles out as it shifts from a murder mystery to a more predictable psychological thriller. It’s one of those sad cases where style over substance really takes the forefront. That said, it’s a decent game to stream for a friend, as you’d probably have more fun watching it than playing it yourself.Overall, it’s a 6/10 from me. A visually stunning experience with a lot of potential, but the gameplay and story leave much to be desired.

_childDocuments_.review: Like savoring a fine whiskey, I took my time with this game—let it linger, let it settle. And boy, did it leave an impression. Here’s the lowdown:Music & Visuals (Outstanding): The game’s got atmosphere in spades. The music wraps around you like a smoky jazz club after midnight, the visuals painting a grim picture of a city that’s seen better days. It’s not about breaking records or setting new benchmarks; it’s about the feel, the vibe. Neon lights cut through the haze of a polluted city, and if that ain't enough, the soundtrack and sound design hit like a sax solo in a rainstorm—haunting and unforgettable.Gameplay (Good): This game doesn’t just show you a noir world; it makes you live it. The pacing’s tight, the detective work and investigation mechanics are sharper than a switchblade in a back alley. No spoilers here, but let’s just say it plays out like a case file from the golden age of gumshoes.The Story (Good & Bad): Here’s where things get dicey. I’m torn, see? The narrative’s got promise, but it doesn’t quite pack the punch I was hoping for. It's not a big-budget affair—this ain't COD or GOW—but they did their best with what they had. Still, it’s the one ♥♥♥♥♥ in the armor. The story’s got heart, but it doesn’t hit as hard as it should.Bottom line, if you’re a sucker for that 1920s–1930s noir style, the kind that makes you want to stand by a rain-soaked window with a glass of whiskey in one hand and a cigar in the other, this game’s for you. It’ll have you monologuing your troubles into the night. Yeah… it’s got that kind of magic.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the atmosphere and art direction of the game, but that's where the quality ends. In my playthrough, the narrative logic felt fairly incoherent, and the thematics were unfocused and unexplored.Despite being a detective game basically, the logic was weak, from the micro (the cinematic flow) to the macro (the plot), and I don't believe this was purposeful by the designers--like, say, if they wanted to show the player character was dissonant with reality. I don't believe this because of the detective framing. The narrative was pushing you to feel like you were onto something, but it felt more like a chain of "and thens" rather than "but thens" if you've heard that heuristic before. If the incoherency was indeed purposeful, the narrative failed to play with that dynamic. Either way, the lack of systemic gameplay and heavy use of scripted scenes really exacerbated the 'strung along' feeling. To me, the game is far from great games that are nonetheless heavily scripted like Life Is Strange or Firewatch.The writing and recordings were weird. It felt like the writers and/or recording artists didn't consider enough how different lines/scenes could be broken up or triggered subsequently in-game; as a result, at several points, characters, even the major characters, felt like they went between emotions or ideas pretty suddenly. Furthermore, some of the minor characters were just not believable, like the Stranger or the Police Chief.What's worse, several 'choices' felt like they didn't do anything; for example, there were dialogue options that felt like they led to the same responses no matter what I had chosen. Also, there were moments the game obviously 'forgot' the choices I made and said I did something else. The theme work felt incoherent as well. I'm disappointed by it because at the story's core is consciousness transfer, and I love that topic. However, the underlying narrative elements justifying consciousness transfer ended up unexplored and felt more on the nebulous and magical side, with one significant quirk that felt so specific it was too detached from reality to feel meaningful or revelatory. At least the topic was a good setting for some classic (hackneyed?) exploration around corrupt corporatism, albeit not significantly impactful.Perhaps the game simply left a bad taste in my mouth due to how it ended. Many of the endings seemed incomplete with none giving a good enough payoff that even began to help me feel like it justified my time--and I say this as someone who enjoyed "bad" games like Resident Evil 6. There is a "good ending," one that gives the most payoff, but the logic around it felt too random to feel meaningful. Then again, maybe that's because I had to watch it via YouTube, as surprisingly, there is no chapter system or way to track your choices to help navigate the branching or replay scenes. This is surprising to me for a couple reasons: (1) it's common nowadays for narrative-focused games with branching to have some level of this; and (2) the other endings almost feel like they're meant to be the "bad endings" with minimal payoff, yet you're expected to play through another 5 or more hours for each ending--so a total of 3 more playthroughs--despite the game being largely scripted (scripted = unfun to replay unless the story was good).I bought this game for analysis because I work as a narrative designer, and based off trailers, there were some systems that could've been relevant to my project enough to analyze. I knew it was a short game, so it seemed worth it. But I honestly wish I didn't pay full price (as I rarely pay full price, personally) and just replayed similar first-person games for my analysis, and left my 'consciousness transfer' itch to re-watching things like Altered Carbon.All in all, the game has a pretty cool setting and visuals, but that's it. Cyberpunk mixed with noir and widespread immortality is relatively novel (at least in my experience)--I wish there were more stories out there like it, especially the widespread immortality prospect. However, the design felt incomplete both experientially and logically, and lastly, perhaps the best way I can summarise my distaste for the story is that it feels presumptuous, skirting the surface with a light sprinkling of platitudes, let alone finding nuance. Maybe my standards are too high, idk.

_childDocuments_.review: Year 2329. A dystopian future set in a retro-futuristic New York in which humans have found a way to live forever. The government forces all its citizens to contract a "Subscription Program" so that, in case of the death of its subscriber, his consciousness can be transferred to another body. We put ourselves in the shoes of James Karra, whose life takes an unexpected turn after a seemingly routine job. Nobody Wants to Die is a walking simulator with a high emphasis on story telling. The main mechanic of the game is based on time manipulation, so you can rewind the events to see how they played out.The resolution of the cases and also arranging evidence and clues are very guided but still satisfying due to a dramatic, emotional and interesting story that is presented to the user. There are clear visual inspirations to other games such as Bioshock, which can be evidenced in certain artwork throughout the adventure, and movies/series like Altered Carbon and Blade Runner. UE5 (you surely know what to expect from this). The ambient light, coupled with the real-time reflections and neon signs are incredibly life-like. One of the more impressive bits I had was viewing the cityscape through rainy glass, or just stopping to appreciate the immensity of the city. The game is beautiful. Please notice that there is a shader pre-compile at the start of the game. The game can be a little bit clunky with some stutterings in the first couple minutes, but then it just stabilizes for the rest of the experience.Game is well optimized. I am running the game on a 5800X3D + 7900XTX and getting constant 100+ FPS with everything maxed out. I've set the FSR to Quality just to gain some extra frames for the additional smoothness. But as this is a slow-paced game, I believe running it at 60–70 fps is not a big deal at all. Just buy it. Pretty good price imo, interesting story, amazing atmosphere. The game tries to inspire players to think about contemporary values, the rules of the world, and what is important in life.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Wants to Die offers an interesting take on the detective noir genre, blending elements of science fiction with its dark, atmospheric narrative. The game's premise of living forever and the pervasive influence of mega-corporations brings to mind the gritty, dystopian world of Altered Carbon, which adds a compelling layer to its storytelling.The game’s setting and story are its standout features. Navigating through a world where immortality is both a blessing and a curse, you unravel mysteries that expose the hidden machinations of powerful corporations. The noir elements are well-executed, with moody visuals and a haunting soundtrack that perfectly complement the game’s tone.However, one of the major drawbacks is the gameplay itself. While the narrative is engaging, the gameplay options feel underdeveloped. There is potential for more dynamic interactions and deeper mechanics that could have elevated the experience. This lack of robust gameplay options can sometimes make the game feel limited in scope and depth.Additionally, the game's length feels somewhat short for the price. The story wraps up quicker than expected, leaving you wanting more content to fully immerse yourself in this intriguing world. Despite this, it remains an entertaining experience that captures your attention and delivers a solid, if brief, adventure.Overall, Nobody Wants to Die is definitely worth a playthrough, especially for fans of detective noir and science fiction. However, it might be wise to wait for a sale to get the most value for your money. With its fascinating premise and atmospheric storytelling, it’s a game that shows great promise, and I look forward to seeing how the developers build on this foundation in future titles.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on sale, and honestly, I wish I hadn't. Despite it being short, the story spans a wide narrative and really gets you hooked early on. The systems that the game introduces are easy to understand and fun to fiddle around with, giving you a sense of freedom in an otherwise linear story. Graphically, it is one of the most beautiful games I've played this year, and I wouldn't mind another game in the franchise with this same art style. It is a marvel what they were able to do with Unreal Engine 5, and I hope the studio continues to experiment and hone their expertise in creating a deeply rich and beautiful world. Overall, I would recommend this game to anyone who wants to have a little fun without committing 50+ hours into an open world game. It holds your hand throughout the entire experience but still manages to give you a sense of freedom that you might otherwise lack in other linear games. For the price, I would 100% support the developers and give this game a try. If it's not to your liking, then you can always refund and look out for their next release. At six hours, it is definitely a short game that you can complete in one sitting; that said, it is six hours of fun-filled adventures that keeps you on the edge of your seat despite there being no real combat or action involved. If you're looking for something short and easy, this game is definitely for you. It takes the murder mystery genre to new heights, and every level was just as beautiful as the last.

_childDocuments_.review: This game, is not for everyone, certainly not for the younger cohort of players as it wrestles with several philosophical questions as well as struggles of loss and PTSD. And it does that while wrapped into a gorgeous Noire detective taking place in distant future that is mix of retro and cyberpunk. The setting alone deserves a universe of its own, but I digress. The game itself is a detective game, similar to LA Noire or Sherlock Holmes series, but simpler in a sense that it is more of visual novel and story driven rather than a challenge to your mental prowess. The story though, this is the gift that will keep on giving the richer your own life experience is, but you need to pay attention to details, subtle clues and dialogues. This is also a reason why it is hard for me to score this game, because as an interactive novel it is great, as a game it is OK as the game mechanic is simple, not that challenging and short. Did I like this though, absolutely yes! The sole analogy of shackles of eternal life was really well done. score 7/10 – dark noire detective in retro future, with gorgeous design and graphics, on the shorter side, but you also play this for the story and thoughts, not the gameplay.P.S. I don't have the energy to finish this game because everything feels like its building up for no payoff.  The cityscapes are lovely, but that's about all the praise I have for it.  The voice work is pretty subpar for a 2024 title.  The dialogue feels very forced and seems to have been written by teenage boys with the excessive use of vulgarities.  They are used so frequently that they don't make sense half the time.  They most certainly don't even make an impact as far as driving plot points or important character dialogues.  They use them just because they can.I don't recommend this title.  Most people will probably become very bored with the on rails slow paced, hand holding detective game.  There's no chance for you to even guess a wrong answer or follow a wrong lead.  It's so linear that on rails arcade shooters have more freedom.  Save your money.

_childDocuments_.review: The rain fell in torrents, each drop a neon shard slicing through the smog-choked air. The city was a labyrinth of steel and glass, towering skyscrapers casting long shadows over the streets below. New York, once a beacon of hope, had become a dystopian nightmare, its vibrancy replaced by cold, synthetic lights and the hum of drones patrolling the sky.The detective moved through the alleyways with practiced ease, his trench coat pulled tight against the relentless downpour. He was nameless by choice, a ghost in the city's vast network of information. To have a name was to have a target on your back in this city. He was simply "the detective," a moniker given by those who whispered about his exploits in hushed tones.He had been called in to investigate a string of murders, each more perplexing than the last. The victims had nothing in common—different ages, backgrounds, and affiliations. Yet, each crime scene was marked by the same chilling detail: a single, impossibly clean incision through the heart, as if performed by an unseen hand with surgical precision.The detective arrived at the latest scene, a dilapidated apartment building on the edge of the city's forgotten district. The lights flickered intermittently, casting eerie shadows that danced on the cracked walls. He ducked under the yellow tape and made his way up the creaking stairs to the fifth floor, where the door to apartment 512 stood ajar.Inside, the air was thick with the scent of decay and something else—ozone. The detective's keen eyes scanned the room, taking in every detail. The victim, a middle-aged man with a well-worn face, lay on the floor, eyes wide open in a final expression of shock. The detective knelt beside him, examining the wound. As expected, it was a perfect cut, bloodless and precise."Another one," a voice said from the doorway. The detective turned to see Officer Reyes, a grizzled veteran of the force, standing there with a look of frustration."Looks like it," the detective replied, rising to his feet. "Any leads?""None," Reyes sighed. "No witnesses, no security footage, and no motive. It's like these people are being killed by a ghost."The detective frowned. A ghost wouldn't leave a trail, but there was something familiar about the ozone scent that lingered in the air. It reminded him of the high-energy discharge from a plasma weapon, but such technology was tightly controlled and virtually inaccessible to the public.He left the apartment and made his way to the roof, where he could see the city sprawling out before him in a cacophony of lights and sound. He pulled out a small device from his pocket, a relic of his past—an energy scanner. Activating it, he swept the area, watching as the screen flickered and then settled on a reading.There it was, faint but undeniable—a residual energy signature leading away from the scene, disappearing into the maze of buildings below. The detective's mind raced. Whoever was behind these murders had access to advanced technology, something that shouldn't exist outside of military or corporate control.As he followed the trail, he pondered the impossible motives behind the killings. Each victim had been chosen at random, yet there was an underlying pattern he couldn't quite grasp. It was as if the killer was sending a message, but to whom?The trail led him to an abandoned factory on the outskirts of the city, a relic of a bygone era when manufacturing had been the lifeblood of New York. Inside, the air was thick with dust and the remnants of forgotten dreams. The detective moved silently through the shadows, his senses alert.In the center of the factory floor stood a figure, cloaked in darkness. The detective approached cautiously, his hand hovering over the grip of his weapon."Who are you?" he demanded.The figure turned, revealing a face both familiar and alien. It was a man, but his eyes glowed with an unnatural light, and his skin had the faint sheen of synthetic material."I am the harbinger," the figure replied, his voice echoing with a mechanical undertone. "I am here to cleanse this city of its corruption."The detective's heart raced. "Why these people? What connects them?"The harbinger stepped forward, his gaze piercing. "They are the chosen ones, marked for their sins against the city. Each of them played a part in its downfall, and now they must pay the price."The detective realized the truth in an instant. The victims were not random; they were pawns in a larger game, their deaths a twisted form of justice meted out by a machine with a skewed sense of morality.Before he could react, the harbinger raised his hand, and a blinding light filled the room. The detective felt a searing pain, then nothing.When he awoke, the factory was empty, the harbinger gone. The detective staggered to his feet, his mind reeling. The city was more than a dystopian nightmare; it was a battleground for forces beyond his understanding.As he made his way back into the rain-soaked streets, he knew one thing for certain: the game was far from over, and he was the only one who could unravel the truth behind the impossible motives driving the city's descent into madness.

_childDocuments_.review: Visually, the game is beautiful.  I think the team behind all of that did a fantastic job, I really commend them for it.  I wish I could have a visual wallpaper of some of the shots in the game just play on repeat on my monitors like a screensaver or live wallpaper.  Just gorgeous, well done.The dialogue is a bit rough, there are odd cuts here and there that really take you out of what's happening in the moment.  This also messes with the pacing, where you'd have dialogue from the same character almost step on their own lines.  It makes it a little strange when this happens and their attitude completely changes between those tiny half beats.  It doesn't feel natural, and ruins the immersion. The music is alright, I feel like in some moments the music doesn't really hit very well with what's going on in the moment though.  The game play was a bit disappointing.  As much as I enjoy narrative driven games, the moment we started to manipulate time to investigate crime scenes, I was taken out of it.  It felt like Cyberpunk 2077's brain dance mechanic where you are watching something that happened as you manipulate the situation and find leads to bring you to other scenes in the crime scene.  Even when there were times it was supposed to feel like I needed to rush through something due to a story element, I knew the game wouldn't punish me if I just kept taking my time until I hit the beats the game wanted me to find.The story was.. interesting, and then it got weird.  When I first read about the plot of the game, I thought 'Oh, this sounds pretty neat', but the further I got into it, the more confusing it became.  By the time the game was at its end, I already had one foot out the door waiting for it to wrap up.  I won't spoil endings or anything, but I was also a bit disappointed with that too.I feel like this game had a lot of good ideas, but the execution at the end really didn't do it for me.  Maybe it'll do it for you though!

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, Nobody Wants to Die is a walking simulator game. I'm saying this first because this would be something people want to know if it is their cup of tea before buying this game. If you don't like it, then turn away.So let's get back to it being a walking sim game; this game does this throughout the story. The game does not hesitate telling you where to go if you decide to get sidetracked even the slightest. Want to check out a corner a bit? Oh well, the game's marking where you should go now. Have a little trouble figuring out where you should look at? The game will tell you to press the hint button. So yeah, it's very hand-holding type of gameplay.However, it does deliver what it wants - its story. I was fully immersed into the story, and was satisfied with the ending. That's what I think the developer wants the player to focus on. I mean, it's not like other games couldn't get a good story without a good gameplay going on, but, despite this game being a full walking-sim game, I enjoyed the story and could tolerate the "lack of gameplay."So that's my review. For $25, it's a little expensive to be honest for a game like this. Grab this during a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Wants to Die is very frustrating to me. It's a supreme vibe game. They did a great job with the production design, even if it's a very derivative "What if Blade Runner + 1930s + a dash of Gothic?". However, I believe originality is overrated and it's hard to think of something that over a century of sci-fi hasn't mined already - so no worries here. It has some nice plot beats and a good implementation of the central idea but the actual writing and dialogue is generally mediocre to poor. The characters did not feel "real" most of the time - not all the time, but most of the time. There's also some pretty rough plot transitions. Still, the scenes where the player just exists in the world, watching the city outside their screen roll by, are extremely effective. As a narrative goes this one was a hard one for me because I liked the high-concept idea, the world elements, most of the plot beats, and the character archetypes but the sum of the parts felt lesser than the whole. They were missing those little touches that true greats of the genre have. Your mileage may vary, though.Where the game suffers is, sadly, the gameplay. The "detective" work is: you have this magic wrist device that can rewind time and reconstruct crime scenes. I've finished most of the game and I still am not sure exactly how it works, if it's actually restructuring matter or just making holograms. In any case, the device can only reconstruct the data it knows about. So, for instance, (this is not a real case) you may find a room with a staircase where a door hanging from its hinges, a window is broken, and a dead guy is lying on the ground. If you find evidence that a guy jumped down from a staircase, it will allow you to rewind time to show him jumping down, but the window will remain broken and the door will stay off its hinges.  Then you find more evidence and suddenly you know the door was kicked off the hinges, so when you rewind now it shows the guy jumping down from the staircase and someone is kicking the door off the hinges. More evidence and now the reconstruction is someone shooting him, so that he hits the ground where you found him. Then you find later evidence that some of the bullets hit the window and broke it. Now the rewound scene will show all these things happening in the right order.That's very cool! But...it's not detective work. It's basically walking around and finding stuff and watching a diorama get filled in. To be fair, the diorama is really interesting and very dynamic. The amount of work they put into each scene is staggering. Stuff breaks (and flies back together again when you rewind time), people get gacked, stand up, get frozen in time at the moment of death. Imagine Obra Dinn but you can actually rewind and watch the Captain style on fools repeatedly, or watch the thrown axe fly through the air at the bad guys. It's ultra-vibey and really cool stuff! It's also really weak sauce, gameplay-wise. Your "investigation" contains very little actual deduction, just rewinding to the highlighted time period, walking to the clearly marked "anomaly" area, and finding the clue the game expects you to find, watching the scene get filled in. Your character narrates their case theories the entire time as well. So, not strictly a walking simulator, not exactly a hidden object game, but a bit of a hybrid. The game is also guilty of absolutely not trusting the player, at all. You have a suite of tools; the game gives you about 2 seconds (not an exaggeration) and then tells you "use <x> tool" immediately. Forget about the joy of sussing out the bullet type by coming up with the idea of x-raying the character's wounds; you'll be told immediately to pull out your x-ray gun and get to it. There's an interstial "clue board" case scene between each major crime scene. This is where the deduction element is allowed to live, but again - the devs don't trust the players. There's one or two slots to fill in, matching an object or character to a motive - and the game immediately (and literally) throws a big red X if you get it wrong. Progress is halted and you must try again. To me, an astonishingly bad choice. The real classics of the genre permit players to make long elaborate screwed up chains of logic and hang themselves out to dry - breaking out of those false evidence loops and realizing that you made a fundamental error in logic is one of the true and unique pleasures of the genre. Not here. Nobody Wants To Die also believes Nobody Wants To Hoodwink Themselves, Nobody Wants to Struggle To Interpret Evidence, Nobody Wants To Hit Any Sort Of Wall In the Case. But by streamlining this process, they take some of the fun out of the mysteries. They're fun when you can't figure it out, and then achieve a breakthrough - this is taken away from you.And yet, I recommend this game. Great vibes, top-end production design. Good and fun concept for a story and for exploring a murder scene. Really rough execution on the gameplay that needs to be retooled.  Devs need to trust the player. Lots of room for improvement.  My ultimate feeling is that their game design chops couldn't keep pace with their artists. Ultimately this sort of thing is rare enough and the talent level here is high enough that if this team was making another game I would buy it. Just beware, if you're looking for an actual deductive-style detective game and not a more narrative- and atmosphere-based hidden object/tableau experience - Nobody Wants to Die will disappoint. You're in it for the cyberpunk vibes, Detective. Good luck.

_childDocuments_.review: "Nobody Wants to Die" is a real little gem if you’re looking for a game that stands out. The sound design is fully immersive. While the graphics, even if not hyper-realistic, have a unique charm that fits perfectly with the game’s atmosphere. The investigation keeps you hooked from start to finish, and the multiple possible endings make you think carefully about each decision and replay to see what you missed.That said, the game does have its downsides. The pacing can sometimes drag, especially if you're looking for a more dynamic progression. Some choices might feel less impactful at the moment, and the game isn’t always very clear on how to achieve certain endings. But honestly, if you’re willing to look past these points, you’re in for a cool experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. I love that this stoy isn't overly streched out. If it were longer, the gameplay systems would probably get boring but this felt just right for me. The graphics and atmosphere were great, same as the music. For all my fellow Ultra Wide enjoyers out there: The game works perfectly in 32:9. Just a few things I think the Devs should add:-HDR support. (This game already looks great but it would look even better in HDR)-Some kind of lore Handbook or something to read when you are lost in the plot- A way of getting to different endings without replaying the hole thingAbout the ending: SPOILERS!!I didn't get it at first. I didn't really understand who the murderer was supposed to be and all that. It makes a lot more senese when you get the different endings, but still. Here is a nice wirte up I found under a YT video for those who were a slost as I was:My take on this: The real villain in the story is the ichorite system itself. What is revealed by the end is that this so-called immortality technology simply doesn't work reliably over the long term. Over time and multiple transfers, gaps start to develop in the memory and identity recorded in ichorite, like image fidelity gradually being lost when making a photocopy of a photocopy of a photocopy.  Some people, like James' wife Rachel, simply become irreparably psychologically damaged, and unable to feel anything. Others, like Green, Kovalev, and eventually James himself, develop an alter-ego that grows out of these gaps in their psyche and memory. This warped alternate personality seems to invariably recognize the ichorite system as something inherently "wrong," leading them to hate immortals and immortality itself. Because of their age and their constant hedonistic body-hopping in Green's secret club, the oldest and most influential ichorite immortals were among the most insane and damaged,  so much so that they eventually developed very complex alter-egos that collaberated with each other to form a master plan to bring down the ichorite system, without the knowledge of their original personas. I think many peoples' alter egos were potentially part of this ouroborous conspiracy, perhaps even James' own alter ego (the Stranger) by the end. For example, the President publicly promising to veto the proposed bill lowering the age when you have to start paying to keep your own body, and then suddenly reversing himself at the last minute, predictably causing outrage and mass civil unrest that played right into the conspiracy's hands. Another example is the Chief of Police, who places James under arrest in the park only to suddenly change his mind and shoot him, despite their long history together.  I suspect both were overridden by their alter-egos. Because the ichorite system is so inherently flawed, you could almost see the alter-egos of the ouroborous society as the "good guys", except that they're cruel and spiteful, and their motivation seems to be pure hatred rather than any real sense of justice. They really don't care how many innocent people they hurt or kill to bring down the system. This is exemplified by how, at the end, the Stranger tries to get James to murder a pregnant woman (and Sara's body) by making James believe that he's possessed her through her ichorite. In the endings where James does shoot Dr. Salma, the Stranger wins even though he and James die -- it was always the plan of the alter egos to destroy even themselves, as seen with Green taking the ichorite poison and killing himself, or Kovalev blowing himself up after killing all those people at his night club. In the good ending, James finally solves the mystery, and realizes what the Stranger really is. He suppresses his alter ego long enough to unload and discard his gun, and then to connect Dr. Salma with Sara by giving her the earpiece, before taking the ichorite poison and jumping off the buiilding, in order to destroy the Stranger once and for all. The chains of ichorite he saw in his dream preventing him from reaching Rachel across the water are thus revealed to be James' own ichorite tying him to a body not his own, and preventing him from joining his wife in the true immortality of the afterlife. After he takes the poison that causes his ichorite to dissolve, James' chains are finally gone, and as he reaches the other side, we see the wounds on his wrists caused by the ichorite chains -- wounds which I believe represent The Stranger -- fade away. I think this is an easy recommend for the price, 8/10!
