_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Wants to Die has all the trappings of a retrofuturist noir mystery and despite its rather brief runtime manages to deliver a few really enjoyable and memorable moments that will leave you wanting more. Some players, myself included, may walk away hung up on a few questionable design and narrative decisions, but for fans of the various genres being mashed up there's a compelling reason to dive into the "shell" of Det. (ret?) James Karras and go out on the beat in the game's gorgeous rain-drenched NYC megalopolis.VISUALS 9/10The first thing you will likely notice about this game is the gorgeous visuals, especially its rendition of a future New York City that blends the rainy evergloom of Ridley Scott's LA in Blade Runner with the verticality of Luc Besson's Fifth Element, with hints of Fritz Lang's Metropolis and yes, more than a few nods to Ken Levine's Rapture in the BioShock series. If you're the kind of player who likes to move slowly through your game environments admiring the work of the level designers, you will love this game for the gorgeous vistas - the buildings and vehicle design is especially sweet. It's like multiple theses in fine art were channeled into the game world, with gorgeous architecture that manages to retain those few subtle details that make it feel like it could have once been the NYC we know rather than some generic future city. However, the closer you admire the details, the higher chances of noticing tiny anomalies that tear you from the uncanny valley, like how the windshield wipers of your flying car act more to hide and show a layer of sploshing raindrops rather that clearing them away only for more raindrops to accumulate. When you stop to admire the moody rays of what little sunlight filters through the arcology in the distance, you see a layer of buildings above and wonder where all the rain is coming from. Still, from the gorgeous neon flashes of the omnipresent technology to the menacing glow of the flames of riotous revolution, this game is eye candy to be savored.GAMEPLAY 6/10You'll see a lot of reviews deriding this game and many like it as a "walking simulator" with a few bells and wistles. While that criticism oversimplifies how players move through the game, you shouldn't expect a bunch of gunplay, complex puzzles, or tense chase sequences. You will be combing through crime scenes, reconstructing the events using a combination of QTE and a handful of "classic" futuristic detective tools including a UV lamp that looks like an opthalmoscope and an X-ray powered magnifying glass, along with time-limited dialog responses and a few "key decisions that will affect the gameplay" or something to that effect. It wasn't entirely clear how my choices impacted the outcome, other than to unlock additional dialogue options and determine which one of what seem to be multiple possible endings. I sometimes really craved some of the gunplay and chasing that was missing clicking to pull a trigger to no avail, but I can understand and maybe even admire the bold decision to focus the gameplay and not bring in more mechanics that might muddy things up. That said, I found the gameplay itself to be the weakest point of Nobody Wants to Die, outshined on all fronts by the visuals, audio, and the themes. You are encouraged to follow a set path when surveying the crime scenes, such that you can't really uncover key clues before their turn, which totally discourages exploration. Even when explained in its neat little sequence, it feels confusing though it's difficult to separate what was done by design from what just feels awkward. The use of very clear UI icons means you are never wondering where to go to interact next, but as a result you pay less attention to the beautifully-detailed environments. While understandably the devs don't want players completely confused as to what to do, the hand holding felt a bit to heavy.NARRATIVE 8/10At its best, this game makes you feel like you're playing out a musty paperback pulp science fiction novel from the mid-20th century, where time, culture, dress, cars, architecture, and music all stood still for centuries in the game's retrofuturist world. It handles immense concepts about life, longevity, and how power corrupts, which the ideas themselves evoke and provoke very interesting thoughts and questions if not managed by the narrative. However, the narration also stumbles at a few points, leaving us in the dark for a little too long before lifting back the curtains where a longer game would take what it reveals and immerse the player in it more, allowing them to affect it and see more of the outcome. They payoff feels puchy, but getting there I was often a bit confused as to what was going on and what happened. I get it that it's a mystery, but even some of the revelations and resolutions feel more like vagaries and plot holes...or maybe setup for a sequel? It's at its worst when it leans too heavily into the tropes of the genres at play, especially noir, or spends way too long forcing the player to their knees in a fit to cough up yet another pint, ho hum. You do grow to feel something about the protagonist and his supporting cast, especially regarding their former lives, the "grade" of their "shell" and the pains of "desynchro" but you barely spend enough time with them before the game rolls the credits...then again, if it leaves you wanting more, does that make it a bad story? And bonus points for randomly littering some environments with great books like Meditations, though I'm not sure what would have made the book's owner a stoic otherwise.SOUND 8/10A lot of reviewers will rightly call out the game's sound as one of its strengths. I definitely think the music, environment and voice acting are all very solid across the board, but I think it also played it safe where it could have done more. The signature whiny brass and harrowing orchestral flourishes of classic film noir are here in spades, and while a few tunes really did stick in my head for hours after one or two play sessions and gave my evenings a bit of extra mood when the game really had me the most engrossed, I couldn't help but notice times when it felt repetitive or cliche when it was meant to drive home a much heavier sentiment. Those mournful moments of loneliness, tenderness or sorrow, where the player might have shared in the heartstring plucking of flashbacks of love lost feel like missed opportunities where in the aforementioned precedents like Blade Runner or Fifth Element the soundtrack pulled you deeper into its world without knowing it until you notice your eyes beginning to well up from what the vibe just conjured up out of your subconscious. The sound could have been used to build a greater sense of dread, or flesh out the world more where the neon signs and advertisements only take things so far on their own. Still, it supported the narrative well throughout and rarely fell flat.VERDICT 7.5/10A compelling but brief look into a gorgeous retrofuturist cybernoir New York City where death is cheated on a macro scale and society teeters on the brink of collapse. Fans of cyberpunk, noir mystery, detective games, narrative-focused games and the like will find the game is worthy of your hard earned dollars. If you are only partially sold, it's still worth wishlisting and picking up on sale for a rainy weekend romp.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody wants to die is a neo-noir detective story set in a bladerunner-esque retro-future version of New York. The gameplay is focused around rebuilding crime scenes with sufficently advanced technology, with a story straight out of the classics. Drunken detective on the outs with his department chief takes a case which skids too close to his personal life not to take personally.The gameplay is walk-and-examine with quicktime events, where you find the thing you need to do to fill in the next bit of the timeline on your magic recreation device. You're led by the nose a lot of the way, with the game dialogue explicitly telling you "Now it's time to use the UV Scanner!", "That looks like a job for the X-Ray Machine!". The way you actually *affect* the game is by choices, in both dialogue and action, which will open up or close down options going forward. There's a great sense of discovering the case alongside the protagonist.The game itself is very pretty, showing off a lot of what Unreal Engine 5 can do with a solid art direction and some care. It's very heavy on the light-bendy effects and clean bright illumination, looking a lot like every tech demo for UE5 you'll have ever seen, and reminds me a lot of the original Bioshock, which is partly due to the retro-future 1920s style. It's not a long game - my first playthough was around 5 hours - and the only reason to replay it would be to get the alternative endings. That's probably worthwhile.The story gathers up speed from a slow start, and ramps up in both intensity and lore being thrown at you towards the end near vertically. I didn't get the good ending - I don't think there really is one - but I also entirely failed to find out what's actually going on, and I don't really know what decision I could have made that would change that. The ending as it was was mechanically very satisfying, but narratively incoherent. At the end I'll say that the version I played - first release - isn't short of bugs. I only had a couple of complete crashes to desktop, but the interface of finding things to interact with is finicky and extremely directionally picky, the camera will occasionally dramatically swing to show an exciting thing that notably stops you from being able to see the UI for the QTE you're in the middle of, and the expository dialogue will frequently cut over itself and leave things unexposited. All of this might be fixed by the time you read this.All in all, I paid £15 for 5 hours of a decent detective story that was very pretty, with a well-thought-out world that the writers clearly loved building. I wouldn't recommend it unreservedly, but if the above sounds like your jam, it probably is.Seven whiskies on the rocks out of ten.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: This is a great 3D visual novel with lots of atmosphere and a cool storyCons: It should really be more upfront about being a visual novel, I keep seeing "Cyberpunk" come up in comparisons and it has literally nothing in common with it besides being set in the future. The "gameplay" is very hand-holdy and linear and tells you what to do every step of the way, so it doesn't really count as an adventure game either as all decisions come down to dialogue and item decision choices like a VN.Secondly, the dialogue occasionally sounds like it was written by a teen. Not that I have some kind of moral hang-up about cursing, but Sara and James curse like they're seniors in high school which really hurts their characterizations; with James having been around for a hundred+ years and Sara being presented as a professional with a cool head I really doubt they'd F this F that every single sentence. In fact, the language over all would benefit from a total rehaul into some form of Cityspeak like in Blade Runner considering how disconnected from the past everyone is supposed to be.Overall it's definitely worth a play, and I hope this game is used to herald in something bigger and closer to Cyberpunk, set in the same world. Maybe an open world prequel that leads up to the train incident, or a different character under one of Green's earlier incarnations. It could also be used as a proof of concept for a Cyberpunk style game with the Blade Runner IP, which would also be awesome. In any case, check it out!

_childDocuments_.review: Meet the game that reminds you of that one girl you’ve always dreamed of. She’s beautiful, smart, and at first glance seems perfect. You’re in ecstasy when you first meet her: her appearance is flawless, and her inner world captivates you. It feels like everything you’ve ever wished for has come to life in her. But, as often happens, the more you get to know her, the more you begin to notice her flaws.This game is just like that girl. The visual design of the game is simply stunning. You’ll find some of the most beautiful landscapes you can imagine. The acting is top-notch, and the world you explore is mesmerizing in its detail and mystery. Do I mentioned visuals? Ah, yes, the visual aspect is undoubtedly one of the game’s main strengths, and it’s worth your attention for that alone.However, as you dive deeper into the gameplay, you start to realize that not everything is as great as it seems. Beneath the shiny surface lies an extremely shallow and illogical plot. The game throws standard clichés at you, like yet another story about a dead wife (seriously?!). The dialogues can sometimes feel absurd, and the characters come across as one-dimensional. The gameplay, while engaging at first, quickly becomes meaningless, and the plot twists fail to surprise or impress.The endings, in particular, leaves you scratching your head, as it hinges on some smalltalk midgame dialogue. It’s crucial to understand the importance of the decision you’re making, but that can be incredibly difficult in the context of the game. The ending leaves you feeling frustrated, with a sense that many important questions remain unanswered, only adding to the confusion.Yes, the game is worth buying and playing, if only for its visuals and atmosphere. But after completing it, you’re left with a sense of disappointment from the meaningless ending and the wasted potential. Despite its merits, I can’t give this game a high rating – there are just too many unanswered questions, and the ending only makes it worse.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: If you're interested in a fun game (with good gameplay), don't buy it. If you're interested in a good story, don't buy it. However, if you're a fan of the retrofuturistic aesthetic, then there is the possibility of having a decent experience in just trying to immerse yourself in this world for a few hours. You'll have to suspend your disbelief pretty hard, but if you do, there are a few enjoyable hours to be had. If you're a fan of the Blade Runner aesthetic, pick this one up... on a sale. In-depth review:TechnicalQuite a rough and overall unpolished game. Janky movement, ultra-finicky "scanning spots" for clues, and a lot of bugs. My first impression of the game was changing the upscaling method off FSR and the game immediately crashing. Luckily that was a one-off, but it didn't set the tone well when it came to the game's technical quality.Quality controlThere's a ton of obvious spelling mistakes, and the voice acting is.. well, it sounds like an anime dub. That same sort of overacting. The mixing isn't great either, so some lines are delivered too quietly, others too loudly. In one moment the actor sounds distressed, and the next line is delivered straight despite the tone of what the conversation is about or what is occurring in the scene not changing.GameplayThe gameplay (read: the lack of it) is really not something to write home about. You walk around, you interact with the environment by using the crime-solving tools over and over... honestly none of it is engaging. It's a game where you do the cyberpunk 2077 braindance thing over and over. It's very linear and there's no actual detective work. The few times you actually do get to draw up what you think is happening on a board, the game will not proceed if you connect the wrong clues. The gameplay is essentially this exact formula: interactable conversation scene (pick between these 2-4 dialogue options), cyberpunk 2077 braindance (rewind time back and forth to reconstruct what occured at a scene and gather clues), put the clues together in order to come to a hypothesis (put the clues together, if they don't go together you get a fat red X, if you put the right clue together, you can proceed), repeat.StoryYou've seen it a thousand times. No spoilers, but it's got all the tropes: disgraced detective picks himself up after meeting a woman, discovers that the corruptness "goes all the way to the top!", has to figure out the case while dodging the law as he has been laid off the force, and so on. It's extremely predictable.AestheticThis is where this game deserves to be praised.I'm a sucker for the retrofuturistic aesthetic, especially Blade Runner. And well, this just oozes Blade Runner (the main characters voice actor sounds like a Harrison Ford impersonator, and his ex-wife is named Rachel... that cannot be coincidental). There is an interesting twist, in that instead of it being retrofuturistic 1980s, it's retrofuturistic 1930s - this adds a far greater element of "vintageness" to the aesthetic, and honestly the noir tropes fit a bit better thematically in this futuristic 30s world, than they did for the futuristic 80s world of Blade Runner. There's tommy guns, crooked cops, the drunk detective, the dame, all the noir tropes that we associate with the 1930s are present. These elements add a nice vintage contrast to the flying cars, neon signs and electrical-powered crime-solving gadgets that we associate with the futuristic detective vibe.

The UE5 Engine really shines in this game! The "Batman: Arkham" detective work is the most interaction that can be done aside from point and click for anything that can be touched.However, the gameplay is VERY minimal and linear. You don't have much interaction to do and the "detective work" is very basic. It is unfortunate that this game doesn't have much of a "game" to play since this is mostly an interactive visual novel.  For this price point, it is forgiven! I'd just wish someday, we'd get a true OPEN WORLD, interactive game in this noir retrofuture universe. It looks great with decent worldbuilding and atmosphere, but the more I played the more annoyed I got with the investigations that practically play themselves. It's like the devs latched on to the most boring aspect of Cyberpunk 2077. The unnecessarily convoluted story has nothing interesting to say. Philip K. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Even the achievement titles are derivative with only surface-level connections to the original material. The dialogue is tone deaf -- wanting to make a profound statement one minute then a snarky joke the next. But if you like this game you may really love Observer.

_childDocuments_.review: Positives:+Atmosphere - The game does well at creating that Noir Detective feeling, the monologues and conversations between characters perfectly resemble what you would aspect.  Additionally, the future dystopian is full of philosophical thought and standard ideas of a future without true death.+Graphics - The game is beautiful, every scene is filled with care.  Even the simplest scenes with your car are beautifully done.+Story - Without any spoilers, the story is your classic murder mystery.  The story is pretty strong at the start, I will say dips a little within the middle.  Overall it was interesting to see each different aspect, and if you pay attention to dialogue, as the player you get to concoct different guesses at the ending.Okay:+ -Gameplay - The tools create an interesting story and gameplay aspect, but rather than letting the player figure out the crime scene with the different tools, it hand holds you throughout the process.  I was hoping to have more control in the story, maybe if you weren't thorough enough you didn't gather enough evidence, leading to different results.  Its not terrible, but does make the game feel more like a telltale game (i.e. movielike, point to click).  There also isn't any combat, so the game has the entire focus on the detective side of things, which wouldn't be as big of a deal if the detective side was strong.  It would have be fun to have some potential conflict, just to get more of the gritty detective feel.+- Game Length - For me, the game was only 5.5 hours long and thats roughly what I see other players have.  Its short, I was hoping for a longer game, maybe with some different types of scenes.  It doesn't kill the game for me, but it does hinder it a bit.+- Characters - I really liked the voice acting and performance of all of the characters.  The only complaint I would have is the lack of conclusions.  The ending credits concludes one story, but leaves open several others.  Its not a big deal, but it definitely could've been better.Negatives:-Choices - Throughout the game you get simple choices that may affect certain dialogue, but doesn't really impact story or character.  If feels more like Telltale games where your choices don't change the story, just adds some personality.  The biggest disappointment is the fact there are multiple endings, which pretty much only rely on a singular choice late in the game.Overall:I would recommend the game for its price, its an enjoyable experience that gives a grand performance.  Just don't go into the game thinking like its Detroit Become Human, its a interactive movie essentially.  Its good for what it is, just falls flat in a few categories.

_childDocuments_.review: So this does fall into more of a walking sim/ guided narrative than a game. The mechanics are simplistic, and  with the over prompting not all that satisfying. However the atmosphere is rich, the narrative dense and compelling, with utterly gorgeous UE 5 graphics (4090 max settings and even a Legion Go with FSR 3 - it's  an absolute looker). There are strong performances too.  I don't know how this wasn't a VR game from the offset as presentation and pace easily lends itself to it - a very easily done mod though.  Personally some abstruce puzzles that felt more like trial and error and some structure quirks (it's a convoluted and confusing shaggy noir tale - that is possibly just a little too hard to unravel) with pacing issues (I get that a noir protagonist is going to blackout a few times - but not this much!) hold it back from greatness. But for little over 15 pounds for 6 hours of stunning mystery I'd recommend and it's a no brainer for the fans of slow paced story driven media if ever on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Story: Great at the beginning and really pulls you in as you go through the game and keeps you really invested. However, the towards the ending of the game it just turns into a mess, it gets really and i mean REALLY rushed and it seems like the plots ending gets thrown at you to finish it up quick instead of taking the time to explore it further as It had great potential, the choice based part of this game means absolutely nothing as then ending has 2 choices and depending on whichever one you pick, it changes the ending so all other choices before those 2, Useless. aside from the story being rushed at the end and not being explored it was interesting and in some ways unique so the story is a 6/10.Gameplay: The gameplay is simple, basically a walking sim but with cool gadgets to use to solve crimes scenes and learn what happened and the tools are unique and cool which is something that's rare with most detective games nowadays. _childDocuments_.review: Love this game! It's just the kind of immersive and interactive narrative heavy game I love. _childDocuments_.review: Nobody Wants to Die is less of a game and more of an interactive adventure; an experience to be had. At its core it’s a walking simulator.You play as a detective in a retro-futuristic 1940’s New York setting complete with all of the tropes we’ve come to know and love. The most interesting thing about the game for me was the concept of capitalist immortality where the rich can live forever and the 99% can support them because they want a bite of the unattainable carrot. 🥕 Unfortunately the game doesn’t delve deep enough into this fascinating concept choosing instead to focus our time on solving the death of a rich dude.Still, it’s a nice little diversion for a few hours and I would recommend giving it a whirl for yourself. 7.5/10
_childDocuments_.name: Nobody Wants to Die

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Wants to Die is all style and not much substance. It is okay that there is no combat in the moment to moment gameplay but the investigative part of the game itself is extremely bare bones and very "handholdy". You don't get to actually investigate, you don't get to actually make meaningful choices with consequences and most importantly you don't get to make mistakes. The first chapter of the game felt decent and refreshing but it never got better and it only went downhill from there plus some of the voice actors are overacting in a hilarious manner and there is no actual replay value here unless you want to get all the achievements in which case it would have been thousand times better to include a chapter select which they did not do sadly.Overall what we have here is an atmospheric although cliche cyberpunk detective noir where all you  get to do is walk forward, interact with highlighted objects, listen to dialogue and make choices which do not actually matter. I could have enjoyed this type of dystopian detective-noir as a show or a movie but as a video game, not so much.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing atmosphere, attention to detail, and world building... All of it. It feels so polished and cared for. I loved the voice acting, and characterizations of everyone. The aesthetics of Art Deco in a dystopic future were so well conceived, and imagined. Every scene was wonderful to feel, hear, and exist in.I played through the whole thing in about 6 hours, and I have no idea if I got a "good ending" or a "bad ending" - or even if there are multiple endings. But I'm curious if playing again I can get a different one.There was a QTE at the end - which I don't care for in games - and I actually lost it. I'm not sure if I was supposed to have lost, or if maybe writing a macro would have saved me. (It was insane - I was two-fingering my left-mouse button at lightning speed). Perhaps there's a setting in the menu to disable the button mash QTE, and I missed it. I'm on the fence about whether or not there's enough replay value in there for me to warrant attempting to find a different ending, as I feel pretty unsatisfied with how it ended... But regardless: I enjoyed the journey through the whole game, and it left me wanting to explore this world more. If you are like me recently, and need to clear your mind of brain-rot games that do nothing new but take your time: then I highly recommend this as a way to immerse yourself and clear it all out.

_childDocuments_.review: Bottom line it's worth playing if you enjoy a story driven experience. The theme and setting really help and there's a lot of thought put into the world building.Yes, there isn't that much in the way of intense interactive puzzle solving or action but I enjoyed the chill feeling of letting the story guide me. The times you are providing input are thought provoking and the writing is fairly well done if not a little corny/leaning a little too hard on the old 'noir' tropes. The voice acting was well done but there were times where the clean up of the audio was not well done. The differences in recording between lines was very noticeable at times. A couple of the lines felt as if they needed to be retaken and directed a little differently as it felt jarring with the tonal shifts. Something they hopefully nail in their next game. A couple of small technical gripes. The motion blur is intense enough to cause dizziness and the graphical load can be too intense for an older series of graphics card. Run it on Epic if you can but you're not going to miss out on too much if you aren't able too. Overall worth playing for the short romp in an interesting world, I look forward to what they make next!

_childDocuments_.review: My first gave review EVER! I'm not going to talk about optimization because with my 4090 I have zero issues. This game is something. I can't describe how much I love the atmosphere. This is just perfect combination of Noir and Blade Runner 1982 vibes. If you’re a big fan of both will definitely will enjoy it. Most games nowadays are a vacuum for dopamine. They are too fast, you don't have time to relax, you always on a go, but not with this game. This game gives you time to walk around, enjoy every bit of level design and visuals. Unfortunately, I'm not a "notes" reader. Most of the games use that to kinda push the game play time. I had the same feelings when I've played Prey 2017 for the first time. For this game I read every single note, listened to every single audio recordings. Because I was there. I was by myself and I wanted to figure out what this all about. Sadly games like this aren't really "blockbuster" games, but we should have games like this so we can have stories, ideas, thoughts through the experience of a main character. I don't know if you can really put this game at the "niche" shelf, but same as a Blade Runner 1982 it was ahead of its time. Same with Nobody Wants to Die. This game is something you have to play again in 10-15 years. 10/10

_childDocuments_.review: This story is genuinely one of the most deep, complicated, deceptive and impressive tales I've seen from a game. I'm not going to put it above Cyberpunk 2077 my beloved, but it's damn close. Don't expect a AAA experience, there's performance issues and minor bugs, but given the size of the team and how smoothly it manages to play regardless is fine enough for me. TLDR; If your a fan of slow (like, really slow) storytelling with big buildups and massive mysteries and have a decent PC, this game is a must play.

_childDocuments_.review: It is crazy what limiting scope and creating a more linear game can do to enhance the level of detail and graphical fidelity. _childDocuments_.review: I think this is a good game, it does have some issues though.First, it could certainly be better optimized, though it is decent at the very least. My biggest complaint though would be that it is a bit too short for this style of game and the investigations are a bit linear for this type of game. These may be cheap complaints, but the main reason these things get to me is that it speeds the mystery along too fast so you don't really get time to stew on the details of the mystery.There are a couple other things to note, that aren't necessarily negative. The dialogue is a bit goofy at times, but I think the fact that it's diving head first into the 1920's noir style makes it enjoyable. Also, some of the marketing made it seem at least partially open world (like you could fly around New York in your car) but it is not open world, which works and makes sense for the game that it is, but I still think it would have been cool to be able to fly around the city.That being said, it does make for a good narrative game as its story is good. And the mechanics are enjoyable with the retro-futuristic detective devices. Plus the world and settings for the investigations are super cool. All-in-all, I would recommend this game if you are looking to play a futuristic noir detective themed narrative game.
_childDocuments_.name: Nobody Wants to Die

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to give this game a thumbs up because it has some fantastic qualities, the issue is that the negatives outweigh the positives.Some of the positives....==== Graphics ====Incredible. The atmosphere is extremely unique, with incredible set pieces and cityscapes that rival the best looking games that have ever been released. Truly a graphical benchmark.==== Noir Setting ====The setting of a noir futuristic dystopia is fantastic. I would liken it to the world of Fallout where you become immersed in the time period and the advancements made in this potential future.Now unfortunately, the negatives....Right from the off, you immediately feel that some of the game mechanics are cumbersome. Clicking around the screen at items, waiting for the next dialog to prompt, or trying to use some of the tools can be very finicky and lead to a frustrating experience. Which goes hand in hand with....There is linear, there is hand-holding, then there is this. I appreciate that the description states "Interactive Noir Thriller", but I didn't think it would be a sitting simulator where you occasionally press buttons and the game takes you on a rail the entire time. Not only are all areas barricaded off completely, you are told specifically what to do, when to do it, and how to do it EVERY. DAMN. TIME. There is no real guess work or detective content to this game, because you click buttons and it tells you everything, that's it.The story ending is atrocious and leaves you with more questions that have been piling up the entire time you have been playing. Just in case you want to try it, i'll mark the below as spoiler so you can formulate your own conclusions and questions:All in all, I was left deeply unsatisfied by the end because of this lack of closure.If this title was deeply, and I mean, deeeeeply discounted, I would say for the atmosphere alone it is worth a play. Do not go in expecting a thrilling story (It is decent, but without conclusion). It is an interactive story book across 5-6 hours of pointing and clicking.- Please, please make a sequel. Take all the feedback you receive and make progress on your next title. It has the opportunity to be incredible. - Polish the story, keep the multiple paths but provide an ending that will leave players satisfied. I can already see so many ideas for the story progression picking up from this point, or even being a prequel.- This could easily be First Person and more interactive with the players figuring out what tool to use and which routes to go. All the animations and graphics such as the large sets and interactions are already there, just need to let loose.

Basically, if you love cyberpunk OR noir, this is an easy buy, especially at less than half the price of a AAA game.Edit: My first completion took 6.5 hours, though I did get what I am interpreting as the "bad" ending.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best cybernoir of the 2020s. This creates a beautifully immersive environment that feels like nothing else.  The story is really engaging and there's a lot of details that stick out on repeat playthroughs.  The main characters are great, especially Karra; he really captures that hardboiled detective archetype perfectly with lots of charisma.  The way they handle the investigation mechanics is really neat, and so are all the choices that shape the story.But honestly, the setting and style are what puts this game to the top of my list. _childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this for the visually striking environments and great jazzy soundtrack, however the most this game does to justify the fact it isn't a movie is by presenting the occasional player choice. I was anticipating at least one new mechanic to be introduced and shake things up, but it seems as though the plot revelations alone were meant to keep me engaged--unfortunately, they didn't. The writing got on my nerves after a while, with frequent quips and swearing in dialogue that came off excessive and unnecessary; at odds with the classic film noir monologues. I'd say the story's premise was more intriguing than its execution. Hopefully, the developers address my criticisms in their next project, as they do show potential.

_childDocuments_.review: got a few hours in.  I also started playing the new Sherlock game a few days ago and I have also played Sunken City and both Alan Wakes.  This game is a detective game like the above mentioned games.  So know what it is before you get mad its not a FPS.   Firstly the good things.  Great art style.  Good acting. Intriguing story.  A little slow at times but nothing too crazy.   So I never finished Sunken city, though I got like 80% done, and I am dragging a bit on Sherlock because they both have this kind of terrible detective mind palace design and you also have to do so much pixel hunting its ridiculous.  I basically had to keep a walk through open for both games to progress because god forbid i didnt turn an object over in just the right angle to get the clue.  It kind of turned me off detective games.  Alan Wake is much more intuitive though still challenging to figure out how to navigate the clue board.  Not sure I ever really fully figured out how it worked.   So I bring those up for comparison if you have payed any of those.  This one uses a sort of mix of the better parts of the Sherlock/Sunken City,  and Alan Wake mechanics.    So there was a few times I felt like I was pixel hunting for a clue, but only like 3 times so far and I think i am almost finished with the game.    Unlike all the other detective games I mention, this one has a few things that make it less frustrating and time wasting.  Firstly, if you get lost a bit about what the next step is, just go back to the previous clue and interact with it, and it will help you out.  Secondly, while pixel hunting, a beeping sound will tell  you if you are getting hotter or colder.  (dont forget to look up for one of the semi-early clues if you cant find it -in the zephyr)  and if you really are out of ideas you can hit "x" on the controller and it will tell you where to walk to (for some parts).   Because I sure dont like walking around in circles, back tracking, re interacting with everything just to progress,.  maybe you dont either.  So this issue has been basically fixed with the mechanic in NobodyWTD.  Finally, someone made an enjoyable detective game. Now the negatives.  So my specs.  12gb 6700Xt AMD GPU,  a 32gb RAM with 3200mhz.  AMD Ryzen 7 5800.  So pretty decent hardware.  I play at 4k resolution.  Usually I can play at ultra everything. Not this game.  I had to reduce quite  a few settings to keep the frame rate from dipping really low.  So I think it needs some optimization.  So far no crashes tho.  The frame rate dipped really low when I was in the car for one scene.  Seems odd.   I also noticed some flickering of scenery that should not be happening.  I think the rain might be an issue. But No other visual bugs that I recall.   So just minor things.  The next bit about bugs is for the devs if they read this. I did find a two bugs in the game.  Or perhaps,,, typo error is more appropriate for the first one.  There is a empty magazine (green i think) you can pick up in the red room, and it gives you the option to "read" it.  And it reads you something from some other item I had picked up earlier.  Cant recall what now, but yeah.  little bug. Second bug.  When doing the equivalent "mind-palace bit", if you choose the wrong clue to link, you get a red shape, and if you hover over it you can remove the incorrect linked clue (remove hypothesis or something like that).  But, for the whole first set, whenever I did this, it would also remove the second to last one too.  So I would have to re-link the previous correct one.  It was just a minor annoyance.  I didn't realize it was a bug until I did the second mind-palace thing and this did not occur.   It also did not occur for the third.  So definitely a bug for the first one.  Doesn't keep you from progressing or anything.  But because the first one is the one you are figuring out this mechanic and making a lot of mistakes, it was more annoying there.  To add to that.  Sometimes the correct one really seemed too far away from the question being asked.  But that is somewhat subjective.  Conclusion:Overall happy with game, glad i bought it.  Pretty good price for such a quality story, beautiful Art Deco art style, pulp fiction, nior feels, and of course, cyberpunk which is basically futuristic pulp fiction.    And I am super super happy that they have improved the detective game-play formula.   Its been needing an overhaul for a while.   If you like walking sims, or detective games, give this one a try.  If you loved Alan Wake, you will like this one. If you wanted to like Sunken City/Sherlock but was finding the frustration ruined it for you, then give this game a try.   There is no combat as far as I can tell.  Its purely story driven.  But you do impact the story by your choices.  Many of the questions and action choices say it will impact the path of the narrative, so I am looking forward to seeing how this works when I finish.

_childDocuments_.review: So right off the top, I'll say that this game is not for everyone. It's very linear and very hand-holdy, to the point of being more akin to a walking simulator. But I'll also say that as someone with high standards for this genre and who didn't care for a lot of walking simulator "darlings", I really enjoyed this one.It's an absolutely stunning looking cyberpunk/1930s detective noir crossover that deals with themes of continuing life, not unlike SOMA in some ways. It's a combination of narrative and detective/investigation sequences, which you can't fail at. There are a number of story-impacting choices and while it's not clear just how big an impact they can have, there are multiple endings as I understand it. There's no chapter select though so if you get one ending, you can't easily go back to get the other(s).The voice acting is excellent and the main characters and their relationship gets nicely fleshed out, with lots of twists and surprises in the story. I did find myself a bit confused where certain things were going or had gone at times though and I wouldn't be surprised if there was a plot hole or two I just didn't catch at the time.The characters and in particular, the world that I've never seen done elsewhere were the big draws to this for me and they make up for the lacking game play. If you're into this kind of game, I highly recommend it, but if you're not sure, there is plenty of time to decide if you'll like it within the Steam refund window.

_childDocuments_.review: Look, this is a good game in general. I recommend it, maybe not for the original price, but if there's a good discount, you should pick it up.However, it has flaws. This game is a choose-your-own-adventure with a bunch of gameplay put on top that mostly translates to "push button A now. Push button B now. Now look there and push button X". Nothing REALLY challenging or mysterious about it. And the biggest problem, the "branching paths" only have ONE real point of divergence, and you may end up going to the right branch purely by accident just because you're given the option. Basically, what should be a "YAH! I solved the mystery!" moment can be chosen by pure casuality, just by not paying much attention. Also, the save system is BAD, you're basically encouraged to keep manual backups of your save file if you want to see everything the game has to offer, or start the story from 0 every time you're curious about some different path. But there's nothing really new to check on those different paths, just different dialogue, different achievements. The overarching story is still the same. It only changes the small details in the end, providing more details if you got the right answer.With the negative taken out of the way, let's talk about the positive. This game is all about vibes. If you like Blade Runner (Or rather, "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?"), you'll feel how this game gives you the shivers just with the feeling of the setting, Noirpunk, may we call it. It's a very similar philosophical outlook on transhumanism too, the limits of what defines us, and what's a moral human to do when those limits become blurred. In order not to spoil the twist I won't give much detail, but this is some deep mystery, and it's a great experience. As I said, much like reading a choose-your-own-adventure book but actually seeing and feeling what's happening. The visuals are also generally great, but the VFX were slightly lacking, I felt like maybe they're trying to rely too much on high-specs machines to pull their weight instead of designing impressive effects themselves (not saying that's wrong, it probably looks stunning on those machines, but mine is not one of them)All in all, as I said, it's recommended when discounted, but don't expect a masterpiece in branching narratives or in detective guesswork. It's more like watching a very interesting interactive movie

_childDocuments_.review: This noir game has the look of Bioshock and the play style of a Telltale title. You play as grizzled detective, James Karra as he returns to work (off the books) solving a unique series of murders in this Bladerunner-like version of New York. The graphics in this game are top notch, with the Unreal engine 5 really flexing its muscle for the players whose PCs can handle it. Gameplay wise, there isn't much to talk about. For most of the game you are given the freedom to move about the environment. However, these environments are rather small and have very little to interact with that doesn't serve the plot. So, for the most part, you just move from set piece to set piece, uncovering clues and trodding along with the story. Throughout the title you will be given dialogue choices. Some choices have time limits and a few choices will change the outcome of the game (mostly by opening up more dialogue trees, but some will affect which of the four endings that you can achieve). If this were all the game had to offer I would probably put it in the not recommend bin, as it would just be a walking simulator. However, there is one other area of the game that stands out, and that is the reconstructions. The theme of this game pulls from other SciFi titles like Altered Carbon. People can upload and download their consciousness at will (for a price), making bodies dispensable. Bodies can be rented, bought, or even stolen. This makes solving murders more difficult since it's a lot harder to kill a person in this world. It also makes solving murders more interesting as one can use data from ichorite cores (the materials used to house consciousness) to reconstruct past moments from a crime scene. The reconstructor allows you to move forward and backwards in time as you look for relevant clues to solve the murder. This part was quite fun, and even though you are still being guided by the nose to your next objective, you have more freedom to adjust these past tableaus and even solve other aspects of a murder that are only ancillary to the main plot. Along the way you will be helped by Sara, the "gal in a chair" who helps you get into locked areas and put together clues. The banter between James and Sara can be fun at times and cringey at others (too much colloquial speak that doesn't land well in a noir setting). Lastly, the game really holds your hand through the entire run, with Sara or James quickly mentioning what tool you should be using in what moment. There is no real room for trial and error learning. One has to go out of their way to actually break from the critical path.To summarize, I think Nobody Wants to Die is a fun title that offers a bit of replay value (ending and conversation collecting), but it's heavy focus on story over gameplay limits the fun and exploration that similar looking titles have. If you like cyberpunk aesthetic and a noir story, but are less sticky about gameplay then I would recommend giving this title a shot...when it is on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Draws heavy inspiration from futuristic noir movies / shows like Blade Runner and Altered Carbon. Nonetheless, it has quite a few contemplative moments reminiscent of the balcony scene (from the 1997 Blade Runner game). It's rare to see a game be reasonably priced nowadays. Even for a 5-6h experience, $20 felt more than adequate considering the overall quality and the fact that this was the first game developed by this studio. Each individual chapter can be finished in 30-45 minutes, making this a great game to play in the evening during multiple sessions. More efforts could have been made in this direction. For example, you learn much about the world by inspecting items in a 3D viewer, like in Crystal Dynamic's rebooted Tomb Raider series. These items usually also include newspapers, leaflets and even comics. Instead of toggling a text overlay to figure out what's written in the fine print, the game should have allowed the player to unfold / open the newspapers and zoom in to be able to read it. It's not unfair to compare this game to an interactive movie. Although this doesn't bother me since I knew what I was buying, I was still a bit disappointed by some plot reveals that felt unearned, not to mention the endings. All in all, the ending is decided by only two decisions (one of which felt inconsequential at the time) and you have a 25% chance of getting the "good ending" (as far as I can tell). Puzzles similar to those in Remember Me in that you can freely control the flow of time and replay the events. Unfortunately, everything is very streamlined. While you're supposed to progressively unlock missing portions of the event in order to reconstruct the moments leading up to the crime, the games doesn't even trust you to make any decision. It tells you where to sit in order to find a clue and even auto-selects the necessary tool (e.g., UV lamp, X-ray visor, etc.)

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Wants to Die has an average yet somehow very confusing story with cliché characters but that would be fine for a video game with great mechanics. Nobody Wants to Die has no really interesting gameplay mechanics which would be fine if it had a great story with well written characters. You see where I'm going with this... I feel sorry for giving this game a negative review because it's apparent that many devs poured their heart in it but for me this game didn't do anything much.My main concern is that this is not a detective game whereas it tries to presents itself as one. You will do button prompt hunting and occasionally trial and error clue matching minigames with extreme levels of hand holding. There's no detective work from the players part, no deductive thinking or true clue hunting or even puzzle solving. The game tells you which tool to use and when then there's a dialogue explaining what you just did and how it progresses the case.There are some tools that seems interesting at first but there's just not enough content for them. The player has no freedom, you can't really try out different things. I know it is not a AAA game but maybe the devs should've just focused on the reconstructor and drop the other tools. After playing games like Return of the Obra Dinn, trying to "investigate" here was really a let down.There are some levels which have really good atmosphere and the world is interesting sometimes but that didn't save the game for me. The visuals seems great at times but the constant glitches (shadows and reflections glitch like hell, there's really few surface in the game which doesn't look like it has a huge noise texture flickering above them).The voice acting is nice however there were multiple times when the sound levels were all over the place and I couldn't really hear the characters even if they were shouting..or if they were me.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Wants to Die is a stunning tribute to contemporary sci-fi, deserving of high praise. This narrative thriller boasts a compelling storyline, immersive experience, and striking visuals. Crafted by creators with a deep understanding of cinema, gaming, and dystopian themes, it stands out as a remarkable achievement. However, the ending feels unfinished, and the decisions made throughout the game don't impact the outcome. Instead, a series of choices at the very end determine the different endings, with only one definitive ending being satisfying, while the others are exasperating and make you feel like your efforts were in vain as you get no final explanation of the plot.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall not a great experience. Also, finished the game in 5 hours...I feel like this game did not get enough play-testing.Dialogues in the game are weird, often make little sense, and add nothing to the story. English lines are read at different volumes and with weird intonation, which makes it a confusing experience. Like they re-recorded parts of it.Game mechanics are finicky. Since the game is so short and linear, I don't understand why the player has so many different tools to use. The x-ray and the lamp add only pointless confusion to the game. I know where the shooter was, why do I need to trace the bullets with the x-ray to forward the story? Blood stains are visible without the lamp, and bullet traces show up in reconstruction... In the bar scene you literally have to scan every bullet wound, even when it is immediately obvious where to go and what to do next. You have to find everything for the game to let you proceed. I got stuck multiple times looking for clues for the next part of the reconstruction while I missed a scan at the previous part. That happened pretty much in every scene. Some clues require you to approach at a very precise angle, so I would walk around them in circles until the prompt appeared.The board mechanic is also questionably designed - there is SO MUCH SPACE, but all the evidence is crammed on one side. This makes the board pretty much unreadable, and strings between the clues a tangled mess.Ending I got was very anti-climatic. I understand there are more endings, but because how bad the gameplay mechanics are, I don't really feel like re-playing the game.Some dialogues are bugged and relate to choices I did not make, happened to me at least once that I noticed.Graphically game is pretty good, performance is OK with DLSS on, but unplayable without it on a 4080. Since it's not a shooter, the weird stuttering that the game has (stuttering at ~90 FPS???) was not a big issue.

_childDocuments_.review: Coming into , I really wasn't sure if I would like it or not. Having loved games where your choices matter, having QTE's, and making sure you either make the right and wrong choices; I was pleasantly surprised with this title - especially when I've never really  detective style games.You do completely lose yourself in the immersion of a cyperpunk - dystopian - New York City in the year 2329. You play as Detective James Karra, who really does take an  approach to investigating crimes, while getting to the bottom of what is going on with the cities elite. You will be uncovering the dark secrets, while utilising the games unique mechanics, which was a solid experience. Making sure to cover all aspects from UV Light, to X-Ray scanning objects (and people) to determine the cause of there death; than having to solve the puzzle and put the story together. Really made for an interactive experience that leaves you on the edge of your seat the whole way through.Although, I did experience one bug towards the final 30min of the game. Where I couldn't look around after a cutscene, that I won't spoil. This functionality did come back after the next one a few minutes later. Important to note, this didn't ruin the overall experience, and will hopefully be fixed in a future bug fix update.Overall, it took me 6hrs from start to finish, looking over everything and making the most of the game. I didn't rush it, but do feel like I would make some different choices in another playthrough, to see how that impacts the overall reactions and end result to the game.Overall, I would honestly give this a solid 8/10, and would be up there as a must-play in my opinion. It is well worth the price tag it currently has!

_childDocuments_.review: The moment I found this game, I knew it was my kind of game. After 7 hours of playing this and finishing my first playthrough, I liked what I saw, but I had mixed feelings about the story, so instead of replaying it again, I decided to watch the other endings on YouTube. I doubt I would have got myself 1 of the 4 endings, which explained the story the best way.Visually and thematically, it's similar to Blade Runner (1982) and Surrogates (2009), except the title of the game is misleading - it should be "Some People Want to Die". Mid-game reminded me of Eyes Wide Shut (1999), but after that, the story derails, literally.There are multiple interesting detective mechanics. While the gameplay reminded me of Detroit Became Human, making sense of the clues was much weaker than for example, Blacksad: Under the Skin.Some may say that the game is not optimized well enough, but I disagree, it's just a very demanding game with a small technical flaw - it doesn't have an Exclusive Fullscreen option in graphics settings, which means you can't change the output resolution, so all the upscalers are forced to scale the image to whatever resolution your desktop has.Luckily, it's a Unreal Engine game, so CurrentResolution and CurrentWindowMode=0 can be changed in %LOCALAPPDATA%\detnoir\Saved\Config\Windows\GameUserSettings.ini file.

_childDocuments_.review: A good game that really utilizes an amazing art direction. I was stunned a couple times with not only how good the game looks graphically but how creative the environments and world was, which is much more important than graphical quality. (Think about how Dishonored is a much more beautiful game than Call of Duty remakes, despite the latter having better graphical quality.) Some may take issue with the fact there is no combat in the game (only snippets from a "memory" which you don't actually control anything, or sections where you can choose to peak at your opponent) or the fact the game is linear and not open world. One of my biggest gripes with the gaming community is insisting that games be open world, I love Fallout NV, I love Fallout 3, I love Far Cry 3, hell I love Rage 2. I do not love Starfield or Fallout 4 (its ok). Not all games have to be open world, and hating on polished linear games is counter intuitive to a diverse (not in the political sense) gaming environment. My issue with the game is thus, it built up a lot of threads story wise that never really got paid off, or explained, after finishing the game it did not leaving me thinking what it all meant or theorizing on who was doing what. The story was super strong at first but fizzled out, in a way that was sort of disappointing. There are so many directions that they could have gone into especially with some of the ancient symbolism, tying their story to more obscure stories written in the past. The story is a 7/10. The beauty of the game and art direction is a 10/10, game play is adequate as it is a "movie game", and the story is a 7/10, so I'll say the game is an 8.5.

_childDocuments_.review: Caution: this game is a motion sickness generator. I can only play for half an hour or so before I need to take a break, and that's with motion blur turned off and the lowest mouse sensitivity! This is a very, very beautiful game. Sitting outside your apartment just watching the traffic flow by is surprisingly relaxing. However, there are a few negatives. Some mechanics aren't actually explained, which leads to a lot of frustrating trial-and-error. The whole game is very, very linear - you can't even take a shower when the game wants you to decontaminate! And the handholding is very real, our partner is constantly "suggesting" stuff that we already gear up to do. That's most annoying, especially in comparison to the mechanics that are not explained. It's a very linear, hand-holding game with interesting ideas and stunning graphics, massively inspired by Altered Carbon and the film noir, but also a dash Dishonored and good old detective work.

_childDocuments_.review: Really liked the start of the game, the way the game looks and feels.It gets repetitive really fast though. They tried to make a "interactive" walking simulator I guess - that didn't work at all for me though. You end up in a cycle of characters talk -> protagonist says "I should use tool x/y" -> you press e to use the tool. Rinse and repeat. You can't change the order of interactions or conclude anything yourself.The deduction-board stuff doesn't work at all. You're not deducing anything here, you can only do what the game tells you to and you're not allowed to make mistakes. Also some conclusions don't make any sense with the info you have at that point.The end of the game is really bad, no other way to say it. An obscure, ambiguous dialog choice towards the end decides if you get the good or bad ending - what you did before does not matter (even though the game pretends like it does). And here you suddenly can make a 'mistake' (or just misunderstand the options), triggering the bad ending with no way to change it without playing through the whole game again.I was really suprised that a point in the story seemed like it was supposed to be a plot twist - anyone will see that coming miles away.And don't even let me get started on the inconsistencies, plot holes, stereotypes and some idiotic characters...This game had a lot of potential and I really like what they are going for here - a short, focused, narrative experience - and for their first game they did a good job, even though they fell short for me.I have high hopes for the next game by this developer, this one wasn't there yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing experience.It is indeed more of an interactive drama/thriller move with alternative endings and some variations in the middle. The atmosphere is one of the best I've experienced in years; the retro-futuristic world feels truly alive, beautiful, and miserable. The characters' motivations and behaviors appeared incredibly believable too, which added to the immersion.I loved the fact that it is a short game. The total of 6 hours allowed me to appreciate every moment without getting bored, and there was plenty of variety in tools and gameplay moments in that time. I would totally buy a separate story set in the same world from this studio.Performance was good on both a Steam Deck and a PC with a 7800X3D + RTX4090. I totally enjoyed the game on both device, although the Steam Deck requires all settings to be set on low and XeSS or FSR on balanced (I was surprised how well it looked, tbh).Totally recommend to anyone who's into retro-futurism and detective stories.

_childDocuments_.review: Not for everyone, but very unique. First of all, let me say that this games art design is fantastic. Very  meets cyberpunk. The design on everything from the vehicles, to the buildings, to the detective tools, and weapons are so incredibly evocative of the interwar period despite this being a futuristic sci-fi. I think that the setting and design of this game are its strongest elements. The world that this game creates is so unique. I wish there was more of it.This game absolutely nails the noir feel in story, atmosphere, art direction, setting, and most of the dialogue. The graphics are pretty good, but the art style elevates them to great heights. Very on-rails with almost no player freedom or choice except for minor dialogue stuff and one binary choice at the end. Short play time ~6 hrs and only way to see alternate ending is by replaying the entire game. Story is fascinating but ends pretty abruptly and doesn't really answer many of the main questions. No modern sociopolitical garbage. I give it a 7/10 if, like me, you like niche noir/decopunk/dystopian stuff. Probably a 4-5/10 otherwise.This game is very much on rails and the only choices you make are minor dialogue decisions that can unlock future dialogue options, and then one big binary decision at the end of the game. The gameplay is very simple with basic movement controls, click to interact with highlighted prompts, and using the detective tools to reconstruct and scan stuff in the environment. Since this game is totally linear, there really isn't much at all that a player could miss or screw up. You play a game like this for the setting and the story.A linear narrative driven game like this lives and dies by of its writing and I think  does a  great job with its story and dialogue. Characters are fairly consistent and well acted, the mystery is intriguing and very gripping, and the setting is fascinating as I've mentioned already. However, I do have a few criticisms. First, every character in the game uses such modern profanity (and lots of it) that it clashed with the old-timey style of everything else in the setting; at least for me. One major character seems to swing wildly around in motivations and demeanor and becomes bafflingly unpredictable (and not in a good, intentional way). There are also a few scripted moments where I almost yelled at the main character for essentially just allowing things to happen despite him seeing them coming a mile away. One example:  "Don't come any closer or I'm going to do X." "Don't you dare do X." "I'm going to do X!"  Without spoiling anything, I was disappointed in the ending, but I immediately started a new game to go back through it. I do wish they allowed you to load back in specific chapters, especially the last one, to try different dialogue options, but you have to start a whole new game. This game is short, about 5.5 hours to complete it, so at least multiple playthroughs aren't that laborious. However, I wish there was more content because this setting is so fascinating and addicting. Graphics are solid for an indie title. The art style elevates the graphics to breathtaking effect many times. I can't overemphasize how much I enjoyed the style and atmosphere of this game.Finally, unless I missed something, this game has no modern sociopolitical garbage bringing down the narrative. To me, this was a breath of fresh air. The story itself is compelling and universal enough that it will still hold up long after our current day troubles are in the rear view mirror. There is a some of the "eat the rich" theme in the story, but that actually fits in with the noir genre pretty well. This dev studio has some great talent and I'm excited to see what more they make. If you are like me and the setting grabs you and you enjoy noir detective stories, then I recommend giving this a playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: This game flew completely under my radar until a recent sale and man can i say this game was amazing. In a world with no death seeing the characters reacting to people dying for the first time in a long time was very interesting. The future setting of this dark and gritty New York along with the classic noir narration really makes it feel like you're in a cheesy cop movie that James loves so much. The gadgets are done well and in interesting ways, the reconstructor being the best getting to put the puzzle together in front of your eyes. This game had me looking in every corner in every room to find all the clues to unlock new dialogue and evidence. The graphics are absolutely beautiful, from the popping colors from the neon signs to the dark and dirty trash littered hallways in the shady parts of town. The attention to detail is amazing, i read everything i could , even the things that had nothing to do with the story. The story had me on the edge of my seat with all the plot twists and trying to solve the crimes and figure out who done it. I may not have loved the ending i got but i don't regret any of the decisions i made. This game is a masterpiece definitely worth the price and I cannot wait to see what the devs do next. 10/10  Get it

_childDocuments_.review: It's a very decent game for a couple of evenings, I enjoyed it! Slightly comparable to Signifier and Observer, but it's a classic noir detective story with it's tropes, so don't expect anything out of the ordinary. Gameplay-wise it's a first-person walking sim with a repeating and familiar time-rewind crime scene investigation gimmick. And a tiny bit qte. Your dialog choices influence the story and further down the road some dialog choices will be locked. I'm not sure if it's because I missed something, or chose a different dialog previously, that leads to it. But generally speaking you maneuvre from good cop to bad cop.Pros: - AMAZING environments! The attention to details is on very high level;- very good job on mixing the 1920s with cyberpunk. At first, I thought it wasn't possible, but the world felt believable enough;- nice voice-acting;- one of the most beautifully made crime scene reconctrustion mechanic. Not just holograms or ghosts as I'm used to seeing, but full immersion high quality sequences. Had a lot of fun just rewinding back and forth and looking at the details; - fun and moody dialogs;- replayable, at least for the second run.Cons: - gameplay felt a little too simple, characters were always annoyingly saying what your next move should be, leaving little space for your own exploration. "Now I better pick up a UV light" I mean, I want to come up with this myself, why are you always telling me?- the crime scene reconstruction minigame was a bit too easy and detached from the narrative. Like a mini-game for a sake of mini-game;- flashlight didn't work in all places, sometimes was very hard to see and explore the details;- huuuuge instrument selection dial, you can scale it down 2-3 times, it won't hurt;- some story points are only hinted at, but don't get development or confirmation. I still have no idea what was going on with their (B)ryan. It was a part of personal tragedy that got neglected;- facial animations.Nitpicking:- narrative is a little naive for my taste. I understand that going with small scope (new technology and all the narrative turns around it) is most of the times good enough for a short narrative driven game like this, but I felt for the setting to fully prove itself there should have been a little more ideas explored than this. I got a feeling like all our characters just got that technology and haven't gotten used to it, because most of the time, they discuss nothing but that or something closely related to that. Snippets into ecological problems were really refreshing to hear, as an example.

_childDocuments_.review: Nobody Wants to Die is a visually stunning, original blend of noir, sci-fi, and political intrigue. The world-building is nothing short of phenomenal—this futuristic, dystopian New York feels alive with its towering skyscrapers, neon rain, and a gritty, politically corrupt underbelly that had me yearning to explore more of it. The writing, while ambitious, deserves credit for attempting to tackle deep, existential themes, and the game's aesthetic is truly a masterpiece of design.However, where Nobody Wants to Die excels in atmosphere and originality, it stumbles in its philosophical execution. The game introduces Ichorite, a mysterious substance that supposedly holds consciousness, memory, and soul—yet the explanations fall apart under scrutiny. Consciousness is not simply a "fluid" to be transferred between bodies. The quantum mind theory, for example, posits that consciousness arises from quantum processes in the brain, something far more nuanced than the game’s reductionist portrayal of memory transference as a mere swapping of Ichorite. Likewise, Vajrayana Buddhism offers an understanding of subtle consciousness that persists beyond death, hinting at layers of awareness that transcend the physical—yet none of this is reflected in the game’s approach, which boils down immortality to something closer to software installation.Even more frustrating, the game leans heavily on psychosis as a narrative shortcut to explain the consequences of body-swapping and immortality, rather than engaging with deeper questions about the mind, self, and identity. The exploration of these themes feels shallow compared to what modern science and philosophy could offer. Despite its incredible visuals and world-building, Nobody Wants to Die misses an opportunity to delve meaningfully into the nature of consciousness.TL;DR:Nobody Wants to Die presents an atmospheric, noir-soaked world with spectacular graphics and bold, original writing. But the story stumbles when it comes to exploring deeper philosophical concepts like consciousness and immortality, treating them in a simplistic and inconsistent manner. Worth playing for the visuals and world-building, but don’t expect a profound narrative on the nature of the mind.

_childDocuments_.review: Good things:1. immersive world. The graphics and art direction gives the city a convincing look combining cyberpunk and steampunk elements, captivating and intimidating at the same time. Making it even better, the world of Nobody Wants to Die is filled with small details that brings the ridiculous world building to life.2. nice acting. Maybe I'm just saying the curtain is blue but at points I think the actor plays our main guy with self-awareness of the noir genre. It was a lot of fun watching him being edgy and awkward at the same time all the time.Bad things:1. writing. The story starts really strong, as demonstrated by the trailer. Yet as it progresses, the writing grows weaker. What seemed to be a novel implementation of social commentary ends up getting all of its weight taken away, by itself, as the player being told the ultimate truth: all the problems you experience is just some imperfect technology and two (2) lunatics losing their minds. Making things worse that revelation is done mostly in exposition dialogue. It pains me to see so much potential of a good sci-fi story goes into waste in such a rush.2. gameplay. This is a nitpick, as this game is mostly a walking simulator, but setting up the gameplay as if it's a detective game only to just have the player clicking around for shiny spots isn't a good look.Verdict: the unsatisfying story, in my opinion, deals the fatal blow for a supposedly narrative-focused game, and I can't recommend it in lieu of all the things it did so well.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one game where I really wish that Steam allowed a "neutral" or "somewhat recommend" rating.  That, if it wasn't obvious, is how I feel about NOBODY WANTS TO DIE.  The game has an amazing concept, really phenomenal art direction (overwhelmingly so at times) the seeds of an excellent mystery, and then...it just doesn't stick the landing - it flops right onto its face, actually.Through its very brisk running time, I simply don't think the story had enough time to properly blossom, drop appropriately sized breadcrumbs, give context clues through worldbuilding, offer clever misdirects, or really make good use of its choice system.  It's either that, or the writing simply was never going to get there - it's really hard work to make a gripping detective narrative that truly works!What you are left with is ultimately a binary choice (neither of which is properly presented - one of them is so obvious it's delivered via forklift [and is also wrong,] the other is so nebulous and without proper context clues that I feel like if the game didn't present me with "Option A: Martians did it.  Option B: This other guy did it." then I wouldn't have guessed.)And that's a darn shame, because the overall concept and philosophical questions proposed by the game are excellent.  So, until Steam allows a half-way point grade, allow this to be my "Thumbs barely up" review.

_childDocuments_.review: My head kept spinning and it felt as if a whole orchestra had decided to all play drums and move into the back of my skull. The summer kept sending waves of immense heat and humidity through my office window as if the world was on fire. Fire. Red fire. Red, like the colour of her hair.I went to my cupboard to bring out that old bottle of bourboun yet again only to realise it was empty. Empty like my heart.I had no choice but to buy Nobody Wants to Die through the Steam store.I knew it was trouble from the start. Trouble. Big trouble. But I also knew I had to poke that beehive and see what flew out of it. Little did I know what awaited me.Noire. Bladerunneresque future. More or less just a walking simulator but oh, what atmosphere. Highly recommended!

I do love the voice actors and BGM in this game though.Overall IMO I think you should buy it when there is a sale and not the full price of it.Hope to see a second game or similar detective game.

The developers did a great work on immersing you into a 1920s futuristic noir megalopolis but if you are willing to ignore the cheesy lines (the ones from the movies the game is inspired of), the immersion breaking delivery lines and the ok story, you have a great 5 hours story telling game which you'll play again so you can get the full experience. _childDocuments_.review: Short, story-driven narrative. This very much falls under "walking simulator". But the emphasis is on the visuals and storytelling. This game was an amazing experience. _childDocuments_.review: Nice game overall, but there're a lot of things to improveThe main disadvantage currently is performance. The game works in 30-50 FPS in 4K on RTX 4090 (also it doesn't allow to set the FPS limit higher than 60, but you won't need it anyways :)). There are a lot of titles, which have much better graphics and better performance. Performance -- The plot is good, but not something incredible. Also it's very ambiguous and illogical sometimes. Plot -- The investigation itself is pretty interesting and also this "reconstruction" gameplay element is enjoyable. Gameplay -- The "will affect the plot" decisions are unclear, so you don't really understand what your choice changes and also it's sometimes hard to predict what it can change. Role play -- Setting is good, the city looks feasible and all decorations are so. Setting -- The last thing I want to mention is that you can't load from some chapter or smth like that, so if you want to check other endings/decisions you need to go from the start. Replayability -- Overall -- I'd give the game 4/10-5/10. Recommend this game only hoping that devs will improve performance & add saves/chapters
_childDocuments_.name: Nobody Wants to Die

_childDocuments_.review: + Voice Acting is great. + The graphic is fantastic. They pulled off the dark, detective vibe so well. The game still runs very well on my 1080ti. No bug or crash at all. + The setting is incredible. From the city to all the rotten going under it. Everything about it is so intriguing for me to figure out more.- Although how good the world was, the great graphics and VA that brought it to life, I feel like the story didn't do them justice. The story was too much about the main character and his struggles, and they were not anything new either. It was short as well. It took me ~6 hours to go through the story and the last 2 hours were about the main character, about who I could not care less.- The gameplay is mostly on rail. You could compare this to Detroit Become Human or Until Dawn. It gets boring pretty fast, but thanks to the short game time, this was not really sticking out.🎖️ I would still recommend this game if you are into LA Noire, like me, and can't wait for a new game like that. I wish they made more of these.
