_childDocuments_.review: I now return to update my review on Frictional's newest game, after having fully completed it and leaving no stone unturned in the titular bunker, in order to provide a more accurate rating of the product.Amnesia: The Bunker was announced unexpectedly about a year ago. After having played and thoroughly enjoyed the game’s Demo version, and upon seeing the scope of the Halloween Update's newly added difficulty and replayability, I made it my priority to get it as soon as possible and personally find out what innovative, experimental terrors the folks at Frictional Games have prepared for us this time. Amnesia: The Bunker's story takes place during the First World War, somewhere at a front of the armed conflict between France and Germany. This time, we step into the shoes of Henri Clément, an amnesiac French soldier who, after a short sequence of flashbacks that provide some context and introduce us to the game's controls, wakes up in the bunker's infirmary, having miraculously survived. Right away, we can see that something isn't right; the place seems deserted and is in utter disrepair. So we begin to look for clues as to what could have happened, find a hand-cranked flashlight, and come upon a set of two doors further down the hallway. One door seems to be bolted from the other side, while the other is locked with a padlock; with no other options, we enter the Officers' Mess Hall. While there, we start hearing pleas for help coming from the kitchen, where we find a wounded soldier. From him, we learn that the officers ran and blew the bunker's exit behind them, and he tells us where to find the dynamite to blow it back open and escape. Before he can tell us more, he's cut off by the sounds of some creature getting closer. Desperate, he gives his revolver to Henri, along with a final request to have his life ended before it can get to him, saying that there are some bullets left in the pantry. However, before we can fulfil his wish, he's attacked and then dragged into the dark hole in the wall as he screams, and moments later, the light goes out. Without much time left before the monster comes back for us, we quickly shoot the padlock off (or smash it with a brick) and make it to the Administration Room. And so, the game begins...This game is vastly different from what the Amnesia series has accustomed us to. Instead of walking around, searching for pieces of a puzzle while trying to avoid getting maimed by some malformed being in the dark or losing our endless battle against insanity, we are now at liberty to explore an intricate bunker while on a quest to locate the tools with which we will fashion our escape, and an actual predator actively trying to stop us. The bunker is divided into a few different sublevels accessed from the main hub, each one sporting a distinct appearance and containing a key item we need to make progress. The Administration Room within the Central Bunker serves as a safe haven where we can save progress, plan our expeditions and keep whatever we manage to carry back from our supply runs nice and organised in a chest. That is also where the Generator Room is, with a generator that you should definitely keep fuelled if you wish to keep the lights on. And being able to see where you're going is fairly important, especially in a place like this. The bunker has been massacred by this feral creature while you were unconscious, and it is littered with traps set up in a futile attempt to fight back against it. Navigating this place without triggering any of these by accident or a way to disarm them can be challenging when you're trying to move around quietly, and exceptionally dangerous if you can't see the trip wires. Aside from that, there are also many dead bodies of soldiers lying around, with abnormally large rats feasting on the fresh corpses. These rats are aggressive and may even go after you if their hissing wasn't enough to discourage you from interrupting their meal. So, if you can't find a way to scare them off or distract them, keep your distance, or you'll be the next thing on their menu.Which finally brings us to  an abomination which indubitably takes the cake as the biggest and scariest threat in the game and is the main reason you'd want to keep the generator running. As you may have noticed, there are strikingly large holes in the walls of the bunker. These aren't there just for the show; the beast actively uses them to move around and hunt its prey. Anything that makes more noise than what can usually be heard within the bunker will eventually pique the beast's curiosity, which will move closer to the source... and wait. Should you continue to make a racket, the beast will either peek out of one of those holes, or emerge fully and begin to diligently look around the area. If it doesn't find or hear anything, it will eventually get sick of being in the light and crawl back into the walls it came from. Of course, that is only the case if there is any light at all...Let’s assume that you made a bold decision to simply scout ahead and search just one more room for supplies before retreating, the generator suddenly runs out of fuel as your flashlight begins to dim. And then you hear the beast emerge. It is now stalking the bunker's corridors while looking for you, never too far away for you to hear. Suddenly you realise that you haven't got the faintest idea of where you are, you can't see a thing, but one thing is certain; you're now in the hunting grounds of a ruthless, active predator, and it is  fault. At this point, other than loading your last save, you have only two options. You can either try to quietly crawl to some distant nook and wait for an opportunity to sneak past it, hoping that the beast won't find you while you're out in the open or hear you accidentally bump into something. Or you can start furiously cranking that antediluvian source of light with your gun ready, making your presence known to every being that inhabits this hell, knowing well that the monster will come back for you, angrier than before and potentially making you spend even more of your scarce, hard-earned ammunition. Choose wisely, you don't have much time left...Overall, it feels like Amnesia: The Bunker combines the strengths of the developers' previous work, with all the little throwbacks to their older games (things like aggressive, mutated animals and deadly holes in the walls in particular giving me strong Penumbra flashbacks, flickering lights when danger is nearby reminding me of the underappreciated Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, and the original pickup sound returning from Amnesia: The Dark Descent just being a heartwarming cherry on top) bringing extra charm to this already thrilling experience. All in all, while it is true that my standards might have been lowered considerably after how the Indie Horror industry had been so persistently entertaining us with spectacularly underwhelming products for the last few years, I can confidently say that my experiences with this game have been undeniably positive, and it far exceeded even my boldest expectations. It does deliver what it promises, and it really isn’t for the faint of heart. As a little side note, I might add that from what I have seen of Frictional Games’ history in video game development, I am under the impression that this is one of those passionate, dedicated studios where the developers actually put their love and souls in their work, despite the unlikely flops they might make. And that even when they do make that occasional mistake, it never truly seems to be to their detriment; they take a step back, analyse what went wrong, and with that knowledge in hand they work extra hard to achieve an even better result in their next experiment. And I will say this: I am really looking forward to whatever comes next from Frictional.

_childDocuments_.review: Another outstanding horror game masterpiece by Frictional Games.You are a WW1 French soldier who wakes up alone in a bunker, with no memories of what has happened while you were unconscious. You must traverse your way in the bunker trying to escape, which requires attention to detail in some cases and brute force in other cases.The most difficult part is you are not alone, the whole time you’re fighting to keep the power on because the creature that stalks you hunts more regularly when the lights go out. If there’s a power outage and you’re nowhere near one of the only save points in the game. You need to crawl your way back to the save point, and that's the most nerve-wracking situation you will experience. The creature never stops stalking. However, its spawns are randomly generated and can be influenced by factors such as power, noise, and campaign milestones. The tension feeling never stops all throughout.

_childDocuments_.review: I find that for horror games you need to put yourself into a mood to allow yourself to feel scared; you need to take the setting seriously, not play with the lights on, and really try your best to empathise with the character you're playing. In that regard I have found myself stuck with most of the heavy lifting when it comes to being scared by a lot of horror games lately. I did not have this problem with The Bunker. Amnesia: The Bunker managed to instil within me a creeping dread that I forgotten games were capable of. The atmosphere setting and sound design are superb but the real star of the show is the games functional mechanics. Just about every game-play option you have is set up as a dilemma, not a problem because problems have solutions but as a dilemma that force you to make a difficult choice with risk in either option. The best example is the flashlight; the flashlight needs to be constantly wound to produce light and this is noise that can potentially attract the monster so you have to chose between fumbling around in the dark or making a small amount of noise. So when you end up fumbling around in the dark it's not because you have no other option it's because you're scared to use one of the options.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very well made, claustrophobic, terrifying adventure in the Amnesia world. It's definitely different than all the other entries as although the story is linear, the entire game is set in the titular bunker. At first you might think "Oh, a bunker. It can't be that large, can it?" It's big enough to keep you on your toes but not overwhelmingly so.Additionally, you can now defend yourself! Although I would treat it as a last resort, as you really shouldn't be using all of your bullets on the monster. That's right, monster; singular. There is ONE monster in this game, and although that sounds boring, it never grew stale for me and I found each encounter interesting.Overall this is a fun and terrifying adventure into the world of the French--the most horrifying aspect.

_childDocuments_.review: This is in my opinion the best Amnesia game of them all! Better than Dark Descent, Better than even SOMA. I would highly recommend that if ever you played any of the Amnesia/SOMA/Panumbra games that you play this one. There is absolutely no chance that this game won't top your expectations if you enjoyed any of the previous titles. The game is so laser focused on telling a specific story, without any padding, it's so refreshing to experience such game development ethos. Straight to the point. A true masterclass in game density. It gets you captivated from the intro all the way to the credits. The introduction of combat mechanics and resource management were exactly what this franchise needed. Allowing for more interaction with the game world and its dangers. I wonder what is next for the this developer as this has left a hopeful glint in my eyes. Even though the run time of the game is short, each time you start a new game the bunker items are randomised in terms of values of key items and also higher levels of difficultly add more modifiers to the game so you can truly play this multiple times if you want too. Great game. Play and finish it at least once.

_childDocuments_.review: I almost never write reviews for games. But after playing this game, I felt compelled to do so. Amnesia: The Bunker sets a new standard for the horror genre, bringing the original Amnesia experience to a whole new level. Buy this game.This game is a fantastic evolution of the series. Amnesia: The Bunker introduces a game design that's quite a new formula to the series, while also evoking traditional mechanics from Amnesia: The Dark Descent. You really don't want to miss out on this banger of an Amnesia title.Amnesia: The Bunker features Henri Clément, a French soldier serving on the Western Front of World War I. After a near-death experience on the front lines, Clément wakes from a coma and finds himself back at his bunker in the infirmary, where his wounds have been tended. His injuries caused him to experience amnesia, but he has more pressing matters to worry about. Clément discovers that something has gone horribly wrong in the bunker. There is no one to be found, and he starts to unravel just what went down before he awoke. Henri realizes that he is trapped within the bunker with a vicious beast, with only one round left in his revolver. With the exits sealed, he must find a way to escape with his life.The story of Amnesia: The Bunker, while a little short, will have you captivated until the very end, giving you many twists and turns along the way. The game's lore also has strong connections to the other games in the series.I'll be honest, although I enjoyed Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs and Amnesia: Rebirth, they were clearly lacking in gameplay. Amnesia: Rebirth really just relied on collecting matches and fuel as the main resource management. Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs didn't even have an inventory system, nor the worry of oil or tinderboxes. These games were also very linear in their progression, and your only real options against enemies are to run or hide. While this isn't bad, most people seem to agree that it has been a bit overdone.It seems like Frictional Games realized these shortcomings, and then dropped Amnesia: The Bunker out of nowhere. Gameplay wise, they scrapped the whole idea of linear progression and went more into an open-world style with this game. There is one main antagonist in this game: The Beast. This monster will be hunting you for most of your time in the game, as he has dug tunnels throughout the bunker - and he HATES light. That's why it's so important to keep the generator fueled up, which provides power to the entire bunker. When the lights are on, it doesn't just provide you a sense of comfort, it actually deters the beast. When you make noise, he will become more active in your area and more likely to emerge from the tunnels. So you still have to worry about him and be conscious about the noise you make. Don't get complacent though - you're on the clock. The game gives you a pocket watch which allows you to time the generator, so you know when it's going to go out. So while you're out there trying to find a way to escape, you can hear that watch ticking away each second. Don't let the generator run out of fuel.Because if it does, the bunker will have a blackout - and this is where ♥♥♥♥ goes down. The beast will constantly roam around the area, and the pitch darkness of the bunker would require the use of the flashlight in order to see. And yes, there is a flashlight! The best part is that the flashlight is unlimited use, but there's a catch. The flashlight is mechanical, as in it uses a little fan to generate electricity. Oh and you bet yourself that it's very noisy. Imagine having a blackout, because you couldn't find enough of the scarce fuel that's around the bunker. And then you need to see in order to get back to the generator, so you're cranking away at that flashlight while the beast is hunting you. It's absolutely terrifying. All while you need to solve puzzles using clues you find around the bunker, and whatever tools you can get, like a gun.For the first time in an Amnesia game, the player has a gun. To be specific, the standard-issue Modèle 1892 for French servicemen in WW1. Like everything other resource, there is a very limited supply of ammunition. This creates a really interesting dynamic in the game, where you can actually fight back against the beast. It requires exceptional bravery to do so, but it will give you some protection. Note however that the beast cannot be killed.It seems like Frictional Games took quite a lot of inspiration from Alien: Isolation, which has a similar resource-management and very similar mechanics with the monster. But I actually think that Amnesia: The Bunker does it better. Frictional Games nailed it with making the game feel like a real survival situation. When you're playing the game, you can feel the tension and the anxiety. This is partly due to Amnesia's great atmosphere, but also the game mechanics really prey on your natural human response to things like fear, urgency, and pressure. So unlike in all other past Amnesia titles, you're thrown into a real survival situation and that is also reflected in the puzzles that you need to solve in order to progress. One wouldn't be wrong to expect that the puzzles are separate from the danger in Amnesia, because that's how it has always been done. But The Bunker does it differently. You're gonna have to solve the puzzles under the pressure of both the beast and the generator.Last but certainly not least, it wouldn't be an Amnesia game without an incredible atmosphere. This game does not fall short of those expectations. Everything from the eerie ambiance of the bunker, to the sounds of the beast crawling through the tunnels of the bunker, stalking you. You will hear the beast scratching within the walls, stomping through the bunker, with its roars reverberating throughout the hallways. You will hear the ticking of your pocket watch as your generator fuel dwindles away. You will hear your ears ringing after firing your gun or tossing a grenade. Everything in this game is masterfully designed to cause the player uneasiness, fright, and panic. I love it.Overall, Frictional Games have outdone themselves here. Some might say that The Bunker is "the BOTW of the Amnesia series," referencing how the Legend of Zelda series was transformed by the carefully crafted mechanics of BOTW. And while the game is short, it is a very solid game. Perhaps the reason why it is short is because this game is meant to gauge the community reaction to the new evolution of the game. But regardless, we must rejoice the support for custom stories, and I cannot wait to see awesome creations by the community.I really hope that you're able to enjoy this game as much as I did and I hope this review was helpful for you.

If you're waiting for Silent Hill, if you're wishing for Ill, if Alan Wake 2 wasn't quite as scary as you wanted, and if you like Amnesia but wanted a weapon, or all of those, you have arrived and found your desire. This is the best thing for now: IMO one of the best psychological survival horror games on the market. Its challenging, interesting, well-detailed. and scary. You know that skin-crawling spine-tingling sensation you experience when you are focused on some task before you, such as removing the screws from a ventilation cover, and you KNOW there is death coming from behind you because you can hear its footsteps and smell its breath? That moment in the kitchen of SOOTH? This whole game is that feeling.One of the best. Have read that the playtime is 6 hours. There's almost (if not absolutely) no scripted events after the intro: if you did a good job at managing fuel, sneaking stealthily and picking some quest item, devs won't teleport the beast behind you just to be a ♥♥♥♥: the game is hard, but it is fair

_childDocuments_.review: The game is the best looking and sounding Amnesia game so far, for sure. But is that enough? It's also one of the most annoying and irritating experiences I've had in a long time.If you are a horror/terror fan, you might enjoy it. But I find it difficult. Second to gameplay I value atmosphere and mood the most, generally speaking. Amnesia the Bunker does have its share of atmosphere, but not close to what other games can offer. Even a childish game like GYLT has better atmosphere if you ask me. Well, I can think of countless of games that do this better.Is playing and making progress for 15 minutes only to die by a trap and restart from the latest save fun? No. Is it scary? Not really. Especially not when the monster shows up. It's better when it stays hidden. I found it a bit thrilling to hide from it while it was in the next room, the first time. But when it finds you and you have to restart... Yawnzzzzzzz... Unfortunately, that's the gameplay The Bunker offers. You quickly learn that you need to go out in the bunker from the central save point (the one and only) for short expeditions, only to return in order to save your progress. There are traps everywhere that will kill you in an instant (seriously, what's fun with that?). I started to cheat and used god mode and infinite ammo. It immediately got much more enjoyable, because I suddenly was able to actually get anywhere and explore. But then a trap killed me despite the so called god mode. Seriously, I hate it. _childDocuments_.review: The game is fairly short, but feels quite dense and the Bunker itself has just enough to explore without feeling overwhelming.  Reminds me a lot of classic PS1 Resident Evil, with a heavy emphasis on inventory management, becoming familiar with a space and having an unstoppable juggernaut pursuer that you can only temporarily drive off.Between the noisy flashlight and the constant pressure of keeping the generator fueled, every decision in the game no matter how small has some kind of resource cost.  Walking is quiet but slower, which means more fuel is used by the generator to keep the beast away.  Running is quicker but louder, which will more likely draw out the monster and possibly risk losing health or at worst wasting precious time from having to run and hide.  For a game where your most complex action will be throwing a brick at wooden doors, there's a satisfying amount of depth to be discovered.The game's length works well with the constant pressure you're under.  If the game was any longer it would've far outstayed its welcome I feel.  That said, despite the game's efforts to increase replay value with randomizing various elements every playthrough, the lack of a deeper mystery to be solved and no multiple endings kills the drive to do multiple playthroughs.  The mystery presented is by no means bad and I did like piecing things together, but not having anything else to bite into after that was basically solved kinda left me not wanting to play after my first playthrough.I do feel $25 is perfect for a title like this.  If it was any higher than that I would not say this is worth the time or money.  While it does lack something like a larger mystery or multiple endings to better entice multiple playthroughs, I'm still going to fondly remember playing through this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: Frictional has a penchant for making games that are so atmospheric that 90% of the fear comes from your paranoia rather than the big eldritch creatures hunting you. Don't be fooled by the addition of the gun like I first was though; having firepower to defend yourself may seem like it would take away from the survival horror aspect, but if anything it does the opposite and makes you feel even more vulnerable than ever. You'd be fooling yourself if you thought you could just shoot the thing and never have to deal with it again.Amnesia: The Bunker and equally, the rest of the Amnesia games, do a great job of taking a very simple premise: you're someone who doesn't remember anything other than your name, you're trapped in a dark, claustrophobic area with eldritch abominations and your goal is to Not Get Caught. Unlike the previous game Rebirth, which many people consider to be on the weaker side due to its emphasis on narrative and world building over gameplay, The Bunker does the opposite and places the gameplay at the top of the hierarchy, letting that - as well as a number of notes and its environments - tell the story. The devs chose to go with a more procedurally generated game this time, extending the replayability and, in my opinion, overall enjoyment of the game as no two playthroughs will ever be the same. I also love the absolutely dire situation it puts you in making such a tragic thought experiment: you're fighting so desperatley to escape the horrors of the bunker that they've almost made returning to an active warzone... appealing? That mere thought alone, removed of the jumpscares, time limits and constant stalking is why the psychological horror element of Frictional's games works so well. Also this game is just... terrifying. The scariest in the series, if you ask me. And yet, I can't stop myself from playing just to hide under a table or in a cupboard or behind a crudely angled barrel for 5 minutes, despite not having even glimpsed the beats until about 3 hours in.I don't really have any cons to speak about when it comes to this game as it's really solid overall. The voice acting is really good for what it's portraying, there are a few places you can clip through walls or items but nothing I've encountered has been immersion breaking and the random-ness of the items spawns provides more of a challenge than an obstacle that casual players who aren't looking to torment themselves with the hardest modes or speedruns can really appreciate and enjoy.Highly recommend this game if you're a fan of the previous Amnesia games, or if you're just looking for a refreshing survival horror experience. 10/10, no notes from me.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: Significantly better than the previous game in the Amnesia series. They dialed it back on having a protagonist who constantly talks and is annoying. The atmosphere is much scarier as you constantly hear the sounds of the monster chasing you, and it all takes place in the underground bunker which is dark and claustrophobic. And this game introduces a new element of resource management with consumable items and a safe room you frequently need to return to which is a suitable mechanic for a horror game.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: best horror game ive ever played. i like how the game gives you little more power as you go, the gun and shot gun both give and power while also being a liability, i hope that makes sense. instead of just running form the beast there are multiple ways of surviving in the bunker i honesty think its the games best feature. cant recommend it more if you liked RD7 or are just a fan of horror games.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: Amnesia the bunker is a really great game, it has some flaws but also a lot of positives. I really love the Amnesia universe and this game delivered when it comes to that universe delivering a strong connection to what the other amnesia games tackled.I've always loved the engine they use to pick up items, do actions via using your mouse like activating something or opening a door, etc. The game is pretty scary. It's really pretty imo when it comes to graphics and my pc is not that advanced.When it comes to flaws, like many people have said, the game is short, I honestly expected to complete the area we wake up in and move to another one, another different bunker or something with an entire whole new area to complete but that really wasn't the case. The game can also be quite frustrating because you're def gonna die a few times.All in all, I'd still heavily recommend the game, I personally loved playing it, I loved the gameplay, the story and everything, I just wished the game was longer.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: This was my first experience playing a game from this developer and although a bit short, I was thoroughly impressed by the challenge, and couldn't put this one down. Starts slow, building a dark atmosphere that soon adds an extreme layer of terror. First impressions of the creature was a Mr. X type of encounter but I soon realized the beast hunting me down in The Bunker is much more sophisticated, unrelenting and unpredictably intense. It took until about 3/4ths of the way through before I felt like I finally had the mechanics figured out and I could begin to breath a little easier. I set the game to hard from the start and I thought maybe I wouldn't be able to complete it after being ruthlessly slaughtered numerous times, but I was able to pull it off with persistence. Scarce weapons, ammo, and lightning help to ramp up the dread. The stealth, item interactions and strategies really set it apart from others in the genre. I tried following the story but it still seems like somewhat of a mystery to me. I can't think of another game that has frightened me as intensely as Amnesia: The Bunker.  Its a true survival horror and a great formula.  Worthy of a 9/10 score for a small developer. Note: be sure to look up how to change config file to run at over 60 FPS, and disable HDR.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: Haven't finished yet but so far have mostly only good things to say. A few pros and cons for now:1) If you liked the first Amnesia and/or Alien Isolation, and didn't care for where Rebirth took the series, then you will like this. 2) Atmosphere-wise, it's the first amnesia. Gameplay-wise, it is a mix of TDD's physics mechanics and Alien's stealth gameplay, but it genuinely does something new as well by combining it with the generator and crafting mechanics. 3) If you want a lot of story then don't expect that here, this entry is atmosphere & gameplay-first.4) The best sound design I have ever heard in a horror game, and I would probably put in my top 5 of all time for any genre.Cons)I wish the map was more interconnected in its layout. I suppose that'd probably be unrealistic for a game set in a ww1 underground bunker, but it feels more metroidvania and less immersive sim in that regard.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: Uniquely brisk-pace survival horror. You lose some of the depths of immersion as the gameplay really demands you to think mechanically if you want to make progress and do it well so if you're making that sacrifice you have to make sure the gameplay carries its own aesthetic. I'd say this succeeds at that and largely outshines all the previous FG titles. Of course we're all nostalgic for the older games, but they were really leaning on presentation over substance back then. If that's what you like, fine, but I loved the frantic and involved feeling of this one. It's all pedal to the metal all the time and then ends right as you start getting the hang of it. For one, that makes it a perfect package, no bloat. But also this sense of only beginning to really grasp how good you can get at the very end of the game serves as the enticement for the new game+. Some randomized key items, alterations to the monster and boom. Now it's a challenge-run type of game. I was satisfied with what I got simply playing through once on normal, but this is clever. This game shows off a matured design-sense which is exciting for future projects.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: Yet another incredible title put out by Frictional. The difficulty options allow for so much flexibility, and keep achievement hunting interesting and keeps the game from ever spoiling its welcome. The Shell Shock difficulty was an exciting change of pace after a couple of playthroughs, and the map design easily avoided the problems many games run into of having 1 or 2 achievements that require replaying half the game to get to. No matter how many times I completed the game, or how low the difficulty was set, the monster and surroundings were continually nothing short of horrifying.When Rebirth released I was disappointed, the game was good, but left much to be desired. And yet, many of the game play and game design techniques implemented in Rebirth have carried into The Bunker and made for one of the greatest horror experiences of the last decade.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: The first few hours of this were terrifying - the beast seems unpredictable, the situation hopeless, the odds heavily stacked against you - and this fear drives every facet of the game; you are forced to make impossible decisions (do I burn fuel to keep the lights on and the beast away? or do I risk venturing into the darkness and stumbling head-first into it?) and cautiously plan every move you make (how far can I get with just a single fuel canister, or what can I afford to leave behind?), which creates this constant, gut-wrenching tension the likes of only Alien: Isolation has seen before. It's awesome. Personally though, this tension mostly evaporated after a couple extended confrontations with the beast, and at a point, once you've learnt it's behaviours and patterns, you start to realise that the situation is not as dire as it originally seems, and you'll be comfortably braving the claustrophobic corridors of the bunker with an abundance of fuel and a confidence that once seemed unimaginable.That being said, the atmosphere - from the sound design, to the lighting, to the dust that falls from the ceiling as the beast stalks your every movement - is immaculate, and the horror and immersive sim (lite) mechanics are still incredibly appealing. They are also clearly the main appeal, though, as the story is predictable, short, and retreads the same ground that other Amnesia games have already walked. It's disappointing. However, combined with an impressively immersive environment and dreadful horror elements, it still manages to be interesting, and certainly drove my motivation forward with each note I collected.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: The claustrophobia gets me here, especially when the power is out. But loot seems to scale faster than progressionI played on Normal difficulty on my first run and had so much loot because I played the early game frugally. By end game, I was running around with the power on 24/7 and throwing frag grenades everywhere. In the finale, I had so many gas grenades saved up that I just made a safe area to solve the puzzle, completely skipping what you were  to doI'm replaying on Shellshock difficulty and omg the loot is sparse. For anyone who is familiar with survival horror games, play Hard (the highest difficulty for first play through), otherwise the end game will be routine

_childDocuments_.review: This game, at the time, had some performance issues.I believe they have most of them fixed and they had added in additional features for this game!Its really good, thrilling and challenging to play.Although, its not a game I can recommend to those that struggle with memory, keeping tabs on certain moments and overall lacking some common sense for this game.You have to be careful, strategic, manage your resources and aware of your surroundings.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: Amnesia: The Bunker is an amazing balance between the Amnesia series and the Penumbra Games. The constant feeling of being stalked and hunted rings feelings of Amnesia while the mechanics and progression feels more or less Penumbra based.A near-complete open area lets you tackle goals in any order with the exclusion of   The sound design is phenomenal, the lighting creates terrifying darkness for the monster to live and lurk in, and the game play loop keeps you in an uncomfortable situation at every turn.The only issue I retain after playing it is in the loading screen it claims that "if you believe something is possible then it probably is" inst necessarily true it gives the illusion that you can do a lot more than you can but the game isn't nearly complex enough to pass this as true, the furthest this really reaches is being able to use explosives as tools which isn't all that new to the series.All in all it isn't best Amnesia, it isn't the best Penumbra, but it is an amazing mix of the two which in a way will fill a gap in long time fans of the series and fill you with dread if you've never experienced them beforePlus there are some REALLY subtle details which by itself isn't terrifying but given other mechanics make you tremble at their sight, which feels like a whole different level of craftsmanship from Frictional.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: DAMN THE RATS!!!! DXEdit upon my completion of Amnesia: The Bunker: For $25, you get a high-quality game. I personally found this game a lot more enjoyable and terrifying than Amnesia: Rebirth. There is a lot more at stake here like you are racing against the clock to the things you need to do before the next refill for the generator or it turns off due to it running out of fuel. I always felt Rebirth played way too safe. There wasn't much repercussion to dying aside from a minor change to the ending drawing plus I felt it wasn't very scary either (not to say Rebirth is a bad game. I would rather play it than Machine for Pigs). In The Bunker, it is stressful and tense. I felt constantly on edge and paranoid because any noise I make will alert the monster to me and/or it deciding to come out of its hole to hunt me. It's even worst when the generator dies as this allows the monster to actively hunt until you get to refilling the generator. The game looks great as well and runs good on my pc. Also, whoever did the sound design for the pistol and shotgun, did a fantastic job. It sounds so meaty and punchy. The story is mostly told through notes but I find it pretty easy to piece things together and the VA for Henri and Lambert did great. I am honestly wondering if Frictional has some bigger in the works because again, $25 is cheap for a game like this. Overall, this game was worth waiting through the delays plus a good game to play in the meantime while waiting for the next two WW1-style horror games Conscript and Ad Infinitum.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: The Rebirth Boss fight was already bad, why did you have to spoil the experience in this amazing game?I might have spoiled the experience already, but hear me out. The experience from start till the end game is incrediable. The atmosphere is so well done, they have beaten themselves from Amnesia Rebirth. WW1 is not romantisied/glazed over and still is portrayed as brutal as it was. The bunker has a small map, so you can't get lost even without a map and it's not hard to save up on fuel. You have to think on how to use the fuel propely, it's not just blindy fueling up, it is thinking.The atmosphere is amazing, from the sound design and the threat of making too much noise to lure out the monster is a constant stress without the stalker being even present. Especially when the flashlight is such an ancient piece of crap that is so loud. The random shutters from above the bunker still representing that war is still going on, giving an extra horror factor. You can easily mix up the Stalker Sound effects with the stuff going on above the bunker.I found it a little wonky sometimes to orient myself with the tasks, since everything (almost) is hidden underneath notes and pictures you gotta find and we sometimes had to pull out a guide for this game to lead us further. The AI is unpredredictable, it is always a 50/50 chance when lights are turned on and you make a bunch of noise, that it comes out or not. Hide or risk it. You'll see the fate. The pressure on when the lights turn off for the first time and you just panic because... what now? Even when you understand the AI pretty much at the end of the game and it might not frighten you anymore, the atmosphere is still nice and you can now fully enjoy the game peacefully... almost.Now back to the headline of the review...Maybe it spoilers a little, sorry. The end absolutely smashed everything. Amnesia Rebirth already brought this out with this sudden new atmosphere, that did NOT match up with the other stuff. I get that it is part of Amnesia lore, did not matter, the problem is with the uncreative Boss Fights they try to make at the end of everything. I feel like in this game, a boss fight was not even neccessary, since you couldnt even fight it for the whole game. Why now? Even if the method was not directly killing it, it still felt empty, annoying and just... made the monster suddenly so harmless and bad. 25 Bucks for this game is okay, better pricing than Rebirth. It is better than Rebirth in any way possible.Play it.

_childDocuments_.review: The Amnesia franchise just keeps getting better! We loved the first one, the second was good, the third was absolutely brilliant. _childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: This game is really good. Possibly my favorite horror game I've played.The beast/stalker is a great enemy to contend with your explorations, the sound design alone keeps me on constant edge when outside safety. The game randomizes quite a bit of elements every playthrough, and it's short length is enough to not overstay it's welcome, even if I do admit it makes me wish there was more of this game, though that is a void that can be filled by custom stories. The generator gives a constant need in the back of your mind to make sure whatever you find, you can get back to there with fuel so you wouldn't need to stumble in the dark not knowing whats in front of your face. Even shooting a gun, something in most horror games would give you a feeling of safety, is obviously loud enough that if you use it on something other than it, it's going to be coming to that area soon, and a highly limited ammo pool encourages you to use it less as a weapon but a general tool.All in all, this is a absolutely fantastic horror game, I can't wait to see fans of this game make custom stories and frictional themselves possibly iterate on the bunkers gameplay in a future project.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: The Dark Descent, which I played back when it was released now almost 14 years ago (whew), quickly gained an iconic status in the horror game genre. I remember the hype leading up to A Machine for Pigs and being ultimately disappointed. I experienced this disappointment once more with Rebirth. It is important to note that while neither of these could match their predecessor, they still had things going for them. Both had interesting concepts and stories that, unfortunately, didn't do it for me. Rebirth in particular I remember being a frustrating experience and I'd rather not think about it.I bought The Bunker soon after its release and played a little, only now returning to it after getting some other games and business out of the way, and let me say that this is easily a better game compared to the previous two. Granted, some of you may enjoy a more linear story and experience (which is fine!) whereas The Bunker is the most open ended of the series. You are never pulled out of the moment by the story which is mostly presented through the environment and papers. Admittedly, I miss some of the presentation that The Dark Descent had going for it, but this is just the sort of storytelling that fits The Bunker well. It is an immersive experience where your task is simple and laid out to you early on: Get the hell out of the bunker! And off you go searching for the necessary parts, guided by notes and environmental clues, this time armed with weapons and tools while facing a monster that reminds me of Alien: Isolation in a good way.I'm fresh out of the game right now and ecstatic so I won't spend much more time on this review other than to say that you really should give this game a try. I feel that The Bunker is just what the series needed and I hope that Frictional keeps experimenting with it. Fantastic. Much love!
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: Amnesia: The Bunker is  new entry into the Amnesia franchise that proves Frictional Games not only still got it but can put numerous other horror titles to complete shame in the process. Amnesia: The Bunker is my favorite horror game of the year easily, and it is easy to see why.I am a huge supporter of Frictional Games, and Amnesia: The Dark Descent is a large part of why I got a degree and am employed in software development. The Bunker looked, to me, like a smaller-scope effort to experiment, iterate on their classic gameplay loop, and provide fans the pure-horror title they want without the risk of a headline game's budget on the line.The result speaks for itself. This game is captivating and terrifying alike, yet it is unequivocally fun!The Bunker takes place in a WW1  (if you could guess) during an extended engagement between France and Germany. After a superb opening trench sequence, you wake up to learn someone pressed the "disturb the ancient tomb" button, cratered the only exit, and left you in the dark with the worst generator ever manufactured. You have limited supplies, a gas guzzling generator, booby traps , and no clear path forward.What this all culminates into is an amazing lesson in what stressful horror games are . Everything balances together into a tense exercise in managing resources and time against a dominating and relentless predator. Light brings relative safety, but dawdling too much could get you stuck without fuel, power, and light in an inopportune spot. Speed can maximize your generator's fuel, but too much noise could get you in trouble anyway. This tightrope forms the brilliance of The Bunker's gameplay loop, especially when some genuine emergent gameplay moments are to be had as well.In short- Amnesia: The Bunker is very scary, very fun, and very fresh. It has all the hallmarks of Frictional's horror titles and exhibits the best of not only Amnesia but also Penumbra- something older fans of the developers will love to see (I know I do).Buy it now and wear the brown pants.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: The thing about Amnesia is that I've seen it in multitudes on the internet. I've never played one myself.I'm no spring chicken, I've played horror before. Cry of Fear is a game I can run with my eyes closed.This game scares the ♥♥♥♥ out of me so hard. The sound design is basically perfect and the gameplay is honed to a fine point. It gives you the end goal of the game right from the start, and it's up to you to figure it out in this cramped, dark, and dusty bunker with  crawling around down here with you.
_childDocuments_.name: Amnesia: The Bunker

_childDocuments_.review: Finally, a return to what makes Amnesia...Amnesia. Don't get me wrong, I'm one of those weirdos who thinks A Machine For Pigs is under rated, and still spent 40 hours playing Rebirth, but the Bunker truly brought me back to the feeling of actual horror. So many different ways to do stuff, very open ended, when you get killed, it's YOUR FAULT. At first I was skeptical about the single save location, but it adds so much. Having to decide between running back to save and put some gas in the generator or to just attempt to get to your objective faster adds such a tension to it, constantly having to second guess yourself, and waste time.Also please never patch the clipping bugs that have existed since HPL Engine V1, it makes speedrunning this game in 3 minutes so funny.

_childDocuments_.review: Very atmospheric game, scary with brutal sounds and noises to accompany the terrifying escape from Alcatraz gameplay. You definitely want to play this alone at night with headphones. But, I quit the game after constantly encountering rats that kept attacking me. With no means of burning them or corpses, or fighting them off, wherever you go you get attacked by them. On top of some very loud monster that's constantly on the hunt for you, it was absurd. You can't kick them, you can't dodge them when they corner you in a pack. You can't even use your flare and wave it at them, it can only be dropped on the floor. You can't use bullets as ammo is massively limited. So what you have to do is keep using bandages, which are in short supply. OR .. Lots and lots of save scumming, which eventually becomes a bit tiresome. I can imagine if you have loads of time to play then it gets rewarding when you finally solve the puzzle. There's a lot of backtracking back and forth, and mostly in the dark where you have to keep charging up your pocket torch. Obviously, this makes sense, as it's a horror-themed puzzle escape game. But, there's only so many times you keep running back to your save room before it starts wearing thin. Eventually you start thinking all I'm going to uncover is more tunnels with more rats, and that darn monster again and again. This game had potential and was nearly a solid thumbs up. I'd give it a 6/10, but thumbing down because of the stupid demon rats.

_childDocuments_.review: i only refunded this because it was too scary for me. i hadn't even seen the monster yet and i was already ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ my pants but from what i played i thought it was really cool to have a central 'base' to save at and having to keep time for when the generator would empty and you'd have to go refill it if you wanted light. pretty clever way of sort of 'punishing' the player if they decide to keep exploring when the lights go out etc. i just wish i wasn't too much of a scaredy cat to play but definitely try it if youre not a ♥♥♥♥♥ like me

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR Great horror game following behind SOMA only because it is short and mechanics seemed to leave more potential. The random elements are not overwhelming to the point that the key paths will not change. For the price, it seems like a fair experience.Pros: Great art direction, sounds are terrifying, and horrifying monster.The controls feel the same as usual (for better or worse).It really gave a claustrophobic feel and darkness does not give the feel of losing sanity in the other games, but more a sense of panic since it'll make the monster more prone to attacking.The game is short, but honestly it made replaying it that much easier and fun.Cons: There are hiccups here and there regarding performance and loading an area stutters.The length feels too short, but only because it has good base gameplay.As usual per other frictional games, "boss" fights are awkward and are kind of anticlimactic.Overall I thoroughly enjoyed playing this game.At this price and length it's good for a short weekend horror night kind of play.

_childDocuments_.review: A great (but short) horror experience.Pros:- Organic gameplay greatly adds to the tension. The game is not bluffing when it says it won't hold your hand. It's up to you to explore, manage resources and avoid danger. Really makes your little victories and discoveries feel hard won.- WW1 setting is nicely realised and adds to the horror in places. The constant rumbling of artillery  were highlights for me.- It scary.Cons:- Some things seem rigged against you in a bad way.  Plenty of locked wooden doors in particular have no way to open quietly, meaning the game is forcing you to summon the monster.- Story is interesting, but very light and almost exclusively told through notes. If (like me) you find the right notes early on, the twist can become obvious much too early.- Small thing but: There are WAY too many steam achievements for every aspect of the game. Having a steam popup every 5 minutes isn't great for immersion, especially in a horror game, so I advise you turn them off.

_childDocuments_.review: I had to refund this game after having massive graphics issues that could not be resolved by any of the settings, deleting config, or updating graphics driver... however, I then bought the game on PS4 and played through it so I can still give a review.I want to start by saying I love Frictional Games. Penumba Black Plague, Amnesia TDD, and SOMA are three of my favorite horror games, and even though people dislike AMFP and Rebirth I still overall enjoyed them even if they were clearly not quite as good. I also want to say that I greatly respect Frictional Games' decision to try something new with this game--especially after the lukewarm reception Rebirth got, however... I think ultimately this game missed the mark so, so much.The game starts with the lie that you can "Experiment" and that "Anything you can think of probably works", but this is absolutely not true. Even basic things often don't work--you can't put a torch to a wooden door, if you throw a grenade at the monster it goes right through it (I assume you can hit it with it but it worked very poorly), if you distract the monster to one area with a large sound and go somewhere else it can still teleport there at a moment's notice, etc. If you die you have to reload your last save and there is only one (well, there's another at the end of the game) save room, so experimenting ultimately winds up being a bad and tedious thing as the monster almost always kills you in one hit--you're much better off finding a strategy that works early on and using it the whole game. There are also randomly (literally) placed traps throughout the game many of which can instantly kill you. Almost all of the items you can use to open doors (shooting locks, grenading wooden doors, etc) result in loud noises forcing the monster to come. This means that ultimately the optimal/safest way to play is "Walk to door. Throw grenade. Return to safe room. Return to grenaded door (often leading to map). Loot room. Return to safe room and examine map. Return back out"... this gets tedious fast, and if you decide to be bold and try to enjoy exploration a bit more you will often get punished with massive throwbacks. I'm actually a fan of the risk of losing progress to not having saved in awhile in games in general like in classic Final Fantasy games or Resident Evil, but because you almost exclusively get one-shot in this game and the monster can teleport it feels completely cheap and infuriating. The attitude of "I can probably also pull this off before returning to the safe room" winds up being extremely punished--it is always better to just go to safe room over and over ad naseum. The only time this save system left me feeling good was when I explored the entire Maintenance area in one go evading the monster several times--however if I had died I guarantee you I would not have enjoyed it looking back. The game is also way too dark. I set the gamma setting to the recommended and you basically cannot see at all without the extremely limited flashlight (which you basically cannot use when monster is near or it will come kill you). I wound up setting it three notches above the recommended level and it still was nearly impossible to see in any dark environment (or if the generator was down) without the flashlight. Charging the flashlight also prevents you from running, so if you are being chased by the monster you literally just have to have the layout memorized since you will be running in total darkness half the time. It is common for Frictional to use diegetic maps on the wall for certain zones and often you have to find out what is inconsistent with the map and the environment like if a hallway collapsed or whatever, and they're tense because you're looking at them in real-time. In this game there is a similar map setup, but it is for the entire game and you can only look at it in the safe room. While I like the diegetic map in small areas in Frictional Games like the prison in TDD, here it just feels completely asinine to not have it be part of your pause screen. In the dev commentary for TDD they discussed the importance of having moments of calm between the scares--solving puzzles, relaxing areas, etc. This game has none of that. The entire game you are in danger. You would think this would make things scarier, but it doesn't. The game is not scary at all. This is partially due to the monster design being the worst in the franchise, but it is moreso because you know how the monster works, you know it will one-shot you, and you will die a lot most likely. Almost instantly the monster changes from being something scary to being something frustrating and annoying. I pretty much exclusively play games on Normal or Hard mode when I start out with them (usually RE I start hard for example), but here I genuinely think Easy might be the best way to play it. You can actually explore in a reasonable way, and the monster may stay somewhat scary for you since it isn't ever-present and extremely tedious. However, for some ungodly reason they do not give you the option to change difficulties in the middle of a playthrough, so I wound up playing through the game on Normal the whole time even though I surely would have lowered it with how tedious it was. I do like the "Metroid-vania" style progression of finding various key items in other areas and returning to earlier ones. It reminds me of the hub areas in TDD or Resident Evil games, however even this is ultimately done poorly due to the pace that you get the items and how easily missable things are. For example, you need the lighter in order to combine the empty bottles with fuel and cloth to make molotovs. These empty bottles are *everywhere*, but you don't get the lighter until the last third of the game (or at least, I didn't--there is some RNG to item placement for some reason too so...) The bolt-cutters I think are necessarily the last item you get before going to the endgame, so the many places throughout the game where you could use bolt-cutters feel extremely pointless. There is also a shotgun that I didn't get, but that I imagine you get at the very end based on the fact that there is a shotgun-wielding enemy. I shot him with revolver but only had one bullet and my molotov didn't finish him off, so I assume you need more ammo or grenades to get the shotgun from him. The segment with the shotgun guy was alright. I liked that it was something different and I liked that it tied into the overall Amnesia lore a little bit.The story overall is extremely bare-bones. There are some notes with some cool tidbits and details connecting things together, but for the most part the notes are to communicate gameplay ("I have the key to x area, I put it in y area"). The intro and ending were very weak with the ending especially being almost nothing. I think you can kill the beast, and maybe that would have given a slightly more involved ending, but the ending I got was literally just sliding out of the bunker and leaving. Horror games are notorious for often having bad final bosses/encounters. In TDD, you literally just push some pillars over with no threat around (or do some other things for different endings), and Rebirth there's a whole annoying running around and hitting switches segment. This final boss was the worst final boss I have ever encountered in any horror game, however. I think if I had grenades or something it may have been trivial, but because I didn't it was awful. The final boss is actually a bit of a microcosm for the entire game: 1. The arena itself has some RNG to it that is completely pointless. 2. You can try to experiment, but it probably won't work (throwing flares to distract him only for him to teleport to me while I was moving boxes anyway), 3. The most tedious strategy is the best (move boxes a little, run around on a loop, come back and move boxes again).I am apparently out of room to write this review lol

_childDocuments_.review: REALLY enjoyed the gameplay of this game!  I'm someone who enjoys punishing survival horror that require resource management that makes you think and approach every situation carefully.  I played it on the hardest difficulty and it gave me just that, which many modern horror games struggle to do.  I do enjoy titles like Dead Space and Resident Evil, but both of those make you feel like a walking tank by the end of the game, this one stayed punishing until the end which I appreciated!  The story was pretty good, nothing to write home about but if you've played previous Amnesia titles you may find it connects to the larger Amnesia universe in an interesting way, if you're not expecting certain things it can definitely have a few interesting twist and turns!  My advice if you're interested in the story: READ ALL THE NOTES!  They're vague enough to not put everything together immediately, but they give enough away to allow you to easily put together what has occurred in the bunker rather easily by the end.  For a short horror game that most will complete in a single playthrough, I cannot recommend it enough for those who enjoy more challenging survival horror experiences.  I really do hope Frictional Games next horror title has the same type of gameplay!

_childDocuments_.review: I'm changing my review. I initially panned this game a bit for the limited puzzle solutions and linearity, but the Halloween update seemed to improve things. Mainly in terms of the monster AI. It acts more unpredictably now, but not as unfairly unpredictable as the Alien in Alien Isolation. In fact, this one is a pretty good sweet spot. Which makes a lot of the anti-monster items more important because you're more likely to have to use them to scare it off. I had some close encounters with it that way whereas before I barely saw it. Infinite fuel runs are still possible but feel more like a natural part of the challenge since you need the fuel more desperately now to keep the monster at bay, and every run I did resulted in me needing to use some items to protect myself or dupe the monster so its still a matter of attrition. It definitely takes notice if you keep visiting the same area and bombing open a door then going immediately back to it will usually result in getting ambushed. It roams around more now and is overall way more aggressive. I even saw it do some smart things like wait for me back at the safe room which made for quite the thrilling encounter. Part of that could just be revisiting the game and playing on hard, but I really can't say for sure because I never played on hard pre-Halloween patch. Still, I would say hard mode is the way this game should be played on first run.  The linearity of progression still bugs me but once you know what to expect in that regard, then having to deal with a more challenging monster while planning around that becomes more fun. I still wish there were more creative solutions, but I feel a lot better about it now that I played on hard mode because it really does encourage a lot more item usage and items are more scarce. I felt like I was actually struggling to survive and optimization was important. One thing that is still pretty bad is the consistency of certain items. I died over and over because I kept shooting the monster two times and it never retreated, but eventually it did retreat on the six or seventh time I double tapped it. Meat also seems buggy and usually doesn't work to lure away rats or even the monster. Gas grenades too, which makes using them to clear rats and then putting on the gas mask kind of pointless. It makes noise and attracts the monster which is totally fine with the gas for some reason even though the other time I gassed it, it retreated. If that bug was fixed I would recommend this game more easily but with that and the fact that the campaign is really short its a hard sell at full price. There is custom story support and they are quite easy to install but I just expected a bit more bang for my buck. Replay-ability is...alright, I guess. Its just different traps and item spawns and codes but the same basic puzzles. Get it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The main point in a horror game is to be scary. Rebirth fell flat because (among other reasons), no matter that I played in a dark room with headphones turned way up and tried my hardest to immerse myself in the atmosphere, it just straight up was not scary. This one however, is. The layout of the map with the hub room as a base and the rest of the map being there from the start with you needing to find ways into different parts was very engaging and felt like a classic escape room game. The monster feels omnipresent, and the generator needing to be fed consumable fuel or else the bunker turns dark (which is when the monster hunts) keeps a constant level of stress. The smaller pieces of gameplay add up really nicely. Like the monster being sound based but your flashlight creating sound. The gun being a handy tool, but the dread that comes with the knowledge that if you have are given a gun, that just means the monster will be more powerful. It does suffer from the same storytelling of finding a thousand notes with scattered bits of story that might make sense if you somehow connect the dots between them, but I find myself forgetting 99% of a note the second I close it. Some complain about it being short. It certainly did not FEEL short, and the game ended right when I started to get to know the monster well enough for it to start losing its novelty and I was just speedrunning around the place without a care. Any longer and it would have become a slog. One thing I'm annoyed they brought over from rebirth was the fact that the body model is still not a viewmodel like it was in SOMA and TDD, but instead a physical entity with a camera taped to it whose view is based on the procedural physical feet position, and awkwardly knocks around into the environment and floor like a game of first-person QWOP. Also, while I obviously don't know the resources over at frictional, I feel like they could be using an engine that isn't nearly a decade old.

_childDocuments_.review: The Bunker is horror-immersive-sim that represents Frictional Games finally deciding to mix gameplay with their trademark hidey-chasey horror and doing a fantastic job of it. The Bunker is claustrophobic and tense and makes excellent use of its setting. But that is almost to be expected. What I did not expect was just how engaging the gameplay is.The Bunker gives you a handful of tools and mechanics and essentially lets you explore its well-designed world in whatever way you want to. There are a few overarching objectives but you are left to complete them in whatever way you choose. Unlocking tools lets you return to old areas and scavenge for items which in turn let you open up new areas and clear new paths. It's a really absorbing gameplay loop made all the more frightening by the most terrifying monster in the franchise.... an old generator. While there is a creature which stalks you around, the object of my greatest fear was a rickety generator which you need to keep fuelled. And this thing guzzles more petrol than a Saudi monarch on a bender. Eventually you start to develop a sort of abusive relationship with a piece of machinery. It always needs more than you can give but you can't stop feeding the almighty generator. Every expedition was wasted unless I got at least one fuel can for this Lovecraftian turbine engine.I will say that the very final sequences of the game are less enjoyable because they move away from the great non-linear imsim mechanics that 90% of the game so interesting. And the climactic boss encounter is...remarkably poor but such is to be expected from any good immersive-sim.Overall though, The Bunker is an intriguing and engaging experiment from Frictional Games and I really hope they develop more games like this. The Bunker is really immersive and kept surprising me with how creative I could get. I thoroughly recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: My key thoughts on this game:- In my opinion, this game is great and surpasses all previous titles from Frictional Games in terms of horror, including Penumbra. While playing the previous titles isn't necessary, there are a handful of references.- Unlike its predecessors, this game is less linear and narrative-driven. You'll need to piece together the story of what happened in the bunker through exploring the many environments.- There's virtually no hand-holding in this game. The main goal is to escape the bunker, so you'll need to embrace being a bit creative and explore through trial and error, in a style reminiscent of Metroid or Hollow Knight.- The game is quite challenging, even on the "Normal" difficulty. Supplies are scarce, and the constant need for fuel for the generator can induce genuine panic. In my playthrough, the monster was very aggressive, despite my caution. It seems that the experience varies among players, so I'm not sure if I somehow managed to anger the monster more than others. Regardless, expect to die—a lot. After the end credits, the game counted over 20 deaths for me.- The game's length appears to vary from player to player. I'm not sure if I was unlucky again, but my first playthrough took around 7 hours, while some others completed it faster. With experience and familiarity with the bunker's layout, I can imagine that this game can be beaten very quickly.- "Amnesia: The Bunker" provided an incredibly captivating experience that left me yearning for more. While the story feels more confined in comparison to "Rebirth" and "TDD", it still manages to leave a lasting impression.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, this game is not at all what I was expecting it to be, but I gotta admit I really like what Frictional did with this! It's so different from Frictional's usual style, which is great because it's been getting kind of stale lately in my opinion, but they didn't change the formula too much and it still feels like an Amnesia game! The puzzles and connecting story that Frictional are known for including in their games are, of course, present in this game, but it's much less focused on narrative and more focused on survival. I've seen some reviewers calling this a survival game, but, honestly, I'd say it's more like a giant escape room challenge than anything else, in fact, your overall objective is literally to escape the bunker, but in order to do so, you must solve many other puzzles to reach items you need to do this all while being as careful as possible not to alert or get caught by the monster, which I must say is definitely one of Frictional's best monsters, it's super terrifying and feels like an ever-present threat! I think almost any horror game player would enjoy this game because it has a lot of lore for those enjoy horror games for their stories and a really well-balanced set of mechanics that offer a challenge for those who enjoy the thrill of surviving in a hostile environment.This is the first horror game I've played in quite a long time that really hasn't given me anything to complain about! Well done Frictional!EDIT: Okay so I have just finished the game tonight and want to update my review with newfound developments. Be warned, this section will contain two massive spoilers to the near end-game section of the game, so if you haven't gotten into the tunnels, then don't read on.This is an absolutely incredible horror game pretty much the entire way through! At first I was wondering whether you'd need to go into all of the major sections of the bunker, but it turned out you do in order to get the bolt cutters to get into the tunnels! Also the monster is seriously one of Frictional's best monsters, I absolutely love how it's like this Frankensteins monster combination of all of the main enemies from the previous Amnesia games! It has the disfigured appearance of the gatherers, it makes lights nearby it flicker the way the manpigs did, and it tunnels through the walls the way the ghouls in Rebirth do! The game managed to remain insanely tense pretty much all the way through as well! The shotgunner scene was truly terrifying and unexpected, his chant will ring in my ears every time I encounter a foggy room in a horror game now, holy hell that's one of the best sequences I've ever seen in a horror game! The rifts between the worlds as seen in Amnesia: Rebirth in the tunnels was a really nice touch that helps remind you that this is set in the same universe, too!EDIT 2: Okay, this is my final edit. I had made my first edit last night after having just completed the game and I was very angry because I had approached and conducted the finale scene in what I have been made aware was probably the most rage-inducing way you possibly could have so I wanted to edit my review because some of the things I said last night were really unfair towards Frictional as developers and I feel the need to take responsibility. It turns out I had completely missed a major area of the tunnels: The hole leading to the pit Henri pulls Lambert out of in the opening act. If I hadn't ran from the tunnels after killing the shotgunner yelling "WHAT THE HELL, HOLY CRAP!" I'd have most likely found out that if I had merely walked forward a few steps in the room where I not only killed the lunatic but got the detonator I would have noticed a hole in the back-left corner of that room leading to the pit, and if I had crawled through that hole I could have found the plush bunny Lambert had lost in the pit. This is what I SHOULD have done. I, in my infinite wisdom, however, ran once I got the detonator because I was freaked out after the shotgunner scene and detonated the explosive and opened up the ending area which I proceeded to enter repeatedly without the plushy and died probably 4 times because I ALSO didn't notice I could raise and lower the bridges and ran in circles while pushing boxes to climb over that wall. TLDR: I died 4 times in a gamer hell of my own making and then blamed Frictional and ranted about it in my review last night, I sincerely apologize.Honestly the finale scene, now that I know what it's supposed to be when some idiot like me doesn't come barreling through it all like a bear and break it over his knee, isn't so bad! The ending where you give Lambert the plushy and then blow up the bridge he's on has the most closure, and honestly, the protagonist being captured by the Germans is still probably better than what he was stuck with prior to that so it's a good ending in a sense. Lambert's fate still haunts me...EDIT 3:You know how I said my last edit was my final edit? Yeah, turns out I lied haha. Frictional updated this game since my last edit and I want to write my thoughts about the new features they added in down somewhere so, here they are. Mostly, I'm talking about the customizable difficulty feature and more specifically the optional fuses and fuse boxes mechanic which honestly I love the layer onto the challenge of Amnesia: The Bunker that fuses and fuse boxes act as! There are a lot of other optional features you can turn on from the new game+ menu and that menu also allows you to tweak Sir Stomps-a-Lot's AI to make the game as much easier or more difficult as you want to alongside a host of other settings you can play with so I definitely recommend trying out a few combinations next time you play! Personally, ever since they've added the new game+ feature, I've started making that my default mode and setting up my desired game every time I start a new run. I think this really helps to ensure the game never looses it's novelty. If you get bored with the way you're playing, you can tweak things next time you play to make it a different challenge. Overall this is one of the best horror games I've ever played, not just because it's downright terrifying the first time you play it but because it is FUN to play and STAYS fun to play over and over again! Cannot recommend enough!

_childDocuments_.review: This is easily the most terrifying piece of fictional media you can possibly experience. No other book, movie, or video game has even come close to providing me with such a raw, visceral sense of terror. On top of that, it's immaculately designed and really, really fun.For starters, I can't possibly think of a better setting for a horror game. There is no other period in human history that is more terrifying than WW1. Combining the godforsaken bleakness of that war with an unkillable monstrosity from the abyss in a dark subterranean hell hole makes for a setting that is a literal waking nightmare. The bunker itself doesn't feel too big or too small either, and every "region" you visit feels quite distinct from the last.Then for the moment-to-moment gameplay, there's so much to talk about. Bringing up the different areas again, the contrast between them also makes you play differently depending on where you are. For instance, the Soldier's Quarters has plenty of places to hide while the Prison has practically none, making you burn through more supplies the more you venture there. Speaking of which, in the beginning, I found a lot of items that I thought were going to be useless. But as supplies, fuel, and bullets began to run out, these items showed their worth as I was forced to adapt.And I was forced to do so since the Stalker AI is designed so damn well. Every time I left the safe area it felt like it was more a matter of 'when' rather than 'if' I was going to have a confrontation. Partly because even if I thought I knew how to control a situation, it would find its own ways to turn my plans of a peaceful outing into a life-or-death altercation by taking an unexpected route or noticing something in the environment had changed by my being there. Now this is just a video game at the end of the day, so there are plenty of predictable behaviors that you can control and anticipate, but that doesn't make it any less terrifying in my opinion, because just look at the thing. It's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ terrifying. It's really hard to keep your composure when something like that is leaping out of an ominous hole in the wall that you weren't expecting, or when it comes screaming, panting, and barreling towards you out of the dark while you run for your life. As for the sound design, good god. You feel every footstep, every piece of rubble dragging on the ground, every crank of the flashlight, just because you're not sure what will rouse the beast. Then when it finally comes looking for you, the lights start flickering, your heart starts pounding- I swear, the first couple of nights that I played this game, I kept jolting awake just as I was about to drift off to sleep because I could still hear the sound of it tunneling through the walls. All of the above provided me with moments where I actually threw my arms up in triumph after accomplishing something I dreaded doing once I came to grasps with what I had to do. It also provided me with that time where I was running like a bat out of hell with the beast on my heels, only to have my cat jump on my desk directly in front of me, making me literally scream out loud in the middle of the night and wake up my upstairs neighbor. This game is just insane. If even a fraction of it sounds interesting, you should play it.
